en: The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra, Volume One, translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Part One: The Mahāvadāna-sūtra (I). The First Section: The Mahāvadāna-sūtra, Number One.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Gṛdhrakūṭa Cave of the Jetavana Grove, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, after their almsround, the bhikṣus gathered in the Hall of the Flower Grove and discussed among themselves, saying: "Venerable bhikṣus!

Only the Unsurpassed Honored One is most extraordinary; his supernormal powers reach far and wide, and his majestic power is vast and great. He knows the countless Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa, severed all fetters, and extinguished all conceptual proliferation."

Furthermore, they know the number of eons of those Buddhas, their names and titles, the clans from which they were born, the food and drink they consumed, the length of their lifespans, and the sufferings and joys they experienced.
Furthermore, he knows that those Buddhas possess such precepts, such teachings, such wisdom, such understanding, and such abidings.
What do you think, worthy ones?
"The Tathāgata is skilled in discerning the nature of phenomena; knowing such matters, he must have been informed by the gods who came to speak with him, and thus he knows this affair.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was in a secluded place, his divine ear being pure, he heard the bhikṣus discussing this matter. He immediately rose from his seat, went to the Hall of the Flower Grove, and sat down upon his seat.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, said: "Monks!
For what purpose have you gathered here? What are you discussing?"
At that time, the bhikṣus answered the Buddha in full detail regarding the matter.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Excellent!"
Excellent! You have left the household life to practice the Way with impartial faith. Regarding all that ought to be practiced, there are two types of activity:
first, the noble ones' discourse on the Dharma; second, the noble ones' noble silence.
What you have discussed is precisely as it should be.

The Tathāgata’s supernormal powers and majestic authority are vast and great; he fully knows the events of countless kalpas in the past because he thoroughly understands the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and also because the devas come to inform him.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Monks gathered in the Dharma Hall, Discoursing on the teachings of the noble ones;
The Tathāgata, dwelling in a quiet chamber, Hears it all with his divine ear.”
The Buddha’s sun-like radiance shines universally, discerning the meaning of the Dharma-realm;
he also knows past events and the three Buddhas’ parinirvāṇas.
He knows their names, clans, and lineages, as well as their stages of birth.
In whatever place they were, my pure eyes perceived them all.
Those devas of great majesty and most dignified countenances also came to inform me that the three Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa.
He fully knows their births, names, and clans, as well as the sounds of their lamenting cranes;
this unsurpassed Honored One among gods and men records the past Buddhas.
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you wish to hear of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of past lives, by which he knows the causal conditions of the Buddhas of the past?
I shall speak of it.”
Then, the bhikṣus said to the Blessed One:
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time; we wish and desire to hear it.”
Excellent, World-Honored One!
Please expound this at the proper time; we shall respectfully practice it.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall analyze and explain it for you.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened attentively.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Ninety-one eons ago, at that time, there was a Buddha in the world named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, who appeared in the world.
Furthermore, monks!"
Thirty-one eons ago, there was a Buddha named Śikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, who appeared in the world.
Furthermore, monks!
Within those same thirty-one eons, there was a Buddha named Viśvabhū Tathāgata, Arhat, who appeared in the world.
Furthermore, monks! In this Bhadrakalpa there were Buddhas named Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa.
Now, I too have attained supreme perfect enlightenment within this same Bhadrakalpa.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was the Buddha Vipaśyin;
thirty-one kalpas later, there was a Buddha named Śikhin."
In that very kalpa, the Tathāgata Viśvabhū appeared.
Now, within this present Bhadrakalpa, after countless nayutas of years,
four great ṛṣis appeared out of compassion for sentient beings:
Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni.
"You should know that during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, the human lifespan was eighty thousand years."
During the time of Śikhin Buddha, the human lifespan was seventy thousand years.
During the time of Viśvabhū Buddha, the human lifespan was sixty thousand years.
During the time of Krakucchanda Buddha, the human lifespan was forty thousand years.
During the time of Konāgamana Buddha, the human lifespan was thirty thousand years.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
Now that I have appeared in the world, the human lifespan is one hundred years, with few exceeding it and most falling short.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"At the time of Vipaśyin, people lived for eighty-four thousand years;
at the time of Śikhin Buddha, the lifespan was seventy thousand years."
During the time of Viśvabhū, the lifespan of humans was sixty thousand years;
during the time of Krakucchanda, the lifespan was forty thousand years;
during the time of Kanakamuni, the lifespan was thirty thousand years.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, people lived for twenty thousand years;
as for people in my own time, their lifespan does not exceed a hundred.
Vipaśyin Buddha was born into the Kṣatriya caste, his clan name being Kauṇḍinya.
The Buddha Śikhin and the Buddha Viśvabhū were likewise of such caste and clan.
The Buddha Krakucchanda was born of the Brahmin caste and the Kāśyapa clan;
the Buddha Kanakamuni and the Buddha Kāśyapa were likewise of such caste and clan.
"I am now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, born of the Kṣatriya caste, named Gautama.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse: "Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Śikhin, Viśvabhū,"
These three Samyaksaṃbuddhas were born of the Kauṇḍinya clan;
the other three Tathāgatas were born of the Kāśyapa clan.
I, now the Unsurpassed Honored One, guide and govern all sentient beings.
The foremost among gods and humans, the valiant one of the Gautama clan;
the first three Perfectly Awakened Ones arose from the Kṣatriya caste;
the latter three Tathāgatas arose from the Brāhmaṇa caste.
I am now the Unsurpassed Honored One; with valor I have emerged from the Kṣatriya caste. Vipaśyin Buddha attained supreme perfect enlightenment while sitting beneath a Pāṭala tree;

Śikhin Buddha attained supreme perfect enlightenment while sitting beneath a Puṇḍarīka tree; Viśvabhū Buddha attained supreme perfect enlightenment while sitting beneath a Śāla tree; Krakucchanda Buddha attained supreme perfect enlightenment while sitting beneath a Śirīṣa tree; Kanakamuni Buddha attained supreme perfect enlightenment while sitting beneath an Udumbara tree; and Kāśyapa Buddha attained supreme perfect enlightenment while sitting beneath a Nyagrodha tree.
"I, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, now sit beneath the Pāṭali tree and have attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Vipaśyin Tathāgata Went to the Pāṭali tree;..."
Right there, he attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
Under the Pundarīka tree, Śikhin realized the Way and extinguished the source of existence.
Vipaśyin Tathāgata sat beneath the Śāla tree;
Having attained the knowledge and vision of liberation, his supernormal powers were unimpeded.
Tathāgata Krakucchanda sat beneath a śirīṣa tree;
with all-knowledge purified, he was untainted and free from attachment.
Kanakamuni sat beneath the Udumbara tree;
at that very spot, he extinguished all greed, sorrow, and affliction.
Kāśyapa Tathāgata sat beneath the Nyagrodha tree.
Right there, at that very spot, he extinguished the root of all existence.
I, Śākyamuni, now sit beneath the Pāṭali tree;
the Tathāgata, honored for his ten powers, has severed and extinguished all fetters and latent tendencies.
Having subdued all demonic adversaries, they proclaim the Great Illumination among the multitudes.
By the power of the seven Buddhas’ diligence, they emit light that extinguishes the darkness;
each sitting beneath a tree, they attain perfect enlightenment therein.

“Vipaśyin Tathāgata held three assemblies for preaching the Dharma: in the first assembly there were one hundred and sixty-eight thousand disciples; in the second assembly there were one hundred thousand disciples; and in the third assembly there were eighty thousand disciples.”

The Tathāgata Śikhin also taught the Dharma in three assemblies: in the first assembly there were one hundred thousand disciples; in the second assembly there were eighty thousand disciples; and in the third assembly there were seventy thousand disciples.
The Tathāgata Viśvabhū preached the Dharma in two assemblies; in the first assembly there were seventy thousand disciples, and in the second assembly there were sixty thousand disciples.
The Tathāgata Krakucchanda preached the Dharma in one assembly, with forty thousand disciples.
The Tathāgata Kanakamuni held one assembly for preaching the Dharma, with thirty thousand disciples.
The Tathāgata Kāśyapa held one assembly for preaching the Dharma, with twenty thousand disciples.
"In this single assembly today, I preach the Dharma, and my disciples number one thousand two hundred and fifty.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Vipaśyin is named 'The Observer'; His wisdom is immeasurable."
All-seeing and fearless, he surveys the assembly of disciples in his three gatherings.
Śikhin’s light is unshakable, able to extinguish all fetters and afflictions;
possessing immeasurable and great majesty, none can fathom him.
That Buddha also had three assemblies, where his disciples gathered together from all sides.
Viśvabhū severed the fetters; the Great Sage’s essential teachings were compiled.
His fame resounded in all directions; his wondrous Dharma possessed great renown.
In his second assembly, the disciples universally expounded the profound and subtle meanings.
In the first assembly of Krakucchanda, he took pity on all and healed their sufferings;
the Guide transformed sentient beings in that single assembly of disciples.
The Tathāgata Kanakamuni was likewise unsurpassed;
his body was the color of purple-polished gold, and his physical features were fully perfected.
In a single assembly, he taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to his multitude of disciples.
In Kāśyapa, every single hair is aligned; his mind is focused without distracted thoughts.
His speech is never redundant, and his assembly of disciples is unified.
The Muni’s intent is tranquil and extinguished; he is the supreme śramaṇa of the Śākya clan.
The God among Gods, most venerable, [spoke thus] to my disciples in this assembly:
"In that assembly, I have manifested the meaning and spread forth the pure teaching;
their minds are always filled with joy, and their outflows are exhausted, ending all further existence."
Vipaśyin had three, Śikhin two, and Viśvabhū one;
each of these four Buddhas [had one], as the Sage explained in the Assembly of Seers.
At that time, Vipaśyin Buddha had two disciples:
The first was named Khaṇḍa and the second was named Tiṣya; they were the foremost among all his disciples.
Śikhin Buddha had two disciples:
the first was named Abhibhū and the second was named Saṃbhava; they were the foremost among all his disciples.
Vipaśyin Buddha had two disciples: the first was named Pūrṇa and the second was named Uttara; they were the foremost among all his disciples. Krakucchanda Buddha had two disciples:
the first was named Śāṇakavāsin and the second was named Vairāṭīputra; they were the foremost among all his disciples.
The Buddha Kanakamuni had two disciples:
the first was named Śubhāna and the second was named Uttara; they were the foremost among all his disciples.
Kāśyapa Buddha had two disciples, the first named Tiṣya and the second named Bharadvāja, who were the foremost among all his disciples.
Now I have two disciples, the first named Śāriputra and the second named Maudgalyāyana, who are the foremost among all my disciples.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Khaṇḍa, Tiṣya, and the others, were disciples of Vipaśyin;
Abhibhū and Tripiṭaka, were disciples of Śikhin.”
Phalgu and Uttara were foremost among the disciples;
both subdued the hosts of Māra. They were disciples of Viśvabhū.
Sañjīva and Vīraka were disciples of Krakucchanda.
Śubhāntara and Uttara were disciples of Krakucchanda;
Tiṣya and Bharadvāja were disciples of Kāśyapa Buddha;
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are my foremost sons.
“Vipaśyin Buddha had an attendant disciple named Aśoka.
Śikhin Buddha’s attendant disciple was named Kṣāntivādin.
Viśvabhū Buddha had an attendant disciple named Upaśānta.”
The Buddha Krakucchanda had an attendant disciple named Sujāta.
The Buddha Kanakamuni had an attendant disciple named Saṃvarta.
"Kāśyapa Buddha had an attendant disciple named Subhadra; my attendant disciple is named Ānanda.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
Aśoka and Kṣāntivādin, Upaśānta and Bhadrajyoti, Saumya and Subhūti, with Ānanda as the seventh.
These were the attendants of the Buddhas, fully endowed with all meaningful purposes;
day and night they were free from negligence, benefiting both themselves and others.
These seven virtuous disciples attended at the sides of the seven Buddhas.
With joy they made offerings, and in tranquility they returned to nirvana.
"Vipaśyin Buddha had a son named Fangying (Square Cheek).
Śikhin Buddha had a son named Wuliang (Immeasurable)."
Vipaśyin Buddha had a son named Sujāta; Krakucchanda Buddha had a son named Varasena;
Kanakamuni Buddha had a son named Vinītarāja.
"Kāśyapa Buddha had a son named Saṃgharakṣita; now I have a son named Rāhula.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Anantaja, Sudarśana and Uttara, Nāyaka, Senāpati, and others— Rāhula is the seventh;
these sons of noble lineage shall carry on the succession of the Buddhas.
He loved the Dharma and delighted in giving alms; he was fearless regarding the noble Dharma.
Vipaśyin Buddha’s father was named Bandhu, of the Kṣatriya royal lineage; his mother was named Bandhumatī; and the city ruled by the king was named Bandhumatī.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Vipāśyī’s father was Bandhumat, And his mother was Bandhumatī;
In the city of Bandhumatī, The Buddha taught the Dharma therein."
“The father of Śikhin Buddha was named Prabhāsa, of the Kṣatriya royal lineage; his mother was named Prabhāvatī, and the city ruled by the king was named Prabhākarī.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Śikhin’s father was Prabhāsa, His mother was named Prabhāvatī.”
In the city of Virocana, his majestic power subdued external enemies.
The father of Viśvabhū Buddha was named Sudīpa, of the Kṣatriya royal lineage; his mother was named Yaśodharā, and the city ruled by the king was called Anupama.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Vipaśyin Buddha’s father was Sudīpa of the Kṣatriya caste;
His mother was named Yaśodharā, and his city was named Anupama."
“Kakusandha Buddha’s father was named Yajñadatta, of the Brahmin caste; his mother was named Sujātā; the king was named Ananda, and because it followed the king’s name, the city was named Ananda.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The Brahmin was named Yajña; his mother's name was Subhaddā.
The king was named Saṃvara, and he resided in the city of Saṃvarapura."

“The father of Konāgamana Buddha was named Mahādeva, of the Brahmin caste; his mother was named Sujayā. At that time, the king’s name was Śuddhodana; because it followed the king’s name, the city was also named Śuddhodana.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"O great virtuous Brahmin, my mother was named Sujayā;
the king was named Śuddhodana, and we resided in the city of Kapilavastu."
"The father of Kāśyapa Buddha was named Brahmadatta, of the Brahmin caste; his mother was named Dhanavatī. At that time, the king was named Kṛkī, and the city ruled by the king was named Vārāṇasī."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Brahmin was named Brahmāśīla; his mother’s name was Dhanavatī.
At that time, there was a king named Kṛkī, residing in the city of Vārāṇasī.”
“My father’s name is Śuddhodana; he is of the Kṣatriya royal lineage. My mother’s name is Mahāmāyā. The city ruled by the king is named Kapilavastu.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Father is the Kṣatriya Śuddhodana, Mother is named Mahāmāyā.”
"The land is vast and its people are abundant; I was born from there.

"These are the causes and conditions, the names, the lineages, and the birthplaces of all Buddhas. What wise person, upon hearing these causes and conditions, would not rejoice and give rise to a heart of love and delight?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now wish to relate the deeds of past Buddhas by means of my knowledge of former existences; do you wish to hear them?"
The bhikṣus replied, “Now is precisely the right time; we wish and desire to hear it!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
"Monks! You should know this constant law of all Buddhas:
when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, he entered through her right side, with right mindfulness and without confusion."

At that time, the earth shook and a great radiance was emitted, universally illuminating the world; even those places not reached by the sun or moon were bathed in this great light, so that sentient beings dwelling in darkness and obscurity were able to see one another and know their respective destinies.

At that time, this radiance further illuminated the palace of Māra; the various devas, Śakra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all other sentient beings were universally graced by this great light, such that the natural radiance of the devas no longer appeared.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Thick clouds gather in the void, And lightning flashes across the world;
When Vipaśyin descended into the womb, The radiance shone forth in just the same way.”
Where the sun and moon do not reach, there is none that does not receive his great brilliance;
dwelling in the womb, he is pure and free from defilement—such is the nature of all Buddhas. "O Bhikṣus!
One should know that this is the constant law of all Buddhas:

when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was in his mother’s womb, he remained mindful and undistracted; four deva kings stood guard over him, holding halberds and spears, so that neither humans nor non-humans could harass or disturb him—this is the constant law.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The four heavenly kings from the four directions, Possessing renown and majestic virtue,
Sent by Śakra, Lord of Devas, Guard the Bodhisattva well."
Constantly grasping halberds and spears, they provide protection without ever departing;
neither humans nor non-humans can cause them harm—this is the constant law of all Buddhas.
They are protected by celestial deities, just as celestial maidens guard the gods.
"The retinues harbor joy; this is the constant law of all Buddhas.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"The constant law of all Buddhas is as follows:"

When Vipaśyin Bodhisattva descended from the Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, he remained mindful and undistracted; his mother’s body was peaceful and secure, free from all afflictions and ailments, and her wisdom increased.
The mother observed her own womb and beheld the body of the Bodhisattva, with all its sense faculties complete, like polished purple-gold, free from any flaw or impurity.
It was as if a person with clear vision were looking at pure lapis lazuli, transparent both inside and out, without any obstructions or veils.
"O monks! This is the constant law of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Like a pure lapis lazuli gem, its brilliance like that of the sun and moon;
when the Benevolent Honored One dwelt in his mother’s womb, his mother was free from affliction and distress.
Wisdom increased within her, and she beheld the fetus as if it were a golden image."
"The mother’s pregnancy is peaceful and blissful; this is the constant law of all Buddhas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"When the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, he remained mindful and undistracted. His mother’s mind was pure, free from all sensual thoughts, and she was not consumed by the fire of lust. This is the constant law of all Buddhas."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva dwells within his mother’s womb; His celestial life ends and celestial merit is perfected.
His mother’s mind is pure and serene, Free from all thoughts of sensual desire."
"Having abandoned all sensual desires, Neither stained by nor associating with them;
Not burned by the fire of desire, The Mother of all Buddhas is eternally pure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is the constant law of all Buddhas:

when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin descended from the Tuṣita Heaven into his mother’s womb, he was mindful and undistracted; his mother observed the five precepts, maintained pure conduct, was deeply faithful and compassionate, accomplished in all virtues, and lived in peace and fearlessness. Upon the dissolution of the body after death, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—this is the constant law."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Bearing the body of the Honored One among Men, With diligence and the full observance of precepts, One will surely receive a celestial body hereafter;
This causal condition is called the Mother of the Buddha.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, he emerged from the right side [of his mother], the earth shook, and a brilliant light shone everywhere."
"At the moment of first entering the womb, there is no place within the darkness that does not receive light; this is the eternal law.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When the Prince was born, the earth shook, And a great radiance shone everywhere."
In this realm and other realms, above, below, and in all directions,
they emit light to bestow pure vision; endowed with celestial bodies,
they proclaim the names of Bodhisattvas with joyful and pure voices.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, he emerged from the right side [of his mother], mindful and undisturbed."
At that time, the Bodhisattva’s mother stood grasping a tree branch, neither sitting nor lying down.
Then, four celestial sons approached with their hands holding fragrant water and stood before her, saying:
"Indeed, O Celestial Mother!"
"A noble son has been born today; do not harbor grief or sorrow.
This is the constant law.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Mother of Buddhas neither sits nor lies down; abiding in the precepts, she cultivates the holy life.
Born noble and free from indolence, she is attended by gods and humans.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, he emerged from his mother’s right side, mindful and undisturbed; his body was pure, untainted by any impurity."
It is just as when a man with sight casts a pure, bright pearl onto white silk; neither defiles the other, for both are pure.
The Bodhisattva’s emergence from the womb is likewise so; this is the constant law.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as a pure, bright mani-jewel, Cast upon silk, is not stained;
When the Bodhisattva emerges from the womb, He is pure and free from defilement."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
when the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, he emerged from his mother’s right side, mindful and undisturbed."
Emerging from his right side, he descended to the ground and took seven steps without anyone supporting him; surveying the four quarters, he raised his hand and declared:
"In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the most honored; I shall deliver all living beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
"This is the constant law.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just like the stride of a lion, / He gazes intently in all four directions."
Upon touching the ground, he walked seven steps; so too did the Lion among Men.
Furthermore, like a great dragon moving, he surveyed the four quarters;
upon touching the ground, he walked seven steps; so too did the Dragon among Men.
When the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings was born, he walked seven paces with steady gait;
looking toward the four quarters and raising his voice, he declared: "I shall bring an end to the suffering of birth and death.
At the very moment of his birth, he was both the peerless and the equal.
"Observing for myself the root of birth and death, this body is my final limit.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is the constant law of all Buddhas:"

When the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, he emerged from his mother’s right side with focused mindfulness and without confusion; two springs gushed forth, one warm and one cool, to provide for his bathing—this is the constant law.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"When the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings was born, Two springs spontaneously gushed forth;
To provide for the Bodhisattva’s use, The All-Seeing One bathed therein, becoming pure."
Two springs gush forth spontaneously; their waters are exceedingly pure and clear.
One is warm and the other is cool, used for bathing the Omniscient One.
"When the Prince was first born, his father King Bandhumat summoned physiognomists and masters of various arts and sciences, ordering them to examine the Prince and discern his fortune."
Then, the physiognomists received their orders and went to observe; they stepped forward and uncovered his robes, seeing that he possessed the marks of greatness. They divined and said:
"One who possesses such marks shall surely go to one of two destinations; of this there is no doubt."

If he remains a householder, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, ruling over the four continents with a complete fourfold army; he shall govern by the True Dharma without partiality or injustice, extending his benevolence throughout the world. The seven treasures will arrive spontaneously, and he shall have a thousand sons, valiant and capable of subduing external enemies; weapons shall not be used, and the world shall enjoy peace.
If he leaves the household life to study the Way, he shall attain Perfect Enlightenment, fully endowed with the ten titles.
At that time, the physiognomists addressed the king, saying:
"The son born to the king possesses the thirty-two marks; he will surely proceed toward one of two destinies, of this there is no doubt."
"If he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
if he leaves the household life, he shall attain Perfect Enlightenment, fully endowed with the ten titles.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"When the Prince of a Hundred Blessings was born, the physiognomists made this prediction:
as recorded in the ancient chronicles, he will undoubtedly follow one of two paths.
If he delights in the household life, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King."
The seven treasures are difficult to obtain, yet as a king’s jewels they come of their own accord.
Made of pure gold, complete with a thousand spokes, and held together by a golden rim all around, it can fly and travel everywhere; therefore, it is called the Celestial Wheel.
Well-tamed, with seven tusks, dwelling in stability; tall and broad, white as snow, capable of flying through the void—this is called the second treasure, the Elephant.
The horse travels throughout the world, departing in the morning and returning by evening to feed.
The vermilion crest of the peacock’s throat is called the third treasure.
The pure lapis lazuli bead emits light for one yojana;
its illumination at night is as bright as day, and it is called the fourth treasure.
In form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, there is none who can equal her;
among all women she is the foremost, known as the fifth treasure.
She presented the King with lapis lazuli jewels, pearls, jade, and various rare treasures.
Offered with joy, it is called the sixth treasure.
Just as the wheel-turning king thinks, his military hosts come and go swiftly;
as agile and fast as the king’s will, it is called the seventh treasure.
These are called the seven treasures: the wheel, the elephant, and the pure white horse;
the householder, the jewel, and the woman treasure; and the military commander treasure as the seventh.
Beholding this, he felt no weariness; delighting himself with the five desires, like an elephant breaking its tether, he left the home life and attained perfect enlightenment.
The King has such a son, the most honored among two-legged human beings.
Turning the Wheel of Dharma while dwelling in the world, he attained the Way without indolence.
At that time, the Father King earnestly and repeatedly asked the physiognomists once more:
"Examine the Prince's thirty-two marks again; what are these names?"
Then the physiognomists immediately removed the prince’s robes and described his thirty-two marks:
"First, his feet are level and even; the soles of his feet are flat and full, treading upon the ground with stability."
Second, the soles of his feet are marked with the sign of the wheel, complete with a thousand spokes, their radiance illuminating one another.
Third, his hands and feet are webbed, like those of the king of geese.
Fourth, his hands and feet are soft and supple, like celestial garments.
Fifth, the fingers of his hands and feet are slender and long, such that none can equal them.
Sixth, the heels of his feet are full and well-fleshed; one never tires of gazing upon them.
Seventh, his calves are like those of a deer, tapering and straight from top to bottom.
Eighth, the hook-locked bones: the joints of the bones are interlocked like a series of linked chains.
Ninth, the male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse.
Tenth, standing upright with arms hanging down, the hands reach below the knees.
Eleventh, a single hair grows from each pore; these hairs curl to the right and are the color of dark lapis lazuli.
Twelfth, the growing hairs curl to the right, are deep blue in color, and lie flat upward.
13. His body is golden in color.
14. His skin is fine and soft, such that it does not retain dust or impurities.
15. His two shoulders are level, full, and perfectly rounded.
16. On his chest is the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel.
17. His body is twice the height of an ordinary person.
18. Seven parts of his body are flat and full.
19. His height and breadth are equal, like those of the nyagrodha tree.
20. His jaws are like those of a lion.
21. His chest is broad and well-proportioned, like that of a lion.
22. His mouth has forty teeth.
23. They are square, even, and level.
24. The teeth are closely set without gaps.
Twenty-five: His teeth are white and brilliant.
Twenty-six: His throat is pure and clear; whatever various flavors he consumes, none fail to be perfectly suited to him.
Twenty-seven: He has a broad and long tongue, with which he can lick both ears from left and right.
28. His Brahma-voice is clear and resonant.
29. His eyes are deep blue. 30.
His eyes are like those of a bull king; both the upper and lower eyelids blink simultaneously.
31. Between his eyebrows is a white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*), soft, fine, and lustrous; it extends one fathom in length, and when released, it curls to the right like a pearl.
32. On the crown of his head is a fleshy protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*). These are the thirty-two marks.
Then he spoke in verse:
"With feet well-placed and supple, No footprints appear upon the ground;
Adorned with the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, Every radiance and color is fully present."
Like a nyagrodha tree, its height and circumference are perfectly equal;
the Tathāgata possesses the unprecedented secret mark of the horse’s sheathed organ.
His body is adorned with gold and jewels, where the various marks reflect one another.
Though he moves in accordance with worldly ways, the dust and soil do not defile him.
His celestial countenance is exceedingly supple; a divine canopy naturally covers him.
With a Brahma-voice and a body of purple-gold, he is like a flower first emerging from a pond.
The king questioned the physiognomist, and the physiognomist respectfully replied to the king:
"I praise the marks of the Bodhisattva; his entire body is endowed with radiance.
From the hands and feet to every joint, there is nothing—inner or outer—that is not manifest."
The flavors of food he consumes are entirely perfect; his body is upright and never slants.
The mark of the wheel appears on the soles of his feet, and his voice is like that of a sorrowful phoenix.
His shanks and thighs are perfectly formed, brought to fruition by the karma of past lives.
His arms and elbows are perfectly rounded; his eyebrows and eyes are most dignified and handsome.
This Honored One, a lion among men, possesses the foremost power and majesty.
His jaw is square and well-proportioned; he lies on his side like a lion.
His forty teeth are square and even, closely set without gaps.
His Brahma-voice is unprecedented, reaching far and near according to conditions.
Standing upright, his body does not lean; with both hands, he touches his knees.
His hands are even and supple; the Honored One among Men is endowed with beautiful marks.
A single hair grows from each pore, and his hands and feet possess the webbed-mark.
He has a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head and deep blue eyes; both the upper and lower eyelids blink together.
His two shoulders are full and rounded, endowed with the thirty-two marks;
his heels are level without unevenness, and his calves are slender and well-proportioned like those of a deer.
The God among Gods has come here, like an elephant breaking free from its tethering ropes.
To liberate sentient beings from the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death,
he preaches the Four Noble Truths out of a heart of compassion;
by expounding the meaning of the Dharma verses, he causes the multitude to revere the Supreme Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When the Bodhisattva Vipaśyin was born, the devas were above him in the void, holding white parasols and precious fans in their hands to shield him from cold and heat, wind and rain, and dust.”
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Unprecedented among men, He was born as the Honored One among bipeds;
All devas, harboring reverence and devotion, Offer him precious canopies and precious fans."
"At that time, the father-king provided him with four nurses:
the first for suckling, the second for bathing, the third for applying fragrant unguents, and the fourth for entertainment."
She nurtured him with joy, never growing weary.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The wet nurse possessed loving-kindness; As soon as the child was born, she was entrusted with his care."
One nursed him at the breast and one bathed him; two anointed him with perfumes for his amusement.
With the most exquisite fragrance in the world, they anointed the Honored One among Men.
When he was a youth, the men and women of the entire kingdom gazed upon him without ever being satiated.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Venerated and beloved by many, like a golden image newly completed,
men and women gaze upon it together, never wearying of the sight."
"When he was a child, the men and women of the entire nation vied with one another to carry him in their arms, as if gazing upon a precious flower.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"When the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings was born, He was revered and loved by many people."
They passed him from hand to hand in turn, holding him as if beholding a precious flower with its fragrance.
When the Bodhisattva was born, his eyes did not blink, just like those of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
"Because he does not blink, he is named Vipaśyin.
Thereupon, a verse was spoken:
"The God among Gods does not blink, just like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Seeing forms and observing them correctly, he is thus named Vipaśyin.
When the Bodhisattva was born, his voice was clear and penetrating, soft, gentle, and elegant, like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a bird of the Snowy Mountains, Drinking the nectar of flowers, sings;
So too is the voice of that Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, Pure and penetrating."
"When the Bodhisattva was born, his eyes could see clearly through one *yojana*.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Through the retribution of pure karmic conduct, He receives the wondrous radiance of the heavens; The Bodhisattva’s eyes, being clear and pure, Can see all things within a *yojana*."
The range of the Bodhisattva’s vision extends for a full yojana.

When the Bodhisattva was born, as he gradually grew to maturity, he resided in the Hall of Heavenly Rectitude; there, he transformed others through the Way, his benevolence reaching the common people, and his fame and virtue spread far and wide.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Though a youth, he dwelt in the Hall of Righteousness, Transforming the world through the Way;
He resolved all matters of state, And was thus named Vipaśyin."
"Pure wisdom is vast and extensive, as profound as the great ocean;
it brings joy to all living beings and causes their wisdom to increase and expand.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, wishing to go out for an excursion, commanded his charioteer to prepare the precious carriage and proceed to the grove to wander and observe.
The charioteer immediately finished preparing the carriage and returned to report:
"Now is precisely the time.
The Prince then mounted the precious chariot and proceeded to that garden for an excursion.
On the way, he saw an old man whose head was white and teeth fallen out, his face wrinkled and body bent; leaning on a staff, he walked with feeble steps, gasping for breath.
The Prince asked his attendant: "Who is this person?"
He replied, "This is an old man.
He asked again:
"What constitutes being old?
He replied, "As for being old, it means that the span of one's life is drawing to a close and little of the remaining lifespan remains; therefore, it is called 'old'."
The Prince asked again:
"Shall I also become like this, unable to escape this affliction? He replied:
"However, birth is inevitably followed by old age, regardless of whether one is noble or lowly.
Thereupon, the Prince was despondent and displeased; he immediately told his attendant to turn the carriage back to the palace and reflected in silent contemplation:
"Reflecting on this suffering of old age, I too shall surely experience it."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Seeing one whose life is nearly spent, Supporting a staff with weary steps;
The Bodhisattva reflects to himself: 'I too shall not escape this hardship.'"
At that time, the father king asked his attendant:
"Did the prince enjoy himself on his excursion? He replied:
"I am not happy.
He was asked again for the reason, and he replied, "I encountered an old man on the road; that is why I am not happy."
At that time, the father king silently reflected to himself:
"In the past, when the physiognomist examined the Prince's marks, he said he would surely renounce the world; seeing him now so dejected, could it not be that this has come to pass?"
"We must devise skillful means to place him within the deep palace, providing him with the pleasures of the five desires to delight his heart, so that he will not leave the household life.
Thereupon, they immediately adorned the palaces and halls and selected beautiful women to entertain him.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"When the Father King heard these words, He skillfully adorned the palace halls;
He increased the five sensory pleasures, Wishing to prevent him from leaving home."
Furthermore, at a later time, the Prince again commanded his charioteer to prepare the carriage for an excursion.

On the way, he encountered a sick man whose body was emaciated and his belly distended; his face was dark and sallow, and he lay alone amidst filth with no one to look after him. He suffered from the most agonizing pain and was unable to speak.
The counselor asked the charioteer,
"Who is this? He replied:
"This is a sick person. He asked,
"In what way is he ill?"
He replied: "As for 'sickness,' it is when various pains press upon one so urgently that there is no certainty as to whether one will survive; hence it is called sickness.
He spoke again:
"I too shall be like this; am I not likewise unable to escape this affliction? He replied, "Indeed."
"Once born, one is subject to illness; there is no distinction between noble and base.
Thereupon, the Prince was despondent and displeased, and immediately commanded his charioteer to turn the carriage back to the palace.
He reflected in silence:
"Reflecting on this suffering of illness, I too shall be like this.
Thereupon, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Seeing that long-suffering patient, whose complexion had grown haggard, he reflected in silence: 'I too shall not escape this affliction.
At that time, the father-king again questioned the charioteer:"
"Did the Prince enjoy himself on his excursion? He replied, "He did not."
When asked again for the reason, he replied, "I encountered a sick person on the road; therefore, I am not joyful.
Thereupon, the father king reflected in silence:
"In the past, when the physiognomist examined the Prince's features, he said that he would surely renounce the household life. Today he appears displeased;
could it be that this is what has come to pass? I shall employ further skillful means, increasing the various musical performances to delight his heart and prevent him from leaving home."
He then once again adorned the palace quarters and selected court ladies to provide him with entertainment.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“Forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and touches— Subtle and delightful to the senses.”
"By the power of the Bodhisattva’s merit, he thus finds delight therein.
Furthermore, at another time, the Prince again commanded his charioteer to prepare the carriage for an excursion.

On the way, he encountered a dead person being escorted out of the city; various colored silk banners preceded and followed him, while his kinsmen and relatives wailed and wept in mourning as they saw him off.
The Prince asked again,
"Who is this person? He replied:
"This is a dead person.
He asked: "In what way is one considered dead?"
He replied: "To die means to come to an end.

The wind-element precedes, followed by the fire-element; the sense faculties are destroyed and decayed, existence and non-existence diverge toward different destinies, and the family is separated—therefore, it is called death."
The Prince asked the charioteer again:
"Am I also destined to be like this, unable to escape this affliction? He replied:
"However, birth must inevitably lead to death; there is no distinction between the noble and the humble.
Thereupon, the Prince was despondent and displeased, and he immediately instructed his charioteer to turn the carriage back to the palace. In silent contemplation, he reflected:
"Reflecting on this suffering of death, it is surely my destiny as well."
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"When I first saw someone die, I knew they would be born again;
In silent contemplation, I reflected: 'I too shall not escape this affliction.'"
At that time, the father-king again asked the charioteer:
"Did the prince enjoy himself on his excursion? He replied:
"I am not happy.
He was asked again for the reason, and he replied, "I encountered a dead person on the road; that is why I am not happy."
Thereupon, the father king silently reflected to himself:

"In the past, when the physiognomists examined the Crown Prince's features, they said he would surely renounce the household life; seeing that he is displeased today, could it be that this will indeed come to pass?"
"I shall employ further skillful means, increasing the variety of music and performances to delight his heart, so that he will not leave the household life.
He then once again adorned the palaces and halls and selected beautiful maidens to provide him with entertainment.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The youth is renowned and surrounded by a host of court ladies;
He delights himself with the five desires, like Śakra, Lord of the Devas."

“Furthermore, at another time, he again commanded his charioteer to prepare the carriage for an excursion. On the way, he encountered a śramaṇa wearing dharma-robes and carrying an alms-bowl, walking while keeping his eyes fixed upon the ground.”
He then asked the charioteer, "Who is this?
The charioteer replied:
"This is a śramaṇa. He asked again,
"What is meant by 'śramaṇa'?"

He replied: "A śramaṇa is one who has abandoned affection and love, left the household life to cultivate the Way, and restrains all the sense faculties; he is not stained by external desires, maintains a heart of compassion for all beings, and does nothing to harm them; encountering suffering, he does not grieve, and meeting with joy, he does not exult; he is able to endure like the earth, and for this reason he is called a śramaṇa."
The Prince said: "Excellent!
This Way is authentic and truly severs the accumulation of worldly dust; it is subtle, wondrous, pure, and void—this alone is what brings joy."
He immediately commanded his charioteer to turn the carriage toward him.
At that time, the Prince asked the śramaṇa,
"Having shaved off your hair and beard, wearing the dharma-robes and holding an alms-bowl, what is it that you seek?"
The śramaṇa replied:

"One who has left the household life desires to subdue the mind and intentions, to be forever free from worldly defilements, to compassionately nurture all living beings without causing them harm or disturbance, and to remain empty-minded and tranquil, making only the Way his primary concern."
The Prince said: "Excellent!
This path is the most true."
He then commanded his charioteer:

"Take my precious robes along with the carriage and return to inform the Great King that I shall now, right here, shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma-robes, and leave the household life to practice the Way."
"Why is this? It is because I wish to subdue my mind and thoughts, cast off worldly defilements, dwell in purity, and seek the way of the Path.
Thereupon, the charioteer returned the precious carriage and the garments that the Prince had ridden in to his father, the King.
Thereafter, the Prince shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and left the household life to practice the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When the Prince saw the old man and the sick man, he understood the suffering and affliction of the world; furthermore, when he saw the dead man, his worldly attachments were extinguished.”
Upon seeing the śramaṇa, he attained great and expansive awakening.
As he descended from his precious chariot, with every step he took he moved further away from bondage and attachment; this is true renunciation, this is true seclusion.

At that time, when the people of that country heard that the prince had shaved off his hair and beard, donned dharma robes, and taken up the alms bowl to leave the household life and practice the Way, they all said to one another:
"This path must be true, for it has caused the prince to renounce the glory of his kingdom and abandon what he held most dear."
At that time, eighty-four thousand people from within the kingdom went to the Prince and requested to become his disciples, leaving the household life to cultivate the Way.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Having selected the profound and wondrous Dharma, they heard it and followed him forth to leave the household life."
"Free from the prison of affection and love, he is without any fetters of worldly attachment.
At that time, the Prince immediately accepted [the gift] and traveled about with him, teaching and transforming beings wherever they went.
Traveling from village to village and from kingdom to kingdom, wherever he went, there was no place where he was not reverently provided with the fourfold offerings.
The Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"I and my great assembly have been wandering through various kingdoms; these human realms are noisy and tumultuous, which is not suitable for me."
When shall I be able to leave this multitude and seek the truth of the Way in a secluded place, so that I may fulfill my aspiration and cultivate the path with single-minded diligence in solitude?
Again, he thought: “Beings are pitiable;

they dwell perpetually in darkness, their bodies fragile and precarious, subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death. They are the gathering place of manifold sufferings, dying here and being born there, passing from there to be born here. Following this aggregate of suffering, they transmigrate without end. When shall I clearly understand this aggregate of suffering and extinguish birth, old age, and death?”
Again, he thought: "From what does birth and death arise?
By what conditions do they exist?"
He then used wisdom to observe the causal origins: from birth come old age and death; birth is the condition for old age and death.
Birth arises from becoming; becoming is the condition for birth.
Becoming arises from grasping; grasping is the condition for becoming.
Grasping arises from craving; craving is the condition for grasping.
Craving arises from feeling; feeling is the condition for craving.
Feeling arises from contact; contact is the condition for feeling.
Contact arises from the six sense bases; the six sense bases are the condition for contact.
The six sense bases arise from name-and-form; name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases.
Name-and-form arises from consciousness; consciousness is the condition for name-and-form.

Consciousness arises from volitional formations; volitional formations are the condition for consciousness. Volitional formations arise from ignorance; ignorance is the condition for volitional formations.

Thus, conditioned by ignorance there are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations there is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases there is contact; conditioned by contact there is feeling; conditioned by feeling there is craving; conditioned by craving there is clinging; conditioned by clinging there is becoming; conditioned by becoming there is birth; conditioned by birth there are old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress—this mass of suffering arises conditioned by birth. This is the origin of suffering.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
when contemplating the aggregate of the origin of suffering, knowledge arises, vision arises, awakening arises, clarity arises, penetration arises, wisdom arises, and realization arises.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further reflected to himself:
"In the absence of what is there no old age and death?
Through the cessation of what does old age and death cease?"
He then used wisdom to observe the causal origins: because birth does not exist, old age and death do not exist; because birth ceases, old age and death cease.
Because existence does not exist, birth does not exist; because existence ceases, birth ceases.
Because grasping does not exist, existence does not exist; because grasping ceases, existence ceases.
Because craving does not exist, grasping does not exist; because craving ceases, grasping ceases.
Because feeling does not exist, craving does not exist; because feeling ceases, craving ceases.
Because contact does not exist, feeling does not exist; because contact ceases, feeling ceases.
Because the six sense bases do not exist, contact does not exist; because the six sense bases cease, contact ceases.
Because name-and-form do not exist, the six sense bases do not exist; because name-and-form cease, the six sense bases cease.
Because consciousness does not exist, name-and-form do not exist; because consciousness ceases, name-and-form cease.

Because of the absence of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*) is absent; because of the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases. Because of the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations are absent; because of the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease. Thus, through the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease;

through the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; through the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) ceases; through the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) cease; through the cessation of the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*) ceases; through the cessation of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) ceases; through the cessation of feeling, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases; through the cessation of craving, clinging (*upādāna*) ceases; through the cessation of clinging, existence (*bhava*) ceases; through the cessation of existence, birth (*jāti*) ceases; and through the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease.
The Bodhisattva reflects:
"When the aggregate of suffering ceases, knowledge arises, vision arises, awakening arises, clarity arises, penetration arises, wisdom arises, and realization arises."

At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order; having known them as they truly are and seen them as they truly are, he immediately attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon his seat.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
“These words are spoken within the assembly; you all should listen well.
This is the Dharma never before heard, contemplated by the Bodhisattvas of the past.”
From what condition does old age and death arise?
By what cause does it exist?
Having contemplated this correctly, one knows that its root originates from birth.
From what condition does birth arise?
By reason of what thing does it exist?
Having reflected thus, one knows that birth originates from becoming.
Having grasped that, and having grasped it further, existence increases through successive stages;
therefore the Tathāgata has said: grasping is the causal condition for existence.
It is like a mass of foul impurities, which the wind blows and causes to flow out as a torrent of filth.
Thus, grasping at signs is the cause, and through craving it becomes widespread.
Craving arises from feeling, serving as the root of the net of suffering;
by means of the conditions of defiled attachment, suffering and pleasure are conjoined.
From what condition does sensation arise?
By what cause does sensation exist?
Having reflected thus, one knows that sensation is born from contact.
From what conditions does contact arise?
By reason of what does contact exist?
Having reflected thus: "Contact is born from the six sense bases."
What is the primary condition for the six sense bases?
By what cause do the six sense bases exist?
Having reflected thus: "The six sense bases arise from name-and-form."
What is the primary condition for name-and-form?
By what cause does name-and-form arise?
Having reflected thus: name-and-form arises from consciousness.
From what condition does consciousness fundamentally arise?
By what cause does consciousness exist?
Having reflected thus, one knows that consciousness is born from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
From what condition do volitional formations arise?
By what cause do volitional formations exist?
Having reflected thus, he understood that volitional formations are born from ignorance.
Such causal conditions are called the cause of ultimate reality;
through the observation of wisdom and skillful means, one can perceive the root of dependent origination.
Suffering is not created by the noble ones, nor does it exist without a cause.
Therefore, the suffering of change is what the wise eliminate.
When ignorance is extinguished, at that time there are no volitional formations;
if there are no volitional formations, then there is also no consciousness.
If consciousness is eternally extinguished, there will likewise be no name-and-form;
once name-and-form has ceased, there are then no sense bases.
If the sense bases are eternally extinguished, then there is likewise no contact.
If contact is eternally extinguished, then there is no feeling;
if feeling is eternally extinguished, then there is no craving;
if craving is eternally extinguished, then there is no grasping.
If grasping is eternally extinguished, then existence (bhava) does not exist;
if existence is eternally extinguished, then birth does not exist;
if birth is eternally extinguished, there are no aggregates of old age, sickness, and suffering.
All things are forever extinguished; this is what the Wise One has taught.
The twelve links of dependent origination are profound, difficult to see, and difficult to comprehend;
only a Buddha can perfectly awaken to them—how they exist because of causes and how they cease to exist.
If one can observe for oneself, then there will be no sense-bases;
one who deeply perceives dependent origination need seek no teacher outside.
One who, regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, has abandoned desire and is undefiled;
Worthy of receiving all offerings, he purifies his reward for the benefactor’s kindness.
If he attains the four analytical knowledges, he will achieve definitive realization;
able to untie the bonds of the multitude, he severs them without negligence.
Form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are like a dilapidated old cart;
one who can contemplate these phenomena with clarity will achieve perfect and complete enlightenment.
Like a bird soaring through the void, flying east and west with the wind;
The Bodhisattva severed all fetters, Like the wind blowing a light garment.
Vipaśyin, in tranquil seclusion, Contemplated all phenomena:
"By what cause do old age and death exist?"
From what does cessation arise?
Having made this contemplation, he gives rise to pure wisdom;
he knows that old age and death are caused by birth, and that with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease.

"When Vipaśyin Buddha first attained the Way, he frequently cultivated two contemplations: the first is called the contemplation of peace and security, and the second is called the contemplation of renunciation.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata, unequaled among equals, Frequently cultivated these two contemplations; ... [as above] ..."
Peaceful and secure, having attained liberation, the Seer has crossed to the other shore.
His mind is sovereign, having severed all fetters and latent tendencies;
ascending the mountain, he gazes upon the four quarters, and for this reason he is named Vipaśyin.
The light of great wisdom dispels the darkness, like using a mirror to see oneself;
it removes the world’s grief and affliction, exhausting the suffering of birth, old age, and death.
In a secluded and quiet place, Vipaśyin Buddha again had this thought:

"I have now attained this unsurpassed Dharma, which is profoundly deep, subtle, difficult to understand, and difficult to see; it is quiescent, pure, known by the wise, and beyond the reach of the ordinary and foolish."

This arises because sentient beings have different levels of tolerance, different views, different inclinations, and different studies; relying on those differing views, each delights in what they seek and each exerts themselves in what they practice.

Therefore, they are unable to comprehend this profound principle of dependent origination; yet the nirvana of the exhaustion of craving is even more difficult to understand. If I were to explain it to them, they would certainly fail to understand and would instead become further disturbed.
Having formed this thought, he remained silent and no longer preached the Dharma.
At that time, Brahmā Śikhin, knowing the thoughts of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, reflected to himself:
"Alas, this world is falling into ruin; it is truly pitiable."
"Vipaśyin Buddha realized this profound and subtle Dharma, yet he did not wish to preach it.

Just as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, he suddenly descended from the Brahma palace and stood before the Buddha; bowing his head to the Buddha's feet in salutation, he withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Brahma King knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma at this opportune moment!

Now these sentient beings have but slight dust and defilement; their faculties are sharp and keen; they possess a heart of reverence and are easily transformed. They fear the unrescued sins of future lives, are able to extinguish evil dharmas, and can give birth to the good paths."
The Buddha told the Brahma King: "So it is! So it is!"
It is as you have said; however, while dwelling in a secluded place, I reflected silently within myself:

"The True Dharma I have attained is exceedingly profound and subtle. If I were to preach it to them, they would certainly not understand it and would instead become further disturbed. Therefore, I remain silent and do not wish to preach the Dharma."

For incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have practiced the supreme path with diligent effort and without slackening; it is only now that I have finally attained this Dharma so difficult to obtain. If I were to preach it to sentient beings who are dominated by lust, anger, and delusion, they would certainly not accept or practice it, and I would merely exhaust myself in vain.
"This Dharma is subtle and profound, contrary to worldly ways; sentient beings, being defiled by desire and shrouded by ignorance, are unable to believe or understand it.
Brahmā King!
Observing this, I remained silent and did not wish to preach the Dharma."
Then, Brahmā Śikhin again entreated him with repeated and earnest sincerity, even up to three times:
"World-Honored One!
If you do not preach the Dharma, this world will now fall into ruin; it is truly to be pitied."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound [the Dharma] at this opportune time, so as not to let sentient beings fall into other realms of existence!

At that time, having heard the Brahma King’s earnest entreaty three times, the World-Honored One immediately surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye, observing that the defilements of sentient beings vary in thickness, their faculties differ in sharpness or dullness, and the teachings vary in difficulty or ease.
Those who are easily taught fear the retribution of future lives; they are able to extinguish unwholesome dharmas and give rise to rebirth in the good realms.

It is like the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers: some have just emerged from the mud but have not yet reached the water; some have already emerged and are level with the water; and some have emerged from the water but have not yet blossomed. Yet none of them are stained or attached by the water, and they are all easily made to bloom.
The sentient beings of the world are also like this.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Brahma King, saying:

"Out of compassion for you all, I shall now open and expound the Dharma-gate of ambrosia. This Dharma is profound and subtle, difficult to understand and know; I shall speak it now for those who believe, accept, and delight in hearing it, but not for those who are intrusive, troublesome, or unbeneficial."

At that time, the Brahma King, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and suddenly vanished.
Not long after they had departed, the Tathāgata remained in silence and reflected to himself:
"To whom should I first preach the Dharma?
He then thought to himself:
"I shall enter the city of Bandhumatī and first open the gate of the Dharma of Immortality for Prince Tiṣya and the minister’s son Khanda.

Thereupon, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, the World-Honored One suddenly vanished from beneath the Bodhi tree and arrived at the Deer Park of King Bandhumān in the city of Bandhumatī, where he spread out his seat and sat down.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"As a lion roams at will through the forest,
so too does that Buddha roam, unimpeded and free from obstruction."
Vipaśyin Buddha said to the park keeper,
"You may enter the city and say to Prince Tiṣya and the minister's son Khanda:
'Do you wish to know?'"
"Vipaśyin Buddha is now in the Deer Park and wishes to see you; you should know that the time has come.
Then, the park keeper, having received these instructions, went to where the two men were and delivered the Buddha’s message in full.
Having heard this, the two went at once to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha gradually taught them the Dharma, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening them:

he spoke on generosity, on morality, and on rebirth in the heavens; he spoke of the impurity of sensual desires and how the outflows of higher realms are a source of affliction; and he praised renunciation as the most subtle, pure, and supreme state.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the minds of these two men were supple and gentle, filled with joy and faith, and capable of receiving the True Dharma, thereupon preached for them the Noble Truth of Suffering, expounding, elucidating, and explaining it in detail; he likewise proclaimed and interpreted the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
"At that time, Prince Tiṣya and the minister’s son Khanda, while still on their seats, became free from dust and defilement and attained the pure Dharma-eye, just as a white cloth is easily dyed."
At that time, the earth deity proclaimed these words:

"The Tathāgata Vipaśyin has turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park at the city of Bandhumatī—a wheel that cannot be turned by any śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, Māras, Brahmās, or other worldly beings."

In this manner, the sound was transmitted from one to another, reaching the Four Heavenly Kings and continuing up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations; in the space of a moment, the sound reached the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"With hearts leaping with joy, they praised the Tathāgata:
'Vipaśyin has attained Buddhahood And turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.'"
First arising from beneath the King of Trees, he went to the city of Bandhumatī;
for Khaṇḍa and Tiṣya, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s transformative teaching, Khaṇḍa and Tiṣya—
Within the pure wheel of Dharma, the holy life is unsurpassed.
The hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, as well as Śakra, Lord of Devas, joyfully inform one another; there are none among the gods who do not hear it.
The Buddha has appeared in the world, turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma;
he increases the hosts of devas and diminishes the asuras.
His fame as a transcendent sage is heard everywhere; with excellent wisdom, he has left the extremes of the world behind.
Attaining mastery over all phenomena, he turns the wheel of Dharma through wisdom.
Observing the equality of all dharmas, his mind is stilled and free from defilement;
having escaped the yoke of birth and death, he turns the wheel of Dharma through wisdom.
Extinguishing suffering and departing from all evils, Transcending desire to attain mastery;
Fleeing the prison of affection and love, With wisdom, he turns the wheel of Dharma.
The Perfectly Awakened One, honored among men, The Honored One among bipeds, the Tamer;
Having attained liberation from all bonds, wisdom turns the wheel of Dharma.
A skillful guide who teaches and transforms others, able to subdue the enmity of Māra;
having departed from all evils, wisdom turns the wheel of Dharma.
With the power of the untainted, he subdues Māra; his faculties are concentrated and unwearied.
Having exhausted the outflows and escaped the bonds of Māra, his wisdom turns the wheel of Dharma.
If one studies the definitive Dharma, one knows that all phenomena are without self.
This is the supreme among dharmas: wisdom that turns the wheel of Dharma.
Not for the sake of gain or offerings, nor seeking fame or reputation, but out of compassion for those sentient beings, wisdom turns the wheel of Dharma.
Seeing sentient beings in distress, oppressed by old age, sickness, and death,
he turns the wheel of Dharma through wisdom for the sake of these three evil realms.
He cuts off greed, hatred, and delusion, and uproots the very source of craving.
Unmoving yet liberated, with wisdom he turns the wheel of Dharma.
Having conquered the unconquerable, having conquered, he has brought himself under control;
having triumphed over the unconquerable Māra, with wisdom he turns the wheel of Dharma.
This unsurpassed wheel of Dharma can only be turned by a Buddha;
among all devas, Māras, Śakras, and Brahmās, there is none who can turn it.
By turning the wheel of Dharma through close proximity, he brings benefit to the multitudes of devas and humans.
"These Teachers of Gods and Humans have attained the further shore.

At that time, Prince Tiṣya and the minister’s son Khaṇḍa, having seen the Dharma and attained the fruit, being true and without deception, and having achieved fearlessness, addressed Vipaśyin Buddha, saying:
"We wish to purely cultivate the holy life within the Dharma of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! My Dharma is pure and sovereign; practice it to bring an end to the limits of suffering."
At that time, the two men immediately received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Not long after their ordination, the Tathāgata further manifested three things for them:

first, the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi*); second, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); and third, instruction and admonition (*avavādānuśāsanī*). Thereupon, they attained the state free from outflows (*anāsrava*), liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*), and the wisdom of non-doubt (*niḥsaṃśaya-jñāna*).

At that time, the many people within the city of Bandhumatī, hearing that two men had left the household life to study the Way, wearing dharma robes and carrying alms bowls to purely cultivate the Brahma-faring, all said to one another:
"That Way must surely be true, for it has caused these men to renounce worldly glory and status, and to cast away what they held most dear."

At that time, eighty-four thousand people from within the city went to the place where Vipaśyin Buddha was in the Deer Park; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha gradually taught him the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him with discourses on giving, discourses on morality, and discourses on rebirth in heaven; he spoke of the impurity of sensual desires and the affliction of the outflows of higher realms, praising renunciation as the most subtle, pure, and supreme state.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the minds of this great assembly were pliant, joyful, faithful, and delighted, and that they were capable of receiving the True Dharma, thereupon preached for them the Noble Truth of Suffering, expounding, elucidating, distributing, and explaining it; he likewise preached the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

At that time, eighty-four thousand people, while still upon their seats, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye. Just as a white cloth easily takes on dye, they saw the Dharma and attained the fruit; realizing it was true and without deception, they achieved fearlessness and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to practice the pure Brahma-faring within the Dharma of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu! My Dharma is pure and sovereign;
practice it so as to bring an end to the limits of suffering."
At that time, eighty-four thousand people immediately attained full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Not long after their ordination, the World-Honored One instructed them through three matters:

first, the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi*); second, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); and third, formal admonition (*anuśāsana*). They immediately attained the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*), liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*), and the wisdom of non-doubt (*niḥsaṃśaya-jñāna*).

When eighty-four thousand people heard that the Buddha had turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park—a wheel that cannot be turned by any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or other worldly beings—they immediately went to the city of Bandhumatī to the place where Vipaśyin Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Just as one whose head is on fire Seeks a place of extinction with all haste;
So too is that person, Who hastens swiftly to the Tathāgata."
At that time, the Buddha preached the Dharma for them in the same manner.

At that moment, there were one hundred and sixty-eight thousand great bhikṣus in the city of Bandhumatī. Among this great assembly, the bhikṣu Tiṣya and the bhikṣu Khaṇḍa ascended into the air, emitting water and fire from their bodies and manifesting various supernatural transformations, while preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the great assembly.
At that time, the Tathāgata thought silently to himself:

"Now, within this city there are one hundred and sixty-eight thousand great bhikṣus; it is fitting that they be sent away to travel, two by two, to various places, and after six years have returned to the city to recite the full precepts."

At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa deva, knowing the Tathāgata’s mind, vanished from that heaven and suddenly appeared here in the space of a strong man bending and extending his arm. He prostrated himself before the World-Honored One with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and after a short while addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is so, World-Honored One!”

"The bhikṣus within this city of Bandhumatī are numerous; it would be well for them to distribute themselves and travel everywhere. After six years have passed, they shall return to this city to recite the Prātimokṣa. I shall provide protection so that no one seeking an opportunity to harm them may find such an opening."
At that time, the Tathāgata heard these words of the deva and silently gave his consent.
When the Śuddhāvāsa deva saw that the Buddha had silently granted permission, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and suddenly vanished, returning to the heavens.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Now, there are many bhikṣus within this city; it is fitting that you each disperse and travel about to teach and transform others. When six years have passed, you shall return and assemble for the recitation of the precepts."
Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“The Buddha has a community entirely free from confusion, Free from desire and free from attachment.”
Majestic as a garuḍa, like a crane abandoning an empty pond.
"At that time, after one year had passed, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven addressed the bhikṣus:
'You have already spent one year wandering; five years remain.'"
"You should know that once the six years have passed, you shall return to the city to recite the precepts.
Thus it continued for six years, until the deva spoke again:
"The six years are now complete; you should return to recite the precepts."

At that time, having heard the words of the deva, the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and returned to the city of Bandhumatī. They went to the place where Vipaśyin Buddha was in the Deer Park, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"Just as a well-trained elephant goes wherever it wishes,
so too does this great assembly return according to the teaching."
At that time, the Tathāgata ascended into the air before the great assembly, sat cross-legged, and preached the Sūtra on the Precepts:
"Patience is the foremost; the Buddha has declared Nirvāṇa to be supreme. One does not become a śramaṇa by merely shaving one's hair and beard while harming others."
At that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven, standing not far from the Buddha, spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s great wisdom is subtle, wondrous, and uniquely supreme;
Perfectly endowed with śamatha and vipaśyanā, he has attained the most perfect enlightenment.”
Out of compassion for all living beings, he attained enlightenment while in the world and,
by means of the Four Noble Truths, taught them for the sake of the śrāvakas:
suffering, the cause of suffering, and the truth of the cessation of suffering.
The Noble Eightfold Path leads to the place of peace and security.
When Vipaśyin Buddha appeared in the world,
he shone among the great assembly like the radiance of the sun.
Having spoken this verse, he suddenly vanished.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I reflected to myself:"
"Once, at one time, while at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, I had this thought:
'The places where I have been born are nowhere not pervasive, with the sole exception of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven; were I to be born in that heaven, I would not return here.'"
"At that time, bhikṣus!
I again had this thought:
'I wish to go to the Heaven of No-Creation.'"
Then, like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, I vanished from this place and appeared in that heaven.
When those devas saw me arrive there, they prostrated themselves with their heads at my feet, stood to one side, and said to me:

"We are all disciples of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin; having been transformed by that Buddha, we have come to be born here. They then related to me in full detail the causes, conditions, beginning, and end concerning that Buddha.
