Furthermore, Śikhin Buddha, Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha were all my teachers; having received transformation and instruction from them, I have therefore been born here.
He also explained the causes, conditions, beginning, and end of all Buddhas, up to their birth among the Akaniṣṭha devas; it was likewise so.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Just as a strong man, in the space of bending and extending his arm,"
By means of my supernormal power, I have reached the Heaven of No-Creation.
To the Seventh Great Sage, who has subdued the two Māras,
who is without fever and beyond perception— I join my palms in reverent salutation.
Like a pārijātaka tree, renowned afar as the Teacher of the Śākyas,
endowed with all the marks of excellence, he reached the Sudarśana Heaven;
like a lotus flower, he was unsullied by the waters.
The World-Honored One is unstained, having attained supreme and great clear vision.
Like the sun first rising, pure and free from dust or obscuration;
like the bright autumn moon, he has reached the ultimate consummation.
These five abodes are purified by sentient beings;
because their minds are pure, they come to where there is no affliction.
Coming with pure hearts, they become disciples of the Buddha.
Having abandoned defiled grasping, he delights in non-grasping.
Having seen the Dharma with certainty, the son of Vipaśyin, with a pure mind, has come forth; he approaches the Great Seer.
The son of Śikhin Buddha, stainless and unconditioned,
has come with a pure mind to visit the Honored One who is detached from existence.
The son of Viśvabhū, his faculties fully perfected, [has likewise arrived].
With a pure mind he approaches me, like the sun shining in the sky.
Kruṣṇa’s son, having abandoned all desires,
approaches me with a pure mind, his wondrous radiance blazing intensely.
The son of Kanakamuni is stainless and unconditioned;
with a pure mind he approaches me, his radiance like that of the full moon.
The disciple of Kāśyapa has all his faculties complete.
With a pure mind, he approached me; his devotion was like that of the gods.
Undistracted toward the Great Sage, whose supernormal powers are foremost, he became a disciple of the Buddha with a steadfast heart.
As a disciple of the Buddha, one pays homage to the Tathāgata and fully proclaims the Honored One among men:
his name, clan, and lineage, as well as his profound knowledge and vision of the Dharma.
They shall attain the unsurpassed path;
free from defilement and dust, through diligent and tireless effort,
they shall sever all fetters of existence.
"This fundamental and derivative causal nexus was expounded by Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this Mahānidāna Sūtra, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced it accordingly.
The Dīrgha Āgama Spoken by the Buddha, Volume One.

2. The Cunda Sūtra (Part 2) The First Division: The Cunda Sūtra, Part Two Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru of Magadha wished to attack Vṛji. The king thought to himself:
"Although they are brave and strong, and their people are powerful, it will not be difficult for me to take them."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru summoned the brahmin minister Varṣākāra and addressed him, saying:
"Go to Vulture Peak Mountain to where the World-Honored One is; bearing my name, prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One and inquire after his well-being, asking:
'Are you light and at ease in your movements? Is your walking strong?'"
Again, he addressed the World-Honored One:

"The people of Vṛji pride themselves on their valor and strength; they are a powerful and arrogant populace who do not submit to me. I wish to go and attack them, but I do not know what instructions the World-Honored One would give."
“If there are instructions to be given, you should remember them well and not let anything be omitted, exactly as they were spoken.
What the Tathāgata says is never false.”

Having received the King’s instructions, the minister Varṣākāra immediately mounted a precious chariot and proceeded to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Upon reaching his destination, he alighted from the chariot and continued on foot until he arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was staying. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“King Ajātaśatru of Magadha bows his head at the Buddha’s feet and inquires with great earnestness:
‘Are you light and well in your daily life? Is your movement vigorous?’”
Again he addressed the World-Honored One:

“The people of Vaṃśa pride themselves on their valor and strength; they are a bold and powerful populace who do not submit to me. I wish to go and attack them, but I do not know what instructions the World-Honored One would give.”
At that time, Ānanda was standing behind the World-Honored One, holding a fan and fanning him. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Have you heard that the people of the Vṛji country frequently assemble together to discuss matters of right conduct?"
He replied, "I have heard it.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If this can be achieved, the young and old will be harmonious and submissive, and the nation will become increasingly prosperous; it will remain secure for a long time, and none shall be able to invade or harm it.
Ānanda! Have you heard that among the people of Vṛji, the ruler and his ministers are harmonious and submissive, and those above and below respect one another?"
He replied, “I have heard it. “Ānanda!

"If this can be achieved, the old and the young will live in harmony and submission, the population will increase further, and the kingdom will remain secure for a long time, incapable of being invaded or harmed.
Ānanda! Have you heard that the people of Vṛji revere the Dharma, observe prohibitions, and do not violate the rules of propriety?"
He replied, “I have heard it. “Ānanda!

If this can be achieved, then the young and the old will live in harmony and accord, the population will flourish ever more, the kingdom will enjoy long-lasting peace, and none shall be able to invade or harm it. Ānanda,
have you heard how the people of Vṛji serve their parents with filial piety and respect and obey their teachers and elders?
He replied, “I have heard it. “Ānanda!

If this can be achieved, the young and the old will be harmonious and compliant, and their excellence will increase further; the kingdom will remain secure for a long time, and none shall be able to invade or harm it.
Ānanda! Have you heard that the people of Vṛji are reverent toward their ancestral temples and pay respectful homage to the spirits and deities?
He replied, "I have heard it. "Ānanda!

If this can be achieved, then the young and the old will be harmonious and compliant, becoming even more so; the kingdom will remain secure for a long time, and none shall be able to invade or harm it.

Ānanda, have you not heard that among the people of Vaṅga, the domestic life is truly upright and pure, free from defilement, such that even in their jesting, their speech never touches upon what is improper?
He replied, “I have heard it. “Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

If this can be achieved, then the old and the young will be harmonious and compliant, the population will flourish even more, the kingdom will remain secure for a long time, and no one will be able to invade or harm it. Ānanda!
Have you not heard that the people of Vṛji revere and serve the śramaṇas, respectfully uphold those who observe the precepts, and look after and nurture them without ever becoming weary?
He replied, “I have heard it. “Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]

"If this can be achieved, the old and the young will live in harmony and accord, the population will flourish ever more, the kingdom will remain secure for a long time, and none shall be able to invade or harm it.
Then the minister Varṣākāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the people of that country were to practice even one of these dharmas, they would still be impossible to plot against; how much more so if they possess all seven?"
"Due to many affairs of state, I now request leave to return home.
The Buddha said, "It is well;
you should know that this is the proper time."
At that time, King Yu She rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew with respectful courtesy.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Command all the bhikṣus in the vicinity of Rājagṛha to assemble in the lecture hall."
He replied, “So be it.
He then proceeded to the city of Rājagṛha, assembled the bhikṣus, and having gathered them all in the lecture hall, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The monks have assembled; let the Noble One know that the time has come.
Then, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, proceeded to the Dharma Hall, took his place upon the seat, and addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall teach you the seven dharmas of non-retrogression; listen attentively!”
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The seven dharmas of non-retrogression are:
first, to gather frequently for assemblies and discuss the correct meaning; thus, the young and old will be harmonious and compliant, and the Dharma cannot be destroyed."

Second, when those above and below are harmonious and united, reverent and compliant without opposition, then the elderly and the young will be harmonious and submissive, and the law cannot be subverted.

Third, when one upholds the Dharma and understands prohibitions, not violating established regulations, then the elderly and the young will be harmonious and submissive, and the law cannot be subverted.

The fourth is: if there is a bhikṣu who has the power to protect the assembly and possesses many spiritual friends, one should serve and honor him; thus, the young and old will be harmonious and compliant, and the Dharma cannot be destroyed.
Fifth, it is to guard the mind with mindfulness, taking filial piety and reverence as primary; thus the old and young will be harmonious and compliant, and the Dharma cannot be destroyed.
Sixth, it is to purely cultivate the Brahma-faring, not following the ways of desire; thus the old and young will be harmonious and compliant, and the Dharma cannot be destroyed.
"Seventh, to put others before oneself and not covet fame or profit; thus, the young and old will be harmonious and compliant, and the Dharma cannot be destroyed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, there are seven dharmas that cause the Dharma to increase and prevent it from declining."
First, one delights in few activities and does not take pleasure in doing much; thus, the Dharma increases and there is no diminution.
Second, one delights in silence and does not take pleasure in speaking much.
Third, one has little sleep and is free from mental dullness.
Fourth, one does not form factions or engage in useless speech.
Fifth, one does not praise oneself for qualities that one lacks.
Sixth, one does not associate with evil persons as companions or partisans.
Seventh, one delights in dwelling alone in the seclusion of mountain forests.
Thus it is, O bhikṣu!
"Then the Dharma will increase and there will be no decline.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, there are seven dharmas that cause the Dharma to increase and prevent any decline."
What are the seven?
First, they possess faith; they believe in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is fully endowed with the ten titles.
Second, they possess a sense of shame; they feel shame regarding their own deficiencies.
Third, they possess a sense of shame, feeling abashed by evil conduct.

Fourth, they are widely learned; that which they have received and upheld is good in its superior, middling, and inferior aspects, profound in meaning and flavor, pure and free from defilement, and fully endowed with the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Fifth, he applies himself with diligence to ascetic practices, extinguishing evil and cultivating good, training with perseverance without abandoning his efforts.
Sixth, he recollects and does not forget what he has previously studied and learned.
Seventh, he cultivates wisdom, understands the law of arising and ceasing, proceeds toward the essentials of the noble ones, and brings all roots of suffering to an end.
"These seven dharmas cause the Dharma to increase and prevent its decline.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, there are seven other dharmas that cause the Dharma to increase and prevent its decline."
What are the seven? First, reverence for the Buddha;

second, reverence for the Dharma; third, reverence for the Saṅgha; fourth, reverence for the precepts; fifth, reverence for meditative concentration; sixth, reverence for and obedience toward one’s parents; seventh, reverence for heedfulness.
"In this way, these seven dharmas cause the Dharma to increase and never diminish.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, there are seven other dharmas that cause the Dharma to increase and never diminish."

What are the seven dharmas? First, contemplating the impurity of the body; second, contemplating the impurity of food; third, taking no delight in the world; fourth, constantly maintaining the perception of death; fifth, giving rise to the perception of impermanence; sixth, the perception of suffering within impermanence; and seventh, the perception of non-self within suffering.
"These seven dharmas lead to the increase of the Dharma and its lack of decline.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, there are seven other dharmas that lead to the increase of the Dharma and its lack of decline."
What are the seven?
First, one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, which is secluded, free from desire, essential for liberation, and unconditioned.
Second, one cultivates the awakening factor of dharma-discernment.
Third, one cultivates the awakening factor of diligence.
Fourth, one cultivates the awakening factor of joy.
Fifth, one cultivates the awakening factor of tranquility.
Sixth is the cultivation of the awakening-factor of concentration.
Seventh is the cultivation of the awakening-factor of equanimity.
Through these seven dharmas, the Dharma increases and suffers no diminution.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are six dharmas of non-retrogression that cause the Dharma to increase and prevent it from declining. What are these six?
First, one constantly practices compassion with the body, refraining from harming sentient beings.
Second, one proclaims benevolence and kindness with the mouth, refraining from uttering evil words.
Third, one maintains a compassionate mind with the intention, refraining from harboring thoughts of destruction or harm.
Fourth, he obtains pure offerings and shares them with the assembly, treating all equally without distinction.
Fifth, he upholds the precepts of the noble ones, free from deficiency or omission, untainted by impurity, and remaining steadfast and immovable.
"Sixth is seeing the noble path that leads to the end of suffering.
Through these six dharmas, the Dharma increases and there is no decline.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Furthermore, there are six dharmas of non-retrogression that cause the Dharma to increase and prevent its decline:

first, mindfulness of the Buddha; second, mindfulness of the Dharma; third, mindfulness of the Saṅgha; fourth, mindfulness of the precepts; fifth, mindfulness of giving; and sixth, mindfulness of the devas."
"By cultivating these six recollections, the Dharma will increase and there shall be no decline.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had stayed as long as was appropriate in Rājagṛha, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"All of you prepare yourselves; I wish to go to the Bamboo Grove."
He replied, “So be it.

He immediately prepared his robes and bowl and, accompanied by the great assembly as his attendants, followed the World-Honored One from the route through Magadha to the Bamboo Grove. Arriving at the hall, he sat down and preached to the bhikṣus on morality, concentration, and wisdom.
By cultivating ethical discipline one attains concentration and gains a great fruit;
by cultivating concentration one attains wisdom and gains a great fruit;
by cultivating wisdom the mind becomes pure, one attains equal liberation, and exhausts the three outflows—the outflow of sensual desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance.
Having attained liberation, he realized the knowledge of liberation:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had stayed at the Bamboo Grove for as long as was appropriate, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
“You all should prepare yourselves; we shall go to the city of Pāṭaliputra. They replied, “So be it.”

He immediately prepared his robes and bowl and, accompanied by the great assembly as his attendants, followed the World-Honored One. Traveling by way of Magadha, they arrived in succession at the city of Pāṭaliputra, where he sat beneath a pāṭala tree.

At that time, when the lay devotees heard that the Buddha and the great assembly had come from afar to this spot beneath the Pāṭali tree, they immediately went out of the city together. From a distance, they saw the World-Honored One beneath the Pāṭali tree, his appearance upright and handsome, his sense-faculties tranquil and stilled, and his mastery of self-discipline supreme.
He is like a great dragon whose waters are clear and limpid, free from dust and impurity;
his body is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
Having seen him, they were filled with joy and gradually approached the Buddha’s presence. They prostrated themselves, touching their heads to his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the lay devotees addressed the Buddha, saying: “We wish to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha.

We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will grant us permission to become upāsakas. From this day forward, we shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants; we shall uphold these precepts without fail.”
"I wish to prepare an offering; I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, will deign to show compassion and grant us your presence.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha was silent, the lay devotees rose from their seats, circumambulated the Buddha three times, paid their respects, and returned home.
He immediately built a great hall for the Tathāgata, leveling the site, sweeping and sprinkling it, burning incense, and solemnly arranging the precious throne.
Once the offerings were prepared, he went to inform the World-Honored One:
"The preparations are complete; may the Holy One know the time."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and together with the great assembly, proceeded to that lecture hall. Having washed his hands and feet, he sat down in the center.
At that time, the bhikṣus were seated on the left side, and the lay devotees (upāsakas) were seated on the right side.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the lay devotees, saying:
"When an ordinary person violates the precepts, there are five forms of decline."
What are these five?
First, when seeking wealth, one's wishes are not fulfilled.
Second, even if something is obtained, it shall daily diminish and waste away.
Third, wherever one goes, one will not be respected by the multitude.
Fourth, one's ugly reputation and evil fame will spread throughout the world.
Fifth, when the body perishes and life ends, one shall enter hell.
He further addressed the lay devotees:
"When ordinary people uphold the precepts, there are five merits.
What are these five?
First, whatever one seeks shall be obtained immediately according to one's wishes.
Second, all one's property and wealth shall increase without diminution.
Third, wherever one goes, one shall be respected and loved by all people.
"Fourth, his good name and fine reputation will spread throughout the world.
Fifth, when his body perishes and his life ends, he will surely be reborn in the heavens.
At that time, it was already midnight; he told the lay devotees that they should each return home.
The lay devotees, having received the Buddha’s instruction, circumambulated him three times, prostrated at his feet, and returned home.

At that time, during the final watch of the night when the light of dawn appeared, the World-Honored One went to a secluded place; with his pure and penetrating divine eye, he saw that the great devas each claimed possession of their respective dwelling sites, while the middle and lower devas likewise claimed possession of their dwelling sites.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned to the lecture hall, took his seat, and because he knew the proper moment, he asked Ānanda:
"Who built this city of Pāṭaliputra?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“This was built by the minister Vasabha to defend against the Vajjis.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“The one who built this city has truly attained the favor of the devas. During the last watch of the night, when the dawn light appears, I shall go to a secluded place and, with my divine eye, see how the great devas each claim their sites for dwellings, and how the middling and lower devas likewise claim their sites for dwellings.”
Ānanda! You should know that wherever people dwell upon lands granted by the great devas, there will be peace, joy, and prosperity.
Those granted by middling devas are inhabited by middling people;
It is a place sealed by lower deities and inhabited by lower beings;
according to the measure of their merit, each dwells wherever they have settled. Ānanda!

This place is where the virtuous dwell and where merchants gather; its national laws are true and free from deception. This city is the most excellent, esteemed by all quarters, and cannot be destroyed.
In the distant future, when this city is about to be destroyed, it will surely be by three things:
first, great floods; second, great fires; and third, when those within the city conspire with those from outside, they shall destroy this city.
At that time, the lay devotees of Pāṭaliputra had prepared the offerings throughout the night; when the time arrived, they informed the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the proper time."

Then, the lay devotee immediately made the necessary preparations; he personally served the food, and when the meal was finished, he provided water for washing. He then took a small seat, spread it out before the Buddha, and sat down.
At that time, the World-Honored One pointed it out to him, saying:
"Now, this place where you reside is inhabited by the virtuous and wise; many here uphold the precepts and purely cultivate the holy life, so that the benevolent deities rejoice."
He then offered a blessing for them:

"May you know how to revere those worthy of reverence and how to serve those worthy of service; may you practice extensive generosity and universal love, possessing a heart of compassion. May you be praised by the devas, always accompanied by goodness, and never meeting with evil."
At that time, having taught the Dharma, the World-Honored One rose from his seat; surrounded by the great assembly, they escorted him back.
As the minister Roca followed behind the Buddha, he thought to himself:
"Now that the śramaṇa Gautama has passed through this city gate, let this gate be named the 'Gautama Gate'."
"Furthermore, observe the place where the Tathāgata has crossed the river; let this very spot be named the Gautama River.

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Pāṭaliputra and arrived at the riverbank. At that moment, there were many people upon the riverbank; some were crossing by boat, some by raft, and others by floating logs as they crossed the river.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, suddenly reached the other shore in the brief interval it takes for a strong man to bend and extend his arm.
Having contemplated this meaning, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Buddha is the master of the ocean-going ship; The Dharma is the bridge across the river's ford."
The carriage of the Mahāyāna path carries all devas and humans across;
it also brings about one's own liberation from fetters, crossing to the shore to attain the state of an immortal.
It causes all disciples to untie their bonds and attain nirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, traveling from the Vṛji country to the village of Kuḷī, stayed beneath a tree in a forest and addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four profound dharmas:
first, noble ethical discipline; second, noble concentration; third, noble wisdom; and fourth, noble liberation."
This Dharma is subtle and difficult to understand; because neither I nor you have fully comprehended it, we have long remained in saṃsāra, wandering through it without end.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having contemplated this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Precepts, concentration, wisdom, and supreme liberation— Only the Buddha can discern them;
He transforms others by departing from suffering, Causing them to sever the habits of birth and death."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having stayed as long as was appropriate in the village of Kūṭi, addressed Ānanda, saying, "Let us go together to the village of Nāda.

Ānanda received the instruction and immediately donned his robes and took up his bowl. Together with the great assembly, he attended upon the World-Honored One. Traveling by way of Vṛji, they arrived at the village of Nāda and stayed at the site of the ghaṇṭā-stūpa.
At that time, Ānanda was in a secluded place, reflecting silently to himself:
"In this village of Nāḍika, there are twelve lay devotees:

first, Gaggara; second, Kāliṅga; third, Vakkala; fourth, Kaliṇḍaka; fifth, Cāru; sixth, Vāru; seventh, Bhadda; eighth, Subhadda; ninth, Todeyya; tenth, Soṇadaṇḍa; eleventh, Jeta; and twelfth, Jetavana."
Where have these people been reborn now that their lives have ended?
Furthermore, fifty people have passed away, and another five hundred have passed away; where have they been reborn?
Having had this thought, he rose from his secluded place and went to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
I retired to a quiet place and reflected silently to myself:
"In this village of Nāḍika, twelve householders including Gārgra have passed away; furthermore, fifty people have passed away, and another five hundred have passed away. Where have they been reborn?"
“I only wish that you would explain this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“Gaggarā and the other twelve individuals have severed the five lower fetters; at the end of their lives they will be reborn in the heavens, where they shall attain parinirvāṇa and no longer return to this world.”

Of those fifty who passed away, having severed the three fetters and attenuated lust, anger, and delusion, they attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*; returning once more to this world, they will bring an end to the root of suffering.

Of those five hundred who passed away, having severed the three fetters, they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; they shall not fall into the evil realms, are destined for enlightenment, and after seven more births of coming and going, they will reach the end of suffering.
Ānanda! Birth is followed by death; this is the constant order of the world, so why should it be considered strange?
If every single person who died were to come and question me about it, would that not be a source of disturbance?
Ānanda replied: “It is so, World-Honored One!
It is indeed a disturbance.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I shall now explain for you the Mirror of Dharma, by which a noble disciple may know the places of rebirth.

Having exhausted the three evil realms and attained the stage of Srotāpanna, they will not undergo more than seven births before they surely reach the end of suffering; furthermore, they are able to explain these matters to others."

Ānanda! As for the "Mirror of the Dharma," it refers to a noble disciple who has attained indestructible faith and rejoices in faith in the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is fully endowed with the ten titles.
Rejoicing with faith in the Dharma:
truly subtle and exquisite, spoken with complete freedom, it is timeless and reveals the path to Nirvana; it is the practice of the wise.

Rejoicing with faith in the Saṃgha, they dwell in excellent harmony; their conduct is upright and sincere, free from flattery and deceit; they have accomplished the fruits of the Path; those above and below are concordant and submissive; and they are fully endowed with the Dharma-body.

Those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry and those who have attained stream-entry; those who are candidates for the fruit of once-returning and those who have attained once-returning; those who are candidates for the fruit of non-returning and those who have attained non-returning; and those who are candidates for arhatship and those who have attained arhatship—these four pairs and eight classes constitute the Tathāgata’s assembly of noble and holy ones. They are most worthy of reverence and are the field of merit for the world.
Faith in the noble precepts:
they are pure and undefiled, without flaw or leakage; practiced by the wise and enlightened, they result in the attainment of samādhi. Ānanda!

This is the mirror of the Dharma, which enables the noble disciple to know the places of rebirth; having exhausted the three evil realms, they attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, and within seven more births at most, they will surely reach the end of suffering, and can also explain these matters to others.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had stayed for as long as was appropriate, he addressed Ānanda, saying, "Let us go together to the kingdom of Vaiśālī.

Having received these instructions, they set out; putting on their robes and taking up their bowls, they accompanied the World-Honored One with the great assembly as attendants. Traveling by way of the Vṛji country, they arrived at Vaiśālī and sat beneath a tree.

There was a courtesan named Āmrapālī who, hearing that the Buddha had arrived at Vaiśālī with his disciples and was sitting beneath a tree, immediately prepared her precious chariot and set out to go to the Buddha’s location to pay homage and make offerings.

Before he had yet arrived, he saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s countenance was upright and handsome, his faculties were exceptionally distinguished, and his marks and signs were complete, like the moon among the stars.

Having seen him, he rejoiced; he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot, gradually approaching the Buddha’s presence. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma for her, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, she gave rise to a heart of joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Triple Gem. I only pray that you will grant me permission to become a lay follower (*upāsikā*) within the True Dharma; for as long as this life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not speak falsely, and not drink intoxicants."
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One and your disciples will graciously accept my invitation to stay at my garden this very evening.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Buddha had granted his silent consent, the woman rose from her seat, prostrated herself at his feet, circumambulated him, and returned home.
Not long after she had departed, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"I shall go with you and the others to visit that garden."
He replied, "So be it.
The Buddha then rose from his seat, took up his robes and bowl, and proceeded to that garden together with his assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples.

At that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, hearing that the Buddha was staying in the Āmrapālī grove, immediately prepared their five-colored precious chariots. Some rode in blue chariots drawn by blue horses, with their clothing, parasols, banners, and attendants all blue; the same was true for the chariots and horses of the other four colors.

At that time, five hundred Licchavis, all dressed in identical attire, were on their way to visit the Buddha. On the road, Ambapālī, who was returning home after bidding farewell to the Buddha, encountered these Licchavis.

At that time, his carriage was traveling at a rapid pace when it collided with and jolted against the other jeweled carriage; the banners and canopies were broken and torn, and he did not yield the road. The charioteer rebuked him, saying:
"By what power do you presume to travel without yielding the road, crashing into and jolting my carriage, thereby breaking and tearing my banners and canopies?"
He replied, “Noble sirs!
I have already invited the Buddha for a meal tomorrow; I am returning home to prepare the offerings, which is why I am traveling so swiftly—it is not possible for me to avoid you.”
The Licchavis then said to the woman, "Set aside your request for now; we shall first give it to us, and we will give you a hundred thousand pieces of gold.
The woman immediately replied:
"The invitations have already been settled; we cannot grant your request.
Then, the Licchavis spoke again to the woman, saying, "We will give you sixteen times one hundred thousand pieces of gold; must we not have the first choice?"
The woman still refused, saying, "My request has already been settled; it cannot be otherwise.
At that time, the Licchavis spoke again to the woman, saying:
"I shall now divide the wealth of the kingdom with you; may you first give it to me?
The woman replied again, "Even if you were to offer the entire wealth and treasures of the kingdom, I would still not take them."
"The reason for this is that the Buddha resides in my garden and has already accepted my invitation; this matter is settled, and I will certainly not share him with you.
Each of the Licchavis shook their hands and lamented:
"Now, because of this woman, our initial merit has been lost."
He then proceeded directly to that grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar five hundred Licchavis approaching with tens of thousands of chariots and horses filling the road, and he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know the manner of play and the gardens of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, their deportment and adornments are no different from these."
"You, bhikṣus! You should restrain your own minds and maintain all dignified deportment.
How does a bhikṣu restrain his own mind?"
Thereupon, a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as body, ardent, unflagging, mindful, and clearly aware, having abandoned worldly desire and grief;
he contemplates the body externally as body, ardent, unflagging, mindful, and clearly aware, having abandoned worldly desire and grief;
he contemplates the body both internally and externally as body, ardent, unflagging, and having abandoned worldly desire and grief.
The same applies to the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena. How does a bhikṣu possess all dignified deportment?

In this regard, a bhikṣu knows when it is appropriate to walk and knows when to stop; he knows how to look to the left and right, how to bend and stretch, and how to bow and raise himself; he maintains his robes and bowl with propriety; in eating, drinking, and taking medicinal decoctions, he does not lose the proper measure; he skillfully employs expedient means to remove the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; whether awake, speaking, or remaining silent—he restrains his mind so that it is not distracted. This is called a bhikṣu who possesses all dignified deportment.

At that time, five hundred Licchavis went to the Āmrapālī grove, intending to approach the place where the Buddha was. They dismounted from their carriages and proceeded on foot; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

As the Tathāgata sat upon his seat, his radiant marks shone forth uniquely, eclipsing the entire assembly; it was like the autumn moon, or like the heavens and earth when clear and bright, free from dust and obscuration, with the sun shining alone in the void.
At that time, five hundred Licchavis were seated surrounding him in attendance. Among the assembly, the Buddha’s radiant marks shone with singular brilliance.

Then, from among those seated, a brahmin named Piṅgiya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
“The King of Magadha and Aṅga Has truly gained a most excellent benefit.”
Clad in armor of precious jewels, the World-Honored One emerges from that land.
His majestic power shakes the three thousandfold world; his fame is as renowned as the Snowy Mountains.
Like a lotus in full bloom, his fragrance is most subtle and wondrous.
Now I behold the Buddha’s radiance, like the sun first rising, like the moon traveling through the void, free from all clouds and obscurations.
The World-Honored One is likewise; his light shines throughout the world.
"Beholding the wisdom of the Tathāgata is like seeing a lamp in the darkness;
he bestows the clear eye upon the multitude and resolves all doubts.
At that time, having heard this verse, the five hundred Licchavis further addressed Pūraṇa:
"You may repeat it once more.
Thereupon, Piṅgiya repeated the verses before the Buddha three times.

When the five hundred Licchavis had heard the verses repeated for a second time, each of them removed his precious robe and offered it to Piṅgiya; Piṅgiya then presented these precious robes to the Tathāgata, and out of compassion for them, the Buddha accepted them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Licchavis of Vaiśālī, saying:
"There are five treasures in the world that are extremely difficult to obtain. What are these five?"
First, it is extremely rare for a Tathāgata, a Truly Realized One, to appear in the world.
Second, it is rare to find a person capable of expounding the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Third, those who are able to believe and understand the Dharma expounded by the Tathāgata are difficult to find.
Fourth, those who are able to accomplish the Dharma expounded by the Tathāgata are difficult to find.
"Fifth, those who rescue others from perilous distress and recognize their obligations are rare to find.
These are called the five treasures that are difficult to obtain.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, exhortation, benefit, and joy, the five hundred Licchavis addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One and your disciples will graciously accept my invitation!
The Buddha told the Licchavi:
“You have already invited me; I have now already received your offering. However, the lady Āmrapālī has already invited me first.”
At that time, having heard that the woman Āmrapālī had already invited the Buddha, five hundred Licchavis each shook their hands and said,
"We intended to make offerings to the Tathāgata, but now this woman has preempted us."
They immediately rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and each returned to their own abodes.

At that time, the woman Āmrapālī prepared various offerings that very night. When the time arrived the following day, the World-Honored One, together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, adjusted his robes, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by his attendants before and behind, went to the place of the invitation and sat upon the seat.
At that time, the lady Āmrapālī prepared a superior meal and offered it to the Buddha and the Sangha.
When they had finished eating and set aside their bowls, she removed the tables and stands.
Then, holding a golden pitcher in her hand, she poured water for washing and, having completed this, stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Of all the parks and groves in this city of Vaiśālī, my park is the most excellent; I now offer this park to the Tathāgata. Out of compassion for me, I pray that you will graciously accept it."
The Buddha told the woman:
"You may offer this garden to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, headed by the Buddha. Why is this so?"

Regarding all the Tathāgata’s groves, dwellings, and the six requisites such as robes and alms bowls, even Māras, Śakras, Brahmās, or gods of great supernatural power are none who could be worthy recipients of such offerings.
Then, the woman, having received these instructions, immediately offered this garden to the Buddha as its head and to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
Out of compassion for her, the Buddha accepted it and spoke this verse:
“Building stūpas and establishing vihāras, Giving gardens and fruits for cool refreshment;”
Building bridges and providing boats to ferry people across, giving water and grass in the vast wilderness,
and offering halls and pavilions— such merit increases day and night;
those who possess the purity of the precepts will surely reach the auspicious realm.

Then, the lady Āṭavikā took a small seat and sat before the Buddha. The Buddha gradually taught her the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening her with a discourse on generosity, a discourse on ethical conduct, and a discourse on rebirth in the heavens;
he explained that sensual desires are a great affliction, defiled and impure, that the higher outflows constitute an obstruction, and that the way of renunciation is supreme.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the woman’s mind was supple and serene, her afflictions were slight, and she was easily capable of being transformed, taught her the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, according to the Dharma of all Buddhas.

At that time, the woman Āmrapālī’s faith was pure and clear, like a clean white woolen cloth that easily takes on dye. Immediately upon her seat, she became free from dust and removed from defilement; the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within her. She saw the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and stood firmly established in certainty. No longer destined for the evil realms and having achieved fearlessness, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Sangha."
Thus she requested a second and a third time:
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will allow me to become a laywoman (*upāsikā*) within the True Dharma!
From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants.”

At that time, having received the five precepts from the Buddha, she abandoned her former habits; her defilements were eliminated, and she immediately rose from her seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having stayed at Vaiśālī for as long as was appropriate, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"All of you prepare yourselves; I wish to go to the Bamboo Grove."
He replied, “So be it.
He then prepared his robes and bowl and, accompanied by the great assembly as his attendants, followed the World-Honored One along the road through Vṛji until they reached that Bamboo Grove.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Viśāṭhya who, hearing that the Buddha had gone with a great assembly to this Bamboo Grove, reflected silently to himself:

"This śramaṇa Gautama’s fame and virtue have spread throughout the four quarters; he is endowed with the ten titles. Among devas, Śakras, Brahmās, Māras, or celestial Māras, śramaṇas, and brahmins, he has realized it for himself and teaches the Dharma to others. His words—whether superior, middling, or inferior—are all entirely true and correct; their meaning and flavor are profound and subtle, and his holy life is complete."
"A true person such as this should be visited and beheld.

At that time, the brahmin emerged from the bamboo thicket and approached the World-Honored One. Having exchanged greetings, he sat to one side. The World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having heard this, the brahmin was filled with joy and immediately invited the World-Honored One and the great assembly for a meal at his home the following day.
At that time, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that he had granted permission, the brahmin rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha, and returned home.
That very night, he prepared food and drink.
When the time arrived the following day, [the host thought], "Only the Noble One knows the proper time.
Then, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and, surrounded by the great assembly, proceeded to that house and sat upon the seat.
At that time, the brahmin prepared various kinds of delicious foods to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha.
When the meal was finished and the bowls had been removed, and after the ritual washing of hands was completed, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse for the sake of the brahmin:
"If one gives food and drink, clothing, and bedding to those who uphold the precepts, one shall obtain a great fruit."
This is a true companion, following from beginning to end;
wherever one goes, it is like a shadow following a form.
Therefore, plant roots of goodness to serve as provisions for future lives.
Merit is the foundation; by it sentient beings find peace.
Merit is protected by the heavens; its practice is free from peril, one encounters no calamities in life, and at death ascends to the celestial realms.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the brahmin, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that moment, grain was expensive and famine prevailed in that land, making it difficult to obtain alms. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Command all the bhikṣus currently present within this country to assemble in the lecture hall."
He replied, "So be it.
He then received the instructions and issued a proclamation that those from near and far should assemble at the lecture hall.
At that time, the great assembly within the kingdom had all gathered. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “The great assembly has already assembled; may the Holy One know the proper time.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, proceeded to the lecture hall, took his place upon the seat, and addressed the bhikṣus:

"In this land there is famine, and it is difficult to obtain alms by begging; you should each divide into groups and go, according to your acquaintances, to Vaiśālī and the kingdom of Vṛji to observe the rains retreat there, so that you may not suffer from want."
I shall dwell here in retreat together with Ānanda alone.
Why is this? I fear there may be a lack of necessities.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and immediately departed, leaving the Buddha and Ānanda alone.
Later, during the summer retreat, a sickness arose in the Buddha’s body; his entire frame was in pain. The Buddha thought to himself:

"Now that this illness has arisen, my whole body is in extreme pain, yet all my disciples are absent. If I were to enter parinirvāṇa now, it would not be appropriate for me. I shall now apply myself with diligence and through my own power preserve my life."
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from his quiet chamber and sat in a cool place.
Having seen this, Ānanda went to him with great haste and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Observing your venerable countenance now, it appears as though your illness has worsened."
Ānanda spoke again:

“The World-Honored One is ill; my heart is filled with dread and anxiety, so confounded that I lose all sense of direction. My breath has not yet ceased, and I still possess a small measure of clarity.”
He reflected silently:

"The Tathāgata has not yet entered parinirvāṇa; the Eye of the World has not yet been extinguished; the Great Dharma has not yet declined. For what reason does he now offer no instruction to his disciples?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Does the Saṃgha have any need of me? If there is anyone who says:
[they require something]"...
"I sustain the Saṃgha; I gather the Saṃgha.
Such a person ought to have instructions and commands over the assembly, yet the Tathāgata does not say:
"I sustain the assembly; I gather the assembly."
"How could I ever issue commands to the assembly?
Ānanda! I have already completed my teaching on both the internal and external; to the very end, I never claimed that what I had seen was fully realized."
"I am already old, nearly eighty years of age.
It is like an old cart that, through skillful means of repair, can still reach its destination.

My body is likewise; by the power of skillful means, I have managed to prolong my life for a short while. Through my own strength and diligence, I endure this painful sensation and, without entertaining any perceptions, enter the state of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti). At that time, my body is peaceful and secure, free from all affliction."
Therefore, Ānanda, you should be a lamp unto yourself, a lamp unto the Dharma, and not rely on any other lamp;
you should take refuge in yourself, take refuge in the Dharma, and not take refuge in anything else.
How is it that one should kindle oneself and kindle the Dharma, rather than being kindled by another;
that one should take refuge in oneself and take refuge in the Dharma, rather than taking refuge in another?
Ānanda! A bhikṣu contemplates the body internally with diligence and without slackening, maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness, and removing worldly greed and sorrow;

he contemplates the body externally, and contemplates the body both internally and externally, with diligence and without slackening, maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness, and removing worldly greed and sorrow.
The same applies to the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena.
This, Ānanda, is called being self-luminous,
luminous through the Dharma, and not luminous through another.
"You should take refuge in yourselves and take refuge in the Dharma; do not take refuge in anything else.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, whoever is able to practice this Dharma shall be my true disciple and the foremost among students."
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Let us go together to the Cāpāla Shrine. He replied:
“Very well,” [he replied].
The Tathāgata then rose, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went beneath a tree, where he said to Ānanda:
“Spread a seat; I am suffering from back pain and wish to rest here.”
He replied, "So be it," and immediately spread out the seats.
After the Tathāgata had sat down, Ānanda spread out a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“Those who cultivate the four bases of psychic power, practicing them extensively and constantly maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness, can, according to their own wish, attain non-death for a kalpa or more.”

Ānanda! The Buddha has already extensively practiced the four bases of psychic power and maintains them with focused mindfulness without forgetfulness. According to his own will, the Tathāgata could remain for another eon or more, dispelling the darkness of the world, bringing great benefit, and granting peace to devas and humans.
At that time, Ānanda remained silent and did not respond; though this was repeated three times, he remained silent once more.
At that moment, Ānanda was shrouded by Māra and, being clouded and lacking realization, he did not recognize the Buddha’s three manifestations of intent nor request [the teaching].
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"You should know that now is the time.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s intention, immediately rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Not far from the Buddha, he sat beneath a tree, reflecting with a tranquil mind.
Before long, Māra Pāpīyas approached the Buddha and said: "The Buddha’s mind is free from desire;
you may now enter parinirvāṇa. Now is the very time; it is fitting that you swiftly pass into extinction."
The Buddha said to Pāpīyas: "Cease! Cease!"

I know my time. The Tathāgata has not yet entered parinirvāṇa; he requires that my bhikṣus assemble. Furthermore, they are able to discipline themselves, being courageous and undaunted, having reached the state of peace and attained their own benefit. They shall act as guides for others, expounding the scriptural teachings and elucidating the meaning of the words and phrases.
If there should be any dissenting views, he is able to subdue them with the True Dharma;
furthermore, through supernormal transformations, he personally realizes and witnesses [the truth].
Yet, such disciples have not all yet assembled.
Furthermore, the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās are all likewise not yet assembled.
Now, I must extensively cultivate the holy life and propagate the factors of awakening, so that all devas and humans may universally behold these divine transformations.
Then, Māra Pāpīyas again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the past, when the Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment at the foot of the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree by the banks of the Nairañjanā River in Uruvelā, I went to the World-Honored One and entreated the Tathāgata to enter parinirvāṇa, saying:
'Now is the very time; it is fitting that you should quickly pass into extinction.'"
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately replied to me, saying:
"Stop! Stop!"

Pāpīyān! I know the time myself; the Tathāgata will not yet enter parinirvāṇa until my disciples have assembled, and even until gods and humans have witnessed my divine transformations before he attains extinction.
"The disciples of the Buddha have now assembled, and even gods and humans witness his spiritual transformations. Now is precisely the right time;
why not enter parinirvāṇa? The Buddha said, "Stop!"
"Stop, Pāpīyan!
The Buddha himself knows the time; he will not remain much longer. Three months from now, at his birthplace in Kuśinagara, between the twin śāla trees in the grove, he shall enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, Māra thought to himself:
"The Buddha does not speak falsely; he will surely enter parinirvāṇa now.
Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, he suddenly vanished from sight.
Not long after Māra had departed, the Buddha entered the samādhi of the *cāpāla* stūpa, relinquishing his natural life-span while maintaining his power over it.

At that moment, the earth shook violently; the people of the entire kingdom were struck with terror, their hair standing on end. The Buddha emitted a great radiance that illuminated all things without limit; even the most obscure and dark places were bathed in light, so that all could see one another.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Amidst the two paths of existence and non-existence, I now abandon all conditioned things;
Internally focused in samādhi, Like a bird emerging from its egg."

At that time, the venerable Ānanda was struck with awe and his hair stood on end; he hurried to the Buddha, prostrated himself at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How strange! How extraordinary!"
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that the earth shakes to such an extent? What are the causes and conditions for this?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Whenever there is an earthquake in the world, there are eight causes and conditions.

What are these eight? Now, the earth rests upon water; the water rests upon wind; and the wind rests upon space. When a great wind occasionally arises within space, the great waters are stirred; when the great waters are stirred, the entire earth shakes—this is the first cause.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

There are times when bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs who have attained the Path, and great, venerable devas perceive the nature of water as predominant and the nature of earth as slight; wishing to test their own power, they cause the entire earth to tremble—this is the second cause.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
When a bodhisattva first descends from the Tuṣita heaven into his mother’s womb, remaining focused and undisturbed, the earth shakes greatly; this is the third [sign].
Furthermore, Ānanda!
When the Bodhisattva first emerges from his mother’s womb, being born from her right side with focused mindfulness and without distraction, the entire earth trembles; this is the fourth [sign].
Furthermore, Ānanda!
When the Bodhisattva first attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, at that very moment the earth shakes violently; this is the fifth [sign].
Furthermore, Ānanda!

When the Buddha first attained the Way and turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma—which cannot be turned by Māras, celestial Māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, or worldlings—the entire earth shook; this is the sixth.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
When the Buddha’s teaching is about to conclude, he focuses his mind without distraction; as he wishes to relinquish his life-force, the entire earth trembles—this is the seventh [sign].
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder, the earth-element quakes; this is the eighth.
By these eight causes and conditions, the earth-element is made to tremble.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Unsurpassed Honored One among bipeds, The Great Śramaṇa who illuminates the world;
Ānanda requests the Teacher of Gods: For what cause and condition does the earth tremble?"
The Tathāgata utters a voice of compassion, A sound like that of the kalaviṅka bird;
Listen as I explain to you The cause by which the earth trembles.
The earth rests upon water, And water abides because of wind.
When the wind arises in the void, the earth shakes violently.
When bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs wish to test their power of supernatural feet,
the mountains, seas, hundreds of grasses and trees, and the great earth all tremble.
Śakra, Brahmā, and all the honored devas intended to move the earth;
the spirits and deities of the mountains and seas caused the great earth to tremble.
The Bodhisattva, the Honored One among bipeds, has already perfected the marks of a hundred merits.
When he first entered his mother’s womb, the earth shook greatly.
For ten months he dwelt within her womb, like a dragon lying upon a fine mat;
when he was finally born from her right side, the earth then shook greatly once more.
When the Buddha was a youth, he extinguished the fetters of the causal conditions;
having attained the immeasurable victory of the Way, the earth shook greatly.
He ascended to the state of the Immortal and turned the Wheel of Dharma within the Deer Park.
When the power of the Way subdues the Māras, the earth shakes greatly.
When the celestial Māras come repeatedly to entreat him, urging the Buddha to enter parinirvāṇa,
the Buddha relinquishes his life-force, and the earth then shakes greatly.
The Honored One among Men, the Great Guide, the last of all seers and gods, having attained extinction while remaining unshakable, the earth then shook violently.
The One of Pure Eyes explained the various conditions; the earth shook through eight causes.
"There is this, and there is also more; at that time, both the earth and the heavens trembled.
*The Buddha-spoken Dīrgha Āgama*, Fascicle Two.
*The Buddha-spoken Dīrgha Āgama*, Fascicle Three.
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
In the second part of the *Caryā-sūtra*,
the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
“There are eight assemblies in the world.

What are the eight? First is the assembly of kṣatriyas; second is the assembly of brāhmaṇas; third is the assembly of householders; fourth is the assembly of śramaṇas; fifth is the assembly of the Four Great Kings; sixth is the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods; seventh is the assembly of Māra; and eighth is the assembly of Brahmā.”

I recall this: "In the past, there were countless instances of me coming and going, sitting and rising, and conversing with assemblies of kṣatriyas; through the power of concentration born of diligence, I was able to manifest myself wherever I wished."
"He possesses a beautiful complexion, yet my complexion surpasses his;
he possesses a wondrous voice, yet my voice surpasses his;
he declines when I retreat, but I do not decline when he retreats."
"Whatever he is able to speak, I too am able to speak;
whatever he is unable to speak, I too am able to speak."— Ānanda!

I extensively expounded the Dharma for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; having done so, I immediately vanished from that place, yet they did not know whether I was a deva or a human.
In this manner, I went as far as the assembly of the Brahmā heavens, making countless journeys back and forth and extensively expounding the Dharma, while no one could discern who I was.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary,
World-Honored One!”
"It is truly unprecedented that you are able to accomplish such a thing.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda, such a subtle and rare Dharma as this— "
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!
This is unprecedented; only a Tathāgata is able to accomplish such a dharma."
Again, he addressed Ānanda:

“The Tathāgata is able to know the arising, abiding, and ceasing of feeling; the arising, abiding, and ceasing of perception; and the arising, abiding, and ceasing of volitional formations. This is a most wonderful, marvelous, and unprecedented quality of the Tathāgata, which you should receive and uphold.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"Let us go together to the Fragrant Stūpa; there, beneath a tree, spread a seat and sit.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Various bhikṣus have appeared on both sides of the Perfumed Stūpa; command them all to assemble in the lecture hall.
Ānanda received these instructions and proclaimed the order for a general assembly.
Ānanda then addressed the Buddha:
“The great assembly has gathered; may the Noble One know the time.
At that moment, the World-Honored One proceeded to the lecture hall, took his seat, and addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should know that I have personally realized this Dharma and attained supreme perfect enlightenment, namely:”

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.

"You all should, within this Dharma, be harmonious and respectful, refraining from dispute. Having received it from the same teacher, like water and milk mixed together, you should diligently study within my Dharma, mutually kindling it and mutually delighting in it."
"Monks, you should know that regarding these teachings, I have realized them for myself and manifested them to others, namely:
the *Sūtra*, the *Geya*, the *Vyākaraṇa*, the *Gāthā*, the *Udāna*, the *Itivṛttaka*, the *Jātaka*, the *Vaipulya*, the *Adbhutadharma*, the *Avadāna*, and the *Upadeśa*."
"You all should properly receive and uphold this, weigh and discern it, and practice accordingly according to its meaning. Why is this?
Before long, after three months from now, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa."

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they were all struck with amazement; overcome by desolation and confusion, they threw themselves upon the ground and cried out at the top of their voices: "How swift this is!"
The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa;
how painful this is! The Eye of the World has been extinguished.
"In this matter, we have already suffered a long-term decline.
Some bhikṣus wept and wailed, rolling about on the ground and sobbing uncontrollably; they were like severed snakes writhing and turning in confusion, not knowing what to rely upon.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Cease, all of you, and do not harbor grief or sorrow.
Among heaven, earth, humans, and things, there is none that is born which does not end. To wish for conditioned phenomena to remain unchanging—such a thing is impossible."

"I have also previously taught that what is loved and cherished is impermanent; there is separation from those with whom one has met, for the body does not belong to oneself, and life does not endure long.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I am now sovereign, having reached the place of peace and security;"
Gathering the great assembly, he spoke this meaning for them:
"I am old, and my remaining life is but little;
what was to be done has been accomplished, and now I shall relinquish my lifespan."
Be mindful and free from negligence; let the bhikṣu be complete in his precepts.
Restraining his own mind through concentration, he guards his heart.
If one is without negligence regarding my Dharma, [he shall attain liberation].
"It can extinguish the root of suffering and bring an end to birth, old age, and death.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Why is it that I now exhort you?"
The Māra Pāpīyas has just now entreated me, saying:
"The Buddha’s mind is free from desire; you may enter parinirvāṇa. Now is precisely the right time; it would be fitting for you to pass into extinction quickly."
I said: "Stop! Stop!"
"Pāpīyan! The Buddha knows the time himself; he requires that my bhikṣus assemble, and even that the devas everywhere behold this miraculous transformation.
Pāpīyan spoke again:
"In the past, when the Buddha first attained the Way of Buddhahood by the banks of the Nairañjanā River at Uruvilvā, beneath the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree, I said to the Buddha:
'The Buddha's mind is free from desire; you may enter parinirvāṇa. Now is precisely the right time; it would be fitting for you to quickly pass into extinction.'"
At that time, the Tathāgata replied to me, saying:
"Stop! Stop!"
Pāpīyān! I know the time myself.

The Tathāgata has not yet entered parinirvāṇa; it must wait until my disciples have assembled, and even until gods and humans have witnessed my supernatural transformations, before I enter parinirvāṇa.
"Now the disciples of the Tathāgata have assembled, and even the devas and humans have witnessed the divine transformations; now is precisely the time, and it is fitting that I enter parinirvāṇa.
I said: "Stop!"
"Stop, Pāpīyan!
The Buddha knows the time himself; he will not remain much longer, for in three months from now he shall enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, Māra thought to himself:
"The Buddha does not speak falsely; he will surely enter parinirvāṇa now.
Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, he suddenly vanished from sight.
Not long after Māra had departed, [the Buddha], at the Cāpāla Stūpa, entered the samādhi of concentrated mind, relinquishing his natural life-span while maintaining his supernormal longevity.

At that moment, the earth shook violently; gods and humans were struck with terror, their hair standing on end. The Buddha emitted a great radiance that illuminated everything boundlessly; even the most obscure and dark places were not left without the benefit of this light, so that all were able to see one another.
At that time, I spoke in verse:
"Between the two paths of existence and non-existence, I now renounce the conditioned;
Internally focused in samādhi, like a bird emerging from its egg."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will remain for a kalpa and not enter parinirvāṇa; out of compassion for sentient beings, may you bring benefit to devas and humans.”
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not respond. When he had been asked this three times, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you have faith in the Tathāgata’s path of perfect enlightenment?"
He replied: "Indeed! It is true."
The Buddha said:
"If you have faith, for what reason have you come three times to disturb me?
You have heard this directly from the Buddha; you have received this directly from the Buddha:"

Those who are able to cultivate the four bases of psychic power, practicing them extensively and constantly mindful without forgetfulness, can, according to their own wishes, attain immortality for a kalpa or more.

The Buddha has already extensively practiced the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), maintaining them with focused mindfulness without forgetfulness. Should he so desire, he could remain for more than an eon without passing away, dispelling the darkness of the world, bringing great benefit, and granting peace to gods and humans.
At that time, why did you not entreat him again so that he would not enter parinirvāṇa?

A second hearing might still have been possible; yet even after hearing it a third time, you still did not exhort him to remain for one kalpa or more, to dispel the darkness of the world and bring great benefit, so that devas and humans might attain peace.
Now, as you speak these words, are you not indeed foolish?
When I manifested the three signs three times, you remained silent all three times. Why did you not then reply to me:
"May the Tathāgata remain for one kalpa, or even more than one kalpa, to dispel the darkness of the world and bring great benefit to many"?
"Stop, Ānanda! I have already renounced my life; it has been cast off and spat out. It is impossible that the Tathāgata would go against his own word."
"It is like a wealthy and noble elder who spits food upon the ground; would anyone ever be willing to go back and take that food up again? He replied, "No."
“The Tathāgata is likewise; having already relinquished and vomited it out, how could he ever again consume his own words?

The Buddha told Ānanda, “Let us go together to the village of Āmrapālī. They immediately prepared their robes and bowls and, accompanied by the great assembly as attendants, followed the World-Honored One. Traveling by way of Vṛji, they arrived at the village of Āmrapālī and stayed in a mountain forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the great assembly concerning precept, concentration, and wisdom.
By cultivating the precepts one attains concentration and gains a great fruit;
by cultivating concentration one attains wisdom and gains a great fruit.
Cultivating wisdom and purifying the mind, one attains equal liberation and exhausts the three outflows—the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, and the outflow of ignorance.
Having attained liberation, the knowledge of liberation arises:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having stayed as long as was appropriate at the village of Āmrapālī, addressed Ānanda:
"All of you, prepare yourselves!"
"You should go to the villages of Campā, Kalandaka, and Bālīva, and proceed to the city of Bhoganagara. He replied, "So be it!"

He immediately prepared his robes and bowl and, accompanied by the great assembly as his attendants, followed the World-Honored One on the road from Vṛji, gradually arriving at another city. To the north of the city of Bhūmi, he stayed in the Śiṃśapā Forest.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now teach you the four great teachings; listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well. The bhikṣus said, "So be it!"
“World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it. “What are the four?”
If there is a bhikṣu who speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!
In that village, that city, or that country, I have personally heard this from the Buddha and have personally received this teaching."

Those who hear this from him should neither disbelieve it nor disparage it; rather, they should investigate its truth or falsehood across various sutras and examine its origins and conclusions in accordance with the Vinaya and the Dharma.
If what they say is not in accordance with the Sūtras, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Dharma, you should say to them:
"The Buddha did not speak this; you have received it erroneously! Why is that?..."
"I rely upon the various sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma; what you have previously said contradicts the Dharma.
Worthy sir! Do not uphold it, do not preach it to others, but rather abandon it."
If what they say is based on the Sūtras, based on the Vinaya, and based on the Dharma, you should say to them:
"What you have said is truly the teaching of the Buddha. Why is this so?"
"I rely upon the sūtras, the vinaya, and the dharma; what you have previously said is in accord with the dharma.
Worthy one! You should receive and uphold it, explain it extensively for others, and take care not to abandon it."
"This is the first great teaching. Furthermore, a bhikṣu might say:
'In that village, that city, or that country, I personally heard from a harmonious Saṃgha of learned elders; I personally received this Dharma, this Vinaya, and this instruction.'"

Those who hear this from him should neither disbelieve it nor disparage it; rather, they should investigate its truth or falsity across the various sūtras, examining its origins and conclusions according to the Dharma and the Vinaya. If what he says is not in accordance with the sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Dharma, they should say to him:
"The Buddha did not speak this; you must have heard and received it erroneously from that assembly!"
Why is this so? I rely on the various sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma; what you previously said contradicts the Dharma.
Worthy sir!
"Do not hold onto this; do not speak of it to others; you should abandon it.
If what he says is based on the Sūtras, based on the Vinaya, and based on the Dharma, you should say to him:
"What you have said is truly the word of the Buddha. Why is that?"
"I rely upon the various sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma; what you have previously said is in accord with the Dharma.
Worthy one! You should receive and uphold it, explain it extensively for others, and take care not to abandon it."
"This is the second great teaching. Furthermore, a bhikṣu might say:

'In that village, that city, or that country, there were many bhikṣus who upheld the Dharma, upheld the Vinaya, and upheld the discipline; from them I personally heard this, and from them I personally received this Dharma, this Vinaya, and this instruction.'"

Those who hear this from him should neither disbelieve it nor disparage it; rather, they should investigate its truth or falsehood across the various sūtras and examine its origins and conclusions in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
If what they say is not in accordance with the Sūtras, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Dharma, one should say to them:
"The Buddha did not speak this; you have heard and received it erroneously from among the many bhikṣus!"
Why is this so? I rely on the various sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma; what you previously said contradicts the Dharma.
Worthy sir!
"You must not accept and uphold it, nor should you speak of it to others; you should abandon it.
If what he says is based on the Sūtras, based on the Vinaya, and based on the Dharma, you should say to him:
"What you have said is truly the word of the Buddha. Why is that? Because..."
"I rely upon the various sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma; what you have previously said is in accord with the Dharma.
Worthy sir! You should receive and uphold it, explain it extensively for others, and take care not to abandon it."
"This is the third great teaching. Furthermore, a bhikṣu speaks thus:

'In that village, that city, or that country, there was a certain bhikṣu who upheld the Dharma, upheld the Vinaya, and upheld the discipline; from him I personally heard, and I personally received this Dharma, this Vinaya, and this instruction.'"

Those who hear this from him should neither disbelieve it nor disparage it; rather, they should investigate its truth or falsehood across all the sūtras and examine its origins and conclusions in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
If what is said is not in accordance with the Sūtras, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not in accordance with the Dharma, one should say to them:
"The Buddha did not speak this; have you perhaps heard it incorrectly from a certain bhikṣu?"
Why is this so? I rely on the various sūtras, on the Dharma, and on the Vinaya; what you have previously said contradicts the Dharma, O worthy one!
"You must not uphold this, nor should you speak it to others; you should abandon it.
If what he says is based on the Sūtras, based on the Vinaya, and based on the Dharma, you should say to him:
"What you have said is truly the word of the Buddha. Why is that?"
"I rely on the various sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Dharma; what you have previously said is in accord with the Dharma.
Worthy one! You should diligently receive and uphold it, explain it extensively for others, and take care not to abandon it."
"This is the fourth great teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having stayed in the city of Pāvā for as long as was appropriate, addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Let us go together to the city of Bhavā.
Ānanda replied, "So be it!"
He immediately prepared his robes and bowl and, accompanied by the great assembly as attendants, followed the World-Honored One on the road from Malla to the city of Pāvā, arriving at the Jeta Grove.

At that time, there was a son of a craftsman named Cunda; hearing that the Buddha had come from Malla to this city, he immediately dressed himself in fine attire and went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sitting to one side.

Then, the Buddha gradually taught the Dharma to Cunda for his correct transformation, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, Cunda felt faith and joy, and immediately invited the World-Honored One to take a meal at his home the following day.
At that time, the Buddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Cunda, knowing that the Buddha had granted his permission, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and returned home.
That very night, he prepared the meal; when the time arrived the following day, he thought, "Only the Holy One knows the proper time."
