At that time, the World-Honored One, wearing his dharma robes and holding his alms bowl, proceeded to the house surrounded by the great assembly and took his seat.

Thereupon, Cunda promptly prepared food and drink to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha; he specially boiled *candana* tree mushrooms—a rare delicacy prized by the world—and presented them exclusively to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Cunda:
"Do not give this bowl to the bhikṣus.
Having received these instructions, Cunda did not dare to give it away.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu among the assembly who had entered the religious life in his later years; while at his seat, he took [his food] with an extra vessel.

Then, when Cunda saw that the assembly had finished eating and the bowls and utensils had been cleared away, and the water for washing had been served, he immediately addressed the Buddha in verse before him, saying:
"I venture to ask the Great Sage of Wisdom, The Perfectly Awakened One, the Honored One among bipeds."
"One who is well-restrained and perfectly disciplined—how many such śramaṇas are there in the world?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Regarding what you have asked, there are four kinds of śramaṇas."
As inclinations differ from one another, you should distinguish them:
first, those who excel in the practice of the Path; second, those who skillfully explain the meaning of the Path;
third, those who live their lives in reliance upon the Path; and fourth, those who defile the Path.
What is called the excellence of the Path?
Skillfully explaining the meaning of the Path, living in accordance with the Path—how could one who practices the Path defile it?
Being able to cross over the thorns of affection and craving, one enters Nirvāṇa without doubt.
Transcending the paths of gods and men, he proclaims this path as supreme.
Skillfully understanding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he speaks of the path free from defilement;
with loving-kindness and benevolence, he resolves the doubts of the multitude—this is what it means to skillfully teach the path.
Skillfully expounding the verses of the Dharma, living in accordance with the Path;
gazing afar toward the stainless field, this is called "living by relying on the Path.
Internally harboring deceit and wickedness, while outwardly appearing pure and white—
Deceptive and lacking sincerity—this is what defiles the Path.
How can good and evil coexist?
When purity and impurity are mixed, they appear outwardly similar to the eye, like copper coated with gold.
When worldly people see this, they say, "The disciples of the Noble One possess such wisdom;
others do not all share this. Do not abandon your pure faith!
A single person may uphold the great assembly, yet be turbid within while appearing pure without.
He manifests the suppression of wicked and depraved traces, yet in reality harbors dissipation.
Do not judge by outward appearance; upon first sight, one may easily become intimate and respectful.
He manifests the suppression of wicked and depraved traces, yet in reality harbors dissipation.
At that time, Cunda took a small seat and sat before the Buddha; the Buddha gradually taught him the Dharma.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, the great assembly surrounded him as he returned with his attendants.
Stopping beneath a single tree along the way, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"I suffer from back pain; you may spread out a seat. He replied:
"Very well," he replied,
and immediately spread out a seat for the World-Honored One to rest.
Then, Ānanda also spread out a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Did Cunda have no sense of regret just now?
If he did, from what cause did it arise?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“Cunda’s offering brings no merit or benefit. Why is this so?
"The Tathāgata will take parinirvāṇa after eating his final meal at his house.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not speak such words!"
Do not speak such words!

Now, Cunda has gained great benefit; he has obtained long life, physical beauty, strength, and a good reputation; he will possess abundant wealth and treasures in this life, and after death, he will be reborn in heaven, where all his desires will be spontaneously fulfilled.

Why is this? Because one who can provide food when the Buddha first attains enlightenment and one who can provide food when the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa—these two merits are exactly equal and without distinction.
"You may now go and say to Cunda:

'I have heard this directly from the Buddha and received this instruction directly from the Buddha: "Cunda, by providing this meal, you have now obtained great benefit and attained a great fruit of retribution."'"
Then Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, went at once to that place and said to Cunda:

“I have heard this directly from the Buddha; I have received this teaching directly from the Buddha: ‘Cunda, by providing this meal, you shall now obtain great benefit and attain a great fruit of retribution.’”

Why is this so? Because the merit of the Buddha being able to eat food when he first attained the Way and the merit of his being able to eat food when he was about to enter parinirvāṇa are exactly equal and no different.
After Cunda had finished eating the meal, he first heard these words:
"The Tathāgata’s illness is extremely grave; his life-force is now about to end.
Although he ate the sandalwood ear-ornaments, his ailment has only increased further."
Traveling on the road while afflicted by illness, he gradually approached the city of Kuśinagara.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat, walked forward a short distance, and went beneath a tree, where he again addressed Ānanda:
"My back pains me greatly; you may spread out a seat."
He replied, "So be it!
He immediately spread out a seat, and the Tathāgata sat down to rest.
After Ānanda had prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side.

At that time, there was a disciple of an arhat named Puṇyavanta who was traveling from the city of Kauśāmbī toward the city of Pāvā. On the road, he saw the Buddha beneath a tree; his appearance was upright and serene, his faculties were tranquil and composed, and he had attained the supreme tranquility of a perfectly disciplined mind.
He was like a great dragon, or like clear water—pure and free from defilement. Upon seeing him, [the Buddha] rejoiced, and a virtuous mind arose within him.
He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is truly extraordinary that those who have left the household life dwell in pure places and delight in secluded abodes.

Once, when my Teacher was staying under a tree by the roadside between the cities of Kauśāmbī and Pāvā, sitting in silent meditation, five hundred chariots passed by his side; though he was awake, he neither heard nor saw the sound of the chariots.
At that time, someone came and asked my teacher,
"Did you see the many carriages that passed by just now? He replied:
"I have not seen it.
He asked again:
"Have you heard it?"
He replied, "I have not heard it.
He asked again:
"Are you here, or are you elsewhere? He replied:
"Here it is! He asked again, "Have you awakened?"
He replied, “I am awake! He asked again:
"Are you awake or asleep?
He replied, "I am not asleep!"
The man thought silently to himself:
"How extraordinary! This renunciant is so single-mindedly focused that he does not even hear the thundering roar of the chariot."
He then said to my teacher:
"Just now five hundred chariots passed along this road; even the rattling sound of those chariots could not be heard by me, so how could anyone else have heard it?"
He immediately paid his respects and departed with joy.
The Buddha said to Pukkusāti: “I now ask you;

answer as you see fit. Between being awakened by the rattling of a multitude of chariots yet not hearing them, and being awakened by thunder shaking heaven and earth yet not hearing it—which would be more difficult?”
Fuguī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The sound of a million chariots—how could it ever equal thunder and lightning?
It would not be difficult to fail to hear the sound of chariots; rather, it is truly difficult to remain asleep and not hear the thunder that shakes heaven and earth.”
The Buddha told Puṇyavanta:
"Once, while traveling through the village of Āvanti, I stayed in a thatched hut.
At that time, a strange cloud suddenly arose, accompanied by thunder and lightning, which struck down four bulls and two brothers who were plowing. A great crowd of people gathered there."

At that time, I emerged from my grass hut and was walking to and fro in meditation. A person from among that great assembly came to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, and followed me as I walked. Knowing the reason, I asked him intentionally:
"What is this great assembly gathered for?"
The man then asked:
"Where has the Buddha been until now?
Is he awake or asleep?"
He replied: "I am here! At this time, I have not slept."

That person also marveled at having attained such a rare concentration as that of the Buddha; though thunder and lightning crashed with a roar that deafened heaven and earth, he remained alone in silent meditative absorption, awake and unaware of the sound.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Just now, strange clouds suddenly arose, accompanied by thunder and lightning strikes that killed four bulls and two brothers who were plowing. That great gathering of people was precisely for this reason."
The man’s heart was filled with joy, and he immediately attained the bliss of Dharma; he prostrated before the Buddha and departed.
At that time, Pukkusāti, clad in two yellow woolen cloths worth hundreds of thousands, rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I now offer these cloths to the World-Honored One; I pray that you will graciously accept them.”
The Buddha told Pukkusa:
"Give one set of robes to me, and give one to Ānanda.
At that time, Pukkusa, following the Buddha’s instruction, offered one to the Tathāgata and gave one to Ānanda.
Out of compassion for him, the Buddha accepted [the gift].
Then, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, Puṇyavanta sat to one side. The Buddha gradually taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him:

he spoke on generosity, on morality, and on rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desires are a great affliction, impure, and defiling, that the higher outflows are obstacles, and that the way of escape is supreme.

At that time, the Buddha, knowing that Puṇyavanta’s mind was joyful and supple, free from the hindrances and entanglements, and easily capable of being transformed, followed the constant law of all Buddhas and immediately preached to him the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

At that time, Puṇyavanta’s faith became pure, like a clean, white cloth that easily takes on dye; immediately upon his seat, he was freed from dust and removed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within him. Having seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma, he became firmly established in certainty, no longer falling into the evil realms, and having achieved fearlessness, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha!"
I take refuge in the Dharma!
I take refuge in the Saṃgha!

May the Tathāgata grant me permission to become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) within the True Dharma. From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking intoxicants. May the World-Honored One grant me permission to become a lay follower within the True Dharma.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If you travel to convert beings and should arrive at the city of Pāvā, I only pray that you would deign to visit my humble village.”

Why is this? It is because I wish to offer all that my household possesses—food and drink, bedding and seats, clothing, and medicinal decoctions—to the World-Honored One; once the World-Honored One has accepted them, my household shall attain peace and security.
The Buddha said, "What you have said is excellent! Then,
the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to Puṇyavanta, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him.
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and departed with joy.
Not long after he had gone, Ānanda sought out yellow silk and offered it to the Tathāgata; out of compassion, the Tathāgata accepted it and draped it over his body.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s countenance was composed and serene, his majestic radiance blazing forth, his faculties pure, and his complexion harmonious and joyful.
Having seen this, Ānanda thought silently to himself:
"In the twenty-five years since I began serving the Buddha, I have never before seen the Blessed One's countenance so luminous and radiant as it is now."
He immediately rose from his seat, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since I have served you for twenty-five years, I have never before seen the Buddha’s radiance as it is now. I wonder what the cause of this may be?"
"I wish to hear its meaning!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are two causes and conditions by which the Tathāgata’s radiance and complexion differ from the ordinary."
First, when the Buddha first attained the Way, achieving supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment;
second, when he was about to enter extinction, relinquishing his life and entering parinirvāṇa.
"Ānanda! Because of these two conditions, his radiance and complexion are extraordinary.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The golden robe is radiant and pleasing, fine, soft, and exceedingly pure;
offered to the World-Honored One by one of noble merit, its white tuft of hair shines like snow.
The Buddha then commanded Ānanda:
"I am thirsty and wish to drink; bring me some water.
Ānanda replied, "Just now five hundred wagons crossed at the upper reaches, so the water is turbid and not yet clear; it may be used for washing the feet, but it is unfit for drinking."
Thus he commanded three times: "Ānanda!
Bring some water here."
Ānanda said, “The Kakutstha River is not far from here; its water is clear and cool, fit for drinking and also for bathing.

At that time, there was a spirit dwelling on Mount Himavat who had deep faith in the Buddha’s Way; he immediately filled his bowl with eight kinds of pure water and offered it to the World-Honored One.
Out of compassion for him, the Buddha immediately accepted it and spoke in verse:
“The Buddha, with his eightfold voice, Commands Ānanda to fetch water:
'I am thirsty and wish to drink now; Having drunk, I shall proceed to Kuśinagara.'"
With a voice supple, harmonious, and elegant, his words gladden the hearts of the multitude.
Attending upon the Buddha at his side, he immediately addressed the World-Honored One:
"Just now there were five hundred chariots that cut across the stream to reach the other shore."
This water is turbid; I fear drinking it would not be good for my body.
Not far from here is the River of Retention (*Ghṛta-nadī*); its water is exquisite, exceedingly clear and cool.
Go there to take some to drink, and you may also bathe your body therein.
In the Snowy Mountains there is a spirit who offered water to the Tathāgata;
having drunk it, his majestic power became strong, and he walked with the stride of a lion among the assembly.
That water was the dwelling place of divine nāgas; it was clear and limpid, free from turbidity or impurity.
"The Holy Countenance is like the Snowy Mountains, calmly crossing the Kakutthā River.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the Kakutthā River; having drunk and bathed there, he departed with the assembly.
Stopping midway beneath a tree, he addressed Cunda, saying:
"Take four folds of your saṃghāṭī robe and spread them out; I am suffering from back pain and wish to rest for a moment."
Cunda, having received these instructions, completed the preparation; the Buddha sat upon it.
After Cunda had paid his respects, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to enter parinirvāṇa!"
"I wish to enter parinirvāṇa!
The Buddha told him,
"Know that now is the time."
Thereupon, Cunda entered parinirvāṇa right before the Buddha, and the Buddha then spoke in verse:
“The Buddha proceeded to the Kakutstha River, Cool and free from turbidity or impurity;
The Honored One among Men entered the water, To bathe and cross to the other shore.”
The foremost leader of the great assembly instructed Cunda:
"I am now utterly exhausted; you must quickly spread out bedding.
Cunda immediately received these instructions and folded his robe into four layers to spread it out.
Once the Tathāgata had ceased speaking, Cunda sat before him and addressed the World-Honored One:
"I wish to attain parinirvāṇa; in a place free from both love and hatred, I shall now go to that realm."
The Most Victorious One, an ocean of immeasurable merit, said to him:
"What you must do has been accomplished; now you should know that the time has come.
Having seen that the Buddha had granted his permission, Cunda redoubled his diligent efforts.
"The practice of cessation leaves nothing remaining, like a lamp whose flame is extinguished when the oil is spent.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and said to him:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, what shall be the method for the funeral rites?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Be silent for now and attend to your own duties; these lay devotees will gladly perform them themselves.
At that time, Ānanda again made his request three times.
"After the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, what shall be the method for his burial? The Buddha said,
"One who wishes to know the method of burial should follow that of a Cakravartin King."
Ānanda asked again,
"What is the funeral rite for a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"According to the funeral rites for a noble king, one first bathes his body with fragrant water, wraps it completely in new *karpāsa* cloth, and then layers five hundred sheets of fine cotton fabric over it in succession."

Having filled the inner golden coffin with sesame oil, they lifted the golden coffin and placed it within the second, larger iron outer coffin; next, a sandalwood coffin was layered over the outside. They piled various famous incenses upon it, covered it thickly, and performed the cremation.

Having completed the collection of the śarīra, he erected a stūpa at a crossroads, with a banner-pole and suspended silk streamers, so that all travelers throughout the land might see the stūpa of the Dharma King, yearn for his righteous transformation, and receive manifold benefits.

Ānanda! When you wish to bury me, first bathe my body with fragrant water, wrap it completely with new *karpāsa* cloth, and then wrap it again in succession with five hundred layers of fine cotton fabric.

Having filled the inner golden coffin with sesame oil, they lifted it and placed it within the second, larger iron outer coffin; next, a sandalwood-fragrant coffin was layered over it on the outside. They piled up various famous incenses, covered them thickly, and performed the cremation.

Having completed the collection of the śarīras, he erected a stūpa at the crossroads, with a bannered *yaṣṭi* and suspended silk streamers, so that all passersby might behold the Buddha’s stūpa, yearn for the Tathāgata’s Dharma-kingly transformation, obtain merit and benefit in this life, and ascend to heaven after death.
At that time, the World-Honored One, contemplating this matter further, spoke in verse:
“Ānanda rose from his seat, And kneeling with long-drawn knees, addressed the World-Honored One:
‘After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, By what dharma should he be enshrined?’”
“Ānanda, you should remain silent for now; reflect upon your own practice.
The faithful lay devotees within the kingdom shall naturally take pleasure in performing it.
After Ānanda had made his request three times, the Buddha spoke of the funeral rites for a wheel-turning monarch.
Desiring to enshrine the body of the Tathāgata, they wrap it in layers of cloth and place it within inner and outer coffins;
at the crossroads, they erect stupas and temples for the benefit of all sentient beings,
so that all who pay homage shall obtain immeasurable merit.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are four kinds of people in the world for whom one ought to erect a stūpa and make offerings of incense, flowers, silken canopies, and music.
What are these four?"
First, a Tathāgata may have a stūpa erected; second, a pratyekabuddha; third, a śrāvaka; and fourth, a cakravartin king. Ānanda!
"These four kinds of persons should have stupas erected for them, and they should be honored with offerings of incense, flowers, silk canopies, and music.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The Buddha deserves the foremost stupa; The Pratyekabuddhas and the Śrāvakas..."
And the wheel-turning sage kings who rule over the four quarters—
these four are worthy of offerings, as recorded by the Tathāgata:
the stupas of the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Śrāvakas, and the wheel-turning kings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"Let us go together to the city of Kuśinagara, to the space between the twin śāla trees of the Mallas. He replied:
“Very well! he replied, and immediately accompanied the great assembly as they surrounded the World-Honored One and proceeded along the road.

A certain brahmin was traveling from the city of Kuśinagara toward the city of Pāvā; midway, he saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s countenance was upright and handsome, and his faculties were serene and composed. Having seen him, he rejoiced and a virtuous mind arose within him spontaneously. He approached the Buddha’s location, and after exchanging greetings, he stood to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The village where I dwell is not far from here; I only wish that Gautama would stay there overnight, and after having eaten in the early morning, proceed to the city.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Stop! For now!"
"Stop! You have already made an offering to me.
At that time, the brahmin earnestly entreated him three times, but the Buddha answered as before and further addressed the brahmin:
“Ānanda is behind you; you may speak to him.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the brahmin went to Ānanda. After exchanging greetings, he stood to one side and said to Ānanda:
“The village where I reside is not far from here. I wish to invite Gautama to stay there overnight; after the morning meal, we shall proceed to the city.”
Ānanda replied, "Stop! Stop!"
"Brahmin! You have already received my acceptance.
The brahmin entreated him again, persisting until the third time, and Ānanda replied:
"The time is already hot, and that village is far distant; the World-Honored One is utterly exhausted, so it would not be right to trouble him further.
At that time, having contemplated this matter, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"With eyes purified, he proceeds on the road; Exhausted, he heads toward the twin trees."
The brahmin saw the Buddha from afar and quickly approached to bow his head.
"My village is now near; out of compassion, please stay for one night.
At dawn I shall provide a modest offering, after which you may proceed to that city."
"O Brahmin, my body is weary; the road is long and I cannot proceed further.
The custodian of the collection is behind me; you may stay here and convey my message.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, he immediately went to where Ānanda was.
"I only pray that you will come to my village, and after eating your morning meal, depart.
Ānanda said, "Stop, stop! It is too hot at this time; we cannot go together.
Though he requested three times, his wish was not granted; he was distressed and found no joy.
Alas! These conditioned phenomena are ever-shifting and do not abide;
now, between the twin trees, I shall extinguish my outflow-free body.
Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—all shall return to extinction.
"Impermanent and devoid of discernment, like fire consuming a mountain forest.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the city of Kuśinagara and proceeded toward his birthplace between the twin śāla trees of the Mallas, where he addressed Ānanda:
"For the Tathāgata, prepare a couch between these twin trees, with the head toward the north and the face toward the west."
"Why is this so? My Dharma shall spread and endure for a long time in the northern regions. He replied:
“Certainly! he replied, and immediately spread out the seat, arranging it with the head toward the north.
At that time, the World-Honored One himself folded his saṃghāṭī robe fourfold, lay down on his right side like a lion king, and rested with one foot upon the other.
At that time, all the spirits and deities between the twin trees who had deep faith in the Buddha scattered out-of-season flowers upon the ground.
Then, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"These tree-spirits have offered me out-of-season flowers; yet this is not an offering to the Tathāgata."
Ānanda said: "What is called 'making offerings to the Tathāgata'?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"One who can receive the Dharma and practice the Dharma is what is called making an offering to the Tathāgata.
Contemplating this meaning, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The Buddha lies between the twin trees, Reclining with a mind undisturbed; The one who can receive the Dharma and Practice the Dharma is called an offering to the Tathāgata."
The tree deity, with a pure mind, scattered flowers over the Buddha.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is called 'making offerings'?"
To receive the Dharma and practice it, and to offer the flower of awakening—this is true worship.
Even scattering golden lotuses like wheels before the Buddha does not constitute the highest offering;
to realize that the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are selfless is called the foremost offering.
At that time, Brahmāna was standing before the Buddha fanning him with a fan.
The Buddha said, "Step aside; do not stand before me.
Then, Ānanda thought to himself silently:
"This Brahmana has always remained by the Buddha's side, providing for all his needs; he should have revered the Tathāgata with never-wearying devotion.
Now, at this final moment when he requires his care, why does the Buddha command him to withdraw? What could be the reason for this?"
Thereupon, Ānanda adjusted his robes, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Brahmāna has always remained by the Buddha's side, providing for all his needs; he should revere the Tathāgata, gazing upon him without ever being satiated."
"Now, at this final moment, he required someone to attend to him, yet you were ordered to withdraw; what could be the reason for this?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"For twelve yojanas outside this city of Kuśinagara, there are the dwellings of the great devas, with not a single empty space."
All these great deities resented this bhikṣu standing before the Buddha, thinking:

"Now that the Buddha is about to enter final nirvana, we deities hope for a single audience with him; yet this bhikṣu possesses such great majestic virtue that his radiance overshadows us, preventing us from drawing near to pay our respects, offer worship, and present offerings."
"Ānanda! For this reason, I have commanded that he be sent back.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“What merit did this venerable bhikṣu accumulate in the past, and what course of action did he cultivate, that his majestic power is now such as this?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in the world named Vipaśyin. At that time, this bhikṣu, with a heart of joy, held a torch of grass in his hand to illuminate that stūpa. By virtue of this cause and condition, his majestic radiance now reaches upward through the twenty-eight heavens, such that it cannot be surpassed by the light of any of the devas.”
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do not enter parinirvāṇa in this desolate, ruined, and lowly small city."

Why is this? There are other great kingdoms—such as the great kingdom of Campā, the kingdom of Vaiśālī, Rājagṛha, Vārāṇasī, Śrāvastī, Kapilavastu, and Vārāṇasī—where the people are numerous and have faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they will certainly be able to reverently honor and make offerings to his relics.
The Buddha said: "Stop! Stop!"
Do not form such a view; do not say that this land is base and inferior. Why is this?

In the past, there was a king in this country named Mahāsudassana. At that time, this city was called Kusāvatī, the capital of the great king, four hundred and eighty *li* in length and two hundred and eighty *li* in breadth.

At that time, grain was abundant and cheap, and the population was flourishing. The city had seven layers of walls, and surrounding the city were likewise seven layers of railings, carved and engraved with intricate patterns and interspersed with hanging jeweled bells.
The foundations of the city were three fathoms deep and twelve fathoms high; the watchtowers atop the walls were twelve fathoms high, with pillars three fathoms in circumference.
There was a golden wall with silver gates, a silver wall with golden gates, a lapis lazuli wall with crystal gates, and a crystal wall with lapis lazuli gates.
"The city was circular and adorned with the four precious substances; its railings were likewise interspersed with the four precious substances.
Golden towers had silver bells, and silver towers had golden bells. There were seven tiers of precious moats, within which grew lotuses:
blue utpala flowers, red padma flowers, yellow kumuda flowers, and white puṇḍarīka flowers."
Below, golden sand is spread across its floor; on both sides of the path grow many *tāla* trees: those that are gold have silver leaves, flowers, and fruits;
those that are silver have gold leaves, flowers, and fruits;
and those that are crystal have lapis lazuli flowers and fruits.
As for the lapis lazuli trees, they have crystal flowers and fruits.
Amidst the tāla trees are many bathing ponds with clear, flowing streams and deep pools, pure and free from impurity, their banks paved with bricks made of the four precious substances.

There were golden stairways with silver steps, silver stairways with golden steps, and lapis lazuli stairways with golden steps; there were lapis lazuli stairways and thresholds with crystal steps, and crystal stairways and thresholds with lapis lazuli steps.

Surrounded by railings that encircle it in continuous succession, this city has *tāla* trees growing everywhere; those trees of gold have silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; those of silver have golden leaves, flowers, and fruits; those of crystal have lapis lazuli flowers and fruits; and those of lapis lazuli have crystal flowers and fruits.
Amidst the trees there were also four kinds of precious ponds, from which grew four kinds of flowers.
The streets and alleys were perfectly aligned, with rows of buildings corresponding to one another; when the wind blew, the various flowers fell in profusion by the roadside.
A gentle breeze arose from all directions, blowing through the various jewel trees and producing soft sounds like celestial music.
The people of that land—men and women, old and young—wandered together among the trees, enjoying themselves.
In that land, there are always ten kinds of sounds:

the sound of conchs, the sound of drums, the sound of *pa-ra* (cymbals), the sound of singing, the sound of dancing, the sound of wind instruments, the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, and the sound of eating, drinking, and joyful laughter.
"At that time, King Mahāsudarśana was endowed with the seven treasures and possessed four virtues as he ruled over the four continents.

What are the seven treasures? First, the precious golden wheel; second, the precious white elephant; third, the precious dark-blue horse; fourth, the precious divine jewel; fifth, the precious queen; sixth, the precious householder; and seventh, the precious military commander."
How did Great King Sudarśana come to possess the precious wheel-treasure?

On the fifteenth day of the month, when the moon was full, the king bathed in fragrant water and ascended a high palace hall, surrounded by his court ladies. Suddenly, the precious wheel appeared before him of its own accord. It had a thousand spokes, was perfectly endowed with radiant colors, and was crafted by celestial artisans; it was not of this world, being made of pure gold, with a diameter of fourteen feet.
King Mahāsudarśana thought to himself:

"I have previously heard from the elders of old that when a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated lineage, on the fifteenth day of the full moon, has bathed in fragrant water and ascended the jeweled palace surrounded by his court ladies, a golden wheel suddenly appears before him. This wheel has a thousand spokes, its radiance and color are perfect, it is fashioned by a celestial craftsman and does not exist in the world; it is made of pure gold and is fourteen feet in diameter. Such a one is called a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin)."
"Now that this wheel has appeared, could it not be so?
I shall now test this precious wheel-treasure.

At that time, King Mahāsudarśana summoned his fourfold army, bared his right shoulder toward the precious golden wheel, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and rubbed the golden wheel with his right hand, saying:
"Go toward the eastern direction and turn according to the Dharma; do not deviate from the established rule.
The wheel then turned eastward.

At that time, King Sudarśana followed behind it with his fourfold army. Four deities led the way before the precious golden wheel, and wherever the wheel halted, the king immediately reined in his chariot.

At that time, the various minor kings of the eastern regions, seeing the Great King arrive, took golden bowls filled with silver grain and silver bowls filled with golden grain, and approached the King's location. Prostrating themselves with their heads at his feet, they said:
"Welcome, Great King!"
"Now this eastern land is prosperous and joyful, its people are numerous and flourishing, their natures are benevolent and harmonious, and they are compassionate, filial, and compliant.
We only pray that the Holy King will govern here; we shall serve as your attendants and receive whatever duties are appropriate."
At that time, the Great King Sudarśana said to the minor kings:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Virtuous ones!

You have already paid me honor; you should now simply govern by means of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), ensuring there is no partiality or injustice, and that no unlawful conduct occurs within the realm. This is what is called 'my governance'."
At that time, having heard these instructions, the minor kings immediately followed the Great King on his tour of the various kingdoms as far as the shores of the eastern sea;
he then proceeded to the south, the west, and the north. Wherever the wheel arrived, the kings of those lands each offered their territories, just as the minor kings of the east had done.

At that time, King Sudarśana, having followed the golden wheel around the four seas, transforming the people through the Way and bringing comfort to the common folk, returned to his own capital city of Kuśāvatī.
At that time, the precious golden wheel remained suspended in the air above the palace gate, and King Mahāsudarśana, leaping for joy, said:
"This precious golden wheel is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
This constitutes the accomplishment of the precious gold wheel.
"How does the Great King Sudarśana accomplish the precious white elephant?

At that time, as the Great King Sudarśana sat upon the main terrace at dawn, the precious elephant suddenly appeared before him of its own accord. Its coat was pure white; it stood evenly on seven parts of its body; it possessed the power of flight; its head was variegated in color; it had six tusks, slender and tapering, inlaid with genuine gold."
At that time, having seen this, the king thought to himself:
"This elephant is noble and excellent; if it were well-trained, it would be fit for riding.
He then tested its training, and found that all its capabilities were fully prepared.

At that time, Great King Sudarśana, wishing to test his elephant himself, mounted it and departed from the city at dawn; having traveled around the four seas, he returned by the time of the midday meal.
At that time, King Śubhavyūha leaped for joy and said, "This precious white elephant is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
This constitutes the perfection of the precious elephant.
"How did Great King Sudarśana come to possess the horse-treasure?

At that time, as Great King Sudarśana was seated upon the main terrace at dawn, the horse-treasure suddenly appeared before him of its own accord. It was deep blue-black in color with crimson mane and tail; its head and neck were like those of an elephant, and it possessed the power to fly."
At that time, having seen this, the king thought to himself:
"This horse is noble and excellent; if it were well-trained, it would be fit for riding.
He immediately tested its training, and found that all its capabilities were fully prepared.
At that time, King Śubhavyūha wished to test his horse-treasure; he mounted it at dawn and traveled around the four seas, returning by the time of the midday meal.
At that time, King Sudarśana leaped for joy and said, "This dark-blue horse treasure is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
This is the accomplishment of the dark-blue horse treasure.
"What is the Great King Śubhavyūha’s accomplishment of the divine jewel?

At that time, as the Great King Śubhavyūha sat upon the main terrace at dawn, a divine jewel suddenly appeared before him; its substance and color were pure and transparent, free from any flaw or impurity."
At that time, having seen it, the king said:
"This jewel is exquisite; if it possesses radiance, it may illuminate the interior of the palace.

Then, King Sudarśana, wishing to test this jewel, immediately summoned the fourfold army and placed the precious jewel atop a high banner. In the darkness of night, he carried the banner out of the city; the radiance of the jewel illuminated the entire host of soldiers as clearly as if it were broad daylight.
Beyond the perimeter of the army, it could further illuminate an area of one yojana.
The people within the city all rose to attend to their tasks, believing it was daytime.
At that time, King Sudarśana leaped for joy and said:
"This divine jewel is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
This is the accomplishment of the divine jewel treasure.
"How does the Great King Sudarśana accomplish the woman-treasure?"

At that time, the Jewel of the Woman suddenly appeared, her complexion serene and her countenance upright. She was neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor delicate, neither too fair nor too dark, and neither too rigid nor too soft. In winter her body was warm, and in summer it was cool; every pore of her body emitted the fragrance of sandalwood, and her mouth exhaled the scent of the utpala lotus. Her speech was gentle, and her movements were composed; she rose before others and sat down after them, never failing to observe proper decorum.
At that time, King Sudarśana was pure and free from attachment; he did not even momentarily entertain such thoughts, much less draw near to them.
Then, King Sudarśana leaped for joy and said:
"This Jewel of the Woman is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
This constitutes the accomplishment of the Jewel of the Woman.
"What is the Great King Sudarśana’s accomplishment of the Householder Jewel?
At that time, a householder suddenly appears of his own accord; treasure stores manifest naturally, and his wealth is immeasurable."
The lay devotee possesses the eye of past merit, which can see through the earth to perceive hidden treasures, whether they have an owner or not; he perceives and knows them all.
Those that have an owner, he protects and safeguards for them; those that have no owner, he takes for the king's use.
At that time, the Householder Jewel went to the king and said:
"Great King! As for whatever needs to be provided, there is no need to worry; I myself am capable of arranging it."
At that time, King Sudarśana, wishing to test the householder-treasure, immediately ordered his ships to be prepared for recreation upon the water and said to the householder:
"I require gold and jewels; give them to me quickly."
The householder replied, "Great King, wait a moment; we must reach the shore.
The king immediately pressed him, saying:
"I require it for my stay; I shall have it here immediately.

At that time, the Householder Jewel, having received the King's strict command, knelt on the ship and placed his right hand into the water. A jeweled jar emerged from the water following his hand, like a caterpillar climbing a tree.
That householder-treasure was likewise; he placed his hand into the water, and by the power of the treasure, [jewels] emerged from his hand and filled the ship. He then addressed the king, saying:
"As for the need for jewels you mentioned earlier, how much do you require?"
At that time, King Sudarśana said to the householder:
"Stop! Stop!"
"I have no need for anything; I was merely testing you!
You have now already performed an offering to me.
When the householder heard these words of the king, he immediately cast the precious objects back into the water.
At that time, King Sudarśana leaped for joy and said, "This Jewel of the Householder is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-turning Sage King.
This constitutes the accomplishment of the Jewel of the Householder.
“What is the accomplishment of the Great King Sudarśana’s military treasure?
At that time, the military treasure suddenly appeared; he was of heroic and fierce wisdom, possessing singular strategic resolve. He immediately went to the king’s presence and said:
‘Great King!...’”
"In matters of military punishment, Your Majesty need not worry; I am capable of managing it myself.
At that time, Great King Sudarśana, wishing to test the Jewel of the Military Commander, immediately assembled the fourfold army and addressed them, saying:
"Now, as you employ the troops, those who have not yet gathered must be gathered, and those already gathered must be released."
"Those who have not arrayed their troops shall be arrayed; those already arrayed shall be dismissed.
Those who have not set out shall set out; those already set out shall remain.
When the Jewel of the Military Commander heard the King's words, he immediately ordered the fourfold army: those not yet assembled were to assemble, and those already assembled were to be dismissed.
He adorned those not yet adorned and released those already adorned;
he sent away those not yet departed and stayed those already departed.
At that time, King Sudarśana spoke with great joy:
"This General-Treasure is truly my auspicious sign; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Ānanda! This is how the Wheel-Turning Sage King Sudarśana accomplished the seven treasures.
"What are the four divine qualities?
First, one possesses longevity and does not die prematurely, such that none can equal it.
Second, one's body is strong and free from ailment, such that none can equal it."
Third, his countenance is upright and handsome, such that none can equal him.
Fourth, his treasuries are overflowing with wealth, such that none can equal him.
These are the seven jewels and four merits accomplished by a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
“Ānanda! At that time, after a long interval, King Sudarśana ordered his carriage prepared and went out to the rear garden. He then instructed his charioteer:
‘You must drive skillfully and proceed with composure.’”
"Why is this? It is because I wish to observe clearly whether the people of the kingdom are at peace and free from affliction.
At that time, the people of the kingdom who were watching by the roadside spoke again to the attendant:
"Please walk slowly; I wish to contemplate the majestic countenance of the Holy King.

Ānanda! At that time, King Sudarśana nurtured all people and things with compassion, as a father loves his son. The citizens adored the king as sons look up to a father; they offered him every kind of rare treasure, praying that he would graciously accept them and bestow them as he pleased.
Then the king replied, "Stop, all of you!"
"I have my own treasures; you may use them as you please.
At another time, the king thought to himself:
"I should now build a palace and pavilions."
As soon as this thought arose, the people of the kingdom went to King Sudarśana and each addressed the king, saying:
"We shall now construct a palace for Your Majesty."
The King replied to him, saying, "I now consider myself fortunate to have received your offerings; I possess precious goods sufficient to accomplish this.
At that time, the people of the kingdom again addressed the King with a further petition:
"I wish to construct a palace for the King.
The King addressed the people,
saying, "Do as you intend."
At that time, having received the king’s command, the people immediately brought eighty-four thousand chariots laden with gold and went to the city of Kuśāvatī to construct the Hall of Dharma.
At that time, the second Deva-putra, Viśvakarman of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, thought silently to himself:
"I alone am capable of erecting the Palace of Right Dharma for King Sudarśana. "Ānanda! [he said].

At that time, the celestial artisan created a Dharma Hall sixty li in length and thirty li in width, adorned with the four precious substances. Its foundation was level and even, and its steps were paved with seven tiers of precious bricks.
The hall had eighty-four thousand pillars: golden pillars with silver capitals, silver pillars with golden capitals, and likewise pillars of lapis lazuli and crystal with corresponding capitals.
Surrounding the perimeter of the hall were four railings, all fashioned from the four precious substances; likewise, the four staircases were also made of the four precious substances.

Above that Dharma Hall were eighty-four thousand jeweled towers: those of gold had windows and doors of silver, those of silver had windows and doors of gold, and the same was true for the towers of crystal and lapis lazuli.

There were golden towers with silver couches and silver towers with golden couches; their cushions were fine and soft, woven from gold thread, spread upon the seats, and the same was true for the crystal and lapis lazuli towers and couches.
The radiance of that palace dazzled the eyes of men, like the intense brilliance of the sun such that none could gaze upon it.
At that time, King Sudarśana thought to himself:
"I should now construct the Tāla Grove and the ponds to the left and right of this palace."
He immediately constructed a garden and pond, one yojana in length and breadth.
Furthermore, he thought to himself:
"I shall construct a Dharma-pond before the Dharma-palace."

He immediately commissioned its construction, measuring one yojana in length and breadth. Its waters were clear and limpid, pure and free from impurity. The bottom was paved with bricks made of the four treasures, and the four sides of the pond were surrounded by railings composed entirely of the four treasures: gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.
In that pond, various kinds of water-born flowers grew:
blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka), emitting subtle and wondrous fragrances that wafted and dispersed in all directions.
On the land surrounding the four sides of that pond grow flowers:
ahimukta flowers, campaka flowers, pāṭala flowers, sumanā flowers, vārṣika flowers, and tagara flowers.
He appointed attendants to manage the pool; whenever travelers passed by, he would lead them in to bathe and sport in the cool waters as they desired.
If they required drink, he gave them drink; if they required food, he gave them food. As for clothing, carriages, horses, incense, flowers, and treasures, he never refused anyone’s request.
"Ānanda! At that time, King Sudarśana had eighty-four thousand elephants, adorned with gold and silver and draped with precious gems; among them, the Elephant King was the foremost."
There were eighty-four thousand horses, adorned with gold and silver and harnessed with precious gems; the King of Powerful Horses was foremost among them.
There were eighty-four thousand chariots, covered with lion skins and decorated with the four treasures; the Jewel of the Golden Wheel was foremost among them.
Of the eighty-four thousand pearls, the divine jewel-treasure is foremost.
Of the eighty-four thousand jade maidens, the jade maiden-treasure is foremost.
Of the eighty-four thousand householders, the householder-treasure is foremost.
Of the eighty-four thousand Kṣatriyas, the Jewel of the Military Commander was foremost.
Of the eighty-four thousand cities, the city of Kuśināgarī was foremost.
Of the eighty-four thousand palaces, the Palace of Righteous Dharma (Saddharmaprāsāda) was foremost.
There were eighty-four thousand towers, with the Great Righteousness Tower being the foremost.
There were eighty-four thousand couches, all fashioned from gold, silver, and various jewels; upon them were spread woolen rugs, carpets, and fine, soft silken hangings.
There were eighty-four trillion garments, with *kṣauma*, *kāśika*, and *karpāsa* fabrics being the foremost.
Eighty-four thousand varieties of food were provided daily, each flavor distinct from the others.

“Ānanda! At that time, King Sudarśana mounted eighty-four thousand elephants whose backs were level with his own and departed from the city of Kuśinagara at dawn. He traveled across the world, circling the four seas, and returned to the city within a mere moment to eat his meal.”
Eighty-four thousand horses, mounted by the Horse-Jewel, went out for a ride at dawn to patrol the world, traveling across the four seas; in a mere instant, they returned to the city to eat.

With eighty-four thousand chariots, riding in a golden-wheeled vehicle drawn by precious powerful horses, he went out on an excursion at the clear dawn to inspect the world, traveling throughout the four seas; in a mere moment, he returned to the city to eat.
There were eighty-four thousand divine jewels; by means of these divine jewels, the interior of the palace was illuminated, remaining perpetually bright day and night.
There were eighty-four thousand jade maidens, among whom the Jade Woman Treasure, Bhadrottamā, attended upon him at his side.
There were eighty-four thousand householders who, in matters of providing gifts and requisites, served as the Jewel of the Householder.
There were eighty-four thousand kṣatriyas who, in matters of military expeditions and punishments, served as the Jewel of the Military Commander.
Of the eighty-four thousand cities he constantly governed, his capital was the city of Kuśinagara.
Of the eighty-four thousand palaces where the king constantly resided, his primary dwelling was the Palace of True Dharma (Saddharmaprāsāda).
Of the eighty-four thousand towers, the one where the king constantly resides is the Great Righteousness Tower.
Of the eighty-four thousand seats, the one where the king constantly resides is the crystal seat, because he dwells there in peaceful meditation.
There were eighty-four thousand billion garments, adorned with the most exquisite jewels, which he wore according to his will out of a sense of shame and modesty.
There were eighty-four thousand kinds of food, the king’s regular fare; he ate naturally produced rice out of contentment.
"At that time, eighty-four thousand elephants appeared. As the king trod upon and charged them, they caused injury to sentient beings beyond counting.
Then the king thought to himself:
'These elephants appear so frequently that they cause much destruction and harm. From this day forward, I shall allow only one elephant to appear every hundred years.'"
"In this manner, appearing once every hundred years in successive order, they cycle back again and forth.
Thus ends the third fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* spoken by the Buddha. [Fascicle Four begins.]
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Part Two of the *Caryā-sūtra*.
Furthermore, at that time, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"By what merits did I originally accumulate, and what roots of goodness did I cultivate, that I now obtain such a magnificent retribution as this?
He further reflected:
"By means of three causes and conditions, one brings about this karmic reward. What are the three?
First is giving; second is upholding the precepts; and third is meditative reflection. Through these causes and conditions, one now obtains this great retribution."
The king further reflected to himself:

"I have now already received the karmic rewards of human fortune; I ought to further cultivate the deeds that lead to celestial blessings. It is fitting that I restrain myself, depart from the clamor and bustle, dwell in seclusion and leisure, and thereby honor the Way."
At that time, the king immediately summoned the noble lady Bhadrā and addressed her, saying:

"I have now already received the blessings and retributions of the human realm; I must now further cultivate the karmic deeds for celestial blessings. You should restrain yourself, depart from the clamor and bustle, dwell in seclusion and quietude, and thereby honor the Way."
The woman said,
"Yes, sir! I shall do as the Great King commands."
He immediately issued orders both inside and outside [the palace] to cease all attendance and audiences.

At that time, the King ascended the Dharma Hall and entered the Golden Pavilion, where he sat upon a silver throne. He contemplated sensual desire and evil, unwholesome states; with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the joy and bliss born of seclusion, he attained the first dhyāna.

Having stilled directed and sustained thought, with internal tranquility and joy, his mind concentrated and unified, without directed or sustained thought, and with the joy and bliss born of concentration, he attained the second dhyāna.

By relinquishing joy and maintaining equanimity, with focused mindfulness and undisturbed attention, one experiences within oneself that bliss which the noble ones seek; thus, through the practice of mindful guarding and bliss, one attains the third dhyāna.

By relinquishing both suffering and pleasure, and having previously eliminated sorrow and joy, one dwells in a state neither painful nor pleasant; through the purity of mindful guarding, one attains the fourth dhyāna.

At that time, King Sudarśana rose from his silver throne, emerged from the golden pavilion, and proceeded to the Great Rectitude Pavilion. There he sat upon a lapis lazuli seat and cultivated a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), pervading one direction; he did likewise for the other directions, until it was all-encompassing, vast, universal, non-dual, and immeasurable. He removed all fetters and resentments, and with a heart free from envy or malice, he found delight in stillness, gentleness, and compassion. He practiced the same with the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
At that time, the Jewel Woman silently thought to herself:
"I have long been separated from his countenance and have longed to attend upon him; now, it would be fitting to present myself before the Great King."
Then, the noble lady Bhadrottamā said to her eighty-four thousand court ladies:
"Each of you should bathe in fragrant water and adorn yourselves with fine garments. Why is this so?"
"We have long been separated from your presence; it is fitting that we should come once more to pay our respects.
Having heard this, the women each dressed themselves in their finest attire and bathed to purify themselves.
At that time, the noble lady Bhadrottamā further commanded the minister Senāpati-ratna to assemble the fourfold army.
"We have been long absent from the court audience; it is fitting that we present ourselves once more.
Thereupon, the Minister of War immediately assembled the fourfold army and addressed the Jewel Woman, saying:
"The fourfold army has been assembled; you should know that now is the time."

Thereupon, the Jewel Woman, accompanied by eighty-four thousand court ladies and escorted by the fourfold army, proceeded to the Kimtalin Garden. The great multitude stirred and their clamor reached the King; having heard the noise, the King looked out from his window and beheld her. The Jewel Woman then stepped forward and stood by the side of the door.
At that time, when the king saw the woman, he immediately said to her, "Stop and do not come forward; I shall go out to see you.

Then, King Sudarśana rose from his crystal throne, emerged from the Great Rectitude Tower, descended from the Hall of Righteous Dharma, and together with the Woman-Jewel, proceeded to the Tālin Garden where he took his seat.
At that time, King Sudarśana’s countenance was more radiant than usual, and the noble lady Bhadrottamā thought to herself:
"The Great King’s complexion now surpasses its ordinary state; what extraordinary omen is this?"
Then the woman immediately addressed the Great King:
"Your countenance today is extraordinary; could this not be an unusual omen that you intend to relinquish your life?
Here now are eighty-four thousand elephants, of which this white elephant-treasure is the foremost."

Adorned with alternating gold and silver, and decorated with precious pearls—all of which belong to Your Majesty—please deign to take some interest in them and enjoy yourself together with us; do not pass away so soon, leaving the myriad people to suffer in solitude.
Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand horses, with the King of Horses as the foremost;
eighty-four thousand chariots, with the Wheel-Treasure as the foremost;
and eighty-four thousand pearls, with the Divine Jewel as the foremost.
There were eighty-four thousand women, of whom the Woman-Jewel was foremost;
eighty-four thousand householders, of whom the Householder-Jewel was foremost;
and eighty-four thousand Kṣatriyas, of whom the Military Commander-Jewel was foremost.
Of the eighty-four thousand cities, the city of Kuśinagara is foremost;
of the eighty-four thousand palaces, the Palace of the True Dharma is foremost;
of the eighty-four thousand towers, the Great Righteous Tower is foremost.
There were eighty-four thousand seats, unsurpassed in their precious adornments;
eighty-four thousand billion garments, unsurpassed in their softness;
and eighty-four thousand kinds of food, each flavor exquisite and rare.

All these various treasures are yours, O King; we pray that you will take some heed and enjoy them together with us, rather than relinquishing your life and abandoning the myriad people to their solitude.
At that time, King Sudarśana replied to the Jewel Woman, saying:
"Since you first began serving me, you have been compassionate, gentle, respectful, and obedient; your speech has never been coarse or careless. Why do you now speak these words?"
The woman said to the king,
"I do not understand what it is about that you have spoken which is improper.
The king told the woman:

"As for what you said just now—that elephants, horses, jeweled chariots, golden wheels, palaces, fine garments, and delicacies are all impermanent and cannot be preserved for long—yet you urge me to remain: how could this possibly be appropriate?"
The daughter addressed the king, saying,
"I do not know what words of kindness and compliance I ought to speak.
The king said to his daughter:

"If you can say: 'Elephants, horses, precious chariots, golden wheels, palaces, famous garments, and delicacies—all these are impermanent and cannot be maintained for long; I pray that you will not harbor attachment to them, lest you weary your spirit and thoughts,'" [then you may come].

Why is this so? Your Majesty’s life span has not long remained; you shall soon pass into the afterlife. For all that is born must die, and all that meets must part. How could there be anyone born here who lives forever?
"You ought to sever your affection so as to preserve your resolve for the Way; this is what is called speaking with reverence and compliance. "Ānanda!
At that time, having heard the King’s instruction, the Jewel Woman wept and wailed; wiping away her tears, she said:"

"Elephants, horses, precious chariots, golden wheels, palaces, renowned garments, and delicacies—all these are impermanent and cannot be maintained for long; I pray you do not remain attached to them, thereby exhausting your spirit and thoughts."

Why is this so? Your Majesty’s life will not last long before you must pass into the afterlife; for birth is followed by death, and meeting is inevitably followed by parting—how could there be one born here who enjoys eternal life?
"You should sever your affection and love in order to preserve your resolve for the Way. "Ānanda!

At the very moment the Jewel of the Woman spoke these words, King Sudarśana suddenly passed away. It was as if a strong man had finished a single meal of fine rice; he experienced no suffering, and his spirit ascended to be reborn in the seventh Brahma Heaven."

Seven days after King Sudarśana passed away, the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure spontaneously vanished. On that same day, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure all met their end. The city walls, moats, Dharma-hall, towers, pavilions, precious ornaments, and the Jeta Grove all transformed into mere earth and wood.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“These conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to change; they inevitably lead to decay and extinction. Greed and desire are never satiated, wasting away human life; one remains attached to affection and love, never knowing contentment.”
Only those who have attained noble wisdom and clearly perceive the Path are able to find contentment. Ānanda!
I recall that in the past, I was a Wheel-Turning Sage King in this very place six times, and each time I left my bones here.

Now that I have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I have again surrendered my life and established myself here. From this day forward, birth and death are forever severed; there shall be no land or region where I may place my body. This is the final limit; I shall never again undergo existence.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in the city of Kuśinagara, at his own birthplace, within the Śāla Grove between the twin trees, as he was about to pass into parinirvāṇa. He addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Enter the city of Kuśinagara and announce to the Mallas:
'O worthy ones!'"

"You should know that at midnight, the Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the Śāla Grove. You may go there to inquire about your doubts and receive his instructions face to face; you should take advantage of this time, lest you later regret it."
At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
Accompanied by a bhikṣu, he walked with tears falling and entered the city of Kuśinagara, where he saw five hundred Mallas gathered in one place for some minor reason.
At that time, when the Mallas saw Ānanda approaching, they immediately rose and paid their respects, standing to one side and addressing Ānanda:
"We wonder, Venerable Sir, why you have entered this city so very late this evening; what do you intend to do?"
Ānanda shed tears and said:
"For your sake, wishing to benefit you, I have come to inform you.

You should know that the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa at midnight. You may go to consult him regarding your doubts and receive his instructions in person; you should take advantage of this moment and not later regret it."

At that time, having heard these words, the Mallas raised their voices in mournful wailing; they rolled about and fell prostrate on the ground, fainting and then reviving again. Like great trees whose roots have been uprooted and whose branches broken off, they all raised their voices together, saying:
"How swift is the Buddha’s passing into parinirvāṇa!"
"The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa; how swift it was!
All living beings suffer a long-term loss; the Eye of the World has been extinguished.
At that time, Ānanda comforted the Mallas, saying:
"Stop! Stop! Do not grieve!"
In heaven and earth, among the myriad things, there is none that does not end in death; to wish for that which is conditioned to exist eternally is impossible.
Did not the Buddha say:
"Where there is meeting, there must be separation; where there is birth, there must be cessation"?
At that time, the Mallas said to one another:
"Let us return home, take our families with us, and each bring five hundred pieces of white cotton cloth; let us go together to the twin trees."

Then, each of the Mallas returned to their respective homes, gathered their families, and taking white cotton cloths with them, they departed from the city of Kuśinagara and went to the space between the twin trees where Ānanda was staying.
Seeing them from afar, Ānanda thought silently to himself:
"The number of people here is vast; if each were to see the Buddha one by one, I fear they would not all have heard him before the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa."
"I should now ensure that they see the Buddha at the same time as the preceding night.

He then took the five hundred Mallas and their families to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side. Ānanda then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Such-and-such Mallas and their families inquire after the World-Honored One’s health and well-being."
The Buddha replied, "I thank you for coming; I shall cause your lifespans to be prolonged, free from illness and pain.
Ānanda was thus able to lead the Mallas and their families so that they might see the World-Honored One.
Then, the Mallas prostrated themselves at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught them the impermanence of all things, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.

At that time, the Mallas, having heard the Dharma with joy, immediately offered five hundred pieces of fine cloth to the World-Honored One. The Buddha accepted them for them; the Mallas then rose from their seats, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.

At that time, within the city of Kuśinagara, there was a brahmin named Subhadra, one hundred and twenty years of age, aged yet possessed of great wisdom. Hearing that the śramaṇa Gautama was to attain parinirvāṇa this very night between the twin śāla trees, he thought to himself:
"I have doubts regarding the Dharma; only Gautama can resolve my mind. I must now take the opportunity and go forth by my own effort."

That very night, he departed from the city of Kuśinagara and went to the space between the twin śāla trees. Arriving at where Ānanda was, he exchanged greetings with him, stood to one side, and said to Ānanda:
“I have heard that the Śramaṇa Gautama will attain parinirvāṇa tonight; therefore, I have come here seeking a single audience.”
"I have doubts regarding the Dharma; I wish to see Gautama so that he may resolve my mind.
Is there any leisure for me to meet with him? Ānanda replied, "Stop!
"Stop, Subhadra! The Buddha's body is ill; do not trouble him."
Subhadra entreated him earnestly, even up to three times:

"I have heard that a Tathāgata appears in the world but once in an aeon, appearing only as rarely as the udumbara flower blooms from time to time; therefore, I have come to seek an audience, desiring to resolve my doubts. Might you have the leisure for a brief meeting?"
Ānanda answered as before:
"The Buddha’s body is ill; do not trouble him.
Then the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do not stop him! Allow him to enter;
he wishes to resolve his doubts and has no intention of causing disturbance. Should he hear my Dharma, he will surely attain understanding."
Ānanda then said to Subhadda,
"If you wish to see the Buddha, you should know that now is the time.
Subhadda immediately entered, and after exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have doubts regarding the Dharma; would there be leisure for me to resolve what I am obstructed by?
The Buddha said, "Ask whatever you wish."
Subhadra then asked: "How so, Gautama?"

There are various other groups who claim to be teachers—Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Sañjayin Vairaḍīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra. Each of these teachers has his own distinct doctrine; is the Śramaṇa Gautama able to know them all completely?
"Do you not know this completely?
The Buddha said, "Stop!"
"Stop! What is the use of discussing this? I already know it all.
Now I shall explain for you the profound and wondrous Dharma; listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well.
Subhadra received the instruction, and the Buddha said to him:
"If, among all phenomena, there were no Noble Eightfold Path, then there would be no first fruit of the śramaṇa, nor the second, third, or fourth fruits of the śramaṇa."
Subhadda! Because the Eightfold Noble Path exists within all phenomena, there are the first fruit of the ascetic life, as well as the second, third, and fourth fruits of the ascetic life.

Subhadra! Within my Dharma today there is the Noble Eightfold Path, and there are the first fruit of śrāmaṇya, as well as the second, third, and fourth fruits of śrāmaṇya; among the various groups of outsiders, there is no fruit of śrāmaṇya.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Subhadra:
"I was twenty-nine years old When I left home to seek the Path of Goodness;
Subhadra, since I attained Buddhahood, Fifty years have now passed."
"Through the practice of morality, concentration, and wisdom, one dwells alone in contemplation;
now I have taught the essence of the Dharma—beyond this, there is no ascetic.
The Buddha said to Subhadda:
"If all bhikṣus were able to exercise self-restraint, then arhats would not be rare in this world.
At that time, Subhadra said to Ānanda:
"All those who have already practiced the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama, those who are practicing it now, and those who shall practice it in the future, will obtain great benefit."

"Ānanda! You have also gained great benefit by practicing the holy life under the Tathāgata; I too have gained great benefit in that I have been able to behold the Tathāgata in person and inquire about my doubts."
"Now, the Tathāgata has distinguished me by bestowing upon me the prediction for disciples.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying,
"May I now go forth in the Dharma of the Tathāgata and receive full ordination?"
The Buddha told Subhadra:

"If there are heterodox brahmins who would practice the holy life within my Dharma, they shall undergo a four-month probationary period to observe their conduct and examine their disposition. Those who maintain all the rules of decorum without fail may then receive full ordination within my Dharma."
"Subhadra! You should know that it depends on the person.
Subhadra spoke again, saying:

“Those of external paths and heterodox schools shall undergo a four-month probation within the Buddha-dharma to observe their conduct and examine their dispositions; only those who possess all dignified deportment without lapse may receive full ordination.”
"Now, having served within the Buddha’s True Dharma for four years, maintaining all dignified deportment without any lapse, I shall receive full ordination.
The Buddha told Subhadra:
"I have already stated previously that it depends entirely on the person."
Thereupon, on that very night, Subhadra went forth and received the precepts. He cultivated the holy life with purity, and within this very life, he realized for himself through direct experience:

"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I have attained true knowledge as it is, and there is no further state of existence."
At that time, before long after nightfall, he attained arhatship; he was the final disciple of the Tathāgata, and thus entered parinirvāṇa first, while the Buddha followed later.
At that moment, Ānanda stood behind the Buddha, leaning on the couch and weeping with such grief that he could not restrain himself; sobbing, he said:
"How swift is the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata!"
"How swift is the passing of the World-Honored One!
How rapid is the sinking and obscuring of the Great Dharma!
All living beings suffer perpetual decline, and the Eye of the World is extinguished. Why is this so?"
"Having received the Buddha's grace, I have attained the stage of training; yet before my task is accomplished, the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?"
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"The bhikṣu Ānanda is now behind the Buddha, leaning against the couch and weeping with grief, unable to restrain himself; sobbing, he says:
'How swift is the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata!'"
"How swift is the passing of the World-Honored One!
How rapid is the submergence and obscuration of the Great Dharma!
All living beings shall suffer long-term decline, for the Eye of the World has been extinguished. Why is this so?"
"I have received the Buddha's grace and attained the stage of a learner (śaikṣa), yet before my practice is perfected, the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Stop!
Cease! Do not grieve, nor weep.
Since you have attended me, your physical conduct has been compassionate, non-dual, and immeasurable.
Your conduct in speech is imbued with loving-kindness, and your conduct in thought is imbued with loving-kindness; it is non-dual and immeasurable. Ānanda!
Your merit in making offerings to me is exceedingly great; were there anyone else to offer to the various devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, none could equal you.
"Simply persevere with diligence, and you shall attain the Way before long.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The attendant disciples of all past Buddhas were also like Ānanda; the attendant disciples of all future Buddhas will also be like Ānanda."
However, while the disciples who attended the Buddhas of the past had to wait until they were told before they knew what was needed, my Ānanda now knows it at a mere glance:
"The Tathāgata requires this; the World-Honored One requires that."
This is an unprecedented quality of Ānanda; you should all uphold it.
A wheel-turning sage king possesses four extraordinary and unprecedented qualities. What are these four?

When the Holy King travels, the people of the entire nation all come forth to welcome him; having seen him, they rejoice, and hearing his teachings, they likewise rejoice; gazing upon his majestic countenance, they can never be satiated.

Whether the Wheel-Turning Sage King stands, sits, or lies down, all the ministers and subjects within his realm come before him; they rejoice upon seeing the king, they rejoice upon hearing his instructions, and they gaze upon his majestic countenance without ever being satiated. These are the four extraordinary qualities of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
Now, Ānanda, I too possess these four extraordinary qualities. What are the four?

When Ānanda enters the assembly of bhikṣus in silence, the assembly is filled with joy; when he preaches the Dharma to the assembly, they are likewise filled with joy upon hearing it; and whether they observe his dignified demeanor or listen to his preaching of the Dharma, they never tire of it.

Furthermore, Ānanda, he silently approaches the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the assembly of upāsakas, and the assembly of upāsikās; seeing them all filled with joy, if he preaches the Dharma to them, they likewise rejoice upon hearing it. Observing their deportment and listening to his preaching of the Dharma, they never tire of it. These are the four unprecedented and extraordinary qualities of Ānanda.
At that time, Ānanda bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

There are currently many elderly śramaṇas from the four directions who possess great wisdom, are well-versed in the Sūtras and Vinaya, and are of pure virtue and noble conduct. When they come to visit the World-Honored One, I am thereby able to pay my respects, behold them personally, and inquire after their welfare.”
"After the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, he will no longer come; having nothing left to behold, what shall we do?
The Buddha told Ānanda: "Do not grieve."
Noble sons always maintain four kinds of mindfulness. What are these four?
First, they mindfully reflect upon the place where the Buddha was born; with joy and a desire to see him, they remember it without forgetting and give rise to a heart of longing and devotion.

The second is to recollect the place where the Buddha first attained the Way, feeling joy and desiring to see it, remembering it without forgetting, and giving rise to a heart of longing and devotion.

The third is to recollect the place where the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma, feeling joy and desiring to see it, remembering it without forgetting, and giving rise to a heart of longing and devotion.
The fourth is to recollect the Buddha’s place of parinirvāṇa, desiring to see it with joy, remembering it without forgetfulness, and giving rise to a heart of longing and devotion. Ānanda!
After my parinirvāṇa, when sons and daughters of good family recollect the Buddha at the time of his birth, their merit shall be thus.
When the Buddha attained the Way, his supernormal powers were such as these.
When he turned the Wheel of Dharma, his saving of sentient beings was such as these.
When he approached his final nirvana, the legacy of his Dharma was such as these.

Having gone to each of those places and having traveled about to pay homage to the various stūpas and temples, they all died and were reborn in the heavens, with the exception of those who had attained the Path.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, when members of the Śākya clan come seeking to enter the Path, you should permit them to leave the household life and confer upon them full ordination; do not create any obstacles."
When followers of other schools and brahmins come seeking the Way, they may likewise be permitted to leave the household life and receive full ordination;
