do not subject them to a four-month probationary period.
Why is this? They hold divergent doctrines, and if they are detained for even a short time, their original views will arise once more.
At that time, Ānanda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣu Caṇḍa is arrogant and self-willed; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, what shall we do with him?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if that Candra does not conform to the rules of decorum and does not accept instruction and admonition, you all should together impose upon him the brahmadanda penalty. Command the bhikṣus that they must not speak with him, nor engage in mutual teaching or business with him."
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, what should be done regarding those women who have not yet received instruction?"
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Do not meet with him. Ānanda spoke again:
"If we should encounter them, what should we do?
The Buddha said,
"Do not speak with them."
Ānanda spoke again:
"If one were to converse with him, how should it be done?
The Buddha said:
"Examine your own mind, Ānanda!
Do you think that after the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, there will be no further protection and you will lose your support?"
"Do not form such a view. The sūtras and precepts I have taught since my attainment of Buddhahood are your protection; they are what you uphold. Ānanda!

From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to relinquish the minor precepts. Those who address one another according to seniority should follow the proper rites and measures; this is the method for those who have left the household life to practice respect and obedience."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“If you have any doubts regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, or if you have any doubts regarding the Path, you should inquire about them immediately. You ought to take advantage of this moment; do not let it be so that you regret it later. While I am still present, I shall explain these matters for you.”
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent and spoke no word.
The Buddha addressed them again, saying:

"If you have any doubts regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, or if you have any doubts regarding the Path, you should quickly inquire about them. You ought to take advantage of this moment; do not let it be so that you later regret it. While I am still present, I shall explain these things for you."
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent once more.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"If you are ashamed and do not dare to ask, you should inquire through those whom you know well; you ought to do so now, lest you regret it later."
At that time, the bhikṣus remained silent once more.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I believe that this assembly all possesses pure faith; there is not a single bhikṣu who doubts the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, nor does anyone doubt the Path."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I myself know that even the youngest bhikṣu in this assembly has seen the path; he will not go to the evil realms, but after at most seven more rebirths, he will surely reach the end of suffering."
At that time, the World-Honored One conferred upon his twelve hundred disciples the prediction of the fruits of the Path they had attained.
Then, the World-Honored One bared his saṃghāṭī robe, revealing his golden arm, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should observe that a Tathāgata appears in the world only from time to time, just as the udumbara flower appears but once in an aeon."
At that time, the World-Honored One, contemplating this meaning again, spoke in verse:
“The right arm is the color of purple gold; The Buddha’s manifestation is like a divine omen.
Coming and going, his actions are impermanent; He manifests extinction so that none may be heedless.”
"Therefore, bhikṣus! Do not be negligent.

It was through non-negligence that I attained perfect enlightenment; all immeasurable virtues were likewise acquired through non-negligence. That 'all things are impermanent'—this is the Tathāgata’s final instruction."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One entered the first dhyāna; arising from the first dhyāna, he entered the second dhyāna;
arising from the second dhyāna, he entered the third dhyāna;
arising from the third dhyāna, he entered the fourth dhyāna.
Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite space;
emerging from the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, he enters the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
emerging from the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the concentration of nothingness.
Emerging from the concentration of non-perception, he entered the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
emerging from the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he entered the attainment of cessation.
At that time, Ānanda asked Aniruddha:
"Has the Blessed One already entered parinirvāṇa?
Anuruddha replied, "Not yet, Ānanda!"
"The World-Honored One is now in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
I have personally heard from the Buddha in the past that one enters parinirvāṇa only after arising from the fourth dhyāna.
At that moment, the World-Honored One arose from the meditative absorption of cessation and entered the meditative absorption of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Arising from the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the attainment of nothingness;
arising from the attainment of nothingness, one enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
arising from the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the attainment of the sphere of infinite space.
Emerging from the concentration on the sphere of infinite space, he enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna;
emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the first dhyāna;
emerging from the first dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna;
emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the third dhyāna.
Emerging from the third dhyāna, he entered the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
At that moment, the great earth shook violently, and all the devas and people of the world were struck with great terror.

In all those dark and obscure places where the light of the sun and moon does not reach, everyone was bathed in great brilliance and was able to see one another; they called out to each other, saying, "A person has been born here!"
"Such a person was born here!
Their radiance was all-pervasive, surpassing the light of all the devas.
At that time, the Trāyastriṃśa devas in the midst of the sky scattered mandārava flowers, utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers over the Tathāgata and upon the assembled multitude.
Furthermore, he scattered celestial *candana* sandalwood powder over the Buddha and upon the great assembly.
After the Buddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, the Brahmā King, from within the void, spoke in verse:
"All beings shrouded in ignorance Must all abandon the aggregates (*skandhas*);"
The Buddha is the Unsurpassed Honored One; in the world, there is no equal to him.
The Tathāgata, the Great Sage and Hero, possesses the power of fearlessness;
may the World-Honored One abide for a long time, yet now he enters parinirvāṇa.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra again spoke in verse:
"The aggregates (skandhas) have no permanence; They are merely subject to the law of arising and decaying.
Of those who are born, none do not die; The Buddha’s extinction is bliss."
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa again spoke in verse:
"The great forest of the tree of merit, The unsurpassed śāla grove of blessings;
A fertile field for receiving offerings— There, between the twin trees, he entered parinirvāṇa."
At that time, Aniruddha again spoke in verse:
“The Buddha abides in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), No longer requiring the inhalation and exhalation of breath;
Having originally come from quiescent extinction (*śānti*), The radiant light has now vanished.”
At that time, the bhikṣu Brahmāna again spoke in verse:
"Not with a mind of indolence or pride, I restrain myself and cultivate supreme wisdom;
Unattached and unstained, Free from craving—the Unsurpassed Honored One."
At that time, the bhikṣu Ānanda again spoke in verse:
“Gods and humans harbor terror, the hair on their bodies stands on end;
all things are fully accomplished— the Perfectly Awakened One has entered parinirvāṇa.”
At that time, the deity Kumbhīra again spoke in verse:
"The world has lost its protection; All living beings are forever in blind darkness.
They shall no longer behold the Perfectly Awakened One, The Hero among Men, the Lion of the Śākyas."
At that time, the Malla Vajrapāṇi again spoke in verse:
"In this world and in the world beyond, Among the Brahmās and all the devas,
We shall never again behold The Lion of the Śākyas, the Hero among Men."
At that time, the Buddha’s mother, Māyā, again spoke in verse:
“The Buddha was born in the Lumbinī Grove, And his Way has spread far and wide;
Now he returns to his place of birth, Forever casting off this impermanent body.”
At that time, the deity of the twin trees again spoke in verse:
"When shall we once more scatter non-seasonal flowers upon the Buddha?
The Tathāgata, endowed with the merits of the Ten Powers, has entered parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the deity of the Śāla grove further spoke in verse:
“This place is most wondrous and blissful; The Buddha was born and grew here.
It is here he turned the wheel of Dharma, And it is here he entered parinirvāṇa.”
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings further spoke in verse:
“The Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom Constantly proclaims the discourse on impermanence;
He unties the bonds of suffering for all living beings And ultimately enters into tranquil extinction.”
At that time, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven again spoke in verse:
“Throughout hundreds of millions of koṭis of kalpas, He sought to accomplish the unsurpassed path;
To untie the bonds of suffering for all living beings, And ultimately enter into nirvāṇa.”
At that time, King Yama further spoke in verse:
"This is the final robe, Wrapping the body of the Tathāgata;
Now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, To whom shall this robe be offered?"
At that time, the King of the Tuṣita Heaven further spoke in verse:
"This is the final body; here the aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus) shall cease.
Free from the notions of sorrow and joy, there will no longer be the affliction of old age and death."
At that time, the Deva-king Vaśavartin further spoke in verse:
"In the latter part of this very night, the Buddha shall lie down on his right side;
here in this Śāla Grove, the Lion of the Śākyas will pass into parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven again spoke in verse:
"The world is forever in decline and darkness; The moon, king of stars, has suddenly fallen.
Enveloped by impermanence, The sun of great wisdom is forever eclipsed."
At that time, another bhikṣu spoke in verse:
"This body is like foam or bubbles; Who could find joy in its precarious fragility?
Even the Buddha’s vajra-body Is still destroyed by impermanence."
"The vajra-bodies of all Buddhas likewise return to impermanence;
they vanish as swiftly as a small amount of snow—what further hope can there be for others?
Thus the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the bhikṣus were overcome with grief and collapsed, throwing themselves upon the ground; they rolled about and wailed, unable to restrain themselves, sobbing as they said:
"How swift is the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa!"
How swift is the passing of the World-Honored One!
How rapid is the submergence of the Great Dharma!
All living beings suffer perpetual decline; the Eye of the World has been extinguished.
"It is as if a great tree has been uprooted and its branches broken;
or like a severed snake that writhes and reels about, not knowing where to turn.
At that time, the bhikṣus were likewise; overcome with grief and despair, they threw themselves upon the ground, rolling about and wailing, unable to restrain themselves, and spoke with sobs:
"How swift is the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa!
How rapid is the World-Honored One’s passing!
How quickly has the Great Dharma been eclipsed!"
"The multitude of beings will steadily decline; the eye of the world is extinguished.
At that time, the Elder Aniruddha addressed the bhikṣus: "Stop!
"Stop! Do not grieve; the devas are above, and they might perhaps reprove you for this.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked Aniruddha:
“How many heavens are there above?
Aniruddha replied, “They fill the entirety of space; how could they possibly be measured?”
They all hovered and flitted about in mid-air, wailing piteously and leaping about in grief, shedding tears as they said:
"How swift is the Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata!"
How swift is the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One!
How rapid is the submergence of the Great Dharma!
All living beings suffer perpetual decline; the Eye of the World has been extinguished.
"It is like a great tree whose roots have been uprooted and whose branches have been broken; or like a severed snake that writhes and turns in confusion, not knowing where to turn for refuge.
At that time, the devas were likewise; they all hovered and flitted about in the air, wailing and leaping in grief, shedding tears as they said:
"The Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata—how swift it has come!"
How swift is the Blessed One’s parinirvāṇa!
How rapid is the submergence of the Great Dharma!
All living beings suffer perpetual decline; the Eye of the World has been extinguished.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had discoursed on the Dharma throughout the entire night until dawn, Anuruddha addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You should enter the city and tell the Mallas:
'The Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa; whatever you wish to offer or perform, you should do so while there is still time.'"

At that time, Ānanda immediately rose, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and taking a bhikṣu with him, entered the city weeping. From afar, he saw five hundred Mallas gathered in one place for some minor reason.
When the Mallas saw Ānanda approaching, they all rose to welcome him, prostrated at his feet, and stood respectfully, saying to Ānanda:
"Why have you come so early? Ānanda replied:
"I have come here this morning desiring to benefit you. You should know:
the Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa last night; whatever you wish to perform, you should do so while there is still time."
When the Mallas heard these words, there was none among them who did not grieve with deep sorrow; wiping away their tears, they said:
"How swift it has been!
The Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa."
"How swift! The Eye of the World has been extinguished. Ānanda replied:
"Stop! Stop! Gentlemen, do not weep; it is impossible for that which is conditioned to remain unchanging."
The Buddha has already said:
"To those who are born there is death; to those who meet there is separation;
all that is dear and loved does not endure eternally."
At that time, the Mallas said to one another,
"We should each return home to prepare various incense, flowers, and musical performances, and quickly go to the twin trees to make offerings to the śarīra."

When the day had ended, they placed the Buddha’s relics upon a bier and had Malla youths lift its four corners. Carrying banners and canopies, burning incense and scattering flowers, they offered music and worship as they entered the eastern city gate and passed through all the streets and alleys, so that the people of the kingdom might all have the opportunity to make offerings.
Thereafter, they exited through the western city gate and went to a high and prominent place to perform the cremation.

When the Mallas had finished this discussion, they each returned to their own homes to prepare incense, flowers, and various musical performances, and then proceeded to the space between the twin trees to make offerings to the śarīra.
When the day had ended, they placed the Buddha’s relics upon the bier; the Mallas and their assembly came forward to lift the bier, but none were able to do so.
At that time, Anuruddha said to the Mallas:
"Cease for a moment! You all must stop!"
"Do not weary yourselves in vain; now the devas wish to lift this bier.
The Mallas asked, "With what intention do the devas wish to lift this bier?"

Aniruddha said: "If you wish to make offerings of incense, flowers, and music to the relics for an entire day, you should place the Buddha’s relics upon a bed and have the Malla youths lift the four corners of the bed. Holding up banners and canopies, burning incense and scattering flowers, and providing offerings with music, enter through the eastern city gate and pass through all the streets and alleys so that the people of the kingdom may all make offerings;
thereafter, exit through the western city gate and proceed to a high and prominent place to perform the cremation."
The devas, desiring to retain the śarīras for seven days so that they might pay homage and make offerings with fragrant flowers, music, and song, then placed the Buddha’s śarīras upon a couch.

They had the Malla youths lift the four corners of the couch, held aloft banners and canopies, scattered flowers, burned incense, and performed various musical performances as an offering to the śarīras.
Entering through the eastern city gate, he traveled through all the streets and alleys so that the people of the kingdom might all have the opportunity to make offerings;
thereafter, exiting through the northern city gate, he crossed the Hiraṇyavatī River and proceeded to Tiara Monastery, where he performed the cremation.
"This is the will of the gods, causing the bed not to move.
The Malla replied, "So be it!"
"How excellent are these words!
We shall follow the will of the devas.
At that time, the Mallas said to one another:
"We should first enter the city to level and repair the roads street by street, sweep and sprinkle them, and burn incense; then we shall return here to make offerings to the śarīra for seven days."

Then the Mallas entered the city together; from street to street, they leveled the roads, swept and sprinkled them, and burned incense. Having finished these tasks, they exited the city and, between the twin trees, made offerings of fragrant flowers and music to the relics.

When the seven days had passed and the sun was turning toward dusk, they placed the Buddha’s *śarīra* upon a couch; the Malla youths lifted its four corners, while they held aloft banners and canopies, burned incense, scattered flowers, and performed various musical performances as they proceeded with calm dignity, escorted by attendants before and behind.

At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven scattered mandārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, puṇḍarīka flowers, and celestial powdered sandalwood over the śarīra, filling the streets and roads.
The devas played music and the spirits sang hymns.
At that time, the Mallas said to one another, "Let us set aside human music;
let us instead provide divine music as an offering to the śarīra."

Thereupon, the Mallas carried the couch forward step by step, entering through the eastern city gate; they halted at every street and lane, burning incense, scattering flowers, and making offerings with music.
At that time, there was a Malla woman named Rūpā who had deep faith in the Buddha’s Way; she held in her hands a golden flower as large as a chariot wheel to make an offering to the śarīra.
Then, an old woman raised her voice and praised him, saying:
"These Mallans have attained great benefit; since the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa here at the very end, the people and officials of the entire nation have been joyfully able to make offerings."

At that time, after the Mallas had completed their offerings, they departed through the north gate of the city, crossed the Hiranyavati River, and arrived at the Makutabandhana Temple. They set down a couch upon the ground and said to Ānanda, "What further offering should we now provide?"

Ānanda replied, "I have heard this directly from the Buddha and received this instruction personally from the Buddha: those who wish to enshrine the śarīra should do so according to the funeral rites for a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
He asked Ānanda again:
"What is the funeral rite for a Wheel-Turning Sage King? He replied:

“The funeral rites for a sage-king are as follows: first, his body is washed with fragrant water; it is then wrapped entirely in new *karpāsa* cloth, followed by five hundred layers of fine cotton cloth wrapped in succession. The body is placed within a golden coffin and filled with sesame oil. Once this is complete, the golden coffin is lifted and placed within a second, larger iron outer coffin. A sandalwood coffin is then layered over that on the outside. Various famous incenses are piled up and spread thickly over them before the cremation is performed.”

Having collected the relics, he erected a stūpa at a crossroads, with a banner atop its spire and silken streamers suspended from it, so that all travelers throughout the kingdom might see the King’s stūpa, yearn for the True Dharma, and receive great benefit.

“Ānanda! When you wish to bury me, first bathe my body with fragrant water, wrap it all around with new *karpāsa* cloth, and then wrap it again with five hundred layers of fine cotton cloth, one after another.”

Having placed the inner golden coffin within and poured sesame oil over it, they lifted the golden coffin and set it inside a second, larger iron outer coffin. A sandalwood coffin was then layered on top of that as an outermost layer. Having piled up various famous incenses and covered them thickly upon the coffins, they performed the cremation.

Having collected the śarīra relics, he erected a stūpa at a crossroads, with a flagpole and suspended silk banners, so that all passersby might see the Buddha’s stūpa, contemplate the Tathāgata’s transformation through the Way of Dharma, obtain merit and benefit in this life, and attain rebirth in heaven after death—except for those who have already attained the Way.
Then, the Mallas said to one another:
"Let us return to the city and prepare the funeral requisites: incense, flowers, cotton cloth, inner and outer coffins, fragrant oils, and white silk."

Then, the Mallas entered the city together, prepared the funeral requisites, and returned to the Tiṣya-cūḍā Monastery. They bathed the Buddha’s body with pure scented water, wrapped it all around with new *karpāsa* cotton cloth, and then layered five hundred pieces of fine linen over it in succession.

The inner golden coffin was filled with fragrant oil; the golden coffin was then respectfully lifted and placed within a second large iron outer coffin. This outer coffin of sandalwood was further layered with heavy garments on its exterior, and various famous incenses were piled upon it.
At that time, there was a Malla minister named Rauruka who, grasping a great torch, sought to ignite the funeral pyre for the Buddha, but the fire would not burn.
Furthermore, another great Malla stepped forward next to light the pyre, yet the fire still would not burn.
Then, Anuruddha said to the Mallas: "Stop! Stop!"
"Venerable sirs!
It is not within your power that the fire has been extinguished and does not burn;
this is the will of the devas. The Mallas asked again:
"Why do the devas cause the fire not to burn?

Aniruddha replied, "The devas know that Mahākāśyapa, leading five hundred disciples from the kingdom of Pāvā, is now halfway there on his way; before the cremation has taken place, he wishes to behold the Buddha’s body. Therefore, the devas have caused the fire not to burn."
The Mallas replied, "We pray that this wish be fulfilled!
At that time, Mahākāśyapa was traveling along the road with five hundred disciples from the country of Pāvā when he encountered a Nirgrantha holding a mandārava flower in his hand.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa saw the Nirgrantha from afar and went toward him to ask,
"Where have you come from? He replied:
"I have come from the city of Kuśinagara.
Kāśyapa asked again,
"Do you know my teacher?"
He replied, “I know. He asked again:
"Is my teacher still living?
He replied, "It has already been seven days since he entered parinirvāṇa; I have come from there and obtained these celestial flowers."
Upon hearing this, Kāśyapa was despondent and displeased.

At that time, when the five hundred bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, they all wept with great sorrow, rolling on the ground and wailing so loudly that they could not restrain themselves;
wiping away their tears, they said: "How swift is the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata!"
How swift was the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One!
How rapid was the sinking and obscuring of the Great Dharma!
All living beings suffer perpetual decline; the Eye of the World has been extinguished.
"It is as if a great tree has been uprooted and its branches broken; it is like a severed snake that writhes and turns about, not knowing where to turn for refuge.
At that time, among the assembly was a son of the Śākyas named Upananda, who addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Do not grieve! Now that the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, I have attained freedom."
He used to say constantly, "One should practice this; one should not practice that.
From this day forward, follow whatever I do.
Having heard this, Kāśyapa was despondent and displeased; he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Quickly prepare your robes and bowls; let us go at once to the twin trees so that we may see the Buddha before his cremation."

At that time, having heard Mahākāśyapa’s words, the bhikṣus rose from their seats and followed him as he proceeded toward the city of Kuśinagara. Crossing the Nairañjanā River, they arrived at the Tiara Monastery and went to where Ānanda was.
Having exchanged greetings, they stood to one side and said to Ānanda:
"We wish to have a private audience with the Śarīra before it has been cremated; would it be possible for us to see it?"
Ānanda replied: “Although the cremation has not yet taken place, it will be difficult to see him again. Why is this so?”
The Buddha’s body, having been washed with fragrant water and wrapped in *karpāsa* cotton, was then successively wrapped in five hundred layers of fine cloth.

It was placed within a golden coffin, which was set inside an iron outer casing; this was further encased in a sandalwood coffin, its exterior heavily draped with cloth, for it was considered that the Buddha’s body would be difficult to behold again.
Kāśyapa requested three times, but Ānanda answered as before:
"It is because the Buddha’s body is difficult to behold again.

At that moment, Mahākāśyapa happened to be facing the incense pyre; then, from within the nested coffins, the Buddha’s two feet emerged together. His feet were of a different color, and having seen this, Kāśyapa asked Ānanda in wonder:
“The Buddha’s body is golden in color; why is it different at his feet?
Ānanda replied, “Just now, there was an old woman who approached in deep sorrow and stroked the Buddha’s feet with her hands; tears fell upon them, and for that reason, the color is different.”
Having heard this, Kāśyapa was once again deeply displeased; he immediately turned toward the incense pyre and paid homage to the Buddha’s relics.
At that moment, the fourfold assembly and the various deities above simultaneously prostrated themselves together, whereupon the Buddha’s feet suddenly vanished.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa circumambulated the funeral pyre three times and spoke this verse:
"The Buddhas are unequaled; Their noble wisdom is beyond measure.
To this peerless noble wisdom, I now prostrate in homage."
The peerless Śramaṇa, supreme and free from all defilement;
the Muni who has severed the branches of craving, the Great Sage, honored among gods and men;
the foremost hero among humanity—to him I now bow my head in homage.
In ascetic practice you have no equal; you teach others while remaining free from attachment.
Untainted and free from the dust of defilement, I bow my head to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Having exhausted the three stains, you delight in the practice of emptiness and stillness.
Without peer and without equal, I bow my head to the Honored One of Ten Powers.
The Sugata is the most supreme, the most honored among those with two feet;
having awakened to the Four Truths and attained cessation, I prostrate to the one of peaceful wisdom.
Supreme among śramaṇas, you turn those on wrong paths toward the Right;
World-Honored One, you bestow nirvāṇa—homage to your serene track.
Without fever and without flaw, your mind is perfectly tranquil and settled.
Having refined and removed all defilements, I bow my head to the Stainless Honored One.
With a wisdom-eye of infinite measure, whose fame is the nectar of cessation;
rare and inconceivable, I bow my head to the Peerless One.
“His roar is like that of a lion; dwelling in the forest, he has no fear.
Having subdued Māra and transcended the four castes—for this reason we bow our heads in worship.

After Mahākāśyapa, who possessed great majestic virtue and was endowed with the four analytical knowledges, had spoken these verses, the funeral pyre of that Buddha ignited spontaneously without being burned. Then the Mallas said to one another:
"Now this fire is fierce and blazing; its flames are so intense they are difficult to stop. When the śarīra are cremated, they may be entirely consumed. Where shall we seek water to extinguish it?"
At that time, there was a Śāla tree deity by the side of the funeral pyre who had profound faith in the Buddha’s Way; he immediately used his supernatural power to extinguish the fire of the pyre.
Then, the Mallas spoke to one another again:
"Let us gather all the fragrant flowers within twelve yojanas around this city of Kuśinagara to offer as an oblation for the Buddha’s relics."
He immediately went to the outskirts of the city, gathered various fragrant flowers, and used them for offering.
At that time, the Malla people of the kingdom of Pāvā, hearing that the Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa between the twin trees, all thought to themselves:
"We should now go and seek a portion of the relics so that we may erect a stūpa in our own land to offer worship."

At that time, the Mallas of Pāvā immediately mobilized the fourfold army of their kingdom—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and proceeded to the city of Kuśinagara. They dispatched a messenger with this message:

"We have heard that the Buddha, the Most Honored One, has entered parinirvāṇa here. He was also our teacher; out of a heart of reverence and longing, we come to request a portion of his relics so that we may erect a stūpa in our own country to offer worship."
The King of Kuśinagara replied: “So it is! So it is!”

It is exactly as you have said; however, since the World-Honored One descended to this land and attained parinirvāṇa here, the people of this realm should provide offerings themselves. You gentlemen have traveled from afar with great effort, but a share of the relics cannot be obtained.

At that time, the Vṛji people of the country of Cāpāla, the Koliya people of the country of Rāmagrāma, the Brahmin community of the country of Vaiśālī, the Śākya people of the country of Kapilavastu, the Licchavi people of the country of Vaiśālī, and King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, hearing that the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara, all thought to themselves:
"I should now go and seek a portion of the relics."

Then, the various kings, including Ajātaśatru, immediately mobilized the fourfold army of their kingdoms—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and advanced across the Ganges River. They then commanded the brahmin named Ghoṣila:
"Carry my name with you, enter the city of Kuśinagara, and inquire after the Mallas:
'Are you all well and at ease? Is your movement vigorous?'"
"Among the worthy ones, I have always held you in mutual respect; our neighboring realms have been harmonious in righteousness, never engaging in dispute or litigation.

I have heard that the Tathāgata attained parinirvāṇa within your kingdom. As he was the Unsurpassed Honored One, he is truly my celestial refuge. Therefore, I have come from afar to request a portion of his relics, desiring to return to my own land to erect a stupa and offer worship."
"If you grant it to me, I shall share all the precious treasures of the entire kingdom with you.
Then, having received the King's instructions, the brahmin of the Kharaka clan went to that city and said to the Mallas:
"The Great King of Magadha sends his boundless greetings:"
"I hope you are maintaining good health and that your movements are vigorous?
I have always held you all in high esteem; our neighboring realms have lived in righteous harmony, never engaging in dispute or litigation."

I have heard that the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa within your kingdom; as he is the Unsurpassed Honored One and truly our celestial protector, I have come from afar to request a portion of his relics, desiring to return to my own land to erect a stūpa and make offerings.
"If you grant it to me, I shall share the precious treasures of the entire kingdom with you.
At that time, the Mallas replied to the one of the Ghoṣila clan: "So be it!"
"So be it! It is exactly as you say.

However, since the World-Honored One descended to this land and attained parinirvāṇa here, the officials and citizens of this country shall naturally provide for his offerings. You have traveled from afar with great effort, but a share of the relics cannot be obtained."
At that time, the various kings immediately assembled their ministers and, after deliberating together, spoke in verse, saying:
"We have reached a peaceful agreement; He has come from afar to prostrate himself, Seeking a portion with humble words. If you do not grant it to him,"
"The fourfold army is here; we shall not spare our lives.
If it cannot be obtained through righteousness, we must take it by force.
At that time, the kingdom of Kuśinagara assembled its ministers, and they all deliberated together, responding with this verse:
"I thank you all for your long journey and for humbling yourselves by bowing your heads;
however, regarding the physical remains of the Tathāgata, I dare not grant them to you.
If they wish to raise an army, I likewise possess such means here."
"When our lives come to an end and we meet one another, there will be no fear.
At that time, the Brahmin of the Gandhāra clan addressed the assembly, saying:
"O worthy ones!"

Having long endured the Buddha’s admonitions, reciting his Dharma words with our mouths and submitting to his benevolent transformation in our hearts, we always desire the peace and security of all sentient beings; how could we possibly contend over the Buddha’s relics and bring about mutual destruction?
"The Tathāgata has left behind his physical remains with the desire to bring widespread benefit; since the śarīra are now present, we should simply divide them.
Everyone acclaimed this as excellent, and they immediately deliberated further, saying:
"Who is capable of dividing them?"
They all said, "The Brahmin Vasiṣṭha is benevolent and impartial; he may be appointed to divide [the relics].
Thereupon, the kings immediately commanded Vasiṣṭha:
"For our sake, divide the Buddha’s śarīra into eight equal portions."

At that time, having heard the words of the kings, Ghoṣila went to the place where the relics were, prostrated himself with his head at their feet, and then slowly stepped forward to take the Buddha’s upper tooth and set it aside.
He immediately dispatched a messenger carrying the Buddha’s upper tooth to the residence of King Ajātaśatru, saying to the messenger:
"In my name, report to the Great King:
'Are you light and well in your daily life? Is your gait strong and vigorous?'"
Have you been waiting for the arrival of the śarīras for an immeasurable length of time?

I now entrust these two upper teeth of the Tathāgata to this messenger; they may both be used for veneration to comfort your longing. When the morning star appears, the distribution of the śarīras will be completed, and I shall personally send them to you.
Then, having received the words of the Brahmin Ghoṣila, the messenger went to King Ajātaśatru and said to him:
"The Brahmin Ghoṣila sends his greetings:
'Are you light and at ease? Is your movement vigorous?'"
Have you been waiting for the arrival of the śarīra relics for an immeasurable length of time?

I now entrust these two upper teeth of the Tathāgata to this messenger; they may both be used for worship to console your longing. When the morning star appears, the distribution of the śarīra will be completed, and I shall personally send them to you.
At that time, the one of the Gandaka clan took a jar with a capacity of about one *shi*, immediately divided the *śarīra* relics into eight equal portions, and addressed the assembly, saying:
"I wish for you all to grant me this jar by common consent, so that I may erect a stūpa in my own home to offer worship."
They all said, "Wise indeed!
This is knowing the proper time; we shall all consent to grant it."
At that time, a man from the village of Pipphalivana addressed the assembly, saying:
"I beg for the charred remains of the ground to erect a stūpa in worship. They all said:
"Give it to them. At that time, the people of Kuśinagara obtained their share of the *śarīra* relics and immediately erected a stūpa in their land to make offerings to them.

The people of Pāvā, Cāla, Rāmagrāma, Vaiśālī, Kapilavastu, Vaiśālī, and King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, having each obtained their shares of the *śarīra*, returned to their respective countries and erected stūpas to make offerings to them.
The Brahmin Ghaṭīkāra took the jar containing the relics and returned to erect a stūpa; the people of Pipphalivana took the charred earth from the site and returned to erect a stūpa.
At that time, eight stūpas were erected for the Tathāgata’s relics: the ninth was the jar-stūpa, the tenth was the charcoal-stūpa, and the eleventh was the hair-stūpa from his birth.
At what time was the Buddha born?
At what time did he attain enlightenment?
At what time did he pass into parinirvāṇa?

He was born when the Puṣya constellation appeared; he left home when the Puṣya constellation appeared; he attained the Way when the Puṣya constellation appeared; he entered parinirvāṇa when the Puṣya constellation appeared. (The commentary on the Dan edition notes: "In the 'Questions,' there should be [an inquiry regarding] at what times one leaves home; this is missing from all other editions.")
What gives birth to the Honored One among Two-legged Beings?
What emerges from the suffering of the thicket?
What attains the supreme path?
What is it that enters the city of Nirvāṇa?
Under the Puṣya star, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings was born; under the Puṣya star, he emerged from the forest of suffering;
under the Puṣya star, he attained the supreme path; under the Puṣya star, he entered the city of Nirvāṇa.
On the eighth day the Tathāgata was born; On the eighth day the Buddha left the home life;
On the eighth day he attained Bodhi; On the eighth day he entered Parinirvāṇa.
On the eighth day the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings was born; On the eighth day he emerged from the suffering of the thicket.
On the eighth day he attained the supreme path; on the eighth day he entered the city of Nirvāṇa.
In the second month the Tathāgata was born; in the second month the Buddha left home;
in the second month he attained Bodhi; on the eighth day he took Nirvāṇa.
In the second month, the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings was born; In the second month, he emerged from the suffering of the thicket;
In the second month, he attained the supreme path; On the eighth day, he entered the city of Nirvāṇa.
The sāla flowers flourish, their various radiant forms illuminating one another;
at his place of birth, the Tathāgata attained parinirvāṇa.
Through his great compassion, he entered parinirvāṇa, praised and venerated by many.
Having completely crossed over all fears, one will certainly attain parinirvāṇa.

(3) *Dianzun jing* (Sūtra on the Venerable Scripture), Part One, Section Three.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, Pañcaśikha, the son of the Gandharva king Citraratha, during a night of profound stillness when no one else was present, emitted a great radiance that illuminated Vulture Peak Mountain as he approached the Buddha’s dwelling. Having prostrated his head at the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side.
Then Pañcaśikha addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Yesterday, Brahmā Sahāmpati went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and deliberated with Śakra Devendra.
I personally heard this from him; may I now relate it to the World-Honored One?"
The Buddha said, "If you wish to speak, you may do so. Pañcaśikha replied:
"At one time, the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven gathered in the Hall of Dharma Discourse to engage in discussion.
At that time, the Four Great Kings each sat in their respective positions according to their quarters: King Dhṛtarāṣṭra sat in the east facing west with Śakra before him;
King Virūḍhaka sat in the south facing north with Śakra before him;"
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa sat in the west facing east, with Śakra before him;
the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa sat in the north facing south, with Śakra before him.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all sat down first, and only then did I sit. Furthermore, there were other great divine beings who, having previously cultivated the pure Brahma-faring under the Buddha, passed away from there and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. They caused those devas to increase in five blessings:
first, celestial longevity; second, celestial complexion; third, celestial renown; fourth, celestial happiness; and fifth, celestial majesty and virtue.
At that time, all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven leaped for joy and said,
"The hosts of devas are increased, and the hosts of asuras are diminished. Then, Śakra Devānām Indra,
knowing that the devas possessed hearts of joy, immediately spoke this verse for the sake of the Trāyastriṃśa gods:
“The devas and humans of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, together with Śakra, enjoy themselves;
they pay homage to the Tathāgata, the supreme King of Dharma.”
The various devas receive the blessings of their reflections: longevity, beauty, renown, happiness, and majesty;
because they practiced the holy life under the Buddha, they have been born here.
Furthermore, there are various devas whose radiance and color are most majestic;
the disciples of the Buddha’s wisdom, having been born here, are even more sublime.
Those of the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens contemplate this and find joy within themselves.
"I pay homage to the Tathāgata, the supreme King of Dharma.
At that time, having heard this verse, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were filled with redoubled joy beyond measure; the hosts of devas increased, while the hosts of asuras diminished.
Seeing the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven filled with joy and delight, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed them, saying:
"Virtuous ones! Would you like to hear of the eight peerless qualities of the Tathāgata?"
Then the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven said,
"We wish to hear it with joy! Śakra replied:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well."
"Virtuous ones!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles—neither in the past, nor in the future, nor in the present, has there ever been seen a Tathāgata, an Arhat, fully endowed with the ten titles, such as this Buddha."

The Buddha-dharma is subtle and wondrous, and can be skillfully expounded; it is the practice of the wise. One does not see anyone—whether in the past, the future, or the present—who possesses a subtle and wondrous Dharma equal to that of the Buddha.

By means of this Dharma, the Buddha attained self-awakening, achieved unimpeded penetration, and found therein his own delight; he saw no one among those of the past, future, or present who could attain self-awakening, achieve unimpeded penetration, and find their own delight in this Dharma as the Buddha has done.
"Venerable friends!
Having personally realized this Dharma through self-awakening, the Buddha is also able to reveal the path to Nirvana, which, when approached and gradually traversed, leads to entry into cessation."
For example, the waters of the Ganges and the Yamunā flow together and enter the great ocean.

The Buddha is likewise; he is well able to reveal the path to nirvāṇa, and by drawing near to it gradually, one enters into quiescent extinction. One does not see anyone in the past, future, or present who can reveal the path to nirvāṇa as the Buddha does.
"Virtuous ones!

The Tathāgata’s retinue is perfected: kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, śramaṇas, and those possessed of wisdom—all these constitute the Tathāgata’s perfected retinue. I do not see any perfection of a retinue in the past, future, or present that is equal to that of the Buddha."
Venerable friends!

The Tathāgata’s assembly is perfected—namely, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—and I do not see any assembly, whether of the past, future, or present, that is as perfected as the Buddha’s.
"Venerable friends!

The Tathāgata’s words and deeds are in accord; what he says accords with his practice, and his practice accords with what he says. Thus, he is one who has achieved the perfection of the Dharma through the Dharma, such that no one else—whether of the past, the future, or the present—is seen to have achieved the perfection of the Dharma through the Dharma with words and deeds in accord as the Buddha does."
Venerable friends!

The Tathāgata brings great benefit and great happiness; with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, he benefits devas and humans. I have not seen anyone in the past, future, or present who brings such great benefit and great happiness as the Buddha does.
"Virtuous ones!
These are the eight peerless qualities of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven spoke thus:
"If there were eight Buddhas to appear in the world, it would greatly increase the hosts of devas and diminish the hosts of asuras.
At that time, the Trāyastriṃśa devas said:

"Setting aside eight Buddhas for a moment, even if seven Buddhas, six Buddhas, or even two Buddhas were to appear in the world, it would still greatly increase the hosts of devas and diminish the hosts of asuras; how much more so in the case of eight Buddhas?"
Then Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:
"I have heard this from the Buddha; I have received it directly from the Buddha: it is impossible for two Buddhas to appear in the world at the same time."

Provided that the Tathāgata remains long in the world, bringing great compassion and great benefit, so that devas and humans may obtain peace, then the hosts of devas will greatly increase and the multitude of asuras will diminish.
At that time, Pañcaśikha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

The reason the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven gather in the Hall of Dharma is to deliberate, reflect, weigh, and examine matters; once they have issued their instructions, they then proclaim them to the Four Great Kings.”
Having received these instructions, the Four Kings each sat in their respective positions. Not long after they were seated, a great and extraordinary light shone forth in the four directions.
At that time, when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven saw this light, they were all greatly startled and asked, "What strange phenomenon does this extraordinary light portend?"
The great deities possessing majesty and virtue were likewise all struck with alarm, wondering:
"What strange omen does this extraordinary light portend?

At that moment, the Great Brahmā King transformed himself into a youth with five topknots of hair; standing in the void above the great assembly, his countenance was upright and peerless among the multitude, his body golden-purple in hue, outshining the radiance of all the devas.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven neither rose to welcome him, nor showed him respect, nor invited him to sit.
The Brahmā-son sat wherever he went; as he sat, he felt a sense of joy, just like a Kṣatriya of the water-sprinkled lineage who leaps for joy and exults when ascending the royal throne.

Not long after he had sat down, he again transformed his body into the form of a youth with five topknots on his head; he sat in the air above the great assembly, as steady and unmoving as a strongman seated upon a comfortable cushion.
And he spoke in verse:
“The devas and humans of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, Together with Śakra, enjoy their pleasures;
Yet they pay homage to the Tathāgata, The supreme King of Dharma.”
The various devas receive the blessings of their shadows: longevity, beauty, renown, happiness, and majesty;
because they practiced the holy life under the Buddha, they have been reborn here.
Furthermore, there are various devas and humans whose radiance and color are most majestic;
the disciples of the Buddha’s wisdom, born here, are even more sublime.
Those of the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens contemplate this as their own bliss.
"I pay homage to the Tathāgata, the supreme King of Dharma.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven said to the youth:
"We have heard the Lord Śakra proclaim the eight peerless qualities of the Tathāgata; we are so filled with joy and exultation that we cannot contain ourselves."
Then, the Brahma youth spoke to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, saying:
"What are the eight peerless qualities of a Tathāgata?
I, too, would delight to hear them."

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately expounded to the youth the Eight Peerless Qualities of the Tathāgata. Upon hearing this teaching, the youth and the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were redoubled in joy, unable to contain themselves; the hosts of devas increased, while the hosts of asuras diminished.
At that time, seeing the gods rejoicing, the youth’s own joy increased even further, and he addressed the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:
"Do you wish to hear a peerless Dharma?"
The deva said, “Excellent!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
The youth said: "If you wish to hear it, listen attentively! Receive it with careful heed!"
"I shall explain it for you.
He then addressed the devas, saying:
"In the past, when the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, he was intelligent and possessed great wisdom in every place where he was born."
Virtuous ones!
You should know that in the distant past, there was a king named Bhūmipati, whose eldest crown prince was named Maitrībala.
The king had a chief minister named Agganna, and the minister had a son named Jyotir-mālā.
The Prince had compassionate friends, and those friends were also friends with six Kṣatriya ministers.

Whenever the Great King, the Lord of the Earth, wished to enter the inner palace for diversion and pleasure, he would entrust the affairs of state to the minister Mahāgovinda before entering the palace to perform music and entertain himself with the five desires.
At that time, when the minister Mahāgovinda wished to attend to state affairs, he would first consult his son before making a decision;
likewise, whenever there was a matter to be disposed of, he would also consult his son.
"Subsequently, the Honored Director suddenly passed away. When King Bhūmipati heard of his death, he was filled with compassion and grief, and beating his breast, he said: 'Alas!'"
"What crime has this worthy pillar of the state committed that he has lost his kingdom?
The Prince, out of compassion, silently thought to himself:
"The King grieves over the loss of his dignified minister; I should now go to admonish the Great King so that he does not give rise to sorrow and suffering because of that loss."

Why is this so? The Venerable Steward has a son named Jyotiṣka, who is intelligent and possessed of great wisdom even exceeding that of his father; he may now be summoned to manage the affairs of state.

At that time, Prince Maitrībala went to the king’s presence and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to his father, the king. Having heard the prince’s words, the king immediately summoned Jvālāmālin and addressed him, saying:
"I shall now appoint you to fill your father's position and confer upon you the seal of state."
At that time, having received the seal of state from Jyotiṣpāla, the king wished to enter the palace and entrusted him with the affairs of state.

Then, Jyotiṣpāla became proficient in governance; he understood everything his father had previously accomplished, and he also understood what his father had not reached. Subsequently, his fame spread throughout the land, and all under heaven called him Mahāgovinda.

Then, the Great Steward later had this thought: "Now King Mahāpaṇḍita is already advanced in years; his remaining lifespan is short. It would not be difficult for the crown prince to succeed him to the throne. I should now go first and speak to those six Kṣatriya ministers, saying: 'Now King Mahāpaṇḍita is already advanced in years; his remaining lifespan is short. It would not be difficult for the crown prince to succeed him to the throne.'"
"You all, too, shall each receive a separate royal domain; on the day you take up your positions, do not forget one another.
At that time, Mahāgovinda went to the six Kṣatriya ministers and addressed them, saying:
"Gentlemen!..."
You should know that King Bhūmipati is now advanced in years and his remaining lifespan is short; if the crown prince succeeds to the throne, it will not be difficult.
"You should go and inform the Prince of this intention: 'We have known Your Honor since childhood; your suffering was our suffering, and your joy was our joy.
Now the King is aged and decrepit, with but little life remaining. It will not be difficult for the Prince to succeed to the royal throne; should you ascend it, you must grant us a fief.'"
At that time, when the six Kṣatriya ministers heard these words, they immediately went to the Prince and related the matter as described above.
The Prince replied:
"If I were to ascend the throne and divide the lands to establish feudal states, with whom else would I share them?"
Not long after, the king suddenly passed away. The high ministers of the kingdom promptly invested the crown prince to fill the throne.
Once the king had ascended the throne, he reflected silently to himself:
"In appointing a prime minister now, I should follow the precedent of my late father."
He further reflected to himself:
"Who is capable of undertaking this task?
It is precisely Mahāgovinda who should be appointed to this position."
At that time, the King, moved by compassion, addressed the Great Steward:
"I now appoint you to the position of Prime Minister and confer upon you the seal of office; you should be diligent and concerned, overseeing and managing the affairs of state."
At that time, having heard the King’s command, Mahāgovinda accepted the seal of authority; whenever the King entered the palace, he would invariably entrust the affairs of state to Mahāgovinda.
Mahāgovinda thought to himself again:
"I should now go to the six kṣatriyas and ask whether they remember what was said in the past.
He immediately went to them and spoke to the kṣatriyas, saying:
"Do you still remember what you said in the past?

Now that the Prince has ascended the throne, he dwells in the secluded inner palace, delighting himself with the five desires. You should go now and ask the King: 'Since Your Majesty occupies the royal station and delights yourself with the five desires, do you still remember what you said in the past?'"
At that time, having heard these words, the six kṣatriyas went at once to the king’s presence and said to the Great King:
“Your Majesty dwells in the celestial station, delighting yourself in the five desires; can you truly remember what was said in the past?”
"To whom should the division of lands and the granting of fiefs belong?
The King said,
"Not forgetting my former words, if it is not you, O Minister, to whom else should they belong?"
The king thought again to himself:
"This land of Jambudvīpa is broad within and narrow without; who is able to divide it into seven portions?
He then thought further:
"Only the Great Steward is capable of dividing this;
you should divide this land of Jambudvīpa into seven parts. He then addressed him, saying: "You may divide this land of Jambudvīpa so as to make it sevenfold."

Then, the Great Steward immediately proceeded to divide them; he apportioned the cities ruled by the king, the villages, towns, districts, and states, all of which were distributed into six parts, and the six Kṣatriya kingdoms were likewise divided.
The king expressed his own joy, saying:
"My wish has been fulfilled!
At that time, the six kṣatriyas likewise rejoiced in their own good fortune.
"My vow has been fulfilled; I have accomplished this task through the power of the Great Minister.
The six Kṣatriya kings then reflected to themselves:
"Our kingdom has just been established and we require a prime minister. Who is capable of bearing this responsibility?"
"Let Mahāgovinda be appointed to oversee the affairs of state.
Then, the six Kṣatriya kings summoned Mahāgovinda and addressed him, saying:
"Our country requires a minister; you shall serve as our minister to oversee the affairs of state."
Thereupon, each of the six kingdoms conferred upon him the seal of state.

When Mahāgovinda had received the seals, the six kings entered their palaces for recreation and pleasure; they then entrusted all matters of state to Mahāgovinda. Mahāgovinda administered the affairs of the seven kingdoms, and there was nothing he did not successfully accomplish.

At that time, there were seven great householders within the kingdom; Mahāgovinda also managed their domestic affairs and was able to instruct seven hundred brahmins in the recitation of the scriptures. The seven kings regarded Mahāgovinda with such reverence as if he were a deity, the seven householders of the kingdom looked upon him as a great king, and the seven hundred brahmins viewed him as Brahmā.
At that time, the seven kings, the seven great householders, and seven hundred brahmins all thought to themselves:
"The Great Steward constantly meets with Brahmā; they converse, sit, and rise together in friendly intimacy."
At that time, Mahāgovinda silently understood the thoughts of the seven kings, householders, and brahmins, thinking:
"I am constantly seen by Brahmā, and we converse and sit together;
yet in truth, I have never actually seen Brahmā nor conversed with him. It would be improper for me to remain silent and accept this reputation in vain."
I have also heard the words of former masters:
"If one dwells in a quiet place during the four months of summer and cultivates the four immeasurables, Brahmā will descend to meet them face to face."
"Now, why should I not cultivate the four immeasurables so that Brahmā will descend, and we may meet one another?
Thereupon, Mahāgovinda went to the seven kings and said to them:
"I pray only that Your Majesties attend to the affairs of state; I wish to cultivate the four immeasurables during the four months of the summer retreat."
The seven kings replied,
"Know that the time has come.
The Great Steward then addressed the seven householders:
"You each should diligently attend to your own duties; I wish to practice the four immeasurables during the four months of summer.
The lay devotee replied, "Yes!"
"You should know that this is the time.
He further addressed the seven hundred brahmins:
"You all should diligently recite [the scriptures] and teach one another; I wish to cultivate the four immeasurables during the four months of the summer retreat."
The brahmin said:
"Yes! Now, Great Master, you should know that the time has come."

Then, the Great Steward built a secluded chamber to the east of that city and stayed there for the four months of the summer retreat, cultivating the four immeasurables. Yet, that Brahmā still did not descend. The Steward thought to himself:
"I have heard from the words of the ancient elders that by cultivating the four immeasurables during the four months of summer, Brahmā descends to appear."
"Now it is utterly still; there is not even a faint trace of it.

At that time, on the fifteenth day when the moon was full, Mahāgovinda emerged from his quiet chamber and sat upon the open ground. Not long after he had sat down, a great light appeared. Mahāgovinda thought to himself:
"Is this extraordinary light perhaps an auspicious omen that Brahmā intends to descend?"

Then, the Brahmā King immediately transformed himself into a youth with five topknots on his head and sat in the air above the Lord of the Sūtra. Having seen this, the Lord of the Sūtra spoke a verse, saying:
"What deity is this whose form appears here?"
"Abiding in the midst of space, his light illuminates the four quarters like a great bonfire blazing.
Then, the Brahmā-juvenile replied in verse:
"Only the devas of the Brahma-world know me as the Brahmā-juvenile."
"The others say of me: 'He performs sacrifices to the Great Deity.
" At that time, Mahāgovinda replied with a verse:
"Now I shall consult and receive [his teaching], honoring his instructions with the utmost reverence."
"I have prepared various kinds of superior flavors; may the gods know my heart's intent.
Then, the Brahma youth replied in verse:
"O Lord of the World, that which you practice—what is it you seek to attain?"
"Now that this offering has been presented, I shall accept it for your sake.
He then addressed Mahāgovinda: "If you have anything to ask, feel free to ask; I shall explain it for you."
At that time, the Great Steward thought to himself:
"Should I now ask about present matters,
or should I ask about future matters?"
He further thought to himself:
"What is the use of asking about the manifest affairs of this present life?
I should ask about the hidden matters of the future."
He then addressed the Brahmā-son with a verse, asking:
"Now I ask the Brahmā-son, who can resolve my doubts so that I am free from them:
By what training and by abiding in what dharma Does one attain birth in the Brahma-heaven?"
Then the Brahmā youth replied in verse:
“One should abandon the notions of ‘self’ and ‘person,’ Dwelling alone to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness;
By removing desire and being free from foul impurities, One may then be born in the Brahma Heaven.”
At that time, having heard this verse, the Great Steward thought to himself:
"The Brahma youth has spoken this verse; it ought to remove foul odors, yet I do not understand it. I should now ask him further."
Then, the Great Steward immediately asked in verse:
“The Brahmā-gāthā speaks of stench and impurity; I pray that you will now explain it to me:
Who opens the gates of the world, Causing one to fall into evil and not be born in heaven?”
Then the Brahma youth replied in verse:
"Deceitful and harboring jealousy, Practicing pride and overweening pride,
With greed, hatred, and delusion, They indulge themselves, concealing these within their hearts."
"This world is foul and impure; I shall now speak so that you may know it.
This opens the door to the world, leading one to fall into evil realms and fail to be born in heaven.
When Mahāgovinda heard this verse, he further thought to himself:

"I have now understood the meaning of 'putridity' as explained by the Brahma-śiṣya; however, those who dwell at home have no means to eliminate it. I would rather now renounce the world to leave the household life, shave off my hair and beard, don the dharma-robes, and cultivate the Way!"
At that time, the Brahma-son, knowing his resolve, addressed him in verse:
"If you possess such courage and this aspiration is so sublime, It is the deed of a wise man;
after death, you shall surely be born in the Brahma-heaven."
"Then, the Brahmā youth suddenly vanished.
At that time, Mahāgovinda returned to the seven kings and said to them: 'Great Kings!'"

I only pray that you will deign to attend to the affairs of state with wisdom. As for me, I now desire to leave the world and enter the homeless life to practice the Way in monastic robes. Why is this?
Because I personally heard the Brahma-Boy speak of foulness and impurity, and my heart finds it utterly loathsome.
"If he remains a householder, there is no way for him to attain liberation.
At that time, the seven kings thought to themselves:
"Brahmins are generally greedy for wealth and treasures; we would now rather open our treasuries wide and let him take whatever he requires, so that he does not go forth from home."
At that time, the seven kings immediately summoned the Venerable Dignity and addressed him, saying:
"Whatever you may require, we shall provide it all to you; there is no need for you to leave the household life."
Then, the Great Steward immediately addressed the King, saying:

"I have already received the King's bounty and possess great wealth myself; I now offer all of it to Your Majesty. I pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life, so that I may fulfill my aspiration."
Then the seven kings again thought to themselves:
"Brahmins are generally greedy for beautiful women; we would now rather bring out the palace ladies to satisfy their desires, so that they will not leave the household life."
The King immediately summoned the Chief Steward and addressed him, saying:
"If you require court ladies, I shall give them all to you; there is no need for you to leave the household life.
The Chief Steward replied:

"I have now already received the King's gift; however, my own household has many female attendants, whom I shall now all dismiss, seeking to leave behind affection and love in order to renounce the world and cultivate the Way."
Why is this so? I personally heard from the Brahma Youth a discourse on foulness, and my heart found it utterly loathsome.
For one who lives at home, there is no way to eliminate it.
Then, the Great Steward addressed King Maitrībala in verse:
"May the King listen to my words; for the King is the most honored among men.
Though he may grant me wealth, jewels, and court ladies, these treasures are not what I desire."
Then, King Maitrībala replied in verse:
“In the city of Dantakhaṇḍa, in the city of Kaliṅga, In the city of Aparagoyānī,
in the city of Uttarakuru, In the city of Aṅga, and in the city of Campā.”
The city of Śrāvastī, the city of Setavyā, and the city of Vārāṇasī—
these were all built by you, O Honored One of the Scriptures.
If there is anything lacking in the five desires, I shall provide it all to you.
"You should manage the affairs of state together; there is no need for you to leave the household life.
At that time, Mahāgovinda replied with a verse:
"I have had no lack of the five desires, yet I myself find no pleasure in the world."
"Having heard what the deva has said, my mind no longer dwells upon returning to the household life.
Then, King Compassionate replied in verse:
"As for what the Great Steward has said, from which deva did you hear it?"
"Having abandoned the five desires, I now ask you;
please answer me. Then, the Great Steward replied in verse:
"Long ago, in a secluded place, sitting alone I reflected within myself:"
"At that time, the Brahmā King arrived, universally emitting great radiance;
having heard this from him, I no longer took pleasure in the world.
Then, King Compassion addressed him in verse:
"Wait a moment, Great Steward; together let us propagate the transformation of the wholesome Dharma.
Thereafter, we shall both leave the household life, and you shall be my teacher."
"Just as the void of space is filled with pure lapis lazuli;
so now my pure faith pervades the entirety of the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, Mahāgovinda again spoke in verse:
“‘All gods and people of the world, Should abandon the five desires,
Eliminate all defilements, And purely cultivate the holy life.’”
At that time, the seven kings said to Mahāgovinda:

"Would it not be well if you were to remain among us for seven years, enjoying the five worldly desires together with us in mutual delight; and thereafter, having renounced your kingdoms and entrusted them each to your sons and younger brothers, you all go forth from the household life together?"
"Whatever you have obtained, I shall likewise obtain.
Then, Mahāgovinda replied to the seven kings: "The world is impermanent;
human life passes swiftly. Even between breaths, it is difficult to preserve; how much more so for seven years—is that not far indeed?"
The seven kings spoke again:

"If seven years is too long, how about six years, five years, or even down to one year? Let us remain in our secluded palaces, enjoying the five worldly desires together for recreation; thereafter, we shall renounce our kingdoms, entrust them each to our sons and younger brothers, and all go forth from home together—would that not be excellent?"
"As you have obtained [this], so too should I. Then, the Great Steward replied to the King:

"In this world, all things are impermanent; human life passes swiftly. Even between breaths, it is difficult to preserve; even a single year is still long. Likewise, seven months, down to a single month, are likewise not possible [to wait]."
The king spoke again, saying:

"Stay for seven days more in the deep palace, enjoying the five worldly desires to the full and delighting one another; after that, you may renounce the kingdom, entrust it each to your own sons and younger brothers, and all go forth together into the homeless life—is this not excellent?"
The Great Steward replied:

"Seven days is not far off; you may remain here. I only pray that Your Majesty will not violate your pledge of faith; if the King does not depart after the seven days have passed, I shall go forth into homelessness myself."
Then, the Great Steward went again to the seven householders and said to them:
"Each of you attend to your own affairs; I wish to leave the household life to cultivate the Way of Non-action."
Why is this so? I personally heard from Brahmā speak of foulness and impurity, and my heart finds it deeply loathsome.
If one remains at home, there is no way to eliminate it.
At that time, the seven householders replied to the Venerable Sthavira: "Excellent!
Such a resolve!"
"You should know that this is the time; we also wish to go forth together with you. Just as you have attained [this state], so too should we.
Then, Mahāgovinda went again to the place where the seven hundred brahmins were and addressed them, saying:

"Gentlemen, you should diligently recite the scriptures and extensively investigate the meaning of the Way, teaching one another in turn. I wish to go forth and cultivate the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
Why is this so? I personally heard from Brahmā that [the world] is foul and impure; my heart loathes it deeply, and if one remains at home, there is no way to eliminate it.
Then, the seven hundred brahmins said to the Venerable Master:
"Great Teacher!
Do not go forth into homelessness."
Those who live at home enjoy peace and happiness, delighting themselves in the five desires, with many attendants and no mental distress or suffering.
Those who have left the home life dwell alone in empty wilds; they lack all that is desired and have nothing to covet or grasp.
The Elder replied: "If I had considered living at home to be happiness and leaving the home life to be suffering, I would never have left the home life;
because I consider living at home to be suffering and leaving the home life to be happiness, that is why I have gone forth."
The brahmin replied:
"When the Great Master leaves the household life, I too shall leave the household life;
whatever the Great Master practices, I too shall practice in its entirety."
Then, the Great Steward went to his wives and addressed them, saying:

"Ladies, you may stay as you wish, or you may return home; I intend to leave the household life to seek the Way of the Unconditioned. He then explained the aforementioned matters in detail, clarifying his intention to renounce the world.

Then the wives replied: "While the Great Steward is alive, he is just like our husband and just like our father. Even if he were now to renounce the household life, we would surely follow him; whatever the Steward practices, we too ought to practice."
"After seven days had passed, the Great Steward immediately shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three Dharma robes, and left the household life.

At that time, seven kings, seven great householders, seven hundred brahmins, and forty ladies-in-waiting—following in this manner, eighty-four thousand people simultaneously went forth from the household life, following the Great Steward."
At that time, the Great Steward traveled through various kingdoms with a great multitude, widely propagating the transformative teachings of the Way and bringing benefit to many.
"At that time," the Brahma King said to the assembly of devas,
"'Was the Great Minister, the Steward, anyone other than this person?'"
Do not form such a view; the present Śākyamuni Buddha is that very person.

After seven days had passed, the World-Honored One left the household life to practice the Way, leading a great multitude of followers as he traveled through various kingdoms, widely propagating the transformative teachings of the Dharma and bringing benefit to many.

If you have any further doubts regarding my words, the World-Honored One is currently at Vulture Peak; you may go there to inquire, and you should receive and uphold them exactly as the Buddha speaks.
Pañcaśikha said: "It is for this reason that I have come here.
Indeed, World-Honored One!"
Was that Great Steward indeed the World-Honored One?

Did the World-Honored One, after seven days had passed, leave the household life to practice the Way, and together with seven kings and as many as eighty-four thousand people, simultaneously renounce the world, travel through various kingdoms, extensively propagate the transformation of the Way, and bring great benefit to many?
The Buddha told Pañcaśikha:
"At that time, was the Great Steward anyone else?
Do not harbor such a thought; he was none other than myself."
At that time, whenever the men and women of the entire country encountered any misfortune or damage in their daily activities, they would immediately raise their voices and say:
"Namo to the Great Honored One, the Prime Minister of the Seven Kings!"
"Homage to the Great Venerable One, the Seven Kings,
the Great Minister! Thus he said three times, Pañcaśikha!

At that time, although Mahāgovinda possessed great power and virtue, he was unable to explain the ultimate path to his disciples, unable to enable them to attain the ultimate holy life, and unable to lead them to the state of peace and security.
The Dharma he taught was received and practiced by his disciples; when their bodies perished and their lives ended, they were reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
Those of the next level, whose practice was shallower, were reborn in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;

next, in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, Tuṣita Heaven, Yāma Heaven, Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; and finally, among the Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, and great households of laymen, where they possessed mastery over all that they desired.

“Pañcasikha! Those disciples of that Great Steward have all left the household life free from doubt; they possess the fruits of retribution and receive instruction, yet it is not the ultimate path. It cannot lead them to the fulfillment of the holy life, nor can it bring them to the state of ultimate peace.”
As for those whose path is superior, it reaches at most as far as the Brahma Heaven.
Now, when I teach the Dharma to my disciples, I am able to enable them to attain the ultimate path, the ultimate holy life, and ultimate peace, so that they finally return to Nirvana.

When my disciples accept and practice the Dharma I have taught, they abandon the outflows (*āsrava*) and become free from them, attaining liberation of mind (*ceto-vimukti*) and liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
In this very life, they realize for themselves:
"Birth and death are ended, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
Next, those whose practice is shallow sever the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*) and attain parinirvāṇa in the heavenly realms, never again returning to this world.
Next, with the exhaustion of the three fetters (*trīṇi saṃyojanāni*) and the attenuation of lust, anger, and delusion, they return to this world once more before attaining parinirvāṇa.

Next, by severing the three fetters, they attain the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*); they do not fall into the evil destinies and, after wandering at most seven times among gods and humans, will certainly attain nirvāṇa.

Pancasikha! My disciples do not doubt their renunciation; it has its fruit and its reward, its instruction and its admonition. It culminates in the Dharma, culminates in the holy life, and culminates in peace and security, ultimately leading to Nirvana.
At that time, Pañcaśikha, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
**The Śāṇakavāsin Sūtra (4)** The Fourth Sūtra of the First Division of the Long Discourses Spoken by the Buddha: The Śāṇakavāsin Sūtra. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Nadi-Kaṇḍaka residence together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was sitting in a quiet room, reflecting silently to himself:
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!"
The Tathāgata’s bestowing of predictions upon others brings great benefit.

When the minister Gaggara passed away, the Tathāgata made a prediction concerning him, saying: "When this person passes away, having severed the five lower fetters, he will attain parinirvāṇa in the heavenly realms and shall not return to this world."

The second was Kaliṅga, the third Vigata, the fourth Kaliśu, the fifth Chala, the sixth Vayala, the seventh Vadhula, the eighth Subhadhula, the ninth Tālisana, the tenth Subhadrisana, the eleventh Yashu, and the twelfth Yashodhara. When these various ministers passed away, the Buddha likewise prophesied that they had severed the five lower fetters (pañca-avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana) and would attain parinirvāṇa in the heavens, no longer returning to this world.

Furthermore, there were another fifty people who passed away, and the Buddha likewise prophesied for them: having severed the three fetters and attenuated lust, anger, and delusion, they have attained the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*; returning once more to this world, they shall bring an end to the limits of suffering.
