Furthermore, five hundred people passed away, and the Buddha likewise prophesied for them that they had exhausted the three fetters and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*; they would not fall into the evil realms, and after at most seven more cycles of rebirth, they would surely reach the end of suffering.

There were disciples of the Buddha who passed away in various places, and the Buddha recorded for each of them that "so-and-so was born in such-and-such a place" and "so-and-so was born in such-and-such a place.

Among the sixteen great kingdoms—Aṅga, Magadha, Kāśī, Kosala, Vṛji, Malla, Ceti, Vatsa, Kurū, Pañcāla, Pāṭhā, Aparāntaka, Vatsa, Surāṣṭra, Gandhāra, and Kaṃpilla—the Buddha recorded the births of all those who passed away. However, as for the people of Magadha, who were all of royal lineage and personally favored by the king, when they passed away, the Buddha did not record their births.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his quiet chamber, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Just now, while I was in my quiet chamber, I reflected silently to myself:
'How extraordinary!'"
How extraordinary!

The Buddha bestows predictions upon people for their great benefit; among those from the sixteen great kingdoms who have passed away, the Buddha has recorded them all, yet alone those from the kingdom of Magadha—those whom the King holds in close confidence—who have passed away, do not receive such a prediction.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us an explanation!
We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us an explanation!
It would benefit all beings, and gods and humans would attain peace.
Furthermore, the Buddha attained the Way in the kingdom of Magadha; yet when the people of that country passed away, he alone did not grant them a prediction [of their destiny].
We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us a prediction!
We only pray that the World-Honored One will grant us a prediction!

Furthermore, King Bimbisāra of the kingdom of Magadha became a lay follower (upāsaka); he placed profound faith in the Buddha and provided extensive offerings before his death. Because of this king, many people came to have faith and understanding, making offerings to the Triple Gem; yet, the Tathāgata has not bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon him.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant a prophecy!
This will benefit sentient beings and bring peace to devas and humans.
At that time, Ānanda, having exhorted the World-Honored One on behalf of the people of Magadha, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and having entered the city of Nāga to beg for food, proceeded to the Great Forest where he sat beneath a tree and contemplated the places where the people of Magadha were reborn after their deaths.
At that time, not far from the Buddha, there was a spirit who announced his own name and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am Janavasabha! I am Janavasabha!"
The Buddha said,
"For what reason do you call yourself by the name Jaṇeṣa? Jaṇeṣa,
in the language of Qin, means 'one who has conquered the fetters' (saṃyojana)."
"By what dharma do you, through your own eloquent words, claim to have seen the traces of the Path?
Śāṇakavāsin replied, "Not by any other place."

"In my former life, I was a king of men and a lay follower (*upāsaka*) within the Dharma of the Tathāgata; because I died with a single-minded recollection of the Buddha, I have been born as the crown prince of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa."

From that time forth, he has constantly illuminated all dharmas and attained the stage of Srotāpanna; he shall not fall into the evil realms, and throughout seven births, he shall always be named Janiṣa.
At that time, having stayed as long as was appropriate at the Great Forest, the World-Honored One went to the Nāḍika Caitya, sat down upon his seat, and addressed a certain bhikṣu:
“Go, convey my voice and summon Ānanda.”
He replied, "So be it!
and immediately following the Buddha’s instruction, went to summon Ānanda.
Ānanda soon arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Observing the Tathāgata’s countenance now, it is more radiant than usual, and all his faculties are serene and composed."
“Abiding in what contemplation has your countenance become such as this?
At that time, the World-Honored One told Ānanda:

“Just now, because the people of Magadha came to me and departed after requesting a prediction, I immediately followed behind them, donned my robes, took up my bowl, and entered the city of Nāla to beg for food. Having finished begging, I went to that great forest and sat beneath a tree, contemplating the places where the people of Magadha were reborn after their deaths.”
At that time, not far from me, there was a spirit who announced its own name and addressed me, saying:
"I am Jñānigupta! I am Jñānigupta!"
"Ānanda! Have you ever heard the name of that Jaṇṇuka?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, saying:
"I have never heard of this before.
Now that I have heard its name, I am even struck with fear, and my hair stands on end.
World-Honored One!"
"This spirit must possess great majesty and virtue; therefore, he is named Janīśa.
The Buddha said:
"I previously asked him: "
"By what dharma do you, through your own eloquent words, claim to have seen the traces of the Path? Jaṇeṣa replied,
"I do not [see them] in any other place, nor in any other dharma."

In the past, when I was a king of men and a disciple of the World-Honored One, I became a lay follower (*upāsaka*) out of firm faith and single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha. Thereafter, at the end of my life, I became a son of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. I attained the stage of *srotāpanna* and did not fall into the evil realms; after seven more rebirths at most, I shall reach the end of suffering. Among these seven births, I have always been named Jaṇeṣu.

At one time, the World-Honored One was sitting beneath a tree in a great forest. At that time, I was riding in a celestial chariot with a thousand spokes made of precious jewels. On some minor business, I was on my way to visit King Virūḍhaka when I saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree. His countenance was upright and handsome, and his faculties were tranquil and stilled, like a deep pool that is clear, still, and transparent. Having seen him, I thought to myself: "I should now go and ask the World-Honored One: 'When people of the kingdom of Magadha reach the end of their lives, where will they be reborn?'"
Furthermore, on another occasion, King Vaiśravaṇa himself spoke these verses among the assembly:
"We do not recall ourselves having experienced such things in the past;
now that we have encountered the World-Honored One, our lifespan has been increased."
"Furthermore, on another occasion, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven gathered in one place for some minor reason.
At that time, the Four Great Kings each sat in their respective positions: Dhṛtarāṣṭra sat in the east facing west, with Śakra before him;
Virūḍhaka sat in the south facing north, with Śakra before him."
The Heavenly King Virūpākṣa sat in the west facing east, with Śakra before him;
the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa sat in the north facing south, with Śakra before him.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings all sat down first, and only then did I sit.

Furthermore, there were other great divine beings who had previously cultivated the pure Brahma-faring under the Buddha; having passed away from this life, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, increasing the number of its inhabitants and enjoying the five celestial blessings:
first, celestial longevity; second, celestial beauty; third, celestial renown; fourth, celestial pleasure; and fifth, celestial majesty and virtue.
At that time, all the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven leaped for joy and said,
"The hosts of devas increase, while the hosts of asuras diminish. Then, Śakra Devānām Indra,
knowing that the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven were filled with joy, spoke this verse:
“The devas and humans of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, together with Śakra, enjoy themselves;
they pay homage to the Tathāgata, the Dharma of the supreme dharmas.”
The various devas receive the blessings of their shadows—longevity, beauty, renown, happiness, and majesty;
because they practiced the holy life under the Buddha, they have now been born here.
Furthermore, there are various devas whose radiance and color are most majestic;
the disciples of the Buddha’s wisdom, having been born here, are even more distinguished.
Those of the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens contemplate this and find joy within themselves.
"I pay homage to the Tathāgata, the supreme Dharma of dharmas.
The deity Jaṇeśa spoke again:

"The reason the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven assemble in the Hall of Dharma is to deliberate and reflect together, to observe and weigh matters, and once they have issued their instructions, to then command the Four Heavenly Kings. Having received these instructions, the Four Kings each sit in their respective positions."

Not long after he had sat down, a great extraordinary light shone in the four directions. At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, seeing this extraordinary light, were all greatly astonished and wondered, "What strange phenomenon will this extraordinary light portend?"
The other great devas possessing majestic power were likewise struck with wonder, thinking, "What strange phenomenon could this extraordinary radiance portend?

At that moment, the Great Brahmā King immediately transformed himself into a youth with five topknots on his head; standing in the void above the host of devas, his countenance was upright and peerless among the multitude, his body golden-purple in hue, eclipsing the light of all the devas.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven did not rise to welcome him, nor did they show him respect, nor did they invite him to sit.
Then, as the Brahmā-son proceeded to his seat, joy arose within him; it was like a Kṣatriya of the water-sprinkled lineage who, upon ascending the royal throne, leaps for joy with exultation.
Not long after he had sat down, he again transformed his body into the form of a youth with five topknots on his head, sitting in the air above the great assembly.
Like a strongman seated upon a comfortable throne, he remained majestic and motionless, and spoke this verse:
"The Unsurpassed Honored One who tames, Teaches the world to give rise to the place of clarity;”
"Proclaiming the Great Illumination of the Dharma, with Brahma-conduct beyond compare,
he causes sentient beings to become pure and be reborn in the Pure and Wondrous Heaven.
When the Brahma youth had spoken this verse, he addressed the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, saying:
"Whatever sound possesses five kinds of purity is called the Brahma-voice. What are these five? First, its tone is upright;

second, its tone is harmonious and elegant; third, its tone is clear and penetrating; fourth, its tone is deep and full; fifth, it is heard everywhere at a great distance. Possessing these five qualities is what is called the Brahma-voice."
I shall now speak further; listen well!

Among the lay disciples of the Magadha country who were followers of the Tathāgata, upon the end of their lives, some attained the stage of Anāgāmin, some attained Sakṛdāgāmin, and some attained Srotāpanna. Some were reborn in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, some in the Nirmāṇarati, Tuṣita, Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa, or Cāturmahārājika Heavens, and some were born into great families of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or householders, where the five desires were spontaneously provided.
Then the Brahma youth spoke in verse:
“The lay followers of Magadha, Of all those who have passed away—
Eighty-four thousand people— I have heard that they have all attained the Way.”
Having attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, they shall no longer fall into the evil realms;
all riding upon the level and upright path, they have attained the Way that can provide salvation.
These classes of sentient beings are sustained by their own merit.
Through wisdom he renounced affection; with shame and dread of blame, he abandoned deceit and falsehood.
To that assembly of devas, the Brahma youth gave this prediction:
"He has attained the stage of Srotāpanna," and all the devas rejoiced.
At that time, having heard this verse, King Vaiśravaṇa spoke with joy: "How extraordinary!
The World-Honored One has appeared in the world and preached the Dharma of reality."
How extraordinary!
This has never occurred before.
Previously, I did not know that the Tathāgata had appeared in the world to preach such a Dharma.
"In a future age, there shall again be a Buddha who will preach such a Dharma as can cause the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to give rise to hearts of joy.
At that time, the Brahma Youth said to King Vaiśravaṇa: "Why do you speak these words?"
That the Tathāgata has appeared in the world and preached such a Dharma is truly marvelous,
truly extraordinary, and unprecedented!

The Tathāgata, through the power of skillful means, speaks of the wholesome and the unwholesome; he expounds the Dharma in its fullness yet finds nothing to be attained. He speaks of the dharmas of emptiness and purity as if there were something to be attained; this Dharma is subtle and wondrous, like the finest clarified butter (sarpis).
Then, the Brahma youth again addressed the Trāyastriṃśa devas, saying:
"Listen attentively! Reflect upon this well; I shall speak further for your sake."
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is well able to analyze and explain the four foundations of mindfulness. What are these four?
First is the contemplation of the internal body, practicing with diligence and without slackening, maintaining focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, and removing worldly greed and sorrow.
Contemplating the body externally, he is diligent and unremitting, focused in mindfulness without forgetfulness, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
Contemplating feelings, mind, and phenomena is likewise: he is diligent and unremitting, focused in mindfulness without forgetfulness, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
Having contemplated one's own body internally, one gives rise to knowledge of other bodies;
having contemplated one's own sensations internally, one gives rise to knowledge of other sensations;
having contemplated one's own mind internally, one gives rise to knowledge of other minds.

Having practiced the dharma of internal contemplation, one gives rise to the knowledge of dharmas regarding other phenomena; this is what is meant by the Tathāgata’s skillful and thorough exposition of the four foundations of mindfulness.
Furthermore, O devas! Listen well!
I shall further explain how the Tathāgata is well able to analyze and teach the seven factors of concentration. What are these seven?

Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness—these are the seven factors of concentration that the Tathāgata is well able to analyze and teach.
Furthermore, O devas!
The Tathāgata is well able to analyze and explain the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*). What are these four?

The first is the basis of spiritual power consisting in the cultivation of the accomplishment of the meditative concentration of desire through the abandonment of mental formations (*chanda-samādhi-prahāṇa-saṃskāra-sampanna-ṛddhipāda*).
Second is the base of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of the meditative concentration on diligence and the cessation of formations.
Third is the base of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of the meditative concentration on intention and the cessation of formations.

Fourth is the base of psychic power accomplished through the cultivation of the meditative concentration on investigation and the cessation of formations. These are the four bases of psychic power that the Tathāgata skillfully distinguishes and explains.
He further addressed the devas:
"The śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past, by means of countless skillful methods, manifested immeasurable supernormal powers; all these arose from the four bases of power (ṛddhipāda).
Even if the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the future were to manifest immeasurable supernormal powers through countless skillful methods, they too would all arise from these four bases of power."
Now, the countless śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the present who manifest immeasurable supernormal powers (ṛddhi) all likewise arise from these four bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda).

At that time, the Brahma youth immediately manifested transformations of his own body into thirty-three forms, sitting together one by one with each of the thirty-three gods, and addressed them, saying:
"Do you now see my power of spiritual transformation?"
He replied, "Indeed, I have seen it. The Brahma youth said:
"I too, by cultivating the four bases of psychic power, am able to manifest such countless transformations.
At that time, each of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven thought to themselves:
"Now this Brahmā-son speaks these words while seated alone upon my seat; yet when that Brahmā-son’s single transformation-body speaks, all the other transformations speak as well."
"One emanation remains silent, and the other emanations likewise remain silent.
Then, that Brahmā youth withdrew his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), took his seat upon the throne of Śakra, and addressed the Trāyastriṃśa devas, saying:
"I shall now speak; listen well!"
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, by his own power has opened three paths and attained perfect enlightenment for himself.
What are these three?

There may be sentient beings who are close to sensual desire and habitually practice unwholesome deeds; yet later, such persons draw near to virtuous friends, hear the words of the Dharma, and achieve realization in each and every teaching. Thereupon, they leave behind desire and abandon unwholesome conduct, attaining a heart of joy, tranquil happiness, and within that happiness, further giving rise to great rapture.
Just as a person who abandons coarse food to eat a hundred-flavored meal feels fully satisfied upon eating it, yet still seeks something superior;

so too does the practitioner, having abandoned unwholesome dharmas and attained the joy of rapture, further gives rise to great joy within that very bliss. This is how the Tathāgata, by his own power, opened the initial path and achieved supreme perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are prone to much anger and do not abandon the evil karma of body, speech, and mind. Later, such a person encounters a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) and hears the words of the Dharma; through the realization of each and every teaching, they leave behind evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, giving rise to a heart of joy, tranquil happiness, and within that happiness, further great delight.
It is like a person who abandons coarse food to eat a meal of a hundred flavors; having eaten their fill, they seek something even more excellent.

The practitioner is thus: having abandoned unwholesome states, they attain the joy of rapture; furthermore, within that joy, great gladness arises once more. This is what the Tathāgata calls opening the second path.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are ignorant and devoid of wisdom; they do not distinguish between good and evil, nor can they know, as it truly is, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Later, such a person encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and hears the words of the Dharma. Through the realization of each dharma, they come to recognize what is wholesome and what is unwholesome, and are able to know, as it truly is, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. They abandon unwholesome conduct and give rise to a heart of joy; they become tranquil and happy, and within that happiness, they further experience great rapture.
It is like a person who abandons coarse food to eat a meal of a hundred flavors; having eaten their fill, they seek something even more excellent.

The practitioner is likewise: having abandoned unwholesome states, they attain joy and happiness; furthermore, within that happiness, great rapture arises. This is what the Tathāgata calls the opening of the third path.

“At that time, the Brahma youth preached this True Dharma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; King Vaiśravaṇa, in turn, preached this True Dharma for his retinue; the deity Janiṣa preached this True Dharma before the Buddha; the World-Honored One, in turn, preached this True Dharma to Ānanda; and Ānanda, in turn, preached this True Dharma to the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.”
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The *Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Five.
The *Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Part 2, Section 5: The Minor Causes and Conditions Sūtra (5). The First Sūtra on Minor Causes and Conditions within the First Part of the Second Division.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Mṛgāramātṛ-upasthāna-śālā in the Śrāvastī Garden of the Faithful with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there were two brahmins who, with firm faith, went to where the Buddha was, left the household life to follow the path, one named Vāseṭṭha and the other named Bhāradvāja.
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from his quiet chamber and was walking back and forth in meditation upon the lecture hall.
Then, Vāseṭṭha saw the Buddha walking and immediately went quickly to Vāmadeva, saying to him: "Do you know?"

"The Tathāgata has now emerged from his quiet chamber and is walking up and down in the hall; we should go together to where the World-Honored One is, so that we might perhaps hear whatever the Tathāgata has to say."

When Vāseṭṭha had heard these words, he immediately went together with him to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and followed the Buddha as they walked in meditation.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vāseṭṭha, saying:
“You two have both emerged from the Brahmin caste; out of firm faith, have you gone forth within my Dharma to practice the path?”
He replied, “It is so! The Buddha said:
"Brahmin! Now that you have gone forth in my Dharma to practice the Path, do the other brahmins not reproach you? He replied:
“Yes, indeed!
Having received the Great Benevolence of the Buddha, I have left the household life to practice the Way; yet I am truly held in contempt and reproached by those brahmins.
The Buddha said:
"For what reason did he reprove you?
He then addressed the Buddha, saying: "He said:"
"Our Brahmin caste is the most supreme; others are base and inferior.
Our caste is pure and bright, while others are dark and obscure.
We Brahmins originate from Brahmā; we are born from the mouth of Brahmā. In this present life, we attain pure liberation, and we shall be pure in the future as well."
"Why have you abandoned your pure lineage to enter the heterodox teachings of that Gautama?
World-Honored One!
Seeing me having left the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma, he rebuked me with such words.
The Buddha said to Vāseṭṭha:
"Observe how these people are ignorant and without understanding, like birds and beasts; yet they falsely claim of themselves:
'The Brahmin caste is the most supreme, while all others are base and inferior.'"
"My lineage is pure and bright, while others are dark and obscure;
I am of the Brahmin caste, born from Brahmā, produced from the mouth of Brahmā, pure in the present and pure in the future."

"Vāseṭṭha! Now, within my unsurpassed, truly correct path, lineage is not required, nor is there any reliance on the prideful mind of 'self. Such things are necessary for worldly dharmas; my dharma is not so."
If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who rely on their own lineage and harbor a mind of arrogance, they shall never attain supreme realization within my Dharma.
If one can renounce their lineage and eliminate the mind of pride, they will attain realization within my Dharma and be worthy of receiving the True Dharma.
While people are base and lowly, my Dharma is not so.
The Buddha told Vāseṭṭha:
"There are four castes, in which both the good and the evil dwell; they are those whom the wise praise and those whom the wise censure. What are these four?
First, the kṣatriya caste; second, the brāhmaṇa caste; third, the vaiśya caste; and fourth, the śūdra caste. Vāseṭṭha!

Listen: among the kṣatriya caste there are those who kill living beings, those who steal, those who commit sexual misconduct, those who speak falsely, those who engage in double-tongued speech, those who use harsh words, those who engage in frivolous chatter, those who are greedy and covetous, those who are jealous, and those who hold wrong views;
it is the same for the brāhmaṇa caste, the vaiśya caste, and the śūdra caste—they all likewise engage in these ten types of unwholesome conduct.

Vāseṭṭha! Unwholesome conduct brings about unwholesome retribution; as a dark and murky deed, it results in a dark and murky retribution. If this retribution were to fall solely upon the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, and not upon the Brāhmaṇa caste, then the Brāhmaṇas might well claim:
"We Brāhmaṇas are the most supreme, while all others are base and inferior."
My lineage is pure and bright, while others are dark and obscure;
I am of the Brahmin caste, born from Brahmā, produced from the mouth of Brahmā, pure in the present and pure in the future.

"If unwholesome conduct were to result in unwholesome retribution, and dark conduct were to result in dark retribution, such that it necessarily fell upon those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, then the Brahmins could not claim for themselves alone:
'Our caste is pure and is the most supreme.'"

“Vāseṭṭha! If among the kṣatriya caste there are those who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not speak falsely, do not use double-tongued speech, do not use harsh words, do not engage in frivolous chatter, are not covetous, are not jealous, and do not hold wrong views;
and if the brāhmaṇa caste, the householder caste, and the śūdra caste are likewise all thus, collectively practicing the ten wholesome paths of action.”

Now, one who practices wholesome dharmas must surely receive a wholesome retribution; one who practices pure conduct must surely receive a pure retribution. If this retribution were to accrue exclusively to the Brahmins and not to the Kṣatriyas, householders, or Śūdras, then the Brahmin caste would be entitled to say:
"Our lineage is pure and is the most supreme."
"If all four castes were to share this same retribution, then the Brahmins could not claim for themselves alone:
'Our lineage is pure and is the most supreme.'"
The Buddha told Vāseṭṭha:
“Now we see before our very eyes that the Brahmin caste marries, gives birth, and procreates no differently from the rest of the world, yet they falsely claim:
‘We are of the lineage of Brahmā; we were born from the mouth of Brahmā; we are pure now, and shall be pure hereafter.’”
"Vāseṭṭha! You should know this now:
my disciples today come from various lineages and have diverse origins; they have gone forth to practice the path within my Dharma.
If someone were to ask them, 'What is your lineage?'"
One should answer him, saying:
"I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
One may also call oneself by that title.
"I am of the Brahmin caste; I was born directly from the mouth [of Brahmā], born through transformation by the Dharma, pure in the present and pure in the future. Why is this so?

The name "Great Brahmā" is itself a title of the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is the eye of the world; the Dharma is the wisdom of the world, the Dharma of the world, the Brahmā of the world, the Wheel of Dharma of the world, the nectar of the world, and the Lord of Dharma of the world.

“Vāseṭṭha! If among the kṣatriya caste there are those who have profound faith in the Buddha—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, endowed with the ten titles—and who have profound faith in the Dharma, believing in the Tathāgata’s Dharma as subtle, pure, practiceable in the present, timeless in its teaching, revealing the essentials of Nirvāṇa, known by the wise, and not something that can be taught to the vulgar and ignorant;

and who have profound faith in the Saṅgha, which is virtuous by nature and upright, accomplished in the fruits of the Path, accomplished in its assembly, and consists of the true disciples of the Buddha who are accomplished in each and every dharma;”

What is called the "assembly" refers to those who have achieved the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
These include those progressing toward the fruit of stream-entry and those who have attained stream-entry;
those progressing toward the fruit of once-returning and those who have attained once-returning.
Those who are candidates for the stage of non-returner attain the state of non-returner;
those who are candidates for arhatship attain the state of arhatship.
These four pairs and eight classes constitute the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples.
Worthy of honor and reverence, he is a field of merit for the world and should receive the offerings of others;

he has firm faith in the precepts and is fully endowed with the noble precepts—without deficiency, without flaw, without blemish, and without stain—praised by the wise and possessed of sublime tranquility.

Vāseṭṭha! The brahmin class, the householder class, and the śūdra class should likewise have such firm faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha, and should achieve noble ethical discipline.
Vāseṭṭha! Among the kṣatriyas, there are also those who make offerings to arhats, honoring and prostrating before them;
likewise, among the brāhmaṇas, householders, and śūdras, all also make offerings to arhats, honoring and prostrating before them.
The Buddha told Vāseṭṭha:
"Now my own kinsmen, the Śākyas, also serve King Prasenajit, honoring and revering him; yet King Prasenajit, in turn, comes to make offerings and pay homage to me. He does not think:
'The śramaṇa Gautama comes from a noble clan, whereas my lineage is lowly;'"

The śramaṇa Gautama was born into a family of great wealth and great majesty, whereas I was born into a lowly, impoverished, and humble family; it is for this reason that I offer worship and pay homage to the Tathāgata.
"King Prasenajit contemplates phenomena within phenomena; having clearly discerned the true from the false, he has given rise to pure faith and pays homage to the Tathāgata. Vāseṭṭha!"
I shall now explain for you the original causes of the four castes.

Regarding the beginning and end of heaven and earth, when the kalpa reaches its destruction and ends, the lives of all sentient beings come to an end and they are all reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. There they are born spontaneously by transformation; they take thought as their food, illuminate themselves with their own radiance, and travel through the air by means of their supernormal powers. Subsequently, this entire earth transforms completely into water, such that there is no place it does not pervade.
At that time, there were no longer suns, moons, or stars, nor were there days, nights, months, years, or seasons; there was only vast darkness.
Subsequently, this water transformed into the great earth, and the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, their merit exhausted and their lives ended, came to be born in this world.

Although they have been reborn here, they still subsist on the food of mindfulness, fly through the air by means of their supernormal power, and illuminate themselves with the radiance of their own bodies; having dwelt here for a long time, they each address one another, saying:
"O sentient beings!"
"O sentient beings!
Thereafter, sweet springs welled up from this ground, appearing like clarified butter and honey.
When those who had previously arrived—naturally frivolous and light-minded—saw these springs, they thought to themselves in silence:
"What is this? You may try it. He then dipped his finger into the spring and tasted it;

doing so repeatedly, he found it increasingly delicious. He then scooped it up with his hand and ate it to his heart's content. Thus becoming attached to its pleasure, he could not find enough. Other beings followed his example and ate it as well; after doing so repeatedly, they too found it delicious and ate without ceasing. Their bodies became coarse and their flesh grew hard and rigid. They lost their celestial splendor and no longer possessed supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); they walked upon the ground, their bodily radiance faded away, and the heavens and earth were plunged into great darkness.

“Vāseṭṭha! You should know that this is the constant law of heaven and earth: after the great darkness, the sun, moon, and constellations must necessarily appear in the void; only then do day and night, light and dark, and the reckoning of days, months, and years come to be.”

At that time, sentient beings subsisted solely on the flavor of the earth and dwelt in the world for a long duration. Among them, those who consumed much of this food became coarse and ugly in appearance;
those who consumed little remained radiant and lustrous. Thus, the distinction between the beautiful and the ugly first arose.
Those who were handsome gave rise to a mind of arrogance and looked down upon the unsightly.
Those who were ugly gave rise to feelings of envy and malice, hating those who were handsome.

Consequently, sentient beings began to quarrel with one another. At that time, the sweet springs naturally dried up. Thereafter, a natural earth-fat (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) grew upon this ground, complete in color and flavor, fragrant, pure, and edible; at that time, sentient beings again took it as food and remained in the world for a long duration.
Those who eat much have coarse and ugly complexions;
those who eat little have complexions that remain bright and lustrous.
Those who are handsome give rise to a mind of arrogance and look down upon the ugly.

Those who were ugly gave rise to feelings of jealousy and malice, hating those who were handsome; consequently, sentient beings began to quarrel and dispute with one another, and at that time, the earth-fat ceased to grow.

Thereafter, coarse and thick earth-fat (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) arose again upon this ground; it was fragrant, delicious, and edible, though not as excellent as the former. At that time, sentient beings again took and ate it, dwelling in the world for a long duration.

Those who ate much became coarse and ugly in appearance, while those who ate little remained radiant and handsome; thus, they began to criticize one another for their beauty or ugliness, leading to disputes and litigation. Consequently, the earth-fertility ceased to grow.
Thereafter, this earth produced natural *śāli* rice, which was free of husks and bran, perfect in color and flavor, fragrant, pure, and fit for consumption.

At that time, sentient beings again took it as food and lived in the world for a long time. Then, male and female appeared; looking at one another, they gradually developed desire and drew closer together. When other sentient beings saw this, they spoke:
"What you have done is wrong!
What you have done is wrong!
they said, immediately ostracizing and banishing him beyond the ranks of men; only after three months had passed did he return home.
The Buddha told Vasiṣṭha:
"What was previously considered wrong is now regarded as right.

At that time, those beings practiced what was not the Dharma and indulged excessively in their desires without regard for the proper seasons. Out of a sense of shame, they consequently built dwellings; thus, houses first came into existence in the world."

As they indulged in unwholesome practices, their lustful desires increased further, and the womb subsequently came into being; born from impurity, the origin of the human womb in this world began from that point.
At that time, those beings ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice, which grew back as soon as it was harvested, never becoming exhausted.
At that time, among those beings, there were some who were indolent and thought to themselves:
"I gather food for my morning meal in the morning and for my evening meal in the evening; this is too much toil for me. Now I wish to gather it all at once to last the entire day."
He immediately gathered it all at once.
Later, when his companions called for him to gather rice together, the man replied:
"I have already gathered it all to provide for one day; if you wish to gather some, you may do as you please."
That man further thought to himself:
"This person is wise and able to store provisions in advance; I too now wish to accumulate grain to provide for three days."
The man immediately stored up more than three days' worth of grain.
Other sentient beings came again and said to him,
"We can go together to gather rice."
He replied, "I have already accumulated more than three days' worth of provisions; if you wish to take them, you may go and fetch them yourself.
That man thought again:
"This man is clever; he has previously accumulated surplus grain sufficient for three days. I shall emulate him and accumulate grain sufficient for five days.
He then went immediately to fetch it.
"At that time, after those beings had vied with one another in hoarding, the non-glutinous rice became overgrown and impure, and husks and chaff began to grow;
once harvested, it would not grow back. Seeing this, those beings were displeased and fell into a state of distress and confusion, each thinking to themselves:

'In the beginning, when we were first born, we took thought as our food, possessed the power of flight through the air, and our bodies were self-illuminating; we dwelt in the world for a long time. Subsequently, a sweet spring gushed forth from this earth, resembling clarified butter and honey, fragrant, delicious, and fit for consumption; at that time, we all ate of it together.'"

As they ate for longer periods, those who ate much became coarse and ugly in appearance, while those who ate little remained radiant and lustrous. Because of this eating, our appearances became different;

consequently, sentient beings each harbored notions of right and wrong and began to harbor mutual hatred and envy. At that time, the sweet springs naturally dried up. Thereafter, a natural "earth-fat" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) grew upon this ground, complete with color and flavor, fragrant, delicious, and edible; at that time, we once again took it as food.

Those who ate much became coarse and ugly in appearance, while those who ate little remained pleasant and radiant in complexion; consequently, sentient beings again harbored notions of right and wrong, harboring mutual hatred and envy, and at that time, the earth-fat ceased to grow.
Thereafter, coarse and thick earth-fat (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) arose, which was likewise fragrant, delicious, and edible; at that time, we again took it as food.

Those who ate much became coarse in appearance, while those who ate little remained pleasant in appearance; thus, disputes arose and they came to harbor mutual hatred and jealousy. At that time, the earth-fat eventually ceased to appear.

"Once again, non-glutinous rice appeared spontaneously, free from husks and chaff; at that time, we took it and ate it, dwelling in the world for a long duration. However, those who were indolent vied with one another to store it up. Because of this, the non-glutinous rice became overgrown and defiled, and husks and chaff began to appear again. Once harvested, it no longer regrows. Now, what shall we do?"
They further said to one another,
"We should divide the land together and establish separate boundary markers.
They immediately proceeded to divide the land and established separate boundary markers.
“Vasiṣṭha! It was through these very causes and conditions that the names ‘field’ and ‘land’ first came into being.

At that time, sentient beings demarcated fields and established boundaries for themselves; gradually, the thought of theft arose, and they would steal the grain of others. When other sentient beings saw this, they said:”
"What you have done is wrong!
What you have done is wrong!
You possess your own fields, yet you take the property of others; from this day forward, do not do so again."

Yet those beings did not desist from their theft. The other beings rebuked them again and again, but they still did not stop; they then seized them by the hand and said to the others, "This man has his own fields and crops, yet he steals the property of others."
The other person replied, "This man struck me. Then,
having witnessed the dispute between the two, the crowd became sorrowful and displeased, speaking with resentment:

"When sentient beings turn toward evil, such unwholesome things arise in the world; they give birth to filth, corruption, and impurity. This is the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death; it is the retribution of afflictions and suffering that leads to falling into the three evil realms. It is because of the existence of fields and lands that these disputes and litigations come to pass."

Now, it would be best to appoint one person as a ruler to govern them; he may protect those who should be protected and reprimand those who deserve reprimand. The multitude shall collectively reduce their rice rations to provide for him, so that he may adjudicate disputes and litigation.
Then, from among that assembly, they selected one man who was tall and large of stature, handsome in appearance, and possessed of majesty and virtue, and said to him:

"You shall now act as our impartial leader; you should protect those who need protection, reprimand those who deserve reprimand, and dismiss those who should be dismissed. We shall collectively gather rice to provide for you."

At that time, having heard the words of the multitude, one man was immediately appointed as their leader to adjudicate disputes; the multitude then gathered together to provide him with rice for his support.
Then, that one person further comforted the multitude with kind words; having heard them, everyone was greatly rejoiced and they all together exclaimed: "Excellent!"
"Great King! Excellent! Great King!"

Thereupon, the title "king" came into existence in the world; because he governed the people with the True Dharma (*saddharma*), he was called a *kṣatriya*, and thus the name *kṣatriya* first arose in the world.
At that time, there was one person alone among the assembly who thought to himself:

"The household life is a great affliction; the household life is a poisonous thorn. I would now rather abandon this domestic life and dwell alone in the mountain forests, practicing the Way in quietude."

He immediately abandoned his home and entered the mountain forests to meditate in silent seclusion. When the time came, he took up his bowl and entered the village to beg for food; when the people saw him, they all joyfully offered their support, praising him with delight: "Excellent!"
"This person is able to renounce home life, dwell alone in the mountains and forests, cultivate the Way in silent seclusion, and abandon all evils.
Thus, for the first time in the world, the name "Brahmin" came into being.

Among those brahmins, there were some who did not delight in dwelling in seclusion for meditation and contemplation; they instead entered human settlements, making the recitation and study of texts their profession, and further declared:
"I am one who does not practice dhyāna!"
"Thereupon, people in the world called him the 'Non-Meditating Brahmin.
Because he entered among human beings, he was named a 'Human Brahmin,' and thus there arose the caste of Brahmins in the world.
Among those sentient beings, there were some who took pleasure in managing household affairs and accumulated much wealth and treasure; because of this, people called them 'Householders' (gahapati)."

Among those beings, there were many who possessed skillful ingenuity and engaged in various crafts; it was from this that the name "śūdra" first came to exist in this world for those skilled in crafts. "Vasiṣṭha!..."
In this world, there are four kinds of names; the fifth is the name "the community of śramaṇas.
Why is this so, Vāseṭṭha?

Within the kṣatriya assembly, there were at times those who grew weary of their own dharma, shaved off their hair and beards, and donned the dharma robes; it was from this that the name "śramaṇa" first came into being.

Whether of the Brahmin caste, the householder caste, or the Śūdra caste, there may at times be someone who, weary of their own dharma, shaves off their hair and beard, dons the religious robes, and practices the Way; such a person is called a śramaṇa.

Vāseṭṭha! Among those of the kṣatriya caste, if one practices unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind, then at the breaking up of the body after death, they will inevitably experience a painful retribution.

Whether one belongs to the Brahmin caste, the householder caste, or the Śūdra caste, if they practice unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind, then at the dissolution of the body after death, they will inevitably experience the retribution of suffering.
Vāseṭṭha! Among the kṣatriyas, there are those who practice virtue in body, speech, and mind; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will certainly receive a pleasant retribution.

Whether among the Brahmins, householders, or Śūdras, those who practice virtue in body, speech, and mind will, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, certainly receive a reward of happiness.

Vāseṭṭha! Among the kṣatriya assembly, there are those who engage in two kinds of bodily conduct and two kinds of verbal and mental conduct; when their bodies disintegrate at the end of life, they receive retribution consisting of suffering and pleasure.

Whether one belongs to the Brahmin caste, the householder caste, or the Śūdra caste, if they engage in two kinds of conduct through the body, and two kinds of conduct through speech and mind, then at the dissolution of the body after death, they will experience the retribution of suffering and pleasure.

“Vāseṭṭha! Among the kṣatriya caste, there are those who shave off their hair and beard, don the dharma-robes, and practice the Way; they cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment and will before long achieve the realization of the Way.”
Why is this? Because that son of good family has gone forth in the dharma-robes to cultivate the unsurpassed holy life, and within this very life he has realized for himself:
"Birth and death are exhausted; the holy life is established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence."

"Among the Brahmins, householders, and Śūdras, there are those who shave off their hair and beards, don the dharma-robes, and cultivate the Way; by practicing the seven factors of enlightenment, they will achieve the Way before long."
Why is this? Because that son of good family has gone forth clad in the Dharma robes and practices the unsurpassed holy life (brahmacarya), personally realizing within this very life:
"Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence."
"Vāseṭṭha! Among these four types, all those who have emerged as Arhats accomplished in clear knowledge and conduct are the very foremost among the five types.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Vāseṭṭha.
The Brahmā King spoke in verse:
"Among those born, the Kṣatriya is supreme; yet he who can renounce his lineage and depart, who has perfected knowledge and conduct—he is the foremost in the world."
The Buddha told Vāseṭṭha:
"This was well-spoken by Brahmā, not ill-spoken;
this was rightly received by Brahmā, not wrongly received."
At that time, I immediately confirmed those words. Why is this?
For now, I, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, also teach this same meaning:
"Among those born, the Kṣatriya is supreme; Yet he who can renounce his lineage and depart [is even more so]."
"One who has perfected knowledge and conduct is the foremost in the world.

When the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja attained the liberation of the mind through the destruction of the outflows; having heard what the Buddha taught, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

6. The Discourse on the Practice of the Wheel-Turning Sage King (6). Spoken by the Buddha, the second discourse in the second division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*: The Discourse on the Practice of the Wheel-Turning Sage King. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Mālava and, together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, gradually arrived at the country of Māluda.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should make yourselves your own lamps and make the Dharma your lamp; do not make anything else your lamp.
You should take refuge in yourselves and take refuge in the Dharma; do not take refuge in anything else."
How should a bhikṣu be self-illuminating, illuminating through the Dharma, rather than being illuminated by another?
How should he take refuge in himself, taking refuge in the Dharma, rather than taking refuge in another?
Thereupon, a bhikṣu contemplates the body within the body, diligent and untiring, with mindfulness undiminished, removing worldly greed and sorrow;
he contemplates the body without the body, and contemplates the body both within and without, diligent and untiring, with mindfulness undiminished, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
The contemplation of feeling, mind, and phenomena is likewise so; this is called a bhikṣu who is self-kindled, kindled by the Dharma, and not kindled by another;
who takes refuge in himself, takes refuge in the Dharma, and does not take refuge in another.
"One who practices in this manner cannot be disturbed by Māra, and their merit increases day by day. Why is this?
In the distant past, long ago, there was a king named Dṛḍhamati, a Kṣatriya of the consecrated lineage, who was a Cakravartin King ruling over the four continents."

At that time, King Īśvara ruled and transformed the realm according to the Dharma; he was preeminent among men and possessed the seven treasures: first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure; fourth, the divine jewel treasure; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the householder treasure; and seventh, the general treasure.
He possesses a full thousand sons, valiant, heroic, and fierce, capable of subduing enemies without the use of weapons or staffs, so that peace prevails naturally.

After King Dṛḍhasmṛti has reigned for a long time, the precious golden wheel suddenly leaves its original place in the sky. At that time, the attendant of the wheel quickly goes to inform the king: "Great King! [The wheel has departed from its place in the sky.]”
"You should know that the Wheel-Treasure has now departed from its original place.
When King Dṛḍha heard this, he thought to himself:
"I have previously heard from the elders and the aged that if the Wheel-Treasure of a Wheel-Turning Sage King moves, the king's life will not last much longer."

I have now already enjoyed the blessings and pleasures of the human realm; it is fitting that I employ further means to enjoy the blessings and pleasures of the heavens. I shall establish the crown prince to govern the four continents and separately grant a village to my barber. I command him to shave off my beard and hair, don the three dharma robes, and leave the household life to cultivate the Way.
Then, King Dṛḍhacitta summoned his crown prince and addressed him, saying:
"Do you know? I have heard from the elders of former times that if the golden wheel of a Wheel-turning Sage King departs from its original place, the king’s life will not last much longer."

"I have now already received the blessings and joys of the human realm; I shall now employ further skillful means to transition to receiving celestial blessings. I now wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, and leave the household life to pursue the Way. I entrust the four continents to you; you should exert yourself and show compassion and care for the people and all things."
At that time, having received the King’s instruction, Prince Dṛḍhamati immediately shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and left the household life to practice the Way.
"At that time, after the King had been ordained for seven days, that precious golden wheel suddenly disappeared. The officer in charge of the wheel went to inform the King, saying:
'Great King!'"
"You should know that the Wheel Treasure has now suddenly disappeared.
At that time, the king was displeased and immediately went to the place where King Dṛḍhamati resided; having arrived, he addressed the king, saying:
"O Father King!"
"You should know that the Wheel-Treasure has now suddenly disappeared.
At that time, King Dṛḍhadhyāna replied to his son: "Do not harbor grief or be displeased.

This Golden Wheel-Treasure was not produced from your father’s lineage; you need only diligently practice the True Dharma of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin). Once you have practiced the True Dharma, on the fifteenth day when the moon is full, having bathed in fragrant water and being surrounded by your court ladies, ascend the Hall of True Dharma, and the divine Golden Wheel-Treasure will naturally appear before you. It shall have a thousand spokes, be perfect in radiance and color, crafted by a celestial artisan, and not of this world."
The son addressed the King, his father:
"What is the True Dharma of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?
How should it be practiced?"
The King said to his son:
"You must rely upon the Dharma; establish the Dharma, fulfill the Dharma, revere and respect it, contemplate the Dharma, take the Dharma as your foremost priority, and protect the True Dharma.

Furthermore, you must instruct the palace ladies according to the Dharma. You must also protect, oversee, and admonish the princes, ministers, officials, the various functionaries, the hundred officers, and all the people—including śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, down to the birds and beasts—all of whom you must protect and care for."
Again, he said to his son:

"Furthermore, within the borders of your realm, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice with purity and sincerity, are fully endowed with merit, and are diligent without indolence; they have abandoned arrogance, are patient and benevolent, and dwell in seclusion practicing alone, attaining cessation alone, and reaching nirvāṇa alone. They have eliminated greed themselves and transform others to eliminate greed;
they have eliminated anger themselves and transform others to eliminate anger."
Having personally eliminated delusion, he transforms others to eliminate delusion.

He is unstained by defilement and uncorrupted by evil; he is not foolish, yet he does not manifest as wise; he may appear to cling, yet he does not cling; he may appear to dwell, yet he does not dwell; he may appear to reside, yet he does not reside.
His bodily conduct was upright, his speech was upright, and his mental intentions were upright;

his bodily conduct was pure, his speech was pure, and his mental intentions were pure; with pure right mindfulness, he possessed tireless benevolence and wisdom, was content with food and clothing, and, carrying his alms bowl for begging, brought blessings to all sentient beings.
If there is such a person as this, you should visit them frequently and inquire from time to time: "In all that I practice, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome?
What constitutes an offense?"
What constitutes non-offense?
Who is worthy of association?
And who is not worthy of association?
What may be done? What may not be done? By practicing what Dharma will one experience happiness throughout the long night?
Having consulted and deliberated with your mind, you should act when it is appropriate to act and relinquish when it is appropriate to relinquish.
As for the widowed and the elderly within the kingdom, you must provide for them;
as for the poor, the destitute, and the lowly who come to you seeking aid, take care never to refuse them.
"The kingdom has ancient laws; do not alter them. These are the practices cultivated by the Wheel-Turning Sage Kings (Cakravartin), which you should uphold and practice.

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "At that time, having received his father's instruction, the Wheel-Turning Sage King practiced exactly as taught. Later, on the fifteenth day when the moon was full, he bathed in fragrant water and ascended the high palace, surrounded by court ladies. Suddenly, the precious wheel appeared before him. It had a thousand spokes, its radiance and color were perfect, it was crafted by a celestial artisan and did not exist in the world, being made of pure gold, with a diameter of fourteen feet."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King thought to himself:

"I have heard from the elders and ancestors of old that when a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated lineage, on the full moon of the fifteenth day, bathes in fragrant water and ascends the jeweled palace surrounded by court ladies, a golden wheel spontaneously appears before him. This wheel has a thousand spokes, its radiance and color are perfect; it is fashioned by a celestial craftsman and does not exist in the world, being made of pure gold. The diameter of the wheel is fourteen feet; such a person is called a Wheel-Turning Holy King."
"Now that this wheel has appeared, could it not be so?
I should now test this precious wheel-treasure.

Then, the Wheel-turning King immediately summoned his fourfold army, bared his right shoulder toward the precious golden wheel, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and stroked the golden wheel with his right hand, saying:
"Go toward the east and turn according to the Dharma; do not deviate from the established rule.
The wheel then turned toward the east.

At that time, the king immediately followed behind it with his fourfold army. Four deities led the way before the precious golden wheel, and wherever the wheel came to rest, the king halted his carriage.

At that time, the minor kings of the eastern regions, seeing the Great King arrive, took golden bowls filled with silver grain and silver bowls filled with golden grain, approached the King's location, bowed their heads, and said:
"Welcome, Great King!"

"Now this land in the eastern direction is abundant and prosperous, its people are numerous, and their dispositions are harmonious and benevolent, compassionate, filial, loyal, and obedient. We only wish that the Holy King would govern and rectify it here; we shall serve as your attendants and receive whatever duties are appropriate."
At that time, the Great Wheel-Turning King said to the minor kings:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Virtuous ones!

Once you have made offerings to me, you must simply govern by the True Dharma; do not allow partiality or injustice, and ensure that no unlawful conduct occurs within the realm. This is what is called 'my governance'."

At that time, having heard these instructions, the minor kings immediately followed the Great King on his tour of the various kingdoms as far as the eastern sea. He then proceeded to the south, the west, and the north; wherever the wheel arrived, the kings of those lands each offered up their territories, just as the minor kingdoms of the east had done.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, having followed the golden wheel as it traveled around the four seas, transformed the people through the Way and brought comfort to the common folk, before returning to his own kingdom.
At that time, the precious golden wheel remained suspended in the air above the palace gate. Then, the Wheel-Turning King leaped for joy and said:
"This precious golden wheel is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage-King. This is the accomplishment of the precious golden wheel.
"Having ruled for a long time, at that moment the Golden Wheel Treasure suddenly left its original place in the sky. The official in charge of the wheel quickly went to inform the king:
'Great King!'"
"You should know that the Wheel-Treasure has now departed from its original place.
When the king heard this, he immediately thought to himself:
"I have previously heard from the elders and the aged that if the Wheel-Treasure of a Wheel-Turning Sage King moves, the king's life will not last much longer."

I have now already enjoyed the blessings and pleasures of the human realm; it is fitting that I employ further means to enjoy the blessings and pleasures of the heavens. I shall establish the crown prince to govern the four continents and separately grant a single town to the barber who shaved my hair, commanding him to shave off my beard and hair, don the three dharma robes, and leave the household life to practice the Way.
Then the king immediately summoned the crown prince and said to him:
"Do you know? I have heard from the elders of former times that if the precious golden wheel of a Wheel-Turning Sage King departs from its original place, the king’s life will not last much longer."

I have now already enjoyed the blessings and pleasures of the human realm; I shall now employ skillful means to transition to the enjoyment of celestial bliss. I now wish to shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and entrust the four continents to you. You should exert yourself and show compassion to the people and all living things.
At that time, having received the King’s instruction, the Prince shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and left the household life to practice the Way.
Seven days after the King had gone forth, the precious golden wheel suddenly disappeared. The official in charge of the golden wheel went to inform the King, saying:
"Great King!..."
"You should know that the Wheel-Treasure has now suddenly disappeared.
When the king heard this, he did not become distressed, nor did he go to inquire about his father-king's intentions.
At that time, his father, the King, suddenly passed away.

From that point onward, six successive universal monarchs had all inherited the throne one after another, ruling according to the True Dharma; yet this one king alone governed the country according to his own will, not following the ancient laws. His administration was unjust, and the world complained and lamented; the realm diminished and the people declined.
At that time, a brahmin minister went to address the king, saying: "Great King!
You should know that the kingdom is now declining, the population is wasting away, and things have become increasingly unlike their former state."

"Your Majesty now has many learned men within the realm who are intelligent and erudite, well-versed in the past and present, and fully acquainted with the methods of governance employed by former kings. Why not command them to assemble and inquire of their knowledge? They will surely provide the answers themselves."
At that time, the king immediately summoned his ministers and questioned them regarding the methods by which his predecessors had governed.

Then, the wise ministers answered him in full detail. Having heard their words, the king immediately implemented the former administration and protected the world according to the Dharma; yet, he was still unable to rescue the orphaned and the elderly, nor extend his aid to the most destitute.

At that time, the people of the kingdom gradually fell into poverty; they subsequently began to plunder one another, and bandits became exceedingly numerous. Those who were apprehended by the watchmen were brought before the king, who was addressed thus:
"This man is a thief; we pray that Your Majesty punish him."
The king then asked,
"Are you truly a thief? He replied:
"It is truly so!
I am poor and hungry, unable to sustain myself, and that is why I became a thief.
Thereupon, the king immediately brought forth goods from the treasury to provide for him and addressed him, saying:
"Use these goods to make offerings to your parents and provide for your kinsmen; from this day forward, do not commit robbery again.

When others heard that the king had provided wealth and treasures to those who committed robbery, they began once more to plunder the property of others. They were subsequently caught by the watchmen and brought before the king, who said to him:
"This man is a thief; we pray that Your Majesty will punish him."
The king asked again,
"Are you truly a thief? He replied:
"It is truly so!
I am poor and hungry, unable to sustain myself, and that is why I became a thief.
At that time, the king again brought forth his treasury's wealth to provide for him, and further addressed him, saying:
"Use these goods to provide for your parents and to show compassion toward your kinsmen; from this day forward, do not commit robbery again.

Furthermore, there was another person who, having heard that a thief had been granted wealth and treasures by the king, subsequently went out to plunder the property of others. He was caught by the watchmen and brought before the king, who said to him:
"This man is a thief; I pray that Your Majesty will punish him."
The king asked again,
"Are you truly a thief? He replied:
"It is truly so!
I am poor and hungry, unable to sustain myself, and that is why I became a thief.
At that time, the king thought to himself:

"Previously, when I saw those who were impoverished, I provided them with wealth and treasures, hoping they would desist from their ways. However, others heard of this and began to emulate one another; thus, bandits increased daily without end. Should I not now instead place these men in shackles and manacles, parading them through the streets and alleys, and then carry them out of the city to execute them in the wilderness, so as to serve as a warning to those who follow?"
At that time, the king immediately commanded his attendants:

"Have him arrested and bound; beat the drums and proclaim this order throughout all the streets and alleys. Once it has been completed, load him onto a carriage and take him out of the city to be executed in the wilderness."
When the people of the country all knew that he was a thief who had been arrested and imprisoned by the king, they were paraded through the streets and lanes before being executed in the wilderness.
At that time, the people passed the word among themselves, saying:
"If we were to become thieves, we too would be treated like this; we would be no different from him."

Thereupon, for the sake of self-protection, the people of the country began to manufacture weapons such as staves, swords, and bows and arrows; they proceeded to harm one another and engage in attacks, plundering, and robbery.

From the time this king arrived, poverty first arose; once there was poverty, robbery first arose; once there was robbery, weapons first arose; once there were weapons, killing first arose; and once there was killing, complexions became haggard and lifespans grew short.

At that time, the human life span was exactly forty thousand years; subsequently, it decreased until the life span was twenty thousand years, yet among those sentient beings there were some who lived long and some who died young, and some who experienced suffering and some who experienced happiness.
Those who suffer give rise to thoughts of sexual misconduct and covetousness; they employ many expedient means to plot for the property of others.

At that time, sentient beings become impoverished, resorting to robbery and killing with weapons; these evils increase ever more, and the lifespan of human beings diminishes until it reaches ten thousand years.

"When ten thousand years had passed, sentient beings again began to plunder one another. Having been caught in the act by those on watch, they were brought before the king, who was addressed as follows:
'This man is a thief; we pray that Your Majesty punish him.'"
The king asked, "Did you truly commit the theft? He replied:
"I will not do it!"—thus he deliberately utters a falsehood in the midst of the assembly.

At that time, because those sentient beings are impoverished, they practice robbery; because of robbery, there is warfare with weapons; because of warfare with weapons, there is killing; because of killing, there is greed for acquisition and sexual misconduct; because of greed for acquisition and sexual misconduct, there is lying; and because of lying, their lifespan diminishes further until it reaches one thousand years.

When the human lifespan was one thousand years, three types of verbal misconduct first appeared in the world: first, double-tongued speech; second, harsh speech; and third, frivolous speech. As these three unwholesome karmas grew increasingly intense, the human lifespan gradually decreased to five hundred years.

At the time of the five-hundred-year lifespan, sentient beings again gave rise to three further types of misconduct: first, unlawful sexual misconduct; second, unlawful greed; and third, wrong views. As these three unwholesome karmas grew increasingly intense, the human lifespan gradually decreased to three hundred and two hundred years. As for people today, they live at most a hundred years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.

"In this manner, as they continue to commit evil without ceasing, their lifespan gradually diminishes until it reaches ten years. At the time when the human lifespan is ten years, girls will marry at only five months of age."

At that time, the names of worldly substances such as ghee, honey, and rock sugar, as well as all sweet and delicious flavors, will no longer be heard. Fine rice and grain will transform into weeds and tares; silks, brocades, damasks, fine cotton, and white woolen cloth—garments renowned in the present age—will all disappear, and people will instead weave coarse woolen threads to make their upper garments.

At that time, this earth will abound with thorns, mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, lice, snakes, vipers, bees, and maggots; venomous insects will be numerous, and gold, silver, lapis lazuli, pearls, and other famous jewels will all sink into the ground, while tiles, stones, sand, and gravel will emerge upon the surface.
"At that time, among the various classes of sentient beings, the names of the ten wholesome actions will never again be heard; instead, the ten unwholesome actions alone will fill the world.
At such a time, even the name of wholesome dharmas will not exist; by what means, then, could those people cultivate virtuous conduct?"

At that time, sentient beings will commit extreme evils; they will be unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, unfaithful and unrighteous, and even rebellious and lawless—and yet such people will receive honor and respect.

Now, those who are able to cultivate wholesome conduct, filially support their parents, respectfully obey their teachers and elders, are loyal and trustworthy while harboring righteousness, and practice in accordance with the Way, shall receive honor and respect.

At that time, sentient beings practiced the ten unwholesome actions extensively and fell frequently into the evil realms; when they saw one another, they constantly desired to kill each other, just as hunters see a herd of deer.
At that time, this land will abound with ditches, pits, mountain torrents, and deep valleys; the terrain will be vast and sparsely populated, making travel perilous.
Then, an era of weapons (śastra-kalpa) shall arise, wherein even grass and wood held in the hand will turn into spears and lances, and for seven days, people will slaughter one another in succession.
At that time, a wise person fled far into the forest and took refuge in a hollow; for seven days, harboring a mind of fear, he uttered words of loving-kindness and compassion:
"May you not harm me, and may I not harm you."
They ate the seeds of grasses and trees to preserve their lives; after seven days had passed, they emerged from the mountain forests.
Those who survived were able to see one another, and with joy and celebration, they said: "Have you not died?"
"Are you not dead?

Just as parents who have only one son, upon meeting after a long separation, feel immeasurable joy, those people likewise each harbored great joy and congratulated one another. They then inquired about his family; they learned that many of his relatives had died, and for seven days they wept and wailed, crying out toward one another.
After seven days had passed, they again celebrated together for another seven days, enjoying themselves with joy and merriment. Then, they thought to themselves:

"Because we have accumulated such extensive evil, we have encountered this calamity; our kinsmen have died and our families have been destroyed. Now we ought to practice virtue together to some small degree. What kind of virtue should we practice?"
"One must not kill living beings.

At that time, all sentient beings harbored hearts of loving-kindness and did not harm one another; consequently, the physical form and lifespan of these beings increased, such that those who lived for ten years now lived for twenty years.
When people lived for twenty years, they further thought to themselves:

"Because we practiced a small amount of wholesome conduct and did not harm one another, our lifespan has been extended to twenty years. Now, it would be well to increase our wholesome practice even further; what wholesome deed should we cultivate?"
"Having already refrained from taking life, one should refrain from stealing.
Once they had cultivated non-stealing, their lifespan was extended to forty years.
When people lived for forty years, they again thought:
"Because we have practiced a small amount of goodness, our lifespans have been extended. Now, we should further increase our small store of merit; what goodness may we practice?
We shall refrain from sexual misconduct."
Thereupon, those people completely refrained from sexual misconduct, and their lifespans were extended to eighty years.
Those who lived for eighty years then thought:

"Because we practiced a small amount of goodness in our youth, our lifespans have been extended; now, would it not be well to further increase our practice of goodness? What kind of goodness might we cultivate?"
"One must not speak falsely.
Thereupon, those people refrained entirely from false speech, and their lifespan extended to one hundred and sixty years.
When they reached one hundred and sixty years, the people again had this thought:
"Because we have practiced a small amount of virtue, our lifespans have been extended. We should now further increase our minor virtues; what virtue may we practice?
We shall refrain from double-tongued speech."
Thereupon, those people completely refrained from double-tongued speech, and their lifespan extended to three hundred and twenty years.
When they reached the age of three hundred and twenty, the people again had this thought:
"Because we practiced a small amount of goodness, our lifespan has been extended; now, would it not be well to further increase our practice of goodness? What kind of goodness can be cultivated?"
"One should not engage in harsh speech.
Thereupon, those people completely refrained from harsh speech, and their lifespan was extended to six hundred and forty [years].
At that time, the people again thought:
"Because we have cultivated wholesome deeds, our lifespans have been extended; now, it would be well for us to further increase our small store of merit. What wholesome deed may we cultivate?
We shall refrain from frivolous speech."
Thereupon, those people completely refrained from frivolous speech, and their lifespan was extended to two thousand years.
When they had lived for two thousand years, the people again thought to themselves:
"Because we have practiced wholesome deeds, our lifespan has been extended; now, would it not be well to further increase our wholesome merit? What wholesome deed may we practice?"
"One should not be stingy or greedy.
Thereupon, those people completely abandoned stinginess and greed and practiced giving, whereby their lifespan was extended to five thousand years.
When they had reached five thousand years, the people again thought:
"Because we have practiced wholesome deeds, our lifespans have been extended. Now, it would be well if we could further increase our small amount of merit; what wholesome deed may we practice?
We shall refrain from envy and cultivate wholesome deeds with a mind of loving-kindness."
Thereupon, those people ceased all jealousy and cultivated goodness with a compassionate heart; their lifespan was extended until it reached ten thousand years.
When their lifespan reached ten thousand years, the people again had this thought:
"Because we have cultivated goodness, our lifespan has been extended. Now, might we not further increase our small amount of merit? What goodness may we cultivate?"
"One should practice right view and not give rise to perversions.
Thereupon, that person fully practiced right view and did not give rise to perversions; his lifespan was extended to twenty thousand years.
When the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, people again had this thought:
"Because we have practiced wholesome deeds, our lifespans have been extended; now, would it not be well to further increase our wholesome practices? What wholesome deed may we practice?"
"One should extinguish three unwholesome dharmas: first, unlawful sexual misconduct; second, unlawful greed; and third, false views.
Thereupon, that person completely extinguished these three unwholesome dharmas, and his lifespan was extended to forty thousand years.
When the human lifespan was forty thousand years, people again had this thought:
"Because we have practiced virtue, our lifespans have been extended; now, would it not be well to further increase our small amount of goodness? What virtue may we practice?"
"One should filially support one's parents and respectfully serve one's teachers and elders.
Thereupon, that person immediately began to filially support their parents and respectfully serve their teachers and elders, and their lifespan was extended to eighty thousand years.
"When the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, women will not go out to marry until they are five hundred years old.

At that time, humans shall have nine kinds of ailments: first, cold; second, heat; third, hunger; fourth, thirst; fifth, excrement; sixth, urine; seventh, desire; eighth, gluttony; and ninth, old age."
