At that time, this great earth was level and smooth, free of ditches, pits, mounds, ruins, or thorns; it was likewise devoid of mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, vipers, and venomous insects. Pottery shards, stones, sand, and gravel were transformed into lapis lazuli. The population flourished, the five grains were abundant and cheap, and there was boundless prosperity and joy.
At that time, eighty thousand great cities shall arise, with villages and towns situated so close together that their roosters can hear one another’s cries.

At that time, a Buddha shall appear in the world named Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles, just as the present Tathāgata is fully endowed with the ten titles. He, among the devas, Śakras, Brahmās, Māras, or celestial Māras, among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans, shall realize [the truth] through his own direct experience, just as I now, among the devas, Śakras, Brahmās, Māras, or celestial Māras, among śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans, realize it through my own direct experience.

He shall preach the Dharma, excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its end; complete in meaning and phrasing, he shall purely cultivate the holy life—just as I today preach the Dharma, with words that are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, all of which are true and correct, complete in meaning and phrasing, and pure in the holy life.
That assembly of disciples numbered countless thousands of myriads, as the number of my own disciples today is several hundred.
At that time, the people called his disciples "Sons of Compassion" (Maitreyaputra), just as my disciples are called "Sons of Śākya" (Śākyaputra).

"At that time, there was a king named Śaṅkha, a Kṣatriya of the consecrated head lineage, a Wheel-Turning Sage King who ruled over the four continents. He governed according to the True Dharma, and all submitted without exception. He was endowed with the seven treasures: first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the dark-blue horse treasure; fourth, the divine jewel treasure; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the householder treasure; and seventh, the military commander treasure."

The king had a thousand sons, valiant and fierce, capable of repelling external enemies; the four quarters were respectful and submissive, such that no weapons or staves were employed, and peace prevailed naturally.
At that time, the Holy King erected a great precious banner, sixteen fathoms in circumference and one thousand fathoms in height; it was adorned with a thousand varieties of colors.
The banner had a hundred facets, each facet having a hundred branches, woven from precious threads and interspersed with various jewels.

Thereupon, the Holy King, having dismantled this banner, bestowed it upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the poor of the kingdom; thereafter, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, left the household life to practice the Way, and cultivated the supreme conduct. Within this present life, he realized it for himself: birth and death were exhausted, the holy life was established, what was to be done had been accomplished, and there would be no further existence.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"You should diligently cultivate wholesome conduct. By cultivating wholesome conduct, one's lifespan will be extended, one's complexion will improve, one will be at peace and happy, one's wealth and treasures will abound, and one's power will be complete—just as when kings follow the ancient laws of the Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), their lifespan is extended, their complexion improves, they are at peace and happy, their wealth and treasures abound, and their power is complete."

In the same way, a bhikṣu should cultivate wholesome dharmas; thus his lifespan will be prolonged, his complexion will improve, he will dwell in peace and happiness, his wealth and treasures will abound, and his power will be fully perfected.
“How does a bhikṣu extend his lifespan?
It is when a bhikṣu cultivates the concentration of desire, practicing with diligence and without slackening, accomplishing the practice of cessation, thereby cultivating the basis of psychic power;

he cultivates the concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation, practicing with diligence and without slackening, accomplishing the practice of cessation, thereby cultivating the basis of psychic power—this is what is meant by extending the lifespan.”
What is meant by a bhikṣu’s countenance being enhanced?

It is when a bhikṣu is fully endowed with the precepts, achieves dignified deportment, perceives even minor offenses as grounds for great dread, and trains equally in all the rules until they are completely fulfilled and perfected; this is called a bhikṣu’s countenance being enhanced.
What is meant by a bhikṣu’s peace and happiness?

In this regard, a bhikṣu abandons sensual desire and removes unwholesome states; with directed thought and evaluation, he enters and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and happiness.

Having stilled directed thought and evaluation, with internal serenity and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and happiness.

Abandoning joy and guarding equanimity, with a concentrated and undistracted mind, he experiences within himself that bliss which the noble ones seek—dwelling with mindfulness and clear comprehension, he enters and abides in the third dhyāna.

Abandoning both suffering and pleasure, and having previously eliminated sorrow and joy, he dwells in neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, with purity of mindfulness through equanimity; he enters and abides in the fourth dhyāna. This is what is meant by a bhikṣu’s peace and happiness.
"What is meant by a bhikṣu being abundant in wealth?

It is when a bhikṣu cultivates a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), pervading one direction, and likewise the other directions, all around, far and wide—unified, immeasurable, free from enmity and resentment, with a heart devoid of jealousy or ill will, serene, compassionate, and gentle, finding his own delight therein. The same applies to the minds of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); this is what it means for a bhikṣu to be abundant in wealth."
What is meant by a bhikṣu being endowed with power?

In this regard, a bhikṣu knows the noble truth of suffering as it truly is, and he likewise knows the truths of its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are; this is what is meant by a bhikṣu being endowed with power.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“I have now surveyed all those who possess power, and none surpasses the power of Māra; yet a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted possesses the power to overcome him.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

7. The Bhismasūtra (VII), Part Two, The Bhismasūtra, Number Three.

At that time, the young woman Kāśyapī was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala with five hundred bhikṣus. Gradually, they arrived at the brahmin village of Svastika. Then, the young woman Kāśyapī stayed in the Śiṃśapā Grove to the north of the village of Svastika.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Pāyāsi who resided in the village of Setavyā.

This village was prosperous and pleasant, with a large population and lush vegetation; King Prasenajit had granted this village to the brahmin Pāyāsi as a private fiefdom, making it his "Brahma-portion."
The brahmin Pāṭikāputta constantly harbored heterodox views and said to others:
"There is no other world, nor is there rebirth, nor is there retribution for good or evil deeds."

At that time, the people of the village of Sāvatthī heard that the maiden Kāśyapa, together with five hundred bhikṣus, had gradually arrived from the kingdom of Kośala at this Śiṃśapā Grove. They said to one another:

"This maiden Kāśyapa has a great reputation; she has already attained arhatship, is an elder of long standing, is widely learned and of vast knowledge, is intelligent and wise, possesses eloquence suited to the occasion, and is skilled in discourse. Would it not be excellent if we were now to see her?"
At that time, those villagers went to visit Kāśyapa day after day in succession.

Then, while Bhṛgu was atop a high tower, he saw the villagers following one another in groups and did not know where they were going; he immediately asked his attendants holding parasols, "For what reason are those people following one another in such a crowd?"

The attendant replied, "I have heard that the maiden Kāśyapa, accompanied by five hundred bhikṣus, is traveling through the country of Kośala and has arrived at the Śiṃśapā Forest. Furthermore, I have heard that she possesses great renown; she has already attained arhatship, is an elder of long standing, is widely learned and of vast knowledge, is brilliant and wise, possesses eloquence suited to the occasion, and is skilled in discourse.
These people are traveling in a group, wishing to go to see Kāśyapa."
Then, the brahmin Pāṭikāputra immediately commanded his attendant:
"Go quickly and tell those people:
'Wait a moment!'"
"We should go together to meet him. Why is this?
That man is deluded and deceives the world;
he claims there is another world, that there is rebirth, and that there are rewards for good and evil deeds, yet in reality there is no other world, nor rebirth, nor rewards for good and evil.
Then, having received these instructions, the messenger went at once and spoke to the people of the village of Sāvatthī, saying:
"The brāhmaṇa says: 'Stay where you are!'"
"We should go together to meet him.
The villagers replied, "Excellent! Excellent!"
"If he is able to come, we shall travel together.
The messenger returned and reported:
"That person has already stopped; you may go as you please."

Then the brahmin descended from the high tower and commanded his attendants to prepare the carriage. Surrounded by the villagers of that village, he proceeded to the Śālavana grove. Upon arrival, he alighted from the carriage and advanced on foot to where Kāśyapa was. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side.

Among those villagers—brahmins and householders—some prostrated themselves before Kāśyapa and then sat down; some, having exchanged greetings, sat down; some, having announced their names, sat down; some, having joined their palms in reverence, sat down; and some sat down in silence.
Then, the brahmin Pāṭikāputra said to the young woman Kāśyapī:
"I now wish to ask a question; would you have the leisure to grant me your attention?"
Kāśyapa replied, "Ask whatever you wish; having heard it, you shall understand. The brāhmaṇa said:
“I, as a proponent of this doctrine, maintain that there is no future world, nor is there rebirth, nor is there retribution for sins or merit;
what do you say to this? Kāśyapa replied, “I shall now question you; answer according to your own understanding. Is the sun and moon above us of this world?”
"Is it for another world?
Is it for humans or for devas? The brāhmaṇa replied:
"The sun and moon belong to the other world, not this world;
they are gods, not humans. Kāśyapa replied:
"By this it can be known that there must be another world, as well as rebirth, and the retribution of good and evil. The Brahmin said,
"Though you claim there is another world, rebirth, and the retribution of good and evil, according to my own view, none of these exist at all."
Kāśyapa asked: "Is there any reason by which one might know that there is no other world, no rebirth, and no retribution for good or evil deeds?"
The brahmin replied, “I have a reason. Kāśyapa asked:
“For what reason do you say there is no other world?
The brāhmaṇa replied, “Kāśyapa!”
"I have a kinsman and acquaintance who has fallen ill and is suffering from disease. I went to visit him and asked:

'The various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas each hold differing views, claiming that those who kill living beings, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, use double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, or frivolous chatter, and who are greedy, jealous, or hold wrong views—all such persons, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, enter hell.'"
At first I did not believe this; why was that?
It is because I have never before seen anyone who, having died, returned to report on the place where they had fallen.
If there were someone who came to tell me of such a place, I would certainly have believed and accepted it.

"You are now my close relative, yet you have committed all ten evil deeds. If what the śramaṇa says is true, you will surely enter the great hells upon death. Now I trust you; let me receive a definitive assurance from you. If there truly are hells, you must return and tell me so that I may know it, and only then shall I believe."
"Kāśyapa! Since his death, he has not returned to this day. He was my kinsman; he ought not to deceive me. Having promised and yet not coming, there must surely be no future world."
Kāśyapa replied: "Those who possess wisdom gain understanding through parables; I shall now provide a parable for you to explain this.

Suppose there were a thief, constantly harboring deceit and fraud, who violated the king’s prohibitive laws. Having been caught by the watchmen, he was brought before the king, who addressed him, saying:"
"This man is a thief; we pray that Your Majesty punish him.
The king immediately commanded his attendants to arrest and bind the man, parading him through all the streets and alleys before loading him onto a cart and taking him out of the city to be executed.
At that time, the attendants led the thief to the executioner, whereupon the thief spoke to the guards with gentle and soft words:
"Release me so that I may see my relatives, speak with them, and bid them farewell, after which I shall return.
What do you think, brahmin? Would those guards be willing to release him?
The brahmin replied, "No! Kāśyapa spoke again:

"If even those of his own kind, who still exist together with him in the present world, he does not release, how much less will he release you—his own kin—who are fully possessed of the ten evil deeds? Upon the death and end of life, you will surely enter hell. The hell-wardens have no compassion, nor are they of your kind; you have died and are born into a different world. Even if he were to seek from the hell-wardens with gentle words, saying:
'Please release me for a moment so that I may return to the world to see my relatives and bid them farewell, and then I shall return,' [he would not be released]."
"Would it be permissible to release him? The Brahmin replied, "No!"
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"By comparing these things with one another, it is sufficient to know [the truth] for oneself; why do you persist in delusion and give rise to false views? The brāhmaṇa said:
"Although you have cited analogies to claim that there is another world, I still say there is none.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Do you perhaps have any further reasons by which one may know that there is no other world?"
The brahmin replied, “I have yet another reason for knowing that there is no other world. Kāśyapa asked:
"By what means is this known? He replied: "Kāśyapa!..."
"I have a kinsman who has fallen gravely ill. I went to him and said:

'Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas each harbor different views; some say there is a future world, claiming that those who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not deceive, do not speak divisively, harshly, falsely, or frivolously, and who are free from greed, envy, and wrong views, will all be reborn in the heavens when their bodies perish and their lives end.
At first, I did not believe this. Why was that?'"
"Never before have I seen anyone who, having died, has returned to report the place where they were reborn.
If someone were to come and tell me of their rebirth, I would certainly believe them;

you, however, are my close relative and are fully endowed with the ten wholesome deeds. If what the śramaṇa says is true, then upon the end of your life, you will surely be reborn in the heavens. I now believe this and rely on you for certainty. If there truly is such a reward in heaven, you must certainly return and tell me so, and only then shall I believe."
"Kāśyapa! Since his death, he has not returned to this day. He was my kinsman and should not have deceived me; having promised and yet not coming, there must certainly be no other world."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables; I shall now provide another parable for you.
It is like a man who has fallen into a deep latrine, his body and head submerged within. The king commands his attendants:"

"Pull this person out and, using bamboo as a comb, scrape his body three times. Then cleanse him with bathing beans and pure ash as if washing him; afterwards, bathe his body with fragrant water. Sprinkle fine powders of various incenses over his body and command the barber to shave his beard and hair clean."

Furthermore, he commands his attendants to bathe him again, doing so up to three times; they wash him with fragrant water, sprinkle him with powdered incense, adorn his body with famous garments and fine robes, satisfy his palate with a hundred flavors of sweet delicacies, and lead him to a lofty hall for the enjoyment of the five desires. Would that man then be able to return to the latrine?
He replied, "I cannot! That place is foul and stinking; how could I return there?"
Kāśyapa said: "The same is true for the devas.
This Jambudvīpa is foul, filthy, and impure; though the devas above are a hundred yojanas away from here, they smell the stench of humans from afar, which is even worse than that of a latrine."

"Brāhmaṇa! Suppose your kinsmen and acquaintances were fully endowed with the ten wholesome paths of action; they would surely be reborn in the heavens, delighting themselves with the five desires and experiencing boundless happiness. Would they ever willingly return again to enter this latrine of Jambudvīpa?"
He replied, "No. Kāśyapa spoke again:
"By comparing these things, one can know for oneself; why then do you persist in delusion and give rise to false views?
The Brahmin replied, "Though you cite analogies and speak of a future world, I still say it does not exist."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Do you perhaps have any other reason by which one might know that there is no future world? The brāhmaṇa replied:
"I have another reason for knowing that there is no other world.
Kāśyapa asked, "By what reason do you know this?"
He replied: "Kāśyapa! I had a kinsman who fell gravely ill; I went to him and said: "

“Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas each harbor different views, asserting that there is a future life and claiming that those who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not deceive, and do not drink intoxicants will all, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
I do not believe this either. Why is that? ”
"Never before have I seen anyone who, having died, has returned to report the place where they were reborn;
if someone were to come and speak of such a rebirth, I would certainly believe them.

Now you are my relative, fully endowed with the five precepts, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, you will surely be born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. I now believe this, and I seek confirmation from you: if there truly is such heavenly bliss, you should return and tell me so that I may know it, and only then shall I believe."

"Kāśyapa! Since his death, he has not returned to this day. He was my kinsman; there should have been no deception. Having given his word and yet failing to come, there must surely be no future world."
Kāśyapa replied:

"A hundred years here correspond to exactly one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; likewise, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. Thus, the lifespan of those devas is one thousand years."
"How is it, brahmin? Your kinsmen were fully endowed with the five precepts; when their bodies perished at the end of life, they were certain to be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Once reborn there in heaven, they formed this thought:"
"Will you ever see him again who said, 'When I was first born here, after playing and sporting for two or three days,
I shall come down to give you my word'?"
He replied: "No!
I have been dead for a long time; by what means could we meet?"
The brāhmaṇa said, "I do not believe you.
Who has come to inform you that there is a Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and that its lifespan is such as this?
Kāśyapa replied:
“Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables; I shall now further provide a parable for you.

Suppose there were a person born blind who did not recognize the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—nor coarse or fine textures, nor long or short shapes. Furthermore, he could not see the sun, the moon, the stars, or the topography of hills and valleys.”
Someone asked, "What are the five colors— blue, yellow, red, and white?
The blind man replied:
"There are no five colors.
In this way, they claim that there is nothing—neither coarse nor fine, long nor short, nor sun, moon, stars, mountains, hills, ravines, nor gullies.
"What do you think,
brahmin? Is what that blind man said a correct answer?"
He replied, "No! Why is that?"

In the world, there currently exist five colors—blue, yellow, red, white—and coarse, fine, long, short, as well as the sun, moon, celestial bodies, mountains, hills, ditches, and ravines; yet they claim these do not exist.
"Brahmin! You are just like this.
The lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa devas truly exists and is not non-existent; yet because you do not see it for yourself, you say that it does not exist."
The brahmin said, "Although you say it exists, I still do not believe you.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"What further conditions did you employ to know that they do not exist? He replied, "Kāśyapa!"
Among the people of the village granted to me by my lord, there was one who committed theft. Having been apprehended through surveillance, he was brought before me, and they said to me:
"This man is a thief; we pray that you will punish him."
I replied: "Bind this man, place him inside a large cauldron, cover it with hide and thick clay to ensure it is airtight and leak-proof, surround it with guards, and boil him with fire."

At that time, wishing to observe and know the place from which his spirit had emerged, I led my attendants to circle the cauldron and examine it, yet I saw no place where the spirit came or went; furthermore, when I opened the cauldron to look inside, I still saw no place for the spirit to have traveled to or from.
"For this reason, one knows that there is no future world.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"I now ask you; if you can answer, respond as you please."
"Brāhmaṇa! When you were resting and sleeping in your high tower, have you ever dreamed of mountain forests, rivers, gardens, bathing pools, cities, towns, streets, or lanes?"
He replied, "I saw it in a dream.
He asked again:
“Brahmin! When you were dreaming, did your household members and kinsmen attend upon you? He replied:
"Attendant! he asked again, "Brahmin!"
“Do your various attendants see your consciousness-spirit entering or exiting?
He replied, “I do not see it.”
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Even while you are alive, the coming and going of the conscious spirit cannot be seen; how much less so in the case of one who is dead?
You must not judge sentient beings based solely on what is manifest before your eyes."

"Brahmin! There is a bhikṣu who, during the first and last watches of the night, casts off sleep and practices with diligence and without slackening, focusing his mindfulness on the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma). By the power of samādhi, he cultivates the pure divine eye;
by the power of the divine eye, he observes sentient beings."

He fully knows and sees how beings die here and are born there, and how they pass from there to be born here; he perceives their long or short lifespans, their beautiful or ugly complexions, and how they experience retribution according to their conduct within the realms of good and evil.
"You must not, with your defiled and turbid fleshly eyes—which cannot penetrate to see where sentient beings go—declare that they do not exist.
O Brahmin! By this you may know that there must certainly be another world."
The brahmin said, "Although you have cited metaphors to speak of the existence of another world, according to what I see, it still does not exist.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Do you have any further reasons for knowing that there is no other world? The brāhmaṇa replied, "I do."
Kāśyapa asked, "By what means do you know this?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"Among the people of the village granted to me, there was one who committed a theft. Having been apprehended through surveillance, he was brought before me, and they said to me:
'This man is a thief; we pray that you punish him.'"
I commanded my attendants to bind this man and flay his skin alive, seeking his *vijñāna* (consciousness), yet it was nowhere to be seen;
again, I commanded my attendants to mince and cut his flesh, seeking the *vijñāna*, yet it was still not seen;
again, I commanded my attendants to sever his tendons, veins, and to search for the spirit within the spaces between his bones, yet it was once more not seen.
He further commanded his attendants to break his bones and extract the marrow, seeking the soul within the marrow, yet it was not to be seen.
"Kāśyapa! By this means, I know that there is no future world."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables; I shall now provide a parable for you.

In the distant past, long ago, there was a country that had been destroyed and remained in ruins, unrecovered. At that time, five hundred merchant wagons passed through that land. There was a brahmin who worshipped the fire deity and habitually stayed in a certain forest."
At that time, all the merchants went there to stay for the night and departed at dawn. Then, a fire-worshipping brahmin thought to himself:
"The merchants who stayed here in this forest have now left; perhaps there is something they have left behind—I should go and look."
He immediately went to that place, but saw nothing at all; there was only a small child, barely one year old, sitting there alone.
The brahmin thought again:
"How can I bear to see this child die before my very eyes?"
"Now, would it not be better to take this child to my own dwelling and raise him?
He then took the child in his arms and went to his residence to nurture him; as the boy grew, he reached the age of ten or more years.
At that time, this brahmin, having a minor matter on which he wished to travel among the people, said to the boy:
"I have a small errand and wish to go out for a short while; you must guard this fire well and take care not to let it go out."
"If the fire should go out, you must drill wood with a fire-drill to fetch fire and kindle it.
Having given these instructions, he departed from the forest to wander about.
After the brahmin had left, the boy was preoccupied with play and did not check on the fire frequently; consequently, the fire went out.
When the boy returned from his play, he saw that the fire had already been extinguished. Distressed, he said: "I have done wrong.
When my father departed, he gave me detailed instructions to guard this fire and take care not to let it go out; yet, out of greed for play, I caused it to be extinguished. What shall I do?"

At that time, the boy blew on the ashes seeking fire, but being unable to find it, he then split firewood with an axe seeking fire, yet again was unable to find it; furthermore, he chopped the wood and placed it in a mortar, pounding it to seek fire, but once more he was unable to find it.
At that time, the brahmin returned from among the people and went to the grove where he asked the boy, "I previously instructed you to guard the fire; has the fire not been extinguished?"
The boy replied, "I went out to play and did not watch over it at the proper time; the fire has now been extinguished.
He questioned the boy again:
“By what means do you seek fire again?
The boy replied, “Fire comes from wood;
I split the wood with an axe to seek fire, yet I could not find it.”
"Furthermore, he chopped it until it was shattered, placed it in a mortar, and pounded it with a pestle seeking fire, yet he could not obtain it.
At that time, the brahmin used a fire-drill to bore into wood to produce fire; having piled up firewood and set it ablaze, he said to the boy:
"In the proper method for seeking fire, one should act in this way; one should not seek it by breaking, splitting, or pulverizing [the wood]."

“Brahmin! You are likewise without skillful means; you flay the skin from a dead person in search of the consciousness-spirit (vijñāna). You cannot discern the nature of sentient beings by observing only what is manifest before your eyes.”

"Brāhmaṇa! There are bhikṣus who, during the first and last watches of the night, cast off sleep and, with diligent and tireless effort, focus their mindfulness on the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā). By the power of samādhi, they cultivate the pure divine eye (dibbacakkhu); and by the power of that divine eye, they observe sentient beings—how they die here and are born there, how they pass from there and are born here; they perceive the length of their lifespans, the beauty or ugliness of their complexions, and how they experience retribution according to their conduct, whether in good or evil destinies—all of which they know and see.
You, however, cannot see through to the destinies of sentient beings with your defiled physical eyes; therefore, you must not say that such things do not exist."
"O Brahmin! By this it can be known that there must be another world. The Brahmin said:
"Although you have cited analogies to claim that there is a future world, according to what I perceive, it simply does not exist.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Do you perhaps have any further reasons for knowing that there is no future world?"
The brahmin said, "There is! Kāśyapa said:
“By what means do you know this?
The brāhmaṇa replied, “A man from my granted village committed a theft; having been caught by a watchman, he was brought before me, and he said to me:”
"This man is a thief; I pray that you punish him.
I then commanded my attendants:
"Take this man and weigh him on the scales."
The attendant, having received these instructions, immediately weighed him on the scales.
The king further commanded the attendant:
"Take this man and kill him slowly and steadily; do not damage his skin or flesh."
He immediately followed my instructions and killed it without causing any harm.
I then commanded my attendants: "Weigh it once more."
Thus, he returns to his original state. Kāśyapa!
When one is called by name, their consciousness still remains; their countenance is joyful and pleasant, they are still able to speak, and their body becomes light.

After death, the body becomes heavy again; consciousness has already ceased, there is no longer any color [in the face], one cannot speak, and the body becomes even heavier. By these reasons, I know that there is no other world.
Kāśyapa said to the brāhmaṇa:
“I shall now question you; answer me as you please.
Suppose a person were to weigh iron: first weighing it when cold, and then weighing it when hot—how could it possess radiance, color, softness, and lightness?”
"Why is it that when it lacks luster and color, it becomes hard and heavy?
The brahmin replied, "Hot iron has color, is soft and light; cold iron lacks color, is rigid and heavy."
Kāśyapa said: "Human beings are also like this: while alive, they have a healthy complexion, are supple and light;
when dead, they lose their complexion, become rigid and heavy."
"By this it can be known that there must be another world.
The Brahmin said, "Though you cite analogies to claim that there is another world, according to what I have observed, there certainly is none."
Kāśyapa said: "For what reason do you know that there is no other world?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"I have a relative who has fallen seriously ill.
At that time, I went to him and said:
'Support this sick person and cause him to lie on his right side.'"
His gazing, stretching and contracting his limbs, and speaking were all as usual;
furthermore, when he was made to lie on his left side and rolled over repeatedly, his stretching and contracting, gazing, and speaking remained as usual, until he suddenly passed away.

I again had people assist him in turning over, lying on his left side and then his right, and observed him closely as he repeatedly turned; yet he no longer flexed or extended his limbs, nor did he look around or speak. By this, I knew for certain that there is no other world.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables; I shall now provide a parable for you.

Once there was a country where the sound of the conch shell had never been heard. At that time, there was a man skilled at blowing the conch who went to that country, entered a village, blew the conch three times, and then set it down on the ground."
At that time, the men and women of the village were startled by the sound and all went to inquire:
"What is this sound? How can it be so sorrowful, harmonious, and clear?"
That man pointed to the conch shell and said,
"This is the sound of that object.
Then, the villager touched the conch shell with his hand and said:
"Make a sound! Make a sound! he cried, but the conch shell did not ring at all;
its owner then took it up, blew into it three times, and set it down on the ground.

Then the villagers said, "That beautiful sound just now was not produced by the power of the conch shell itself; it had hands and a mouth, and only after someone blew upon it with breath did it resound."

"Human beings are also like this: when they possess life-force (*jīva*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the inhalation and exhalation of breath, they are able to bend and stretch, look about, and speak;
when they lack life-force, lack consciousness, and lack the inhalation and exhalation of breath, they cannot bend or stretch, look about, or speak."
He further said to the brāhmaṇa:
"You should now abandon this evil and false view; do not increase your own suffering and affliction for the sake of the long night.
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"I cannot relinquish it. Why is this so? Since my birth, I have recited it through the long night;
I have studied and mastered it with firm resolve—how could I possibly relinquish it?"
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables; I shall now provide a further illustration for you.
Long ago, in the distant past, there was a kingdom whose borders were desolate and its people ruined."
In that country there were two men, one wise and one foolish, who said to each other:
"I am your kinsman; let us go out of the city together to seek wealth as companions."
They immediately followed one another to an empty village. Seeing hemp on the ground, the wise man said to the fool:
"Let us gather some and carry it back.
At that time, the two of them each took a load. Continuing on, they passed by a previous village and saw hemp fibers; then the wise man spoke:
"The hemp fibers have been successfully processed; they are light and fine, and thus acceptable.
Another person said, "I have already taken the hemp and bound it firmly; I cannot let it go."
The one who was wise immediately took the hemp fibers and departed with his heavy burden;
they continued forward together until they saw some hempen cloth, whereupon the wise one said:
"This hempen cloth is finished and ready; it is light and fine, and may be taken."
The first person said:
"I have already taken the hemp and bound it so firmly that I cannot let it go.
The wise man among them immediately abandoned the hemp fibers and took cloth for his own weight.
They proceeded together once more and saw some cotton cloth (*karpāsa*).
One of the wise men said, "Cotton cloth is expensive; it is light and fine, so we should take it. The other man said:
"I have already taken this hemp; it is securely bound and I have carried it a long distance, so I cannot abandon it.
At that time, a wise person immediately discarded the hemp cloth and took the cotton.
"Proceeding in this manner, he saw cotton thread, then white cloth, then white copper, then white silver, then gold. One wise man said:

'If there is no gold, one should take white silver; if there is no white silver, one should take white copper, and so on down to the hemp thread; if there is no hemp thread, one should take the hemp itself.'"

"In this village there is now a great abundance of gold, the most excellent of all treasures; you should abandon your hemp and I shall abandon my silver, so that we may together take the gold and return home with it as our own."
The other man said:
"I have taken this hemp and bound it firmly; having carried it over a long distance, I cannot abandon it.
If you wish to take it, do as you please."

The one who was wise discarded the silver and took the gold; carrying his heavy burden, he returned home. When his kinsmen saw from afar that he had obtained such great wealth in gold and jewels, they welcomed him with joy.
At that time, the one who had obtained gold saw his kinsmen coming to meet him and was filled with great joy.

However, when the ignorant man returned home carrying the hemp, his kinsmen saw him and were displeased; they neither greeted him nor rose to welcome him, causing the man carrying the hemp to feel redoubled shame and remorse.

"Brahmin! You should now abandon your evil habits and false views; do not increase your own suffering and affliction for the sake of the long night. It would be like a man carrying hemp who remains firm in his resolve and refuses to take gold and jewels; he returns home carrying only hemp, exhausting himself in vain, displeasing his kinsmen, and remaining poor through the long night, thereby increasing his own grief and pain."
The brāhmaṇa said: "I can never abandon this view. Why is that?
It is because I have taught much through this view and brought great benefit to many; the kings of the four quarters all know my name, and they all know that I am a proponent of annihilationism."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables; I shall now provide a further illustration for you.
Long ago, in the distant past, there was a kingdom whose borders were desolate and its people ruined."
At that time, there was a merchant with a thousand wagons passing through that land; as water, grain, firewood, and fodder were not sufficient for their needs, the merchant leader thought to himself:
"Our company is large, yet water, grain, firewood, and fodder are not sufficient for our needs. It would be best now to divide ourselves into two groups, and let one group set out ahead."
Before him, the Guide saw a man with a coarse and large body, red eyes, and a black face, his body smeared with mud; seeing him approaching from afar, he immediately asked:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied, "I have come from the village ahead.
He was asked again:
"Is there an abundance of water, grain, firewood, and grass where you have come from?

The man replied, "Where I have come from, there is an abundance of water and grain, and there is no lack of firewood and grass. On the way here, I encountered a heavy rain from the heavens; that place had much water and was likewise rich in firewood and grass."
He further said to the caravan leader:
"If you have grain or fodder upon your carts, you may discard it all; they already possess these in abundance, so there is no need for heavy loads."
Then, that merchant leader said to the merchants:
"As I was traveling forward, I saw a man with red eyes and a black face, his body smeared with mud. From afar, I asked him:
'Where have you come from?'"
He immediately replied to me, saying,
"I have come from the village ahead.
I then asked him again:
"Is there an abundance of water, grain, firewood, and grass in the place from which you have come?
He replied to me: "It is indeed very abundant there."
He further said to me:
"Just now, on the way, we encountered a heavy rainstorm; this place has plenty of water and is rich in firewood and grass.
He spoke to me again:
"If there is any grain or straw upon your carts, you may discard it all; he has it in abundance himself, so there is no need for heavy loads.
You should each cast away the grain and straw, and proceed quickly with lightened carts.
They immediately acted according to those words, each discarding their grain and fodder, and the light chariots advanced swiftly.
In this manner, they did not see water or grass for one day; nor for two days, three days, and even up to seven days, whereupon they again saw none.
At that time, the merchants were exhausted in the vast wilderness and were devoured by ghosts.

Subsequently, another group proceeded along the road; the caravan leader then encountered a man ahead of him who had red eyes and a black face, with mud smeared over his body. Seeing him from afar, he asked:
"Where have you come from?"
That person replied,
"I have come from the village ahead.
He asked again:
"Is there an abundance of water, grain, firewood, and grass where you have come from? The man replied,
"There is indeed great abundance."
He spoke again to the caravan leader:
"On the way, I encountered a heavy rain from the heavens; that place has much water and is also abundant in firewood and grass.
He spoke again to the caravan leader:
"If you have grain or grass upon your carts, you may discard it; they already have it in abundance, so there is no need for heavy loads.
Then, the merchant leader returned and said to the other merchants, "As I was traveling forward, I saw a man who spoke of this matter as follows:"
"If there is any grain or straw upon your carts, you may discard it all; they have it in abundance themselves, so there is no need for heavy loads.
Then the caravan leader said, "You must not discard your grain or straw. You should keep them until you obtain new supplies, at which point you may discard them. Why is that?"
"Only when the new supply meets with the old shall we be able to cross this wilderness.
At that time, those merchants traveled with heavily laden carts; thus they went for one day without seeing water or grass, and for two days, three days, up to seven days, yet still saw none.
"I only see that the person ahead has been devoured by a ghost, his bones scattered in disarray. 'Brahmin!
That one with red eyes and a black face is a rākṣasa ghost.'"
Those who follow your instructions will likewise suffer for a long night, just as they did.
Because the merchants of the first caravan lacked wisdom, they followed the words of their guide and brought about their own destruction.

"O Brahmin! Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas possess diligence and wisdom, those who receive and follow their teachings will obtain peace for a long night, just as that latter group of merchants, by virtue of their wisdom, was able to escape danger."
“Brahmin! You should now rather abandon this evil view; do not increase your own suffering and affliction for the sake of a long night. The Brahmin said:
"I can never abandon my view; even if someone were to come and forcefully admonish me, it would only provoke my anger, for I will never relinquish this view.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Those who possess wisdom gain understanding through parables; I shall now provide another illustration for you."
In the distant past, there was a certain land whose borders were desolate and its people had fallen into ruin.
At that time, there was a man who delighted in raising pigs; he went to an abandoned village and saw some dry dung. He thought to himself:
"There is plenty of dung here, yet my pigs are hungry. I shall now take this dry dung, wrap it in grass, and carry it back on my head."

He immediately sought out some grass, wrapped the excrement in it, and carried it upon his head. On the way, he encountered a heavy rain; the liquid from the excrement flowed down until it reached his heels. When the people saw this, they all said, "A madman!"
"This place is filled with the stench of excrement; even when the weather is clear, one should not wear it, let alone walk about wearing it in the rain!
The man then became enraged and reviled them, saying, "You yourselves are fools, for you do not know that my pigs and piglets are starving!"
If you knew this, you would not say, "I am deluded. O brāhmaṇa!
You should now rather abandon this evil view; do not persist in your confusion and suffer for a long night.

"It is like that foolish son who walked while carrying excrement on his head; though the multitude rebuked and admonished him, he instead grew angry and cursed them back, saying they did not understand.

The Brahmin said to Kāśyapa, "If you say that practicing goodness leads to birth in heaven and that death is superior to life, then you should have taken your own lives by cutting yourselves with knives, drinking poison, binding yourselves in five ways, or throwing yourselves from high cliffs. Since you now covet life and cannot kill yourselves, it is clear that death is not superior to life."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables; I shall now provide a further illustration for you.
Long ago, in this village of Svastika, there was a brahmin, an elder of long standing, one hundred and twenty years of age."
He had two wives: one already had a son, while the other was newly pregnant.
At that time, the brahmin died not long after; the mother of the elder son said to the mother of the younger son, "All the wealth and treasures should be given entirely to me; you have no share."
Then the stepmother said: "Wait a moment;
you must wait until I have delivered my child. If it is a boy, there should be a share of the wealth for him;
if it is a girl, you may marry her yourself and shall obtain the property."
The son earnestly and repeatedly demanded the wealth, but his stepmother answered as she had before;
when the son continued to press her without ceasing, the stepmother then took a sharp knife and cut open her own belly to see whether it was a boy or a girl.
He said to the brahmin:
"The mother now commits suicide and further harms her unborn child; you, O brahmin, are just the same—you have already taken your own life and now wish to kill another."

If śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas diligently cultivate goodness, are fully endowed with the virtue of precepts, and remain long in the world, they will bring great benefit to many, and gods and humans will attain peace.
I shall now provide you with a final illustration to make you understand the calamity of wrong views.
Long ago, in this village of Sarpaka, there were two performers skilled at juggling balls. The two competed in their arts, and one emerged victorious.
Then the one who had lost said to the victor, "Let us stop for today; we shall try again tomorrow.
The loser immediately returned home, took his play-balls, smeared them with poison, and dried them in the sun. The next day, he took these balls to the victor’s place and said:
"Let us compete in a contest of skills.
He then stepped forward and played with him; first, he gave a poisonous pill to his opponent who had won, saying:
"The victor shall swallow it immediately."
To the one who was inferior, he further gave a poisonous pill; having received it, the man swallowed it immediately. As the poison circulated through his body, his entire frame trembled.
Then, the inferior man reviled him with these verses:
"I coated this pill with medicine, yet you swallowed it without realizing it."
"O little performer, you have swallowed [poison]; after a long time, you shall know it for yourself.
Kāśyapa said to the brāhmaṇa:
"You should now quickly abandon this evil view; do not remain obstinately deluded and increase your own bitter suffering, like that performer who swallowed poison without realizing it."

Then the brahmin said to Kāśyapa, "Venerable sir, when you first offered the analogy of the moon, I already understood it. The reason I went back and forth and did not accept [the invitation] immediately was that I wished to see Kāśyapa’s eloquence and wisdom, so as to give rise to firm faith."
"I now accept with faith and take refuge in Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa replied, "Do not take refuge in me.
You should take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One, in whom I myself have taken refuge."
The brāhmaṇa asked, "I wonder where the Unsurpassed Honored One has gone;
where is he now? Kāśyapa replied:
"Now it has not been long since our teacher, the World-Honored One, entered parinirvāṇa. The brāhmaṇa said:
"If the World-Honored One were still present, I would not have avoided distance or proximity; I would have gone to see him in person, take refuge in him, and pay him homage."
Now, having heard the words of Kāśyapa,
"The Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa," I now take refuge in the Tathāgata who has entered parinirvāṇa, as well as in the Dharma and the Saṃgha.
“Kāśyapa! Listen as I become a lay follower (*upāsaka*) within the True Dharma!

From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, deceive, or drink intoxicants; I shall now perform great acts of giving for the sake of all beings.”
Kāśyapa said: "If you slaughter living beings and beat your servants to hold such a feast, this is not pure merit.
It is like planting in stony, barren soil where thorns abound; whatever is sown therein will surely yield nothing."
If you slaughter living beings and beat your servants to hold a great assembly for the sake of those with wrong views, this is not pure merit.
If you give a great gift without harming living beings, without inflicting whips or canes upon your servants, and joyfully provide a feast for a pure assembly, then you shall obtain great merit.
"It is just like a fertile field: if one plants at the proper time, one will surely obtain fruit.
"Kāśyapa! From this day forward, you must always provide pure offerings to the Saṃgha so that they never cease."
At that time, there was a young brahmin named Māṭhara standing behind Pāyāsi, to whom Pāyāsi looked back and said:
"I wish to provide a great universal gift; you should manage and arrange it for me."
Then, having heard the words of Pāyāsi, the young brahmin immediately made preparations; having performed a great act of giving, he spoke these words:
"May Pāyāsi not obtain the fruit of merit in this world or in future lives."
At that time, having heard that the brahmin had made preparations for the offering, Pāyāsi spoke these words:
"May Pāyāsi not obtain the fruit of retribution in this life or in future lives."
He immediately summoned the brahmin and addressed him, saying:
"Did you indeed speak these words? He replied:
"It is so! Indeed, these words are true. Why is this? Because..."

"The food now prepared is coarse, harsh, and of poor quality; if one were to offer this to the Saṃgha, yet show it to the King, the King would not even be able to momentarily direct his hand toward it, let alone eat it."
"What is currently being provided is not something to be delighted in; how could one obtain pure karmic retribution in future lives from this?
Your Majesty’s gift of monastic robes consists entirely of hempen cloth; if it were shown to you, Your Majesty would not even be able to direct a single step toward it, much less wear it yourself."
"What you are currently giving cannot bring joy; by what means could you obtain a pure retribution in future lives?
At that time, the Brahmin further told the Vaiśya:
"From this day forward, you shall give my food and my clothes to the assembly of monks."
Then, the brahmin immediately followed these instructions and offered the king’s food and the king’s robes to the assembly of monks.

At that time, because the brahmin had made this pure offering, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in a lower heaven. As for the brahmin who managed the assembly, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, the brahmin Pāṭikāputra, the young brahmacārins, the brahmin Subhadda, the householders, and the others, having heard what the maiden Kāśyapa had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Seven.
The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Eight.
Translated during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian.
8. Sandhāna Sūtra (8), Part Two, Sandhāna Sūtra, Chapter Four.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Mount Vaibhāra, in the Saptaparṇa Cave, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a householder in the city of Rājagṛha named Sandhāna, who delighted in wandering and sightseeing; every day he went out of the city to visit the World-Honored One.
Then, that householder looked up at the time of day and thought to himself:

"Now is not the time to go and visit the Buddha; the World-Honored One must currently be in his quiet chamber in meditative concentration, and the assembly of bhikṣus will likewise be practicing dhyāna. I would do better to go now to the grove of the brahmin woman Utpalavarṇā; when the proper time arrives, I shall go to the World-Honored One to pay respects, offer greetings, and inquire after his well-being, and also go to where the bhikṣus are to pay my respects and inquire after their well-being."
At that time, there was a brahmin named Nyagrodha living in a forest with five hundred brahmin youths.
Once, the assembly of brahmins gathered in one place and engaged in loud, heated debate, spending the entire day speaking only defiled and confused words that obstruct the path.

Sometimes they discussed state affairs; sometimes they discussed matters of warfare and weaponry; sometimes they discussed matters of national righteousness and diplomacy; sometimes they discussed the affairs of high ministers and commoners; sometimes they discussed carriages, horses, and excursions to gardens and groves; sometimes they discussed seating arrangements, clothing, food and drink, and women; or they discussed mountains, seas, tortoises, and turtles. They spoke only of such worldly discourses that obstruct the Path, spending their entire day in this manner.
At that time, seeing the householder Sandhāna approaching from afar, the brahmin immediately commanded his assembly to remain silent, saying:
"For what reason? [Because he is coming]."

"A disciple of that ascetic Gautama has now come from outside; among the white-robed lay disciples of the ascetic Gautama, he is the most eminent. He will surely come here, so you should remain silent."
At that time, the brahmins each remained silent.
The householder Sandhāna went to where the brahmins were, and after exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and said to them:

"My teacher, the World-Honored One, always delights in seclusion and quietude and does not favor clamor and bustle, unlike you who dwell among people with your disciples, raising your voices in loud debate and speaking only of obstructive and useless words."
The brahmin spoke again to the householder, saying:
"Has the śramaṇa Gautama ever engaged in discourse with others?
By what means do people come to know that the śramaṇa possesses great wisdom?"

Your teacher always prefers to dwell alone in remote places, just like a blind ox grazing that wanders only toward what it can see; your teacher Gautama is exactly the same, preferring solitary views and delighting in uninhabited spots.
If your teacher comes here, we shall call him a "blind ox."

He has always claimed for himself great wisdom; yet with a single word I have exhausted him, rendering him silent like a tortoise withdrawing its six limbs. Thinking he might be free from harm, I shall strike him with a single arrow, leaving him no place to flee.

At that time, while the World-Honored One was in a quiet chamber, he heard with his divine ear such a discussion among the brahmins and householders. He immediately emerged from the Saptaparṇa Cave and proceeded to the grove of the brahmin woman Utpalavarṇā.
At that time, the brahmin saw the Buddha approaching from afar and commanded his disciples:

"All of you remain silent. The śramaṇa Gautama wishes to come here; you must take care not to rise to meet him, nor offer him respectful prostrations, nor invite him to sit. Take a separate seat and give it to him so that he may sit.
Once he is seated, you should ask him: "
“Śramaṇa Gautama! From the beginning, by what teaching have you instructed your disciples so that they attain peaceful concentration and purely cultivate the holy life?”

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually arrived at that garden. Then, the brahmin, without realizing it, rose of his own accord and went forward to meet the World-Honored One, saying: "Welcome, Gautama!"
"Welcome, śramaṇa! It has been a long time since we last met; for what reason have you come here today?
Please come forward and sit for a moment."
At that time, the World-Honored One took his seat and smiled with joyful composure, silently reflecting to himself:
"These foolish people cannot maintain self-restraint; though they first established their solemn vow, they have ultimately failed to fulfill it entirely."
"Why is this so? It is because the Buddha’s spiritual power causes that evil mind to naturally perish.
At that time, the householder Sandhāna prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
After the brahmin Nyagrodha had exchanged greetings with the Buddha, he sat down to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! From the very beginning, by what teaching have you instructed and exhorted your disciples so that they attain peaceful stability and purely cultivate the holy life?"
The World-Honored One said: "Stop, brahmin!"

My Dharma is profound and vast; from the very beginning, I have instructed my disciples so that they may attain the state of peace and security and purely cultivate the holy life—this is not within your reach.
He further addressed the brahmin:
"Even if there were pure and impure aspects to the path and dharma practiced by your teacher and your disciples, I am fully capable of explaining them all."
At that time, the five hundred disciples of the brahmins each raised their voices and said to one another:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great majesty and great supernormal power; when others question him on his own doctrine, he instead elucidates the doctrines of others."
Then, the brahmin Nigrodha addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent, Gautama!”
"I pray that you will analyze this for me.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
I shall speak for you.
The brahmin replied:
“I would gladly wish to hear it! The Buddha told the brahmin:

“The practices you follow are all base and vulgar: you go about naked, shielding yourself with your hands; you do not accept food from a jar, nor from a bowl; you do not accept food from between two walls, nor from between two people, nor from between two knives, nor from between two bowls; you do not accept food from a household where they eat together, nor from a household where a woman is pregnant; seeing a dog at the door, you do not accept food from that house; you do not accept food from a household with many flies, nor food offered by invitation; and if another says, ‘I know him well,’ you do not accept food from that person.”

He did not eat fish, he did not eat meat, he did not drink alcohol, and he did not eat from two vessels. He would take a single meal and swallow it once, stopping at seven meals; when receiving additional food from others, he would not exceed seven portions.
Sometimes he ate once a day, or once every two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days.

Alternatively, he ate fruits, or he ate weeds, or he ate rice-water, or he ate hemp and rice, or he ate wild rice, or he ate cow dung, or he ate deer dung, or he ate roots, branches, leaves, and fruits of trees, or he ate fruit that had fallen naturally.

Some wear garments of bark, some wear robes of *śāṇa* grass, some wear tree bark, some cover their bodies with grass, some wear deerskins, some let their hair grow long, some wear woven wool, some wear shrouds from burial mounds, some constantly hold their hands aloft, some do not sit on beds or mats, some remain constantly in a squatting posture, some shave their heads but leave their topknots and beards, some lie upon thorns, some lie upon gourds and melons, and some lie naked upon cow dung;
some bathe three times a day, some bathe three times a night—thus they afflict this body with countless forms of suffering and toil.
"Nikūṭa, how is it? Can one who practices in this manner be said to possess pure dharmas?
The brahmin replied:
"This dharma is pure; it is not impure.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"What you call 'pure,' I shall declare to be defiled within that very dharma of yours which you consider pure."
The brahmin said: "Excellent, Gautama!"
"You may speak of it; I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Those ascetics constantly reflect and deliberate within themselves:"
"To think, 'By practicing in this way, I shall receive offerings, honor, and respectful service'—
this is defilement. When that ascetic,

having received offerings, becomes firmly attached to them, stained by craving and unable to relinquish them, failing to understand detachment and not knowing the path to liberation— this is defilement."
When those ascetics see someone approaching from afar, they all sit in meditation together; yet when no one is present, they sit or lie down as they please—this constitutes defilement.
“That ascetic, upon hearing the righteous Dharma from others, refuses to acknowledge it; this is a defilement.
That ascetic, when others pose a righteous question, begrudges answering it; this is a defilement.
That ascetic, upon seeing someone making offerings to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, rebukes and stops them; this is a defilement.”
If that ascetic, upon seeing śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who produce further [unwholesome] states while eating, censures them, this is a defilement.

If that ascetic possesses impure food yet refuses to give it to others, or possesses pure food yet is greedily attached to eating it himself, failing to see his own faults and ignorant of the way to liberation, this is a defilement.
If that ascetic praises his own virtues and disparages others, this is a defilement.
That ascetic commits killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, envy, and wrong views; these constitute defilements.
"That ascetic is indolent and prone to forgetfulness; he does not practice meditative concentration and lacks wisdom, being like a bird or beast—this is a defilement.
That ascetic prizes high status and is arrogant and conceited—this is a defilement.

That ascetic lacks integrity and faithfulness, and is ungrateful; he does not maintain pure precepts, cannot apply himself diligently to receiving instruction, and constantly associates with evil people, never ceasing his wickedness—this is a defilement."

Those ascetics harbor much resentment and take pleasure in artifice and hypocrisy; relying on their own views, they seek out the faults of others and constantly maintain wrong views, accompanied by extreme views—these constitute their defilements.
"Nigrodha, how is it? Can one who practices in such a manner be said to be pure? He replied:
"This is impure; it is not pure.
The Buddha said, "Now, within these defiled dharmas of yours, I shall further explain the pure dharmas that are free from defilement."
The brahmin said, "I only pray that you will explain it! The Buddha said:
"Those ascetics do not harbor such thoughts as:
'By practicing in this way, I shall receive offerings, respect, and veneration.
This is the stainless dharma of asceticism."

When that ascetic has received offerings, his mind is free from attachment; he clearly understands detachment, knows the Dharma of the essential way out, and this is the stainless dharma of asceticism.
That practitioner of asceticism maintains a constant practice in meditation whether people are present or absent, regarding them as no different; this is the stainless dharma of asceticism.
That practitioner of asceticism hears the correct teachings of others and receives them with joy and approval; this is the stainless dharma of asceticism.
That practitioner of asceticism, when questioned correctly by others, explains with joy; this is the dharma of asceticism free from defilement.

“If that ascetic, upon seeing someone making offerings to śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, rejoices on their behalf rather than rebuking or stopping them—this is the practice of asceticism free from defilement.
If that ascetic, seeing śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas eating food grown again (regenerative food), does not reproach them—this is the practice of asceticism free from defilement.

If that ascetic, regarding impure food, has no mind of stinginess, and regarding pure food, is without attachment, being able to see his own faults and knowing the Dharma of the essential way out—this is the practice of asceticism free from defilement.”
That ascetic does not praise himself nor disparage others; this is the stainless dharma of asceticism.

That ascetic refrains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, envy, and wrong views; this is the stainless dharma of asceticism.

"That ascetic is diligent and never forgetful, delights in practicing meditative cultivation, and extensively develops wisdom; he is not as ignorant as a beast—this is the practice of austerity free from defilement.
That ascetic does not act out of nobility, arrogance, or conceit—this is the practice of austerity free from defilement.

That ascetic always harbors faith and integrity, cultivates acts of reciprocity, is able to maintain pure precepts, diligently receives instruction, constantly keeps company with virtuous people, and accumulates goodness without ceasing—this is the practice of austerity free from defilement."

That ascetic harbors no resentment, practices no artifice, does not rely on his own views, seeks not the faults of others, maintains no false views, and is free from extreme views; this is the practice of asceticism that is free from defilement.
"Vāsiṣṭha, what do you think?
Is such asceticism the dharma that is pure and free from defilement? He replied:
"So it is! This is indeed the pure and stainless Dharma.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is practicing these ascetic disciplines together sufficient to be called the foremost firm practice?
The Buddha said, “Not yet.”
"It was merely the bark at first.
The brahmin said, "I pray you, speak of the tree's knots!"
The Buddha told the brahmin: "Listen well!
I shall now speak."
The brahmin said:
“Indeed! I wish most earnestly to hear it.”

“O Brahmin! That ascetic does not kill living beings himself, nor does he instruct others to kill; he does not steal himself, nor does he instruct others to steal; he does not engage in sexual misconduct himself, nor does he instruct others to do so; he does not speak falsely himself, nor does he instruct others to do so.

With a mind of loving-kindness, he pervades one direction, and likewise the other directions; his loving-kindness is vast, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and pervades the entire world. His minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are also like this. Asceticism up to this point is called ‘the joint of the tree.’”
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will explain the meaning of the steadfastness of ascetic practice.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall now explain it."
The brahmin said: “Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said:

"Those ascetics do not kill living beings themselves and teach others not to kill; they do not steal themselves and teach others not to steal; they do not engage in sexual misconduct themselves and teach others not to engage in sexual misconduct; they do not speak falsely themselves and teach others not to speak falsely."

He pervades one direction with a mind of loving-kindness, and likewise the other directions; his loving-kindness is vast, non-dual, immeasurable, and free from enmity, pervading the entire world. His minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are also like this.

That ascetic, through his own recollection, knows the events of countless past kalpas—from one birth, two births, up to countless births; he sees and knows entirely the formation and destruction of lands, and the beginning and end of kalpa-cycles.

Furthermore, he personally perceives and knows: "I was once born into such a clan, with such a name, such food and drink, such a lifespan, and such experiences of suffering and pleasure; from that place I came here, and from here I went there. In this way, he fully remembers the events of countless kalpas.
"This, brahmin, is what makes that ascetic firm and indestructible.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the foremost? The Buddha said, "Brahmin!"
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall now explain it to you.
The brahmin said:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha said:

"Those ascetics do not kill living beings themselves and teach others not to kill; they do not steal themselves and teach others not to steal; they do not engage in sexual misconduct themselves and teach others not to engage in sexual misconduct; they do not speak falsely themselves and teach others not to deceive."

He pervades one direction with a mind of loving-kindness; he does likewise for the other directions. This mind of loving-kindness is vast, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity and resentment, and pervades the entire world. It is the same for the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

That ascetic, through his own recollection, knows the events of countless kalpas in the past—whether one birth, two births, or up to countless births; he perceives and knows entirely the formation and destruction of lands and the beginning and end of kalpas.

Furthermore, he knows and sees for himself: "I was born into such a clan, with such a name, such food and drink, and such a lifespan; such were the sufferings and joys I experienced. He remembers all such matters from countless kalpas, including how he passed from that life to this, and from this life to that.

With the pure divine eye, he observes the various classes of sentient beings—dying here and being born there; their beautiful or ugly complexions; the good or evil destinies they follow; and where they fall according to their conduct—he perceives and knows them all entirely.

Furthermore, he knows that sentient beings engage in unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind; they revile the noble ones and hold false, perverted views; thus, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the three evil realms.

There are some sentient beings whose bodily conduct is wholesome, and whose speech and mind are also wholesome; they do not revile the noble ones, but see correctly and practice with faith. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among gods or humans.

The practitioner, with the purified divine eye, observes and sees sentient beings, even as they fall according to their conduct; there is nothing he does not see or know. This is the foremost excellence of ascetic practice.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Within this Dharma there is yet something superior; it is with this Dharma that I constantly transform my śrāvakas, and by means of this Dharma they are able to cultivate the holy life."
Then, the five hundred disciples of the brahmins each raised their voices and said to one another:
"Now we see that the World-Honored One is the most supreme; our teacher does not equal him."
Then, the householder Sandhāna said to the brahmin:
"Just now you yourself said:
'If Gautama comes, we shall call him a blind ox.'"
“The World-Honored One has now arrived; why do you not address him?
Furthermore, you previously said:

‘I shall exhaust that Gautama with a single word so that he falls silent, like a tortoise withdrawing its six limbs, thinking itself free from harm, only for me to strike it with a single arrow, leaving it no place to escape.’”
"Why do you not now exhaust the Tathāgata with that single word of yours?
The Buddha asked the brahmin,
"Do you recall having said such a thing in the past?"
He replied, "Indeed there are!
The Buddha said to the brahmin:

"Have you not heard from the venerable brahmins of old that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas dwell alone in mountain forests, delighting in secluded and quiet places, just as I today delight in living in seclusion?
Is it not contrary to your own dharma to delight in clamor and spend your days speaking useless matters?"
The brahmin said:
"I have heard that the Buddhas of the past delighted in seclusion and dwelt alone in mountain forests, just as the World-Honored One does now;
they were not like my own Dharma, which delights in clamor and spends the whole day speaking useless matters!"
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Do you not recall that you thought,
'The śramaṇa Gautama is able to speak of bodhi'?"
One who is able to discipline oneself is able to discipline others;
one who has attained tranquility for oneself is able to bring others to tranquility;
one who has crossed to the other shore oneself is able to cause others to cross.
"Having attained liberation yourself, you are able to liberate others;
having attained nirvāṇa yourself, you are able to lead others to nirvāṇa.
At that time, the brahmin rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's feet], and touching the Buddha's feet with his hands, spoke his own name, saying:
“I am the brahmin Nyagrodha! I am the brahmin Nyagrodha!
I now take refuge and pay homage at the feet of the World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to the brahmin: "Stop! Stop!"
"Wait! If your mind attains understanding, that itself shall constitute your salutation.
Then, that brahmin prostrated again at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Do you perhaps think that the Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of gain and offerings?
Do not give rise to such a thought!"
If there is any gain or offering, I shall give it all to you.
The Dharma I teach is subtle and supreme; it serves to extinguish unwholesome states and increase wholesome dharmas.
He further addressed the brahmin:

"Do you not think that the Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of his reputation, for the sake of being honored, for the sake of being a leader, for the sake of his retinue, or for the sake of the great assembly?"
"Do not give rise to such thoughts!
Your retinue now belongs entirely to you.
The Dharma I teach is for the purpose of extinguishing unwholesome states and increasing wholesome dharmas."
He further addressed the brahmin:
"Do you not think that the Buddha has placed you among the mass of the unwholesome or within the mass of darkness?
Do not harbor such a thought!"
"Abandon all the masses of unwholesome and dark-and-gloomy qualities; I shall personally explain the pure and wholesome Dharma for you.
He further addressed the brahmin:
"Do you not think that the Buddha has excluded you from the assembly of wholesome dharmas and the assembly of purity?"
"Do not give rise to such thoughts!

You need only apply yourself diligently to the collection of wholesome qualities and the collection of pure virtues; I shall myself explain for you the most excellent and pure dharmas, so that unwholesome conduct is extinguished and wholesome dharmas are increased."
At that time, the five hundred disciples of the brahmins all straightened their hearts and rectified their intentions to listen to what the Buddha was saying.
Then, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"These five hundred disciples of the brahmins have straightened their hearts and rectified their intentions to listen to the Dharma from the Buddha; I should now go and ruin their resolve."
At that time, the evil Māra used his own power to corrupt and disturb their minds.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Sandhāna, saying:

"These five hundred sons of brahmans have focused their hearts and rectified their intentions to listen to the Dharma from me; however, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān has corrupted and disturbed their minds. Now I wish to return, and you may go with me."
At that time, the World-Honored One took the householder Sandhāna by his right hand, placed him upon his palm, and returned through the air.
Then, the householder Sandhāna, the brahmin Nyagrodha, and five hundred brahmin youths, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. Saṅgīti Sutta (9). The Fifth Discourse of the Second Division of the Long Discourses Spoken by the Buddha, the Saṅgīti Sutta. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the Mallas together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikkhus, and gradually arrived at the Jātukaṇṇa mango grove near the city of Pāvā.
At that time, on the night of the full moon on the fifteenth day, the World-Honored One sat in the open air, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him.
After the World-Honored One had preached the Dharma extensively during the night, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:

"Now the bhikṣus from the four directions have gathered here; they are all practicing with diligence and have cast off sleep. I suffer from back pain and wish to rest for a while; you may now preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus."
He replied, "Indeed! I shall act according to the Holy Teaching."
At that time, the World-Honored One folded his saṃghāṭī robe into four layers, lay down on his right side like a lion with his feet stacked one upon the other, and went to sleep.
Then Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:

"In this city of Pāvā, a Nirgrantha has recently passed away. Since then, his disciples have split into two factions who constantly engage in disputes and litigation, seeking out each other's faults, reviling one another, and each asserting what is right and wrong."
"I know this Dharma, whereas you do not;
you abide in false views, whereas I abide in the True Dharma.
Their speech was thus confused and devoid of logical sequence.
He proclaimed his own words, asserting them to be the truth:
"What I have said is superior; what you have said is defeated. I am now the master of this discourse; if you have anything to ask, you may come and question me."
“O bhikṣus! At that time, the people of the country who followed the Nirgranthas grew weary of the sounds of their quarrels and disputes, for their doctrine was not true and correct.
