Since a doctrine that is not true and correct provides no means of escape from suffering—just as a decaying stupa cannot be restored by plastering—it was not taught by a Samyaksaṃbuddha.”

"O Bhikṣus! Only my Dharma, the unsurpassed teaching of Śākya, is truly authentic and capable of leading to deliverance; it is like a new stupa that is easily adorned. This is what the Samyaksaṃbuddhas have taught."

"O Bhikṣus! We should now assemble the Dharma and the Vinaya in order to prevent disputes and litigation, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and granting peace to devas and humans."
"O Bhikṣus! The Tathāgata has taught one true Dharma: all sentient beings depend upon food for their existence.

Furthermore, the Tathāgata has taught another one Dharma: all sentient beings proceed by means of action. This is the one Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; you should collectively gather it so as to prevent disputes and litigation, to ensure that the holy life (brahmacarya) endures long, to bring great benefit, and to grant peace to gods and humans."
“Monks! The Tathāgata has taught two categories of true dharma:
first, name; second, form.”
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
first, delusion; second, craving.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
There is the view of existence and the view of non-existence.
Furthermore, there are two further factors:
first, lack of shame; second, lack of dread.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
first, having a sense of shame (hrī); second, having a sense of dread (apatrāpya).
Furthermore, there are two dharmas:
First is the knowledge of exhaustion, and second is the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, there are two factors, two causes, and two conditions that give rise to sensual desire:
first, pure and exquisite forms; second, the failure to practice right reflection.
Furthermore, there are two factors, two causes, and two conditions that give rise to anger:
first, resentment; second, lack of reflection.
Furthermore, there are two factors, two causes, and two conditions that give rise to wrong views:
The first is hearing from others; the second is wrong reflection.
Furthermore, there are two factors, two causes and two conditions, by which right view arises:
the first is hearing from others; the second is correct reflection.
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, with two causes and two conditions:
first, the liberation of those in training (*śaikṣa-vimukti*); second, the liberation of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa-vimukti*).
Furthermore, there are two dharmas, with two causes and two conditions:
"First is the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), and second is the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*). Monks!

These are what the Tathāgata has taught; you should collectively compile them to prevent disputes, so that the holy life (*brahmacarya*) may long endure, bringing great benefit and granting peace to gods and humans."
“Monks! The Tathāgata has taught three true dharmas, namely the three unwholesome roots:
first, greed; second, hatred; and third, delusion.”
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three roots of goodness:
first, non-greed; second, non-anger; and third, non-delusion.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three unwholesome courses of action:
First, unwholesome bodily conduct; second, unwholesome verbal conduct; third, unwholesome mental conduct.
Furthermore, there are three factors, namely the three types of unwholesome conduct:
unwholesome bodily conduct, unwholesome verbal conduct, and unwholesome mental conduct.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three types of unwholesome conduct:
unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three types of wholesome conduct:
There are wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas, namely the three unwholesome perceptions:
the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of harmfulness.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three wholesome perceptions:
the perception of non-desire, the perception of non-ill will, and the perception of non-harming.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three unwholesome volitions:
There are thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness.
Furthermore, there are three other factors, namely the three wholesome thoughts:
thoughts of non-sensual desire, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harmfulness.
“Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three meritorious actions:
the action of giving, the action of impartiality, and the action of reflection.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three feelings:”
There are pleasant feelings, painful feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three cravings:
craving for sensory desires, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three outflows (*āsrava*):
the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*).
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three fires:
The fire of desire, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three searches:
the search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three types of proliferation:
proliferation of the self, proliferation of the world, and proliferation of phenomena.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three realms:
The realm of sensual desire, the realm of ill will, and the realm of harmfulness.
Furthermore, there are three other dharmas, namely the three realms:
the realm of renunciation, the realm of non-ill will, and the realm of non-harmfulness.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three realms:
the realm of form, the formless realm, and the realm of exhaustion.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three aggregates:
The aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three types of morality:
the morality of increase, the increase of intention, and the increase of wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three samādhis:
the emptiness samādhi, the wishlessness samādhi, and the signlessness samādhi.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three marks:"
The sign of tranquility, the sign of exertion, and the sign of equanimity.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*):
the clear knowledge of the recollection of past lives, the clear knowledge of the divine eye, and the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three transformations:
first, the transformation of supernormal power; second, knowing the minds of others and preaching the Dharma according to their inclinations; and third, instruction and admonition.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three origins of desire:

first, through the desire for the manifest, one is born among humans and devas; second, through the desire for transformation, one is born as a deva of the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (Nirmāṇarati); third, through the desire for the transformations of others, one is born as a deva of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmitavaśavartin).
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three arisings of joy:
first, sentient beings spontaneously accomplish [their aims] and give rise to a joyful mind, as when the devas of the Brahma-ābhāsvara Heaven are first born.
Second, there are sentient beings who take joy in mindfulness, exclaiming "Excellent! like those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Third, they attain the bliss of tranquility, like those in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
“Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three types of suffering:
the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three faculties (*indriya*):”
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "having known.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three halls:
the hall of the noble ones, the hall of heaven, and the hall of Brahmā.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three types of arousal:
arousal through seeing, arousal through hearing, and arousal through doubt.
Furthermore, there are three things, namely the three types of discourse:
In the past there were such events and such discourses;
in the future there will be such events and such discourses;
in the present there are such events and such discourses.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three groups:
the group of those fixed in rightness, the group of those fixed in error, and the group of those who are not fixed.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three types of sorrow:
There is distress of body, distress of speech, and distress of mind.
Furthermore, there are three things called the three types of elders:
the elder by seniority of years, the elder by the Dharma, and the elder by office.
Furthermore, there are three dharmas, namely the three eyes:
the flesh eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye. O bhikṣus!

"This is the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; we should compile it together to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and peace to devas and humans."
“Monks! The Tathāgata has taught four right dharmas, namely the four types of verbal misconduct:
first, false speech; second, divisive speech; third, harsh speech; and fourth, frivolous speech.”
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four types of wholesome verbal conduct:
first, truthful speech; second, gentle speech; third, the absence of frivolous speech; and fourth, the absence of divisive speech.
“Furthermore, there are four things, namely the four non-noble statements:
to say one has seen what one has not seen; to say one has heard what one has not heard; to say one has sensed what one has not sensed; and to say one has known what one has not known.”
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four noble modes of speech:
to say one has seen when one has seen; to say one has heard when one has heard; to say one has sensed when one has sensed; and to say one has known when one has known.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four kinds of nutriment:
edible food, contact-nutriment, mental volition-nutriment, and consciousness-nutriment.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four types of feeling:
There are those who currently practice asceticism and later receive a painful retribution;
there are those who currently practice asceticism and later receive a pleasant retribution;
and there are those who currently practice pleasant conduct and later receive a painful retribution.
There are those who perform pleasant actions in the present and subsequently receive pleasant retribution.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four clingings (*upādāna*):
clinging to sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*), clinging to self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*), clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*), and clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*).
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four bonds:
the bodily bond of sensual desire, the bodily bond of ill will, the bodily bond of attachment to precepts and rituals, and the bodily bond of the view of self.
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four thorns:"
The thorn of desire, the thorn of hatred, the thorn of views, and the thorn of pride.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four modes of birth:
birth from an egg, birth from a womb, birth from moisture, and birth by transformation.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four foundations of mindfulness:
herein, a bhikṣu contemplates the body within the body, practicing with diligence and without slackening, maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness, and abandoning worldly greed and sorrow;
he contemplates the body without the body, practicing with diligence and without slackening, maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness, and abandoning worldly greed and sorrow.
One contemplates the body internally and externally with diligence and without slackening, maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness, and relinquishing worldly greed and sorrow.
The same applies to the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and phenomena.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four right efforts (*catur-samyakprahāṇa*):
herein, a bhikṣu employs skillful means to prevent unarisen evil dharmas from arising,
and employs skillful means to eliminate evil dharmas that have already arisen.
"Exert skillful means to cause wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise;
exert skillful means through reflection to cause wholesome states that have already arisen to increase and expand.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda)."
Thereupon, the bhikṣu contemplates the concentration of desire as the accomplishment of the practice of cessation;
it is likewise for the concentration of energy, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of contemplation.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four dhyānas:
herein, a bhikṣu, having removed sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, enters the first dhyāna.

With the cessation of directed thought and evaluation, and with internal confidence and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, he enters the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.

Free from joy, he cultivates equanimity, mindfulness, and vigilance; experiencing bliss with his body, he enters the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and blissful."

Free from pleasure and pain, and having previously stilled sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and is characterized by equanimity and pure mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas known as the four brahma-vihāras:
first, loving-kindness; second, compassion; third, sympathetic joy; and fourth, equanimity.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). In this regard, a bhikṣu transcends all perceptions of form;

having first exhausted perceptions of aversion and no longer attending to perceptions of diversity, he contemplates the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Having relinquished the sphere of infinite space, he enters the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); having relinquished the sphere of infinite consciousness, he enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); and having relinquished the sphere of nothingness, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four foundations of dharma:
the foundation of non-greed for dharmas, the foundation of non-aversion for dharmas, the foundation of right mindfulness for dharmas, and the foundation of right concentration for dharmas.”
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four lineages of the noble ones (*āryavaṃśa*).

In this regard, a bhikṣu is content with his robes; he does not rejoice when obtaining good ones, nor does he grieve when encountering poor ones. He is neither stained nor attached, knows what is forbidden, and knows the path of deliverance. Within these dharmas, he exerts himself with diligence and without slackening, accomplishing the task without deficiency or diminution, and is also able to teach others to accomplish this same task. This is the first lineage of the noble ones: dwelling in contentment.
From the beginning until now, he has never been troubled or disturbed;
no gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, or people of the world have been able to revile him.
Furthermore, regarding food, drink, bedding, seating, and medicinal requisites for illness, he is likewise entirely content.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*):
generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four factors of stream-entry (*srotaāpattyaṅga*):
A bhikṣu attains indestructible faith in the Buddha, and indestructible faith in the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas known as the four realizations:
realization through seeing forms, realization through bodily contact with cessation, realization through recollecting past lives, and realization through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four paths:
the path of suffering with slow attainment, the path of suffering with swift attainment, the path of pleasure with slow attainment, and the path of pleasure with swift attainment.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four noble truths:
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four fruits of śrāmaṇya:
the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, and the fruit of arhat.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four bases:
the basis of reality, the basis of giving, the basis of wisdom, and the basis of cessation.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four knowledges:
The knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of the unknown (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*):
consciousness abides in form, taking form as its object, dwelling in form, and increasing together with craving; it likewise abides in feeling, perception, and mental formations.
Furthermore, there are four things, namely the four yokes:
the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
Furthermore, there are four things, namely the four non-yokes:
There is no yoke of desire, no yoke of existence, no yoke of views, and no yoke of ignorance.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four purities:
purity of virtue, purity of mind, purity of view, and purity through the overcoming of doubt.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four kinds of knowledge:
knowing what is to be accepted as acceptance, knowing what is to be practiced as practice, knowing what is to be delighted in as delight, and knowing what is to be relinquished as relinquishment.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four modes of deportment:
One knows when it is appropriate to walk, one knows when it is appropriate to stand, one knows when it is appropriate to sit, and one knows when it is appropriate to lie down.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the four modes of reflection:
limited reflection, expansive reflection, immeasurable reflection, and reflection on nothingness.
Furthermore, there are four methods, namely the four types of categorical exposition:
categorical exposition, analytical exposition, interrogative exposition, and setting aside.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas, namely the Tathāgata’s four ways of being beyond protection (*caturvidha-arakṣya*):
the Tathāgata’s bodily conduct is pure, being without deficiency or flaw such that it requires no self-protection;
his verbal conduct, mental conduct, and livelihood are likewise pure.

This is the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; we should compile it together to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and granting peace to gods and humans.
"Furthermore, monks! The Tathāgata has taught five right dharmas, namely the five entrances:
eye and form, ear and sound, nose and odor, tongue and flavor, body and tangibility."
Furthermore, there are five things, namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandhāḥ*):
the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-, saṃjñā-, saṃskāra-, vijñāna-skandhas*).
Furthermore, there are five things, namely the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇāni*):
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
Furthermore, there are five factors known as the five lower fetters:
the fetter of the view of a self-identity, the fetter of attachment to precepts and rituals, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of sensual desire, and the fetter of ill will.
Furthermore, there are five factors, namely the five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*):
attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Furthermore, there are five factors, namely the five faculties (*pañcendriya*):
The faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas known as the five powers:
the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
“Furthermore, there are five dharmas called the branches of cessation:
first, a bhikṣu has faith in the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is fully endowed with the ten titles.”
Second, the bhikṣu is free from illness and his body is always at ease.
Third, he is upright and honest, devoid of flattery and deceit. To one who can act in this manner, the Tathāgata reveals the path to nirvāṇa.
Fourth, one should concentrate the mind so that it does not become confused or distracted, and maintain in memory without forgetting what was previously recited.
Fifth, one should skillfully observe the arising and ceasing of phenomena, employing the conduct of the noble ones to exhaust the root of suffering.
Furthermore, there are five things, namely the five types of instigation:
untimely instigation, false instigation, instigation that is not meaningful, instigation consisting of empty words, and instigation lacking compassion.
Furthermore, there are five things, namely the five types of virtuous instigation:
There is then the arousal [of speech] that is timely, the arousal of truth, the arousal of meaning, the arousal of harmonious words, and the arousal of a compassionate mind.
Furthermore, there are five things called the five types of envy:
envy regarding one’s dwelling place, envy regarding donors, envy regarding material gains, envy regarding physical appearance, and envy regarding the Dharma.
“Furthermore, there are five dharmas, namely the liberations from the five destinies:

first, the perception of the impurity of the body; second, the perception of the impurity of food; third, the perception of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena; fourth, the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds; and fifth, the perception of death.”
Furthermore, there are five dharmas, namely the five elements of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-dhātu*):

First, a bhikṣu finds no delight in sensual desires and remains unshaken; he does not associate with them, but contemplates renunciation alone, delights in seclusion, and associates with it without indolence. His mind becomes pliant, and through renunciation and the departure from desire, those outflows (*āsrava*) and fetters (*paryavasthāna*) that arise because of desire are completely abandoned, extinguished, and he attains liberation. This is called the renunciation of desire.
The same applies to the escape from ill will, the escape from envy, the escape from sensual form, and the escape from the view of a self-identity.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas, namely, the five liberations through joy.

If a bhikṣu is diligent and untiring, delights in secluded places, and focuses his mind with single-minded concentration, he will attain what was not yet understood, reach what was not yet exhausted, and find what was not yet settled.

What are the five? In this regard, a bhikṣu hears the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, or hears a fellow practitioner of the holy life (brahmacaryā) preach, or hears a teacher preach the Dharma; he reflects upon and examines it, discerning the meaning of the Dharma, and his mind attains joy. Having attained joy, he attains love for the Dharma. Having attained love for the Dharma, his body and mind become tranquil and secure. Once his body and mind are tranquil and secure, he attains meditative concentration (dhyāna). Having attained meditative concentration, he attains true knowledge and vision. This is the first entrance into liberation.

Thereupon, having heard the Dharma with joy, the bhikṣu receives, maintains, and recites it with joy; he explains it to others with joy; he reflects upon and analyzes it with joy; and his attainment of meditative concentration regarding the Dharma is likewise joyful.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas, namely five types of persons:

those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, those who attain parinirvāṇa without exertion, those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion, and those who ascend to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

"O bhikṣus! This is the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; you should compile it together in order to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and granting peace to devas and humans."
"Furthermore, monks! The Tathāgata has taught six right dharmas, namely the six internal sense bases:
the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base."
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*):
the base of form, the base of sound, the base of odor, the base of taste, the base of tangibles, and the base of mental phenomena.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*).
The group of visual consciousness, and the groups of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six groups of contact:
the group of visual contact, and the groups of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six groups of feeling (ṣaḍ vedanākāyāḥ):
the group of feeling of the eye, and the groups of feeling of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six groups of perception (ṣaṭ saṃjñākāyāḥ):
The perception of forms, the perception of sounds, the perception of odors, the perception of tastes, the perception of tangibles, and the perception of mental phenomena.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six groups of volition:
volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, volition regarding odors, volition regarding tastes, volition regarding tangibles, and volition regarding mental phenomena.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six bases of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*):
the base of craving for forms, and the bases of craving for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six roots of dispute:

If a bhikṣu is prone to anger and does not relinquish it, he does not revere the Tathāgata, nor does he revere the Dharma, nor does he revere the Saṃgha; his observance of the precepts is perforated and leaking, defiled and impure;
he delights in engendering much strife and litigation within the assembly, is detested by others, disturbs the pure community, and brings unease to devas and humans alike.

"O Bhikṣus! You should each examine yourselves within. If there is resentment or malice, as in that case of the one who caused the disturbance, you should assemble the harmonious Saṃgha and employ extensive skillful means to uproot this source of contention.

Furthermore, you should maintain focused mindfulness and observe yourselves; once the knot of hatred has been extinguished, you should employ even more skillful means to restrain the mind so that it does not arise again."

"O bhikṣus! It is likewise with those who are stubborn and unreflective, stingy and envious, skillful in deception and falsehood, who rely on their own views, erroneously accept [views] and do not relinquish them, who are deluded by wrong views, and who are possessed of extreme views."
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six elements:
the earth element, the fire element, the water element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six modes of observation:
The eye perceives forms; the ear [perceives] sounds, the nose odors, the tongue tastes, the body tangibles, and the mind perceives mental phenomena.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six elements of renunciation.
If a bhikṣu should say:
"I have cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, yet anger still arises," other bhikṣus should say to him:

"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata does not say that it is possible for one who cultivates the liberation of loving-kindness to give rise again to thoughts of ill will—such a thing cannot be."
The Buddha said:
"Only after one has eliminated ill will can one attain loving-kindness. If a bhikṣu says:
"When practicing the liberation of compassion, a mind of resentment and envy arises;
when practicing the liberation of sympathetic joy, a mind of sorrow and affliction arises;
when practicing the liberation of equanimity, a mind of aversion and attachment arises."
"Practicing the path of non-self gives rise to a mind of doubt;
practicing the path of non-perception gives rise to various disordered thoughts. It is also thus.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six unsurpassed qualities:
unsurpassed seeing, unsurpassed hearing, unsurpassed gain, unsurpassed precepts, unsurpassed respect, and unsurpassed mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are six dharmas, namely the six recollections:
recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of the precepts, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the devas.

These are the true dharmas taught by the Tathāgata; they should be compiled together to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and granting peace to gods and humans.
“Monks! The Tathāgata has taught seven right dharmas, which are the opposites of the seven unrighteous dharmas:
lack of faith, lack of shame, lack of dread, little learning, laziness, forgetfulness, and lack of wisdom.”
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven right dharmas:
having faith, having a sense of shame, having a sense of dread of blame, being learned, being energetic, possessing retentive memory, and possessing great wisdom.
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
There are sentient beings who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; these are gods and humans, which is the first station of consciousness.
There are sentient beings who possess diverse bodies but a single perception; these are the Brahmakāyika gods at the time of their initial birth, which is the second station of consciousness.
There are some sentient beings who have a single body but various perceptions; these are the Ābhāsvara devas, and this is the third station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
There are some sentient beings who have a single body and a single perception; these are the Śubhakṛtsna devas, and this is the fourth station of consciousness.
There are also some sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness.
“Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven dharmas of diligence:

first, a bhikṣu is diligent in the practice of the precepts; second, he is diligent in extinguishing greed and desire; third, he is diligent in destroying false views; fourth, he is diligent in extensive learning; fifth, he is diligent in vigor; sixth, he is diligent in right mindfulness; and seventh, he is diligent in meditative concentration.”
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven perceptions:

the perception of impurity, the perception of the impurity of food, the perception that all worlds are not to be delighted in, the perception of non-existence, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, and the perception of non-self in suffering.
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven factors of concentration:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness.
Furthermore, there are seven dharmas, namely the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga):

the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of dharma-discernment, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.

This is the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; we should compile it together to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and securing peace for gods and humans.
“Monks! The Tathāgata has taught the eight right dharmas, namely the eight worldly conditions:
gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure.”
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas, namely the eight liberations:
perceiving forms while having form internally is the first liberation;
not perceiving forms internally while perceiving forms externally is the second liberation;
The liberation of the pure is the third liberation;
transcending perceptions of form and extinguishing perceptions of aversion, one dwells in the liberation of the sphere of infinite space, which is the fourth liberation;
transcending the sphere of infinite space, one dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness, which is the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one dwells in the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; this is the eighth liberation.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas, namely the Eightfold Noble Path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Furthermore, there are eight dharmas, namely the eight persons:

the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-pratipannaka), the stream-enterer (srotāpanna); the candidate for the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka), the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin); the candidate for the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-pratipannaka), the non-returner (anāgāmin); the candidate for the fruit of arhatship (arhattva-pratipannaka), and the arhat.

"This is the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; we should compile it together in order to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and granting peace to gods and humans."
“Monks! The Tathāgata has taught nine true dharmas, namely the nine abodes of sentient beings:
there are some sentient beings who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions—these are gods and humans; this is the first abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who possess various bodies but a single perception; this refers to those first born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and this is the second abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who possess a single body but various perceptions; this refers to the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and this is the third abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who possess a single body and a single perception; this refers to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, and this is the fourth abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are without thought and without cognitive awareness; this refers to the Heaven of No-Thought, which is the fifth abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of infinite space; this is the sixth abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the seventh abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the eighth abode of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the ninth abode of sentient beings.

This is the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; we should compile it together to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and granting peace to gods and humans.

“Monks! The Tathāgata has taught ten right dharmas, namely the ten dharmas of one beyond training: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right effort, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation.”

This is the True Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; we should compile it together in order to prevent disputes, so that the holy life may endure for a long time, bringing great benefit and peace to gods and humans.
At that time, the World-Honored One confirmed what Śāriputra had said.
Then, having heard what Śāriputra had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Eight.
The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Nine.
Translated during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty by Buddhayaśas together with Zhu Fonian.
10. The Discourse on the Ten Superiorities (10). Second Division, The Sixth Discourse on the Ten Superiorities.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Aṅga together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The World-Honored One traveled to the city of Campā and stayed by the side of the Gaggarā Pond.
On the fifteenth day, when the moon was full, the World-Honored One sat in the open air surrounded by a great assembly. He preached the Dharma throughout the night and addressed Śāriputra:

"At present, bhikṣus from the four directions have gathered; they are all diligent, having cast off sleepiness, and desire to hear the Dharma. I am suffering from back pain and wish to rest for a short while. You should now preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus."

Then, having received the Buddha’s instruction, Śāriputra departed. At that time, the World-Honored One folded his saṃghāṭī robe fourfold, lay down on his right side like a lion, and rested with one foot upon the other.
At that time, the Elder Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall teach the Dharma; its words—beginning, middle, and end—are all entirely true and correct, complete in meaning and flavor, and pure in the holy life (brahmacarya). Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
At that time, the bhikṣus received the instruction and listened.
Śāriputra addressed the bhikṣus:

“There are ten superior dharmas that eliminate the various fetters and bonds, leading to Nirvāṇa and the end of suffering; furthermore, they are fully endowed with five hundred and fifty dharmas. I shall now analyze them; listen well.”

"Monks! There is one thing that leads to accomplishment, one thing that leads to cultivation, one thing that leads to awakening, one thing that leads to cessation, one thing that leads to decline, one thing that leads to increase, one thing that is difficult to understand, one thing that leads to birth, one thing that leads to knowledge, and one thing that leads to realization."
What is the one dharma to be accomplished?
It is non-negligence regarding all wholesome dharmas.
What is the one dharma to be cultivated?
It means constantly reflecting upon the body oneself.
What is the single factor of awakening?
It is tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*).
What is the one dharma that is subject to cessation?
It is the conceit "I am.
What is the one dharma that is subject to decline?
That is to say, it is not the contemplation of impurity.
What is the one increasing factor?
It is the contemplation of impurity.
What is the one dharma difficult to understand?
It is the concentration of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-samādhi*). What is the one dharma that arises?
This refers to liberation with outflows (*sāsrava-vimukti*).
What is the single knowledge of phenomena?
It is that all sentient beings subsist by depending on food.
What is the one dharma to be realized?
It is the unimpeded liberation of the mind.

Furthermore, there are two dharmas to be accomplished, two dharmas to be cultivated, two dharmas to be awakened to, two dharmas to be extinguished, two dharmas subject to decline, two dharmas subject to increase, two dharmas difficult to understand, two dharmas to be produced, two dharmas to be known, and two dharmas to be realized.
What are the two factors that constitute the Dharma?
They are a sense of shame and a sense of dread of blame.
What are the two factors to be cultivated?
That is to say, serenity (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā).
What are the two factors of awakening?
That is to say, name (nāma) and form (rūpa).
What are the two factors that lead to cessation?
They are ignorance and craving.
What are the two factors that lead to decline?
This refers to the violation of precepts and the destruction of right view.
What are the two factors of increase?
They are the perfection of precepts and the perfection of right view.
What are the two difficult-to-understand dharmas?
There are causes and conditions by which sentient beings give rise to defilement;
there are causes and conditions by which sentient beings attain purity.
What are the two types of dharmas that have been realized?
The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
What are the two types of dharmas that are known?
That is to say: the possible and the impossible.
What are the two qualities that are to be realized?
They are clarity and liberation.

"Furthermore, there are three dharmas of accomplishment, three dharmas of cultivation, three dharmas of awakening, three dharmas of cessation, three dharmas of decline, three dharmas of increase, three dharmas difficult to understand, three dharmas of arising, three dharmas of knowledge, and three dharmas of realization."
What are the three factors for accomplishment?
First, associating with virtuous friends; second, hearing the sound of the Dharma with one's ears; third, the accomplishment of each and every dharma.
What are the three dharmas to be cultivated?
This refers to the three samādhis:
the emptiness samādhi, the signless samādhi, and the wishless samādhi.
What are the three factors of awakening?
That is to say, the three feelings:
painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What are the three things subject to cessation?
That is to say, the three cravings:
craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
What are the three factors that lead to decline?
They are the three unwholesome roots:
the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
What are the three factors of increase?
They are the three roots of goodness:
the root of goodness of non-attachment, the root of goodness of non-hatred, and the root of goodness of non-delusion.
What are the three things that are difficult to understand?
It refers to three things that are difficult to understand:
the difficulty for noble sages to understand, the difficulty of understanding the Dharma upon hearing it, and the difficulty of understanding the Tathāgata.
What are the three factors of arising?
That is to say, the three characteristics:
the characteristic of cessation, the characteristic of diligence, and the characteristic of equanimity.
What are the three ways of knowing the Dharma?
This refers to the three realms of transcendence:
transcending the realm of desire to reach the realm of form; transcending the realm of form to reach the formless realm;
and abandoning all conditioned phenomena—that is called "exhaustion."
What are the three verified dharmas? They are the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*):
the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
"Monks! These are the thirty dharmas that are real and not false; having realized them, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with impartiality.

Furthermore, there are four dharmas for accomplishment, four dharmas for cultivation, four dharmas for awakening, four dharmas for cessation, four dharmas for decline, four dharmas for increase, four dharmas difficult to understand, four dharmas for arising, four dharmas for knowledge, and four dharmas for realization."
What are the four factors for accomplishment? They are the four wheels:
first, dwelling in a central land; second, associating with virtuous friends; third, exercising self-restraint; and fourth, having planted roots of goodness in past lives.
What are the four dharmas to be cultivated?
They are the four foundations of mindfulness:

A bhikṣu contemplates the body within the body, practicing with diligence and without slackening, maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness, and relinquishing worldly greed and sorrow; [he likewise contemplates feelings, mind, and phenomena].
Contemplating the body as a body externally, he is diligent and untiring, mindful and not forgetful, abandoning worldly greed and sorrow;
contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally, he is diligent and untiring, mindful and not forgetful, abandoning worldly greed and sorrow.
The contemplation of sensation, mind, and mental phenomena is likewise.
What are the four conditions for the arising of consciousness?
They are the four nutriments:
The food of physical morsels, the food of contact, the food of volition, and the food of consciousness.
What are the four things subject to cessation?
They are the four types of feeling.
The clinging to sensual pleasures, the clinging to self, the clinging to precepts and vows, and the clinging to views.
What are the four states of decline?
They are the four yokes.
The yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
What are the four factors for increase?
They are the four yokeless states.
There is no yoke of desire, no yoke of existence, no yoke of views, and no yoke of ignorance.
What are the four difficult-to-understand phenomena?
They are the four noble truths.
The truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
What are the four dharmas of birth?
They are the four knowledges:
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and knowledge of the minds of others.
What are the four knowledges of phenomena?
They are the four analytical eloquences (pratisaṃvid):
The discrimination of phenomena, the discrimination of meaning, the discrimination of language, and the discrimination of eloquence.
What are the four verified dharmas?
They are the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
Monks, these are the forty dharmas, which are real and not false; having realized them through direct knowledge, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with impartiality.

“Furthermore, there are five factors of accomplishment, five factors of cultivation, five factors of awakening, five factors of cessation, five factors of decline, five factors of increase, five factors difficult to understand, five factors of arising, five factors of knowledge, and five factors of realization.”
What are the five factors for accomplishment?
They are the five branches of cessation:
first, faith in the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, who is fully endowed with the ten titles;
Second, they shall be free from illness, their bodies always remaining peaceful and secure;
third, they shall be upright and sincere, devoid of flattery or deceit, proceeding directly upon the path to the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa;
fourth, they shall be single-minded and undistracted, reciting and chanting without forgetfulness.
Fifth, one is skillful in observing the arising and ceasing of phenomena, thereby exhausting the root of suffering through the practice of the noble ones.
What are the five things to be cultivated? They are the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*).
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
What are the five factors of enlightenment?
They are the five aggregates of clinging:
The aggregate of form-feeling, the aggregate of feeling-feeling, the aggregate of perception-feeling, the aggregate of formations-feeling, and the aggregate of consciousness-feeling.
"What are the five things to be abandoned?
They are the five hindrances:"
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
What are the five factors leading to decline?
They are the five mental fetters of obstruction:
First, a bhikṣu doubts the Buddha; having doubted the Buddha, he does not draw near to him; not drawing near to him, he does not revere him—this is the first mental fetter of obstruction.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu harbors flawed conduct, improper conduct, and defiled conduct toward the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the Precepts; he does not draw near to the Precepts nor does he revere them—these are the four mental fetters of obstruction.

Moreover, a bhikṣu conceives thoughts of malice toward those who lead the holy life (brahmacārin); his heart finds no joy in them, and he reviles and abuses them with coarse and evil words—this is the fifth mental fetter of obstruction.
What are the five factors of increase?
They are the five bases of joy:
first, rapture; second, mindfulness; third, tranquility; fourth, bliss; and fifth, concentration.
“What are the five dhammas that are difficult to understand?
They are the five bases of liberation:

if a bhikkhu is diligent and untiring, delights in secluded places, and is single-mindedly focused, he attains what was not yet attained, realizes what was not yet realized, and achieves what was not yet achieved.”

What are the five? If a bhikṣu hears the Buddha teaching the Dharma, or hears fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin) teach, or hears his teachers and elders teach; he reflects upon and examines them, discerning the meaning of the teachings, and his mind attains joy. Having attained joy, he then attains love for the Dharma (dharmatṛṣṇā). Having attained love for the Dharma, his body and mind become tranquil and secure. Once his body and mind are tranquil and secure, he attains meditative concentration (dhyāna). Having attained meditative concentration, he attains knowledge in accordance with reality (yathābhūtajñāna). This is the first entrance into liberation.

Thereupon, the bhikṣu rejoiced upon hearing the Dharma; he received, upheld, and recited it with joy; he also rejoiced in explaining it to others; he likewise rejoiced in reflecting upon and analyzing it; and he likewise attained meditative concentration in the Dharma in the same way.
"What are the five dharmas that lead to birth?
They are the five noble knowledges of concentration (*pañca-ārya-jñāna-samādhi*):
first, the cultivation of *samādhi* which brings present happiness and future happiness, giving rise to internal and external knowledge."
Second, the noble ones are free from craving, giving rise to internal and external wisdom.
Third, that which is practiced by the Buddhas and noble ones gives rise to internal and external wisdom.
Fourth, relying on the mark of quiescent extinction, solitary and without companion, one gives rise to internal and external wisdom.
Fifth, entering one-pointedly into samādhi and arising from it one-pointedly, one gives rise to internal and external knowledge.
What are the five ways of knowing phenomena?
They are the five elements of renunciation:

First, a bhikṣu takes no delight in sensual desires, does not dwell upon them, and does not associate with them; he dwells only on the way of escape, delights in seclusion, and associates with it without indolence. His mind becomes pliant and supple; through this escape from desire and freedom from passion, the outflows arising from desire are exhausted, abandoned, and extinguished, whereby he attains liberation. This is the way of escape regarding desire. The ways of escape regarding ill-will, envy, form, and the view of a self-body are likewise the same.
What are the five realized dharmas?
They are the five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa):

the aggregate of morality, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. These constitute the fifty dharmas.
Knowing this as it truly is, without falsehood, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with equanimity.

Furthermore, there are six factors for accomplishment, six factors for cultivation, six factors for awakening, six factors for cessation, six factors for decline, six factors for increase, six factors difficult to understand, six factors for arising, six factors for knowledge, and six factors for realization.
What are the six factors for the perfection of the Dharma? They are the six principles of respect:
if a bhikṣu cultivates these six principles of respect, he will be worthy of honor and esteem, live in harmony with the community, remain free from disputes, and walk alone without entanglement.
What are the six?

In this regard, a bhikṣu constantly practices loving-kindness with his body, respects those who practice the holy life, and dwells in a heart of benevolence and compassion. This is called "valuing the Dharma. He is worthy of respect and honor; he lives in harmony with the community, free from dispute and contention, and walks alone without entanglement.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu practices loving-kindness in speech and loving-kindness in mind; he shares with others whatever sustenance he has obtained through the Dharma and whatever remains in his alms bowl, without harboring thoughts of "self" or "other."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu observes the precepts practiced by the noble ones: he does not transgress them nor defile them; they are unstained, praised by the wise, perfectly maintained, and bring about the accomplishment of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu who has accomplished the noble way of escape, who brings an equal end to suffering through right view and the various holy practices, is said to "revere the Dharma. Such a person is worthy of honor and respect; they live in harmony with the community, free from dispute, and walk alone without entanglement.
"What are the six dharmas to be cultivated?
They are the six recollections:
recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṃgha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the devas."
What are the six factors of awakening?
They are the six internal bases: the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base.
What are the six factors of cessation?
They are the six cravings:
craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena.
What are the six states of decline?
This refers to the six things that are not objects of reverence:

lack of reverence for the Buddha, lack of reverence for the Dharma, lack of reverence for the Saṅgha, lack of reverence for the precepts, lack of reverence for meditative concentration, and lack of reverence for one's parents.
What are the six increasing dharmas?
They are the six dharmas of reverence:
reverence for the Buddha, reverence for the Dharma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the precepts, reverence for meditative concentration, and reverence for one's parents.
What are the six dharmas that are difficult to understand? They are the six unsurpassed qualities:
unsurpassed seeing, unsurpassed hearing, unsurpassed gain, unsurpassed precepts, unsurpassed respect, and unsurpassed mindfulness.
What are the six dharmas that arise?
They are the six pairs of dharmas:

herein, a bhikṣu sees forms with the eye without sorrow or joy, dwelling in equanimity with mindfulness and clear comprehension; likewise, he hears sounds with the ear, smells odors with the nose, tastes flavors with the tongue, feels tangibles with the body, and cognizes mental objects with the mind, being neither glad nor sad, but dwelling in equanimity with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
“What are the six things to be known?
They are the six elements of renunciation. If a bhikṣu should say:”
"I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, yet anger arose again.
Other bhikṣus said, "Do not speak these words;
do not slander the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata does not say such a thing. It is impossible that one who cultivates the liberation of loving-kindness would have anger arise again."
The Buddha said:
"Only after one has eliminated ill will can one attain loving-kindness. If a bhikṣu says:
"When I practice the liberation of compassion, a mind of resentment and envy arises;
when I practice the liberation of sympathetic joy, a mind of grief and affliction arises;
when I practice the liberation of equanimity, a mind of aversion and attachment arises."
"Practicing the path of non-self gives rise to a mind of doubt;
practicing the path of non-perception gives rise to various confused thoughts. It is also thus.
What are the six realized dharmas? They are the six supernormal powers:

first, the realization of the power of psychic transformation; second, the realization of the power of the divine ear; third, the realization of the power of knowing the minds of others; fourth, the realization of the power of recollecting past lives; fifth, the realization of the power of the divine eye; and sixth, the realization of the power of the exhaustion of outflows.
These are the sixty dharmas.
O bhikṣus! Having known them as they truly are, without falsehood, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with equanimity.

Furthermore, there are seven things that lead to success, seven things to be cultivated, seven factors of awakening, seven things that lead to cessation, seven things that lead to decline, seven things that lead to increase, seven things difficult to understand, seven things leading to birth, seven things to be known, and seven things to be realized.
What are the seven factors of accomplishment?
They are the seven treasures:

the treasure of faith, the treasure of ethical discipline, the treasure of moral shame, the treasure of dread of blame, the treasure of learning, the treasure of generosity, and the treasure of wisdom; these constitute the seven treasures.
What are the seven factors of cultivation?
They are the seven factors of enlightenment.
In this regard, a bhikṣu cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and based on relinquishment;

He cultivates the practice of equanimity, the practice of concentration, the practice of tranquility, the practice of joy, the practice of energy, and the practice of virtue; he does so based on dispassion, based on cessation, and based on relinquishment.
"What are the seven factors of awakening?
They are the seven stations of consciousness:
if there are sentient beings who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions—namely, gods and humans—this is the first station of consciousness."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who have diverse bodies but a single perception; this refers to those born at the very beginning of the Ābhāsvara Heaven (the Heaven of Radiant Sound), which is the second station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who have a single body but diverse perceptions; this refers to the Ābhāsvara Heaven, which is the third station of consciousness.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who possess a single body and a single perception; these are the Śubhakṛtsna devas, and this constitutes the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

There are also sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of infinite space; this is the fifth station of consciousness. Or there are those who dwell in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the sixth station of consciousness.
Or, abiding in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these are the seven stations of consciousness.
What are the seven things subject to cessation? They are the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

The latent tendency of sensual desire, the latent tendency of existence, the latent tendency of views, the latent tendency of pride, the latent tendency of ill will, the latent tendency of ignorance, and the latent tendency of doubt.
"What are the seven factors leading to decline?"
These are the seven unrighteous qualities:
this bhikṣu lacks faith, lacks shame, lacks dread of wrongdoing, has little learning, is indolent, is forgetful, and lacks wisdom.
What are the seven progressive qualities?
That is to say, the seven true dharmas:
herein, a bhikṣu possesses faith, possesses a sense of shame, possesses a sense of dread, is learned, is not indolent, has a strong memory, and possesses wisdom.
What are the seven factors that are difficult to understand?
They are the seven right and wholesome qualities:

herein, a bhikṣu is fond of meaning, fond of the Dharma, fond of knowing the proper time, fond of contentment, fond of self-restraint, fond of gathering the assembly, and fond of discerning individuals.
What is the dharma of seven births?
It refers to the seven perceptions:

the perception of impurity, the perception of the impurity of food, the perception that all worlds are not worth delighting in, the perception of death, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, and the perception of non-self in suffering.
"What are the seven factors of knowledge? They are the seven types of diligence:

diligence in ethical conduct, diligence in extinguishing craving, diligence in destroying wrong views, diligence in extensive learning, diligence in energetic effort, diligence in right mindfulness, and diligence in meditative concentration."
What are the seven factors of realization?

They are the seven powers of the destruction of the taints (*āsrava-kṣaya-bala*): herein, a monk whose taints are destroyed knows and sees, as they truly are, all suffering, its origin, its cessation, its gratification, its peril, and the escape from it.
One contemplates desire as a pit of fire and also like a sword; knowing desire and seeing desire, one does not crave desire, and the mind does not dwell upon desire.

A bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted observes both in direct and reverse order; having realized it as it truly is and seen it as it truly is, worldly greed, envy, and evil unwholesome states do not leak forth nor arise. He cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, practicing them extensively and repeatedly; he cultivates the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path, practicing them extensively and repeatedly.
"O bhikṣus! These are the seventy dharmas, which are real and not false; having realized them, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with impartiality.

Furthermore, there are the eight dharmas of accomplishment, the eight dharmas of cultivation, the eight dharmas of awakening, the eight dharmas of cessation, the eight dharmas of decline, the eight dharmas of increase, the eight dharmas difficult to understand, the eight dharmas of arising, the eight dharmas of knowledge, and the eight dharmas of realization."
What are the eight factors? They are the eight causes and conditions:
one attains wisdom without having attained the holy life, and once the holy life has been attained, wisdom increases further.
What are the eight?

In this regard, a bhikkhu dwells in dependence upon the Blessed One, or upon his teachers, or upon wise fellow-practitioners of the holy life; he gives rise to a sense of shame and dread of blame, possessing affection and reverence. This is called the first causal condition: by means of which one who has not yet attained the holy life gains wisdom, and having attained the holy life, wisdom increases further.
Furthermore, by dwelling in reliance upon the World-Honored One and inquiring at the appropriate times, "What is the meaning of this Dharma?
Toward what does its significance lead?
the elders will then expound for them the profound principles and meanings; these constitute the second set of causes and conditions.
Having heard the Dharma, one finds joy in the stillness of body and mind; this is the third causal condition.

Having found joy in stillness, one does not engage in obstructive, useless, or frivolous discourse; when entering among the assembly, whether preaching the Dharma oneself or requesting another to do so, one nevertheless does not abandon the noble silence; this is the fourth causal condition.

Having heard extensively and widely, one maintains it without forgetting; the various dharmas are profound and subtle, good in the beginning, middle, and end, with meanings and flavors that are true and sincere, and the holy life (brahmacarya) is fully perfected. Having heard this, it enters the heart, and one’s vision does not waver—these are the five causes and conditions.
To practice with diligence, to eliminate evil and increase goodness, to exert effort and remain capable, and not to abandon this Dharma—these are the six causes and conditions.
To possess wisdom that knows the dharma of arising and ceasing, to follow the path of the noble ones, and to be able to reach the end of suffering—this is the seventh cause and condition.

Contemplating the five aggregates of clinging, one observes their characteristics of arising and their characteristics of cessation: "This is form, this is the origination of form, this is the cessation of form; this is feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; this is the origination of consciousness, this is the cessation of consciousness. These constitute the eight causal conditions.
"One possesses wisdom even before attaining the holy life, and once the holy life has been attained, wisdom increases further.
What are the eight things to be cultivated?
They are the Noble Eightfold Path."
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
What are the eight factors of enlightenment?
These are the eight worldly dharmas:
gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure.
What are the eight dharmas that lead to their cessation?
They are the eight wrong paths:
wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration.
What are the eight qualities leading to decline?
This refers to the eight factors of indolence. What are the eight factors of indolence?
A bhikṣu, having failed to obtain food while begging for alms, thinks to himself:

"Today I went to the village to beg for food but did not receive any; my body is utterly exhausted and I am unable to endure sitting in meditation or walking meditation. I should now lie down and rest."

The indolent bhikṣu then lies down to rest, refusing to apply himself with diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to acquire what has not yet been acquired, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is the first form of indolence.
When a lazy bhikṣu has obtained sufficient food, he further thinks:

"This morning I entered the village to beg for food and received more than enough; my body is heavy and weary, and I am unable to endure sitting meditation or walking meditation. It would be best now to lie down and rest."

The indolent bhikṣu then goes to sleep; he is unable to be diligent in order to attain what has not yet been attained, to acquire what has not yet been acquired, or to realize what has not yet been realized.
Even if the indolent bhikṣu has a small amount of administrative work, he thinks to himself:
"Today I have performed administrative duties and my body is utterly exhausted; I am unable to endure sitting meditation or walking meditation. It is now best that I go to sleep."
The indolent bhikṣu then goes to sleep.
Even if the indolent bhikṣu intends to attend to his duties, he thinks to himself:
"If I attend to my duties tomorrow, I will surely become utterly exhausted; I cannot practice sitting meditation or walking meditation today, so I should lie down and rest in advance."
The indolent bhikṣu then lay down to rest.
Even if the indolent bhikṣu had walked for a short distance, he would think to himself:
"I have walked this morning until my body is utterly exhausted; I am unable to endure sitting in meditation or walking meditation. It is fitting that I now lie down to rest."
The indolent bhikṣu then lay down to rest.
Even if the indolent bhikṣu wished to practice a little, he would think to himself:
"I shall practice tomorrow; I will surely become exhausted. I cannot sit in meditation or walk in *caṅkrama* now, so I must lie down and rest in advance."

The indolent bhikṣu immediately seeks rest and sleep; he is unable to apply himself with diligence to that which is not yet attained, to that which is not yet acquired, or to that which is not yet realized. This is the sixth type of indolent bhikṣu.
If he encounters even a minor ailment, he immediately thinks:
"I have contracted a grave illness; I am so debilitated and emaciated that I am unable to endure sitting meditation or walking meditation, and must instead rest."

The indolent bhikṣu immediately went to sleep; he was unable to apply himself with diligence to attain what had not yet been attained, to acquire what had not yet been acquired, or to realize what had not yet been realized.
Once the indolent bhikṣu’s illness had subsided, he again thought to himself:
"My illness has not long since been cured, and my body is still weak and emaciated; I am unable to endure sitting meditation or walking meditation, so it is best that I rest."

The indolent bhikṣu then immediately goes to sleep; he is unable to apply himself with diligence to that which has not yet been attained he wishes to attain, that which has not yet been acquired he wishes to acquire, and that which has not yet been realized he wishes to realize.
What are the eight factors of increase?
This refers to the eight forms of non-laziness.
What are the eight types of diligence?
When a bhikṣu enters a village to beg for food and returns without having obtained any, he immediately reflects thus:
"My body is light and agile, and I require little sleep; it is fitting that I should apply myself with diligence to sitting meditation and walking meditation.

Thus, he strives to attain what has not yet been attained, to achieve what has not yet been achieved, and to realize what has not yet been realized. Thereupon, the bhikṣu exerts himself with diligence; this is called the first type of diligent bhikṣu.
Having obtained sufficient almsfood, he thought to himself:

"I have now entered the village and received enough food to satisfy my hunger; my physical strength is restored. It is fitting that I should apply myself diligently to sitting meditation and walking meditation."
"May I attain what has not yet been attained, acquire what has not yet been acquired, and realize what has not yet been realized. Thereupon, the bhikṣu immediately applies himself with diligence.
If that diligent bhikṣu has some administrative duties, he reflects thus:
"I have been occupied with administrative duties and have neglected my practice of the Path; now I should apply myself diligently to sitting meditation and walking meditation."
"May I attain what has not yet been attained, acquire what has not yet been acquired, and realize what has not yet been realized. Thereupon, the bhikṣu immediately applies himself with diligence.
If a diligent bhikṣu is about to take up administrative duties, he reflects thus: "I shall attend to administrative duties tomorrow;
that will hinder my practice of the Path. For now, I should apply myself to sitting meditation and walking meditation with diligence."
"Having not yet attained, may I attain; having not yet acquired, may I acquire; having not yet realized, may I realize. Thus, the bhikṣu exerts himself with diligence.
When a diligent bhikṣu goes about his business, he reflects:
"I have been occupied with coming and going this morning, which has hindered my practice of the path; now I should exert myself in seated meditation and walking meditation."
"Those not yet attained shall be attained; those not yet acquired shall be acquired; those not yet realized shall be realized. Thereupon, the bhikṣu immediately applies himself with diligence.
If a diligent bhikṣu intends to travel, he reflects thus: "I shall travel tomorrow, which will interrupt my practice of the Way;
it is fitting that I now apply myself with diligence to sitting meditation and walking meditation."
"May I attain what has not yet been attained, acquire what has not yet been acquired, and realize what has not yet been realized.
Thus, the bhikṣu applies himself with diligence. When a diligent bhikṣu encounters illness, he reflects:
"I am gravely ill; my life may come to an end. Now is the time for diligence."
"Having not yet attained what is to be attained, not yet acquired what is to be acquired, and not yet realized what is to be realized, this bhikṣu then applies himself with diligence.
As the bhikṣu’s illness begins to subside through his diligence, he further reflects:
'My illness has only recently improved; it might flare up again and cause me to abandon my practice of the Way. I should now apply myself diligently to sitting meditation and walking meditation.'"

"Those not yet attained will be attained; those not yet acquired will be acquired; those not yet realized will be realized. Thereupon, the bhikṣu applies himself with diligence to sitting meditation and walking meditation; this is the eighth.
"What are the eight unfavorable conditions that obstruct the Dharma?
They are the eight states of lack of leisure that hinder the cultivation of the holy life.
What are these eight?"

When a Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world and teaches the subtle, wondrous Dharma—tranquil, unconditioned, and leading toward the path of Bodhi—if there is someone born in the hells, this constitutes an unfavorable place where one cannot practice the holy life.

When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, appears in the world and teaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma—quiescent, unconditioned, and leading toward the path of Bodhi—there are still sentient beings among the animals, among the hungry ghosts, among the long-lived devas, or in remote borderlands where there is no knowledge and no Buddha-Dharma; these are called "unfamiliar places" (akṣaṇa), where one cannot practice the holy life (brahmacarya).

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world and teaches the subtle Dharma—tranquil, unconditioned, and leading toward the path of enlightenment—there may be sentient beings born in the Central Land who nevertheless hold wrong views, harbor perverted minds, and accomplish evil deeds; they will inevitably enter hell. This is called an "unfamiliar place," where one cannot practice the holy life.

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world and proclaims the subtle Dharma—tranquil, unconditioned, and leading toward the path of enlightenment—there may be sentient beings born in the Central Land who are deaf, blind, or mute, such that they are unable to hear the Dharma or practice the holy life; this is called being "unskilled" (avyavakīrṇa).

If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha does not appear in the world, there can be no one to preach the subtle Dharma—tranquil, unconditioned, and leading toward the path of Bodhi—and yet a sentient being is born in a central land, with all faculties complete and capable of receiving the holy teaching, but fails to encounter a Buddha and cannot practice the Brahma-faring; this is the eighth lack of leisure.
"What are the eight things that lead to birth?
They are the eight awakenings of a great man:
the Path consists in having few desires; to have many desires is not the Path."
The Way requires contentment; insatiability is not the Way.
The Way requires seclusion and stillness; delighting in crowds is not the Way.
The Way requires self-restraint; frivolous laughter is not the Way.
The Way requires diligent effort; indolence is not the Way.
The Way requires focused mindfulness; excessive forgetfulness is not the Way.
The Way requires a concentrated mind; a distracted mind is not the Way.
The Path consists of wisdom; ignorance is not the Path.
What are the eight knowledges? They are the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited, whether beautiful or ugly, observing them constantly and maintaining mindfulness; this is the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as immeasurable, whether beautiful or ugly, observing them constantly and maintaining mindfulness; this is the second sphere of mastery.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited, whether beautiful or ugly, constantly observing and constantly mindful of them; this is the third base of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
