The Sūtra on the Questions of Śakra Devānām Indra (14) The Tenth Sūtra of the Second Division of the Long Discourses Spoken by the Buddha: The Sūtra on the Questions of Śakra Devānām Indra. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Magadha, north of the village of Ambala, within the Indrasāla Cave on Mount Vebhāra.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra conceived a subtle and virtuous mind, desiring to come and see the Buddha, thinking:
"I shall now go to the place where the World-Honored One resides.

When the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard that Śakra Devānām Indra had conceived this sublime and virtuous mind and wished to approach the Buddha’s dwelling, they immediately went to Śakra and said to him:
“Excellent, Śakra! Since you have conceived such a sublime and virtuous mind to go to the Tathāgata, we too would delight in attending upon you as we go to the presence of the World-Honored One.”
Then Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the musician god Pañcaśikha, saying:
"I now wish to go to the place where the World-Honored One resides; you may accompany me, and these gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven shall also go with me to the Buddha's dwelling."
He replied, "So be it!
Then, Pañcaśikha took up his lapis lazuli lute and played before Śakra, amidst the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, as an offering.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, and Pañcaśikha suddenly vanished from the Dharma Hall; in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, they arrived at Mount Vipula in the northern part of the kingdom of Magadha.
At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Fire-Flame Samādhi, and Mount Vidyā became one color with fire. When the people of the country saw this, they said to one another:
"This Mount Vidyā has become one color with fire; this must be through the power of the Tathāgata and the devas."
Then Śakra Devānām Indra said to Pañcaśikha:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is extremely difficult to behold; yet he has condescended to visit this secluded place, which is silent and still, with birds and beasts for companions. This place is constantly guarded by great divine beings who attend upon the World-Honored One. You may go before him and entertain the World-Honored One by playing your lapis lazuli lute, while I and the other devas shall follow behind."
He replied, “So be it!
Having received these instructions, he took his lapis lazuli lute and went before the Buddha first.
Not far from the Buddha, she played a lapis lazuli lute and sang in verse:
“Bhadra, I pay homage to your father; your father is most upright and majestic.
When you were born, there was auspiciousness; my heart is filled with great love and joy.”
Originally arising from a minor cause, the desire-mind grew therein;
it expanded and increased further, as if making offerings to an arhat.
The sons of Śākya are devoted to the four dhyānas and always delight in dwelling in seclusion.
With right intention I seek the nectar of immortality; my single-minded devotion is likewise so.
When the Sage of Benevolence resolved upon the mind of enlightenment, he was determined to achieve perfect awakening;
as I now seek that woman, my determination to meet her is likewise so.
My mind has given rise to defiled attachment; I cherish it and cannot let it go.
Though I wish to abandon it, I am unable to leave, like an elephant restrained by a hook.
It is as if one who encounters a cool breeze after heat, or as if one who is thirsty finds a cold spring.
Like one who attains nirvāṇa, as water extinguishes fire;
like a sick man finding a skilled physician, or a hungry person obtaining fine food;
sufficiency brings happiness, like an arhat wandering in the Dharma.
Like an elephant pierced by a deep hook, yet still refusing to submit;
charging and butting about, difficult to restrain, its heedlessness knows no stopping.
It is like a cool, clear pond, with various flowers covering the surface of the water.
As an elephant exhausted by heat bathes, its entire body attains coolness;
so too, whatever offerings I have previously bestowed in worshiping the arhats—
may all those who possess merit in this world receive that same offering.
If you die, I shall surely die with you; if you are gone, what is the use of my living?
It would be better for my own body to perish than for me to exist without you.
Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, has now granted my wish.
"I commend you for your possession of proper etiquette; you have reflected upon this well.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and addressed Pañcaśikha, saying: "Excellent!"
"Excellent, Pañcaśikha!

You are able to praise the Tathāgata with a pure voice while playing the lapis lazuli lute; the sound of the lute and your voice are neither too long nor too short, harmonious and plaintive, moving the hearts of men."
In what you play upon the lute, all meanings are fully contained: it speaks of the bonds of desire, it speaks of the holy life, it speaks of the śramaṇa, and it speaks of nirvāṇa.
At that time, Pañcaśikha addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall, World-Honored One, when you were formerly by the waters of the Nairañjanā River at Uruvilvā, beneath the Ajapāla-nyagrodha tree, having first attained the Way of the Buddha. At that time, the son of the celestial general Śīkhadhara and the daughter of the king of the Gandharvas were together in one place, indulging only in sensual pleasures. Seeing their state of mind at that moment, I immediately composed a verse for them. That verse spoke of the bonds of desire, and also spoke of the holy life (brahmacarya), and also spoke of the śramaṇa, and also spoke of nirvāṇa."
At that time, having heard my verses, the goddess raised her eyes, smiled, and said to me: "Pañcaśikha!

I have not yet seen the Tathāgata; however, I once heard the devas in the Dharma-preaching hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven praising the Tathāgata, saying that he possesses such virtues and such powers."
"You have always harbored faith and drawn near to the Tathāgata; I now wish to become your spiritual friend.
"World-Honored One!
After I had spoken those few words with him at that time, I did not speak with him again."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra had this thought:
"Pañcaśikha has already entertained the Tathāgata; I should now rather attend to that man."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately thought of that man.
Then Pañcaśikha also gave rise to this thought:
"Now Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has been able to think of me."
He then took his lapis lazuli lute and went to the abode of Śakra.
Śakra addressed him, saying:
"In my name and on behalf of the intention of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, inquire after the World-Honored One’s welfare."
"Are you light and at ease in your movements? Is your gait strong?

At that time, Pañcaśikha, having received the instruction of Śakra, went immediately to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"On behalf of Śakra Devānām-indra and the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he has sent me to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health."
“Are you physically light and at ease? Is your movement vigorous?
The World-Honored One replied, “May you, Śakra, and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have long lives, happiness, and freedom from affliction.”
Why is this so? Because all sentient beings—the gods, the people of the world, and the asuras—equally crave long life, peace and happiness, and freedom from affliction.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself again:
"We should go to pay our respects and visit the World-Honored One.
He immediately went with the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I do not know how far from the World-Honored One I may sit.
The Buddha said to Śakra:
"You gods are many; simply sit near me.
At that moment, the Indra Cave where the World-Honored One was staying naturally became spacious and vast, without any obstruction.
At that time, Śakra, together with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the Pañcaśikhas, all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Once, when the Buddha was at the residence of a brahmin in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the World-Honored One entered the Fire-Flame Samādhi. At that time, due to a minor matter, I was riding a precious chariot with a thousand spokes on my way to the abode of King Virūḍhaka; as I passed through the air, I saw a celestial maiden standing before the World-Honored One with her palms joined. I immediately said to her:
‘When the World-Honored One emerges from his samādhi, you should announce my name and inquire after his well-being:’”
"Are you physically light and well, and is your movement strong?
I wonder, World-Honored One, whether that woman ultimately succeeded in conveying this message of mine to him?"
“Are you able to recall this matter?
The Buddha said,
“I do recall it!”
"She then inquired after me using your voice; as I arose from my meditative absorption, I still heard the sound of your chariot.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, on account of a minor matter, I was gathered with the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven in the Hall of Dharma. Those elder devas all spoke thus:"
"If a Tathāgata appears in the world, the hosts of devas increase and the hosts of asuras decrease.

Now, having personally seen the World-Honored One, having personally known it for myself, and having personally realized it through my own testimony, I know that a Tathāgata, a Worthy One, has appeared in the world, whereby the hosts of devas increase and the hosts of asuras decrease.

There was this daughter of the Śākya clan, Gopī, who practiced the pure life under the World-Honored One; when her body perished and her life ended, she was reborn in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and has now become my son.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven all exclaimed:
"The Great Son of Heaven, Gopī, possesses great merit and great power.

Furthermore, there were three other bhikṣus who, having purified themselves in the holy life under the World-Honored One, were reborn after the dissolution of their bodies and the end of their lives among the lowly music-playing deities. They came daily to serve me; when Gopī saw them, she provoked them with a verse, saying:
"You are now a disciple of the Buddha; when I was formerly a householder, I provided you with food and clothing, and paid you homage with the utmost reverence."
Who are you that have personally received the Buddha’s instructions?
You have failed to examine what was spoken by the One of Pure Vision.
I originally paid homage to you, having heard the supreme Dharma from the Buddha;
I was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three as a son of Śakra.
Why do you not observe this?
By virtue of all my merits;
formerly having been a woman’s body, I am now a son of Śakra.
You all were originally together with me, practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) in common.
Now dwelling alone in lowliness and meanness, you serve as our attendant;
because you originally committed wicked deeds, you now receive this retribution—
dwelling alone in lowliness and meanness, serving as our attendant.
Born in this place of impurity, One is tormented by the touch of others;
Having heard this, one should feel weary and loathe it— This place is truly to be loathed.
From now on, you should apply yourself with diligence, And never again be made a servant for others.
The two of them applied themselves with diligent vigor, contemplating the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
They abandoned what they cherished and clung to, observing that the practice of desire is impure;
the bonds of desire are unreal, deceiving and deluding the world.
Like an elephant freed from its tether, he has transcended the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have gathered in the Hall of Dharma.
By his own heroic power, he has transcended the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Śakra marveled at this unprecedented event, and the devas likewise beheld it.
"This is a son of Śākya who has transcended the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
weary of the bonds of desire," thus spoke Gopī.
In the kingdom of Magadha there was a Buddha named Śākyamuni;
his son lost his mindfulness greatly, but later regained it.
One among these three men is therefore the musician deity.
Two who have seen the Truth of the Path surpass those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One, the disciples harbor no doubt;
two who together hear the Dharma are superior to that one alone.
"Having seen their own excellence, they were all reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
having observed them, I have therefore come to the presence of the Buddha.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray that you will grant me the leisure to resolve my doubts.
The Buddha said,
“Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain each point for you one by one.”
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"With what fetters are the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and other sentient beings bound, such that they even face one another with enmity, hostility, swords, and staves?"
The Buddha told Śakra:

"The arising of enmity and resentment all stems from greed and jealousy; it is because of this that devas, humans, asuras, and other sentient beings inflict harm upon one another with swords and staves."
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The arising of the bond of enmity is due to greed and jealousy; it causes gods, worldlings, asuras, and other sentient beings to strike one another with swords and staves.

Having now heard what the Buddha has taught, the net of my doubts has been entirely cleared away; I no longer have any uncertainty. However, I do not understand from what cause this greed and envy arise.
By what cause and by what condition?
Who is the primary source?
From whom does it arise?
"From what does it cease to exist?
The Buddha told Śakra:

"The arising of greed and envy is entirely due to love and hatred. Love and hatred are the cause, love and hatred are the condition, and love and hatred are the primary factor; from these they come into being, and without these, they do not exist."
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”

The arising of greed and envy all stems from love and hatred; love and hatred act as the cause, love and hatred act as the condition, and love and hatred are the primary factor. From these they come into being; without them, they do not exist.
Having now heard what the Buddha has taught, my delusions have been entirely removed and I no longer have any doubts.
However, I do not understand from what cause and by what conditions love and hatred arise;
what are their roots and their conditions?
Who is the primordial source?
From whom does it arise?
From whom does it cease?
The Buddha told Śakra:
"The arising of love and hatred is entirely due to desire; it is caused by desire and conditioned by desire, with desire as its primary source. From this they exist; without this, they do not exist."
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”

The arising of love and hatred both stems from desire; they are caused by desire and conditioned by desire, with desire as their primary source. From this they exist, and without this, they do not exist.
Having now heard what the Buddha has taught, my delusions have been entirely removed and I no longer have any doubts.
I only do not know by what means this desire arises again;
what is its cause and what is its condition?
Who is the primordial source?
From whom does it come to be?
From whom does it cease to be?
The Buddha told Śakra:
"Craving arises from perception; it is caused by perception and conditioned by perception. Perception is the primary source; from this it comes into being, and without this, it does not exist."
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
Craving arises from perception; with perception as its cause and perception as its condition, perception is the primary source. From this it exists, and without this it does not exist.
Having now heard what the Buddha has taught, I no longer have any doubt.
Yet I do not understand from what source this perception arises;
by what cause and by what condition?
Who is its original source?
"From whom does it exist?
From whom does it not exist?
The Buddha told Śakra:
“The arising of perception is due to frivolity; with frivolity as its cause and frivolity as its condition, frivolity is the primary source. From this it exists, and without this, it does not exist.”

Śakra! If there is no frivolous play, then there is no conceptualization; if there is no conceptualization, then there is no desire; if there is no desire, then there is no love or hatred; if there is no love or hatred, then there is no greed or envy. If there is no greed or envy, then all sentient beings will not harm one another.

Śakra! It is simply that tranquility is the root; because of tranquility and conditioned by tranquility, tranquility is the primary source. From this comes perception; from perception comes desire; from desire come love and hatred; from love and hatred come greed and envy.
Because of greed and envy, all living beings cause one another harm.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”

By means of tranquility (*śamatha*), with tranquility as the cause and tranquility as the condition, tranquility is the primary source. From this, perception arises through tranquility; without tranquility, there is no perception.

If there were fundamentally no tranquility, there would be no perception; without perception, there is no desire; without desire, there is no love or hatred; without love or hatred, there is no greed or envy; and without greed or envy, all living beings would not harm one another.

But perception arises from mental application; with mental application as its cause and mental application as its condition, mental application is the primary source. From mental application comes perception; from perception comes desire; from desire come love and hatred; from love and hatred come greed and envy; and from greed and envy, all sentient beings cause mutual injury to one another.
"Having now heard what the Buddha has taught, my delusions are entirely removed, and I have no further doubts.
At that time, Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Do all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas completely eliminate frivolous play and abide in the state of cessation?"
"Is it that some have not yet eliminated frivolity while abiding in the state of cessation?
The Buddha told Śakra:
"Not all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have completely eliminated frivolity while abiding in the state of cessation."

Why is this so? Śakra, there are various realms in the world, and sentient beings each rely upon their own realm, holding fast to it with firm resolve and unable to relinquish it; they claim their own to be real and all else to be false.
"Therefore, Śakra! No śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have reached the cessation of tracks without first completely eliminating frivolous play.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed it is so, World-Honored One!

There are various kinds of sentient beings in the world, each relying upon their own realm, holding fast to it with firm resolve, unable to relinquish it; they claim themselves to be right and others to be false.”
Therefore, all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have not yet exhausted their frivolous play cannot abide in the cessation of traces.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, my doubts are entirely dispelled; I have no further uncertainty.
Śakra again addressed the Buddha, saying,
“To what extent does one abide in tranquility within the state of cessation?
The Buddha told Śakra:
"There are three kinds of frivolous speech:
first, that of the mouth; second, that of thought; and third, that of seeking.
That which is spoken by the mouth may harm oneself, harm others, or harm both."
Having abandoned these words, he acts as he has spoken: neither harming himself, nor harming others, nor harming both.
A bhikkhu who knows the proper time acts according to his words, with focused mindfulness and without distraction. He likewise abandons the thoughts that harm himself, harm others, or harm both;

having abandoned these thoughts, he acts according to what he has thought: neither harming himself, nor harming others, nor harming both. A bhikkhu who knows the proper time acts according to what he has thought, with focused mindfulness and without distraction.
"Śakra! Seeking [sensual pleasures] harms oneself, harms others, and harms both;

having abandoned such seeking, one does not harm oneself, does not harm others, and does not harm both, according to what is sought. A bhikṣu who knows the proper time, according to what is sought, remains focused and undistracted."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said,
"Having heard what the Buddha has spoken, I no longer have any doubts.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"How many names for the noble and holy ones' mind of relinquishment are there?
The Buddha told Śakra: "There are three kinds of the mind of relinquishment: [the relinquishment of the body, the relinquishment of possessions, and the relinquishment of views]."
First is the body of joy, second is the body of sorrow, and third is the body of equanimity.
O Śakra! That which is the body of joy harms oneself, harms others, and harms both.

Having abandoned this joy, one does not harm oneself as one rejoices, nor harm others, nor harm both; knowing the proper time, the bhikṣu remains focused and mindful without forgetfulness—this is called receiving full ordination.
"Śakra! Those who are distressed by their bodies harm themselves, harm others, and harm both;

having abandoned such distress, they do not harm themselves, harm others, or harm both as they previously did. When a bhikṣu knows the proper time, remains focused in mindfulness without forgetfulness, he is said to have received full ordination."
Furthermore, Śakra!
That person who abandons the body harms themselves, harms others, and harms both;

whereas having abandoned this body, as it has been abandoned, one neither harms oneself nor harms others, nor harms both. A bhikṣu who knows the proper time and maintains focused mindfulness without forgetfulness—this is what is called receiving full ordination.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Having heard what the Buddha has spoken, I have no further doubts.
He then addressed the Buddha again:
"To what extent are those called 'worthy ones' (ariya) and 'noble ones' (ariyapuggala), whose faculties are fully perfected?
The Buddha told Śakra:
"Regarding the eye's cognition of forms, I say there are two [types]: [the noble and the ignoble]."
There are those that are to be cultivated and those that are not to be cultivated.
Regarding sounds for the ear, odors for the nose, tastes for the tongue, tangibles for the body, and mental phenomena for the mind, I say there are two kinds:
those that are to be cultivated and those that are not to be cultivated.
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has spoken in brief without yet providing a detailed analysis, yet I have understood it fully.”
Regarding the eye’s cognition of forms, I say there are two kinds:
those that are to be cultivated and those that are not to be cultivated.
Regarding the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena, there are likewise two kinds.
"Venerable One, there are those who may be associated with and those who may not be associated with.
Just as when the eye perceives forms and wholesome qualities diminish while unwholesome qualities increase— such perception of forms by the eye, I say, should not be associated with."

When sounds are heard by the ear, odors by the nose, flavors by the tongue, tangibles by the body, and mental objects are cognized by the mind, if wholesome qualities diminish and unwholesome qualities increase, I say that such [objects] are not to be associated with.
"Bhagavān! Just as when the eye sees forms, wholesome qualities increase and unwholesome qualities decrease, so too when the eye cognizes forms, I say it is to be cultivated.

When the ear cognizes sounds, the nose cognizes odors, the tongue cognizes tastes, the body cognizes tangibles, and the mind cognizes mental phenomena, wholesome qualities increase and unwholesome qualities decrease; I say these are to be cultivated."
The Buddha said to Śakra: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"This is called the noble and holy discipline of having the faculties fully complete.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Having heard what the Buddha has taught, I have no further doubts."
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To what extent is a bhikṣu said to have reached the ultimate, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate peace and security, and the ultimate state without remainder?"
The Buddha told Śakra:
"For one who, being afflicted by craving, attains the cessation of the body—this is the ultimate, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate peace, and the ultimate state without remainder."
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying, “For a long night, I have harbored a web of doubts; now the Tathāgata has opened up and resolved what I doubted.
The Buddha told Śakra:
“Have you ever previously gone to the presence of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas to inquire about this meaning?
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I recall from my own memory:”
In the past, I once went to the dwellings of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to inquire about this matter.
Formerly, on one occasion, I gathered in the lecture hall and discussed it with the assembly of devas:
"Has the Tathāgata appeared in the world, or has he not yet appeared?"
At that time, we searched together but did not see the Tathāgata appearing in the world; each of us returned to our palaces to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
World-Honored One!
Later, I again saw those great divine beings who, having indulged in the five desires at will, gradually passed away one by one.
At that time, World-Honored One,
I was seized by great terror, and my hair stood on end. Then,
seeing śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas dwelling in seclusion, having left home and abandoned desire, I immediately went to where they were and asked them:
"What do you mean by 'ultimate'?
I asked regarding this matter, but he was unable to answer.
Since he did not know, he instead questioned me in return, saying:
"Who are you? I immediately replied, "I am Śakra Devānām Indra."
He asked me again, "Which Śākya are you?
At that time, I replied:
"I am Śakra, Lord of the Devas; having a doubt in my mind, I have come to question you.
At that time, I explained the meaning of "Śakra" to him according to what I knew and saw.
He asked me, saying:

"I have become your disciple once again; I am now a disciple of the Buddha, having attained the stage of Srotāpanna. I shall not fall into other realms of existence, and after at most seven more cycles of rebirth, I will surely realize the fruit of the path. I only pray that the World-Honored One will certify me as a Sakṛdāgāmin."
Having spoken these words, he further uttered this verse:
"Because of those defiled perceptions, I gave rise to doubt;
throughout the long night, Together with the devas, I sought the Tathāgata."
Seeing various renunciants always dwelling in secluded and quiet places, he thought they were the Buddha, the World-Honored One; thus he went to them, bowed his head, and said:
"I have now come specifically to ask: what constitutes ultimate liberation?"
Having been questioned, he was unable to answer regarding the destination of the path’s tracks.
Today, the Peerless Honored One—whom I have long sought—is here;
having observed his own conduct, his mind is already rightly concentrated.
Only the Sage has already known the course of my mind;
regarding the practices cultivated throughout the long night, I pray that the One with Pure Eyes will record them.
I take refuge in the Supreme among Men, the Infinite Honored One of the Three Realms.
"Able to sever the thorns of affection and love, I now pay homage to the Honored One, the Sun-Light.
The Buddha said to Śakra:
"Do you remember when you first attained joy and mindfulness of bliss?"
Śakra replied: “It is so, World-Honored One!
I recall the joy and happiness I experienced in the past, and I remember that happiness.”

"Bhagavān! In the past, I once engaged in battle with the asuras. When I was victorious and the asuras retreated, I returned home feeling joy and mindfulness of happiness. Compared to this joy and mindfulness of happiness, the joy and happiness derived from being free of defilement, evil, weapons, and staves, and the joy and happiness of being free from strife and contention, [the former] is far superior."
"Now, regarding the joy and mindful delight I have found in the Buddha, there is no joy therein involving weapons, staves, strife, or litigation.
The Buddha said to Śakra:
"Now that you have attained this joy and mindful delight, what fruit of merit do you seek within it?"
At that time, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Within the joy of delight and the joy of mindfulness, I wish to seek the fruit of five merits. What are these five?”
He then spoke in verse: "If,
after my life here ends, I relinquish this celestial longevity,
may I dwell in the womb without suffering, so that my heart may be filled with joy."
The Buddha delivers those not yet delivered, being able to proclaim the true and correct path;
within the Dharma of the Three Buddhas, I shall practice the holy life.
Abiding in the body of wisdom, my mind directly perceives the true reality.
Having attained the realization of the origin from which all arises, one is thereby forever liberated.
One should simply practice with diligence and cultivate the Buddha’s true wisdom;
even if one does not attain the realization of the Path, such merit remains superior to that of the heavens.
All those wondrous and sublime devas, such as those of Akaniṣṭha and the rest;
down to my final body, I shall surely be born in those places.
Now, in this very place, I receive a pure celestial body.
"Furthermore, I shall obtain an increase in lifespan; this pure eye I know for myself.
Having spoken this verse, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Within joy and mindfulness of joy, I desire to attain these five fruits of merit."
At that time, Śakra addressed the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, saying:
"It was well that you previously paid respectful homage before the Brahma-Boy in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; that you now again offer this reverence before the Buddha is likewise most excellent!"
Before these words had even faded, the Brahma youth suddenly appeared in the midst of the celestial host in the sky and addressed Śakra, Lord of Devas, in verse:
“The King of Devas practices pure conduct And brings great benefit to sentient beings;
Śakra, Lord of Magadha, Is able to inquire about the meaning of the Tathāgata.”
When the Brahma youth had spoken these verses, he suddenly vanished.

At that time, Śakra rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and withdrew by retreating backward. The various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and Pañcaśikha likewise prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew by retreating backward.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, proceeded a short distance further and looked back to address Pañcaśikha, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"

"You shall first entertain us by playing the lute before the Buddha; only then will I and the other devas arrive behind you. I now recognize that you shall succeed to your father's position and become the foremost among the Gandharvas; therefore, I shall give you the daughter of King Bhadra-gandharva to be your wife."
When the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, eighty-four thousand devas became free from dust and defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, and Pañcaśikha, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Mithilā, in the region of Ānandī, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Āṇāiya to beg for food.
Then, the World-Honored One thought silently to himself:
"It is still early for me to beg for food now; it would be appropriate to go and visit the park of the brahmin Bhārgava."
The bhikṣu waited until the proper time had arrived before going for alms.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to that grove. When the brahmin saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he rose to welcome him, and after exchanging greetings, said: "Welcome, Gautama!"
"It has been a long time since we last met face to face; for what reason have you now deigned to visit us?
We only pray that Gautama will take a seat here!
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately took his seat.
Then, that brahmin, having sat down to one side, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Last night, the Licchavi bhikṣu Sunakṣatra came to my place and said to me:
'O Great Master!'"
"I do not practice the holy life under the Buddha.
Why is this? Because the Buddha has cast me out."
"Even though that man spoke thus, recounting the faults of Gautama, I shall not accept his words.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I know that you will not accept what Sunakṣatra has said."
Once, while I was staying at the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, assembled in the Dharma Hall, this Sunakṣatra came to where I was and said to me:
"The Tathāgata has excluded me; I shall no longer practice the holy life under the Tathāgata."
I then said to him: "For what reason do you say:
'I have not practiced the holy life under the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is outside of me'?"
Sukhāvatī replied to me, saying,
"The Tathāgata did not manifest his supernatural powers and transformations for me.
At that time, I said to him:
"Shall I invite you to practice the pure life (brahmacarya) within my Dharma, and shall I manifest supernormal powers (ṛddhi) for you?
Or shall you say to me:
'The Tathāgata should first manifest supernormal transformations for me, and only then shall I practice the pure life'?"
At that time, Sunakṣatra replied to me, saying: "No,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha told Sunakṣatra: "I did not say to you:
'If you practice the pure brahma-faring within my Dharma, I shall manifest for you a transformation through supernormal powers.'"
"You have also not said that one should practice the holy life because the Tathāgata manifests supernormal powers for you.
What do you think, Sunakṣatra?
Do you believe that the Tathāgata is able to manifest supernormal powers, or is he unable?"
"Is the Dharma that I teach capable of leading to the definitive exit [from suffering] and the exhaustion of the limits of dukkha?
Sunakṣatra replied to the Buddha,
"It is so, World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgata is able to manifest supernormal powers; it is not that he is unable. The Dharma he teaches enables one to attain the essential way out and exhaust the limits of all suffering; it is not that he does not exhaust them.

"Therefore, Sunakṣatra! Regarding the Dharma I have taught for the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya), those who can manifest supernormal powers (ṛddhi) are not incapable of doing so; those who seek the essential departure [from suffering] and leave behind suffering are not incapable of leaving it behind. What do you seek within this Dharma?"
Sunakṣatra said: “World-Honored One!
You do not teach me according to the proper time. Your father possessed secret arts that you, World-Honored One, know completely; yet you are stingy and do not teach them to me.”
The Buddha said:
"Sunakṣatra! Have I ever said this?"
"You who practice the holy life within my Dharma, do you teach your father's craft?
Would you perhaps say:
'One who teaches me my father's craft should be the one under whom I practice the holy life'?"
He replied, "No. [The Buddha said: "Therefore, Sunakṣatra!"
"I did not say such a thing previously, nor have you said it; why do you speak these words now?
What do you think, Sunakṣatra!
Do you believe that the Tathāgata is able to explain the secret arts of your father, or is he unable to do so?"
"Is it possible that the Dharma he can preach will enable one to attain the essential way out and reach the end of suffering?
Sunakṣatra replied, "The Tathāgata is indeed able to preach his father’s secret arts; it is not that he is incapable."
"I am able to preach the Dharma that leads to the essential way out and can bring an end to the limits of suffering;
it is not that I am incapable. The Buddha told Sunakṣatra:
"If I can preach your father’s secret arts, and I can also preach the Dharma that leads to the essential way out and liberation from suffering, what more do you seek within my teaching?"
He further addressed Sunakṣatra:
"Previously, in the land of Vaiśālī and Vāsavagrāma, you used countless skillful means to praise the Tathāgata, praise the True Dharma, and praise the Saṃgha."
It is, for example, as if someone were to praise that cool pond with eight qualities to make people desire it:
first, it is cold; second, light; third, soft; fourth, clear; fifth, sweet; sixth, stainless; seventh, one never tires of drinking it; and eighth, it is beneficial to the body.
You, too, are like this: in the land of Vaiśālī, among the Vṛjis, you praise the Tathāgata, praise the True Dharma, and praise the Saṅgha, causing people to have faith and joy.
"Sunakṣatra!
You should know that because you have now fallen away, people in the world will again say:

'The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra had many acquaintances, was personally favored by the World-Honored One, and was a disciple of the World-Honored One; yet he was unable to practice the pure brahmacarya throughout his life, but instead abandoned the precepts to return to secular life and engage in lowly conduct.'"
"O Brahmin! You should know that at that time, although I spoke fully to him, he did not follow my instruction; he abandoned the precepts and returned to secular life. O Brahmin!"

At one time, I was staying at the Dharma Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha named Kārūṣa who resided there; he was honored and respected by people, his fame was heard afar, he had many acquaintances, and he was fully provided with offerings and gains.
At that time, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Vaiśālī to beg for food. Gradually, he made his way to where the Nirgranthas were.
Thereupon, Sunakṣatra questioned the Nirgranthas regarding profound and far-reaching meanings; they were unable to answer him and consequently gave rise to anger.
Sunakṣatra thought to himself:
"I have provoked this man; will I not suffer the retribution of pain and affliction for a long night? O Brahmin!

You should know that at that time, after his almsround, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra took up his robes and bowl, came to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, and sat to one side; yet at that time, Sunakṣatra did not inform me of this matter, so I said to him:
"Foolish man!..."
"Can you truly call yourself a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya?
Sunakṣatra immediately replied to me, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Why do you call me foolish?
Should I not call myself a son of the Śākyas? I said to him:
"O fool! You once went to the place of the Nirgranthas and asked them about profound and far-reaching meanings; they were unable to answer, and you immediately gave rise to anger.
At that time, you thought to yourself:"
"I have now touched this Nirgrantha; will I not suffer the retribution of affliction for a long night?
Do you not have such a thought?
Sunakṣatra replied to the Buddha:
"He is an Arhat; for what reason could he harbor such a mind of jealousy and anger?
At that time, I replied: "Fool!..."
"On what basis do Arhats harbor jealousy and anger?

It is not that I, as an Arhat, possess jealousy and anger; rather, you yourself now claim that he is an Arhat, yet he possesses seven ascetic practices which he has maintained throughout the long night."
What are the seven?
First, for as long as life lasts, one does not wear clothes.
Second, for as long as life lasts, one does not drink alcohol or eat meat, nor does one eat rice or flour-based foods.
Third, for as long as life lasts, he shall not violate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Fourth, for as long as life lasts, he shall not leave the four stone stūpas of Vaiśālī—the one in the east named Udyāna-stūpa, the one in the south named Hasty-śaila-stūpa, the one in the west named Bahuputra-stūpa, and the one in the north named Saptaparṇa-stūpa—but shall perform four ascetic practices before them.
Afterward, having violated these seven ascetic practices, he will pass away outside the city of Vaiśālī.
Just as a jackal, suffering from scabies and wasting diseases, dies among the burial mounds, so too is that Nirgrantha;
he established his own restrictive laws, yet later violated them all.
He had originally vowed:
"I shall not wear clothes for as long as my life lasts," yet later he returned to wearing clothes.
He had originally vowed:
For as long as life lasts, he vowed not to drink alcohol or eat meat, nor to eat cooked rice or flour-based foods, eating only after [the meal was finished]; yet,
while originally swearing an oath not to violate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), he later violated it as well.
The original statement says:
"Do not overstep the four stupas—the Eastern Grove Stupa, the Southern Elephant Stupa, the Western Bahuputra Stupa, and the Northern Saptaparna Stupa";
now, one should completely distance oneself from them and no longer draw near.
Having himself violated these seven vows, that man departed from the city of Vaiśālī and passed away among the tombs.
The Buddha said to Sunakṣatra:
‘Foolish man!’
"If you do not believe my words, go and see for yourself; then you shall know it.
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"At one time, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, having dressed and taken his bowl, entered the city to beg for food. Having finished begging, he was returning out of the city when he saw a Nirgrantha who had died among the empty tombs."
Having seen me, he came to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, and sat to one side; yet he did not speak to me regarding this matter, O Brahmin!
"You should know that at that time I said to Sunakṣatra:
'What do you think, Sunakṣatra!
Was what I previously predicted regarding the Nirgranthas exactly as I have spoken?'"
He replied: "So it is, just as the World-Honored One has said. O Brahmin!
"You should know that when I manifested supernatural powers for Śubhavyūha as a testimony, he said:
'The World-Honored One did not manifest them for me.

Furthermore, on another occasion, I was in the city of Pāṭaliputra in the kingdom of Mithilā. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha named Kūṭadanta who resided in Pāṭaliputra; he was honored and respected by people, his fame was heard afar, and he received much gain and support."

At that time, having put on my robes and taken up my alms bowl, I entered the city to beg for food. The bhikṣu Sunakṣatra followed behind me and saw the Nirgrantha Kūladatta lying prostrate upon a heap of dung, licking dregs and husks.
"Brahmin! You should know that when the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra saw this Nirgrantha prostrate himself upon a heap of dung and lick the dregs and husks, he thought to himself:
'Among all those in the world who are Arhats or those progressing toward the path of Arhatship, none can equal this man. This Nirgrantha’s way is the most supreme. Why is this so?'"
"Such is the asceticism of this man that he has been able to cast aside arrogance and lie prostrate upon a heap of refuse to lick the dregs of grain. "Brahmin!
At that time, I turned to the right and said to Sunakṣatra:"
“You are a fool! Do you truly consider yourself a son of the Śākyas?
Sunakṣatra replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Why do you call me ignorant? Should I not call myself a son of the Śākyas?”
The Buddha said to Sunakṣatra:
"You fool! Observe this Kūlāyika squatting upon a heap of dung, prostrate and eating chaff and dregs. Having seen him, you thought to yourself:"
Among all those in the world who are arhats or those progressing toward arhatship, this Kūṭadanta is the most eminent. Why is that?
Because this Kūṭadanta is now capable of practicing austerities; he has abandoned pride and arrogance, squatting upon a heap of dung and prostrating himself to lick the dregs of grain.
"Do you have such a thought?
He replied to me, "Indeed, I do."
Sujāta spoke again: "For what reason,
World-Honored One?"
"I have conceived a mind of envy toward an Arhat.
The Buddha said to the foolish man, "I do not conceive a mind of envy toward an Arhat; why would one conceive a mind of envy toward an Arhat?"

"You fool! You claim that Kūṭadanta is a true Arhat; yet this man shall, seven days from now, die of abdominal distension and be reborn among the hungry ghosts of the *vetāla* class, constantly suffering from hunger. After his life ends, he will be dragged by a reed rope to the cemetery."
"If you do not believe me, you may go there first and speak to him.
Then, Sunakṣatra went to where Kūṭadanta was and said:
"That śramaṇa Gautama has prophesied concerning you:"
"Seven days from now, your belly shall swell and you will die, reborn among the hungry ghosts known as 'corpse-raisers. After death, you will be bound with reed ropes and dragged to the cemetery.
Sunakṣatra replied again, "You must moderate your food intake, lest his words prove true."

"O Brahmin! You should know that after seven full days had passed, Kauśika died of abdominal distension; he was immediately reborn among the hungry ghosts as a *vetāla*, and his corpse was dragged to the cemetery, bound with reed ropes."

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Sunakṣatra counted the days on his fingers; when the seven days had passed, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra went to the village of the naked ascetics, and upon arrival, he asked the villagers:
"O worthy ones!..."
"Where is Kaurati now? He replied,
"She has already passed away."
He asked, "What is the harm in dying? He replied:
"He has abdominal distension. He asked,
"How shall he be coffined and sent off?"
He replied: "They were tied with reed ropes and dragged to the cemetery.
"Brahmin! [the Buddha said.]

At that time, having heard these words, Sunakṣatra immediately went to the cemetery. As he was about to reach, but had not yet reached, it, the corpse moved its knees and feet and suddenly crouched up. Then Sunakṣatra proceeded forward to where the corpse was and said: "Kauravya!"
"Have you passed away? The corpse replied,
"I have indeed passed away."
He asked, "By what ailment did you pass away?
The corpse replied:
"Gautama predicted that seven days from now I would die of abdominal distension; as he had said, when the seven days were complete, I died of abdominal distension.
Sunakṣatra asked again, "Where have you been reborn?"
The corpse then replied:
"That which Gautama predicted—that I would be reborn among the hungry ghosts as a *vetāla*—has come true; today I have been reborn among the hungry ghosts as a *vetāla*."
Sunasoma asked, "When you pass away, how will you be buried?
The corpse replied:
"What Gautama predicted—that it would be tied with a reed-cord and dragged to the cemetery—is indeed true; it has been tied with a reed-cord and dragged to the cemetery.
Then, the corpse said to Sunakṣatra, "Though you have left the household life, you have not attained any wholesome benefit."
“‘The śramaṇa Gautama has spoken such matters, yet you have always disbelieved them.
Having said these words, the corpse lay down again. ‘O Brahmin!’”
At that time, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra came to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, and sat to one side; yet he did not speak to me regarding this matter.
I immediately said to him: "Is it truly as I have predicted concerning Kūṭadanta?"
He replied: "It is indeed so, just as the World-Honored One has said. O Brahmin!
Although I have thus repeatedly manifested supernatural powers as a demonstration for the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, he still says:
"The World-Honored One has not manifested supernatural powers for me."
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"Once, when I was at the Dharma Lecture Hall by the Monkey Pond, there was a brahmin named Pāṭikāputra residing there. He was honored and respected by people, his fame was heard afar, and he received much material support. In the midst of the great assembly at Vaiśālī, he spoke thus:
'The śramaṇa Gautama claims to possess wisdom; I too possess wisdom.'"
The śramaṇa Gautama claims to possess supernormal powers, yet I too possess supernormal powers;
the śramaṇa Gautama has attained the path of transcendence, yet I too have attained the path of transcendence.
"I shall manifest supernatural powers alongside him: when the śramaṇa manifests one, I shall manifest two;
when the śramaṇa manifests two, I shall manifest four;
when the śramaṇa manifests eight, I shall manifest sixteen."
"If the śramaṇa manifests sixteen, I shall manifest thirty-two;
if the śramaṇa manifests thirty-two, I shall manifest sixty-four.
Whatever the number manifested by that śramaṇa may be, I shall always double it."
“Brahmin! At that time, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, having dressed and taken his bowl, entered the city to beg for food. He saw the brahmin Pāṭali speaking thus among the great assembly:
‘The śramaṇa Gautama claims to possess wisdom; I too possess wisdom.’”
The śramaṇa Gautama claims to possess supernormal powers, yet I too possess supernormal powers;
the śramaṇa Gautama has attained the path of transcendence, yet I too have attained the path of transcendence.
"I shall manifest supernatural powers together with him: when the śramaṇa manifests one, I shall manifest two;
when the śramaṇa manifests four, I shall manifest eight;
indeed, I am able to double whatever number the śramaṇa manifests."
At that time, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, having finished his almsround, came to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, sat to one side, and said to me:
"This morning, having dressed and taken up my bowl, I entered the city to beg for food. At that time, I heard the son of Vṛjī from Vaiśālī making this statement in the midst of a great assembly:
'The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great wisdom; I too possess great wisdom.'"
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses supernormal powers, and I too possess supernormal powers;
if Gautama manifests one, I shall manifest two;
indeed, for as many as Gautama manifests, I am able to double them all."
"He reported this matter to me in full detail, and I said to Sunakṣatra:
'It is absolutely impossible that Pāṭikāputra would come to me without having renounced these words, these views, and this pride within the great assembly.'"
If he were to think:
"I will not abandon this speech, I will not abandon this view, and I will not abandon this pride, yet go to where the śramaṇa Gautama is," his head would immediately split into seven pieces.
"If one wishes to cause that person not to abandon these words, not to abandon their views and conceit, yet still come here—that is impossible.
Sunakṣatra said, "The World-Honored One guards his speech; the Tathāgata guards his speech."
The Buddha said to Sunakṣatra:
"For what reason do you say:
'The World-Honored One guards his speech; the Tathāgata guards his speech'?"
Sujāta said: "That Pāṭikaputra possesses great majestic power and great spiritual strength; could it be that he will come here, thereby making the World-Honored One’s words false?"
The Buddha asked Sunakṣatra,
"Is there any duality in what the Tathāgata has spoken? He replied:
"No. He further addressed Sunakṣatra:
"If there were no duality, why did you say:..."
“Does the World-Honored One guard his speech? Does the Tathāgata guard his speech?
Sunakṣatra replied to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, do you know and see that Pāṭikāputra yourself, or did the devas come and tell you?”
The Buddha said:

"I know this myself, and I also know it because the devas came to tell me: 'This great general Āyu of Vaiśālī, upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, has been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.'"
He came and said to me:

"The brahmin youth Pāṭali, lacking shame and modesty, has violated the precepts and spoken falsely. While in Vaiśālī, amidst the great assembly, he uttered such slanderous words: 'The general Āyudha, upon the dissolution of his body at the end of his life, was reborn among the vetāla ghosts; however, I, in truth, upon the dissolution of my body at the end of my life, was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.'"
"Regarding Pāṭikāputra, I already knew this myself, and I also know it because the devas came and told me.

The Buddha said to the foolish Sona Koḷivisa, "If you do not believe my words, go into Vaiśālī and proclaim as you wish; after I have finished my meal, I shall go to the place where the brahmin youth Pāṭikāputra is."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Then, after that night had passed, Sunakṣatra put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms.
At that time, Sunakṣatra spoke these words in full to the many brahmins, śramaṇas, and brahmacārins within the city of Vaiśālī:"
The brahmin youth Pāṭika addressed the great assembly, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom;
the śramaṇa Gautama possesses great power, and I too possess great power."
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal powers, and I too possess great supernormal powers.
If the śramaṇa manifests one, I shall manifest two;
and so on, for however many he manifests, I shall always double it."

"Now the śramaṇa Gautama wishes to go to where Pāṭikāputra is; all of you should go there as well. At that time, the brahmin Pāṭika was walking along the road; seeing him, Sunakṣatra quickly approached him and said:

"In the great assembly at Vaiśālī, you spoke these words: 'The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom,' and so forth, up to: 'Whatever amount of supernormal power the śramaṇa Gautama displays, I shall double it.'"
"Gautama has heard these words and now wishes to come to your place;
you should return quickly. He replied, "I shall indeed return!"
"I shall surely return!

Having spoken these words, he was immediately seized with terror; his hair stood on end, and instead of returning to his own place, he went to the forest of the Paribbājaka Brahmin Pāṭikāputta at the head of the road, where he sat upon a rope-couch, distressed and bewildered.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"After my meal, I went with a large company of Licchavis, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, brahmins, and householders to the dwelling place of Pāṭikāputra, where we took our seats."
In that assembly, there was a brahmin named Cāla. At that time, the people called out to Cāla and said to him:
"Go to the forest at the head of the road and say to Pāṭikaputta:
'Now many Licchavis, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, brahmins, and householders have all gathered in your forest, and they are deliberating together, saying:'"
The brahmin Pāṭali proclaimed these words among the great assembly:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom; even to whatever extent Gautama manifests supernormal powers, I am able to double them all."
“The ascetic Gautama has come specifically to your grove; you should go and see him.
Thereupon, having heard the words of the multitude, Cāla went to the road-side grove and said to Pāṭikaputta:
“That great multitude of Licchavis—ascetics, brahmins, mendicants, and householders—all have gathered in your grove, and they are discussing it together, saying:”
“The brahmin Pāṭikāputra has declared this himself in the midst of the great assembly:

‘The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom; even regarding the supernormal powers manifested by the śramaṇa Gautama, for however many he displays, I am able to double them all.’”
"Gautama is currently in that grove; Pāli, why should you not return now?
At that time, the brahmin Pāli replied to Cāra: "I shall return!"
"O, may I return!
Having spoken these words, he turned and tossed about restlessly upon the rope bed.
At that time, the rope bed again caught his feet, so that he was unable to leave the bed; how much less could he walk to where the World-Honored One was?
Then Cāra said to Pāli: "You yourself lack wisdom; you merely utter empty sounds when you say, 'I shall return!'"
“I am paralyzed!
I cannot even leave this rope bed; how could I possibly reach the place where the great assembly is?
Having thus rebuked Pāṭiputra, he immediately returned to the place of the great assembly and reported:
"By means of my mastery over the voices of all beings, I went to speak with Pāṭikāputra, and he replied to me, saying:
'You must return! You must return!'"
He immediately shifted his body upon the rope bed, but the bed stuck to his feet so that he could not move; since he could not even leave his rope bed, how could he have come to this assembly?
At that time, there was a Mālava youth sitting among the assembly who rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the multitude, saying:
"Wait a moment, great assembly; I shall now go myself and bring that man here."
The Buddha said: "At that time, I spoke to the young Licchavi Sumana, saying:
'That person speaks such words, harbors such views, and gives rise to such pride; it is impossible for him to come to the place where the Buddha is.'"

"Tamali! Even if you were bound with heavy leather thongs and a herd of oxen pulled you together until your body was shattered, you would still never be able to abandon such words, such views, and such pride to come to me."
"If you do not believe my words, go there yourself and see.
At that time, the Licchavi youth Dhammika went to Pāṭikāputra and said to him:
"A great multitude of Licchavis, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, ascetics, and householders have all gathered in your grove, and they are all deliberating together, saying:"
“The brahmin Pāṭikāputra proclaimed with his own mouth in the midst of the great assembly:
‘The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom... even when the śramaṇa Gautama displays his supernormal powers, whatever he displays, I am able to double it.’”
“The śramaṇa Gautama is now in that forest; you may return.
At that time, Pāṭikāputra replied: “I shall return!”
"Help me! Help me!

Having spoken these words, he shifted his body upon the rope bed; at that moment, the rope bed became stuck to his feet, so that he was unable to free himself from it, let alone walk to where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, Dharmika said to Pāṭikāputra:
"You yourself lack wisdom; you merely utter empty sounds, saying:
'I shall take refuge!'"
“I am paralyzed!
I cannot even leave this rope-bed; by what means could I possibly reach the place where the great assembly is?
Then Dhūma spoke again to Pāṭali:

"Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables. Long ago, in the distant past, there was a lion, king of beasts, dwelling in a deep forest. When the lion first emerged from his cave at dawn, he surveyed the four directions, shook himself vigorously, let out three roars, and then wandered about to select and eat meat."

"Pālitaputra! After that lion, the king of beasts, has eaten and returned to the forest, a jackal always follows behind him to eat the remains. Once his strength was fully restored, he said to himself:
'What kind of beast is this lion in the forest after all?'"
"Can he truly defeat me?

It would be better for me now to take sole possession of this forest; emerging from my cave at the clear dawn, looking in all four directions, letting out three thunderous roars with vigor, and only then wandering about to choose my meat for food!"
He soon went alone into a forest; at dawn he emerged from his cave, shook himself, and let out three roars, yet instead of roaming about to give a lion’s roar, he made the cry of a jackal.
Pāṭikāputra! You are just like that now:
having received the Buddha’s majestic grace, you remain alive in this world and receive the offerings of people, yet now you further seek to compete with the Tathāgata.
Then, the son of Dharmaruci rebuked him with these verses:
"A jackal claims to be a lion, Deeming himself the king of beasts;
Wishing to let out a lion’s roar, He still produces only the cry of a jackal."
Dwelling alone in the empty forest, he calls himself the king of beasts;
wishing to let out a lion’s roar, he instead utters the cry of a jackal.
He kneels on the ground seeking a burrowing rat; he digs through graves searching for a corpse.
"Desiring to let out a lion’s roar, you instead produce the sound of a jackal.
Māṇava replied, "You are just like this:
having received the power of the Buddha's grace to remain alive in this world and receive the offerings of men, you now seek to compete with the Tathāgata."
Then, having rebuked him face-to-face with four similes, the son of Dharmaruci returned to the great assembly and reported:
"I called out to Pāṭikāputra using the voices of all the people; he replied to me, saying:
'You should return!'"
"I must return!
he cried, and as he shifted his body upon the rope-cot, the cot immediately stuck to his feet so that he could not move away;
since he could not even leave the rope-cot himself, how could he have come here to this assembly?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Dhammika, saying:
"I told you before that it is impossible for this man to come to where the Buddha is."

"Even if you were to bind them with heavy leather thongs and a herd of oxen were to pull them together until their bodies were shattered to pieces, they would ultimately refuse to abandon such speech, such views, and such pride, nor would they come to me."

"O Brahmin! At that time, I immediately preached various teachings to that great assembly, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them. In the midst of that assembly, I uttered the three lion-roars, ascended into the air, and returned to my original place."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
'The entire world was created by Brahmā, the Lord of Heaven.'"
I asked him: "Is it true that all the world was created by Brahmā, the Lord?
He was unable to answer and instead questioned me in return:
"Gautama! What do you say to this? I replied to him:

"Or, when this world was first undergoing dissolution, there were certain beings whose life-span and karma were exhausted; they passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn in another empty Brahmā realm.

There, they conceived a craving and developed a mind of attachment and delight, desiring that other beings should also come to be born in that place. Then, when those other beings' life-span and karma were exhausted, they were likewise reborn there."
At that time, those beings formed this thought:
"I am now the Great Brahma King; I have appeared suddenly, and there is no creator of me.
I am able to fully comprehend the ultimate meaning of all things, and I possess supreme sovereignty over a thousand worlds."
He is capable of creation and transformation, supreme and subtle, acting as the father and mother of humanity.
I arrived here first, alone and without companion; by my power these sentient beings came to be, and I am the creator of these sentient beings.

Those other sentient beings likewise follow me; he is called the Brahmā King, appearing suddenly, fully comprehending all meanings, possessing the greatest sovereignty over a thousand worlds, capable of creation and transformation, supreme and subtle, the father and mother of humanity. He existed first, and only later did we come to be; this Great Brahmā King has manifested us through his creative power.

These sentient beings, having reached the end of their respective lifespans, come to be born in this realm; as they gradually grow up, they shave off their hair and beards, don the three dharma robes, and leave the household life to pursue the Way.
Entering into the concentration of meditative absorption, he follows that concentrated mind to recollect his original birth, and speaks these words:

"This Great Brahmā Heaven appeared suddenly; there is no creator. He has fully mastered all meanings and possesses supreme sovereignty over a thousand worlds. He is able to create and transform; he is subtle and sublime beyond compare, the father and mother of all beings."

"That Great Brahmā Heaven is eternally abiding and immutable, possessing no quality of change; we, however, are emanations of that Brahmā Heaven, and for this reason we are impermanent, unable to abide long, and subject to the law of change."
"In this way, brahmin! For these reasons, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas each claim that Brahmā, the Sovereign God, created this world."
"O Brahmin! The creator of this world is beyond the reach of others; only a Buddha can know it.

Furthermore, there are matters even beyond this that a Buddha knows completely. Though he knows them, he does not cling to suffering, its origin, its cessation, gratification, peril, or the escape from it. He knows them as they truly are, and through the contemplation of equality, attains liberation without remainder; thus he is called a Tathāgata."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus:
'Amusement, laughter, and indolence are the beginning of sentient beings.'"
I said to them: "How can you truly say that joking, laughter, and indolence are the beginning of sentient beings?
They were unable to answer and instead questioned me in return:
"Gautama! What do you say to this?
At that time, I replied:

“Or there may be beings of the Ābhāsvara Heaven who, through indulgence in joy, play, and laughter, become lax; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn here in this world. As they gradually grow up, they shave off their hair and beards, don the three Dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and enter the samādhi of mental concentration. By the power of that samādhi, they recognize their original place of birth and say:
‘Those other beings do not indulge in joy, play, or laughter, but remain constantly in that place, dwelling forever without change.
Because we frequently indulged in joy, play, and laughter, we have come to this impermanence and become subject to the law of transformation.’”

"Thus it is, brahmin! Because of these reasons, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas claim that play and laughter are the beginning of sentient beings. The Buddha knows this completely; he knows what transcends this as well. Knowing yet remaining unattached—being unattached to suffering, its origin, its cessation, its gratification, its peril, and the escape from it—he knows them as they truly are. Having observed with equanimity, he is liberated without remainder; he is called the Tathāgata."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
'Loss of mindfulness is the beginning of sentient beings.'"
I said to them: "Do you truly say that the loss of mindfulness is the beginning of sentient beings?"
Not knowing how to answer, he instead asked me:
"Gautama! What do you say to this?"

I said to them: "There may be sentient beings who, after looking at one another in succession, lose their mindfulness; because of this, they die and are reborn in this realm. As they gradually grow up, they shave off their hair and beards, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and enter the samādhi of mental concentration. By the power of that samādhi, they recognize their original place of birth and speak thus:
'Just as those sentient beings did not look at one another in succession and thus did not lose their mindfulness, they remain eternally present and unchanging.'"
"Having looked at one another there again and again, we lost our mindfulness, resulting in this impermanence; it is a phenomenon subject to change.
Thus it is, O Brahmin!

For these reasons, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak erroneously, claiming that the mind is the beginning of sentient beings; this is known only by the Buddha, and he knows what transcends this as well. Having known it, he is not attached to suffering, its origin, its cessation, its gratification, its peril, or the escape from it, knowing them as they truly are. Having known them, he contemplates with equanimity the liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
'I have arisen without cause.'"
I said to them: "Do you truly say that they originally emerged without a cause?"
He was unable to answer and instead came to question me; I then replied:

"There are sentient beings who are without thought and without cognition. If those beings give rise to thought, they immediately pass away and are reborn here in this world. Gradually growing up, they shave off their hair and beards, don the three dharma-robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and enter the samādhi of mental concentration. By the power of that samādhi, they recognize their original place of birth and speak thus:
'I originally did not exist, but now I have suddenly come to be.'"
"This world was originally non-existent, but now it exists; this alone is real, and all else is false.

Thus, brahmin, because of such reasons, some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas claim that things arise without cause. Only the Buddha knows this, and he knows what transcends it as well. Having known it, he does not cling to suffering, its origin, its cessation, its gratification, its danger, or the escape from it; he knows these as they truly are. Having contemplated them with equanimity, he is liberated without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"What I have taught is thus: there may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, in private, slander me, saying:
'The śramaṇa Gautama claims that his disciples enter into pure liberation and accomplish pure conduct; they know purity, yet they do not fully comprehend purity.'"
"However, I do not say this:
'My disciple enters pure liberation, accomplishes pure conduct, and while he knows purity, he does not fully comprehend purity.'"
"O Brahmin! I myself declare:
'My disciples enter into pure liberation, accomplish pure conduct, and they know purity as universal purity.'"
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"He has failed to gain any wholesome benefit, for he slanders the śramaṇa Gautama, saying:
'The śramaṇa claims for himself:'"
‘My disciples enter the liberation of purity and accomplish pure conduct; they know purity, yet they do not fully comprehend purity.
However, the Blessed One does not speak thus; the Blessed One himself says:
‘My disciples enter the liberation of purity and accomplish pure conduct; they know purity and fully comprehend all that is pure.’”
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I, too, shall enter this pure liberation, accomplish pure conduct, and attain all-encompassing knowledge.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"If you wish to enter, it will be exceedingly difficult.
Since you hold different views, different tolerances, and different practices, it will be hard for you to attain pure liberation by relying on other views;
however, if you cherish the Buddha with an unceasing heart, you shall always find peace and happiness throughout the long night."
At that time, the brahmin Bhārgava, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
16. The Sūtra on Sujāta (16) The Twelfth Sūtra on Sujāta, from the Second Division of the Long Discourses Spoken by the Buddha. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, when the hour had come, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

At that moment, there was a son of an elder in the city of Rājagṛha named Sujāta. Early in the morning, he left the city to go and stroll through a garden; having just finished bathing, his entire body was still wet as he paid homage toward the various directions—the east, west, south, north, above, and below—traversing them all completely.

At that time, the World-Honored One saw the elder’s son Sujāta approaching the garden for recreation; having just finished his bath, his entire body was wet as he paid homage toward the various directions.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One went to where he was and said to Sujāta:
"For what reason have you come out of the city at dawn, with your entire body drenched, prostrating toward the various directions within the grove?"
At that time, Sujāta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When my father was approaching the end of his life, he left me this final instruction:
'If you wish to pay homage, you should first pay homage to the east, the south, the west, the north, the zenith, and the nadir.'"

I have respectfully followed my father’s instructions and dared not disobey them; therefore, having finished bathing, I first joined my palms and faced east to pay homage to the eastern direction, and likewise to the south, west, north, and all directions above and below, encompassing every quarter.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Sujāta:
"Son of a householder!
This direction exists; it is not that it does not exist."
"However, in my noble and holy Dharma, one does not pay homage by means of these six directions.
Sujāta addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will skillfully explain to me the method for paying homage to the six directions within the noble and holy Dharma!"
The Buddha said to the son of a householder:
"Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!"
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake.
Sujāta replied, "Indeed, I wish most earnestly to hear it!"
The Buddha told Sujāta:

"If a householder or a householder’s son understands the four karmas of fetters and does not commit evil deeds in the four places, and furthermore can understand the six karmas that deplete wealth—this, Sujāta, is what is meant by [a wise person]."
Householder, householder’s son, by abstaining from the four types of misconduct and paying reverence to the six directions, you will be virtuous in this life and obtain a good reward in the future;

you will have a foundation in this life and a foundation in the next life. You will be praised by the wise in the present existence, attain the fruits of this world, and after the body breaks up at the end of life, you will be reborn in a heavenly realm, a place of excellence.
"Sunetra! You should know that there are four types of conduct involving fetters:
first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; and fourth, false speech—these are the four types of conduct involving fetters."
What are the four bases?
First, desire; second, malice; third, fear; and fourth, delusion.
If a householder or a householder’s son commits evil regarding these four bases, they will suffer loss and decline.
After the Buddha had spoken these words, he further uttered this verse:
“Desire, hatred, fear, and delusion— Whoever possesses these four qualities Will see their reputation diminish daily,
Like the moon waning toward the dark fortnight.”
The Buddha told Sujāta:
"If a householder or a householder’s son does no evil in these four places, there will be increase.
At that time, the World-Honored One further spoke in verse:
"One who does not commit evil deeds out of desire, anger, fear, or delusion,
sees their reputation increase daily, like the moon waxing toward its fullness.
Thus the Buddha spoke to Sujāta.
"There are six activities that deplete wealth:

first, indulgence in alcohol; second, gambling; third, profligacy; fourth, infatuation with music and performance; fifth, associating with evil friends; and sixth, indolence. These are the six activities that deplete wealth."
"Śāṇakavāsin!

If a householder or a householder’s son understands the practice regarding the four fetters and does not commit unwholesome deeds in the four places, and furthermore understands the six ways in which wealth is depleted—this, Śāṇakavāsin, is [the teaching]."

One attains freedom from the four states, makes offerings to the six directions, is virtuous in both present and future, establishes a foundation for this life and the next, is praised by the wise in the present existence, attains the first fruit of the world, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, is reborn in a heavenly, auspicious realm.
"Good Birth! You should know that there are six losses resulting from drinking alcohol:

first, the loss of wealth; second, the onset of illness; third, quarreling and strife; fourth, the spread of an evil reputation; fifth, the sudden arising of violent anger; and sixth, the daily diminution of wisdom."
"Śreṇika! If that householder or his son drinks alcohol without ceasing, the family's wealth and estate will diminish day by day. Śreṇika!"
There are six failings associated with gambling. What are these six?

First, one's wealth and property diminish daily; second, even when victorious, one engenders resentment; third, one is censured by the wise; fourth, people do not respect or trust one; fifth, one is alienated and excluded by others; sixth, one gives rise to a mind of theft and pilfering.
"Good sir! These are the six losses of gambling.
If a householder or a householder’s son gambles incessantly, his family estate will diminish day by day. There are also six losses of dissipation: "

First, one does not protect one's own body; second, one does not protect one's wealth; third, one does not protect one's children and grandchildren; fourth, one is constantly filled with alarm and fear; fifth, various suffering and unwholesome dharmas constantly entangle one's person; sixth, one delights in giving rise to falsehoods—these are the six losses of dissipation.
If a householder or a householder’s son is unrestrained and dissolute without ceasing, the family's wealth and property will diminish day by day.
"Sujāta! There are six further losses resulting from being deluded by music and pleasure: [text continues]"
First, seeking songs; second, seeking dances; third, seeking lutes and zithers; fourth, *pānai-zao*; fifth, *tālapan*; sixth, *śūhana*. These are the six failings of musical performance.

If a householder or a householder’s son indulges incessantly in music and entertainment, his family’s wealth and property will diminish day by day. Furthermore, there are six ways in which associating with evil friends leads to ruin:
