first, employing means to practice deception; second, taking pleasure in secret, private places; third, seducing the family members of others; fourth, plotting to seize the property of others; fifth, directing all profit and gain toward oneself; and sixth, delighting in exposing the faults of others. These are the six ways in which evil friends cause ruin.

If a householder or a householder’s son associates with evil friends without ceasing, the wealth and property of his household will diminish day by day. There are six losses resulting from indolence: first, being unwilling to work despite having wealth and pleasure;

second, being unwilling to apply diligent effort despite being poor; third, being unwilling to apply diligent effort during cold weather; fourth, being unwilling to apply diligent effort during hot weather; fifth, being unwilling to apply diligent effort when it is early in the day; sixth, being unwilling to apply diligent effort when it is late in the day. These are the six losses of indolence.
"If a householder or a householder’s son does not cease his indolence, the wealth and business of his household will diminish day by day.
Having spoken thus, the Buddha further uttered these verses:
"For those who are deluded by alcohol, There will likewise be a circle of drinking companions; [The wealth of such a person] will surely decline."
Wealth was gathered, yet as soon as it was his own, it was spent again.
Drinking without moderation, he constantly delighted in song, dance, and play;
wandering through the houses of others by day, he thereby brought himself to ruin.
Following evil friends without reforming, slandering those who have left the household life;
such wrong views are ridiculed by the world, and such defiled conduct is rejected by others.
Attached to external forms, they concern themselves only with matters of victory and defeat.
Lacking filial piety and failing to repay kindness, one’s conduct is defiled and rejected by others.
Ruined and deluded by wine, one lacks self-awareness regarding poverty;
being light on wealth and fond of extravagant spending, one destroys the family and brings about calamity.
Gambling and drinking in crowds, consorting together to seek out other women’s wives;
indulging in base and vulgar conduct like the moon approaching its waning phase—
by committing evil one receives evil, for one associates with and acts as an equal to evil friends.
In this life and in the next, one will ultimately gain nothing from beginning to end.
By day one indulges in sleep; by night, upon waking, one is full of longing.
Utterly muddled and lacking virtuous friends, one is unable to attend to the affairs of the household.
Morning and evening one refuses to work; in both cold and heat, one again succumbs to indolence.
What one undertakes is not brought to completion, and even what has been achieved is ruined.
If one disregards the cold and heat, and diligently applies oneself morning and evening;
"Your undertakings shall never fail, and until the end you shall have no sorrow or affliction.
The Buddha told Sujāta:
"There are four enemies who appear as friends; you should recognize them."
"What are the four? First, intimidation; second, flattery; third, servile compliance; and fourth, evil companions.
The Buddha told Sujāta:
“There are four ways of being cowed by fear.

What are these four? First, giving first and then taking back; second, giving little while expecting much; third, feigning intimacy out of fear; and fourth, befriending others for the sake of profit. These are the four ways of being cowed by fear.”
The Buddha told Sujāta: "There are four further matters regarding being a pleasant-spoken friend.

What are these four? First, one accords with both good and evil; second, one abandons and leaves you in times of difficulty; third, when others come from without, one secretly restrains them; fourth, upon seeing a perilous situation, one immediately provides assistance and rescue. These are the four matters of being a pleasant-spoken friend."
There are four matters for honoring and obeying one's parents.

What are these four? First, deceiving them beforehand; second, deceiving them afterwards; third, deceiving them in their presence; and fourth, inflicting corporal punishment upon seeing even a minor transgression. These are the four matters for honoring and obeying one's parents.
There are four further ways in which one associates with evil friends.

What are these four? First, being a friend when drinking alcohol; second, being a friend when gambling; third, being a friend when indulging in lustful excesses; and fourth, being a friend when engaged in singing and dancing. These are the four ways of associating with evil friends.
When the Blessed One had finished speaking this, he further uttered these verses:
"To one who is submissive out of fear yet acts as a close friend, and likewise to one who is a friend through pleasant speech;
to one who is respectful and compliant yet deceitful— these evil companions constitute harmful friends."
"One should not rely on such kin; the wise should realize this.
One ought to distance oneself from them quickly, as one would avoid a perilous path.
The Buddha told Sujāta:
“There are four kinds of kinsmen who are worthy of being relied upon, who provide great benefit, and who act as protectors for others.

What are these four? First, they refrain from wrongdoing; second, they possess compassion; third, they benefit others; and fourth, they share in common activities. These are the four kinds of kinsmen who are worthy of being relied upon, who provide great benefit, and who act as protectors for others; one should draw near to them.”
"Good Birth!
That cessation has four aspects that bring great benefit and provide protection for people.
What are these four?"

First, seeing others commit evil, one is able to restrain them; second, one demonstrates rectitude to others; third, one regards them with a compassionate heart; fourth, one shows others the path to the heavens.
These are the four kinds of non-contention, which bring great benefit and serve as protection for others.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of compassionate sympathy:

first, rejoicing on behalf of others when seeing their gain; second, feeling concern on their behalf when seeing their suffering; third, praising the virtues of others; and fourth, being able to restrain others when seeing them speak ill. These are the four kinds of compassionate sympathy, which bring great benefit and serve as protection for others.
There are four benefits. What are the four? First, protecting others so as not to allow them to become negligent;

second, protecting them from losing their wealth through negligence; third, protecting them so that they do not fall into fear; and fourth, instructing and admonishing them in private. These are the four benefits for a person who brings much advantage and serves as a protector for others.
There are four kinds of sameness of purpose (*samānārthatā*). What are the four?

First, for the sake of others, not sparing one's own body or life; second, for the sake of others, not sparing one's wealth or treasures; third, for the sake of others, rescuing them from their fears; fourth, for the sake of others, providing private instruction and admonition. These are the four kinds of sameness of purpose, which bring great benefit and provide protection for others.
When the Blessed One had spoken thus, he further uttered these verses:
“Restraint is kin who wards off evil; Compassion is kin toward others;
Benefiting others and aiding them is kin; Sharing in common activities is kin equal to oneself.”
This relative is truly worthy of being relied upon; he is one whom the wise draw near to.
Among all relatives, there is no relative equal to this: as a compassionate mother toward her child.
If you wish to rely on those worthy of reliance, you should rely on a steadfast relative.
"Those who possess the fullness of the precepts are like the light of a fire illuminating people.
The Buddha told Sujāta:
"You should know the six directions. What are these six directions?"

Parents are the eastern direction; teachers and elders are the southern direction; wives and concubines are the western direction; kinsmen and associates are the northern direction; servants and laborers are the downward direction; and śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and those of noble conduct are the upward direction.
"Sunetra! As a son, one should honor and comply with one’s parents through five matters. What are these five? First, providing for their needs so that they lack nothing;

second, first informing the parents of whatever one intends to do; third, being respectful and compliant toward whatever the parents do, never opposing them; fourth, not daring to disobey the righteous commands of the parents; and fifth, not interrupting the righteous activities of the parents."
"Sunetra! As a son, one should honor and comply with one's parents through these five matters; the parents, in turn, should honor and care for their son through five matters.
What are these five?"

First, they restrain their children from committing evil; second, they instruct and show them the way of goodness; third, their compassionate love penetrates to the very marrow of their bones; fourth, they seek virtuous marriages for their children; and fifth, they provide whatever is necessary at all times.
"Son of Good Birth!
If you respect, obey, and reverently serve your parents, then that quarter will be peaceful and secure, free from anxiety and fear.
Son of Good Birth!"
There are five further matters by which a disciple reverently serves their teacher.

What are these five? First, providing whatever is required for service; second, paying homage and making offerings; third, honoring and looking up to them with reverence; fourth, respectfully following the teacher’s instructions and commands without opposition; and fifth, hearing the Dharma from the teacher and retaining it well without forgetting.
"Śāṇakavāsin!
A disciple should serve his preceptor and elders with these five dharmas, and the preceptor and elders, in turn, should regard their disciples with five matters. What are these five?"

First, to guide others in accordance with the Dharma; second, to instruct them in what they have not yet heard; third, to enable them to skillfully understand the meaning according to their questions; fourth, to introduce them to virtuous friends; and fifth, to exhaustively impart all that one knows without parsimony.
"Son of Good Birth!
When a disciple is respectful, compliant, and reverently serves his teacher, that quarter will be peaceful and secure, free from anxiety and fear.
Son of Good Birth!"
A husband’s respectful treatment of his wife also consists of five matters.

What are these five? First, treating her with propriety; second, maintaining a dignified presence without being harsh; third, providing food and clothing according to the season; fourth, arranging her adornments at the proper times; and fifth, entrusting her with the management of the household.
"Son of Good Birth!
If a husband treats his wife with respect by means of these five matters, and the wife in turn honors her husband with five matters, what are these five?
First, rising before him; second, sitting after him; third, speaking with gentle words; fourth, being respectful and compliant; and fifth, anticipating his wishes and carrying out his intentions."
"Son of Good Birth!
This is how a husband should treat his wife with respect; by doing so, she will be secure and free from anxiety or fear.
Son of Good Birth!"
Now, as a person, one ought to treat one's kinsmen with affection and respect through five matters.
What are these five? First is giving; second is kind speech; third is providing benefit; fourth is sharing common interests; and fifth is not deceiving.
"Son of a Good Family!
These are the five ways one should show affection and respect to one's kinsmen, and likewise, the five ways kinsmen show affection and respect to others.

What are these five? First, protecting them from negligence; second, protecting them from the loss of wealth due to negligence; third, protecting those who are terrified; fourth, instructing and admonishing them in private; and fifth, constantly praising one another."
"Son of Good Birth!
By thus honoring and looking after one's kinsmen, that quarter will be peaceful and secure, free from anxiety and fear.
Son of Good Birth!"
A master instructs his servants and attendants through five matters.

What are these five? First, employing them according to their abilities; second, providing food and drink at the proper times; third, granting rewards for their labor at the proper times; fourth, providing medical care when they are ill; and fifth, allowing them leave and rest.
"Sunetra! These are the five matters for instructing servants; servants, in turn, serve their masters through five matters.

What are these five? First, rising early; second, performing tasks with thoroughness; third, not taking what is not given; fourth, attending to duties in proper order; and fifth, praising the master’s name."
"In this way, when one serves as a master to servants and laborers, that region will be peaceful and secure, free from anxiety and fear. 'Sujāta!
A donor should provide for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas with five things. What are these five?'"

First, practicing loving-kindness through bodily action; second, practicing loving-kindness through verbal action; third, practicing loving-kindness through mental action; fourth, giving at the appropriate time; and fifth, not obstructing the door.
"Son of Good Birth!
If a donor provides for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas with these five things, the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas should in turn instruct them with six things. What are these six?"

First, to protect them so they do not commit evil; second, to instruct them toward wholesome states; third, to teach them to harbor a virtuous mind; fourth, to cause those who have not heard [the Dharma] to hear it; fifth, to enable those who have already heard it to understand it well; and sixth, to reveal the path to heaven.
"Son of Good Birth!
When a donor thus reverently serves śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, that region will be peaceful and secure, free from anxiety and fear.
Having spoken thus, the World-Honored One further recited these verses:
"Parents are the eastern direction; teachers and elders are named the southern direction;
wives and spouses are the western direction; kinsmen are the northern direction;
servants and attendants are the downward direction; and śramaṇas are the upward direction."
Those sons of noble families who pay homage in all directions,
who act with reverence and obedience without missing the proper time, shall all be reborn in heaven after death.
Through generous giving and gentle speech, they bring great benefit and profit to many people.
Sharing benefits equally with others and giving all that one possesses to them—
these four carry a heavy burden, as weighty as a chariot wheel;
without these four in the world, there would be no filial piety or support for parents.
This Dharma exists in the world, selected by the wise;
practicing it, one obtains great fruit, and one's fame spreads far and wide.
Adorning the seats and couches, and providing the finest food and drink;
Providing what is required, one’s fame spreads far and wide;
not neglecting kinsmen and friends, one shows them beneficial matters;
with superiors and subordinates always in harmony, one gains a good reputation therein.
First one should practice the arts and skills, and only then acquire wealth and property;
once wealth and property are fully acquired, one should protect them well.
When spending wealth, one should not be extravagant, and should carefully select those with whom one deals.
To those who are deceitful and aggressive, it is better to give even what has not yet been gathered.
Wealth accumulates from small beginnings, just as bees gather from many flowers;
as riches increase day by day, they will never suffer depletion until the end.
First, know contentment with one meal; second, cultivate your practice without indolence;
third, you should first store up provisions to prepare for times of scarcity;
fourth, engage in farming and commerce, and provide watered lands for grazing.
Fifth, one should erect stupas and temples; sixth, one should establish monastic dwellings.
A householder should diligently attend to these six tasks and cultivate them well without missing the proper time.
For one who practices in this manner, the household will suffer no decline.
"Wealth and treasures increase daily, like the ocean swallowing all streams.
At that time, Sujāta addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Excellent! It is most excellent!"
“World-Honored One!

Truly this exceeds my original expectations and surpasses the instructions of my father; you have been able to cause those who were prostrate to look upward, those who were closed in to find opening, and those who were lost to attain awakening—like lighting a lamp in a dark room so that those with eyes may see.”
What the Tathāgata has taught is likewise so: by means of countless skillful expedients, he awakens those who are ignorant and deluded, manifesting the pure and white dharmas. Why is this?
The Buddha is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; therefore, he is able to reveal and teach, serving as the enlightened guide for the world.

Now I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha. I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me the status of an upāsaka within the True Dharma. From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, I shall refrain from killing, refrain from stealing, refrain from sexual misconduct, refrain from lying, and refrain from drinking intoxicants.
At that time, Sujāta, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Scroll 11. *The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Scroll 12.
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
17. The Sūtra on Purity (17), Part Two, Number Thirteen. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Kapilavastu, in the Mṛgadāva forest of the upāsaka Cunda, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, the śrāmaṇera Cunda was in the kingdom of Pāvā. Having completed his summer retreat, he took up his robes and bowl and gradually made his way to the Jeta Grove in Kapilavastu. Arriving at Ānanda’s location, he prostrated himself at the elder’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed him, saying:

"In the city of Pāvā, there was a Nirgrantha who died not long ago. His disciples have now split into two factions, each disputing with the other, reviling one another face to face without any sense of seniority or hierarchy.
They take turns seeking out each other's faults, contending over their knowledge and views, saying: 'I know this, but you do not;'"
My practice is authentic, whereas yours is based on false views.
You take what precedes as what follows, and what follows as what precedes; thus you are inverted and confused, lacking any consistent principle.
"What I have done is excellent; what you have said is not so. If you have any doubts, you should consult me. Venerable Ānanda!
At that time, the people of that country who served the Nirgranthas, having heard this dispute, gave rise to a sense of revulsion and weariness.
Ānanda said to the novice Cunda:
"We have something we wish to inform the World-Honored One; let us go together now to present this matter. Whatever instructions the World-Honored One may give, we shall together carry them out."
At that time, having heard Ānanda’s words, the novice Cunda immediately went together with him to the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This novice Cunda, having completed the summer retreat in the kingdom of Pāvā, took up his robes and bowl and gradually arrived here. He prostrated at my feet and said to me:

'In the kingdom of Pāvā, there was a Nirgrantha who died not long ago; his disciples have now split into two factions, each disputing with the other, reviling one another face to face, disregarding seniority, seeking out each other's faults, and contending over their respective knowledge and views:'"
"I am able to know this, whereas you cannot;
my practice is authentic, whereas yours is based on false views.
You take the former for the latter and the latter for the former; you are inverted and confused, lacking any systematic principle."
"What I say is correct; what you say is incorrect. If you have any doubts, you should consult me.
At that time, the people of that country who served the Nirgranthas, having heard this dispute, gave rise to a sense of weariness and revulsion.
The World-Honored One said to the śrāmaṇera Cunda: "So it is, Cunda!"
Those who dwell in such unrighteousness are unworthy of being heard; these are not the words spoken by the Samyaksaṃbuddha. They are like a dilapidated stupa that cannot be stained with color.
Although they have teachers, all harbor false views; although they possess teachings, none are authentic or true.
They are unworthy of being heard or adopted, for they cannot lead to liberation. These are not the words spoken by the Samyaksaṃbuddha; they are like an old stupa that cannot be stained.
Among those disciples, there may be some who do not comply with his teaching; they abandon those heterodox views and practice right view. Cunda!
Suppose someone were to come and say to those disciples:
"Virtuous ones! Your teacher’s Dharma is correct; you should practice within it, so why do you abandon it?
Those disciples who believe his words will lose the Way in both cases and incur immeasurable demerit. Why is this? Because...
Although that teacher possesses a doctrine, it is not true or authentic. Cunda!

If a teacher is free from wrong views, his doctrine is true and authentic; it is worthy of being heard and adopted, capable of leading to liberation, and spoken by the Samyak-saṃbuddha—just as a new stupa is easily colored.

However, among these disciples, some are unable to practice diligently within this Dharma and fail to achieve accomplishment; they abandon the path of equanimity and enter into false views. Suppose someone were to come and say to those disciples:
"Venerable friends!..."
"Your teacher’s Dharma is correct; you ought to practice within it. Why have you abandoned it to enter into false views?
If that disciple believes these words, then both will see what is truly correct and obtain immeasurable merit.
"Why is this? Because that Dharma is true and correct.
The Buddha told Cunda:
"Although he has a teacher, he harbors wrong views;

although he possesses teachings, they are entirely not true or correct, unworthy of being heard or adopted, incapable of leading to liberation, and not spoken by the Samyak-saṃbuddhas—just as a dilapidated stupa cannot be beautified with colors."
Those disciples have achieved mastery in their respective doctrines and follow their practices, yet they give rise to various wrong views. Cunda!
Suppose someone were to come and say to those disciples:
"If your teacher’s Dharma is correct and what you practice is right, then by practicing with such diligent austerity as this, you should achieve the fruit of the Path in this very life.
Those disciples who believe and accept these words will lose the Path in both cases and incur immeasurable demerit.
Why is this? Because the Dharma is not genuine and true. Cunda!

If the teacher does not hold wrong views, his Dharma is authentic and true, worthy of being heard and adopted; it can lead to the essential way of liberation and was spoken by the Samyaksaṃbuddha. It is like a new stupa that is easily dyed with color.
Furthermore, his disciples have achieved mastery in each and every teaching; they practice in accordance with them and give rise to right view. If someone were to come and say to those disciples:
"Your teacher’s Dharma is correct and what you practice is right; since your current cultivation involves such diligent hardship, you should achieve the fruit of the Path within this very life."
Those disciples believed and accepted his words; both possessed right view and obtained immeasurable merit.
Why was this? Because the Dharma is true and correct.
"Cunda! There may be a teacher who appears in the world and causes his disciples to give rise to sorrow;
there may also be a teacher who appears in the world and causes his disciples to be without sorrow."
"How is it that the appearance of a Teacher in the world causes his disciples to give rise to sorrow? Cunda!

When a Teacher has newly appeared in the world and it has not been long since he attained the Way, his Dharma is complete and his holy life is pure; yet, before he has fully manifested the true essentials as they really are, that Teacher quickly enters parinirvāṇa. His disciples, unable to practice, all become distressed and say:"

"Since the Teacher first appeared in the world, not long after he attained the Way, his Dharma has been pure and his holy life complete; yet its true and essential reality has never been fully revealed. Now that the Teacher, our Guide, is about to pass into parinirvāṇa so soon, we disciples will have no opportunity to practice."
"This is what it means for the Teacher to appear in the world while his disciples are filled with sorrow and anxiety.
What does it mean for the Teacher to appear in the world such that his disciples do not grieve?

It means that when the Teacher appears in the world, his Dharma is pure, his holy life (*brahmacarya*) is complete, and he widely disseminates the true essentials as they truly are; only then does the Teacher pass into parinirvāṇa. His disciples are all able to practice accordingly and do not harbor words of grief, saying:"

"When our Teacher first appeared in the world, not long after he had attained the Way, his Dharma was pure and his holy life was complete; yet the true essentials were not yet widely revealed. Now that the Teacher has so quickly entered parinirvāṇa, it prevents us, his disciples, from practicing."
"In this way, Cunda, when a Teacher has appeared in the world, his disciples have no sorrow.
The Buddha said to Cunda:

"This factor fulfills the holy life: namely, when the Teacher has appeared in the world, but it has not been long since his renunciation and his fame has not yet spread widely; this is called the incompleteness of the factors of the holy life."

Cunda! The Teacher has appeared in the world and has long been a renunciant; his fame is far-reaching and extensive. This is called being fully endowed with the factors of the holy life (*brahmacariya*). Cunda!

The Teacher has appeared in the world and has long been a renunciant; his fame is widespread, yet his disciples have not yet received instruction, have not perfected the holy life (*brahmacarya*), have not reached the state of peace, and have not attained their own benefit. They are unable to receive the Dharma and distribute it through exposition, and when heterodox arguments arise, they cannot go forth to extinguish them according to the Dharma. They have not yet achieved the transformations of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) or realization; thus, these factors of the holy life are incomplete.

Cunda! When a Teacher appears in the world, having long since gone forth from the household life, his fame is widespread; and all his disciples receive his instructions, becoming fully endowed with the holy life (*brahmacarya*), reaching the state of peace and security, and having already attained their own benefit. Furthermore, they are able to receive the Dharma and explain it in detail, to extinguish heterodox arguments in accordance with the Dharma as they arise, and to possess the transformations that constitute the realization of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This is called being fully perfected in the limbs of the holy life.

"Cunda! Although the Teacher has appeared in the world and has long since gone forth, and although his fame is widespread, the bhikṣuṇīs have not yet received instruction; they have not yet reached a state of peace, nor have they attained their own benefit. They are unable to receive, distribute, and expound the Dharma, and when heterodox arguments arise, they cannot eliminate them according to the Dharma as it truly is. They have not yet been able to manifest transformations or realize supernatural powers. This is what is meant by the factors of the holy life being incomplete."

"Cunda! The Teacher has appeared in the world and has long been a renunciant; his fame is widespread. All the bhikṣuṇīs have received his instruction and training, are fully endowed with the holy life (brahmacarya), and have reached the state of peace and security. Having already attained their own benefit, they are further able to receive the Dharma, analyze it, and expound it; when heterodox arguments arise, they can extinguish them in accordance with the Dharma; they are fully endowed with transformations and have realized the supernormal powers (abhijñā). This is called being fully perfected in the factors of the holy life."
Cunda! It is the same for all upāsakas and upāsikās who extensively cultivate the holy life, even unto the full accomplishment of transformations and the realization of supernormal powers.

“Cunda! If the Teacher were not present in the world, if he were without renown, and if his gains and offerings were diminished, then the factors of the holy life would not be complete and fulfilled.”
If the Teacher were still in the world, and his fame, gain, and offerings were all fully possessed without any diminution, then the factor of the holy life would be complete and fulfilled.

If the Teacher is in the world and his fame and material gains are fully complete, yet the bhikṣus lack such fame and material gains, this constitutes an incompleteness in the factors of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

If the Teacher remains in the world, and his fame, gain, and offerings are fully provided without deficiency, and the community of bhikṣus is likewise complete, then the factor of the holy life is fulfilled; the same applies to the community of bhikṣuṇīs.

“Cunda! I have been a renunciant for a long time, and my fame has spread far and wide. My bhikṣus have already received my instructions and reached the state of peace; they have attained their own benefit and are further able to receive the Dharma and preach it for others. When divergent arguments arise, they are able to extinguish them according to the Dharma. They are fully endowed with transformations and have realized supernormal powers; the bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās are all likewise.”
Cunda! I have widely disseminated the holy life—up to the point of having fully perfected the transformations and realized the superknowledges. Cunda!
Among all the teachers in the entire world, I do not see anyone whose fame, renown, gain, and offerings equal those of me, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Cunda! Among all the assemblies in the world, there is none that possesses fame and gain equal to my own assembly, Cunda!"
If one wishes to speak correctly, one should say that he sees the unseen.
How does he see the unseen?
When all the pure holy life is fully perfected, proclaimed, and manifested, this is called seeing the unseen.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Udraka Rāmaputra made this statement in the midst of the great assembly:
'There is seeing and not seeing. What is meant by "seeing and not seeing"?'"
"Just as a sword can be seen, but its edge cannot be seen. "Monks!
That son has cited the words of an ignorant worldling to serve as a simile; it is thus, Cunda!"
If one wishes to speak correctly, one should say "seen" or "not seen. How so?
You should speak correctly, saying:
" 'The complete purity of the entire holy life (brahmacarya) is proclaimed and disseminated, yet it is invisible.
Cunda! That which is a continuous dharma may be obtained when incomplete; that which is a non-continuous dharma is not obtained even when complete."
"Cunda! Among all dharmas, the holy life (brahmacarya) is like the cream within curd.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“I have personally realized this Dharma through my own direct experience—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four bases of psychic power, the four right efforts, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. You all should fully harmonize and not give rise to disputes;
with one teacher and one reception, like water and milk blending together, you should yourselves blaze forth within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and swiftly attain peace and happiness.”
Having attained peace and happiness, if there is a bhikṣu who, while preaching the Dharma, says:
"The phrases he has spoken are incorrect; their meaning and principle are incorrect."
Having heard this, the bhikṣu should neither say "it is so" nor say "it is not so," but should instead say to that bhikṣu: "How is it, O worthy ones?"
"My position is thus, and your position is thus;
my meaning is thus, and your meaning is thus.
Which of these is superior?"
"What constitutes a defeat?
If that bhikṣu replies: "My statement is thus; my meaning is thus;"
"Your phrasing is thus, and your meaning is thus;
your phrasing is superior, and your meaning is also superior.
When that bhikṣu says this, one may neither condemn it nor affirm it.
You should admonish that bhikṣu, you should rebuke him and stop him, and you should investigate together; thus, all should remain in harmony, without giving rise to disputes.
Sharing the same reception, the same teacher, and the same milk, you should make yourselves a beacon within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, attaining swift peace and happiness.
"Once they have attained peace and happiness, if there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma, and among them another bhikṣu says:
'The phrases he speaks are not correct, but the meaning is correct.'"
Having heard this, the bhikṣu should neither say "it is so" nor say "it is not so," but should instead say to that bhikṣu:
"What do you mean, bhikṣu?"
"My position is thus, and your position is thus;
which of these is correct and which is incorrect? If that bhikṣu replies:
"Your statement is thus, my statement is thus, yet your statement is superior.
When that bhikṣu says this, one may neither say it is so nor say it is not so.
You should admonish that bhikṣu, you should rebuke him and stop him, and you should investigate the matter together. In this way, you should all remain in harmony, without giving rise to disputes;

sharing the same teacher and receiving the same teaching, like water and milk mixed together, you should make yourselves a beacon for the Tathāgata’s true Dharma and swiftly attain peace and happiness.
“Once they have attained peace and happiness, if there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma, and among them another bhikṣu says:
‘The phrases he speaks are correct, but the meaning is not correct.’”
Having heard this, the bhikṣu should neither affirm it as correct nor deny it as incorrect, but should say to that bhikṣu:
"What do you mean, bhikṣu?"
"My position is thus, and your position is thus;
which of these is correct, and which is incorrect? If he should reply:
"My position is thus, and your position is thus; yet your position is superior.
When that bhikṣu has said this, he may neither say "it is so" nor may he say "it is not so."

You should admonish that bhikṣu, you should rebuke him, and you should stop him; you should investigate the matter together. In this way, all bhikṣus should remain in harmony, without giving rise to disputes, sharing the same teacher and receiving the same teaching, like water and milk mixed together.
Within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, you should make yourselves a beacon of light, so that you may swiftly attain peace and happiness.
"Once they have attained peace and happiness, if there is a bhikṣu who preaches the Dharma, and among them another bhikṣu should say:
'The phrases he speaks are correct; their meaning is correct.'"
When a bhikṣu has heard this, he must not say it is wrong; rather, he should praise those words, saying:
"What you have said is correct; what you have said is correct. Therefore, bhikṣus!

Regarding the twelve divisions of the scriptures, you shall personally realize them and cause them to be widely disseminated: first, the *Sūtra*; second, the *Geya*; third, the *Vyākaraṇa*; fourth, the *Gāthā*; fifth, the *Dharmapada*; sixth, the *Saṃyukta*; seventh, the *Itivṛttaka*; eighth, the *Jātaka*; ninth, the *Vaipulya*; tenth, the *Adbhutadharma*; eleventh, the *Avadāna*; and twelfth, the *Upadeśa*. You should properly receive and uphold them, weigh and examine them, and extensively expound and distribute them.

“Monks! Regarding the robes I have prescribed—whether they be robes from cemeteries, robes from householders, or coarse and humble robes—these robes are sufficient to ward off cold and heat, and to protect against mosquitoes and gadflies; they are sufficient to cover the four limbs.”
"O Bhikṣus! Regarding the food I have prescribed— whether it be alms-food or the food of householders—
if this food is sufficient, yet the body suffers affliction and various ailments press upon it such that death may be imminent, then I permit this food, provided one remains content with it."
"O Bhikṣus! Regarding the dwellings I have prescribed— whether under a tree, in the open air, within a room, atop a multi-storied pavilion, inside a cave, or in various other types of dwellings—
these places are sufficient for protection against cold and heat, wind and rain, and mosquitoes and gadflies, down to providing a quiet and secluded place for rest."
"O Bhikṣus! Regarding the medicines I have prescribed—namely, excrement and urine, ghee, oil, honey, and black rock sugar—these medicines are sufficient in themselves.
If physical suffering arises and various ailments press upon you so severely that you fear death will follow, I therefore permit these medicines."
The Buddha said:
"There may be certain non-Buddhist brahmins who come and say:
'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, amuse themselves with various pleasures.'"
If anyone should speak these words, you should reply as follows:
"Do not say such things, claiming that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, delight themselves with manifold pleasures."
Why is this so? There are those who delight in self-entertainment whom the Tathāgata censures;
there are those who delight in self-entertainment whom the Tathāgata praises.
If non-Buddhist brahmins should ask, saying:
"What pleasure do you yourself enjoy that you, Gautama, condemn it?
should such words be spoken, you should reply as follows:

"The qualities of the five desires are lovely and delightful, and are objects of people's craving and attachment. What are these five? They are: forms known by the eye, which are lovely and delightful, and objects of people's craving and attachment;

[sounds known by the ear, odors known by the nose, tastes known by the tongue, and tangibles known by the body, which are likewise lovely and delightful, and objects of people's craving and attachment]."
The ear hears sounds, the nose perceives fragrances, the tongue perceives flavors, and the body perceives tangibles—all of which are lovely, delightful, and objects of people's craving.
Venerable friends!
Such joy and pleasure arising from these five desires is what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has censured.
It is, for example, like a person who intentionally kills a living being and considers it a source of pleasure; this is what the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has condemned.
Just as there may be someone who secretly commits theft and considers it a pleasure—this is what the Tathāgata censures.
Just as there may be someone who violates the holy life (brahmacarya) and considers it a pleasure—this is what the Tathāgata censures.
It is as if there were someone who intentionally speaks falsehoods, considering it a pleasure; this is what the Tathāgata censures.
It is as if there were someone who is dissolute and self-indulgent; this is what the Tathāgata censures.
It is like a person who practices external austerities that are not the right practice taught by the Tathāgata; though they consider it happiness themselves, this is what the Tathāgata censures.
“Monks! One should censure the five qualities of sensual desire to which people are greedily attached.
What are these five?
The eye perceives forms that are lovely and delightful, to which people are attached;
the ear hears sounds, the nose perceives odors, the tongue perceives tastes, and the body perceives tangibles—all of which are lovely and delightful, to which people are attached.
Such pleasures as these do not exist for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
It is as if there were someone who intentionally kills living beings and takes pleasure therein; such is not the pleasure of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.
It is as if there were someone who openly acts as a thief and considers it a pleasure; such is not the pleasure of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.
It is as if there were someone who, having violated the holy life, considers it a pleasure; such a pleasure as this does not belong to the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
It is as if there were someone who, having intentionally uttered a falsehood, considers it a pleasure; such a pleasure as this does not belong to the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
It is as if there were someone who is dissolute and self-indulgent, considering such things to be pleasure; the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, have no such pleasure.
It is as if there were someone who practices external austerities, considering such things to be pleasure; the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, have no such pleasure.
"Monks, if non-Buddhist brahmins were to ask: 'What is the pleasure that brings self-delight, which is praised by the śramaṇa Gautama?
[you should answer thus]."
If he should speak these words, you should answer him thus:
"Venerable sirs!
There are five strands of sensual pleasure which are lovely, delightful, and objects of people's craving."
What are the five?
They are the eye cognizing forms—up to the body cognizing tangibles—which are lovely, delightful, and objects of people's craving.
O Venerable Ones!
The pleasure born from the causes and conditions of the five desires should be swiftly eradicated.
It is like a person who intentionally kills sentient beings and considers it a pleasure;
since such a pleasure exists, it should be swiftly eradicated.
It is just as if there were someone who openly acts as a thief and considers it a pleasure;
such a pleasure should be swiftly eliminated.
It is just as if there were someone who violates the holy life (brahmacarya) and considers it a pleasure.
There is such pleasure as this, which should be swiftly eliminated.
It is like a person who deliberately utters falsehoods and considers it a pleasure;
there is such pleasure as this, which should be swiftly eliminated.
It is like a person who is dissolute and self-indulgent, considering this to be happiness;
such happiness as this should be swiftly eliminated.
It is like a person who practices external austerities, considering this to be happiness.
There is such pleasure as this that should be swiftly eliminated.

It is like a person who has departed from sensual desire and is free from unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, they enter the first dhyāna, which is characterized by joy and pleasure.
Such pleasure is praised by the Buddha.

Just as a person, with the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, with internal joy and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna,
which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss— such bliss is praised by the Buddha.

Just as someone, having removed joy and entered into equanimity, experiences bodily happiness with mindfulness and single-mindedness—this happiness sought by the noble ones and protected by right awareness—and enters the third dhyāna;
such is the happiness praised by the Buddha.

With the fading away of pleasure and the fading away of pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by the purity of equanimity and mindfulness;
such is the pleasure praised by the Buddha.
"If any non-Buddhist brahmin should ask:
'In this pleasure, what fruits and merits do you seek?
you should answer him thus:"
"This bliss shall have seven fruits and virtues. What are the seven?
In this present life, one attains the realization of the Path; even if one does not attain it then, at the time of death, one shall attain the realization of the Path."

If one does not achieve it even at the time of death, one should exhaust the five lower fetters and attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, parinirvāṇa upon being reborn there, parinirvāṇa through exertion, parinirvāṇa without exertion, or parinirvāṇa as an upstreamer reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Venerable friends!
These are the seven virtues of this pleasure.
Venerable friends!
If a bhikṣu on the stage of training (śaikṣa-bhūmi) desires to ascend and seek a state of peace and security, yet has not yet eliminated the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa), what are these five? They are:

the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of ill will (vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of sloth and torpor (styānamiddha-nīvaraṇa), the hindrance of restlessness and remorse (auddhatyakaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa), and the hindrance of doubt (vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa).

If that training bhikṣu, while desiring to seek higher attainment and seeking a state of peace and security, has not yet extinguished the five hindrances, cannot apply himself diligently to the four foundations of mindfulness, and cannot zealously cultivate the seven factors of awakening, yet wishes to attain the states of superior men and the flourishing of noble wisdom, seeking to know and see—that is impossible.
Venerable friends!
A bhikkhu on the stage of training who desires to seek higher and seeks a state of security is able to extinguish the five hindrances:
the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.

Furthermore, if one can be diligent in the four foundations of mindfulness and practice the seven factors of enlightenment as they truly are, desiring to attain the state of a superior person and the exalted wisdom of the noble ones, seeking to know and see—that is possible.
Venerable friends!

If there is a bhikkhu who is an arahant with taints destroyed, who has accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, and is liberated through right knowledge, he does not engage in nine matters.
What are the nine? First, refraining from killing;

second, refraining from stealing; third, refraining from sexual misconduct; fourth, refraining from false speech; fifth, not abandoning the Path; sixth, not following desire; seventh, not following anger; eighth, not following fear; ninth, not following delusion.
Venerable friends!

This is the Arhat whose taints are exhausted, who has done what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, liberated through right knowledge, and remains far removed from the nine matters.
"Or if there are non-Buddhist brahmins who say:
'The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas possess a dharma of non-abiding,' one should reply to them as follows:"
"Venerable friends!
Do not speak thus:
'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, possess a nature that does not abide.'"

Why is this so? The Dharma of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, is eternally abiding and cannot be moved; it is like the threshold of a door, which stands eternally without moving. The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are likewise: their Dharma is eternally abiding, without any shifting.
"Or there may be certain heterodox brahmins who say this:
'The śramaṇa Gautama knows all matters of the past, but he does not know matters of the future.'"
"That bhikṣu and those heterodox brahmins differ in their knowledge and differ in their contemplation; what they say is false.
Regarding past events, the Tathāgata knows and sees them as if they were before his eyes;
regarding the future, he gives rise to the knowledge of the path."
Matters of the past that are false and unreal are not worth rejoicing over and provide no benefit; thus, the Buddha does not provide a prediction regarding them.
Or, if matters of the past are real, yet lack anything worth rejoicing over and provide no benefit, the Buddha likewise does not provide a prediction.
If matters of the past are real and worth rejoicing over, yet provide no benefit, the Buddha likewise does not provide a prediction.
If past events were real, pleasant, and beneficial, the Tathāgata fully knows them and then records them;
it is likewise for the future and the present.

Regarding the past, future, and present, the Tathāgata speaks at the appropriate time, speaks truthfully, speaks meaningfully, speaks beneficially, speaks in accordance with the Dharma, and speaks in accordance with the Vinaya; there is nothing false in his words.

From the time the Buddha attained supreme perfect enlightenment during the first watch of the night until the final watch of the night, everything he spoke in the interval was entirely in accordance with reality; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, that which the Tathāgata speaks is as it is, and that which is as it is is what he speaks; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
In what sense is he called the Samyaksaṃbuddha?
"Whatever the Buddha knows and sees, whatever he has extinguished, and whatever he has awakened to—the Buddha has fully realized all this;
therefore, he is called the Truly and Fully Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
"Furthermore, there are certain non-Buddhist brahmins who speak thus: 'The world is eternal; only this is true, and all else is false.'"
Or again, some may say:
"This world is impermanent; only this is true, and all else is false.
Or again, there may be those who say:
"The world is both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false. Or again, some say:
"This world is neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false."
Or again, some may say:
"This world is finite; this alone is true, and all else is false.
Or again, some may say:
"The world is infinite; only this is true, and all else is false.
Or again, some say: "The world is both finite and infinite; only this is true, and all else is false."
Or again, some may say:
"The world is neither finite nor infinite; only this is true, and all else is false.
Or again, some may say:
"This life is the self; this is the truth, and all else is false.
Or again, some say: "Life is not the self; this is the truth, and all else is false."
Or again, some say: "The life-principle is different from the body; this alone is true, all else is false. Or again, some say:
"The life-principle is not different from the body; this alone is true, and all else is false.
Or again, there are those who say:
"The Tathāgata undergoes cessation; this alone is true, and all else is false."
Or again, some might say:
"The Tathāgata does not pass away; this is true and all else is false.
Or again, some might say:
"The Tathāgata neither passes away nor does he not pass away; this alone is true, all else is false.
Or again, there may be those who say:
"The Tathāgata neither passes away nor does he not pass away; this alone is true, all else is false."
"Those who hold such views are said to have 'original birth' and 'original views. I now declare this for you:

'This world is eternal'—up to and including 'the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end'—claiming that only this is true and all else is false; this is what constitutes original view and original birth."
"I shall grant you a prediction regarding this:
'As for that which has not yet been seen and has not yet arisen, I likewise grant a prediction concerning it.
What is it that has not yet been seen and has not yet arisen, which I thus predict?"
"Form is the self, which ends with perception; this alone is true, all else is false.
Or, formlessness is the self, which ends with perception.
Or, both form and formlessness are the self, which ends with perception."
The self is neither with form nor without form; it ends with perception.
The self is finite, the self is infinite, the self is both finite and infinite, or the self is neither finite nor infinite; it ends with perception.
"I have pleasure, which ends with perception;
I have no pleasure, which ends with perception;
I have both pain and pleasure, which ends with perception."
I am neither suffering nor pleasure; my existence ends with perception.
"I am a single perception"—my existence ends with that perception.
"I am manifold perceptions"—my existence ends with those perceptions.
"To have a limited perception [of self], which ends with that perception;
or to have an infinite perception [of self], which ends with that perception—this alone is true, all else is false.
This, I declare, is the root of wrong view, the origin of views, and their arising.
“Or there may be certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
‘This world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—up to: ‘The infinite perception is the self; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
If those śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas further speak and hold such a view as this:
"This alone is true; all else is false," you should reply to them as follows:
"If you truly propound this doctrine, how can it be that this world is eternal?
That this alone is real and all else is false—
such speech is not permitted by the Buddha."

Why is this? Within each of these views there are respective fetters and afflictions. When I examine them through reason, among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, there is none who equals me, much less one who could surpass me.
"These various wrong views are mere words; they are not to be discussed with me—even the view that 'an infinite perception is the self' is likewise so.
"Or there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
'This world was created by itself.'"
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
"This world was created by another.
Or again, there are those who say:
"Created by oneself or created by another," or again, some say:
"Neither created by oneself nor created by another; it exists suddenly."

As for those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who claim that the world is self-created, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas all do so because of the causal condition of contact (sparśa); it is impossible that one could speak thus while being separated from the cause of contact.

Why is this so? Because from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arises contact (*sparśa*); from contact arises feeling (*vedanā*); from feeling arises craving (*tṛṣṇā*); from craving arises grasping (*upādāna*); from grasping arises becoming (*bhava*); from becoming arises birth (*jāti*); and from birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—the great mass of afflictions.

If there are no six sense bases, then there is no contact; if there is no contact, then there is no feeling; if there is no feeling, then there is no craving; if there is no craving, then there is no grasping; if there is no grasping, then there is no becoming; if there is no becoming, then there is no birth; and if there is no birth, then there is no old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction—the great mass of calamities that is the accumulation of the aggregates.

Furthermore, it is likewise said that this world was created by another, or that this world was created by both self and another, or that this world was neither created by self nor created by another but arose suddenly; yet it exists because of contact, and without contact, it does not exist.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to extinguish these various false and evil views, you should cultivate three practices regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni).
What are the three practices that a bhikṣu should cultivate regarding the four foundations of mindfulness in order to extinguish these evils?
A bhikṣu contemplates the body internally, ardent, unflagging, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow;
he contemplates the body externally, ardent, unflagging, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow;
he contemplates the body both internally and externally, mindful and unforgetting, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
The contemplation of feelings, the mind, and mental phenomena is likewise so.
This constitutes the threefold cultivation within the four foundations of mindfulness for the purpose of extinguishing all unwholesome dharmas.
There are eight liberations; what are these eight?
Perceiving forms while contemplating forms is the first liberation.
Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms; this is the second liberation.
The liberation of the beautiful is the third liberation.
Transcending perceptions of form and extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, one dwells in the sphere of infinite space; this is the fourth liberation.
Abandoning the sphere of infinite space, one dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the fifth liberation.
Abandoning the sphere of infinite consciousness, one dwells in the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
"Abandoning the sphere of nothingness, one dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.
The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling is the eighth liberation.

At that time, Ānanda was standing behind the World-Honored One fanning him; he then bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous!
World-Honored One!
This Dharma is pure, subtle, and supreme."
"How should it be named?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra is named 'Purity'; you should uphold it with purity.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
18. The Sūtra on Self-Rejoicing (18) The Fourteenth Discourse in the Second Division of the Long Āgama Spoken by the Buddha: The Sūtra on Self-Rejoicing. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the city of Nālandā in the Pāvārika-amba grove, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, while in a secluded place, the Elder Śāriputra thought to himself in silence:

"I am certain in my mind that regarding the wisdom, supernormal powers, merit, and power of the path of the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past, future, and present, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Then, Śāriputra rose from his quiet chamber and went to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Just now, while in my quiet chamber, I reflected in silence:

among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past, future, and present, there are none whose wisdom, supernormal powers, merit, and power of the path can equal that of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “Excellent! Excellent!”
That you are able to speak such words before the Buddha, upholding them single-mindedly and uttering this true lion’s roar—no other śramaṇas or brahmins can equal you.
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Are you able to know what was thought in the minds of the past Buddhas—whether those Buddhas possessed such precepts, such Dharma, such wisdom, such liberation, and such abode of liberation?"
He replied, "I do not know. [The Buddha said,] "How is this so, Śāriputra?"
Are you able to know what is being thought in the minds of all future Buddhas—whether they possess such precepts, such dharmas, such wisdom, such liberation, and such abode of liberation?
He replied, “I do not know. [The Buddha asked,] “How is it, Śāriputra?”
"Can you know what is currently in the mind of me, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—namely, such morality, such Dharma, such wisdom, such liberation, and such abode of liberation?"
He replied, “I do not know.
He then addressed Śāriputra again:
"You do not know what is being thought in the minds of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present; why then do you definitively form such a thought?"
On account of what matter did you give rise to this thought, that you have so resolutely maintained this lion’s roar? If other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas were to hear your words:

“I definitively know that regarding the wisdom, supernormal powers, merits, and power of the path of the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past, future, and present, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
"You should not believe what you say.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I cannot know the thoughts within the minds of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present; however, I am able to know the general characteristics of the Dharma."

The Tathāgata has taught me the Dharma, ever more exalted and ever more sublime; he has taught the dark and bright dharmas, the conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, and the luminous and non-luminous dharmas. What the Tathāgata has spoken is ever more exalted and ever more sublime. Having heard the Dharma, I have understood each and every teaching and reached the ultimate realization of the Dharma. I place my faith in the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; I place my faith in the Tathāgata’s Dharma, which is well-differentiated; I place my faith in the Tathāgata’s accomplishment of the cessation of all suffering. Among all wholesome dharmas, this is the most supreme.

The World-Honored One’s wisdom is without remainder, and his supernormal powers are without remainder; among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who can equal the Tathāgata, much less surpass him.
“Furthermore, there is a further excellence in the World-Honored One’s teaching, namely, the established rules (*prajñapti-dharma*).

As for the established rules, they refer to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path; this is the unsurpassed establishment.”

With wisdom without remainder and supernormal powers without remainder, among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in all the worlds, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less any who could surpass him.
“Furthermore, there is a further excellence in the World-Honored One’s teaching, namely, the restraint of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
As for the sense bases, they are: the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena.

Just as the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones also restrained these sense bases—namely, the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena—even so will the future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones also restrain these sense bases—namely, the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena.”
Now, I, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, have likewise established this entrance—namely, the eye and forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena.

This Dharma is unsurpassed; none can surpass it. My wisdom is complete and my supernormal powers are complete. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who can equal the Tathāgata, much less one who could excel above him.
“Furthermore, there is a further excellence in the Blessed One’s teaching regarding the entry of consciousness into the womb.

As for those who enter the womb, there are four types: first, those who enter confusedly, dwell confusedly, and emerge confusedly; second, those who enter without confusion, dwell confusedly, and emerge confusedly; third, those who enter without confusion and dwell without confusion, but emerge confusedly; and fourth, those who enter without confusion, dwell without confusion, and emerge without confusion.”
He who enters without confusion, dwells without confusion, and emerges without confusion is supreme among those entering the womb.
This Dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is complete, his supernormal powers are complete, and among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, none can equal the Tathāgata, let alone surpass him.
“The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata has that which is even more supreme, namely the Path (*mārga*).

As for what is called the Path: various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of the mind of concentration and wisdom; following that samādhi-mind, they cultivate the awakening-factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), relying on desire, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and relying on renunciation.

Likewise, they cultivate the awakening-factors of dharma, diligence, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, relying on desire, relying on detachment, relying on cessation, and relying on renunciation.”
This Dharma is supreme; its wisdom is unsurpassed, and its supernormal powers are unsurpassed. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, none can equal the Tathāgata, much less surpass him.
“There is yet another superior way for the Tathāgata to teach the Dharma, namely: for the sake of cessation.
Regarding cessation: if suffering is extinguished but attained slowly, both are base;
if suffering is extinguished and attained quickly, only the suffering is base.”
If the cessation of pleasure is attained slowly, it is merely slow and base;
if the cessation of pleasure is attained quickly, yet it is not extensive and universal, it is called base because it is not extensive and universal.
"Now the Tathāgata has attained the bliss of cessation swiftly and extensively, even unto the point that devas and humans witness his spiritual transformations.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The teaching spoken by the World-Honored One is subtle and supreme; even down to women, they are able to receive and uphold it, exhausting all outflows to achieve the state of no-outflow, attaining liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and realizing this for themselves within the present life, declaring: 'Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been done, and there will be no further existence after this.'"
Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence.

This is what the Tathāgata calls the unsurpassed cessation. This Dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is without remainder, and his supernormal powers are without remainder. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, none can equal the Tathāgata, much less surpass him.
“There is yet another superior aspect to the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, namely, purity of speech.

As for purity of speech: the World-Honored One does not utter useless or false words among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; his speech seeks no victory, nor does he take sides; what he says is gentle, timely, and never uttered in vain—this is called purity of speech.”

This Dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is without remainder, and his supernormal powers are without remainder. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less any who could surpass him.
“There is yet another superior form of the Tathāgata’s teaching, namely, the concentration of vision (*darśana-samādhi*).

As for that concentration of vision: there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various means, enter the samādhi of a concentrated mind; following the mind in samādhi, they contemplate from head to foot and from foot to head, observing the skin both inside and out. They see nothing but impurities: hair, body hair, nails, liver, lungs, intestines, stomach, spleen, kidneys, the five viscera, sweat, fat, marrow, brain, excrement, urine, mucus, and tears—all foul-smelling and impure, with not a single thing worthy of desire. This is the first concentration of vision.”

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas employ diverse skillful means to enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following that concentrated mind, they remove all external impurities such as skin and flesh, contemplating only the white bones and teeth—this is the second type of fixed view.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas employ diverse skillful means to enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following that concentrated mind, they remove all external impurities such as skin and flesh along with the white bones, observing only where the consciousness of the mind dwells.
Is it in this present life?
Or is it in a future life?
It is neither interrupted in this present life nor interrupted in a future life.
"Not liberated in this life, nor liberated in future lives"—this is the third fixed view.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following the mind in that samādhi, they remove all external impurities such as skin and flesh, and even remove the white bones, further contemplating consciousness repeatedly:
"Consciousness exists in future lives, but not in this life."
"Cessation in this life but not in future lives;
liberation in this life but not in future lives"—these are the four fixed views.

There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following the mind of that samādhi, they remove all external impurities such as skin and flesh, and even the white bones. They then further contemplate consciousness, finding it neither in this life nor in future lives.
Having severed both and being liberated from both, this constitutes the certainty of the five views.

This Dharma is unsurpassed; its wisdom is exhaustive, and its supernormal powers are exhaustive. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, none are equal to the Tathāgata, let alone those who would wish to surpass him.
“Furthermore, there is a superior form of the Tathāgata’s teaching, namely, the teaching of the eternal dharma (*nitya-dharma*).

Regarding the eternal dharma: various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through various means, enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and following the mind of that concentration, they recollect twenty eons of the world’s formation and destruction.
They then declare: ‘The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, and all else is false. Why is this so?’”

Based on what I recollect and recognize, I know that there are such eons of formation and destruction; however, regarding other past eons that I do not know, and the future eons of formation and destruction, I likewise do not know them.
This person, morning and evening, speaks out of ignorance, saying:
"The world is eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false.
This is the first doctrine of eternalism.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following that concentrated mind, they recollect and recognize forty eons of formation and destruction, and they speak thus:
"This world is eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false."

Why is this? Because through my recollection and awareness, I know the kalpas of formation and destruction; furthermore, I can transcend these and know the past kalpas of formation and destruction, yet I do not know the formation and destruction of future kalpas.
This teaching speaks of knowing the beginning, but does not speak of knowing the end; such a person, morning and evening, speaks with ignorance, saying:
"The world is eternal; only this is true, and all else is false."
"This is the second eternal principle.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through various skillful means, enter meditative concentration (samādhi) and, following the mind in that samādhi, recollect and recognize eighty eons of formation and destruction.
They declare: 'This world is eternal; all else is false.'"

Why is this? Because through my recollection and awareness, I know there are kalpas of formation and destruction; furthermore, beyond this, I know the past kalpas of formation and destruction, and I also fully know the formation and destruction of future kalpas.
This person, morning and evening, speaks out of ignorance, saying:
"The world is eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false.
These are the three things that are considered eternally existing.

This Dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is without remainder, and his supernormal powers are without remainder. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who can equal the Tathāgata, much less surpass him.
“The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata has yet another superior aspect, namely, observation (*vipaśyanā*).

As for observation: there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who observe through conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), [thinking], ‘The mind of another is thus inclined; this mind is thus inclined. When that person forms such a thought, it may be either false or true; this constitutes one form of observation.”
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do not examine through perception; yet, having heard the speech of devas or non-humans, they say to them:
"Your mind is thus; your mind is thus."
"This too may be either true or false; these are the two types of observation.

There may be a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who does not observe by means of perception, nor has he heard the speech of devas or non-humans, yet observes his own body and hears the words of others, and says to that person:
'Your mind is thus; your mind is thus.'"
This also has both the real and the false; these constitute the three types of observation.

There may be a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who does not observe by means of perception, nor hears the speech of devas or non-humans, and furthermore neither observes himself nor observes others; having eliminated initial and sustained application of thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), he attains the samādhi of a concentrated mind and observes the minds of others, saying to them:
"Your mind is thus; your mind is thus."
"To observe in this manner is the truth; these are the four observations. This Dharma is unsurpassed;
its wisdom is complete and its supernormal powers are complete. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less one who could surpass him."
“The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has yet another superior aspect, namely, instruction (*anuśāsana*).

As for instruction: there may be someone who does not violate the instruction, exhausting all out-flows (*āsrava*) and becoming free from them, attaining liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. In this very life, they realize for themselves through direct experience:
‘Birth and death have been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence. This is the first instruction.”

Furthermore, there may be someone who does not violate the instructions and, having exhausted the five lower fetters, attains parinirvāṇa there and does not return to this world; this is the second instruction.

Or, there may be someone who does not violate the instructions, whereby the three fetters are exhausted and lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated; such a person attains the stage of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) and returns to this world to attain final nirvāṇa—this constitutes the third instruction.

Furthermore, there may be someone who does not violate the instructions; having exhausted the three fetters, they attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*, returning at most seven times before attaining the ultimate fruit of the path and never falling into the evil destinies. These are the four instructions.

This Dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is without remainder, and his supernormal powers are without remainder. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less one who could surpass him.
“The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has yet another superior aspect: he teaches the Dharma to others so that their precepts may be pure.

As for purity of precepts, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas whose speech is sincere and free from double-tonguedness; they are always self-respectful and solemn, having cast off sleepiness and harboring no crookedness or flattery; their mouths do not utter falsehoods, nor do they prognosticate good or bad fortune for worldly people; they do not boast of gains received from others to show them to others, nor do they seek further profit from others; they practice dhyāna and cultivate wisdom, possessing unimpeded eloquence, maintaining focused mindfulness without distraction, and exerting themselves with diligence without weariness.”

This Dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is without remainder, and his supernormal powers are without remainder. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less one who could surpass him.
“There is yet another superior aspect to the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma, namely, the knowledge of liberation.
Regarding this knowledge of liberation, the World-Honored One, through internal reflection based on other causes and conditions, declares:
‘This person is a srotāpanna; this one is a sakṛdāgāmin; this one is an anāgāmin; this one is an arhat.’”

"This Dharma is unsurpassed; its wisdom is exhaustive, and its supernormal powers are exhaustive. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less one who could surpass him."
“The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata has yet another superior aspect, namely, the realization through the knowledge of recollecting one’s own past lives.

By means of various skillful means, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following that concentrated mind, they personally recollect the events of countless past lives—one birth, two births, and so on up to hundreds of thousands of births, through kalpas of formation and destruction. In this way, they recollect their countless past existences: ‘I was born in such a place, with such a name, of such a caste and clan, with such a lifespan, eating such food, and experiencing such suffering and pleasure;

from here I went there, and from there I came here,’ thus recollecting their past lives across countless kalpas with all their various characteristics, constantly mindful day and night of what they have experienced.”
"This is form; this is the formless;
