this is perception; this is non-perception; this is neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—all these he remembers and knows completely.

This dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is exhaustive, his supernormal powers are exhaustive; among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, none are equal to the Tathāgata, much less those who would wish to surpass him.
“The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma has yet another superior aspect, namely, the knowledge of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-jñāna*).

As for this knowledge of the divine eye: through various means, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following that concentrated mind, they observe all sentient beings—those dying and those being born, those of beautiful form and those of ugly form, those in good destinations and those in evil destinations, whether handsome or hideous—seeing and knowing them all exactly according to their respective deeds.”

There may be sentient beings who have committed evil deeds of body, speech, and mind, who slander the noble ones, and who hold false and inverted views; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the three evil realms.

There are some sentient beings who practice virtue in body, speak virtuously with their speech, and maintain virtuous thoughts in their minds; they do not revile the noble ones, but perceive and believe in the right path. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among gods or humans. With the purified divine eye, they observe all sentient beings and know and see them as they truly are.

This Dharma is unsurpassed; his wisdom is without remainder, as is his supernormal power. Among all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world, there is none who is equal to the Tathāgata, much less one who could surpass him.
“There is yet another superior aspect to the Tathāgata’s teaching, namely, the realization of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*).

As for the realization of the bases of supernormal power, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through diverse means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; following that concentrated mind, they exercise countless supernormal powers: they can transform a single body into countless bodies, and merge those countless bodies back into a single body; they pass through stone walls without obstruction and sit cross-legged in mid-air.”
Just as a flying bird enters and exits the earth;
just as one is in water, treading upon water as if upon solid ground;
and from his body issuing smoke and fire, like a blazing mass of flames.
If one could touch the sun and moon with one's hand and reach the Brahma Heaven in an instant, and if any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa were to claim such supernormal power, you should reply to them:
"Such supernormal power exists; it is not that it does not exist."
This supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) is base, lowly, and inferior; it is practiced by ordinary worldlings and is not that which is cultivated by the noble ones (ārya).
If a bhikṣu is untainted by attachment to the forms beloved in the world, and having abandoned these, acts as he ought to act—this is what is called the supernormal power of the noble ones.
Regarding forms that do not evoke joy, one feels neither aversion nor attraction; having relinquished these, one acts as is appropriate—this is called the noble supernormal power (*ārya-ṛddhipāda*).
Having relinquished both attractive and unattractive forms within the world, one cultivates equanimity and maintains mindfulness without forgetfulness—this is called the noble supernormal power.

Just as the World-Honored One is diligent and courageous, possesses great wisdom, has knowledge and awakening, and has attained the supreme awakening, he is therefore called the Equally Awakened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha).

"World-Honored One, you likewise do not delight in sensual desires, nor do you delight in the practices of base and vulgar worldlings, nor do you weary yourself by undergoing various sufferings and afflictions.

World-Honored One, if you wish to eliminate unwholesome and evil dharmas, you may dwell in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), born of seclusion, and filled with joy and bliss; in this way, you can eliminate those unwholesome and evil dharmas.
It is the same for the second, third, and fourth dhyānas."
“With diligence and valor, possessing great wisdom, having knowledge and awareness, and having attained the foremost awakening, he is therefore called ‘Equally Awakened’ (Samyaksaṃbuddha).
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“If any heterodox practitioners or followers of other teachings should come and ask you:”
"If they were to ask you, 'Were the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past equal to the śramaṇa Gautama? how would you answer?
They then asked again:
"If someone were to ask you, 'Will future śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas be equal to the śramaṇa Gautama? how would you answer?
Furthermore, if they were to ask, 'Are present śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas equal to the śramaṇa Gautama? how would you answer?"
"How would you answer?
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If such a question were asked:"
"Are the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past equal to the Buddha?
One should answer: "There are."
If it is asked,
"Will the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the future be equal to the Buddha?
one should answer:
"There are. Suppose one were to ask:
"Are the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the present equal to the Buddha?"
"You should answer, 'No. The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Those non-Buddhist brahmins may further ask:
'For what reason do you sometimes say "it exists" and sometimes say "it does not exist"?'"
"How would you respond? Śāriputra said, "I would reply to him:"

"The Tathāgatas of the past were equal to the Tathāgata; the Tathāgatas of the future will be equal to the Tathāgata. I have personally heard this from the Buddha: it is impossible for there to be a Tathāgata of the present who is equal to the Tathāgata."
“World-Honored One!
Having answered in this way according to what I have heard, in accordance with the Dharma and following the Dharma, will there not be some fault?
The Buddha said:
“Answering thus is in accordance with the Dharma and follows the Dharma; it does not contradict it.

Why is this so? Because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past were equal to us, and the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future will be equal to us. It is impossible for two Buddhas to appear in the world simultaneously in the present.”
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him with a fan. The Buddha said to him:

"Udāyin, you should observe how the Blessed One is of few desires and content; though I now possess great supernormal power and great majesty, I am of few desires and content, and do not delight in sensual pleasures."

Udāyin! If any other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas were able to attain even a single dharma through diligent exertion within this Dharma, they would immediately raise a banner and announce to the four quarters:

"The Tathāgata is now one of few desires and contentment; behold now the Tathāgata’s fewness of desires and contentment! The Tathāgata possesses great supernormal power and great majestic virtue, yet he does not rely on sensual desires."
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How extraordinary!
World-Honored One!

Few are those who possess such few desires and contentment as the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One possesses great supernormal power and great majestic virtue, yet does not rely upon sensual desires.

Furthermore, if there were any other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through diligent effort within this Dharma, could attain even a single dharma, they would be able to raise their banners and proclaim to the four quarters:
"The World-Honored One is now one of few desires and contentment."

“Śāriputra! You should frequently expound this Dharma for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās. If they have any doubts regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, or the Path, upon hearing this Dharma expounded, their web of doubt will no longer remain.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“You should frequently expound this Dharma for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.”
"Why is this? Those who have doubts regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the Path will surely attain understanding upon hearing what you say. He replied:
"So be it, World-Honored One!

At that time, Śāriputra repeatedly preached the Dharma for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās; because he did so for the sake of his own purification, it is therefore called the "Sutra of Purification."
At that time, Śāriputra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
19. The Sūtra on the Great Assembly (19) The Fifteenth Discourse in the Second Division of the Long Āgama Spoken by the Buddha: The Sūtra on the Great Assembly. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats. Furthermore, the various sublime devas from the ten directions all came to the assembly to pay homage to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the four devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens each thought to themselves within their celestial abodes:

"Now, the World-Honored One is in the Śākavardhana forest at Kapilavastu, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom have attained arhatship; furthermore, various sublime devas from the ten directions have all come to assemble, paying homage to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus."
"We, too, should now go together to the place where the World-Honored One is, and each of us shall praise the Tathāgata with verses.
At that time, the four devas of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, like a strong man extending or contracting his arm, vanished from that heaven and arrived at the Śākavati-kāpiṣṭhila forest grove.
At that time, the four devas of the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven arrived, prostrated themselves at [the Buddha’s] feet with their heads, and stood to one side.
Then, one of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, before the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“Today this great assembly has gathered; All the celestial deities have assembled here.”
"We have all come for the sake of the Dharma, wishing to pay homage to the unsurpassed assembly.
Having spoken this verse, they withdrew to one side and stood there.
Then, another deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven further spoke in verse:
“The bhikṣu beholds the manifold impurities; with a composed mind, he guards himself.
Desire is like the ocean swallowing rivers; the wise man protects his sense faculties.
Having spoken this verse, he withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, another deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven further spoke in verse:
“He has severed the thorns and leveled the pit of craving, And filled in the trench of ignorance;
He wanders alone upon the field of purity, Like a well-trained elephant under control.”
Having spoken this verse, he withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, another deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven further spoke in verse:
"Those who take refuge in the Buddha Shall never fall into the evil realms."
"Having cast off this human form, they receive the pure body of a deva.

At that time, after the four devas of the Pure Abodes had spoken this verse, the World-Honored One gave his approval; they then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and suddenly vanished.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Now the great assembly of devas has gathered; now the great assembly of devas has gathered. Among the wondrous devas of the ten directions, there are none who have not come here to pay homage to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus."
"O bhikṣus! The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past also had great assemblies of devas, just as I have today;
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the future will also have great assemblies of devas, just as I have today."

"O Bhikṣus! Now the great assembly of devas has gathered; there are no divine beings from the ten directions who have not come here to pay homage to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus. You should likewise recite their names and speak verses for them."
Bhikṣus, you should know:
“Those who dwell among the earth, mountains, and valleys, appearing hidden yet terrifying;
though their bodies are clad in pure white garments, they are clean and free from defilement.”
Having heard this, the devas and humans all returned to the Brahma Heaven;
now I shall proclaim their names in proper sequence without error.
O Bhikṣu, you should know that the hosts of devas have now arrived.
The worldly wisdom of ordinary people does not perceive even one in a hundred;
how then could they see the seventy thousand hosts of ghosts and spirits?
Even if they were to see a hundred thousand ghosts, they would still not see even a single side [of the truth].
"How much more so for the various spirits who pervade the world!

There were seven thousand yakṣas of various kinds among the earth deities, all possessing supernormal powers, distinct forms, complexions, and reputations; with hearts full of joy, they came to the grove where the assembly of bhikṣus was gathered.

At that time, there was a mountain spirit of the Snowy Mountains who, accompanied by six thousand yakṣas of various kinds—each possessing supernormal powers, distinct physical forms, complexions, and reputations—approached the forest where the community of bhikṣus resided with a heart full of joy.

There was a Śālā-deva who, accompanied by three thousand yakṣas of various kinds—each possessing supernormal powers, distinct forms, complexions, and reputations—approached the grove where the community of bhikṣus resided with a heart full of joy.

These sixteen thousand spirits, yakṣas, and various other kinds of beings—each possessing supernormal powers, physical forms, complexions, and renown—came with hearts full of joy to the forest grove where the assembly of bhikṣus was gathered.
Furthermore, there was the spirit Vibhīṣaṇa, who resided in the country of Aśvaka, leading five hundred ghosts, all of whom possessed supernormal powers and majestic virtue.
There was also the spirit Kumbhīra, who dwelt on Mount Vipula at Rājagṛha, surrounded by countless spirits and ghosts who paid him reverent homage.

Furthermore, there is the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east, who leads the gandharva deities; he possesses great majesty and virtue, has ninety-one sons, all of whom are named Indra and possess great supernormal powers.

In the south is the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, who leads the various dragon kings; he possesses great majestic power and has ninety-one sons, each also named Indra, who likewise possess great supernormal powers.

In the western quarter, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa leads the kumbhāṇḍa spirits; he possesses great majesty and virtue, has ninety-one sons, and they too are named Indra and possess great supernormal powers.

The Heavenly King of the North is named Vaiśravaṇa; he leads the yakṣas and spirits, possesses great majesty and virtue, and has ninety-one sons, each also named Indra, who possess great supernormal powers.
These Four Heavenly Kings, who protect and sustain the world, possess great majestic power; emitting light from their bodies, they came to the Kāpiśī grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to subdue their illusory, deceitful, and false minds, uttered this incantation:

“Makula-makula, vilola-vilola, ādānagamaceti, kāṇeyan-dau, nayan-dau, panāsu-uhu-nu-nu-cu, devasumura, mathura, citrāsana, gandharva, naracu, janiśa, śiha, vāindara, vipamitara, tucendara, naruniha, dhuburu, śuci-pavajiva. Thus, the various kings, gandharvas, and rākṣasas, all possessing supernormal powers, physical forms, and majestic appearances, came with hearts full of joy to the forest where the assembly of bhikṣus resided.
At that time, the World-Honored One again bound this mantra, saying:
"Akṣaṇā-dhe."
That Vaiśālī Sahā.

"Jitavajra."

*Namo bhañje jātadhara-gandharva-sāhasra-ti-su-vira-ya-akhe-gaṇe bhikṣu samiti bhavani ti bhavani.* At that time,
there were another fifteen hundred Brahmins possessing the five supernatural powers, for whom the Tathāgata likewise bound this incantation.
At that time, the Brahmā King of this world-system and all the Brahmā devas possessed supernatural powers; among them was a Brahmā youth named Tiṣya, who possessed great supernormal power.
Furthermore, there were other Brahma Kings from the ten directions, each surrounded by their retinues, who came forth.
Crossing over a thousand worlds, a Great Brahma King, seeing the great assembly at the World-Honored One’s place, immediately came with his retinue surrounding him.
At that time, the Māra King, seeing the great assembly in the presence of the World-Honored One, conceived a mind of malice and immediately thought to himself:
"I shall lead my ghostly armies to destroy that assembly; I will surround them and seize them all, leaving none behind."

At that time, he immediately summoned the fourfold army and struck his chariot with his hand; the sound was like a thunderclap, and there were none among those who saw it who were not struck with terror. He unleashed great winds and rains, along with lightning and thunderbolts, toward the Kapilavastu grove, surrounding the great assembly.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus who were fond of this assembly:
"You should know that today the hosts of Māra have come with evil intent.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"You should now show reverence and compliance, establishing yourself in the Buddha-dharma;
you must destroy this host of Māras, as an elephant crushes a cluster of flowers.
Be single-minded in mindfulness and free from negligence, remaining fully endowed with pure precepts."
With a concentrated mind, reflect within yourself and well-guard your intentions.
If, within the True Dharma, one is able to be heedful,
then one will cross over the realm of old age and death, forever exhausting the root of all suffering.
Having heard this, all disciples should apply themselves with diligent effort;
transcending all desires, they shall not waver even a single hair.
This assembly is most excellent, possessing great wisdom and renown.
"The disciples are all valiant and courageous, and are revered by the multitude.

At that time, the devas, spirits, ghosts, and seers possessing the five supernatural powers all gathered within the Garden of Kapilavastu; seeing what Māra had done, they marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.
When the Buddha taught this Dharma, eighty-four thousand devas were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

3.20 The Āmaṅkura Sūtra (20) The Third Section: The Āmaṅkura Sūtra, First Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the Kosalā country together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. He arrived at Icchānaṅgalā, a brahmin village of the Kosalas, and stayed there for the night in the Icchānaṅgala Forest.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Puṣkarasādi who resided in the village of Ukkaḷā. That village was prosperous and flourishing, with a dense population; King Prasenajit had granted this village to the brahmin Puṣkarasādi as his *brahmadeya* (a land grant for religious purposes).

This Brahmin has maintained pure descent from both his father and mother for seven generations; he is not disparaged by others. He has mastered the recitation of the three ancient Vedas and can discern the meaning of all various scriptures. Furthermore, he is skilled in interpreting the marks of great men and the rituals of sacrifice, and he teaches five hundred disciples without ceasing.

The foremost disciple of that Māṇava was named Āmrapālī; for seven generations his lineage on both sides had been pure and true, such that he was never disparaged by others. He was proficient in reciting the three Vedas and could distinguish the various scriptures; furthermore, he was skilled in interpreting the marks of great men and the rituals of sacrifice. He also had five hundred Māṇava disciples whom he taught without ceasing, being no different from his own teacher.

At that time, the brahmin Pukkusāti heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who had left home to attain the Way, was traveling with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus to Icchānaṅgala, a brahmin village of the Kosalans, where he was staying in the Icchānaṅgala forest. He possessed a great reputation that resounded throughout the world; he was the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among gods, humans, Māras, or those belonging to the realm of Māra, among śramaṇas and brahmins, he had realized it for himself and taught the Dharma to others—a teaching excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, complete in meaning and phrasing, and pure in holy conduct.

"Such a true person should be visited and personally attended upon; I should now go to see the śramaṇa Gautama to see whether he truly possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man, whose fame has spread abroad, and whether he is as his reputation suggests."
"By what means can the marks of the Buddha be seen?
He then thought further:

"Now my disciple Āmātya has been of pure parentage for seven generations; he is not disparaged by others, and he has mastered the recitation of the three ancient Vedas. He is able to distinguish all kinds of scriptures and is skilled in interpreting the marks of a Great Man as well as the rituals of sacrifice. Only this man may be sent to observe the Buddha to determine whether these marks exist."
Then the brahmin immediately summoned his disciple Āmātya and said to him:
"Go and observe that śramaṇa Gautama; does he truly possess the thirty-two marks, or is it false?"
Then, Amātya immediately addressed his teacher, saying:
"By what means may I examine the marks of Gautama to discern whether they are real or false?
The teacher then replied:
"I now tell you this: whoever is endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man will certainly proceed to one of two destinations; of this there is no doubt.

If he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents, governing the people and all things through the Dharma, and possessing the seven treasures:

first, the treasure of the golden wheel; second, the treasure of the white elephant; third, the treasure of the dark-blue horse; fourth, the treasure of the divine jewel; fifth, the treasure of the jade-like woman; sixth, the treasure of the householder; and seventh, the treasure of the military commander."

The king had a thousand sons, valiant and highly wise, who subdued all enemies without the use of weapons; the world was in great peace, and within the realm, both people and creatures had nothing to fear.
If he does not delight in the world but leaves the household life to seek the Way, he shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
By this, one may know the truth or falsehood regarding Gautama.

Then, having received his teacher’s instruction, Ambaṭṭha immediately prepared his precious chariot and, taking five hundred young brahmin disciples, set out from the village at dawn and proceeded to the Icchānaṅgala forest.
Having arrived, he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot to where the World-Honored One was.
While the Buddha sat and he stood, or while the Buddha stood and he sat, they conversed together on the principles of the Dharma between them.
The Buddha asked the Māṇava,
"Have you ever engaged in such a discussion with the elder, long-established great Brahmins?
The Māṇava replied to the Buddha:
"What do you mean by this?
the Buddha asked the Māṇava.
"I am sitting while you stand; I am standing while you sit. We have been discussing together in between. Is such the manner in which your teacher discusses the Dharma?"
The Māṇava addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In our Brahminical discourse on the Dharma, when we sit, we sit together; when we stand, we stand together; and when we lie down, we lie down together."

Now these śramaṇas have disfigured their appearances and live as solitary widowers; they are lowly and inferior, practicing the dark and obscure teachings. When I engage in debate on the meaning of the Dharma with such as these, they show no restraint in their sitting or rising.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to him:
"You, Māṇava, have not yet been tamed.
When the Māṇava heard the World-Honored One address him as "you" and heard that he had not yet been tamed, he immediately became angry and resentful, and spoke in slander against the Buddha, saying:
"These Śākya seedlings are fond of harboring envy and malice; they possess neither righteousness nor the Dharma.
The Buddha said to the Māṇava:
"What fault do the Śākya seedlings have toward you?"
The Māṇava said: “Once, on a certain occasion, I was in the kingdom of Kapilavastu for the sake of some minor business concerning my teacher.

At that time, a great multitude of Śākya youths had gathered in the lecture hall for some small matter; seeing me coming from afar, they treated me with contempt and mockery, failing to observe proper etiquette and showing me no respect.”
The Buddha told the Māṇava:
"Those Śākya sons have returned to their own country, sporting and acting as they please, just like flying birds that enter and exit their nests and groves with complete freedom."
"The Śākya clansmen, while in their own country, sport with such sovereign ease; it is just like this.
The Māṇava addressed the Buddha, saying:

"In the world there are four castes—the Kṣatriyas, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vaiśyas, and the Śūdras. Among them, those of the other three castes always respect, revere, and make offerings to the Brāhmaṇas."
"The claim that those sons of the Śākyas should be treated in such a manner is incorrect.
Those Śākyas are commoners, lowly, base, and inferior, yet they do not show respect to me, a brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself in silence:
“O Māṇava! You repeatedly revile me with insults and speak of me as a low-born servant; shall I now recount my past origins to subdue you?
The Buddha addressed the Māṇava:
“What is your clan? The Māṇava replied, “My clan is Śabdavatsa.”
The Buddha told the māṇava:
"If your lineage is such, then you are of the Śākya slave caste.
At that time, those five hundred māṇava disciples all raised their voices and said to the Buddha:
"Do not speak these words! Namely:
'This Māṇava is of Śākya slave lineage.'"
Why is this? This great Māṇava is a true son of noble family;
he is handsome in appearance, possesses eloquence suited to the occasion, and is widely learned and well-informed, such that he is fully capable of engaging in debate with Gautama.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five hundred young brahmins:
"If your teacher is entirely as you have described him not to be, you should abandon him and debate with me;
but if your teacher possesses the qualities you have described, you should remain silent, and I shall debate with your teacher."
Then the five hundred māṇavas said to the Buddha,
“We shall remain silent and listen as we debate with our teacher.
Thereupon, all five hundred māṇavas became completely silent.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Āmātya:
"In the distant past, long ago, there was a king named Śrīghoṣa.
The king had four sons:
The first was named Mukhaprabha, the second Hastibhakṣa, the third Mārgadarśin, and the fourth Alaṃkāra.

When these four sons of the king committed a minor offense, the king banished them from the kingdom. They went to the south of the Snowy Mountains and dwelt in a forest of straight trees. Their mother and the rest of their family members all missed them and, having deliberated together, went to King Śreṇika and said: "Great King!"
"You should know that we have been separated from our four sons for a long time and wish to go see them.
The king then replied, "Go as you please."
At that time, having heard the king’s command, the mothers’ kinsfolk went to the Forest of Straight Trees on the southern side of the Snowy Mountains and arrived where the four sons were.
Then the mothers said:

"I give my daughter to your son, and you give your daughter to my son; let us thus be joined as couples and become husband and wife. Later, when a son is born, he shall be of handsome and upright appearance."

At that time, King Śreṇya heard that his four sons had each taken their respective mothers as wives, and that they had fathered sons who were handsome and upright. The king was immediately filled with joy and spoke these words:
"These are truly Śākyas!"
"O true Śākya youth!
You are able to establish yourself; for this reason you are named Śākya-Śākya.
In the language of Qin, this means "Able to Stand Firm in the Straight Forest."
Therefore it is called "Śākya.
"Śākya" in the language of Qin is also translated as "Direct."
King Śreṇika was formerly a member of the Śākya clan.

The king had a maidservant named Fangmian (Sīmantinī), who was of upright countenance. She entered into a liaison with a certain Brahmin and subsequently became pregnant, giving birth to a young son of the Mānava class. As soon as he fell to the ground, he was able to speak, and immediately addressed his parents:
"You should bathe me to remove all impurities and foulness."
‘When I have grown older, I shall personally repay his kindness.
Because he was able to speak immediately upon birth, he was named King of Sound (Śabdavasu).
Just as people today are terrified when someone can speak at birth, and thus call such a child "Frightening" (Bhīṣaṇaka); [so it was with him].
He was likewise; he was able to speak as soon as he was born, and was therefore named Śabdārāja.
From that time forward, the Brahmin caste took Śabdārāja as their clan name.
He further addressed the māṇava:
"Have you ever heard from the elders, the aged, or the great brahmins regarding the causal origins of this clan?
At that time, the māṇava remained silent and did not reply.
When he was asked thus a second time, he again did not answer.
When the Buddha asked a third time, he said to the Māṇava:

"I have asked you three times; you should answer quickly. If you do not answer, the Mārīcika Vajrapāṇi, who stands at my side holding a golden mallet, shall immediately split your head into seven pieces."

At that time, the Malla Vajrapāṇi stood in the air above the head of the māṇava, holding a golden mallet; if the māṇava did not answer the questions immediately, he would bring down the golden mallet and crush the māṇava’s head.
The Buddha said to the Mānava, "Look up.

The Mānava looked up and saw the Vajrapāṇi Mahākāla standing in mid-air, holding a golden mallet in his hand. Having seen him, he was struck with terror; his hair stood on end, and he immediately rose to move his seat closer to the World-Honored One. Relying upon the World-Honored One for protection and refuge, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Blessed One, please ask; I shall now answer.
The Buddha then addressed the Māṇava:
“Have you ever heard from the venerable elders and great brahmins such an account regarding one’s lineage?”
The Māṇava replied, “I have indeed heard it; such a thing truly exists.
At that time, the five hundred Māṇava disciples all raised their voices and said to one another:
"This Āmrapālī is truly of the Śākya slave lineage.
What the śramaṇa Gautama has spoken is the truth, yet we have acted improperly, harboring a mind of contempt."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"These five hundred young brahmins will surely harbor arrogance in the future and call him a slave; I shall now employ an expedient means to eliminate the name 'slave' for him."
He then addressed the five hundred māṇavas, saying: "All of you!
Be careful not to call him a man of slave stock."
Why is this so? That former brahmin was a great seer of immense power; when he demanded the king’s daughter from King Śreṇya, the king, out of fear, gave her to him immediately.
By these words of the Buddha, he was freed from the name of "slave.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Āmrapālī’s son, saying:
"What do you think, māṇava?"

Māṇava, if there is a Kṣatriya woman whose lineage has been pure for seven generations on both her father’s and mother’s sides, such that she is not disparaged by others, and she becomes the wife of a Brāhmaṇa and bears him a son—Māṇava!
"Suppose one were of upright appearance and entered among the Kṣatriya caste; would he be permitted to sit and receive water and recite the Kṣatriya dharma? He replied, "He would not."
“Did you obtain your father’s wealth and estate? He replied, “I did not.”
“Did you succeed to your father’s office? He replied, “I did not.”

“How is it, Māṇava? If there is a Brahmin girl whose lineage has been pure for seven generations on both her father’s and mother’s side, who has not been disparaged by others, and she becomes the wife of a Kṣatriya and gives birth to a boy of handsome appearance— would that boy, upon entering the assembly of Brahmins, be permitted to sit, rise, and receive water?”
He replied, "Yes. [The King asked:
"Can he recite the Brahminical laws, inherit his father’s estate, and succeed to his father’s office?"
He replied, “I have. [The Buddha asked: “How so, māṇava?”
"If a brahmin were to expel another brahmin and join the kṣatriya caste, would he be permitted to sit, rise, receive water, and recite the dharma of the kṣatriyas? He replied, "He would not."
“Having obtained his father’s inherited wealth, does he succeed to his father’s office? He replied, “He does not.”

“If a member of the kṣatriya caste were to expel another kṣatriya and take refuge with a brāhmaṇa, would he be permitted to sit and rise [in their company], receive water, recite the brāhmaṇa dharma, inherit his father’s estate, and succeed to his father’s office?”
He replied, “Yes. “Therefore, Māṇava! [he said.]
"Among women, the Kṣatriya woman is superior; among men, the Kṣatriya man is superior;
it is not the Brāhmaṇa. Brahmā himself spoke this verse:
"The Kṣatriya is supreme among those born, And his lineage is also pure."
“Perfectly endowed with knowledge and conduct, he is the most supreme among gods and humans.
The Buddha told the Māṇava:
“The Brahmā spoke this verse; it was well-spoken and not ill-spoken, and I approve of it. Why is that?”
I, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, also speak this meaning:
"The Kṣatriya is supreme among those born; his lineage is also pure and true.
Fully endowed with knowledge and conduct, he is the most excellent among gods and humans."
The Māṇava addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Gautama! Who is the unsurpassed person, perfected in knowledge and conduct?”
The Buddha told the māṇava:
“Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!”
"Reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake. He replied, "Indeed!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told the Māṇava:

"If a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, a Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, a Sugata, a Lokavid, an Anuttara, a Puruṣadamyasārathi, a Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, a Buddha, a Bhagavān—he realizes for himself alone among all the gods, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, māras, and Brahmās, and he teaches the Dharma to others."
The beginning is excellent, the middle is excellent, and the end is excellent; it is complete in meaning and phrasing, revealing pure conduct.
When householders, sons of householders, or those of other castes hear this True Dharma, they immediately give rise to faith and joy. With a heart of faith and joy, they think:
"I am currently a householder, bound by wife and children, unable to purely cultivate the holy life in its entirety."
"Now it would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the home life to practice the Way.

At another time, he abandoned his family wealth, renounced his kin, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, and left the home life to practice the Way. Together with other renunciants, he discarded all finery and ornaments, fulfilled all the precepts, and refrained from harming living beings.
"To lay aside the sword and staff, to harbor a sense of shame and remorse, and to regard all beings with loving-kindness—this is non-killing.
To lay aside the intent to steal, not taking what is not given, with a mind that is pure and free from any thought of private theft—this is non-stealing.
To abandon lustful desire, to purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), to be diligent and energetic, to remain unstained by desire, and to abide in purity—this is non-lust."
To abandon false speech, to be sincere and without deception, and not to mislead others—this is non-false speech.

To abandon divisive speech: if one hears something here, one does not transmit it there; if one hears something there, one does not transmit it here. One brings about reconciliation for those who are estranged, causing them to become affectionate and respectful toward one another. Whatever one says is harmonious and timely—this is non-divisive speech. To abandon harsh speech:

that which is coarse and rugged, which delights in distressing others and causes them to give rise to resentment and enmity—one abandons such words. One’s speech is instead gentle and soft, giving rise to no malice or harm, being of great benefit and loved by all people; they delight in hearing one's words—this is non-harsh speech.

Abandoning frivolous speech, one speaks at the appropriate time, truthfully and in accordance with the Dharma; one settles disputes according to the Vinaya, speaks only when there is a relevant cause, and does not utter words in vain—this is the abandonment of frivolous speech.

One abandons the drinking of intoxicants and stays away from occasions of heedlessness; one does not wear perfumes, flowers, or necklaces; one does not go to watch or listen to singing, dancing, or theatrical performances; one does not sit on high beds; one does not eat at improper times; one does not take or use gold, silver, or the seven treasures; one does not marry a wife or concubine; one does not keep slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, oxen, chickens, dogs, pigs, sheep, fields, houses, gardens, or pavilions; one does not deceive others with false measures or scales; one does not drag or pull others by the hands or fists; one does not extort debts through intimidation, nor does one slander or deceive others, nor act with hypocrisy or fraud.

Abandoning such evils and extinguishing all unwholesome matters of contention, he acts with knowledge of the proper time and does not act at improper times. He eats according to the capacity of his belly without hoarding, and wears clothing according to the needs of his body, taking only what is sufficient. His Dharma robes and alms bowl are always with him, just as the wings of a flying bird follow its body; so too is it for the bhikṣu who has no attachments.
“Māṇava! Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having received the faithful offerings of others, seek further accumulations and have no satiety regarding clothing and food;
those who enter my Dharma do not engage in such things.”
"Mañjuśrī! While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the offerings of the faithful, engage in their own livelihood by planting trees as dwellings for spirits and deities—
those who have entered my Dharma do not do such things."

"Mañjuśrī! While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the offerings of the faithful, further employ expedient means to seek various gains— such as ivory, assorted jewels, high and wide couches, various embroidered fabrics, and silken coverlets—
those who have entered my Dharma do not engage in such matters."

"Mañjuśrī! Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having received the offerings of the faithful, further employ various means to seek self-adornment: they rub their bodies with ghee and oil, bathe with scented water, smear themselves with fragrant powders, comb their hair with perfumed ointments, wear fine flower garlands, dye their eyes dark blue, apply cosmetics to beautify their faces, cleanse themselves with rings and clasps, look at themselves in mirrors, wear multicolored leather sandals, upper garments of pure white, carry swords and staves, have attendants, and travel in decorated jeweled carriages with jeweled canopies and fans.
Those who enter my Dharma do not engage in such things."

"Mañjuśrī! While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who consume the offerings of the faithful devote themselves exclusively to amusements— playing at chess, board games, and various games with eight, ten, or a hundred paths, up to all manner of paths and diverse jests—
those who have entered my Dharma do not engage in such things."

“Māṇava! Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, speak only of useless words that obstruct the Path—matters of kings, warfare, and military horses; matters of court officials, ministers, and the processions of mounted riders; matters of pleasure gardens and excursions; discussions of sleeping and waking, walking, and women; matters of clothing, food and drink, and kinsmen; and they also speak of entering the sea to gather treasures.
Those who enter my Dharma do not engage in such things.”

"Mañjuśrī! There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, employ countless expedients to engage in wrong livelihood—using flattery and pleasing words, manifesting signs, disparaging others, and seeking profit through profit.
Among those who have entered my Dharma, such things do not exist."

"Mañjuśrī! Just as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, engage only in disputes—whether in gardens and groves, at bathing pools, or in halls—mutually asserting their own correctness and criticizing others, saying:
'I know the sūtras and the vinaya, whereas you know nothing;'"
I follow the right path, while you head toward a deviant track;
you place the former after the latter and the latter before the former;
I am able to endure you, but you cannot endure me.
"Everything you have said is neither true nor correct;
if you have any doubts, you should come and ask me, for I am able to answer them all.
For one who enters my Dharma, such things do not exist."

“Māṇava! There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, further employ means to seek out diplomatic missions—acting as messengers for kings, royal ministers, brāhmaṇas, or householders, traveling from here to there and from there to here, carrying messages from this side to deliver to that side, or from that side to deliver to this side, whether acting on their own behalf or instructing others to do so.
For one who has entered my Dharma, such things do not exist.”

Māṇava! There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, devote themselves solely to matters of military arrays and combat; or they practice with swords and staves, bows and arrows; or they engage in fighting cocks, dogs, pigs, sheep, elephants, horses, oxen, and camels; or they engage in fighting men and women, and produce various sounds:
the sound of conchs, the sound of drums, the sound of singing, the sound of dancing, the hoisting of banners, and various kinds of acrobatic performances.
Among those who have entered my Dharma, there is no such thing. Māṇava!

Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive dharmas and maintain themselves through wrong livelihoods; they observe the physiognomy of men and women—whether they are auspicious or inauspicious, beautiful or ugly—as well as the physiognomy of animals, in order to seek gain and support.
"Those who enter my Dharma do not engage in such matters. Māṇava!

There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and live by wrong livelihoods; they summon spirits or expel them, or cause them to remain; they perform various incantations and prayers through countless methods, intimidating people, gathering or dispersing them, causing suffering or joy; they also perform rites for stabilizing the womb or producing clothing, and can curse people to become donkeys or horses, or cause others to become blind, deaf, or mute; they display various technical skills, join their palms toward the sun and moon, and perform various austerities in pursuit of gain and support."
For one who has entered my Dharma, such things do not exist.

Māṇava! Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and live by wrong livelihoods; they perform incantations for the sick, recite malevolent spells, or perform auspicious charms, or practice medical arts, acupuncture, moxibustion, and herbal remedies to treat various ailments.
For one who has entered my Dharma, such things do not exist. Māṇava!

There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and maintain themselves through wrong livelihoods: some by reciting spells over water and fire; some by performing exorcisms for spirits; some by reciting spells for kṣatriyas, spells for birds, or spells for the limbs of the body; some by using talismanic spells for pacifying dwellings; some by performing incantations to undo the effects of fire burns or rat bites; some by reciting books on the separation of death and birth, or reading books on dreams; some by examining the hands and faces of others, or reciting books on celestial phenomena, or reciting books on all manner of sounds.
Among those who have entered my Dharma, such things do not exist. Māṇava!

There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and maintain themselves through wrong livelihood; they observe the signs of the heavens and predict whether it will rain or not, whether prices will rise or fall, whether there will be much sickness or little, and whether there will be terror or peace. They may speak of earthquakes, comets, or the eclipses of the sun and moon; they may say that a star has been eclipsed or that it has not been eclipsed; they speak thus of auspicious omens and thus of evil portents.
"Those who have entered my Dharma do not engage in such matters. Māṇava!

There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive dharmas and live by wrong livelihoods, saying: 'This country is superior to that one; that country is not as good as this.'"
Some say that their country is superior to this one, while this country is inferior;
they observe signs for good or ill fortune and speak of its prosperity or decline.
Those who enter my Dharma do not engage in such matters.

One should simply cultivate the noble precepts with a mind free from defiled attachment, harboring inner joy and happiness. Although the eyes see forms, one does not grasp at their signs; the eye is not bound or fettered by forms. Firmly established in tranquility, one is without craving or clinging, and likewise without sorrow or affliction. One does not leak out any evils, steadfastly upholding the categories of the precepts and skillfully guarding the faculty of the eye. The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Skillfully governing the six contacts, one protects, maintains, and subdues them to attain peace and security; it is like a chariot drawn by four horses on level ground, where a skilled driver, holding the whip and reins, ensures they do not stray from the track. In this same way, a bhikṣu governs the horses of the six sense faculties, remaining secure and without fail.

He possesses such noble ethical discipline and attains the noble faculty of the eye; he knows moderation in eating and does not crave flavors, consuming food merely to sustain the body so that it remains free from affliction and suffering, without becoming arrogant. He harmonizes his body so that old suffering is extinguished and new suffering does not arise, maintaining strength without toil, so that his body may dwell in peace and happiness.
It is just as if someone were to apply medicine to a wound, seeking only to heal it and not for the sake of adornment or to exalt himself. Māṇava!
In this same way, a bhikṣu consumes food merely to sustain his body, harboring no arrogance or self-indulgence.
Furthermore, it is like oiling a carriage so that it may run smoothly for the purpose of transport and reach its destination;
in the same way, a bhikṣu consumes food merely to sustain the body, desiring to practice the Path.

“Māṇava! When a bhikṣu is thus endowed with noble ethical discipline, has attained noble faculties, knows moderation in eating, and practices diligence and wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night—”
Furthermore, during the day, whether walking or sitting, he constantly maintains single-minded mindfulness to eliminate the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
During the first watch of the night, whether walking or sitting, he constantly maintains single-minded mindfulness to eliminate the various hindrances;
continuing thus until the middle watch, he lies down on his right side, mindful that it is time to rise, fixing his attention on light so that his mind remains undisturbed.
When the latter part of the night arrives, he rises to engage in reflection; whether walking or sitting, he constantly maintains single-minded mindfulness to eliminate the various hindrances.

A bhikṣu who is thus fully endowed with noble ethical discipline, possesses noble faculties, knows moderation in eating, and applies himself with diligence to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, remains constantly mindful and single-minded without confusion.
"What is meant by a bhikṣu’s mindfulness being undisturbed?
It is when a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally as body, diligent and unflagging, with mindfulness established and not forgotten, removing worldly greed and sorrow;

he contemplates the body externally as body, and both internally and externally as body, diligent and unflagging, with mindfulness established and not forgotten, removing worldly greed and sorrow. The same applies to the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and phenomena. This is called a bhikṣu’s mindfulness being undisturbed."
What is one-pointedness of mind?

It is when a bhikṣu, whether walking or entering and leaving, looking to the left or right, bending or stretching, lifting or lowering his body, holding his robes and bowl, receiving food and drink, attending to the calls of nature, sleeping or waking, sitting or standing, speaking or remaining silent—at all times constantly maintains mindfulness with a single mind and does not lose his dignified deportment; this is called one-pointedness of mind.
It is like a person traveling with a great multitude; whether they are at the front, in the middle, or at the rear, they always attain peace and security, free from all fear.
"Mañjuśrī! When a bhikṣu walks, stands, sits, or lies down—indeed, from his speech to his silence—he is always mindful with a single-pointed mind, free from anxiety and fear.

Possessing such noble precepts and noble faculties, knowing moderation in eating, he applies himself with diligence to wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night; he is always mindful with a single-pointed mind, without confusion, and delights in staying in quiet places, at the foot of trees, or among burial mounds."

Whether in a mountain cave, or in the open air, or among heaps of refuse, when the time comes for alms, he returns, washes his hands and feet, sets aside his robes and bowl, sits cross-legged, straightens his body and composes his mind, and fixes his mindfulness before him.

He eliminates stinginess and greed, so that the mind does not dwell with them; he extinguishes anger and resentment, so that there is no enmity or bondage; his mind abides in purity and constantly maintains loving-kindness and compassion;
he eliminates drowsiness, fixing his attention on clarity; his mindfulness is without confusion, and he cuts off frivolous playfulness, so that the mind does not dwell with it.

Internally practicing tranquility, he extinguishes the restless and playful mind, cuts off doubt and confusion, and having already crossed over the net of uncertainty, his mind is single-mindedly focused upon wholesome dharmas.
It is like a servant who, having been granted a noble surname by his master, attains peace and liberation, is freed from servitude, and with a joyful heart, is no longer subject to anxiety or fear.

"Furthermore, it is like a person who borrows wealth to engage in business and returns with a great profit. Having returned the original principal to the owner and possessing sufficient remaining wealth for their own use, they think to themselves:

'When I first borrowed the wealth, I feared things might not go as hoped; now, having returned the principal to the owner and having enough remaining wealth for my needs, I am free from further anxiety or fear,' and they experience great joy."

It is like a person who has suffered from a long illness; having recovered from that illness, with his food and drink now properly digested and his physical strength and complexion fully restored, he thinks to himself:

"I previously had this illness, but now I have recovered; my food and drink are digested and my strength and complexion are sufficient. I no longer have any anxiety or fear," and he gives rise to great joy.
Furthermore, it is like a person who has been long confined in a prison and is safely released; he thinks to himself:
"I was previously imprisoned, but now I am liberated; there is no longer any sorrow or fear," and he gives rise to great joy.
Furthermore, it is like a person who, carrying much wealth and treasure, traverses a vast wilderness without encountering bandits or thieves and passes through safely; he thinks to himself:
"I have carried my wealth and treasure across this perilous difficulty; I have no further cause for worry or fear. He gives rise to great joy, and his mind is peaceful and blissful.
“Māṇava! A bhikṣu who is covered by the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) is constantly filled with anxiety and fear, just like a slave.

He is like a debtor, one long ill, one in prison, or one traveling through a vast wilderness; he sees for himself that he has not yet escaped. With his mind shrouded by the various aggregates and hindrances, obscured and darkened, his eye of wisdom is not clear. He then applies himself with diligence to abandon sensual desires and unwholesome states; accompanied by directed thought (vitakka) and evaluation (vicāra), and born of seclusion, he attains the joy and happiness of the first dhyāna.”
That joy and rapture moisten and saturate his body, pervading it completely and overflowing until there is no part that is not filled.
It is like a skilled person who places various medicinal herbs in a vessel for bathing and douses it with water; both the interior and exterior become moistened, with nothing left unpervaded.
In this way, a bhikṣu attains the first dhyāna; joy and bliss pervade his entire body, filling it completely without exception.
Thus it is, māṇava! This is the first instance of attaining happiness in the present life. Why is that?
"This results from diligence, mindfulness free from confusion, and that which is attained by delighting in quiet seclusion.

"He, having abandoned applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), gives rise to faith; with one-pointed concentration, being without applied or sustained thought, he enters the second dhyāna, wherein joy and bliss born of concentration arise."

Having thus become moistened by the body through one-pointed joy and delight, it becomes completely saturated and overflows everywhere until there is no part that is not filled. It is like a spring of cool water on a mountain peak that wells up from within and does not come from without; from this very pool, pure water emerges and soaks itself, pervading everything without exception.

“Māṇava! When a bhikṣu thus enters the second dhyāna, there arises joy and bliss born of concentration, filling him completely; this is the second instance of attaining happiness in the present body.”

“Having abandoned joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware; he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones say, ‘He dwells in happiness who is equanimous and mindful,’ and thus enters the third dhyāna.”

His body is devoid of rapture, yet it is saturated, permeated, and completely suffused with bliss, such that there is no part of it not filled. It is like the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers, which have just emerged from the mud but have not yet risen above the water; their roots, stalks, branches, and leaves are all saturated with water, such that there is nothing of them that is not thoroughly pervaded.
Māṇava! In this way, a bhikṣu enters the third dhyāna.
Detached from joy, he dwells in bliss, saturating his body so that there is no part of it not pervaded by it; this is the third instance of attaining bliss in the present life.

"He abandons joy and pleasure; with the prior cessation of sorrow and rapture, he enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity and mindfulness, pure and refined. His body and mind are purified, filled to overflowing, and there is no part that is not thoroughly pervaded."
It is just as if there were a person who has bathed and cleansed themselves, covering their body with a new white cotton cloth, so that their entire frame is pure. Māṇava!

In this way, a bhikṣu enters the fourth dhyāna; his mind is pure and fills his body, pervading it without exception. Furthermore, having entered the fourth dhyāna, his mind neither increases nor decreases, nor does it waver; he dwells in a state free from craving and hatred, a ground of immovability.

It is like a sealed chamber, both inside and out coated and treated, with doors and windows firmly shut so that there is no wind or dust; within it a lamp is lit, undisturbed by any contact, and its flame remains perfectly still and motionless.

"Mañjuśrī! When a bhikṣu thus enters the fourth dhyāna, his mind is without increase or decrease, nor does it waver; he abides in a state free from craving and aversion, a ground of immovability. This is the fourth instance of attaining happiness in the present life. Why is this so?"
"This is obtained through diligent and unremitting effort, through mindfulness that is not confused, and through delighting in dwelling in quiet seclusion.

Having attained a concentrated mind that is pure and free from defilement, supple and well-tamed, and abiding on the stage of immovability, he gives rise within his own body to a mind of transformation and creates another body, complete with all limbs and joints and lacking no sense faculties. He reflects thus:

'This physical body, composed of the four great elements, has transformed into that other body; this body is one thing and that body is another. From this body a mind arises, which transforms into that body, complete with all sense faculties and lacking no limbs or joints.'"
"It is, for example, like a person who draws a sword from its scabbard and thinks:
'The scabbard is one thing and the sword is another, yet the sword has emerged from the scabbard.
Or again, it is like a person who twists hemp fibers into a rope and thinks:"
"Just as the hemp is one thing and the rope another, yet the rope emerges from the hemp;
or again, as if someone were to take a snake out of a basket and think:
'The basket is one thing and the snake another, yet the snake emerges from the basket.'"
"Furthermore, Maṇava, it is as if someone were to take a garment out of a chest and think:
'The chest is one thing and the garment is another, yet the garment has come out from the chest.'"
The bhikṣu is also like this; this is the supreme dharma first attained. Why is this so?
It is because it is obtained through diligence, through mindfulness that is not confused, and through delighting in dwelling in quiet seclusion.

“Having attained a concentrated mind that is pure and stainless, supple, tamed, and established on the immovable stage, he directs his mind from within his own physical body composed of the four great elements and creates a transformation body, complete with all sense faculties and limbs. He then reflects:

‘This body is a composite of the four great elements, while that body exists as a transformation; this body is one thing and that body is another. This mind, which resided within this body and depended upon it for its dwelling, has now entered into the transformation body.’”

"It is like lapis lazuli or a mani-jewel, polished until it is exceedingly bright, pure, and free from defilement. If one were to thread it with blue, yellow, or red cords, a person with sight who held it in the palm of their hand and examined it would know that the jewel is distinct from the cord and the cord is distinct [from the jewel], yet the cord depends upon the jewel, passing from one jewel to the next."
"Mañjuśrī! A bhikṣu contemplates the mind as it abides dependent upon this body; even when he transforms into another body, it is likewise so. This is the second supreme dharma of a bhikṣu."
Why is this so? It is because it is attained through diligent effort, unconfused mindfulness, and the delight in dwelling alone in seclusion.

With a concentrated mind that is pure and stainless, supple and well-tamed, abiding on the stage of immovability, he single-mindedly cultivates the realization of the knowledge of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), being able to perform various transformations: transforming a single body into countless bodies, and merging those countless bodies back into one.
The body can fly, encountering no obstruction from stone walls;
one wanders through the air like a bird and treads upon water as if on land;
and the body emits smoke and flames like a great conflagration.
They can touch the sun and moon with their hands and reach the Brahma Heaven in an instant.
It is like a skilled potter who, having well-prepared his clay, can fashion whatever vessel he desires according to his will, bringing great benefit to many.
It is also like a skilled carpenter who is well able to treat wood; he can create whatever he desires at will and accomplish it with mastery, bringing great benefit to many.

It is also like a master ivory-carver who skillfully treats elephant tusks, or like a goldsmith who skillfully refines pure gold; they can create whatever they desire at will, bringing great benefit to many.

"Mañjuśrī! When a bhikṣu’s mind is thus concentrated and pure, abiding in the stage of immovability, he can manifest transformations at will, even reaching out his hand to touch the sun and moon and standing as far as the Brahma Heaven; this is the third supreme quality of a bhikṣu."
"With his mind concentrated, pure and stainless, supple and well-tamed, abiding in the stage of immovability, he cultivates with single-minded focus and realizes the knowledge of the divine ear."
The divine ear of that being is pure and surpasses the human ear; it hears two kinds of sounds:
celestial sounds and human sounds.

It is like a great lecture hall within a city, high, wide, and spacious; if a person with keen hearing dwells inside this hall, they hear every variety of sound within the hall without exerting any effort to listen.
In this way, bhikṣu, because his mind is concentrated, his divine ear becomes purified, and he hears two kinds of sounds.
Māṇava, this is the fourth superior quality of a bhikṣu.
"With a mind concentrated, pure and stainless, supple and well-tamed, abiding in the stage of immovability, he cultivates with single-mindedness and realizes the knowledge of others' minds."

He knows the minds of others—whether they possess desire or are free from desire, whether they are defiled or undefiled, whether they possess delusion or are free from delusion; he knows whether the mind is expansive or narrow, small or great, concentrated or distracted, bound or liberated, superior or inferior, up to the unsurpassed mind—he knows them all completely.
For example, if a person looks at themselves in clear water, they will certainly discern their own beauty or flaws;
so it is with a bhikṣu: because his mind is pure, he is able to know the minds of others.
"Mañjuśrī! This is the fifth supreme quality of a bhikṣu.

With his mind concentrated, pure and stainless, supple and subdued, abiding in the stage of immovability, he practices with single-mindedness to realize the knowledge of past lives. He is then able to recollect and recognize numerous various kinds of past existences: from one life up to countless lives; the cycles of kalpas of formation and destruction; dying here and being born there; names, surnames, and lineages; the quality of food and drink; the length of lifespan; the suffering and happiness experienced; and the physical form, appearance, and characteristics—all these he fully recollects and recognizes."

For example, suppose there is a person who travels from his own village to another country or town; while staying there, whether walking or standing, speaking or remaining silent, he then travels from that country to yet another, and so on in succession until he returns to his native land. Without exerting any mental or physical effort, he is able to recall everything he experienced in all the countries he visited—from where he went to where, and from where he came to here—including every instance of walking, standing, speaking, and remaining silent. He remembers them all completely.

"Mañjuśrī! When a bhikṣu, with a concentrated mind that is pure and stainless, abides in the stage of immovability, is able to recollect the events of countless eons through the knowledge of past lives—this is the first supreme attainment of a bhikṣu."

Ignorance is eternally extinguished and the dharma of great illumination arises; darkness is eliminated and the dharma of radiance arises. This is the bhikṣu’s clear knowledge of past lives. Why is this so?
"This arises from diligent effort, mindfulness free from confusion, and the attainment gained by delighting in solitary seclusion.
With a concentrated mind, pure and stainless, supple and subdued, abiding in the unmoving state, he single-mindedly cultivates the realization of the wisdom that perceives birth and death."

With his purified divine eye, he sees beings dying here and being born there, passing from that place to this one; he perceives their beautiful or ugly forms, their good or evil karmic fruits, their noble or lowly status, and knows all the causes and conditions of the retributive consequences of the deeds they have performed.

This person acts wickedly in body, speaks wickedly with the mouth, and thinks wickedly with the mind; they slander the noble and holy ones, believe in heterodox and inverted views, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, fall into the three evil realms.

This person acts virtuously in body, speaks virtuously with the mouth, and thinks virtuously with the mind; they do not slander the noble and holy ones, but perceive correctly and practice with faith; upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they are reborn among devas or humans.

With the purity of the divine eye, he sees all sentient beings according to their karmic conditions, coming and going through the five realms of existence. It is like a person with clear vision standing atop a great, lofty tower at a crossroads on a wide, level plain within a city, observing all the people traveling east, west, south, and north, seeing all their movements and actions in their entirety.
Māṇava! When a bhikṣu, with a mind thus purified by concentration, abides in the state of imperturbability, he realizes the knowledge of birth and death.

With the purified divine eye, he sees all beings as they perform good and evil deeds, how they undergo rebirth according to their karma, and how they come and go through the five destinies; he knows all this. This is the second clear knowledge attained by a bhikṣu.

To sever ignorance and give rise to the light of wisdom, to abandon darkness and bring forth the radiance of insight—this is the realization of the knowledge that witnesses the birth and death of sentient beings.
Why is this so? It is because it is attained through diligent effort, through mindfulness that is undisturbed, and through delighting in solitary seclusion.
With a concentrated mind—pure, stainless, supple, and well-tamed—he dwells on the stage of immovability and single-mindedly cultivates the realization of untainted wisdom.

He knows the noble truth of suffering as it really is; he knows the origin of the outflows as it really is; he knows the cessation of the outflows as it really is; and he knows the path leading to the cessation of the outflows as it really is.

Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflows of sensuality, existence, and ignorance; he attains the knowledge of liberation. Birth and death have come to an end, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence.
For example, in clear water there may be wood, stones, fish, turtles, and other aquatic creatures moving here and there; a person with sight perceives them clearly, knowing:
"This is wood or stone; these are fish and turtles."

“Māṇava! When a bhikṣu, with a mind thus purified by concentration, dwells in the stage of immovability and attains the realization of untainted knowledge, up to the point of not undergoing further existence—this is the bhikṣu’s attainment of the third clear knowledge.”
To sever ignorance and give rise to the light of wisdom, to abandon darkness and bring forth the radiance of great knowledge—this is the untainted light of wisdom. Why is this so?
"This is obtained through diligent effort, undistracted mindfulness, and delighting in solitary seclusion. Māṇava!
This is the unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct; what do you think of this?"
"Is such clear conduct as this correct or incorrect?
The Buddha told the Māṇava:
"There are those who, unable to attain the unsurpassed perfection of clear conduct, nevertheless practice four skillful means. What are these four?"

Māṇava! There may be someone who, not having attained the unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct, carries a carrying-pole basket upon his shoulder and enters the mountains to seek medicinal herbs, eating the roots of trees.
This is it, Māṇava! One who has not attained the unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct practices the foremost skillful means. How so, Māṇava?
"This is the first skillful means; do you and your teacher practice this dharma? He replied, "No."
The Buddha told the Māṇava:

"You are of humble origin and do not distinguish between the true and the false; yet you have slandered and reviled the sons of the Śākya, thereby planting the roots of your own transgressions and lengthening the foundations for rebirth in hell."
Furthermore, Māṇava!

There is a person who is unable to attain the unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct, yet he carries a water-pot in his hand, holds a staff, practices arithmetic, enters the mountain forests, and eats fruits that have fallen of their own accord.
This is it, Māṇava! Without having attained the unsurpassed perfection of knowledge and conduct, one practices the second expedient. What do you think, Māṇava?
Do you and your teacher practice this dharma?
He replied, “No. The Buddha said to the Māṇava:

"You are of humble and lowly station, yet you fail to distinguish truth from falsehood; by thus slandering and showing contempt for the sons of Śākya, you plant the roots of sin and lengthen the foundation of hell."
Furthermore, Māṇava!

Without having attained unsurpassed perfection in knowledge and conduct, one might abandon the previous gathering of medicinal herbs and picking of fallen fruits, return toward the village to rely upon human society, erect a grass hut, and subsist on leaves of plants and trees.
Māṇava! This is called failing to attain the perfection of knowledge and conduct, yet practicing the third method.
What do you think, Māṇava?
"Do you and your teacher practice this dharma? He replied, "No."
The Buddha told the Māṇava:

"You, being so lowly and ignorant of the true from the false, have slandered and treated with contempt the sons of the Śākya; you have thus planted the roots of sin for yourself and extended the foundation of hell—this constitutes the third expedient means."
Furthermore, Māṇava!

One who has not attained unsurpassed perfection in knowledge and conduct (vidyā-caraṇa-sampanna), yet does not eat medicinal herbs, does not eat fallen fruits, and does not eat grass or leaves, but instead builds great halls and pavilions in villages and cities to provide for all travelers passing by from the east, west, south, and north according to their needs—this is practicing the fourth means (upāya) while failing to attain unsurpassed perfection in knowledge and conduct.
"What do you think, Māṇava?
Do you and your teacher practice this Dharma? He replied:
"No," the Buddha told the Māṇava.

"Since you are so lowly and ignorant of the true from the false, yet you have slandered and treated the sons of the Śākya with contempt, you have planted the roots of sin for yourself and extended the foundation of hell. How is this, Māṇava?"
The ancient brahmins and various ṛṣis possessed many arts and skills, and they praised and recited what they had originally studied and practiced, just as the brahmins of today recite and proclaim:

first, Aṭama; second, Vāma; third, Vāmadeva; fourth, Viśvāmitra; fifth, Indrota; sixth, Yājñavalkya; seventh, Parāśara; eighth, Kāśyapa; ninth, Āruṇi; tenth, Gautama; eleventh, Śaunaka; twelfth, Bhāradvāja.
"Do all such great seers and brahmins dig moats and erect halls and pavilions, as your teacher and his disciples now do? He replied, "No."
“Did those great sages ever build walls and moats around their dwellings to reside within them, as your teachers and disciples do now?”
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked:
“Do those great seers ever occupy high beds with thick mattresses and fine, soft rugs, as your teachers and disciples do now?”
He replied, “No.
[The King asked,] “Do those great seers ever amuse themselves with gold, silver, necklaces, garlands of various colors, and beautiful women, as your teachers and disciples do?”

Do those great seers ride in precious chariots, led by attendants holding fly-whisks, with white canopies shading them, holding jeweled whisks in their hands, wearing multicolored jeweled sandals, and clad in pure white cotton garments—just as you and your disciples are dressed now?
He replied, "No, Mañava. "Mañava! [the Buddha said.]

You, being of such lowly and humble station, fail to distinguish between the true and the false; yet you have slandered and treated with contempt the sons of the Śākyas, thereby planting the roots of your own sin and lengthening the foundation for rebirth in hell.
"What do you think, Māṇava?

Suppose those great seers and ancient brāhmaṇas praised and recited what they had traditionally chanted, just as the brāhmaṇas of today praise and recite the *Aṭṭhaka* and other such texts; if one were to transmit what they said and teach it to others in the hope of being reborn in the Brahmā world, such a thing is impossible."

It is just as if, Māṇava, King Pasenadi were deliberating with others—whether with other kings, or with ministers, brahmins, or householders—and some common person, having overheard them, were to enter the city of Śrāvastī and, upon meeting someone, say: "King Pasenadi has spoken thus."
"What do you think, Māṇava?
Would the king engage in discussion with such a person? He replied:
"No. "Māṇava! If this person were to recite the king’s words and speak them to others, would he be fit to serve as a minister to the king?"
He replied, "That is impossible, Māṇava. "Māṇava! [the other asked].

If you today transmit the teachings of the ancient seers, the great sages, and the former brahmins, reciting them for others with the desire to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven, such a thing is impossible.
"How is it, Māṇava? When you receive offerings from others, are you able to practice in accordance with the Dharma?"
He replied, “It is so,
Gautama! Having received the offerings of others, one should practice in accordance with the Dharma.”

“Māṇava! Your teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa has received a royal village grant, yet when he debates with King Pasenadi, he speaks irrelevant and useless words rather than admonishing him with matters of right conduct. You should now examine both yourself and your teacher’s faults; set this matter aside for a moment and simply seek the reason for which you have come.”

The Māṇava immediately raised his eyes to behold the body of the Tathāgata, seeking the various marks and signs; he saw all the other marks completely, yet failed to see two signs, and his mind was instantly filled with doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought silently to himself:
"Now this Māṇava does not perceive the two marks; for this reason, he has given rise to doubt.
He then immediately displayed the mark of the broad and long tongue, licking his ears and covering his face.
At that time, that māṇava again had doubts regarding one particular mark. The World-Honored One thought to himself, "This māṇava still harbors doubts about one mark.
He then employed his supernormal powers to cause the māṇava alone to see the sheathed organ of a stallion.
At that time, having fully observed the marks, the Māṇava no longer harbored any doubt regarding the Tathāgata; he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.
Then, the brahmin Vairaṭīputra was standing outside the gate; seeing his disciple approaching from afar, he went out to meet him and asked:
"Did you observe whether Gautama truly possesses the marks?"
"Are his merit and spiritual power truly as you have heard?
He then addressed his teacher, saying:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama is fully endowed with all thirty-two marks; his merit and spiritual power are indeed as you have heard."
The teacher asked again:
"Have you had even a brief conversation with Gautama? He replied:
“I have indeed exchanged words with Gautama.
The teacher asked again:
“What matters did you discuss with Gautama?”
Then, the young brahmin related his discussion with the Buddha in full to his teacher. The teacher said:
"Now that I have produced such an intelligent disciple as this, we shall enter hell before long. Why is that? Because..."
