"You spoke words praising the various desires and disparaging Gautama, causing him displeasure and making him grow distant from me. You and your clever disciples have brought this about; it will not be long before you cause me to enter hell."
Thereupon, his teacher, harboring resentment and a mind of malice, immediately kicked the young brahmin student so that he fell, while the teacher himself mounted the carriage.
At that moment, as the young brahmin student was falling from the carriage, he instantly developed white leprosy.
At that time, the brahmin Pokkharasāda looked up at the sun and thought to himself:
"It is not the right time now to visit the śramaṇa Gautama; I must wait until tomorrow before going to visit and inquire."

On the following morning, he prepared his precious carriage and, surrounded by five hundred disciples in attendance before and behind him, proceeded to the Icchānaṅgala forest. There, he alighted from the carriage and advanced on foot until he reached the place where the World-Honored One was. After exchanging greetings, he sat to one side and gazed up at the body of the Tathāgata; he beheld all the marks of excellence, yet he failed to see two of them.
At that time, the brahmin harbored doubts regarding two marks; the Buddha, knowing his thoughts, immediately manifested the mark of the broad and long tongue, licking his ears and covering his face.
Then, the brahmin again harbored doubts regarding one mark; the Buddha, knowing his thoughts, employed his supernormal powers to cause him to see the sheathed horse organ.
At that time, the brahmin fully beheld the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks; his mind was immediately awakened and he was no longer in doubt. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If, while I am traveling, I encounter the Buddha on the road and briefly stop my vehicle, you should know that I have already paid homage to the World-Honored One. Why is this so?"
“I have received a fief from another village; if I were to dismount, I would lose this fief and my ill repute would spread.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If I were to dismount, unsheathe my sword, remove my parasol, set aside my banner and standard, and take off my water-pot and sandals, you should know that I have already paid homage to the Tathāgata. Why is this so?”
"I have received a fief from another, and thus I possess the five dignified deportments; if I were to prostrate, I would immediately lose my fief, and a bad reputation would spread.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If, while among the assembly, I see the Buddha and rise, or if I bare my right shoulder and announce my clan and name, it should be known that I have already paid homage to the Tathāgata. Why is this so?"
"I have received a fief from another; if I were to perform prostrations, I would lose my domain and a bad reputation would spread.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṃgha. Please accept me as an upāsaka within the True Dharma!"

"From this day forward, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants; I only pray that the World-Honored One and the great assembly will accept my invitation."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the Buddha was silent, the brahmin knew he had granted his consent; he immediately rose from his seat and, without even realizing it, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Upon returning, he prepared a meal; once the provisions were ready, he returned to inform [the Buddha]:
"The time has come.
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty people, went to his house and sat down upon the seats.

At that time, the brahmin personally served various kinds of sweet delicacies to the Buddha and the Sangha. When the meal was finished and the bowls removed, and after the water for washing had been offered, the brahmin took the arm of his disciple Āmātya with his right hand and approached the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant him permission to repent!"
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will grant him permission to repent!
Thus he requested three times, and again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Just as a well-trained elephant or horse may stumble but returns once more to the correct path, so it is with this man; though he has committed a transgression, I pray you will grant him permission to repent.”
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I shall cause your lifespan to be extended and grant you peace and security in this present life; I shall also cause your disciple’s white leprosy to be cured."
As soon as the Buddha had finished speaking, that disciple’s white leprosy was immediately cured.

Then, the brahmin took a small seat and sat before the Buddha. The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma to the brahmin, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him. He spoke on generosity, on ethical discipline, and on rebirth in heaven; he explained that sensual desires are defilements, that the outflows are afflictions, and that the way of escape is supreme, thus unfolding the teaching of purity.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the brahmin’s mind was already pliant, pure, and stainless, and capable of receiving the teachings of the Way, spoke—according to the constant dharma of all Buddhas—the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Escape from Suffering.

At that time, the brahmin, while still on his seat, was distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; just as a clean, white cloth is easily dyed, so it was with the brahmin Puṣkarasādi.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma, he became certain of the fruit of the Path, ceased to believe in other paths, and attained fearlessness. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now take refuge three times in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; please accept me as a lay follower within the True Dharma!"

"For as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, deception, and drinking alcohol. I only pray that the World-Honored One and the great assembly, out of compassion for me, will accept my invitation for seven days."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Thereupon, the brahmin provided various kinds of offerings to the Buddha and the great assembly for seven days.
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One set out to travel among the people.
Not long after the Buddha had departed, the brahmin Puṣkarasādi fell ill and passed away.
When the bhikṣus heard that this brahmin had passed away after making offerings to the Buddha for seven days, they each thought to themselves:
"Now that he has died, in which realm of existence will he be reborn?"
At that time, a group of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated before the Buddha, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After that brahmin had made offerings to the Buddha for seven days, at the dissolution of his body and the end of his life, where will he be reborn?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"This son of good family has universally gathered all virtues and is fully endowed with every dharma; he does not violate the practice of the Dharma, has severed the five lower fetters, and will attain parinirvāṇa there, never again returning to this world."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Thirteen.
*The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Fascicle Fourteen.
Translated by Buddhayaśas together with Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
21. Brahmajāla Sūtra (21). Part Three: The Brahmajāla Sūtra, Second.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus. While wandering among the people, he arrived at the Bamboo Grove and stayed overnight at the Royal Hall.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Sunetra; Sunetra’s disciple was named Brahmāda. Master and disciple were constantly following behind the Buddha. Yet, the brahmin Sunetra used countless skillful means to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, while his disciple Brahmāda used countless skillful means to praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. Thus, the two, master and disciple, each harbored different intentions and were in mutual opposition.
Why is this so? It is because of different practices, different views, and different associations.
At that time, after their almsround, a great number of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall and engaged in this discussion:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!
The World-Honored One possesses great supernormal powers and is fully endowed with majestic virtue; he knows completely the inclinations and intentions of all sentient beings."
Thus, the brahmin Sunakṣatra and his disciple Brahmadatta followed the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus;

yet the brahmin Sunakṣatra used countless skillful means to slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, while his disciple Brahmadatta used countless skillful means to praise the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
This was because the teacher and disciple each harbored different intentions, held different views, practiced differently, and associated with different circles.

At that time, the World-Honored One, while in his private chamber, heard with his divine ear—which surpasses that of humans—the discussion among the bhikṣus. The World-Honored One rose from his chamber and went to the lecture hall; sitting before the great assembly, he asked them knowingly:
"Bhikṣus! [What have you been discussing?]"
"For what reason and by what cause have you gathered here in this lecture hall?
What is it that you are discussing?
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"After we had finished our almsround, we gathered in this lecture hall and discussed together, saying:
'How extraordinary! How marvelous! "
The Tathāgata possesses great supernormal powers and is fully endowed with majestic virtue; he knows completely the inclinations and intentions of all sentient beings.

Now, while the brahmin Sunanda and his disciple Brahmadatta constantly follow the Tathāgata and the community of monks, Sunanda uses countless skillful means to slander the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, whereas his disciple Brahmadatta uses countless skillful means to praise the Tathāgata, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
"Why is this? It is because they hold different views, practice different disciplines, and associate with different companions.
Thus did they deliberate on this matter while gathered in the lecture hall.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there are those who, through some pretext, slander the Tathāgata, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha, you must not harbor resentment or malice toward them. Why is this? Because..."

If you should slander me, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus, and if you harbor resentment and a fettered mind, giving rise to thoughts of harm, you will thereby sink into ruin yourselves. Therefore, you must not harbor resentment and a fettered mind, nor harbor thoughts of harm toward them.
If a bhikṣu praises the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, you should not feel joy or rejoice on that account. Why is this?
If you were to give rise to a heart of joy, you would immediately fall into delusion; therefore, you should not give rise to joy.

Why is this? This is merely a minor matter of the precepts of deportment; ordinary people of little learning do not comprehend its profound meaning, but simply offer praise according to what they perceive as being true.
"How is it that one of limited scope, regarding mere conduct and precepts, being an ordinary person of little learning, directly praises what he has seen as it truly is?
He offers this praise, saying:
'The Śramaṇa Gautama has ceased killing and eliminated killing; he has laid aside the sword and staff, possesses a heart of shame and remorse, and is compassionate toward all beings.'"
"This is a minor matter concerning the precepts of deportment; it is on this basis that an unlearned worldling praises the Buddha.
He further praised him, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned taking what is not given and extinguished taking what is not given; he possesses no intent to steal."
He further sighed:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned sensual desire and purely cultivated the holy life; he is single-mindedly protective of the precepts, does not indulge in lustful excess, and his conduct is pure."
Again he sighed:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned and extinguished false speech; his words are most sincere and what he says is true, so that he does not deceive the people of the world.
The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned and extinguished divisive speech; he does not use these words to disrupt those, nor does he use those words to disrupt these."

He is able to reconcile those who are in dispute; he increases the joy of those already reconciled; whatever he says does not depart from harmony; his words are sincere and penetrate the heart; and he knows the proper time for what he speaks.
The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned and extinguished harsh speech; as for coarse words that wound others, increase their resentment, and prolong hatred, he does not utter any such coarse words at all.
He always uses kind words that please the hearts of people, which are beloved by the multitude and never heard to satiety; he speaks only such words.

The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned and extinguished frivolous speech; he speaks words that are timely, truthful, beneficial, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and words that put a stop to what is improper—he speaks only such words as these.

“The śramaṇa Gautama has abandoned drinking alcohol; he does not wear fragrant flowers; he does not watch singing or dancing; he does not sit on high beds; he does not eat at improper times; he does not handle gold or silver; he does not keep a wife, children, servants, or slaves; he does not keep elephants, horses, pigs, sheep, chickens, dogs, or various birds and beasts; he does not maintain elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, or infantry; he does not own fields or houses for the cultivation of the five grains; he does not strike others with his fists; he does not deceive others with false measures or scales; he does not engage in trade by means of contracts or bonds; he does not accept collateral or take up debts without cause; he does not plot secretly with double-faced intent; and he does not act at improper times.”

To nourish the body and sustain life, he eats according to the capacity of his belly; wherever he goes, his robes and alms bowl accompany him, just as the wings and feathers are inseparable from a flying bird.
"This is a minor instance of his observance of the precepts, yet by this, that unlearned worldling praises the Buddha:

'While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having received the faithful offerings of others, seek further accumulation and have no satiety regarding clothing and food, the śramaṇa Gautama has no such thing.'"

"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, engage in their own livelihoods by planting trees that serve as dwellings for spirits; the śramaṇa Gautama does not do such things."

While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the offerings of the faithful, further employ expedients to seek various gains—such as ivory, assorted jewels, high and wide beds, various embroidered fabrics, woolen rugs, fine carpets, and bedspreads—the śramaṇa Gautama does not engage in such matters.

While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the offerings of the faithful, employ further means to seek self-adornment—rubbing their bodies with ghee and oil, bathing with scented water, smearing themselves with fragrant powders, combing their hair with perfumed ointments, wearing fine flower garlands, tinting their eyes dark blue, wiping and decorating their faces, cleansing themselves with rings and clasps, looking at themselves in mirrors, wearing jeweled leather sandals, dressing in pure white upper garments, carrying canopies and whisks, and adorning themselves with banners and streamers—the śramaṇa Gautama does no such thing.

"Whereas other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas devote themselves exclusively to games and pastimes—such as board games, dice, and various gaming methods with eight paths, ten paths, up to a hundred thousand paths—for their own amusement, the śramaṇa Gautama has no such things."

"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, speak only of useless words that obstruct the path—matters of kings, warfare, and military horses; the attendance of officials and ministers, their mounting and dismounting, and their excursions to parks and gardens; discussions of sleeping and waking, walking, and women; matters of clothing, food and drink, and kinsmen; and even talk of entering the sea to gather treasures. The śramaṇa Gautama has no such things."

"Whereas other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, employ countless expedients to engage in wrong livelihood—using flattery and sweet words, manifesting signs, and disparaging others to seek profit through profit—the śramaṇa Gautama does not do such things."

Just as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the offerings of the faithful, engage only in disputes—whether in gardens and groves, at bathing pools, or in halls—criticizing one another, saying:
"I know the sūtras and the vinaya, while you know nothing;
I follow the right path, while you follow a deviant track."
He places what was previously worn behind and what was later worn in front;
he says, "I am able to endure, but you cannot endure";
and "everything you say is neither true nor correct."
"If you have any doubts, you should come and ask me, and I shall answer them all.
But the śramaṇa Gautama does not do such things.

"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the offerings of the faithful, further employ expedient means to seek out missions as messengers—for kings, royal ministers, brāhmaṇas, or householders—going from here to there and from there to here, carrying this message to deliver to that person, or carrying that message to deliver to this person; whether acting for themselves or instructing others to act, the śramaṇa Gautama does not do such things."

While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who consume the offerings of the faithful devote themselves solely to matters of warfare and strife—practicing with swords, staves, bows, and arrows; or fighting cocks, dogs, pigs, sheep, elephants, horses, oxen, camels, and various beasts; or fighting men and women; or making various sounds such as the blowing of horns, the beating of drums, singing, and dancing; or performing acrobatic feats on poles and engaging in all manner of theatrical entertainments—the śramaṇa Gautama does not engage in such things.

While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, having consumed the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and maintain themselves through wrong livelihood by physiognomizing men and women for signs of fortune or misfortune, beauty or ugliness, and even by physiognomizing animals to seek gain and support—such things are not found in the śramaṇa Gautama.

"Whereas other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and maintain themselves through wrong livelihood—summoning spirits or exorcising them, performing various incantations and prayers, employing countless methods to terrify people, causing them to gather or disperse, bringing them suffering or joy, performing rites for women to stabilize their pregnancies or deliver clothing, cursing people to become donkeys or horses, or making them deaf, blind, or mute; displaying such technical skills, joining their palms toward the sun and moon, and practicing various austerities to seek gain and offerings—the śramaṇa Gautama does not engage in such things."

While other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, consuming the offerings of the faithful, engage in practices that obstruct the path and sustain themselves through wrong livelihood—whether by casting spells for others' illnesses, reciting malevolent incantations, reciting auspicious incantations, or practicing medicine, acupuncture, moxibustion, and pharmacology to treat various ailments—the śramaṇa Gautama does not do such things.

Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and maintain themselves through wrong livelihood; some cast spells over water and fire, some perform exorcisms for spirits, some recite spells for kṣatriyas, some recite elephant spells, some recite spells for the limbs of the body, some recite talismanic spells for pacifying dwellings, some perform incantations to undo the effects of fire or rat bites, some recite books on knowing death and rebirth, some recite books on dreams, some practice physiognomy of hands and faces, some recite books on celestial phenomena, and some recite books on all sounds—the Śramaṇa Gautama does none of these things.

"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and maintain themselves through wrong livelihoods; they observe the celestial seasons and predict whether it will rain or not, whether grain will be expensive or cheap, whether there will be much sickness or little, and whether there will be terror or peace. They may speak of earthquakes, comets, lunar eclipses, solar eclipses, or stellar eclipses, or declare that there will be no eclipses, and they can accurately record the directions and locations [of these phenomena]. The śramaṇa Gautama does not engage in such matters."

Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, practice obstructive arts and maintain themselves through wrong livelihood; some say, "This country shall prevail, and that country shall not," or they say, "That country shall prevail, and this country shall not. They observe omens of good and ill fortune and predict prosperity or decline. The śramaṇa Gautama does nothing of the sort.
"O bhikṣus! This is a minor cause and condition for upholding the precepts, yet by means of it, that ignorant worldling praises the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are further dharmas—profound, subtle, and great dharmas of light—whereby only the noble disciples are able to praise the Tathāgata with these words."
What is this profound, subtle, and great light of the Dharma, by which the noble disciples are able to praise the Tathāgata?

All those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the past eons and past views, or the future eons and future views, speak in various and innumerable ways according to their own inclinations—all such teachings are entirely contained within the sixty-two views;

all those who speak in various and innumerable ways according to their own inclinations regarding the past eons and past views, or the future eons and future views, are entirely unable to transcend these sixty-two views.

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding views concerning the past eons and the past, as well as views concerning the future eons and the future—various and innumerable, each speaking according to their own inclinations—all fall within these sixty-two views and do not exceed them?

Regarding the various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, concerning the past eons and their views, speak in countless diverse ways according to their own inclinations, they all fall within the eighteen views;
regarding the past eons and their views, however numerous and diverse they may be, spoken of according to their own inclinations, none can transcend these eighteen views.

By what conditions do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the views on the past and the eons, express various and countless opinions according to their own inclinations, all of which fall within the eighteen views and do not exceed this limit?
Regarding the various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the past eons, give rise to the doctrine of eternalism,
saying, "The self and the world are eternal," all such positions are included within four views.
Regarding views on the past and the origin of the world, they declare:
"The self and the world are eternal.
All such views are included within four types of views; they do not exceed these.
"For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eons and past views, give rise to the doctrine of eternalism, saying:
'The self and the world are eternal'?"
"All these are included within the four views; they do not go beyond this.
Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind, and with a mind in samādhi, recollect twenty eons of formation and destruction.
They declare: 'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Why is that?'"

By means of various skillful means, I entered the samādhi of concentrated mind and, with a mind in samādhi, recollected twenty eons of formation and destruction; therein, sentient beings neither increased nor decreased, always gathering together and never dispersing. By this I know:
"I and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false."
"This is the first view.
Based on this, recluses and brahmins, regarding the past and views concerning the past, reckon that the self and the world are eternal; among the four views, they do not go beyond this."
“Or there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various means, enter a state of meditative concentration; with a mind in samādhi, they recollect forty eons of formation and destruction.
They declare: ‘I and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Why is that? Because—’”

By means of various skillful methods, I entered the samādhi of concentrated mind and, with that concentrated mind, recollected forty eons of formation and destruction. During those periods, sentient beings neither increased nor decreased; they always gathered together and did not disperse. By this I know that both I and the world are eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false.

"These are two views; based on these, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eons and past views, reckon that the self and the world are eternal. Among the four views, they do not go beyond this."

"There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter into meditative concentration (samādhi) and, with a concentrated mind, recollect eighty eons of formation and destruction. They declare:
'The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Why is that?'"

By means of various skillful methods, I entered the samādhi of concentrated mind; with this concentrated mind, I recollected eighty eons of formation and destruction. During that time, sentient beings neither increased nor decreased, always gathering together without dispersing. By this I know that I and the world are eternal; this alone is true, and all else is false.
These are the three views.
Based on these, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eons and past views, reckon that the self and the world are eternal; among the four views, they do not go beyond this.

"There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess the wisdom of swift discernment and are skilled in observation. Using the skillful means of this wisdom of swift discernment, they observe and consider it to be definitive; based on their own vision and their own eloquence, they speak thus:
'I and the world are eternal.'"
These are the four views.

Based on these, recluses and brahmins, regarding the past and their views concerning the beginning of the eon, reckon that the self and the world are eternal; among these four views, they do not go beyond this.

Regarding these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on their views concerning the past, reckon that the self and the world are eternal—all such positions are entirely subsumed within four views; "the self and the world are eternal" does not exceed these four views.
Only the Tathāgata knows this locus of views—how they are maintained and how they are grasped—and he also knows their retribution.

What the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this; though he knows it, he does not cling to it. Being without clinging, he attains tranquility. He understands the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding sensation. Through impartial contemplation, he attains liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is yet another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata; what is it?
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the views concerning the past eons (*pūrvakalpa*), formulate the theory:
"Both myself and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal.

Based on these views concerning the past eons, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas reckon that both themselves and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal; among these four views, they do not exceed this limit, nor do they go beyond it.

There may be a time when this kalpa first begins to form; there are certain beings whose merit, lifespan, and karma have been exhausted who, passing away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven, are reborn in the empty Brahmā Heaven. There, they immediately develop a mind of attachment and further wish for other beings to be born together with them in this place.

Once this being had conceived such attachment and aspiration, there were others whose life-span, karma, and merit were exhausted; they passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn among the Śūnyatā-Brahmā devas.
The being who was born first then thought to himself: "In this place, I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā;

I exist spontaneously, and there is no one who created me. I fully know all treatises and meanings; I am sovereign over a thousand worlds, most noble and honored, capable of transformation, subtle and supreme."

‘He is the father of all sentient beings; he alone existed first, while other sentient beings came later. These later sentient beings were created and transformed by me. Subsequently, those later sentient beings also had this thought: ‘He is Mahābrahmā;

he is able to create himself, and there is no one who created him. He fully knows all treatises and scriptures, possesses sovereign power over a thousand worlds, is the most noble and honorable, capable of transformations, and is the foremost in subtlety. He is the father of all sentient beings; he alone existed first, and we came into existence later. We sentient beings were created and transformed by him.’”

When the life and karma of those Brahmā-parishioners were exhausted, they were reborn in this world. As they gradually grew up, they shaved off their hair and beards, donned the three dharma robes, and left the household life to practice the Way. Entering the samādhi of concentrated mind, they perceived their own past lives through the power of that samādhi and spoke thus:

"That Great Brahmā is able to create himself; there is no creator of him. He fully knows all meanings and scriptures, possesses sovereignty over a thousand worlds, is the most noble and honored, and is capable of transformations that are subtle and supreme."
He is the father of sentient beings, eternally abiding and unchanging; yet that Brahmā created us, and we are impermanent and subject to change, unable to abide for long. Therefore, one should know:
both the self and the world are half-eternal and half-impermanent; this alone is true, and all else is false.
This is called the first view.

On this basis, recluses and brahmins give rise to theories regarding the past and views concerning the beginning of the eon, asserting that "half is eternal and half is non-eternal. Among the four views, they do not go beyond this.

“Suppose there are sentient beings who delight in play, laughter, and indolence, repeatedly amusing themselves with play and laughter. While they are thus amusing themselves, their bodies become utterly exhausted and they lose consciousness; having lost consciousness, they pass away and are reborn in this world. As they gradually grow up, they shave off their hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). With a mind established in *samādhi*, they recollect their own past lives and say:

‘Those other sentient beings were not born again and again, nor did they repeatedly amuse themselves with play and laughter; they remained constantly in that place, dwelling forever without change. Because I repeatedly amused myself with play and laughter, I have met with this impermanence and become subject to the law of transformation. Therefore, I know:’”
Both myself and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
This is the second view.

Based on this, recluses and brahmins give rise to theories concerning the past and views regarding the origin of the eon, asserting that "I and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal. Among these four views, none go beyond this.

"Suppose there are sentient beings who, after looking at one another repeatedly, lose their mindfulness; because of this, they pass away and are reborn in this world. As they gradually grow up, they shave off their hair and beards, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and enter the samādhi of concentrated mind. With a mind in samādhi, they recognize their original place of birth and say:
'Just as those sentient beings did not lose their mindfulness because they did not look at one another repeatedly, they remain constant and unchanging;
whereas we looked at one another many times, and having looked repeatedly, we lost our mindfulness, resulting in this impermanence and the nature of change. By this I know:'"
"Both myself and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
This is the third view.
Based on this, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas give rise to theories concerning the past eons and views regarding the origin of the world:
“I and the world are both partly eternal and partly non-eternal.
Within these four views, one does not go beyond this.

“There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess swift analytical wisdom and are skilled in observation; by means of that swift wisdom of analytical observation, they speak with their own intellectual eloquence, saying:”
“I and the world are both partly eternal and partly non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
This is the fourth view.
On account of this, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas give rise to theories concerning the past eons and views regarding the origin of the world:
"I and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal"—within these four views, they do not go beyond this.

Whatever recluses and brahmins, concerning the past and their views on the origin of things, propound the theory that "I and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal," all fall within these four views; they do not go beyond this.
Only a Buddha can know this locus of views—how they are maintained and how they are grasped—and he also knows their karmic retribution.

What the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this; though he knows it, he does not cling to it. Because he does not cling, he attains tranquility. He knows the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding feeling. Through the contemplation of equality, he attains liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is yet another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
What are those teachings?
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the views on the past and the origin of the world, propound the theory:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite."
"Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on this, give rise to theories regarding the past eons and past views, asserting:
'The self and the world are both finite and infinite.
Within these four views, they do not go beyond this."

There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; with a mind in samādhi they contemplate the world and give rise to the notion of finitude, saying:
"This world is finite; this alone is true, all else is false. Why is that?"

By means of various skillful methods, I enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; with a mind in samādhi, I contemplate that the world has limits, and therefore I know that the world has limits—this alone is true, and all else is false.
This is called the first view.
On this basis, certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas give rise to the theory regarding the past and the origin of the world:
"The self and the world are finite. Among these four views, they do not go beyond this.

“Or there may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, by means of various skillful methods, enter into meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and with a mind in samādhi observe the world, giving rise to the perception of its boundlessness. They say:
‘The world is infinite; this alone is true and all else is false. Why is that? Because—’”

By means of various skillful methods, I enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; with this mind of samādhi, I contemplate that the world is boundless, and thus I know that the world is boundless—this is the truth, and all else is false.
This is the second view.
Based on this, certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas formulate a theory regarding the past and views concerning the origin of the eon:
"The self and the world are infinite. Among these four views, it does not go beyond this.

"Or there may be certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter a state of meditative concentration and, with a concentrated mind, contemplate the world, asserting that it is finite above but infinite in the four directions. They say:
'The world is both finite and infinite; this alone is true, and all else is false. Why is that?'"

By means of various skillful methods, I entered the samādhi of concentrated mind; with this concentrated mind, I observed that the zenith has a limit while the four directions are limitless. Therefore, I know that the world is both finite and infinite; this alone is true, and all else is false.
This is the third view.
Based on this, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas give rise to theories regarding the past eons and the views concerning the origin:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite. Within these four views, they do not go beyond this.

“Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess swift and penetrating wisdom and are skilled in observation. By means of that swift wisdom of observation, they declare through their own intellectual discernment:
‘Both the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this alone is the truth, and all else is false.’”
This is the fourth view.
Based on this, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas give rise to theories regarding the past eons and past views, asserting:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite; this alone is true, all else is false. Among these four views, none go beyond this.

This is how these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the theories of the past and views concerning the origin of the world, give rise to the doctrine that "the self and the world are both finite and infinite"; all such positions are included within four views, and none exceed this limit.
Only the Buddha can know this locus of views—how they are maintained and how they are clung to—and he also knows their retribution.

That which the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this; though he knows it, he does not cling to it. Because he does not cling, he attains tranquility. He knows the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding feeling. Through the contemplation of equality, he attains liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma illumination that enables noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is yet another profound, subtle, and great Dharma illumination that enables noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata; what is it?

Regarding the past eons and views, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas ask different questions and give different answers; when asked about this or that, they ask differently and answer differently, yet within these four views, they do not go beyond them.

Because of this, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding their views on the past and their speculations about the eons, provide various answers to various questions; within these four views, they do not go beyond them.
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and maintain such a view:
"I neither see nor know whether there is a retribution for good and evil, or whether there is no retribution."
Because I neither see nor know [this], I speak thus:
Is there retribution for good and evil?
Or is there no retribution?

"In this world, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are broad-minded and widely learned, intelligent and wise, who always delight in seclusion and tranquility, whose eloquence is subtle and refined, who are respected by the world, and who are able to skillfully distinguish between various views through their wisdom."

If someone were to question me regarding profound meanings and I were unable to answer, I would feel ashamed before them and have fear of them; therefore, one should take this answer as one's refuge, as an island, as a shelter, and as the ultimate path.
If someone were to ask such questions, one should answer them as follows:
"This matter is thus; this matter is real; this matter is different; this matter is not different; this matter is neither different nor not different."
This is the first view.
Because of this, some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas give different answers to different questions; among these four views, they do not go beyond this.
"Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and maintain such a view: [text continues]"
"I do not see or know whether there is another world or whether there is no other world.
Yet those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the world who possess the divine eye and the knowledge of others' minds can perceive distant things; though they are close to others, those others do not see them.
"Such persons as these are able to know whether there is a future world or no future world;
I do not know and do not see whether there is a future world or no future world.
If I were to speak on this matter, it would be a falsehood. I loathe and fear falsehood; therefore, I take [the Dharma] as my refuge, my island, my shelter, and my ultimate path."
If someone were to ask such questions, one should answer thus:
"This matter is thus; this matter is real; this matter is different; this matter is not different; this matter is neither different nor not different."
This is the second view.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who give different answers to these questions, none go beyond these four views.
“Or there may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:
‘I do not know and do not see what is wholesome.’”
"What is unwholesome?
I do not know and do not see; thus I say, 'Is this wholesome or unwholesome?
I then give rise to craving toward this; from craving arises aversion. When there is craving and aversion, there is the arising of feeling."
I have gone forth to practice the holy life desiring to extinguish feeling;
yet those wicked ones fear feeling, and thus they take it as their refuge, their island, their shelter, and their ultimate path.
To one who asks such questions, one should answer thus:
"This matter is thus; this matter is real; this matter is different; this matter is not different; this matter is neither different nor not different."
This is the third view.
Among the various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who give different answers to this question, none go beyond these four views.
"There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are ignorant, dull-witted, and dark-minded; when others question them, they answer according to those others' words:
'This matter is thus; this matter is real; this matter is different; this matter is not different; this matter is neither different nor not different.'"
These are the four views.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on these, provide various questions and various answers; among these four views, they do not go beyond them.
There may be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, regarding the past eons and past views, provide various questions and various answers; they all fall within four views and do not exceed this limit.
Only a Buddha can know this locus of views—how they are maintained and how they are clung to—and he also knows their retribution.

What the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this; though he knows it, he does not cling to it. Because he does not cling, he attains nirvāṇa. He knows the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding feeling. Through the contemplation of equality, he attains liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is the profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata; what is it?

There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, regarding the past eons and past views, maintain that this world arises without a cause; they are all included within two views. Regarding the past eons and past views that this world arises without a cause, they do not exceed these two views.
For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eons and past views, claim that things exist without a cause? Within these two views, why do they not go beyond this?

There are sentient beings who are without thought and without cognition; if those beings give rise to a thought, they immediately pass away and are reborn in this world. As they gradually grow up, they shave their hair and beards, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and enter the samādhi of concentrated mind.

With a mind in samādhi, they recognize their original place of birth and speak these words: "I did not exist before, but now I have suddenly come to be. This world did not exist before, but now it exists. This alone is real; all else is false."
This is the first view.

On this basis, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas hold views concerning the past eons and the origin of existence, asserting that things exist without a cause; among these two types of views, they do not go beyond this.

"There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess swift and keen wisdom and are skilled in observation; having observed with their swift and keen wisdom, they are able to speak thus through their own intellectual discernment:
'This world exists without cause; this alone is true, all else is false.'"
"This is the second view.
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, based on this, hold views regarding the past eons and the origin of the world—that it exists without cause—within these two views, they do not go beyond this."

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas hold views concerning the past eons and the origins of things, asserting that they exist without cause—all such views fall within two categories and do not exceed them; that the Buddha alone knows this is likewise so.

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be who, regarding the past eons and views, speak according to their own inclinations in countless various ways—they all fall within these eighteen views concerning the past eons and views, spoken in countless various ways according to their own inclinations;
they do not exceed these eighteen views. Only a Buddha can know this, and it is likewise so.
"Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light. What is it?
There are various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the final eon and the views concerning the final eon, speak in countless and diverse ways according to their own inclinations;

all of these fall within the forty-four views. Regarding the final eon and the views concerning the final eon, whatever they say in countless and diverse ways according to their inclinations does not exceed these forty-four views."

There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on various matters regarding the future eon and future views, speak according to their own inclinations in countless diverse ways; yet among these forty-four views, they do not go beyond this.

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, regarding the final eon and the views concerning the end, give rise to theories of perception and declare that the world possesses perception—they all fall within these sixteen views.

Regarding the final eon and the views concerning the end, they give rise to theories of perception and declare that the world possesses perception; among these sixteen views, they do not exceed this limit.

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on matters concerning the final eon and final views, give rise to speculative theories regarding perception and assert that the world possesses perception? They are all included within these sixteen views; they do not exceed this limit.
“There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and such a view, saying:
‘After my death, I shall be born with form and with perception; this alone is true, all else is false.’”
This is the first view.
Based on this, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas give rise to speculative theories regarding the future during the final age, asserting that the world possesses perception;
among the sixteen views, they do not go beyond this.
Some say: "After my death here, I shall be born in the formless realm with perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death here, I shall be born with form and without form, yet possessing perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death here, I shall be born neither with form nor without form, yet possessing perception; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death, I shall exist with a finite existence and perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death here, I shall be born with the perception of infinite existence; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others say: "After my death here, I shall be born with the perception of both finite and infinite existence; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death, I shall be reborn with perception that is neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death here, I shall be reborn as one who possesses exclusively pleasure and perception; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others say: "After my death here, I shall be reborn as one who possesses exclusively suffering and perception; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death, I shall be born with pleasure, with pain, and with perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my passing, I shall be born with neither-painful-nor-pleasant perception; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others say: "After my passing, I shall be born with a single perception; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death, I shall be born with a certain number of perceptions; this alone is real, and all else is false. Others say:
"After my passing, I shall be reborn with limited perceptions; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others say: "After my passing, I shall be reborn with immeasurable perceptions; this alone is true, all else is false."
These constitute the sixteen views.

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, regarding the final eon and final views, give rise to theories of perception and assert that the world possesses perception—none of these exceed the scope of these sixteen views; that only the Buddha can know them is likewise the case.
"Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light. What is this Dharma?
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the final eon and the views of the final eon, give rise to the doctrine of non-perception, asserting that the world is without perception.
They all fall within eight views; regarding the final eon and the views of the final eon, they give rise to the doctrine of non-perception, and among these eight views, they do not exceed this."

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the final age and final views, give rise to the doctrine of non-perception and declare that the world is without perception—such that among these eight views, they do not go beyond this?
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:
"After my death, I shall be born with form but without perception; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death here, I shall be reborn in the formless realm without perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death, I shall be born with form, yet without perception; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others say: "After my death, I shall be born neither with form nor without form, and without perception; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death, I shall be born with a finite existence and without perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death, I shall be reborn in the realm of infinite non-perception; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others say: "After my death, I shall be reborn in the realm of both finite and infinite non-perception; this alone is true, all else is false."
Others say: "After my death, I shall be reborn in a state that is neither finite nor infinite, and is without perception; this alone is true, and all else is false.
These constitute the eight views.

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, based on this, during the final age and with final views, give rise to the doctrine of non-perception and declare that the world is without perception, they all fall within these eight views and do not exceed them; that only the Buddha can know them is likewise the case.
“Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light. What is this Dharma?

There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the final eon and the views concerning the final eon, give rise to the doctrine of ‘neither-perception-nor-non-perception’ and declare that this world is neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving.

They all fall within the eight views; regarding the final eon and the views concerning the final eon, they formulate the doctrine of ‘neither-perception-nor-non-perception’ and declare the world to be neither-perceiving-nor-non-perceiving. Within these eight views, they do not go beyond this.”

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the final eon and the views of the final eon, give rise to the doctrine of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," asserting that the world is neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, such that among the eight views, they do not go beyond this?
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas hold such a doctrine and maintain such a view:
"After my death, I shall be born with form, neither percipient nor non-percipient; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death here, I shall be reborn in the formless realm, in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death here, I shall be born with form and without form, neither percipient nor non-percipient; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death here, I shall be born neither with form nor without form, neither percipient nor non-percipient; this alone is true, all else is false."
Some say: "After my death, I shall be born with a finite existence in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"After my death here, I shall be reborn in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception which is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
Others say: "After my death here, I shall be reborn in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception which is both finite and infinite; this alone is true, all else is false."
Others say: "After my death, I shall be neither finite nor infinite, neither percipient nor non-percipient; this alone is true, all else is false.
These constitute the eight views.

If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, based on this, during the final age and with final views, give rise to the doctrine of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," asserting that the world is neither percipient nor non-percipient;
they are all included within these eight views and do not exceed them. That only the Buddha can know [the truth] is likewise so.
“Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light. What is this Dharma?

There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the final eon and the view of the end, give rise to the doctrine of annihilationism, asserting that sentient beings are annihilated without remainder.

They all fall within seven views; regarding the final eon and the view of the end, they give rise to the doctrine of annihilationism, asserting that sentient beings are annihilated without remainder, and among these seven views, they do not exceed this.”

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the final eon and the views concerning the end, give rise to the doctrine of annihilationism, asserting that sentient beings are annihilated without remainder? Within these seven views, how is it that they do not go beyond this?
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and maintain such a view:

"This body of mine—composed of the four great elements and the six sense bases—is born of father and mother, nurtured by milk and food, raised on clothing and sustenance, and protected by being massaged and embraced; yet it is impermanent and must inevitably meet with destruction. This is what is called annihilation."
This is the first view.
Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus, saying:
"This self does not undergo annihilation; rather, when the self is annihilated without remainder in the heavens of the desire realm, this constitutes annihilation."
These are the two views.
Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus, saying:
"This is not annihilation; my transformation-body in the form realm, with all faculties complete, is annihilated without remainder—this is annihilation."
Some say: "This is not annihilation; I shall attain annihilation in the sphere of infinite space, which is formless. Others say:
"This is not annihilation; I am annihilated in the sphere of infinite consciousness, which is formless. Others say:
"This is not annihilation; I am annihilated in the sphere of nothingness, which is formless."
Some say: "This is not annihilation; rather, it is the annihilation of my existence in the formless realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh annihilation.
These constitute the seven views.
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on this, hold views regarding the final eon and the final end, claiming that these classes of sentient beings are annihilated without remainder;
among the seven views, they do not go beyond this, and it is likewise only the Buddha who can know them.
“Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma illumination. What is this Dharma?

There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the final eon and the views of the final eon, maintain a theory of Nirvāṇa in the present life, asserting that sentient beings attain Nirvāṇa while still existing in the present.
They all fall within the five views; those who speak of Nirvāṇa in the present life regarding the final eon and the views of the final eon do not exceed these five views.”

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the final age and final views, claim that sentient beings currently possess nirvāṇa? Within these five views, how is it that they do not exceed this?
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such views and maintain such doctrines, saying:
"I indulge in the five sensual pleasures in the present life; this is my attainment of nirvāṇa in the present."
This is the first view.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
"This is the present nirvāṇa; it is not that it does not exist. Yet there is another, more subtle and supreme present nirvāṇa which you do not know, but which I alone know."

Just as I have gone beyond desire and unwholesome, evil states, with directed thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, filled with joy and happiness, and entered the first dhyāna—this is called nirvāṇa in the present.
"This is the second view.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus:
'This is the present nirvāṇa; it is not that it does not exist. Moreover, there is another present nirvāṇa, subtle and supreme, which you do not know, but which I alone know.'"

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, with internal clarity and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and evaluation, I entered the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss.
"This is what is called present nirvāṇa; this is the third view.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus, saying:
'This is present nirvāṇa, and it is not that it does not exist; yet there is another present nirvāṇa, subtle and supreme, which you do not know, but which I alone know.'"

Just as I, having removed directed thought and evaluation, and with equanimity and mindfulness, dwelt in happiness, guarding mindfulness and unifying the mind, experienced the bliss of which the noble ones speak, and entered the third dhyāna.
"This is what is called present nirvāṇa; this is the fourth view.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak thus, saying:
'This is present nirvāṇa, and it is not otherwise. Yet there is another subtle and supreme present nirvāṇa which you do not know, but which I alone know.'"

"Just as I have attained the cessation of pleasure and the cessation of pain, having first eliminated sorrow and joy, and abiding in neither-pain-nor-pleasure with pure mindfulness and equanimity, I enter the fourth dhyāna.
This is called the first nirvāṇa; this constitutes the fifth view.

If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, regarding the final eon and final views, give rise to the doctrine of attaining nirvāṇa in the present life, they do not exceed these five views; that only the Buddha can know this is likewise so.

"Whatever śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas there may be who hold views regarding the future eon—those being innumerable and of various kinds, spoken according to their own inclinations—all do not exceed these forty-four views; only the Buddha can know the basis of all these views, and it is likewise so."

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be who, regarding the past eons and views, or the future eons and views, speak according to their inclinations in countless various ways—all these are entirely included within these sixty-two views;

whatever they speak according to their inclinations in countless various ways regarding the past eons and views, or the future eons and views, does not exceed these sixty-two views. Only the Tathāgata knows these bases of views, and it is likewise so.
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the past eons and past views, give rise to the doctrine of eternalism, asserting:
"The self and the world are eternal.

Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas produce this knowledge through various forms of faith, various desires, various hearsays, various conditions, various cognitions, various views, various concentrations, and various tolerances; they produce knowledge based on these. Because they hold such rarefied views, it is called "clinging"—and so it is even up to their present nirvāṇa. It is likewise in all such cases.
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold the doctrine of eternalism, asserting: "The world is eternal.

Because they grasp at conditions, craving arises and grows; yet they do not realize this for themselves, becoming defiled by and attached to craving, and being overcome by craving—even up to their present nirvāṇa, it is likewise so.
Regarding those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, concerning the past eons and past views, give rise to the doctrine of eternalism, claiming:

"The world is eternal," because they rely on the condition of contact (*sparśa-pratyaya*), it is impossible for them to establish such a doctrine apart from the condition of contact—this remains true even up to the present nirvāṇa. It is likewise so.

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas there may be who, regarding views on the past eons and past views, or views on the future eons and future views, each speak according to their own perspectives—they all fall within these sixty-two views; each speaks according to their own perspective, all relying upon and remaining within the middle, not exceeding this limit.

It is just as when a skilled fisherman covers a small pond with a fine-meshed net; you should know that all aquatic creatures within the pond will enter the net, having no place to escape, and none can pass beyond it.

It is the same for all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas: regarding their various assertions concerning the past eons and past views, as well as the future eons and future views, they are all included within the sixty-two views; they do not go beyond this.

“If a bhikkhu knows, as they really are, the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, he is preeminent and transcends those various views.”

The Tathāgata himself knows that birth and death have been exhausted; yet he maintains a body because he desires to bring blessings and deliver all devas and humans. If he were without a body, then all devas and worldlings would have nothing to rely upon, just as a tāla tree whose head has been severed can never grow again.
"The Buddha is also like this; having already severed birth and death, he will never again be born.
When the Buddha spoke these words, the great trichiliocosm shook in six ways, three times over.
At that time, Ānanda was behind the Buddha fanning him; with his right shoulder bared, he knelt on his right knee with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This Dharma is most profound; by what name should it be called?"
"How should it be upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This sutra should be named 'The Movement of Meaning,' 'The Movement of Dharma,' 'The Movement of Views,' 'The Movement of Māras,' and 'The Movement of Brahmās.'"
At that time, Ānanda, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

(22) *Sūtra on the Merit of Lineage*, Part Three, Chapter Three: "The Merit of Lineage.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Aṅga, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Traveling through the human world, he stayed at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in the city of Campā.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Jotipāla who resided in the city of Campā. The people of that city were numerous, flourishing, and prosperous; King Prasenajit had bestowed this city upon the brahmin Jotipāla as his hereditary domain.

This Brahmin has maintained pure lineage for seven generations on both his paternal and maternal sides and is not disparaged by others. He has mastered the recitation of the three Vedas and is proficient in various scriptures; there is no subtle or profound point in worldly classics that he has not thoroughly mastered. Furthermore, he is skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the divination of auspicious and inauspicious omens, and the rituals of sacrifice. He has five hundred disciples, whom he teaches without ceasing.

At that time, the brahmins, elders, and householders within the city of Campā heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan who had left home to attain the Way, was traveling through the human world from the kingdom of Aṅga and had arrived at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in Campā. He possessed great renown that spread throughout the world; he was a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brahmins, he had realized it for himself and taught the Dharma to others; his words—superior, middling, and inferior—were all entirely true and correct, complete in meaning and flavor, and pure in holy conduct.
"Such a True Person (sappurisa) ought to be visited; I shall now go to meet him.
Having said this, they immediately led one another out of the city of Campā, following in groups, desiring to go to the Buddha.
At that time, the brahmin Jyotipāla was atop a high terrace; seeing from afar the crowds of people following one another in groups, he asked his attendant:
"For what reason are those people following one another in groups?"
“Where do you wish to go?

The attendant replied, “I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who left home to attain the Way, is traveling among the people in the kingdom of Aṅga and has arrived at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in the city of Campā. He possesses great renown that spreads throughout the world; he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among the devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he has realized this for himself and proclaims it to others. His words—superior, middling, and inferior—are all entirely true and authentic, complete in meaning and flavor, and his holy life is pure.”
"This multitude of brahmins, elders, and householders from the city of Campā have gathered together and are following one another, wishing to go and pay their respects to the śramaṇa Gautama.
At that time, the brahmin Gotamaka immediately commanded his attendant:
"Go quickly with my words and tell those people:"
“Wait a moment, sirs; you must wait until I have gone there, and then we shall go together to that Gautama.
Then, with a voice of various virtues, that attendant went and said to the people:
“Sirs, wait for a moment; you must wait until I have arrived, and then we shall go together to that Gautama.”
Then, the people replied to the attendant, saying, "Return quickly and inform the brahmin, saying:
'Now is precisely the right time; it is fitting that we go together.'"
The attendant returned and reported:
"The people have already gathered and say:
'Now is precisely the time; we should go together.'"
At that time, the Brahmin Gotama immediately descended from the dais and stood at the middle gate.

At that moment, there were five hundred other Brahmins who had previously gathered at the gate for some minor reason; seeing the Brahmin Gotama approaching, they all rose to greet him and asked: "Great Brahmin!"
"Where do you wish to go? Jotika replied: "There is a śramaṇa, Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who has left the household life and attained the Way.

He is traveling among the people in the kingdom of Aṅga and has arrived at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in the city of Campā. He possesses great renown that spreads throughout the world; he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he has realized it for himself and teaches the Dharma to others. His words—superior, middling, and inferior—are all entirely true and correct, complete in meaning and flavor, and his holy life is pure."
"Such a true person is worthy of being visited for an audience; I now wish to go there to meet him.
At that time, the five hundred brahmins addressed Svāgata, saying:
"Do not go to see him. Why is this?"
He should come here; we should not go there.
Now, this great brāhmaṇa has been of pure descent from both his father and mother for seven generations, and is not disparaged by others;
if one is accomplished in such qualities, he should come here, and we should not go to him.

Furthermore, this great brahmin was proficient in the recitation of the three Vedas of the heterodox schools; he could analyze all manner of scriptures and was thoroughly versed in the subtlest points of worldly treatises. He was also skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the divination of auspiciousness and misfortune, and the rituals of sacrifice.
Having mastered these arts, he knew that such a person as himself should approach him, but that he should not approach them.
Furthermore, this great brahmin has a handsome countenance and possesses the physical appearance of Brahmā;
one who has accomplished such a dharma as this should come here, and I should not go to him.
Furthermore, since this great brahmin excels in the virtue of his precepts and has accomplished wisdom,
one who has accomplished these qualities should go to him, and he should not go to him.
"Furthermore, the Great Brahmin’s speech is gentle and his eloquence is complete; the meaning and flavor of his words are pure.
One who has accomplished such qualities should come here, and we should not go to him."
Furthermore, there is a great brahmin who acts as a master with many disciples;
one who has accomplished this Dharma should go to him, and he should not go to him.
Furthermore, the Great Brahmin constantly instructs five hundred brahmins;
those who have mastered this Dharma should come to him, and he should not go to them.

Furthermore, great brahmins and scholars from the four quarters all came to request instruction; when they asked about various technical arts and the methods of sacrifice, he was able to answer them all completely.
He established this rule: "One who has mastered these dharmas should come here; one should not go there."
Furthermore, this great brahmin is venerated and supported by King Prasenajit and King Bimbisāra;
one who has accomplished this Dharma should go to him, but he should not go to him.
Furthermore, there is a great brahmin who possesses abundant wealth and treasures, his storehouses overflowing;
one who has accomplished this Dharma should go to him, but he should not go to him.
Furthermore, this great brahmin is wise and discerning, his speech is fluent and eloquent, and he is free from timidity;
as one who has accomplished these qualities, he should come here, and we should not go to him.
At that time, Jotipāla said to the brahmins: "So it is! So it is!"
As you have said, I do indeed possess these virtues; it is not that I lack them.
You should listen to what I say: regarding all the merits possessed by the śramaṇa Gautama, we ought to go to him; he should not come here.
The śramaṇa Gautama has had pure and authentic parents for seven generations and is not subject to the contempt or disparagement of others;
since he has accomplished these qualities, we should go to him, and he should not come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is handsome in appearance and born of the kṣatriya caste;
since he has accomplished these qualities, I should go to him, and he should not come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama was born into a noble and honorable station and left the household life to pursue the Way;
since he has accomplished this Dharma, I ought to go to him, and he should not have to come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with radiant complexion and possesses a truly noble lineage; he has left the household life to practice the Way.
Since he has accomplished such qualities, I ought to go to him, and he should not have to come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama was born into a wealthy family and possesses great power; he has left the household life to pursue the Way.
One who has accomplished such a dharma as this, I should go to him, and he should not have to come here.
"Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with the precepts of the noble ones and has perfected wisdom;
since he has accomplished these dharmas, I should go to him, and he should not come here."
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is skilled in speech, which is soft, gentle, and refined;
since he has accomplished such qualities, I should go to him, and he should not come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is a teacher of the multitude with many disciples;
as one who has accomplished this Dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come here.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama has eternally extinguished sensual desire; he is free from sudden outbursts of violence, his anxieties and fears have been eliminated, and his hair does not stand on end. He is joyful and serene, greeting others with kindness, skillfully explaining the retribution of actions, and never disparaging other paths.
Since he has accomplished these qualities, I ought to go to him; he should not come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is constantly honored and provided for by Kings Prasenajit and Bimbisāra;
since he has accomplished these qualities, I should go to him, and he should not come here.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is honored and provided for by the brahmin Poṭṭhapāda; he is also seen to be honored and provided for by the brahmins Brahmāyu, Tārukkha, and Kokanada the son of Māṭhara.
Since he has accomplished these qualities, I should go to him; he should not come here.

"Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is revered, honored, and supported by his śrāvaka disciples; he is also respected by the devas and other hosts of spirits, and the Śākyas, Koliyas, Malla, Vṛji, Malla, and Soma clans all revere him.
Since he has accomplished these dharmas, I should go to him; he should not have to come here."
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama has conferred the three refuges and the five precepts upon King Prasenajit and King Bimbisāra;
since he is one who has accomplished these dharmas, I should go to him, and he should not come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama has bestowed the three refuges and the five precepts upon the brahmin Puṣkarasādi and others;
since he has accomplished these dharmas, I should go to him, and he should not come here.
