Furthermore, the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama receive the three refuges and the five precepts; the devas, the Śākyas, the Koliyas, and others all likewise receive the three refuges and the five precepts.
Since those who have accomplished this Dharma should come to me, they ought not to come here.
"Furthermore, when the śramaṇa Gautama travels, he is honored and provided for by all people;
since he has accomplished these qualities, I should go to him, and he should not come here."
Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes—to cities, towns, or villages—he is honored by people;
since he has accomplished these dharmas, I should go to him, and he should not come here.
Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, non-humans and spirits do not dare to disturb him;
since he has accomplished such a dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come here.
Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, the people of that place all behold a brilliant light and hear the sound of celestial music;
since he has accomplished such dharmas, I ought to go to him, and he should not come here.
Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, when he is about to depart, the multitude will follow him with longing and weep as they see him off;
since he has accomplished such qualities, I should go to him, and he should not come here.
"Furthermore, when the śramaṇa Gautama first left the household life, his parents wept and wailed, cherishing him with love and longing;
since he has accomplished this Dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come here."
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama left home in his youth and vigor, renouncing all ornaments, elephants, horses, precious chariots, the five desires, and necklaces;
since he has accomplished this dharma, I ought to go to him, and he should not come here.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama has renounced the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin) to leave the household life and pursue the Way. Had he remained at home, he would have presided over the four continents, ruling over all people and things, and we would all have been his subjects.
Since he has accomplished this dharma, I ought to go to him; he should not come here.
"Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama clearly understands the Brahma-dharma and is able to expound it for others; he also converses with the Brahmā gods.
Since he has accomplished this dharma, I should go to him; he should not have to come here."
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks;
since he has accomplished these qualities, I should go to him, and he should not have to come here.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama possesses penetrating wisdom and is free from timidity;
since he has accomplished these qualities, I ought to go to him, and he should not have to come here.
"That Gautama has now arrived here at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in the city of Campā; he is my superior and also a distinguished guest, so it is fitting that we go to pay him our respects."
At that time, the five hundred brahmins said to Jātiśroṇa:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
Are his meritorious virtues indeed such as these?
If he were able to accomplish even one of those virtues, we should not have come; how much more so now that he possesses them all!
We ought to lead one another and go together to pay our respects.
Viśvāmitra replied, "If you wish to go, you should know that now is the time. Thereupon,
Viśvāmitra immediately prepared his precious chariot and, surrounded by five hundred brahmins as well as the brahmins, elders, and householders of the city of Campā, proceeded to Lake Gaggara.
Not far from the pond, he thought to himself:
"If I were to question the Gautama, perhaps it would not accord with his views; that ascetic Gautama might rebuke me, saying:
'One should ask in this way, one should not ask in that way.'"
When the multitude hears this, they will say that I am ignorant and will damage my reputation.
Furthermore, if the śramaṇa Gautama questions me on a matter of principle, my answer might not accord with his intention, and that śramaṇa would surely rebuke me, saying:
"One should have answered thus; one should not have answered thus."
"When the multitude hears this, they will say that I am ignorant and will damage my reputation.
If I were to remain silent and return from here, the multitude would say:
'This man knows nothing.'"
"In the end, I was unable to reach the place where the śramaṇa Gautama is, which has damaged my reputation.
Had the śramaṇa Gautama questioned me regarding the Dharma of the brāhmaṇas, my answers would have been sufficient to satisfy his mind."

Then, having formed this thought by the side of the Gaggarā Pond, Soṇadaṇḍa proceeded forward, alighted from his carriage, and approached the World-Honored One on foot; after exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side.

At that time, among the brahmins, elders, and householders of the city of Campā, some sat after paying homage to the Buddha; some sat after exchanging greetings; some sat after announcing their names; some sat with palms joined toward the Buddha; and others sat in silence.
When the assembly was seated, the Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the brahmin Jotidāsa, addressed him, saying:
"As for what you have contemplated, it shall be according to your wish!"
The Buddha asked Jotidāsa:
"Brahmin, how many qualities have you perfected such that what you say is truthful and free from falsehood?"
At that time, Jotipāla thought to himself in silence:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
“The Śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal power; he perceives the minds of others and asks me about this matter just as I was thinking it.
Then, the Brahmin Saṅgharakṣita sat upright with his body composed, looked around at the great assembly, and with a joyful smile, replied to the Buddha’s words:
“I, a Brahmin, have accomplished five qualities; what I say is most sincere and free from falsehood.”
What are the five? First, his paternal and maternal lineages have been authentic for seven generations back, such that he is not disparaged by others.

Second, he is proficient in reciting the three Vedas of the heterodox schools; he can fully analyze all manner of scriptures, has mastered even the most profound and subtle secular classics, and is further skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the discernment of auspiciousness and misfortune, and the rituals of sacrifice.
Third, his countenance is upright and handsome;
fourth, he is fully endowed with the observance of the precepts;
fifth, his wisdom is thoroughly penetrating.
These are the five, Gautama!
When a brahmin is accomplished in these five qualities, his words are truthful and free from falsehood.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Jotika!"
Is there any brahmin who, among these five qualities, abandons one and possesses four, yet whose speech is truthful and free from falsehood, such that he may be called a brahmin?
Jingde addressed the Buddha, saying, “There is. Why is this so?
"Gautama! What is the use of being born?

If a Brahmin of other schools has mastered the recitation of the three Vedas, can distinguish all various scriptures, and has thoroughly cultivated the subtle and profound points of worldly classics; if he is further skilled in the physiognomy of great men, discerns auspiciousness and misfortune, and is proficient in the rituals of sacrifice; if his countenance is upright and handsome, his observance of the precepts is complete, and his wisdom is penetrating."
"One who possesses these four qualities speaks with sincerity and truthfulness, free from all falsehood; such a person is called a brāhmaṇa.
The Buddha said to Śuklodana: "Excellent!"
Excellent! If one were to abandon one of these four qualities and possess the other three, would that person also be called a brāhmaṇa, as their speech is truthful and free from falsehood?
Jingde replied, “There is. Why is this so?”
What is the use of birth or recitation?

If a brāhmaṇa possesses a handsome appearance, is fully endowed with the observance of precepts, and has attained mastery of wisdom—if he accomplishes these three qualities, his words are sincere and free from falsehood; such a one is called a brāhmaṇa.
The Buddha said, “Excellent! Excellent!”
How so? If, among these three qualities, one abandons one and possesses two, would he also be called a brāhmaṇa, provided his words are sincere and free from falsehood?
He replied: "There is. Why is that? Because..."
"What is the use of birth, recitation, and physical beauty? At that time,
the five hundred brahmins each raised their voices and said to the brahmin Jātiśroṇa,
"Why do you rebuke and stop us from speaking of birth, recitation, and beauty, claiming they are useless?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five hundred brahmins, saying:

"If the brahmin Jotipāla is of ugly appearance, lacks noble lineage, is unskilled in recitation, and possesses neither eloquence, wisdom, nor the ability to answer well—such that he cannot engage in discourse with me—you may speak.

However, if Jotipāla is handsome in appearance, endowed with noble lineage, proficient in recitation, and possesses wisdom and eloquence such that he is skilled in questioning and answering, and is fully capable of debating the meaning of the Dharma with me, then you should remain silent and listen to what this man has to say."
At that time, the brahmin Gotamīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that Gautama will pause for a moment!
I myself shall go and instruct this man according to the Dharma.”
At that time, Sonadanda immediately addressed the five hundred brahmins, saying:
"Aṅga Māṇava is here among this assembly; he is my nephew. Do you see him?"
Now this great assembly has gathered here together; with the sole exception of Gautama, who is upright in countenance, none among them can equal this young brahmin (māṇava).
Yet this māṇava kills living beings, commits theft, indulges in lust, lacks propriety, speaks falsehoods, practices deception, burns people with fire, obstructs roads, and does evil.
"O Brahmins! This young man Aṅgaka is possessed of every evil; yet what is the use of his recitation and his physical beauty?
At that time, the five hundred Brahmins remained silent and did not reply.
Zhongde addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one is fully endowed with the observance of precepts and possesses penetrating wisdom, then their words will be ultimate sincerity, free from falsehood; such a person may be called a Brahmin."
The Buddha said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"What do you think, O Guṇabhadra!
If, within two dharmas, one were to abandon one and establish the other, would that person also be called a brāhmaṇa, provided their speech is truthful and free from falsehood?"
He replied, "I cannot. Why is that?"
Precepts are wisdom, and wisdom is precepts;
when one possesses both precepts and wisdom, then what one says is truthful and free from falsehood—I call such a person a Brahmin.
The Buddha said: “Excellent! Excellent!”
As you have said, where there is precept there is wisdom, and where there is wisdom there is precept;
precept can purify wisdom, and wisdom can purify precept.
O Planter of Merit!
It is like a person washing their hands: the left and right hands require one another; the left can cleanse the right, and the right can cleanse the left.
This is also like this: where there is wisdom, there is precept; where there is precept, there is wisdom. Precept can purify wisdom, and wisdom can purify precept.
“Brahmin! One who is endowed with both precepts and wisdom—I call him a bhikṣu.
At that time, the brahmin Saṅgharakṣita addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by precepts?
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!"
"Listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well; I shall explain it to you in detail, point by point. He replied:
"So be it! We wish and desire to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin, saying:

“If a Tathāgata appears in the world—an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of men, a teacher of devas and humans, a Buddha, a World-Honored One—he, having realized it for himself through direct experience among gods, humans, śramaṇas, and brahmins, proclaims it to others; his words—superior, middling, and inferior—are all entirely true, complete in meaning and phrasing, and pure in holy life.”
If a householder or a householder’s son hears this Dharma, their faith becomes pure;
once their faith is purified, they reflect thus:
"Living as a householder is difficult, like being bound in shackles."
‘I wish to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), yet I cannot attain mastery over it.
Now, I would rather shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way.

At another time, he abandoned his family wealth and business, cast aside his kinsmen, donned the three dharma robes, removed all ornaments, recited the Vinaya, and became fully endowed with the precepts. He renounced killing and abstained from it—up until attaining the joy and bliss of the four dhyānas of the mind and mental factors in this very life.
Why is this so? It is because it is obtained through diligent effort, focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, and the delight in dwelling alone in seclusion. O Brahmin!
"This is what it means to be endowed with precepts. He asked again:
"What is meant by wisdom?"
The Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu, with a mind purified by samādhi, free from defilement, supple and subdued, abides in the state of immovability—until he attains the three knowledges (trividyā), eliminates ignorance, gives rise to the light of wisdom, extinguishes darkness, produces the great light of the Dharma, and brings forth the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna)."
Why is this so? It is obtained through diligent effort, focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, and the delight in dwelling alone in seclusion. O Brahmin!
"This is what it means to be fully endowed with wisdom.
At that time, the brahmin Jyotipāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha; I only pray that you will accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) within the True Dharma!"
“From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, I shall not steal, I shall not engage in sexual misconduct, I shall not deceive, and I shall not drink intoxicants.
At that time, the brahmin Jotidāsa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
23. The Kūṭadanta Sūtra (23). The Fourth Sūtra of the Third Division of the Long Discourses Spoken by the Buddha: The Kūṭadanta Sūtra. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. While traveling through the human realm, he arrived at the north of the brahmin village of Khānumata in Kośala and stayed overnight in the Śiṃśapā forest.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Kūṭadanta who resided in the village of Khānumata. That village was prosperous and flourishing, with a dense population; it possessed gardens, groves, and bathing pools, and its trees provided refreshing shade. King Prasenajit had granted this village to the brahmin Kūṭadanta as his *brahmadeya* (a royal endowment for a priest).

This brahmin has maintained pure descent from both his father and mother for seven generations; he is not disparaged by others. He has mastered the recitation of the three Vedas and is proficient in various scriptures, discerning all their contents. There is no subtle or profound point in worldly treatises that he has not thoroughly mastered. Furthermore, he is skilled in the physiognomy of great men, in divining auspicious and inauspicious signs, and in the rituals of sacrifice; he has five hundred disciples whom he teaches without ceasing.

At that time, a brahmin wished to perform a great sacrifice; he prepared five hundred bulls, five hundred cows, five hundred male calves, five hundred female calves, five hundred rams, and five hundred wethers, intending to provide them for the offering.

At that time, the brahmins, householders, and lay devotees of the village of Khānumata heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan who had left home to attain the Way, was wandering through the human realms of the kingdom of Kośala and had arrived at the Śiṃśapā Forest north of the village of Khānumata. He possessed great renown that spread throughout the world; he was a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he realized it for himself and taught the Dharma to others; his words—superior, middling, and inferior—were all entirely true, complete in meaning and flavor, and pure in holy conduct.
"Such a True Person (sappurisa) ought to be visited; let us now go together to see him.
Having spoken these words, they immediately led one another out of the village of Khānumata, proceeding in groups and following one another, desiring to go to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the brahmin Kūṭadanta was atop a high tower; seeing from afar the multitude of people following one another in groups, he turned to his attendants and asked:
"For what reason are those people following one another in groups?"
"Where do you wish to go? The attendant replied:

"I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who left home to attain the Way, is traveling among the people in the kingdom of Kośala and has arrived at the Śiṃśapā forest north of the village of Khānumata. He possesses great renown that has spread throughout the world; he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among devas, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he has realized it for himself and teaches the Dharma to others. His words—superior, middling, and inferior—are all entirely true and correct, complete in meaning and flavor, and his holy life is pure."
"The brahmins, elders, and householders of this village have gathered together and are following one another, wishing only to go and pay their respects to the śramaṇa Gautama.
At that time, the brahmin Kuṭadanta immediately commanded his attendant:
"Go quickly with my words and tell those people: [The brahmin Kuṭadanta says: 'I am ill and suffering.'"
"Wait a moment, sirs; you must wait for me to go, so that we may go together to the śramaṇa Gautama.
Then, the attendant, having received these instructions, went and said to the people: "Wait! Wait!"
"Wait until we have arrived; we shall go together to the place where the śramaṇa Gautama is.
The people replied to the messenger, saying:
"Return quickly and inform the brāhmaṇa:"
"Now is precisely the right time; we should go together.
The attendant returned and reported that the people had already stopped, saying, "Now is precisely the right time; we should go together."
Then, the brahmin immediately descended from the upper story and stood outside the middle gate.

At that time, there were five hundred other brahmins sitting outside the middle gate, assisting Kūṭadanta in preparing for the great sacrifice; seeing Kūṭadanta, they all rose to greet him and asked: "Great Brahmin!"

"Where do you intend to go? He replied: "I have heard that there is a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas who has left home and attained the Way; he is wandering among the people in the kingdom of Kośala and has arrived at the Śiṃśapā Forest north of the village of Khānumata. He possesses great renown that spreads throughout the world; he is a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among gods, humans, śramaṇas, and brahmins, he has realized this for himself and teaches the Dharma to others; his words—superior, middling, and inferior—are all entirely true, complete in meaning and flavor, and pure in holy conduct."
"A true person such as this should be visited for an audience. O Brahmins!

I have further heard that Gautama knows the three types of sacrifice and the sixteen sacrificial requisites—things that even those among us who are long-established scholars cannot know. Now, I wish to perform a great sacrifice; the cattle and sheep are already prepared. I intend to go to Gautama to inquire about the three types of sacrifice and the sixteen sacrificial requisites. Once we have obtained these sacrificial methods, our merit will be complete and our fame will spread far and wide."
Then, five hundred brahmins said to Kūṭadanta:
"Great Teacher, do not go. Why is this?
He should come here; you should not go there."

For seven generations back, the Master’s parents have been of pure lineage and have never been disparaged by others; if one has accomplished this dharma, that person should come here, and one should not go to them.

He further said: "The Great Master has mastered the recitation of the three Vedas of the heterodox schools; he can distinguish all manner of scriptures and treatises; there is no subtle or profound point in secular classics that he has not thoroughly studied. Furthermore, he is skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the divination of auspicious and inauspicious signs, and the rituals of sacrifice. One who has perfected such qualities as these should go to him, and he should not go to him."

Furthermore, the Great Master’s countenance is upright and handsome, and he has attained the Brahma-like appearance; as one who has perfected this Dharma, he should come to us, and we should not go to him. Moreover, the Great Master’s virtue of precepts is supreme and his wisdom is accomplished; as one who has perfected this Dharma, he should come to us, and we should not go to him.

Furthermore, since the Great Master’s speech is gentle and harmonious, his eloquence is complete, and the meaning and flavor of his words are pure, one who has perfected this Dharma should go to him; he should not go to him. He should not go to him.
"Furthermore, as the Great Teacher is the leader of the assembly and his disciples are numerous, those who have perfected this Dharma should come to him; he should not go to them."
Furthermore, the Great Master constantly instructs five hundred brahmins; those who have perfected this Dharma should come to him, and he should not go to them.

Moreover, students from all four directions come to the Great Master to request instruction and inquire about various arts and sacrificial rites, and he is able to answer them all completely; those who have perfected this Dharma should come to him, and he should not go to them.
Furthermore, since the Great Teacher was venerated and supported by King Prasenajit and King Bimbisāra, those who have perfected this Dharma should go to him, and he should not go to them.
Furthermore, the Great Teacher is wealthy and possesses abundant treasures, his storehouses overflowing; one who has accomplished this Dharma should go to him, but he should not go to such a person.

Moreover, the Great Teacher’s wisdom is clear and penetrating, his speech is fluent and eloquent, and he is free from timidity; one who has accomplished this Dharma should go to him, but he should not go to such a person.
“If the Great Master is endowed with these eleven qualities, he should come here; you should not go there.
Then Kūṭadanta said, “So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said.”

We truly possess these virtues; it is not that we lack them. You should listen further to what I say: regarding the merits and virtues achieved by the śramaṇa Gautama, we ought to go to him; he should not come here.

The śramaṇa Gautama has had pure and genuine parents for seven generations; he is not disparaged or reviled by others. Since he has accomplished these qualities, we should go to him; he should not have to come to us.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is handsome in appearance and born of the Kṣatriya caste; since he has accomplished this Dharma, I should go to him, and he should not have to come to me.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama was born into a noble family and left the household life to pursue the Way; since he has accomplished this Dharma, I ought to go to him, and he should not have to come here.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with radiant light and possesses a truly noble lineage; having left the household life to practice the path and accomplished this Dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come to me.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama was born into a wealthy family and possesses great power; having left the household life to practice the Way and accomplished this Dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come to me.
"Furthermore, the ascetic Gautama is endowed with the precepts of the noble ones and has achieved wisdom; since he has perfected these dharmas, I should go to him, and he should not come to me."
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is skilled in speech; his words are gentle, harmonious, and elegant. Since he has perfected these qualities, I should go to him; he should not have to come to me.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is a leader of the multitude with many disciples; since he has perfected this Dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come to me.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama has eternally extinguished sensual desire; he is free from sudden violence, his anxieties and fears have been eliminated, and his hair does not stand on end. He is joyful and serene, praising others when he sees them, skillfully explaining the retribution of actions, and not disparaging other paths. Since he has accomplished these qualities, I should go to him; he should not come to me.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is constantly honored and supported with offerings by King Prasenajit and King Bimbisāra; since he has perfected this Dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come to me.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is honored and provided for with offerings by the brahmin Vokkāṇa; he is also revered and provided for with offerings by the brahmins Brahmāyu, Tārukkha, Sañjaya, and the young brahmin student Suka, son of Todeyya. Since he has accomplished these qualities, I should go to him; he should not come to me.

“Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is honored, revered, and supported by his disciples of the śrāvaka vehicle; he is also respected by the devas and various spirits. The Śākyas, Koliyas, Malla-Neṇiyas, Vṛjis, Mallas, and Soma all revere him. Since he has accomplished this Dharma, I should go to him; he should not have to come to me.”

Furthermore, since King Prasenajit and King Bimbisāra have received the three refuges and the five precepts from the śramaṇa Gautama, and have thus perfected this Dharma, I ought to go to him; he should not come to me.
Furthermore, since the śramaṇa Gautama and the brahmin Puṣkarasādi have received the three refuges and the five precepts and perfected these dharmas, I should go to them; they should not come to me.

Furthermore, the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama receive the three refuges and the five precepts; so too do the devas, the Śākyas, the Koliyas, and others who receive the three refuges and the five precepts and perfect this Dharma. To such persons as these, I should go; they should not come to me.
"Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama travels, he is honored and supported by all people; since he has accomplished this dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come to me."

Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes—to cities, towns, or villages—there is none who does not move with devotion, paying him honor and making offerings. Since he has accomplished such a dharma, I should go to him; he should not come to me.
Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, non-humans and spirits do not dare to disturb him; since he has accomplished such a dharma, I should go to him, and he should not come to me.

Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, the people of that place all behold a brilliant light and hear the sounds of celestial music; since he has accomplished this Dharma, I ought to go to him, and he should not come to me.

Furthermore, wherever the śramaṇa Gautama goes, when he wishes to depart, the multitude follows him with longing and weeps as they see him off; since he has accomplished such a dharma, I ought to go to him, and he should not come here.

"Furthermore, when the śramaṇa Gautama first left the household life, his parents and kinsmen wept and were filled with longing and regret. Since he has accomplished this Dharma, I ought to go to him; he should not have to come here."

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama left home in his youth and vigor, renouncing all ornaments, elephants, horses, precious chariots, the five desires, and necklaces; since he has accomplished this Dharma, I ought to go to him, and he should not have to come to me.

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama has renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch to leave the household life and cultivate the Way. Had he remained at home, he would have ruled over the four quarters of the world, governing both people and things, and we would all have been his subjects. Since he has accomplished this Dharma, I ought to go to him; he should not come to me.

"Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama clearly understands the Brahma-dharma and is able to expound it for others; he even converses with the Brahmā gods. One who has accomplished such a dharma, I should go to him; he should not have to come to me."

Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama clearly understands the three kinds of sacrifices and the sixteen sacrificial requisites, which we elders have been unable to know; since he has perfected these dharmas, I should go to him, and he should not come to me.
Furthermore, the śramaṇa Gautama is endowed with the thirty-two marks; one who has accomplished such a dharma as this, I ought to go to him, and he should not come to me.
Moreover, the śramaṇa Gautama possesses penetrating wisdom and is free from timidity; one who has accomplished such a dharma as this, I ought to go to him, and he should not come to me.
"That Gautama has come here to this village of Khānumata; he is our superior and a distinguished guest. We ought to go and pay him our respects.
Then, five hundred brahmins said to Kūṭadanta:
"How extraordinary!"
"How extraordinary! Are his merits truly such as these?
If the Gautama had accomplished even one of these virtues, he should not have come here; how much less so now that he possesses them all?"
"It would be fitting for us all to lead one another and go together to pay our respects. Kūṭadanta said,
"Those who wish to go, you should know that now is the time."

Then, the brahmin immediately prepared his precious chariot and, surrounded by five hundred brahmins as well as the brahmins, elders, and householders of Khānumata, proceeded to the Śiṃśapā Grove. Having arrived, he alighted from the chariot and advanced on foot to where the World-Honored One was. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side.

At that time, the various brahmins, elders, and householders either sat after bowing to the Buddha, or sat after exchanging greetings, or sat after announcing their names, or sat with palms joined toward the Buddha, or sat in silence.
When the assembly had taken their seats, Kūṭadanta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if you have the leisure and would grant me leave to do so, I would venture to inquire."
The Buddha said,
"Ask whatever you wish. Then,
the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We have heard that Gautama clearly understands the three types of sacrifice and the sixteen sacrificial requisites, which even our long-lived elders could not know. We now wish to perform a great sacrifice; we have already prepared five hundred bulls, five hundred cows, five hundred young bulls, five hundred young cows, five hundred rams, and five hundred wethers, intending to offer them in sacrifice. We have come today specifically to inquire about the methods of the three sacrifices and the sixteen requisites. If this sacrifice is successfully accomplished, one will obtain a great reward, one's fame will spread far and wide, and one will be honored by gods and men."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin Kūṭadanta, saying:
"Listen attentively now, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake."
The brahmin said: "Indeed it is so, Gautama!"
"I wish to hear it with joy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Kūṭadanta, saying:

"In the distant past, long ago, there was a Kṣatriya king of the *abhiṣecita* (consecrated) lineage who wished to perform a great sacrifice. He assembled the Brahmins and his ministers and said to them:"

"I now possess great wealth and treasures in abundance; I indulge freely in the five desires. My years have advanced, yet my troops are powerful and strong, devoid of any cowardice, and my treasuries are overflowing."
"Now we wish to perform a great sacrifice; you all must explain the sacrificial rites—what is required for this?
At that time, the minister addressed the king, saying: "It is so."
"Great King! As Your Majesty has said, the kingdom is wealthy, the army is strong, and the treasuries are overflowing.

However, the people and their possessions mostly harbor evil intentions and practice various unrighteous acts. If one were to perform a sacrifice at such a time, the ritual laws would not be fulfilled; it would be like sending a thief to pursue a thief—the mission would not succeed."
"Great King! Do not harbor such thoughts as: 'These are my subjects; I can strike them, I can kill them, I can rebuke them, or I can restrain them.

Those who serve the King should be provided with what they require; those who engage in commerce should be provided with wealth and treasures; and those who cultivate the fields should be provided with oxen, calves, and seed-grain, so that each may attend to their own affairs."
“When the king does not oppress his subjects, the people will live in peace and security, raising their children and grandchildren, and enjoying themselves together.
The Buddha told Kūṭadanta:

“At that time, having heard the words of his ministers, the king provided clothing and food to those close to him, bestowed wealth and treasures upon the merchants, and gave oxen and seeds to those who cultivated the fields.”
"At that time, the people each attended to their own affairs, did not harm one another, raised their children and grandchildren, and enjoyed themselves together.
The Buddha said:
"Then, the king again summoned his ministers and spoke to them:"

"Our country is wealthy and its military is strong; our treasuries are overflowing. We provide for all our people so that none lack anything, raising up our children and grandchildren, and enjoying ourselves together."
"I now wish to perform a great sacrifice; tell me what is required for the sacrificial rites.
The ministers replied to the king:
"It is so, it is so, just as Your Majesty has said."

The state is wealthy and the army is strong; the treasuries are overflowing, providing for all the people so that none lack anything, while they raise their children and grandchildren and enjoy themselves together.
"Should the King wish to perform a sacrifice, he may inform those within the palace.
At that time, the King followed the minister's words and entered to speak to those within the palace:
"My country is wealthy and my army is strong; my treasuries are overflowing with many riches and treasures, and I wish to establish a great sacrifice."
Then the ladies immediately said to the king:
"It is so, it is so, just as Your Majesty has said.
The kingdom is wealthy and the army is strong; the treasuries are overflowing and filled with many precious jewels. We wish to perform a great sacrifice; now is precisely the right time."
The king went out and informed his ministers, saying:

"My country is wealthy and my army is strong; the treasuries are overflowing. I provide for all the people so that they lack for nothing, allowing them to raise their children and grandchildren and enjoy themselves together."
"Now we wish to perform a great sacrifice; we have already informed those within the palace. Tell me everything you know: what items will be required in this brief interval?
At that time, the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"So be it, so be it; it is exactly as Your Majesty has said."

"I wish to prepare for a great sacrifice; I have already informed those within the palace, but have not yet informed the crown prince, the princes, the high ministers, and the generals. Your Majesty should inform them."
At that time, having heard the words of his ministers, the king immediately addressed the crown prince, the princes, the various officials, and the generals and soldiers, saying:
"My country is wealthy and my army is strong; my treasuries are overflowing. I wish to perform a great sacrifice."
At that time, the crown prince, the princes, and all the ministers and generals immediately said to the king:
"So it is, so it is, Great King!"
"Now the nation is wealthy and the army is strong; the treasuries are overflowing. If you wish to establish a sacrifice, now is precisely the right time.
Then, the king again addressed his ministers, saying:
"My country is wealthy and my army is strong, and I possess abundant treasures. I wish to perform a great sacrifice."
Having spoken thus to those within the palace, the crown prince, the princes, and even the generals and soldiers, he asked: "I now wish to perform a great sacrifice; what is required for this?
The ministers replied to the king:
"As the Great King has said, if you wish to establish a sacrifice, now is precisely the right time."

Having heard these words, the king immediately erected a new hall to the east of the city. The king entered the new residence, donned a deer-skin garment, and anointed his body with fragrant ghee. He also placed a deer horn upon his head, smeared cow dung upon the ground, and sat and lay upon it. Together with the first consort, the brahmins, and the ministers, he selected a single yellow cow; one portion of its milk was for the king’s food, one for the consort’s food, one for the ministers’ food, and one was offered to the assembly, while the remainder was given to the calf.
"At that time, the king shall accomplish eight qualities, and the minister shall accomplish four qualities.
"What are the eight qualities accomplished by the king?

That Kṣatriya king has been of pure descent from both his father and mother for seven generations, such that he is not looked down upon or disparaged by others; this is the accomplishment of the first quality."
That king is handsome in appearance and belongs to the Kṣatriya caste; these are the two qualities.
That king’s virtue of precepts flourishes and he is fully endowed with wisdom; these are the three qualities.

That king practiced various arts and skills—riding elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as the methods of combat with swords, spears, bows, and arrows—and there was nothing he did not fully know; these constitute the four dharmas.
That king possesses great power and majesty, subduing all minor kings so that none do not submit; this is the fifth quality.
That king is skilled in speech, his words are gentle, and they are complete in both meaning and flavor; this is the sixth quality.
That king possesses abundant wealth and treasures, and his storehouses are overflowing; this is the seventh quality.
That king is wise, strategic, brave, and decisive, and is no longer timid or weak; this is the eighth quality.
"That Kṣatriya king accomplishes these eight dharmas.
What are the four dharmas accomplished by the minister?
That Brāhmaṇa minister has had parents of pure lineage for seven generations and is not looked down upon or reviled by others; this is the first dharma."

Furthermore, that minister was proficient in reciting the three Vedas of the heterodox schools; he could analyze various scriptures and was thoroughly versed in even the most profound and subtle points of worldly classics. Moreover, he was skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the observation of auspicious and inauspicious signs, and the rituals of sacrifice—these constitute the second set of qualities.
Furthermore, a minister is skilled in speech; his words are gentle and harmonious, and they are complete in both meaning and flavor—this is the third quality.
Furthermore, a minister possesses wisdom, strategy, courage, and decisiveness, and he is never timid or weak; he understands all the rites of sacrifice—this is the fourth quality.

At that time, that king was accomplished in eight qualities; the brahmin ministers were accomplished in four qualities; and that king possessed four supports, three sacrificial rites, and sixteen sacrificial implements.
At that time, the brahmin minister, at his new residence, used sixteen points to explain the matter and resolve the king's doubts.
What are these sixteen?
The minister addressed the king, saying: "Some people have remarked:
'Now this Kṣatriya king wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet for seven generations his parents have been of impure lineage and has constantly been held in contempt and disparagement by others.'"
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King.
Why is this? Because for seven generations back, the King’s parents have been of pure lineage, and he has never been subject to the contempt or disparagement of others."
Suppose someone were to say:
"This Kṣatriya king wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet his countenance is ugly and he is not of the Kṣatriya lineage.
Even if such words are spoken, they cannot defile the king. Why is this so?
The king’s countenance was upright and handsome, and he belonged to the Kṣatriya caste. Some people said:
"Now this Kṣatriya king wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet he lacks superior discipline and is not endowed with wisdom."
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this?
Because the King’s virtue of the precepts is supreme and his wisdom is complete.
Or someone might say:

"Now this Kṣatriya king wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet he is unskilled in various arts; he cannot understand or master riding elephants, horse-drawn chariots, or the various methods of military strategy."
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this?
Because the King is skilled in all arts and crafts, and there is no strategy of battle or military science he does not understand."
Suppose someone were to say:
"The King wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet he lacks the great power to bring the subordinate kings under his control.
Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this so?
"The King possesses great power and authority, bringing all the minor kings under his sway. Or someone might say:
"The King intends to perform a great sacrifice, yet he is unskilled in speech; what he says is coarse and harsh, lacking in meaningful depth."
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this?
Because the King is skilled in speech; what he says is gentle and his words are complete in both meaning and flavor."
Suppose someone were to say:
"The King wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet he lacks abundant wealth and treasures.
Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King; why is this so?
The king’s treasuries were overflowing and he possessed abundant wealth and treasures.
Yet some people said:
"The king wishes to perform a great sacrifice, but he lacks strategic wisdom and his will is timid and weak."
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the king. Why is this?
Because the king possesses wisdom, strategy, courage, and decisiveness, and is free from any timidity or weakness.
Or someone might say:
"The King intends to perform a great sacrifice, yet he has not informed those within the palace.
Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this so?
Because when the King desires to perform a sacrifice, he first informs those within the palace.
Suppose someone were to say:
"The King intends to perform a great sacrifice, yet he has not informed the Crown Prince or the princes.
Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King; why is this so?
When the king wished to perform a sacrifice, he first informed the crown prince and the royal sons.
Yet some people said:
"The king wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet he does not inform the assembly of ministers."
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this?
Because when the King intended to perform a great sacrifice, he first informed his ministers.
Then, someone might have said:"
"If the King intends to perform a great sacrifice, he does not inform his generals and soldiers.
Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this?
Because when the King wishes to perform a sacrifice, he first informs his generals and soldiers.
“Some people say: ‘The King intends to perform a great sacrifice, yet the Brahmin ministers have not had pure parentage for seven generations; they are constantly despised and reviled by others.’”
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this?
For seven generations back, my parents have been of pure and upright lineage, never having been subject to the contempt or disparagement of others."
Some people might say:

"The King wishes to perform a great sacrifice, yet his ministers are ill-suited to recite the three Vedas of the heterodox schools; they cannot discern various scriptures, nor have they mastered the subtle mysteries of worldly treatises. Furthermore, they are not skilled in the physiognomy of great men, in divining good and bad fortune, or in the rituals of sacrificial offerings."
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this? I have recited and mastered the three classes of heterodox scriptures;

I am able to discern all manner of secular texts; there is nothing among the profound subtleties of worldly treatises that I have not thoroughly studied; furthermore, I am skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the observation of auspicious and inauspicious omens, and the rituals of sacrifice."
Suppose someone were to say:
"The King intends to perform a great sacrifice, yet his ministers are not skilled in speech; what they say is coarse and vulgar, lacking in profound meaning.
Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this so?
I am skilled in speech; what I say is gentle and harmonious, and it is complete in both meaning and flavor. Yet some may say:
"The King wishes to perform a great sacrifice, but his chief ministers lack wisdom and strategy, their will is timid and weak, and they do not understand the sacrificial rites."
"Even if such words were spoken, they could not defile the King. Why is this?
My wisdom, strategy, courage, and decisiveness are free from any timidity; furthermore, there is no ritual of sacrifice that I do not understand."
The Buddha told Kūṭadanta:
"That king had doubts regarding sixteen matters, and that minister resolved the king's mind by means of sixteen points."
The Buddha said:
“At that time, the minister, in that new residence, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the king with ten points of practice. What are these ten?”
The minister said:

"When the King performs a sacrifice, to all those who have assembled—whether they have taken life or not—he gives equally. If one who has taken life comes, he gives to them as well; they shall know for themselves. If one who has not taken life comes, he likewise gives to them. He gives for this reason, giving with such a mind."

Furthermore, if there are those who come to this assembly who commit theft, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, frivolous talk, greed, envy, or hold wrong views, he still gives to them; they shall know for themselves. Likewise, if there are those who do not steal, up to and including those with right view, he also gives to them. He gives for this reason, giving with such a mind.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"That great minister instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him by means of these ten practices.
He further told the brahmin:
"At that time, three regrets arose in the mind of that Kṣatriya king regarding his new residence, which his ministers extinguished.
What were the three? The king gave voice to these regrets: [text follows]"

"I have now performed this great sacrifice; it has already been a great sacrifice, it shall be a great sacrifice, and it is currently a great sacrifice. Having conceived these three thoughts, which involve the expenditure of much wealth and treasure, he harbors regret and remorse.

The minister said: "Your Majesty has already performed this great sacrifice; having given, you shall give, and you are giving now. You should not give rise to regret regarding this meritorious offering."
"Thus, when the king enters his new residence, three kinds of regretful thoughts arise within him, which the ministers extinguish.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:

"At that time, the Kṣatriya king, the consecrated one by the sprinkling of water, on the fifteenth day when the moon was full, went out from that new residence. In the open space before the residence, he lit a great bonfire and, holding an oil jar in his hand, poured it onto the fire, proclaiming:"

"Give! Give! At that time, the king’s consort heard that when the fifteenth day of the month arrived and the moon was full, the king had gone out from his new palace and kindled a great bonfire before it, holding an oil jar in his hand and pouring it onto the flames while crying out, "Give! Give!"
Then those ladies and court attendants, taking with them much wealth and treasure, came to where the king was and addressed him, saying:
"These various precious gems shall assist Your Majesty in performing the sacrifice."
"O Brahmin! That king immediately said to his queen and court ladies: 'Stop!'"
"Stop! You have already made your offering; I myself possess great wealth and treasures, sufficient for the sacrifice.
Then the various ladies and court maids thought to themselves:
"We ought not to take these precious objects back to the palace; rather, when the King performs a great sacrifice in the eastern region, we should use them to assist him. O Brahmin!
"Subsequently, when the King was performing a great sacrifice in the eastern region, the Queen and the court ladies used these precious objects to assist in the preparations for the great sacrifice.

At that time, the Crown Prince and the royal sons heard that on the fifteenth day, when the moon was full, the King had gone out to his new palace and was lighting a great pyre of fire before it. Holding an oil flask in his hand, he poured the oil onto the flames and cried out: 'Give! Give!'"
Then those princes and royal sons, carrying much wealth and treasure, came to the king’s presence and said to him:
“With these precious objects, we shall assist you in your great sacrifice.”
The king said: "Stop! Stop!"
"You have already performed the offering; I myself possess great wealth and treasures, which are sufficient for the sacrifice.
Then the princes and royal sons thought to themselves:
"It is not fitting that we should take these precious objects back; if the King performs a great sacrifice in the south, we shall provide assistance with them."
"In this manner, the ministers brought precious objects, saying:
'We pray that you may assist the King in performing the western sacrifice.
The generals and soldiers also brought precious objects."
"I pray that you will assist the King in performing a sacrifice in the north.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
"When that king performs his great sacrifice, he does not kill oxen, sheep, or any other living beings; he uses only ghee, milk, sesame oil, honey, dark honey, and rock sugar for the sacrifice."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"When that kṣatriya king performs a great sacrifice, he is joyful at the beginning, joyful in the middle, and joyful at the end; this is the method for successfully accomplishing the sacrifice."
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"After that kṣatriya king has performed the great sacrifice, he shaves off his hair and beard, dons the three dharma robes, leaves the household life to follow the path, and cultivates the four immeasurable minds. When his body perishes and his life ends, he is reborn in the Brahma Heaven."

At that time, having performed great acts of giving, the King’s consort likewise shaved her hair, donned the three dharma robes, left the household life to practice the Way, and cultivated the four brahma-vihāras; when her body perished and her life ended, she was reborn in the Brahmā Heaven.

After the brahmin minister had instructed the king to perform sacrifices in the four directions and also made great offerings, he then shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, left the household life to practice the Way, and cultivated the four Brahma-abodes; when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"At that time, the king performed the three sacrificial rites and prepared sixteen sacrificial implements to complete the great sacrifice. What do you think of this?"
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, Kūṭadanta remained silent and did not respond.
Then, the five hundred brahmins said to Kūṭadanta, “The words of the śramaṇa Gautama are subtle and profound; why does our great teacher remain silent and not answer?”
Kūṭadanta replied: "The teaching of the śramaṇa Gautama is subtle and profound; it is not that I do not approve of it, but for this reason I remained silent."
I reflected within myself: "The śramaṇa Gautama speaks of this matter without saying that he heard it from another; I silently pondered:
'Could it be that the śramaṇa Gautama is that very Kṣatriya king himself?'"
"Or perhaps he is that brahmin minister?
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Kūṭadanta: "Excellent!"
Excellent! Your observation of the Tathāgata is most appropriate.
At that time, was the Kṣatriya king who performed the great sacrifice anyone else?
"Do not form such a view; it was I myself who was there at that time, and I exercised the wisdom of great generosity.
Kūṭadanta said to the Buddha, "Is there anything superior to these three sacrifices and sixteen sacrificial requisites for obtaining a great reward?"
The Buddha said, "There are. He asked:
"What are these? The Buddha said:

"If one can constantly provide offerings to the Sangha with these three sacrifices and sixteen sacrificial requisites, ensuring they are never interrupted, the merit will surpass that [of the former]."
He asked again:

"Regarding the three sacrifices and the sixteen sacrificial requisites, if one can constantly provide offerings to the Saṃgha so that they do not cease, is this merit the most supreme, or is there something even more supreme?"
The Buddha said, “There are.
He asked again:
“What is this? The Buddha said:

“If one were to perform the three types of sacrifices along with the sixteen sacrificial implements and provide for the Saṃgha so that these offerings never cease, it would not equal the merit of building monasteries, halls, and pavilions for the Saṃgha of the four quarters; this latter gift is supreme.”
He asked again:

"Regarding the three types of sacrifices and the sixteen sacrificial requisites, as well as providing for the Sangha so that offerings never cease, and building monasteries, halls, and pavilions for the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters—is this merit the most supreme, or is there something even more supreme?"
The Buddha said, "There are.
He asked again:

“What is this? The Buddha said: “If one performs three kinds of sacrifices with sixteen ritual implements to provide for the Saṃgha so that offerings do not cease, or builds monasteries, halls, and pavilions for the Saṃgha of the four quarters, it is not as good as giving rise to a heart of joy and speaking these words oneself:”
"To take refuge in the Buddha, to take refuge in the Dharma, and to take refuge in the Sangha—
this merit is most supreme.
He asked again:
"Is it by these three refuges alone that one obtains such great fruit and retribution?
Or is there something superior?
The Buddha said:
“There is. He asked again: “What is it?”
The Buddha said:

"If one receives and practices the five precepts with a joyful heart—refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts—this merit is most supreme."
He asked again:
"By observing these three sacrifices up to the five precepts, does one obtain a great karmic fruit?
Or is there something even more excellent?"
The Buddha said, "There are.
He asked again:
"What is this? the Buddha said, "If one can contemplate all sentient beings with a mind of loving-kindness for even as long as it takes to milk a cow, that merit is most supreme."
He asked again:
"By performing these three types of sacrifices up to the practice of a compassionate heart, does one obtain a great reward?
Or is there something superior?"
The Buddha said, "There are.
He asked again:

“What is this? The Buddha said: “If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, and there is someone who leaves the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma, becoming fully endowed with all virtues, even attaining the three types of supernormal knowledge (*traividyā*), extinguishing all darkness of delusion, and perfecting the light of wisdom. Why is this so? Because...”
"Because of non-negligence and delighting in seclusion and quietude, this merit is most supreme.
Kūṭadanta addressed the Buddha again, saying: "Gautama!..."
"For the sake of sacrifice, I have prepared five hundred oxen and five hundred sheep; I now release them all, allowing them to roam freely as they please, following water and grass.

I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha. Please accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) within the True Dharma. From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not commit sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants. I only pray that the World-Honored One and the great assembly will graciously accept my invitation."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

When the brahmin saw that the Buddha had accepted his invitation through silence, he immediately rose, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and departed. He returned home and prepared various kinds of delicacies.

When the time arrived the following day, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, proceeded to the brahmin’s house and sat down upon the prepared seat.

Then the brahmin personally served the food with his own hands to the Buddha and the Saṅgha. When the meal was finished, he removed the bowls, and after the ritual washing of the hands was completed, the Buddha spoke these verses for the sake of the brahmin:
"Fire is supreme among sacrifices; Recitation is supreme among poetic compositions;
The king is supreme among human beings; The ocean is supreme among all flowing waters."
Among the stars, the moon is supreme; among luminous bodies, the sun is supreme.
Throughout the upper and lower realms and the four directions, among all things that have come into being—including the gods and the people of the world—the Buddha alone is the most supreme.
"Those who seek great merit should make offerings to the Triple Gem.
At that time, the brahmin Kuṭadanta took a small seat and sat before the Buddha.

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught the Dharma for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them with discourses on generosity, morality, and rebirth in heaven; he explained how sensual desires are a great affliction, how the outflows are an obstruction, and that the way of departure is supreme, thereby revealing and manifesting all pure practices.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed that the brahmin’s disposition was supple and his hindrances were slight, making him easy to discipline. In accordance with the constant dharma of all Buddhas, he taught him the Truth of Suffering, analyzing and revealing it; he then taught the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of the Origin, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to Deliverance.
At that time, the brahmin Kuṭadanta, while still seated upon his mat, was freed from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

Just as a clean, white cloth easily takes dye, so it was with the brahmin Kuṭadanta; he saw the Dharma and attained the Dharma, realized the fruit and remained steadfastly established therein. No longer relying on the faith of others, he attained fearlessness and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I now take refuge for a second and third time in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Saṅgha. May the Buddha accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*) within the True Dharma. From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants."
He addressed the Buddha again, saying,
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will further accept my invitation for seven more days.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted it by remaining silent.
At that time, for seven days, the brahmin personally served the Buddha and the Sangha with his own hands; once the seven days had passed, the World-Honored One traveled among the people.
Not long after the Buddha had departed, the brahmin Kuṭadanta fell ill and passed away.
When many bhikṣus heard that Kuṭadanta, who had provided offerings to the Buddha for seven days, had fallen ill and passed away shortly after the Buddha’s departure, they thought to themselves:
"Now that this man has passed away, where will he go?"
Then, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
"The Kūṭadanta has now passed away; where will he be reborn? they asked.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“That person has purely cultivated the brahma-faring and achieved perfection in each dharma; furthermore, he does not cause any disturbance within the dharmas. Having severed the five lower fetters, he attains parinirvāṇa there in this very life and does not return to this world.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Scroll Fifteen; *The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra*, Scroll Sixteen.
Translated by Buddhayaśas together with Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
24. The Sūtra on Firmness (XXIV), Part Three, The Fifth Sūtra on Firmness.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Pāpāliyañca Grove near the city of Nālandā, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was the son of a householder named Sthira who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then, the householder’s son Sthira addressed the Buddha, saying: “Excellent!
"Blessed One!
We only pray that you would now command the bhikṣus:
'If any brahmins, sons of elders, or householders come, you should manifest supernormal powers for them and display the dharmas of a superior person.'"
The Buddha told Sthiramati:
"I never instruct the bhikṣus to manifest supernormal powers or the superhuman dharmas for the sake of brahmins, elders, or householders."

I merely instruct my disciples to contemplate the Way in silence within secluded places; if they possess merit, they should conceal it themselves, and if they have faults, they should disclose them themselves.
Then, the elder’s son Dṛḍha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will command the bhikṣus:
‘If any brāhmaṇas, elders, or householders come, you should manifest supernormal powers for them and reveal the qualities of a superior person.’”
The Buddha again addressed Sthiramati:
"I never instruct the bhikṣus to manifest supernormal powers or the superhuman dharmas for the sake of brahmins, elders, or householders."

I merely instruct my disciples to contemplate the Way in silence within secluded places; if they possess merit, they should conceal it themselves, and if they have faults, they should disclose them themselves.
Then, the elder’s son Dṛḍha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I have no doubt regarding the superhuman qualities of the World-Honored One.

However, this city of Nālandā is prosperous and peaceful, with a flourishing population; if you were to manifest supernatural powers there, it would bring great benefit, and the Buddha and the great assembly would excellently propagate the transformation of the Way.”
The Buddha again addressed Sthiramati:
"I never instruct a bhikṣu to manifest supernormal powers or the superhuman dharmas for the sake of brahmins, sons of elders, or householders."

I merely instruct my disciples to contemplate the Way in silence within secluded places; if they possess merit, they should conceal it themselves, and if they have faults, they should reveal them themselves.
Why is that? Because there are three bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*). What are the three?
The first is the supernormal power of psychic travel; the second is the observation of others' minds; the third is instruction and admonition.
What is meant by the supernormal power of psychic travel?
O son of a householder!

A bhikṣu practices the immeasurable bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*); he is able to transform a single body into countless bodies, and to merge those countless bodies back into one. Whether far or near, mountains, rivers, stones, or walls, he moves through them with sovereign non-obstruction, as if traveling through space;
he sits cross-legged in mid-air like a flying bird;
and he enters and emerges from the great earth as if it were water.
If he walks upon water, it is as if he were treading on land;
his body emits smoke and fire like a great mass of flames; with his hands he touches the sun and moon; and standing, he reaches as far as the Brahma-heaven.

If there are wealthy householders or lay devotees who have gained faith, and who see this bhikṣu manifest immeasurable supernormal powers, standing poised up to the Brahma-heaven, they should go to other wealthy householders or lay devotees who have not yet gained faith and say to them:
"I saw a bhikṣu manifest immeasurable supernormal powers, standing poised up to the Brahma-heaven."
That householder or layman who had not yet attained faith said to those who had attained faith:
"I have heard that there is a *kūrma* spell capable of manifesting such immeasurable supernatural transformations, even reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven."
The Buddha again addressed the elder's son Sthira:
"That person who lacks faith has spoken such words; are these not indeed words of slander?
Sthira replied to the Buddha:
"This is indeed a slanderous statement.

The Buddha said, "For this reason, I do not command the bhikṣus to manifest supernatural transformations; rather, I teach my disciples to contemplate the Way in silence within secluded places. If one possesses merit, one should keep it concealed; if one has faults, one should disclose them."
Thus it is, householder!
This is the supernormal power manifested by my bhikṣus.
What is called "the supernormal power of observing the minds of others"?

Thereupon, the bhikṣu manifested the supernormal power of immeasurable observation; he perceived the dharmas contemplated in the minds of all sentient beings and was able to recognize everything they did in secret.

If there is a wealthy householder or lay devotee who has gained faith, and who sees a bhikṣu manifesting immeasurable miraculous powers of observation, perceiving the mental states of other sentient beings, and knowing all that is done in secret places, he will then go to other wealthy householders or lay devotees who have not yet gained faith and say to them:
"I have seen a bhikṣu manifest immeasurable miraculous powers of observation; he perceives the mental states of other sentient beings and is able to know all that is done in secret places."
When those faithless elders and householders heard these words, they gave rise to slanderous remarks, saying:
"There is a Gandhāra spell capable of observing the minds of others, by which one can know everything done in secret corners."
"What do you think, son of a householder!
Is this not indeed a slanderous statement?
Sthiramati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This is indeed a slanderous statement," the Buddha said.

"For this reason, I do not command the bhikṣus to manifest supernatural transformations; rather, I instruct my disciples to contemplate the Way in silence within secluded places. If they possess merit, they should conceal it; if they have faults, they should disclose them."
"In this way, son of a householder!
This is my bhikṣu’s supernormal power of present observation.
What is the supernormal power of instruction?
"O Son of a Householder!

If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, endowed with the ten titles, having realized it for himself among gods, humans, Māras, or Māra-devas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he teaches the Dharma to others; his words—superior, middling, and inferior—are all entirely true, their meaning and flavor are pure, and they are complete in the holy life."
If a householder or a layperson, having heard this, gains faith therein; and having gained faith, reflects upon it within himself:
"It is not fitting for me to remain at home; for if one remains at home, they are bound together like a chain, unable to practice the holy life with purity."

I would now rather shave off my hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and fulfill all meritorious virtues, even to the point of accomplishing the three types of supernormal knowledge, extinguishing all darkness and giving rise to the great light of wisdom.
"Why is this so? It is obtained through diligent effort, delighting in solitary seclusion, and focused mindfulness without forgetfulness.
"O Son of a Householder!"
"This is my bhikṣu’s present teaching through supernormal power (ṛddhi).
At that time, the young householder Sthira addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is there any bhikṣu who has accomplished these three supernormal powers?"
The Buddha told the son of a householder:
"I do not say that there is a fixed number; there are many bhikṣus who have accomplished these three bases of supernormal power.
Son of a householder!"
"I have a bhikṣu among this assembly who reflects to himself:
'By what means shall these four great elements of this body—earth, water, fire, and wind—be eternally extinguished?'"
That bhikṣu suddenly took the path to the heavens and went to where the Four Great Kings were, asking them:
"By what means are these four great elements of this body—earth, water, fire, and wind—permanently extinguished?"
"O son of a householder!
Those Four Heavenly Kings replied to the bhikṣu, saying:
'We do not know by what means the four great elements are eternally extinguished.'"
Above me there is a heaven named Trāyastriṃśa, which is most subtle and supreme, possessing great wisdom; that heaven is able to know by what cause the four great elements perish.
Having heard this, that bhikṣu immediately and swiftly ascended to the heavenly realm, went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and asked the devas:
"By what means are these four great elements of the body—earth, water, fire, and wind—permanently extinguished?"
The deva of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven replied to the bhikṣu, saying:

"I do not know by what cause the four great elements cease. Above us there is another heaven named Yama; it is the most subtle and supreme, and its inhabitants possess great wisdom. That heaven is able to know."
He immediately went to question them, but they also said they did not know.
Proceeding in this manner through successive stages, he reached the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, yet all of them said:
"I do not know by what cause the four great elements perish."

Above this, there is another heaven, most subtle and supreme, possessing great wisdom, named Brahmakāyika; the gods therein are able to know by what means the four great elements are eternally extinguished.
That bhikṣu immediately and swiftly proceeded toward the Brahma-path; arriving at the Brahma Heaven, he asked:
"By what means are these four great elements of this body—earth, water, fire, and wind—permanently extinguished?"

That Brahmā replied to the bhikṣu, saying: "I do not know by what cause the four great elements are eternally extinguished. Now there is the Great Brahmā King, whom none can surpass; he governs a thousand worlds, possessing wealth, nobility, and majesty, having attained the highest sovereignty. He is able to create and transform all things and is the father and mother of all sentient beings. He is the one who knows by what cause the four great elements are eternally extinguished."
"O son of a householder!
That bhikṣu then asked:
'Where is that Great Brahmā King currently located?'"
The deva replied, "I do not know where the Great Brahmā is now, but judging by my own thoughts, he will appear before long.
Not long after, the Brahma King suddenly appeared.
"Householder!
That bhikṣu went to the Brahmā King and asked:
'By what means are these four great elements of this body—earth, water, fire, and wind—permanently extinguished?'"
That Great Brahmā King addressed the bhikṣu, saying:

"I, the Brahmā Deva-king, am invincible; I govern a thousand worlds, possessing wealth, honor, and nobility, having attained the highest sovereignty. I am the creator of all things and the father and mother of all sentient beings."
Then, that bhikṣu said to the Brahmā King:
"I did not ask about this matter; I asked about the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and by what means are they eternally extinguished?"
"O son of a householder!
That Brahmā King replied to the bhikṣu, saying:
'I am Mahābrahmā, the Heavenly King; there is none who can surpass me. I am the creator of all things, the father and mother of all sentient beings.'"
The bhikṣu spoke again: "I am not asking about this;
I ask myself by what means the four great elements are eternally extinguished.
"O son of a householder! [the bhikṣu continued].
The Brahma King thus repeated this up to three times, yet he was unable to answer the bhikṣu as to why the four great elements were eternally extinguished.
Then, the Great Brahma King took the bhikṣu by the right hand, led him to a secluded place, and said: "Bhikṣu!..."
Now all the Brahma Kings consider me to be foremost in wisdom, with nothing that I do not know or see; therefore, I cannot give you the answer:
"I do not know or see by what means these four great elements will be permanently extinguished."
He further said to the bhikṣu:
"You are greatly deluded!
You have abandoned the Tathāgata to go among the devas to inquire about this matter."
"You should go to the World-Honored One and inquire about this matter; you must receive and uphold well whatever the Buddha explains.
He further addressed the bhikṣu:
"The Buddha is currently at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī; you may go there and ask him."
“O son of a householder!
At that time, the bhikṣu suddenly vanished from the Brahma Heaven.

In the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, he arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. He came to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, sat to one side, and addressed me, saying:”
“World-Honored One!
By what cause do these four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—cease?
At that time, I replied:

“Bhikṣus! It is just as a merchant who, carrying a hawk on his arm, enters the sea; he releases that hawk to fly through the air toward the east, west, south, or north. If it finds dry land, it will stop there; if there is no dry land, it returns once more to the ship.”
"Monk! You are just like this; even when questioned on such a matter as far as the Brahma-world, you failed to establish it and have returned to me.
Now, I shall cause you to establish this meaning."
He then spoke in verse:
"By what means do the four great elements cease—earth, water, fire, and wind?
By what means do the coarse and the subtle, as well as the long and the short, the beautiful and the ugly, cease?"
By what means are name-and-form extinguished forever without remainder?
One should answer: consciousness is formless; it possesses its own immeasurable light.
When this is extinguished, the four great elements are extinguished; the coarse and the subtle, the beautiful and the ugly, are all extinguished.
"With the cessation of this name-and-form, consciousness ceases and the rest also cease.
At that time, the elder’s son Dṛḍha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the name of this bhikṣu?
How should he be addressed? The Buddha told the son of the householder:
“This bhikṣu is named Aśvajit; you should receive and uphold this.
At that time, the elder’s son Dṛḍha, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
25. The Discourse on the Naked Ascetic (25). Spoken by the Buddha, the sixth discourse in the third division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*: The Discourse on the Naked Ascetic. Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Vajji, in the Kimpaṭṭa Deer Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a naked ascetic of the Kāśyapa clan who went to where the World-Honored One was; having exchanged greetings, he sat to one side.
The naked ascetic Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that the Śramaṇa Gautama reviles all methods of sacrifice and insults those who practice austerities, calling them base and defiled."
"Gotama! If someone were to say:
'The śramaṇa Gotama reviles all sacrificial rites and insults those who practice asceticism, calling them base and corrupt.'"
"One who speaks these words is speaking in accordance with the Dharma; they have accomplished the Dharma and do not slander the śramaṇa Gautama.
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!"
If he should say:
"The śramaṇa Gautama reviles all sacrificial rites and insults those who practice asceticism as being base and filthy," that is not a true statement;
it is a false doctrine, a perversion of the Dharma, a slander against me, and not a truthful word.
Why is that? Kāśyapa! I see those practitioners of asceticism who, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, fall into hell.
Furthermore, one sees practitioners of asceticism who, upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in a favorable heavenly realm;
or one sees practitioners of asceticism who delight in practicing austerities, yet upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in hell;
or one sees practitioners of asceticism who delight in practicing austerities, and upon the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in a favorable heavenly realm.
