Kāśyapa! Regarding these two destinies and the places where their retributions are received, I know them all and see them all; how could I possibly reproach those who practice asceticism as being base and defiled?
When I say it is so, they say it is not; when I say it is not, they say it is so.
Kāśyapa, there are matters on which śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas agree, and there are matters on which śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas disagree.
“Kāśyapa! As for those who are not the same as that, I set them aside, because this Dharma is not shared with śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas. Kāśyapa!”

A wise person reflects in this way: "Between the ascetic Gautama and those other teachers, regarding unwholesome states—those that are heavy, turbid, dark, and not the qualities of the noble ones—who is capable of bringing these states to an end?"
Kāśyapa! When those wise ones contemplate in this way, they know and see thus: "Only the śramaṇa Gautama is able to extinguish these phenomena. Kāśyapa!
When those wise ones observe in this way, investigate in this way, and discourse in this way, I shall attain renown therein.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:

A wise person reflects in this way: "Between the disciples of the ascetic Gautama regarding unwholesome states—those that are heavy, turbid, dark, and unholy—and the disciples of other teachers regarding unwholesome states—those that are heavy, turbid, dark, and unholy—who among them is capable of extinguishing these states?"
Kāśyapa! A wise person makes such an observation and has such knowledge and vision: "Only the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama can extinguish these phenomena. Kāśyapa!
When those wise ones contemplate in this way, investigate in this way, and discourse in this way, my disciples shall then receive renown.
"Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"

A wise person would reflect in this way: "Between the ascetic Gautama regarding wholesome, pure, sublime, and noble dharmas, and those other teachers regarding wholesome, pure, sublime, and noble dharmas—who is capable of increasing and expanding their practice?"
Kāśyapa! A wise person makes such an observation and gains such insight: "Only the śramaṇa Gautama is capable of increasing and cultivating this Dharma."
Kāśyapa! When those wise ones contemplate in this way, investigate in this way, and discourse in this way, I shall possess renown therein.

“Kāśyapa! A wise person would observe this: Between the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama regarding all wholesome dharmas, pure and white, subtle and sublime, as well as the dharmas of the noble ones, and the disciples of other teachers regarding all wholesome dharmas, pure and white, subtle and sublime, as well as the dharmas of the noble ones—who among them is capable of increasing and practicing them?”
Kāśyapa! A wise person observes in this way and perceives in this way: only the disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama are capable of increasing their cultivation and practice of this Dharma.
Kāśyapa! When those who possess wisdom contemplate in this way, investigate in this way, and discourse in this way, they shall attain renown among my disciples.

Kāśyapa! There is a path and there is a track; when a bhikṣu practices therein, he knows for himself and sees for himself that the śramaṇa Gautama speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks according to the Dharma, and speaks according to the Vinaya.
“Kāśyapa! What is the path? What is the track?”

A bhikkhu practices therein, knowing for himself and seeing for himself that the ascetic Gotama speaks at the proper time, speaks truthfully, speaks meaningfully, speaks in accordance with the Dhamma, and speaks in accordance with the Vinaya.
Kāśyapa! In this regard, a bhikṣu cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on tranquility, relying on dispassion, and relying on renunciation;
he cultivates the awakening factors of dharma-discernment, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, relying on tranquility, relying on dispassion, and relying on renunciation.

Kāśyapa! This is the path, this is the track. A bhikṣu who practices within it knows for himself and sees for himself that the śramaṇa Gautama speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks with meaning, speaks according to the Dharma, and speaks according to the Vinaya.
Kāśyapa said: “Gautama!
There is only this path and this track; within it, a bhikṣu practices, knowing for himself and seeing for himself.”
The śramaṇa Gautama speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dharma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
Yet, there are those who, through ascetic practices that are defiled, obtain the name of "brāhmaṇa," and there are those who obtain the name of "śramaṇa."
"What constitutes the defilement of ascetic practices by which one obtains the name of a *brāhmaṇa* or the name of a *śramaṇa*, O Gautama?

[They are: being naked and devoid of clothing; covering oneself with one's hands; not accepting food at night; not accepting stale food; not accepting food from between two walls; not accepting food from between two people; not accepting food from between two knives; not accepting food from between two pestles; not accepting food from a household where a meal is being shared; not accepting food from a household where a woman is pregnant; not eating when a dog is at the door; not accepting food from a household where flies are present; and not accepting invited meals."

He declared that he would not accept food from those he had previously known; he did not eat fish, nor meat, nor drink wine; he did not eat from two vessels at once; he ate only one mouthful at a time, stopping after seven mouthfuls; when receiving additional food from others, he accepted no more than seven portions; and he would eat only once a day, or once every two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days.

Some eat fruits, some eat weeds, some eat rice-water, some eat hemp and rice, some eat wild rice, some eat cow dung, some eat deer dung, some eat roots, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of trees, or they eat fallen fruit;

some wear robes, some wear grass-cloth, some wear tree bark, some cover their bodies with straw, some wear deerskins, some let their hair grow long, some wear woven wool, or some wear shrouds from burial mounds;

some constantly hold their hands aloft, some do not sit on beds or mats, some remain constantly in a squatting posture, some shave their heads but keep their mustaches and beards, some lie upon thorns, some lie upon gourds and melons, and some lie naked upon cow dung.
"Sometimes bathing three times a day, or sometimes bathing three times a night, they exhaust this body with countless hardships.
Gautama! This is the defilement of asceticism; by it, one may obtain the name of a śramaṇa, or obtain the name of a brāhmaṇa."
The Buddha said, "Kāśyapa!

Those who discard clothing and go naked employ countless expedient means to torment this body; yet their precepts are not fulfilled, their vision is not fulfilled, they cannot practice with diligence, nor do they practice extensively."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way is one complete in ethical discipline?
In what way is one complete in view?"
"It surpasses all ascetic practices and is the most subtle and supreme.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Listen attentively and reflect well upon this; I shall speak for your sake."
Kāśyapa said: "Indeed it is so, Gautama!"
"I wish to hear it with eager joy.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If a Tathāgata, an Arhat, appears in the world, he attains happiness within the present life, up to the fourth dhyāna."
Why is this so? It is because of diligent effort, single-minded concentration, delighting in seclusion and tranquility, and being free from negligence. Kāśyapa!
"This is what constitutes the perfection of precepts and the perfection of vision; it surpasses all ascetic practices and is the most subtle and supreme.
Kāśyapa said, "Gautama!"

Although it is said that the perfection of precepts and the perfection of view surpass all ascetic practices and are the most subtle and supreme, yet the Dharma of the śramaṇas is difficult, and the Dharma of the brāhmaṇas is difficult.
The Buddha said,
“Kāśyapa! This is a unique quality (āveṇika-dharma) of the world.”
Regarding what are called the dharmas of śramaṇas and the dharmas of brāhmaṇas, Kāśyapa, even upāsikās can know these dharmas.
They may discard their robes and go naked, or employ countless expedient means to subject this body to ascetic toil; yet they do not understand its mind.
Is there a mind of ill will, or is there no mind of ill will? Is there a mind of resentment, or is there no mind of resentment? Is there a mind of harm, or is there no mind of harm?
One who knows such a mind is not called a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa; it is because they do not know this that being a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa is difficult to achieve.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is a śramaṇa and what is a brāhmaṇa who is fully endowed with ethical discipline and fully endowed with right view—such as is supreme, preeminent, subtle, and foremost?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall speak for your sake. Kāśyapa said:
“Indeed, Gautama! We wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha said, “Kāśyapa! That bhikṣu,

by means of the mind of samādhi, attains even the three supernormal knowledges (vidyā), extinguishing all darkness of delusion and giving rise to the light of wisdom— namely, the arising of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna).”
Why is this? It is because of their diligent application, their focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, their delight in solitary seclusion, and their lack of negligence. Kāśyapa!
"These are called śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are complete in ethical discipline and complete in right view; they are the most excellent, the most supreme, the subtle and wondrous, the foremost.
Kāśyapa said: "Gautama!"
Although it is said that among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, those who are complete in vision and complete in ethical discipline are supreme, excellent, subtle, and foremost,
yet the dharma of the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas is exceedingly difficult!
"It is extremely difficult!
A śramaṇa is difficult to know, and a brāhmaṇa is also difficult to know.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“An upāsaka can also practice this dharma. He replied:

“From this day forward, I am able to refrain from wearing clothes and go naked, even to the point of subjecting this body to hardship through countless expedient means; yet one cannot be called a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa on account of such conduct. If one were to be called a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa by virtue of this conduct, then it could not be said that being a śramaṇa is extremely difficult!”
"Brahmins are truly rare!
It is not because they practice these deeds that they are called śramaṇas and brahmins; rather, it is because [true] śramaṇas are truly rare and brahmins are truly rare!"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Once, in the past, while I was at Rājagṛha in the Seven-Leaf Cave on the high mountain, I taught pure asceticism to the brahmin Nyagrodha."
At that time, the brahmin gave rise to a heart of joy and attained pure faith; he made offerings to me and praised me, offering the foremost of offerings and praises unto me.
Kāśyapa said: “Gautama!
Who would not feel the highest joy, pure faith, reverence, and praise toward Gautama?”
"Now, toward Gautama, I too have conceived the foremost joy and attained pure faith; I shall make offerings, offer praise, and take refuge in Gautama.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Among all the various precepts that exist in the world, there are none equal to this supreme precept (adhiśīla), much less any that could surpass it."

Among all samādhis, wisdoms, liberations, and the vision and knowledge of liberation, there is none equal to this superior samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation; how much less could there be one that surpasses it?

Kāśyapa! That which is called the lion is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; because the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma extensively within the great assembly with sovereign fearlessness, he is named the Lion.
"What do you think, Kāśyapa?
Do you think that when the Tathāgata utters the lion’s roar, he is not courageous?
Do not form such a view; the Tathāgata’s lion’s roar is courageous and fearless."
Kāśyapa! Do you think that when the Tathāgata utters the courageous lion’s roar, he is not in the midst of the great assembly?
Do not hold such a view; the Tathāgata utters the courageous lion’s roar while in the midst of the great assembly.
Kāśyapa! Do you think that the Tathāgata, while roaring the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly, is unable to preach the Dharma?
Do not entertain such a view.
Why is this? The Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, is courageous and fearless, making the lion’s roar and being well able to preach the Dharma.
"What do you think, Kāśyapa?"

Do you think that when the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, is courageous and fearless, letting out the lion’s roar and skillfully preaching the Dharma, the listeners in the gathering are not single-minded?
Do not form such a view. Why is this?

The Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, is courageous and fearless, letting out the lion’s roar; he is skillfully able to preach the Dharma, and all those who have gathered to hear him listen with single-minded attention.
"What do you think, Kāśyapa?

Do you believe that when the Tathāgata stands amidst the great assembly, courageous and fearless, uttering the lion’s roar and skillfully preaching the Dharma, those who have gathered there will not all listen with single-minded attention, nor joyfully accept it in faith and put it into practice?"
Do not form such a view. Why is this?

The Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, is courageous and possesses great strength; he can roar the lion’s roar and is skilled in preaching the Dharma. All those who have gathered to hear him listen with single-minded attention, receiving it with joy and faith.

Kāśyapa! Do you suppose that the Tathāgata, who fearlessly roars the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly and skillfully preaches the Dharma, so that all those gathered there receive it with joy and faith, yet remains without offerings?

Do not form such a view; for the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, is courageous and fearless, roaring the lion's roar and skillfully preaching the Dharma. All those who have gathered listen with a single mind, receiving it with joy and faith, and making offerings.

“Kāśyapa! Do you think that the Tathāgata, being courageous and fearless amidst the great assembly, utters the lion’s roar, and even receives faithful veneration and offerings, yet does not shave off his beard and hair, don the three dharma robes, and leave the household life to practice the Way?”
Do not form such a view. Why is this?

It is because the Tathāgata, amidst the great assembly, is courageous and fearless; he is even worthy of faith, reverence, and offerings, having shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, and left the household life to cultivate the Way.

Kāśyapa! Do you think that although the Tathāgata is courageous and fearless amidst the great assembly, and even after leaving the household life to practice the Way, he has not perfected the holy life, nor reached the state of peace and security, the Nirvāṇa without remainder?
Do not form such a view. Why is this?

The Tathāgata is courageous and fearless amidst the great assembly; he has even gone forth to practice the Way, perfected the holy life, reached the state of peace and security, and attained Nirvāṇa without remainder.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying: "How is it, Gautama?
May I go forth within this Dharma and receive full ordination?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"If followers of other teachings wish to enter my Dharma to leave the household life and practice the Way, they should be retained for four months of observation; once they have met with the approval of the assembly, they may then leave the household life and receive the precepts."
"Kāśyapa! Although such a dharma exists, one must still observe the person. Kāśyapa said:

"If there are followers of other teachings who wish to enter the Buddha-dharma to practice the holy life (brahmacarya), they should be made to observe for four months; once they have met with the approval of the assembly, they may then go forth and receive the precepts."
"I am now able to observe within the Buddha-dharma for four years; once I have met with the approval of the assembly, I shall then leave the household life and receive the precepts.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I have already spoken; I simply wish to observe the person."
At that time, Kāśyapa immediately went forth in the Buddha’s Dharma and received full ordination.

Not long after receiving the precepts, Kāśyapa cultivated the unsurpassed holy life with pure faith; in this very life, he realized it for himself through direct experience: birth and death were exhausted, the holy life was established, what was to be done had been accomplished, and there would be no further existence. Thus, he became an Arhat.
At that time, Kāśyapa, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

**26. The Discourse on the Threefold Knowledge (Skt. *Traividya-sūtra*)** The third discourse in the third division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the seventh discourse, the *Traividya-sūtra*, as I have heard it:

At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kośala with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. He arrived at Icchānaṅgala, a village of the Kośalan brahmins, and stayed overnight in the Icchānaṅgala forest.
At that time, there were two brahmins named Pukkusāti and Tārukkha who, for some minor reason, went to the village of Icchānaṅgala.

This Brahmin Puṣkarasādi has maintained pure descent from both paternal and maternal lines for seven generations; he is not disparaged by others, and he has mastered the recitation of the three Vedas, being well-versed in distinguishing the various scriptures.

Furthermore, he was skilled in the methods for discerning the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*), in observing auspiciousness and misfortune, and in the rituals of sacrifice; he had five hundred disciples whom he taught without ceasing.

One of his disciples was named Vatsīputra, whose lineage of parents had remained pure for seven generations and who was never disparaged by others. He had mastered the recitation of the three collections of heterodox scriptures and could thoroughly distinguish all kinds of treatises. He was also skilled in the physiognomy of great men, capable of observing auspicious and inauspicious signs, and proficient in the rituals of sacrifice; he likewise had five hundred disciples whom he taught without ceasing.

The Tāliya brāhmaṇa was likewise of pure descent for seven generations on both his father’s and mother’s side, and was not held in contempt or disparaged by others. He had mastered the recitation of the three Vedas of the heterodox schools and could thoroughly distinguish the various scriptures; he was also skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the observation of auspicious and inauspicious signs, and the rituals of sacrifice, and he maintained a school of five hundred disciples, teaching them without ceasing.

One of his disciples was named Pāṭhadra; for seven generations his parents had been of pure lineage, such that he was never disparaged by others. He could recite the three Vedas with complete fluency, could distinguish all manner of scriptures, and was also skilled in the physiognomy of great men, the observation of auspicious and inauspicious signs, and the rituals of sacrifice. He also had five hundred disciples, whom he taught without ceasing.
At that time, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja went together to the park at dawn and began to debate their doctrines, each asserting his own position as right and the other's as wrong.
Then Vāseṭṭha said to Bhāradvāja:
"My path is true and correct; it enables one to attain liberation and reach the Brahma-world. This is what was taught by our great teacher, the brahmin Vessāmitta."
Pāṭikāputra spoke again: "My path is true and correct;
it is able to provide the means for deliverance, leading as far as the Brahma-heaven. This is what was taught by my great teacher, the Brahmin Tārukkha."

In this manner, Vāseṭṭha repeatedly asserted that his own path was the true and correct one, and Pūraṇa likewise repeatedly asserted that his own path was the true and correct one; as the two debated together, neither was able to reach a definitive conclusion.
Then Vāseṭṭha said to Bhāradvāja:

"I have heard that the ascetic Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan who left home to achieve enlightenment, is currently wandering among the people in the kingdom of Kosala, staying now in the Icchānaṅgala forest. He possesses great renown that has spread throughout the world; he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles."

Among gods, worldlings, Māras, or Māra-devas, śramaṇas, and brahmins, he has realized it for himself and teaches the Dharma to others; his words—whether superior, middling, or inferior—are entirely true and authentic, complete in meaning and phrasing, and pure in holy conduct.
Such a true person ought to be visited for an audience.

I have heard that this Gautama knows the path to the Brahma world and can explain it to others; he constantly engages in dialogue with Brahmā. We should go together to this Gautama to resolve this matter.
"Whatever the śramaṇa Gautama may say, we shall together receive and uphold it.
At that time, the two men, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, accompanied each other to the Icchānaṅgala forest; having approached the World-Honored One and exchanged greetings, they sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those two men, addressed Vāseṭṭha, saying:
"This morning, you two came to the grove and engaged in such a discussion, mutually disputing right and wrong."
You alone have said:
"My teaching is true and authentic, capable of leading to deliverance and reaching the Brahma-heaven; this is what was taught by the Great Teacher Pūraṇa Kāśyapa."
One of them said: "My teaching is true and correct;
it can lead to the definitive escape and reach the Brahma-heaven. This is what the Great Teacher Tārukkha has taught."
Thus they spoke back and forth three times, disputing with one another: "Is such a thing as this true?
At that time, when Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja heard these words from the Buddha, they were all struck with amazement; their hair stood on end, and they thought to themselves:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great spiritual power and virtue; he knows the minds of others beforehand. That which we intended to discuss, the śramaṇa Gautama has already spoken of in full."
Then Vāseṭṭha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This path and that path are both called true and authentic; both lead to liberation and reach the Brahma-world. Is it the teaching of the brahmin Pokkharasāti that is correct?"
"Is what was said by the Brahmin Tārukkha correct? The Buddha said, "Indeed so, Vāseṭṭha!"

"This path and that path are the true and correct means of deliverance, leading to the Brahma-heaven; why do you spend the early morning in the grove disputing with one another, even up to three times?"
Then Vāseṭṭha addressed the Buddha, saying:

“There are certain Brahmins possessing the three knowledges who teach various paths—the path of mastery over desire, the path of self-creation, and the path of Brahmā. These three paths all lead toward the Brahmā world.”
"Gautama! It is like a village camp where all the various roads lead toward the city; likewise, although the various brahmins teach many different paths, they all lead toward Brahmā."
The Buddha said to Vatsa:
"Do those various paths all lead to the Brahma world? He replied:
"All lead there.
The Buddha asked again, a second and a third time:
"Do all the various paths lead entirely to the Brahma Heaven?"
He replied, "They all go there.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having confirmed his words, addressed Vāseṭṭha, saying:
“Among the brahmins who possess the three types of clear knowledge, is there even a single person who has been able to see Brahmā?
He replied, “There is no one who has seen him.”
“Vasiṣṭha, how is it? Among the former teachers of the三明 (trividyā) Brahmins, was there anyone who actually attained the vision of Brahmā? He replied:
“There is no one who sees.

“How is this so, Vāseṭṭha? In the past, there were seers of the three knowledges, ancient Brahmins who had mastered their recitations and were able to explain to others the ancient hymns, songs, and poems—namely, the Brahmin Aṭṭhaka, the Brahmin Vāmaka, the Brahmin Vāmadeva, the Brahmin Vessāmitta, the Brahmin Yamataggi, the Brahmin Aṅgīrasa, the Brahmin Bhāradvāja, the Brahmin Vāseṭṭha, the Brahmin Kassapa, the Brahmin Bhagu, and the Brahmin Bhagu. Did they also see Brahmā?”
He replied, "There is no one who sees.
The Buddha said:

"If among those Triveda Brahmins there is not a single one who has seen Brahmā, nor among the former teachers of the Triveda Brahmins is there anyone who has seen Brahmā, and furthermore, even the ancient great seers such as Aṭama and others, who were Triveda Brahmins, have not seen Brahmā—then it should be known that what the Triveda Brahmins say is not true."
He further addressed Vāseṭṭha:
"Suppose there were a lustful man who said:
'I have had sexual intercourse with that beautiful woman,' and he praised the act of lust."
Another person said to him,
"Do you know that woman? Where is she?"
"Is it from the east, the west, the south, or the north? He replied, "I do not know."
He asked again:
"Do you know the land, city, town, or village where that woman resides? He replied:
"I do not know. He asked again:
"Do you recognize that woman's parents, as well as her family name and given name?"
He replied, "I do not know. He asked again:
"Do you know whether that woman is the daughter of a kṣatriya, or the daughter of a brāhmaṇa, a householder,
or a śūdra? He replied,
"I do not know."
He asked again:
"Do you know whether that woman is tall or short, thick or thin, black or white, beautiful or ugly? He replied:
"I do not know. "In that case, Vāseṭṭha,
would that person’s praise be considered true?"
He replied, "It is not real. [The Buddha said,] "So it is."
Vāseṭṭha! What the brahmins learned in the three Vedas say is likewise; it is not true. Why is that, Vāseṭṭha?
When you, O Brahmins of the Three Vedas, see the sun and moon as they travel through their courses of rising and setting, you join your palms in worship and can say:
"This path is true and correct; by it one shall attain liberation and reach the place where the sun and moon dwell."
"Is this not so? He replied, "It is so."
The Brahmins of the Three Vedas, seeing the places where the sun and moon travel, rise, and set, join their palms in worship, yet they cannot say:
"This path is true and correct; by it one shall attain liberation and reach the abode of the sun and moon."
"So it is, Vāseṭṭha!"
The Brahmins of the Three Vedas, seeing the places where the sun and moon travel, rise, and set, join their palms in worship, yet they cannot say:
"This path is true and correct; by it one shall attain liberation and reach the abode of the sun and moon."
"And yet, he constantly joins his palms in worship and shows them reverence;
is this not, then, false? He replied, "It is so."
"Gautama! That is indeed false.
The Buddha said:
“Suppose, for example, someone were setting up a ladder in an open space, and another person asked him,
‘What is the purpose of setting up this ladder?
He would reply:”
"I wish to ascend to the hall," he said.
He was asked again,
"Where is the hall located?"
"Is it east, west, south, or north? He replied, "I do not know."
"What do you think,
Vāseṭṭha? Is this person who sets up a ladder intending to climb onto the hall not acting in vain?"
He replied, “It is so; that is indeed false.
The Buddha said:
“O Brahmins of the Three Vedas, it is likewise so: they are deceptive and without reality.
Vāseṭṭha! The five sensual pleasures are pure and exceedingly delightful.”
What are the five? One sees forms with the eye that are exceedingly lovely and delightful;
likewise, sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, and tangibles felt by the body are exceedingly lovely and delightful.
Within my noble and holy Dharma, these are attachments, fetters, and shackles.

Those brahmins of the three Vedas, being defiled by the five sensual desires, possess firm attachment and do not perceive their faults; they do not know the way of escape and are thus bound by the five sensual desires.
Even if one were to serve the sun, moon, water, and fire, and proclaim,
"Support me and lead me to be born in the Brahma Heaven," such a thing is impossible.

It is like the river Aciravatī, whose waters reach the banks so that crows and birds may drink from them; suppose there were a person on this bank, their body bound with heavy fetters, who cried out across the river to the other side, saying:
"Come and carry me across!"
"Would someone from the other shore come across to ferry this person over? He replied, "No."
“Vāseṭṭha! The five sensual pleasures are pure and exceedingly delightful, yet within the Dharma of the Noble Ones they are like shackles.
Those brahmins of the three Vedas are defiled by these five sensual pleasures; their attachment is firm, they do not perceive their faults, and they do not know the way of escape.”
Bound by the five desires, even if one were to serve the sun, moon, water, and fire, proclaiming:
"Support me and take me to be born in the Brahma Heaven."
"It is likewise impossible; such a thing can never happen. Vāseṭṭha!

Suppose there is the river Aciravatī, its water level with the banks so that crows may drink from it; if someone wished to cross it, could they do so without using the strength of their hands, feet, or body, and without relying on a boat or raft?"
He replied, "I cannot. "Vasita! [the Buddha said.]

It is the same for the Brahmins of the Three Vedas: if they do not cultivate the pure brahmacarya of a śramaṇa, but instead cultivate other paths and impure practices while desiring to seek birth in the Brahma Heaven, such a thing is impossible.

Vāseṭṭha! It is just as if a mountain river were to rise in a violent torrent, sweeping away many people, and there were neither boats nor rafts, nor any bridges. Suppose a traveler came along wishing to cross to the other shore; seeing the mountain river rise in a violent torrent, sweeping away many people, and finding neither boats nor rafts, nor any bridges, that person would think to himself:
"Shall I now gather plenty of grass and wood, bind them firmly together to make a raft, and cross to the other shore by my own physical strength?"
He then immediately sought out and bound together a raft, and by his own physical strength, he safely crossed over.
Vāseṭṭha! It is just the same in this case:
if a bhikṣu abandons what is not the conduct of a śramaṇa and is impure, and practices the pure brahma-conduct of a śramaṇa, desiring to be born in the Brahmā world, then such a thing is possible.
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does the Brahmā have a mind of ill will?
Or does he have no mind of ill will?"
He replied, "I have no mind of anger.
He asked again:
“Do the三明 (trividyā) Brahmins have a mind of ill-will, or do they have no mind of ill-will?
He replied: “They have a mind of ill-will.”

“Vāseṭṭha! The Brahmā is free from a mind of ill-will, whereas the三明 (trividyā) Brahmins possess a mind of ill-will. A mind with ill-will and a mind without ill-will do not coexist; they are not liberated together, they do not move toward the same goal, and for this reason, the Brahmā and the Brahmins do not share in common.”
"How is it, Vāseṭṭha! Does the Brahmā have a mind of anger, or is he free from a mind of anger? He replied:
"He has no mind of anger.
He asked again:
"Do the三明 (trividyā) Brahmins have a mind of anger, or do they have no mind of anger?"
He replied, "I have a mind of anger.
The Buddha said:

“The Brahmā deva is free from a mind of ill will, whereas the brahmins of the three knowledges possess a mind of ill will. Since those with a mind of ill will and those without a mind of ill will do not share the same destination and do not share the same liberation, for this reason, the Brahmā deva and the brahmins are not alike.”
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does the Brahmā possess a mind of resentment, or is his mind free from resentment? He replied:
"Is he free from resentment?
He asked again,
"Do the Brahmins who possess the three knowledges have resentment, or are they free from resentment?"
He replied, “I have a heart of resentment.
The Buddha said:

“The Brahmā is free from resentment, whereas the三明 (trividyā) Brahmins harbor resentment; since those with resentment and those without resentment do not share the same destination nor the same liberation, for this reason the Brahmā and the Brahmins are not alike.”
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does Brahmā have a family and property? He replied:
"No. He asked again: "Do the Brahmins of the Three Vedas have families and property?"
He replied, "There is. The Buddha said:

“Brahmā has no family or property, whereas the brahmins of the three knowledges have families and property. Having families and property versus having no families or property constitutes different destinies and different liberations; therefore, Brahmā and the brahmins do not share the same path.”
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does the Brahmā possess mastery, or does he not possess mastery? He replied:
“He has attained mastery.
He asked again:
“Do the三明 (trividyā) Brahmins attain mastery, or do they not attain mastery?”
He replied, "I have not attained mastery.
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā possesses mastery, whereas the brahmins of the three knowledges do not possess mastery. Since those who lack mastery and those who possess mastery have different destinies and different liberations, Brahmā and the brahmins are not of one accord.”
The Buddha said,
"If someone were to come and pose difficult questions regarding profound meanings to those Trividyā Brahmins, they would be unable to answer them fully.
Is this not indeed so?"
He replied, “It is so.
Then, both Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja addressed the Buddha together, saying:

"Setting aside other matters for now, I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama clearly understands the path to Brahmā and is able to explain it to others; furthermore, he meets with Brahmā and converses with him. I only pray that out of compassion, the śramaṇa Gautama will explain the path to Brahmā, revealing and disseminating it."
The Buddha said to Vāseṭṭha:
“I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit.
What do you think, Vāseṭṭha?”
"He thinks of that country; how far is it from here?
He replied, "It is near."
“If there were a person born and raised in that country, and another person asked him for the way to that country, what do you think, Vāseṭṭha?
Would that person, being born and raised in that country, have any doubt when answering about the way?”
He replied: "There is no doubt. Why is this? Because..."
"Because he was born and raised in that country.
The Buddha said,
"Even if that person were born and raised in that country, there might still be doubt;"
If anyone were to come and ask me about the Brahma-way, I would have no doubt. Why is this?
Because I have constantly and repeatedly taught that Brahma-way.
Then Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja both addressed the Buddha, saying: “Let us set aside this discussion for now.

We have heard that the Śramaṇa Gautama clearly knows the path to Brahmā and is able to explain it to others; furthermore, he has met with Brahmā and conversed with him. We only pray that the Śramaṇa Gautama, out of compassion, will speak of the path to Brahmā, revealing and expounding it for us.”
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively and reflect well; I shall speak for you. He replied:
“Yes, indeed; we wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles, and even attains the four dhyānas, he finds delight therein within this very life.”
Why is this so? It is because he is diligent, maintains focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, delights in solitude and tranquility, and is not negligent.

With a mind of loving-kindness, he pervades one direction; he does likewise for the other directions, spreading it boundlessly, without duality, immeasurable, free from resentment, and free from harm. He sports with this mind and finds delight therein:

With a mind of compassion, joy, and equanimity, he pervades one direction; likewise the other directions, extending them boundlessly, without duality, immeasurably, free from resentment, and without intent to harm—sporting with this mind as his own delight.
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does the Brahmā have a mind of ill will, or is his mind free from ill will? He replied:
"He has no mind of ill will.
He asked again:
"Does a bhikkhu who practices loving-kindness have a mind of ill will, or does he not?"
He replied, "I have no mind of ill will.
The Buddha said:

“The Brahmā is free from a mind of ill will; the bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness is also free from a mind of ill will. This mind free from ill will and that mind free from ill will share the same destination and the same liberation; therefore, the Brahmā and the bhikṣu are alike.”
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does Brahmā have a mind of anger?
Or does he have no mind of anger?"
He replied, “There is none. He asked again:
“Does a bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness have a mind of anger or not? He replied: “No.”
The Buddha said:

"The Brahmā has no mind of ill-will; the bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness has no mind of ill-will. Since the mind of no ill-will and the mind of no ill-will share the same destination and the same liberation, the Brahmā and the bhikṣu are thus identical."
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does the Brahmā have a mind of resentment, or is his mind free from resentment? He replied:
"No. He asked again: "Does a bhikkhu who practices loving-kindness harbor a mind of resentment, or is he without resentment?"
He replied, “No. The Buddha said:

“The Brahmā is free from ill will; the bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness is also free from ill will. This state of being free from ill will leads to the same destination and the same liberation; therefore, the bhikṣu and the Brahmā are alike.”
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does Brahmā have a family or possessions? He replied:
"No. He asked again: "Does the bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness have a family and property?"
He replied, “There is none. The Buddha said:

“The Brahmā has no family or possessions; the bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness likewise has no family or possessions. Having no family or possessions, they share the same destination and the same liberation. Therefore, the Brahmā and the bhikṣu are alike.”
"What do you think, Vāseṭṭha!
Does Brahmā possess mastery? He replied:
"He has attained mastery.
He asked again:
"Does the bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness attain mastery?"
He replied, “I have attained mastery.
The Buddha said:

“The Brahmā has attained mastery; the bhikṣu who practices loving-kindness has attained mastery. Having attained mastery, they share the same destination and the same liberation; therefore, the Brahmā and the bhikṣu are alike.”
The Buddha told Vāseṭṭha:
"You should know that when a bhikkhu who practices loving-kindness passes away at the breaking up of the body, he is reborn in the Brahmā heaven as quickly as an arrow is shot."

When the Buddha had spoken this Dharma, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, while still on their seats, were freed from dust and removed from defilement, and the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose within them.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had taught, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra, Volume Sixteen; The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra, Volume Seventeen.
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
27. The Sāmaññaphala Sutta (27). Third Division. The Sāmaññaphala Sutta, the Eighth.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Ambavana, the grove of the Elder’s Son, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, son of Vaidehī, on the night of the full moon on the fifteenth day, summoned a lady of the court and addressed her, saying:
"This night is clear and bright, no different from the day; what should we do?"
The lady said to the king:
"Tonight, on the fifteenth day when the moon is full, it is no different from day; you should wash your hair and bathe, and enjoy yourself with the five desires together with your court ladies."
Then the king again summoned his eldest son, Prince Udayabhadda, and addressed him, saying:
"Tonight is the fifteenth day of the month when the moon is full; it is no different from day. What should be done?"
The Prince addressed the King, saying:

"Tonight is the fifteenth day when the moon is full; it is no different from day. You should assemble the fourfold army and deliberate together on how to strike against the rebels at the border, and thereafter return here to enjoy ourselves together."
At that time, the king again summoned the valiant great general and addressed him, saying:
"Now, on the fifteenth day when the moon is full, the night will be clear and bright, no different from the day; what should be done?"
The Great General addressed him, saying:

"This night is clear and bright, no different from the day; it would be appropriate to assemble the fourfold army and conduct a tour of inspection throughout the world to ascertain who is rebellious and who is compliant."
Then the king again summoned the brahmin Vassakāra and said to him:
"Now, on the fifteenth day when the moon is full, the night will be clear and bright, no different from the day. To which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should I go so that he may enlighten my mind?"
Then Vṛṣala addressed him, saying:
“Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day.

There is Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who serves as the leader among the great assembly; he has many acquaintances, his fame is heard afar, and like the great ocean that receives all, he is honored by the multitude.”
"Great King!
You should go to him to pay your respects; if Your Majesty sees him, your mind may perhaps attain awakening.
The king then summoned Varṣākāra’s younger brother, Sunidha, and said to him:
"Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day; to which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should I go so that they may awaken my mind?
Sunidha replied, "Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day."

There was Makkhali Gosāla, who served as a leader among the great assembly; he had many followers, his fame was heard afar, and like the great ocean that receives all things, he was honored by the multitude.
"Great King!
You should go to him to pay your respects; if Your Majesty should see him, your mind may perhaps attain awakening.
The King then commanded his minister in charge of affairs, saying:
“Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day; to what śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should we go who might be able to awaken my mind?
The minister Mahāgovinda replied:

“There is Ajita Keśakambalin, who is a leader among the great assembly, possesses many followers, has a far-reaching reputation, is as all-embracing as the great ocean, and is honored by the multitude.”
"Great King!
You should go to him to pay your respects; if Your Majesty sees him, your mind may perhaps attain awakening.
The king then commanded the gatekeeper Kāla, saying to him:
"Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day; to which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should I go so that he may awaken my mind?

The gatekeeper Kāla replied, "There is Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who is the leader among the great assembly, possesses many followers, and whose fame is heard afar. He is like the great ocean that accepts all things, and is honored by the multitude."
"Great King!
You should go to him to pay your respects; if Your Majesty should see him, your mind may perhaps attain awakening.
The King then commanded Udāyin, the son of Māṭhara, saying:
"Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day; to which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should I go so that he may awaken my mind?

Udāyin replied, "There is Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, who is a leader among the great assembly, widely known and of far-reaching renown; like the great ocean, there is nothing it does not accommodate, and he is honored by all."
"Great King!
You should go to him to pay your respects; if Your Majesty should see him, your mind may perhaps attain awakening.
The king then commanded his younger brother, Abhaya, saying:
"Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day; to which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should we go so that he may awaken our minds?

His younger brother Abhaya replied, "There is a Nirgrantha who serves as a leader among the great assembly; he is widely learned, his fame is heard afar, like the great ocean that accepts all, and he is honored by the multitude."
"Great King!
You ought to go to him to pay your respects; if Your Majesty should see him, your mind may perhaps attain awakening.
The King then commanded the youth Āyuṣmān, saying to him:
"Tonight is clear and bright, no different from the day; to which śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa should I go so that they may awaken my mind?
The youth Āyuṣmat replied, "There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who is now in my Āmra grove."
"Great King!
You should go to him to pay your respects; if Your Majesty sees him, your mind will surely attain awakening.
The King then commanded Āyuṣmat, saying:
"Adorn the precious elephant upon which I ride, as well as the other five hundred white elephants.
Following these instructions, the elder immediately finished adorning the king’s elephant and the five hundred elephants, and addressed the king, saying:
"The preparations for the procession are complete; we pray only that Your Majesty will know the time is right."

King Ajātaśatru mounted his own precious elephant, while he had five hundred ladies-in-waiting mount five hundred female elephants; each holding a torch in her hand, they manifested the king’s majestic authority as they departed from Rājagṛha, intending to go to where the Buddha was.
The Minor Leader approached Āyuṣmān and said, "You have now deceived me and ensnared me; you are leading my great assembly to deliver it to our enemies."
Āyuṣmān said: "Great King!
I do not dare deceive Your Majesty, nor do I dare entrap Your Majesty or lead Your Majesty’s great assembly into the hands of an enemy."
"O King, proceed forward alone; you shall surely obtain blessings and auspiciousness.
At that time, the king advanced a short distance further and said to Āyuṣmat:
"You have deceived me and ensnared me firmly; you wish to lead my followers away to hand them over to my enemies."
Thus he repeated this twice more. Why was this?
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty people in that great assembly; they were silent and made no sound, as if they were plotting something.
Āyuṣmān addressed the Great King once more, saying: "Great King!
I do not dare to deceive or entrap you, nor would I lead you and your great assembly into the hands of your enemies."
"Your Majesty, simply proceed forward; you will surely obtain blessings and auspiciousness. Why is this?
That śramaṇa’s dharma always delights in solitude and stillness; for this reason, there is no sound."
"Your Majesty, proceed only; the gardens have already appeared.
King Ajātaśatru reached the garden gate, dismounted from his elephant, unsheathed his sword, set aside his parasol, and removed the five royal insignia.
He entered the garden gate on foot and addressed Jīvaka, saying, "Where is the Buddha, the World-Honored One, at this moment?"
Āyuṣmān replied, "Great King!

The Buddha is currently in the high hall with a bright lamp before him; the World-Honored One is seated upon a lion throne facing south. Approach slightly, O King, and you shall see the World-Honored One for yourself."

At that time, King Ajātaśatru went to the lecture hall; having washed his feet outside, he then ascended the hall, gazed silently in all directions, and with a heart filled with joy, spoke these words himself:

"Now these śramaṇas are tranquil and silent, fully endowed with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. I pray that my crown prince Udayibhadra may likewise achieve perfection in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, so that he is no different from them."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to King Ajātaśatru:
"Out of concern for your son, you have spoken these words yourself:
'I pray that Prince Udayibhadra may also achieve the perfection of tranquility and insight, no different from this.'"
"You may come forward and sit.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru immediately stepped forward, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to ask a question; if you have the leisure, I venture to inquire."
The Buddha said: "Great King!
If you have any questions you wish to ask, you may do so."
King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Just as people today ride elephants, horses, and chariots, and practice the arts of the sword, spear, blade, bow and arrow, weaponry, and combat; or as princes, wrestlers, strongmen, servants, leather-workers, barbers, garland-makers, carriage-makers, potters, bamboo-workers, and reed-workers all sustain their lives through various crafts and skills, enjoying themselves at will, and together with their parents, wives, children, slaves, and servants, find mutual pleasure—such livelihoods as these clearly yield present fruits and retributions.”
"Do the various śramaṇas who practice now obtain the fruits of their retribution in the present?
The Buddha told the king:
"Have you ever gone to the dwellings of various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to ask about such matters?"
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I once went to the dwellings of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to inquire about such matters as these.
I recall a time when I went to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and asked him:"
"Just as a person who rides elephants, horses, or chariots, studies the art of war, or engages in various means of livelihood currently experiences their karmic fruits and rewards;
do those in this assembly who are now practicing the Path likewise experience such fruits and rewards in the present?"
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa replied to me, saying:

"Whether one acts for oneself or instructs others to act—to hack and fell, to injure and harm, to boil, roast, and cut; to afflict and disturb sentient beings, causing them grief, lamentation, and weeping; to kill living beings, steal, engage in lustful excesses, and speak falsehoods; to leap over walls and plunder, to set fires and burn, or to block the roads and commit evil."
"Great King!
To act in such a manner is not an evil deed.
Great King!"
If one were to use a sharp sword to carve up all sentient beings, piling their flesh into heaps that fill the world, this would not constitute evil, nor would there be any karmic retribution for it.
To the south of the Ganges River, one may butcher and dismember sentient beings, yet there will be no evil retribution.

To the north bank of the Ganges River, one may hold great assemblies of giving, bestowing upon all multitudes; benefiting others as one benefits oneself, yet there will likewise be no meritorious reward.
The King said to the Buddha:
"It is as if someone were asked about a melon and replied with a plum, or asked about a plum and replied with a melon.
He was just like that; I asked whether one receives retribution in the present life."
He replied to me that there is no retribution for sin or merit.
I then thought to myself:
"I am a Kṣatriya king of the head-anointed lineage; it is not fitting for me to kill, bind, or expel a renunciant."
“At that time, harboring resentment and a bound heart, after I had formed this thought, I immediately departed.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“On one occasion, I went to where Makkhali Gosāla was and asked him:”
"Just as people nowadays who ride elephants, horses, or chariots, study the art of war, or engage in various means of livelihood all presently experience their karmic fruits;
do those in this assembly who currently cultivate the Path likewise receive their retribution in the present?"
He replied to me, saying: "Great King!

There is no giving, no offering, and no ritual of sacrifice; there is neither good nor evil, nor is there retribution for good and evil deeds. There is no present world, nor is there a future world; there is no father and no mother; there are no devas, no spontaneously born beings, and no living creatures. In this world, there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who practice with equanimity, nor is there a present world or a future world that one can personally realize and manifest to others."
"All that which is said to 'exist' is entirely false and illusory.
"World-Honored One!
It is just as if someone were asked about a melon and replied with a plum, or asked about a plum and replied with a melon."
He was also like this; when I asked whether he had attained the fruit of retribution in the present life, he answered with something irrelevant.
I then thought to myself:
"I am a Kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkled lineage; it is not fitting for me to kill, bind, or drive away those who have left the household life.
Having formed this thought with a heart bound by resentment, I immediately departed.
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At one time, I went to where Ajita Keśakambalin was and asked him:
'Venerable Sir!'"
Just as when people ride elephants, horses, or chariots, practice the arts of war, or engage in various means of livelihood, all of these yield manifest results;
now, as this assembly currently practices the Path, do they obtain manifest results?
He replied to me, saying:

"When one who is composed of the four great elements meets the end of life, the earth element returns to earth, water returns to water, fire returns to fire, and wind returns to wind; all are utterly destroyed, and the sense faculties return to emptiness."

When a person dies, their body is lifted onto a bier and placed in a cemetery; their bones are burned by fire until they become the color of a pigeon, or turn into ash and dust. Whether foolish or wise, all who have reached the end of life are utterly destroyed and subject to the law of annihilation.
"World-Honored One!

It is just as if someone were asked about the ripening of a plum fruit, and he would answer in that same way; when I asked whether there is a ripening experienced in the present, he answered me with the doctrine of annihilation."
I then thought to myself:
"I am a Kṣatriya king, of the lineage consecrated by the sprinkling of water; there is no cause for me to kill an ordained person, nor to bind or expel them.
At that time, harboring resentment and a bound heart, having formed this thought, I immediately departed.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Once in the past, I went to where Pūtigandhaka Cañcāyanī was and asked him:
'Venerable Sir!'"
Just as when people ride elephants, horses, or chariots, practice the arts of war, or engage in various means of livelihood, all of these yield manifest fruits and retributions;
now, as this assembly currently practices the Way, do they obtain such retribution?

He replied to me: "Great King! There is no power and no vigor; humans have neither power nor skillful means. Without cause or condition, sentient beings become defiled and attached; without cause or condition, sentient beings become pure. All sentient beings who possess life are entirely without power and lack self-mastery. Among those destined for this number of births, there is no fixed enmity; within these six realms of birth, they undergo various forms of suffering and joy."
"It is just as if one were to ask about a plum and receive an answer regarding a melon, or ask about a melon and receive an answer regarding a plum.
It is the same in this case: when I asked whether he receives retribution in the present life, he was already unable to answer me."
I then thought to myself:
"I am a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated head-lineage; there is no cause for me to kill, bind, or drive away those who have left the household life."
"At that time, harboring resentment and a bound heart, having formed this thought, I immediately departed.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Once in the past, I went to where Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra was and asked him:"
"Venerable Sir!
Just as when people ride elephants or horse-drawn chariots, practice military strategy, or engage in various means of livelihood, all of these yield manifest results;
now, do those in this assembly who currently cultivate the Path likewise obtain manifest retribution?"
He replied to me, saying: "Great King!

There currently exists the fruit of retribution for a śramaṇa; when asked thus, the answer to this matter is as follows: this matter is real, this matter is different, and this matter is neither different nor not different."
"Great King!

There is no present fruition of the fruits of recluseship. When asked such a thing, one answers: 'This matter is thus; this matter is real; this matter is different; this matter is neither different nor not-different.'"
"Great King!

There currently exists no fruit of the ascetic life (śrāmaṇyaphala). To such questions, one answers: 'This matter is thus,' 'This matter is real,' 'This matter is different,' or 'This matter is neither different nor not-different.'"
"Great King!

The fruits of the śramaṇa's life are neither existent nor non-existent in the present. To such questions, one should answer: 'This matter is thus; this matter is real; this matter is different; this matter is neither different nor not different.'"
"World-Honored One!
It is just as if someone were to ask about the ripening of a plum and receive an answer regarding a melon, or ask about a melon and receive an answer regarding a plum.
It is the same in this case: I asked whether one receives retribution in the present life."
When those opponents replied to me, I thought to myself:
"I am a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated head lineage; there is no reason for me to kill, bind, or expel a renunciant."
"At that time, harboring resentment and a bound heart, after forming this thought, I immediately departed.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Once in the past, I went to the place of the Nirgranthas and asked them:"
"Venerable Sir!
Just as when a person rides an elephant, a horse, or a chariot, or engages in various means of livelihood, there is an immediate manifestation of the fruit and retribution;
does this assembly, which now practices the Path, likewise obtain retribution in the present?"
He replied to me, saying: "Great King!

I am one who possesses all-knowledge and all-seeing; I know everything without exception, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, awakening to all things without remainder, with wisdom ever present before me."
"World-Honored One!
It is just as if someone were to ask about the ripening of a plum and receive an answer regarding a melon, or ask about a melon and receive an answer regarding a plum.
It is the same in this case: I asked whether one receives retribution in the present life."
He answered me with [the claim of] omniscience, whereupon I thought to myself:
"I am a Kṣatriya king of the water-sprinkled lineage; there is no cause for me to kill, bind, or drive away a renunciant."
“At that time, harboring resentment and a bound heart, after forming this thought, I immediately departed.
Therefore, World-Honored One, I have now come here to inquire about such a matter:
just as a person who rides elephants or horse-drawn chariots, practices the arts of war, or engages in various means of livelihood, all of which presently yield visible fruits and retributions;”
"Now, when a śramaṇa currently practices the Path in the present life, does he receive its retribution in the present?
The Buddha said to King Ajātaśatru:
"I shall now question you in return; answer as you see fit."
"What do you think, Great King?

When the servants and laborers of the royal household, both internal and external, see the King on the fifteenth day when the moon is full, having washed his hair and bathed, enjoying himself upon a high palace terrace together with his court ladies, they will think to themselves: 'Alas!'"
"Is the karmic fruit of such conduct as this indeed so great?

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, on the full moon of the fifteenth day, had washed his hair and bathed; he was upon a high palace terrace, amusing himself with the five desires in the company of many court ladies.
"Who is able to know that this is indeed the retribution for past actions?
Subsequently, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, left the household life to practice the Way, and practiced the Dharma of equanimity.
How so? Great King! When Your Majesty sees this person coming from afar, would you ever again give rise to the thought: [that he is your son]?
"Is he my servant? The king said to the Buddha, "No."
“World-Honored One!
If you see him coming, you should rise to welcome him and invite him to be seated.
The Buddha said:
"Is this not the present retribution received by the śramaṇa?
The king replied, "It is so."
“World-Honored One!
This is the fruit of retribution for being a śramaṇa obtained in the present life. “Furthermore, Great King!”

If a guest residing within the king’s realm eats from the king’s granary, he may see the king on the fifteenth day, when the moon is full, having washed his hair and bathed, sitting upon a high terrace and delighting himself with the five desires together with his court ladies.
He thought to himself:
"Alas! Is the retribution for such conduct truly like this?"
"Who is able to know that this is indeed the retribution of past actions?
Later, he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma robes, left the household life to practice the Way, and practiced the Dharma of equality.
"What do you think, Great King?
If Your Majesty were to see this man coming from afar, would you think to yourself:
'This is my tenant; he eats from my granary'?"
"Is it so? The King replied, "No."
"If I see him coming from afar, I shall rise to meet him, pay him homage, inquire after his well-being, and invite him to sit.
"How is this, Great King? Is this not the fruit and reward manifested by a śramaṇa?"
The King said: "It is so;
one receives the retribution of a śramaṇa in the present life.
"Furthermore, Great King!"

When a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, those who enter my Dharma attain even the three types of higher knowledge, extinguishing all darkness and giving rise to the great light of wisdom—namely, the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows.
Why is this so? It is because of diligent effort, focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, delighting in solitary seclusion, and the absence of negligence.
What do you think, Great King?
"This is not the present fruit of retribution for a śramaṇa. The King replied,
"So it is, World-Honored One!"
“This is truly the present retribution for being a śramaṇa.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my confession of transgression. Driven by madness, folly, ignorance, and delusion, I lacked discernment; my father, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, governed according to the Dharma without partiality or injustice, yet I, infatuated by the five desires, actually murdered my royal father. I only pray that the World-Honored One will show me compassion and pity, and accept my confession of transgression.”
The Buddha said to the king:

"You were foolish, ignorant, and lacking in discernment; you merely repent now for your own sake. Having been deluded by the five desires, you brought harm upon your father, the king. Now, that you are able to repent within the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones, you will thereby benefit yourself."
"Out of compassion for you, I accept your confession.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the king immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha. Please accept me as an upāsaka within the True Dharma. From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants. I only pray that the World-Honored One and the great assembly will graciously accept my invitation.”
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent by remaining silent.
When the king saw that the Buddha had accepted his invitation through silence, he immediately rose, paid homage to the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, and returned.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"The transgressions and offenses of this King Ajātaśatru have been diminished; he has already uprooted his grave guilt.
Had King Ajātaśatru not killed his father, he would have attained the pure Dharma-eye while sitting right here on this seat."
"Now King Ajātaśatru has repented of his transgressions; his offenses have been diminished, and he has already uprooted his heavy guilt.
At that time, as King Ajātaśatru was on the road, he addressed the youth Jīvaka, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent! You have now brought me great benefit.

It was only after you first praised and elucidated what the Tathāgata had instructed and revealed that you led me to the presence of the World-Honored One, where I was able to receive awakening. I deeply recognize your kindness and shall never forget it.

At that time, the king returned to his palace and prepared various delicacies and diverse foods. When the time for the meal arrived the following day, he thought, "Only the Holy One knows the proper time.

Then the World-Honored One, having donned his robes and taken up his alms bowl, went together with his assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples to the royal palace and sat upon the seat provided.

At that time, the king personally served the food to the Buddha and the Saṃgha. When the meal was finished and the bowls removed, and after the ritual washing of hands was completed, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and said:

"I now repent my transgressions again and again. Driven by madness, folly, delusion, and ignorance, while my father, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, governed according to the Dharma without partiality or injustice, I became infatuated with the five desires and actually murdered my father, the king. I only pray that the World-Honored One will show me compassion and pity, and accept my repentance."
The Buddha said to the king:

"You were foolish and ignorant, deluded by the five desires, that you murdered your father, the king; yet, if you can now repent within the Dharma of the Worthy and Holy Ones, you will thereby benefit yourself."
"I now take pity on you and accept your confession of remorse.

At that time, the king prostrated at the Buddha's feet, took a small seat, and sat before the Buddha; the Buddha then preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the king addressed the Buddha again, saying:

“I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha for a second and third time. I pray only that you will accept me as an upāsaka within the True Dharma; from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants.”
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to King Ajātaśatru, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then, King Ajātaśatru and the youth Jīvaka, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
28. The Pāṭikāputra Sūtra (28). The Ninth Discourse of the Third Division of the Long Āgama Spoken by the Buddha: Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Then the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"It is still too early for begging for food today; I shall instead go to the forest grove of the brahmin Pāṭahapūra to observe it, and when the time arrives, I will then beg for food."
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the grove of the brahmins.
When the brahmin Pāṭikāputra saw the Buddha approaching from afar, he rose to meet him and said:
"Welcome, Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"It has been a long time since you last came here; for what reason have you deigned to visit us today?
Please come forward and take your seat.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One took his seat and addressed Pāṭahālaputra, saying:
“You have gathered here; what are you doing? For what purpose are you teaching?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Yesterday, many brahmins, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas gathered here in this brāhmaṇa hall and discussed such matters, engaging in contradictory and opposing arguments.”
"Gautama! There are some brahmins who speak thus:

'For a person, perception arises without cause and without condition, and perception ceases without cause and without condition; perception has coming and going—when it comes, perception arises, and when it goes, perception ceases.'"
"O Gautama! There are some brahmins who speak thus:
'From life, perception arises; by life, perception ceases. That perception has coming and going: when it comes, perception arises; when it goes, perception ceases.'"
"O Gautama! There are some brahmins who say:
'As was previously stated, that is impossible.'"

There are great spirits of immense power; they depart with their perceptions and they arrive with their perceptions. When they depart with their perceptions, those perceptions cease; when they arrive with their perceptions, those perceptions arise.

"Because of this, I have given rise to a thought: that the śramaṇa Gautama must have previously known this meaning, and he will certainly be able to skillfully know the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
At that time, the World-Honored One told the brahmin: "All those theorists are at fault."

To say that perception arises without cause or condition, and that perception ceases without cause or condition, and that perception has coming and going—such that it arises when it comes and ceases when it goes—is [incorrect].
Some say that perception arises because of life and ceases because of life; perception has coming and going—when it comes, perception arises, and when it goes, perception ceases.
Others say: "That is not possible;
there is a great spirit who brings perception here and takes perception away; when he brings it, perception arises, and when he takes it away, perception ceases."
"Such statements as these all contain faults. Why is this so? O Brahmin!"
“With causes and conditions, perception arises; with causes and conditions, perception ceases.

‘If a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is truly self-awakened, perfectly enlightened, and endowed with the ten titles—and if someone goes forth from home into homelessness within the Buddha’s Dharma to practice the path, even to the point of extinguishing the five hindrances that shroud the mind, removing desires and unwholesome states, and entering the first dhyāna—which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and filled with joy and happiness—then they first extinguish the perception of desire and give rise to the perception of joy and happiness.’”
"O Brahmin! By this you should know that there is a causal condition for the arising of perception, and a causal condition for the cessation of perception.

With the subsiding of directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), with internal joy and one-pointedness of mind, free from directed thought and sustained thought, born of concentration, joy and bliss, one enters the second dhyāna."
"O Brahmin!

When the perception of the first dhyāna ceases and the perception of the second dhyāna arises, by this one knows that there is a causal condition for the cessation of perception and a causal condition for the arising of perception."

Having abandoned joy and cultivated equanimity, with focused mindfulness and one-pointed concentration, he experiences within himself that bliss which the noble ones seek; with pure mindful equanimity, he enters the third dhyāna. O Brahmin!

In that second dhyāna, perception ceases and the perception of the third dhyāna arises; for this reason, one knows that there is a causal condition for the cessation of perception and a causal condition for the arising of perception.
Abandoning suffering and abandoning pleasure, and having previously stilled sorrow and joy, one enters the fourth dhyāna with pure mindfulness and equanimity.

"Brahmin! When the perception of the third dhyāna ceases and the perception of the fourth dhyāna arises, by this one knows that perceptions arise through causes and conditions and cease through causes and conditions."
"Having abandoned all perceptions of form, having stilled ill-will, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space. Brahmin!

When all perceptions of form have ceased and the perception of the sphere of infinite space has arisen, by this you should know that there is a causal condition for the cessation of perceptions and a causal condition for the arising of perceptions."
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. O Brahmin!

As the perception of the sphere of infinite space ceases and the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness arises, one thereby knows that perceptions arise through causes and conditions and cease through causes and conditions.
"Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters the sphere of nothingness. O Brahmin!

Therein, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness ceases and the perception of the sphere of nothingness arises. For this reason, it is known that perceptions arise through causes and conditions, and perceptions cease through causes and conditions."
Abandoning the sphere of nothingness, he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Brahmin!

When the perception of the sphere of nothingness ceases and the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises, one thereby knows that perceptions arise through causes and conditions and cease through causes and conditions.
Having relinquished the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. O Brahmin!

When perception in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception ceases, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; for this reason, it is known that there is a causal condition for the arising of perception, and there is a causal condition for the cessation of perception.
Having attained this perception, he thinks:
"To have thought is evil; to be without thought is good.
While he is thinking thus, that subtle perception does not cease, and a coarser perception arises.
He further thought to himself:
"I would now rather not engage in mental application nor give rise to discursive thought.
Having ceased mental application and refrained from giving rise to discursive thought, subtle perceptions ceased and coarse perceptions did not arise.

When he does not engage in mental activity, does not give rise to volitional thought, subtle perceptions have ceased, and coarse perceptions do not arise, he enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
What do you think, brahmin?
"From the very beginning, have you ever heard of the causes and conditions for this sequential cessation of perception?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From the very beginning, even though I have had faith, I have never heard of such causes and conditions for the sequential cessation of perception."
He again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have now given rise to this thought: 'This is with perception; this is without perception. Or, having perceived that there is perception, he thinks:
'To have mindfulness is evil; to be without mindfulness is good.'"
While he was thinking this, subtle perceptions did not cease, and coarse perceptions arose again. He then thought further:
"I would rather now not engage in mental activity and not give rise to volitional reflection."
When he does not engage in mental application and does not give rise to reflection, subtle perceptions cease and coarse perceptions do not arise.

When he does not engage in mental application and does not give rise to reflection, such that subtle perceptions have ceased and coarse perceptions do not arise, he immediately enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti).
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"This is the sequential attainment of the cessation of perception within the Dharma of the noble ones.
The brahmin spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"Among all these perceptions, which is the unsurpassed perception?"
The Buddha told the brahmin,
“The perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is supreme.
The brahmin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Among all perceptions (*saṃjñā*), which is the foremost and unsurpassed perception?
The Buddha said:

"Among all perceptions and all expressions of non-perception, that which can successively attain the cessation of perception and cognition (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*)—this is the foremost and unsurpassed perception."
The brahmin asked again:
"Is it a single perception, or many perceptions?
The Buddha said:
“There is one perception, but no manifold perceptions.
The brahmin asked again:
“Does perception arise first, and then wisdom?”
"Does wisdom arise first and then perception,
or do perception and wisdom arise simultaneously?
The Buddha said:
“First there is the arising of perception, and subsequently wisdom; it is through perception that wisdom exists.
The brahmin asked again:
“Is perception itself the self?”
The Buddha said to the brahmin,
"Whom do you describe as being 'I'?
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
