"I do not say that a person is the self; rather, I say that the physical body—composed of the four great elements, the six sense bases, born and raised by parents, nourished with milk, grown, adorned with clothing, and subject to the laws of impermanence and decay—is what I call 'this person is the self.'"
The Buddha told the brahmin:

“You say that this physical body—composed of the four great elements, consisting of the six sense bases, born and raised by parents, nourished with milk, grown up, adorned with clothing, and subject to impermanence and decay—is what you call ‘this person is me.’”
"O Brahmin! Let aside this 'self' for a moment; it is merely the perception of a person that arises and the perception of a person that ceases.
The Brahmin said:
“I do not say that a human being is the self; I say that a deva of the desire realm is the self.
The Buddha said:
“Setting aside for a moment whether a deva of the desire realm is the self, it is simply that the perception of a human being arises and the perception of a human being ceases.”
The brahmin said:
"I do not say that a person is the self; I myself say that a deva of the form realm is the self.
The Buddha said:

“Setting aside for a moment the thought that the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are the self, let us consider only the arising of the perception of a person and the cessation of the perception of a person.
The brahmin said:

“I do not say that a person is the self; I myself say that the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—the gods of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)—are the self.”
The Buddha said:

"Set aside the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as well as the formless heavens, and consider them as 'I'; rather, it is only the perception of a person that arises and the perception of a person that ceases."
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, Gautama? Might I come to know the arising of the perception of a person and the cessation of the perception of a person?”
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"If you wish to know how the perception of a person arises and how the perception of a person ceases, it is extremely difficult!
It is extremely difficult!"
"Why is that? Because you have different views, different practices, different tolerances, and different acceptances, relying upon different teachings.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, Gautama! Because my views are different,

my practices are different, my tolerances are different, my acceptances are different, and I rely upon different teachings, it is extremely difficult for me to know how the perception of a person arises and how the perception of a person ceases."
This is extremely difficult!
Why is that? Because [one claims]:
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The self and the world are impermanent; this alone is true, all else is false.
"The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this alone is true, all else is false.
"The self and the world are neither permanent nor impermanent; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The self and the world are finite; this alone is true, all else is false.
"The self and the world are infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
This life-principle is the body; this alone is true, all else is false.
The life-principle is one thing and the body is another; this alone is true, all else is false."
The body and life are neither different nor not different; this is the truth, and all else is false.
There is no life and no body; this is the truth, and all else is false.
The Tathāgata’s passing away: this is the truth, and all else is false.
That the Tathāgata does not pass away—this is real, the rest is false;
that the Tathāgata both passes away and does not pass away—this is real, the rest is false;
that the Tathāgata neither passes away nor does not pass away—this is real, the rest is false.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Whether the world is eternal, or even whether the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end—these are matters I do not declare.
The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Gautama! For what reason do you not provide a definitive teaching on whether the self and the world are eternal, and so forth, up to whether the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end—why do you refrain from teaching all of these?"
The Buddha said:

"This is not consistent with the meaning, nor is it consistent with the Dharma; it is not the holy life, not the absence of desire, not the unconditioned, not cessation, not tranquility, not perfect enlightenment, not the state of a śramaṇa, and not nirvāṇa. Therefore, I do not provide a prediction regarding it."
The brahmin asked again:
"What is meant by 'conformity with meaning' and 'conformity with the Dharma'?
What constitutes the beginning of the holy life?"
What is the unconditioned?
What is desirelessness? What is cessation?
What is tranquility?
What is right awakening? What is a śramaṇa?
"What is Nirvana? What is meant by 'prediction'?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

“I declare the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Why is this?

Because these are consistent with the meaning, consistent with the Dharma; they are the beginning of the holy life, free from desire, unconditioned, tranquil, cessation, stillness, perfect awakening, the state of a śramaṇa, and nirvāṇa. Therefore, I declare them.”
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the brahmin, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him; having done so, he rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after the Buddha had left, the other brahmins said to the brahmin Pāṭahapūra:
"Why did you listen to what the śramaṇa Gautama said, approving every single word?"
Gautama said:
"To say that 'I and the world are eternal,' or even that 'the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end,' does not accord with the truth; therefore, I do not declare it."
"Why do you approve of these words?
We cannot accept what the śramaṇa Gautama has thus spoken.
Puṭṭabālā replied to the brahmins:
"The statement made by the śramaṇa Gautama—'The self and the world are eternal,' up to 'the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end'—does not accord with the meaning; therefore, I do not declare it."
I, too, do not approve of these words.

However, that śramaṇa Gautama abides in accordance with the Dharma; since he speaks according to the Dharma and has transcended by means of the Dharma, how could I possibly go against such wise speech?
“The subtle and wondrous Dharma words of the Śramaṇa Gautama must not be contravened.
Later, on another occasion, the brahmin Pāṭahapūra, together with Śāriputra Khaṇḍadravya, went to where the World-Honored One was; after exchanging greetings, they sat to one side.
After Hastiśīrṣa Śāriputra had paid homage to the Buddha and sat down, a brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha was previously at my place, not long after he had departed. Subsequently, other brahmins said to me:
'Why do you listen to what the śramaṇa Gautama says, and approve of every word? "
Gautama said:
"The views that 'the self and the world are eternal,' and so forth, up to 'the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end,' are inconsistent with the true Dharma;
therefore, I do not declare them. Why, then, do you approve of such statements?"
"We cannot accept what the śramaṇa Gautama has thus spoken.
I replied to them, saying:
"As for what the śramaṇa Gautama has spoken:"
"I do not affirm this statement: 'The world is eternal,' up to and including 'the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end,' because these do not accord with the true meaning;
therefore, I do not provide a definitive teaching on them. I, too, do not endorse this claim.

However, that śramaṇa Gautama abides in the Dharma and dwells by the Dharma; since he speaks according to the Dharma and has transcended through the Dharma, on what grounds could we oppose these words of wisdom?
“The subtle and wondrous words of the Dharma spoken by the Śramaṇa Gautama cannot be contravened.
The Buddha said to the brahmin: “The various brahmins say:”
"Why do you listen to what the śramaṇa Gautama says and approve of every word?
These words are faulty. Why is this so?
The Dharma I teach includes that which is definitively declared and that which is not definitively declared.
What is meant by "not definitively declared"?
Such statements as "the self and the world are eternal," up to "the Tathāgata neither ends nor does not end"—I also speak these words, yet I do not definitively declare them.

Why is this so? Because this does not accord with the meaning, it does not accord with the Dharma; it is not the beginning of the holy life, nor is it freedom from desire, nor is it the unconditioned, nor is it cessation, nor is it tranquility, nor is it perfect awakening, nor is it the state of a śramaṇa, nor is it nirvāṇa.
Therefore, brahmin, although I have spoken these words, I do not provide a definitive declaration.
What is meant by a "definitive declaration"?
I have declared the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin of suffering, the truth of the cessation of suffering, and the truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Why is this?
Because these are in accord with the Dharma and in accord with its meaning; they are the beginning of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and they are neither fixed nor indeterminate.

"Brahmin! There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, regarding one state in this world—desirelessness, the unconditioned, cessation, tranquility, perfect awakening, the state of a śramaṇa, and nirvāṇa—declare it with a definitive prediction; therefore, I speak of them as having made a definitive declaration."
“Brahmin! There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding one part of the world, declare it to be exclusively happy. I say to them:
‘Do you truly say that one part of the world is exclusively happy?’”
He replied to me, saying, "It is so. I then spoke to him again, saying:
"Do you know or see a single place in the world that is exclusively pleasant? He replied to me,
"I neither know nor see such a thing."
I spoke to him again, saying:
"Have you ever seen a single place in the world where all the devas experience nothing but constant bliss? He replied to me:
“I do not know; I do not see. He asked him again:
“Among those various devas in that one world-realm, have you ever sat, stood, or conversed with them as they diligently practiced meditative concentration?”
He answered me, saying, "No. I then asked him again:
"Has any of those gods from that single realm of the world who experience exclusively pleasure ever come to say to you:
'Because your conduct has been upright and sincere, you shall be reborn in that heaven of exclusive pleasure'?"
"Is it because I acted with such integrity that I have been born there to experience this shared joy?
They replied to me, saying:

"No. I then asked him again: "Are you able to give rise to the thought of manifesting another body composed of the four great elements from your own person, such that it is complete in all its parts and lacks no sense faculties?"
He answered me, saying: "I cannot. How so, brahmin?
"Are the words spoken by those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas truthful, and are they in accordance with the Dharma?
The brahmin replied to the Buddha:
"These are not truthful; they are words contrary to the Dharma."
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"Suppose there were a person who said:
'I have had sexual intercourse with that beautiful woman.'"
He praised the courtesan. Others asked him,
"Do you know that woman?"
"In what location does it reside?
Is it in the east, the west, the south, or the north? He replied:
“I do not know. He asked again,
“Do you know the land, city, town, or village where that woman resides?”
He replied, "I do not know. He asked again:
"Do you know that woman's parents, as well as her family name and given name? He replied, "I do not."
He asked again:
"Do you know whether that woman is the daughter of a Kṣatriya, or the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a Śūdra? He replied:
“I do not know. He asked again,
“Do you know whether that woman is tall or short, thick or thin, black or white, beautiful or ugly?”
He replied, “I do not know. “How is that so, brahmin?”
"Is what this person says truthful? He replied, "No."
“Brahmin! Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are likewise; they possess no reality. Brahmin!”
It is like a person setting up a ladder in an open space, and another person asks:
"For what purpose are you setting up this ladder? He replies:
"I wish to ascend to the hall," he said.
He was asked again,
"Where is the hall located?"
He replied, “I do not know. “How is that so, brahmin? he asked.
"Is that person who sets up the ladder not indeed acting in falsehood?
He replied, "It is so;
he is truly acting in falsehood."
The Buddha said:
"All śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are likewise thus—vain and without reality.
The Buddha addressed Potaliputra:

"You say that you take as 'self' this body—composed of the four great elements and the six sense bases, produced by parents, nourished by milk, grown through food, adorned with clothing—which is impermanent and subject to decay."
I have spoken of this as defilement, as purification, and as liberation.
Do you perhaps think that defiled phenomena cannot be extinguished, that purified phenomena cannot arise, and that one remains forever within suffering?
Do not harbor such thoughts.

Why is this? Defiled phenomena can be extinguished, and pure phenomena can be brought forth; one dwells in a state of peace and happiness, with joy and delight, maintaining single-minded concentration, so that wisdom increases and expands.
"O Brahmin!

Regarding the devas of the desire realm, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, I declare them to be defiled, I also declare them to be pure, and I also declare that liberation is attained therein."
You may think that defiled phenomena cannot be extinguished and pure phenomena cannot arise, and that one remains forever in suffering.
Do not entertain such a thought. Why is this?

Defilements may be extinguished and pure dharmas may arise; dwelling in a state of peace and bliss, one experiences joy and delight, focuses the mind with single-mindedness, and wisdom increases and expands.
At that time, Śāriputra Elephant-Head addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,

when there is a human body of the desire realm composed of the four great elements and the various sense faculties, are there also simultaneously present the bodies of the gods of the desire realm, the gods of the form realm, and the gods of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"

"Bhagavān! When there is the body of a deva of the desire realm, are there also simultaneously the four great elements and the sense faculties of a human body in the desire realm, as well as the bodies of devas of the form realm, and the bodies of devas of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?"

"Bhagavān! When one possesses the body of a deva of the form realm, do the four great elements and the various faculties of a human body in the desire realm, as well as the bodies of a deva of the form realm and the bodies of devas of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, all exist simultaneously?"

In this way, when one reaches the state of the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, do the four great elements and the sense faculties of a human body in the desire realm, as well as the bodies of gods in the desire realm, the bodies of gods in the form realm, and the bodies of gods in the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness, all exist simultaneously?
The Buddha told Śāriputra Elephant-Head:

"If there are the four great elements and the various faculties of a human body in the desire realm, at that time there are precisely the four great elements and the various faculties of a human body in the desire realm, and not those of a celestial body in the desire realm, nor those of a celestial body in the form realm, nor those of celestial bodies in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."

In this manner, up until the time one possesses the body of a deva in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, at that time one truly possesses the body of a deva in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, and lacks the four great elements and the sense faculties of a human body in the Desire Realm, as well as the bodies of devas in the Desire Realm, the bodies of devas in the Form Realm, and the bodies of devas in the Spheres of Infinite Space, Infinite Consciousness, and Nothingness.
Hastishirṣa! It is like cow's milk: the milk transforms into curd; the curd into fresh butter; the fresh butter into clarified butter; the clarified butter into ghee; and ghee is the foremost.
"Elephant Head!

When there is milk, it is called only 'milk'; it is not called curd, butter, or clarified butter (ghṛta). In this manner, progressing step by step until one reaches clarified butter, it is called only 'clarified butter,' and is not called milk, nor curd, nor butter."
Elephant Head!

It is just so: when there is a human body of the desire realm with its four great elements and various faculties, there is no body of a desire realm deity, no body of a deity of the form realm, nor even a body of a deity of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Thus it continues in succession; when there is a body of a deity of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is only that body of a deity of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and there is no human body of the desire realm with its four great elements and various faculties, nor a body of a desire realm deity, a body of a form realm deity, nor even a body of a deity up to the sphere of nothingness.
"Elephant Head! What do you think?
If someone were to ask you this: [text continues]"
"If there is a past body, are there also future and present bodies existing simultaneously?
If there is a future body, are there also past and present bodies existing simultaneously?"
"When there is a present body, are there also past and future bodies existing at that same time?
If someone were to ask this question, how would you answer?"
Hastishirsa said: "If such a question were asked, I would reply:
'When there is a past body, there is only that past body; there is no future or present body.'"
When there is a future body, it is exclusively a future body, without past or present bodies.
When there is a present body, it is exclusively a present body, without past or future bodies.
"Elephant Head! It is just the same in this case:

when there is a human body of the desire realm with its four great elements and various faculties, there is no body of the desire realm heavens, nor bodies of the form realm heavens, up to the bodies of the heavens of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Continuing in this manner, when there is a body of the heavens of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there is no human body of the desire realm with its four great elements and various faculties, nor bodies of the desire realm heavens, the form realm heavens, up to the bodies of the heavens of the sphere of nothingness."
"Furthermore, Hastikaśīrṣa!
Suppose someone were to ask you:
'Have you ever existed in the past that has now ceased? "
"Will it arise in the future?
Does it exist now in the present?
If such a question were asked, how would you answer?
Hastishirṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If there should be one who asks such a question, I would answer him thus:
‘I indeed existed in the past and have already ceased; it is not that I did not exist.’”
"That which is yet to come and will arise exists; it is not non-existent.
That which is present now exists; it is not non-existent.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Elephant-Head! It is just the same here:

when there is the body of a human being in the desire realm with its four great elements and sense faculties, there is no body of a celestial being in the desire realm, nor even a body of a celestial being up to the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-perception.

Thus it continues in succession; when one reaches the body of a celestial being in the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-perception, there is no longer the body of a human being in the desire realm with its four great elements and sense faculties, nor the body of a celestial being in the desire realm, nor even the body of a celestial being up to the Heaven of Nothingness."
At that time, Hastiśīrṣa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. Please accept me as an upāsaka within the True Dharma; from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants.”
At that time, the brahmin Pāṭahāra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May I go forth within the Buddha’s Dharma and receive the precepts?
The Buddha said to the brahmin:

"If there are followers of other teachings who wish to leave the household life and practice the Path within my Dharma, they must first undergo a four-month period of observation; only when they meet with the approval of the assembly may they then go forth and receive the precepts."
"Although this rule exists, it is still applied according to the person.

The brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying, "If those of other schools wish to leave the household life and receive the precepts within the Buddha's Dharma, they should first undergo a four-month period of observation; only after they have met with the approval of the assembly may they then leave the household life and receive the precepts."
As I am now, I must first observe within the Buddha-dharma for four years to accord with the wishes of the assembly, and only then may I hope to go forth and receive the precepts.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I have already told you that although such a teaching exists, one must examine the person.
At that time, the brahmin immediately went forth as a monk within the True Dharma and received the precepts.

In this way, before long, with faith made firm, he purified his holy life; in this very life, he realized for himself that birth and death were exhausted, what was to be done had been accomplished, and there would be no further existence, thus becoming an Arhat.
At that time, Pāṭikāputra, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 29.
The Lohitya Sūtra (29) The Tenth Discourse in the Third Division of the Long Āgama Spoken by the Buddha: The Lohitya Sūtra. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was wandering among the people of Kośala together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. He proceeded to the village of the brahmin Vāsiṣṭha and stayed for the night in the Śiṃśapā Forest to its north.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Lūḍha who resided in the Brahmadatta Forest. That village was prosperous and flourishing, with a dense population; King Prasenajit had granted this village to the brahmin as his *brahmadeya* (a religious endowment).

This brahmin has maintained pure lineage through seven generations of ancestors, such that he is not disparaged by others; he is proficient in reciting the three Vedas and can thoroughly analyze all manner of scriptures. Furthermore, he is skilled in the physiognomy of great men, in divining auspicious and inauspicious omens, and in the rituals of sacrificial offerings.

I have heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākyas who has left the household life and attained the Way, is wandering among the people in the kingdom of Kośala and has arrived at the Śiṃśapā Grove. He possesses great renown that spreads throughout the world; he is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles. Among the assembly of devas, humans, Māras, or Māra-devas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he has realized it for himself and teaches the Dharma to others—a teaching that is excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, complete in meaning and phrasing, and pure in its holy life (brahmacarya).
"Such a True Person ought to be visited; I should now go to meet him.
Thereupon, the brahmin departed from that village and went to the Śiṃśapā forest, arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was. After exchanging greetings, he sat down to one side.
The Buddha taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him. Having heard the Dharma, the brahmin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the great assembly will graciously accept my invitation for tomorrow."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing the Buddha’s silence, the brahmin knew he had granted his permission; he immediately rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.
Not far from the Buddha, he gave rise to an evil view and said:

"The śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess much knowledge of the wholesome Dharma and have achieved many realizations should not speak of them to others; they should know them for themselves and desist from speaking of them to others."
"It is just as if someone were to demolish an old prison and construct a new one; this is merely the greed, evil, and unwholesome dharmas.
At that time, the brahmin returned to the Brahma Forest and, during that very night, prepared various kinds of delicacies and food and drink.
When the time arrived, he said to his barber:
"Carry my words to the Śiṃśapā forest and say to the śramaṇa Gautama:
'The hour has come; you should know that it is time.'"
The barber, having received these instructions, immediately set out for the Buddha’s dwelling. Upon arriving, he prostrated at the World-Honored One’s feet and said:
“The time has come; please know that it is now the hour.”
At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and set out for the Bālakī forest accompanied by his twelve hundred and fifty disciples.
The barber who attended upon the World-Honored One bared his right shoulder, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Not far from the Buddha is the brahmin Lohitya, who has conceived a wrong view and says:..."

"Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have extensive knowledge of wholesome dharmas and have attained much realization, they should not speak of them to others; rather, they should know them for themselves and desist from speaking of them to others."
"It is as if someone were to demolish an old prison and build a new one; this is merely the greed, evil, and unwholesome dharmas.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will eliminate their wrong views."
The Buddha said to the barber, "This is a minor matter; he will be easily converted.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to the brahmin’s house and sat down upon the seat prepared for him.

At that time, the brahmin personally served various kinds of sweet delicacies to the Buddha and the Sangha. When they had finished eating and the bowls were removed, and after the water for washing was offered, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha told Lūṣa:
"Yesterday, not far from me, you gave rise to an evil view and said:

'Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess much knowledge of the wholesome Dharma and have realized much should not speak of it to others... [down to] ...even those who are greedy for evil and unwholesome dharmas.'"
"Is it true that such words were spoken? Luṣa replied, "Yes, it is indeed so."
The Buddha told Luṣa:
"Do not again give rise to such an evil view. Why is this?"
In the world, there are three teachers by whom one may admonish oneself. What are these three?

First, one who has shaved off beard and hair, donned the three dharma robes, and left the household life to practice the Way; who, within this present life, can eliminate afflictions and further increase his attainment of the qualities of a superior person.

Yet, in this present life, he does not eliminate the afflictions nor attain the qualities of a superior person; while his own task remains unaccomplished, he preaches the Dharma to his disciples, who do not honor or serve him, yet continue to rely upon him and dwell together with him.
Lūṣa! Those disciples said to their teacher:

"Teacher, you have now shaved off your hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, and left the household life to practice the Way; within this present life, you have been able to eliminate all afflictions and attain the supreme state of a noble person."
Yet, in this present life, he is unable to eliminate the afflictions nor attain the superior, sublime Dharma.

While his own task remains unaccomplished, he preaches the Dharma to his disciples, causing them no longer to revere, serve, or make offerings to him, but merely to rely upon him and dwell together with him.
The Buddha said: "Lūṣa!
It is just as if someone were to demolish an old prison and construct a new one; this is what is called the defiled and evil dharma of greed."
"This is the one teacher by whom you may admonish yourselves.
This is the precept of the noble ones, the precept of the discipline, the precept of decorum, and the precept of the proper time.
He further addressed Luca:

"The second teacher is one who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three Dharma robes, and left the household life to practice the Way. Although he may have attained the removal of various afflictions within this present life, he has not increased his attainment to reach the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*); yet, even though he cannot remove all afflictions in this present life, he has nonetheless attained some degree of the superior and sublime states of a superior person. While his own task remains unfulfilled, he preaches the Dharma to his disciples, but those disciples do not honor or serve him, even as they continue to rely upon him and dwell together with him."
Lūṣa! Those disciples said to their teacher:

"Teacher, you have now shaved off your hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, left the household life to practice the Way, and within this present life have attained the removal of all afflictions and realized the state of a superior person."

Now, being unable to eliminate the various afflictions within this present life, even though he has attained some degree of the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), his own benefit remains unaccomplished; yet he preaches the Dharma to his disciples, causing them no longer to revere, serve, or make offerings to him, but merely to rely upon him for their common residence and cohabitation.
The Buddha said: "Lūśa!
It is just as if someone were walking behind another person and stroking their back with his hand; this is what is called the evil dharma of greed and corruption."
"These are the two teachers by which one may admonish oneself.
These are the precepts of the noble ones, the precepts of the discipline, the precepts of decorum, and the precepts of the proper time.
He further addressed Luṣa:

"The third teacher is one who has shaved off his hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, and left the household life to practice the Way. He is capable of eliminating afflictions within this present life and is further able to increase his attainment of the qualities of a superior person; yet, he is unable to eliminate all afflictions within this present life, and although he has attained some degree of the qualities of a superior person, his own benefit remains unfulfilled as he teaches the Dharma to his disciples, who then respectfully serve him, rely upon him, and dwell with him."
Loocha! Those disciples said to their teacher:

"Teacher, you have now shaved off your hair and beard, donned the three dharma-robes, and left the household life to practice the Way. You thought that within this present life you could eliminate all afflictions and attain various degrees of the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*); yet now, within this present life, you cannot eliminate all afflictions. Although you have attained various degrees of the superhuman states, your own benefit remains unaccomplished as you preach the Dharma to your disciples, who respectfully serve you, dwell together with you, and live in your company."
The Buddha said: "Loocha!
It is just as if someone were to abandon their own crops and weed another's field; this is what is called the evil dharma of greed and corruption."
These are the three teachers by which one may admonish oneself.
These are the precepts of the noble ones, the precepts of the discipline, the precepts of decorum, and the precepts of the proper time. Loocha!
There is one World-Honored One who does not abide in the world and cannot be shaken. What is this one?

It is when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, and so forth, until attaining the three knowledges (*traividyā*): he eradicates ignorance, gives rise to the light of wisdom, dispels all darkness, and brings forth the great light of the Dharma—namely, the realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
Why is this so? It is because it is attained through diligent effort, focused mindfulness without forgetfulness, and the delight in dwelling alone in seclusion. Loocha!
This is the first [reason] why the World-Honored One, though no longer in the world, cannot be shaken. Loocha!
There are four fruits of the ascetic life.
What are the four?
They are the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), and the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala).
What do you think, Loṣṭaka?
There may be someone who, upon hearing the Dharma, ought to attain these four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
If someone were to obstruct them by saying,
"Do not preach the Dharma to him," [it would be a transgression].
"If one were to act according to those words, would that person hear the Dharma and attain the fruit? He replied, "No."
He asked again:
"If one does not attain the fruit [of the path], can one still be reborn in heaven? He replied:
"It is not permitted.
He asked again:
"If one obstructs another from preaching the Dharma, causing them to fail to attain the fruits [of the path] and fail to be reborn in heaven, is this not so?"
"Is this a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind?
He replied, "It is unwholesome."
He asked again:
"Does one with an unwholesome mind take birth in a happy realm, or does one fall into an evil realm? He replied:
“They will be reborn in the evil realms. “Lauḍha!
It is just as if someone were to say to King Prasenajit:”
"Whatever wealth exists within the kingdom belonging to the king, let the king consume it all himself and give nothing to others.
What do you think, Roca? If one were to follow those people's words, would one not have to cut off the provisions for others?
He replied, "It should be severed.
He asked again:
“Is the one who cuts off another’s offerings acting with a virtuous mind or an unvirtuous mind?
He replied, “With an unvirtuous mind.”
He asked again:
"Does one with an unwholesome mind take birth in a happy realm, or does one fall into an evil destiny? He replied:
“They fall into the evil realms.
“Lauḍha! It is just so with that person: having heard the Dharma, they ought to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.”
If someone were to say,
"Do not preach the Dharma," and one were to follow those words, would that person hear the Dharma and attain its fruit?
He replied, “I have not. He asked again:
"If one does not attain the fruit [of the path], can one still be born in heaven? He replied, "One cannot."
He asked again:
"If one obstructs another from preaching the Dharma, preventing them from attaining the fruits of the Path or being reborn in heaven—
is that a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind?"
He replied, "It is unwholesome.
He asked again:
"If one possesses an unwholesome mind, will they be reborn in a happy realm or fall into an evil destiny?
He replied, "They will fall into an evil destiny."
“Roca! Suppose someone were to say to you:
‘All the wealth and property belonging to the village of Pāvāvatī is yours.’”
"Rocaka! Use it yourself;
do not give it to others. One should use things for oneself—what is the use of giving them to another?
What do you think, Rocaka?
"If one were to adopt their words, should the offerings to others be discontinued?
He replied, "They should be discontinued."
He asked again:
"If one instructs another to sever their offerings, is this a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind? He replied:
"Unwholesome. He asked again:
"Does one with an unwholesome mind take birth in a happy realm, or does one fall into an evil destiny?"
He replied, “They fall into the evil realms. “Lauḍha! [he said.]
It is just like this: suppose there is a person who, upon hearing the Dharma, would attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
If someone were to say to them, "Do not preach the Dharma," and they were to follow those words, would that person still attain the fruits upon hearing the Dharma?
He replied, "I cannot. He asked again:
"If one does not attain the fruit [of the path], can one still be reborn in heaven? He replied, "One cannot."
He asked again:
"If one obstructs another from preaching the Dharma, preventing them from attaining the fruits [of the path] or being reborn in heaven—
is this a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind?"
He replied, "It is unwholesome.
He asked again:
"If one possesses an unwholesome mind, will they be born in a happy realm or fall into an evil destiny?
He replied, "They will fall into an evil destiny."
At that time, the brahmin Lūḍaca addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṅgha. I pray that you will accept me as a lay follower within the True Dharma; from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, not steal, not engage in sexual misconduct, not deceive, and not drink intoxicants."
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, the brahmin Lohicca, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Section Four, Part Thirty: The Sūtra on the Record of the Ages (30). The Fourth Part: The Sūtra on the Record of the Ages. Chapter One: The Continent of Jambudvīpa.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Anāthapiṇḍada Park, within the Kuṭāgāra Cave, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, after the meal, the assembly of bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall and deliberated, saying:
"Virtuous ones! This is unprecedented: by what cause will this world-system now be destroyed?"
"By what means is it accomplished?
What is the nature of the lands where sentient beings dwell?
At that time, the World-Honored One, while in a secluded place, heard with his divine ear the monks gathered in the lecture hall after their meal, discussing these matters.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his secluded dwelling, went to the lecture hall, and sat down. Knowing [the matter] yet asking for the sake of instruction, he questioned the bhikṣus:
"Regarding what you were discussing just now, what was the subject of your discussion?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"After our meal, we gathered at the Dharma Hall and discussed, saying:
'O Venerable Ones!'"
"How marvelous! By what cause does this heaven and earth now perish?
By what cause is it formed?
And of what nature are the lands where sentient beings dwell?"
"We have gathered in the hall to deliberate on this matter.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Excellent!"
Excellent! All who have left the household life should practice two dharmas:
first, the noble silence; second, the discourse on the Dharma.
Gathered here in this lecture hall, you too should remain thus in noble silence and discourse on the words of the Dharma.
O bhikṣus! Do you wish to hear the Tathāgata’s account of the formation and destruction of the world-systems, and the lands and cities where sentient beings dwell?
Then, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“Indeed it is so,
World-Honored One!”
"Now is precisely the right time; we wish most earnestly to hear it.
Once the World-Honored One has spoken, we shall uphold it.
The Buddha said:
“Monks! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall speak for your sake.
Thus the Buddha addressed the monks.
"Just as a single sun and moon traverse the four continents, illuminating with their radiance such a thousandfold world-system;
within that thousandfold world-system, there are a thousand suns and moons, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, four thousand continents,
four thousand great continents, four thousand seas, and four thousand great oceans."
There were four thousand nāgas, four thousand great nāgas, four thousand garuḍas,
four thousand great garuḍas, four thousand evil paths, four thousand great evil paths, four thousand kings, four thousand great kings,
seven thousand great trees, eight thousand great hells, ten thousand great mountains, and one thousand Yama kings.
One thousand Four Heavenly Kings, one thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens, one thousand Yāma heavens, one thousand Tuṣita heavens,
one thousand Nirmāṇarati heavens, one thousand Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, and one thousand Brahmā heavens—
this constitutes a small chiliocosm.
As there is one small thousand-world system, so many small thousand-world systems constitute a medium thousand-world system.
As there is one medium thousand-world system, so many medium thousand-world systems constitute a trichiliocosm (a great trichiliocosm).
"In this manner, the worlds surrounding one another undergo formation and destruction; the dwelling place of sentient beings is called a single Buddha-field.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Now, this great earth is sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas deep, its boundaries being limitless. The earth rests upon water, which is three thousand thirty yojanas deep, its boundaries being limitless. The water rests upon wind, which is six thousand forty yojanas deep, its boundaries being limitless."

"O Bhikṣus! That great ocean is eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, its boundaries being limitless. Sumeru, the King of Mountains, enters the waters of the ocean for eighty-four thousand yojanas and rises above the water for eighty-four thousand yojanas. Its base is connected to the earth, resting upon a vast and solid foundation; the mountain rises straight up without any curvature. It produces various kinds of trees that emit manifold fragrances, the scent of which pervades the mountain forests. It is the dwelling place of many sages and holy ones, and of the great, wondrous devas."

The foundation at the base of that mountain consists entirely of golden sand. On its four sides, four terraces protrude, each seven hundred yojanas high, interspersed with various colors and composed of the seven treasures; these four terraces slope downward, curving over the sea.

“Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, has stairways made of the seven treasures. Its lower stairway is sixty yojanas wide. Flanking both sides of the path are sevenfold walls of treasure, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees. There are golden walls with silver gates, silver walls with golden gates, crystal walls with lapis lazuli gates, lapis lazuli walls with crystal gates, red pearl walls with agate gates, agate walls with red pearl gates, and musaragalva walls with gates of various treasures.”

As for its railings: there were golden railings with silver crossbars, silver railings with golden crossbars, crystal railings with lapis lazuli crossbars, lapis lazuli railings with crystal crossbars, ruby railings with agate crossbars, agate railings with ruby crossbars, and musaragalva railings with crossbars made of various jewels.

Upon those railings were jeweled nets: beneath the golden nets hung silver bells; beneath the silver nets hung golden bells; the lapis lazuli nets hung crystal bells; the crystal nets hung lapis lazuli bells; the red pearl nets hung agate bells; the agate nets hung red pearl bells; and the musaragalva nets hung bells made of various jewels.

As for the gold trees, they have golden roots and branches with silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees have silver roots and branches with golden leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees have crystal roots and branches with lapis lazuli flowers and leaves; the lapis lazuli trees have lapis lazuli roots and branches with crystal flowers and leaves; the red pearl trees have red pearl roots and branches with agate flowers and leaves; the agate trees have agate roots and branches with red pearl flowers and leaves; and the musaragalva trees have musaragalva roots and branches with flowers and leaves made of various jewels.

"These sevenfold walls have four gates, each gate with railings; atop the sevenfold walls are pavilions and towers. Surrounding them are gardens and bathing pools where various precious flowers and leaves grow, and rows of jewel-trees stand in dense clusters, their fruits and blossoms flourishing. Fragrant breezes rise from all sides, delighting the hearts of men, while thousands of species of extraordinary birds—ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and other wondrous varieties—sing together in harmony."

Furthermore, the middle terrace of Sumeru, King of Mountains, is forty yojanas wide; flanking both sides of the path are sevenfold rows of precious walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, even unto countless birds singing in harmony with one another, just as on the lower terrace.

The upper terrace is twenty yojanas wide; flanking both sides of the path are sevenfold rows of precious walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, even unto countless birds singing in harmony together, just as on the middle terrace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"On the lower staircase there dwells a yakṣa named Garuḍapāda;
on the middle staircase there dwells a yakṣa named Mālādhāra."
On its upper stairways dwell spirits and deities named *Nandana* (Joy).

Its four terraces rise forty-two thousand *yojanas* high; there are the palaces where the Four Great Heavenly Kings reside, featuring sevenfold jeweled walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees. From the various jeweled bells to the countless birds, all singing in harmony with one another, it is just as described before.

On the summit of Mount Sumeru is the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa devas, with sevenfold rows of jeweled walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees; even down to the countless birds singing in harmony, it is exactly as described before.

One yojana beyond the Heaven of the Thirty-three is the palace of the Yāma Heaven; one yojana beyond the palace of the Yāma Heaven is the palace of the Tuṣita Heaven; one yojana beyond the palace of the Tuṣita Heaven is the palace of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; one yojana beyond the palace of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; and one yojana beyond the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven is the palace of the Brahmakāyika Heaven.

"Between the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations and the Brahmakāyika Heaven, there is a celestial palace, six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees; even up to the countless birds singing in harmony with one another, it is exactly like that."
One yojana beyond the Brahmakāyika celestial palace is the Ābhāsvara celestial palace;
one yojana beyond the Ābhāsvara celestial palace is the Śubhakṛtsna celestial palace; one yojana beyond the Śubhakṛtsna celestial palace is the Bṛhatphala celestial palace;
one yojana beyond the Bṛhatphala celestial palace is the Asaṃjñisattva celestial palace; beyond the Asaṃjñisattva...
One *yojana* beyond the Heaven of Perception (*saṃjñā-deva*) is the palace of the Heaven of No-Making (*anabhraka*);
one *yojana* beyond the Heaven of No-Making is the palace of the Heaven of No-Heat (*atapa*); one *yojana* beyond the Heaven of No-Heat is the palace of the Heaven of Good Vision (*sudṛśa*);
one *yojana* beyond the Heaven of Good Vision is the palace of the Heaven of Great Good Vision (*sudarśana*); [one *yojana*] beyond the Heaven of Great Good Vision...
At a distance of one *yojana* from here lies the celestial palace of Akaniṣṭha (the Ultimate of Form).

Above the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, there are the realms of the gods of the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.
Up to this point is designated as the limit of sentient beings and the world of sentient beings; all sentient beings [reside] therein.
"Birth, old age, sickness, death, the aggregates of sensation, and the experience of existence—beyond these there is nothing more.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"To the north of Mount Sumeru is a world called Uttarakuru; its land is square, measuring ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and the faces of its people are likewise square, corresponding to the shape of that terrain."

To the east of Mount Sumeru is a world named Pūrvavideha; its land is perfectly circular, measuring nine thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise circular, corresponding to the shape of that terrain.

To the west of Mount Sumeru is a world named Godānīya; its land is shaped like a half-moon, measuring eight thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and the faces of its inhabitants are likewise shaped according to that terrain.

To the south of Mount Sumeru is a world called Jambudvīpa; its land is narrow in the south and broad in the north, measuring seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and the faces of the people there are likewise shaped according to this topography.
The northern face of Mount Sumeru is composed of celestial gold, its light illuminating the north.
The eastern face of Mount Sumeru is composed of celestial silver, its light illuminating the east.
The western face of Mount Sumeru is composed of crystal, and its light illuminates the west.
The southern face of Mount Sumeru is composed of lapis lazuli, and its light illuminates the south.
“In Uttarakuru there is a great king of trees named Āmra, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all four directions.”

In Pūrvavideha there is a great king of trees named Kālāmbu; it is seven yojanas in circumference, one hundred yojanas in height, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all four directions.
In Godānīya there is a great king of trees named Kiṃpaka, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions;
furthermore, beneath that tree stands a stone ox-pillar, one yojana in height.

In Jambudvīpa there is a great king of trees named Jambu; its circumference is seven yojanas, its height is one hundred yojanas, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all four directions.

The tree of the Garuḍa King and the Dragon King is named Kūṭaśālmali; it is seven yojanas in circumference, one hundred yojanas in height, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all four directions.
The Asura King has a tree named Suvicitra, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all four directions.

In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is a tree named Pārijāta; it is seven yojanas in circumference, one hundred yojanas in height, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all four directions.

"On the side of Mount Sumeru there is a mountain named Gādha, forty-two thousand yojanas in height and forty-two thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its perimeter is vast and far-reaching, variegated with interspersed colors, and composed of the seven treasures. This mountain is eighty-four thousand yojanas distant from Mount Sumeru; in the space between them grow exclusively blue utpala flowers, red padma flowers, yellow kumuda flowers, and white puṇḍarīka flowers. Reeds, pines, and bamboo grow in thickets therein, emitting various fragrances that pervade everywhere."

Not far from Mount Khadiraka is a mountain named Aiṣadhara, twenty-one thousand yojanas high and twenty-one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its perimeter is vast and wide, variegated with interspersed colors, and composed of the seven precious gems. It is forty-two thousand yojanas distant from Mount Khadiraka; in the space between them grow exclusively blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka). Reeds, pines, and bamboo grow in thickets there, emitting various fragrances whose scent pervades everywhere.

Not far from Mount Īṣādhara there is a mountain named Śuklodara, twelve thousand yojanas in height and twelve thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its perimeter is vast and far-reaching, variegated with interspersed colors, and composed of the seven precious jewels.

Twenty-one thousand yojanas from Mount Īṣādhara, there grows exclusively a variety of four kinds of flowers; reeds, pines, and bamboo grow thickly therein, emitting all manner of fragrances whose scent pervades everywhere.

Not far from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa there is a mountain named Sudarśana, six thousand yojanas in height and six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its perimeter is vast and wide, variegated with diverse colors, and composed of the seven precious gems. It stands twelve thousand yojanas away from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; in the space between them grow exclusively four kinds of variegated flowers, while reeds, pines, and bamboos grow in thickets therein, emitting various fragrances that pervade everywhere.

"Not far from Mount Sudarśana there is a mountain named Aśvakarṇa (Horse-Ear), three thousand yojanas high and three thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its perimeter is vast and wide, variegated with interspersed colors, and composed of the seven precious substances. It is six thousand yojanas from Mount Sudarśana; in the space between them grow exclusively four kinds of miscellaneous flowers, and reeds, pines, and bamboo grow in thickets therein, emitting various fragrances whose scent pervades everywhere."

Not far from Mount Aśvakarṇa is a mountain named Nimindhara, twelve hundred yojanas high and twelve hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Its perimeter is vast and wide, variegated with diverse colors, and composed of the seven precious gems. It is three thousand yojanas distant from Mount Aśvakarṇa; in the space between them grow exclusively four kinds of variegated flowers, while reeds, pines, and bamboos grow in thickets therein, emitting various fragrances whose scent pervades everywhere.

Not far from Mount Nimindhara is a mountain named Vinataka, six hundred yojanas high and six hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Its perimeter is vast and wide, variegated with many colors, and composed of the seven precious gems. It stands twelve hundred yojanas away from Mount Nimindhara; in the space between them grow exclusively four kinds of miscellaneous flowers, while reeds, pines, and bamboo grow in thickets therein, emitting various fragrances that permeate everywhere.

Not far from Mount Vinataka is a mountain named Vajrāvalī, three hundred yojanas high and three hundred yojanas in length and breadth; its perimeter is vast and wide, interspersed with various colors, and composed of the seven precious jewels. It is six hundred yojanas from Mount Vinataka, and in the space between them grow exclusively four kinds of variegated flowers, with reeds, pines, and bamboos growing in thickets, emitting all manner of fragrances whose scent permeates everywhere.

"Not far from Mount Mahāvajra there is a great ocean. On the northern shore of this ocean stands a king of trees named Jambu, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with its branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions. Beyond it, on the empty ground, there is another grove named Āmra, fifty yojanas in length and breadth."
Furthermore, there is a grove named Jambū, fifty yojanas in length and breadth;
there is also another grove named Sāla, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Tālā, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Natālā, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Puruṣa (The Male), fifty yojanas in length and breadth;
there is also a grove named Strī (The Female), fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Man-nü (Strī-puruṣa), fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named San-na (Sana), fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Candana, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Khadira, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Pāṇḍava, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Vīra, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Gandhāmravana, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Amalaka, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Anshiliu (Aśmāparānta), fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Weigan (Madhura), fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Harītakī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth;
and there is another grove named Viśālā, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Āmalaka, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Āmalī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Āmra, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is another grove named Ikṣu, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is yet another grove named Naḍa, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Bamboo, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is another grove named Śāla, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is yet another grove named Śālakalyāṇī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Papaya, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Great Papaya, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Liberation Flower, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Campaka, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Bharara, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Sumana, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Vārṣika, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Tālī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Furthermore, there is a grove named Gayā, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
There is also a grove named Grape, fifty yojanas in length and breadth.

Beyond this empty land, within that empty space, there are further flower ponds, each fifty yojanas in length and breadth; furthermore, there are ponds of padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers, all filled with venomous snakes, each measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Beyond this empty land, within that emptiness, there is a great ocean called Ucchana; beneath these waters lies the path of the Cakravartin kings, twelve yojanas in width.

On both sides of the road, there are seven layers of walls, seven layers of railings, seven layers of nets, and seven rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures. When a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King appears in the world of Jambudvīpa, the water naturally recedes and the road becomes level and manifest.

Not far from the sea there is a mountain named Ujjhāna; the mountain is majestic and its trees are lush and thick, with flowers and fruits in profusion and a fragrance of manifold perfumes wafting abroad, while every kind of bird and beast is found there.

Not far from Mount Udayana is a mountain named Suvarṇakuṭa (Golden Wall), within which there are eighty thousand rock caves. Eighty thousand elephant kings dwell in these caves; their bodies are pure white, their heads are variegated in color, they have six tusks, and the spaces between their teeth are inlaid with gold.

Having passed Mount Kanbhika, there is a mountain named Himavat, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth and five hundred yojanas in depth, extending east and west into the ocean. In the midst of the Snowy Mountains is a jeweled mountain twenty yojanas high.

“A peak of the Snowy Mountains rises one hundred yojanas high; upon its summit is Lake Anavatapta, fifty yojanas in length and breadth. Its waters are cool and clear, transparent and free from impurity. It is bordered by embankments of the seven treasures, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all composed of the seven treasures and displaying various wonderful colors.”

As for its railings: there were golden railings with silver crossbars, silver railings with golden crossbars, lapis lazuli railings with crystal crossbars, crystal railings with lapis lazuli crossbars, ruby railings with agate crossbars, agate railings with ruby crossbars, and musaragalva railings composed of various jewels.

There were golden nets with silver bells, silver nets with golden bells, lapis lazuli nets with crystal bells, and crystal nets with lapis lazuli bells; there were also nets of musāragalva made of the seven precious jewels.

There were *tāla* trees with golden roots and golden branches, silver leaves and silver fruits; silver *tāla* trees with silver roots and silver branches, golden leaves and golden fruits; crystal trees with crystal roots and branches and lapis lazuli flowers and fruits; red pearl trees with red pearl roots and branches, agate leaves and agate flowers and fruits; and musaragalva trees with musaragalva roots and branches and flowers and fruits made of various jewels.

"On the shores of Lake Anavatapta, there are gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools where various flowers are gathered; the leaves of diverse trees are lush, and fruits and blossoms flourish. Various fragrant breezes spread their sweet scents in all directions, and birds of many different species warble in harmony with one another."
At the bottom of Lake Anavatapta, golden sand fills it completely.

On all four sides of the lake there are stairways: gold railings with silver steps, silver railings with gold steps, lapis lazuli railings with crystal steps, crystal railings with lapis lazuli steps, red pearl railings with agate steps, agate railings with red pearl steps, and musaragalva railings with steps made of various jewels.

Encircling the pond on all sides are railings, where four kinds of flowers—blue, yellow, red, and white—grow in a variegated array. The blossoms are as large as chariot wheels and their roots are like chariot hubs; from these roots flows a sap that is white in color like milk and sweet in taste like honey.
To the east of Lake Anavatapta is the Gaṅgā River, which issues from the Ox Mouth and flows through five hundred rivers into the eastern ocean.
To the south of Lake Anavatapta is the Sindhu River, which issues from the Lion Mouth and flows through five hundred rivers into the southern ocean.
To the west of Lake Anavatapta is the Vakṣu River, which issues from the horse’s mouth and flows through five hundred tributaries into the western ocean.
To the north of Lake Anavatapta is the Sītā River, which issues from the elephant’s mouth and flows through five hundred tributaries into the northern ocean.
"In the palace of Anavatapta there is a hall with five pillars, where the Dragon King Anavatapta constantly dwells.
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason is he named Anavatapta?"
What is the meaning of "Anavatapta"?
All dragon kings (nāgarāja) in this Jambudvīpa suffer from three afflictions; only the Dragon King Anavatapta is free from these three afflictions.
What are these three?

First, all the nāgas throughout Jambudvīpa have their bodies struck by hot winds and hot sands, which burn their skin and flesh, as well as their marrow and bones, causing them great suffering; only the nāga of Anavatapta is free from this affliction.

Second, all the dragon palaces throughout Jambudvīpa are struck by violent, evil winds that blow through their interiors, causing them to lose their jeweled ornaments and robes; the dragons' own bodies then become exposed, leading to great distress—except for the Dragon King Anavatapta, who alone is free from such affliction.

Third, when all the nāga kings throughout Jambudvīpa are enjoying themselves within their respective palaces, the great garuḍa bird enters their palaces to seize them—either by force or through skillful means—with the intent to eat them as food. All the nāgas are terrified and constantly harbor burning distress; however, the Anavatapta nāga alone is free from such affliction.

If the garuḍa bird even conceives the thought of going there, he immediately meets his death. Therefore, he is named Anavatapta; "Anavatapta" in the language of Qin means "Free from Burning Distress."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"On the southern slope of the Snowy Mountains there is a city named Vaiśālī. To the north of that city are the Seven Black Mountains; to the north of the Seven Black Mountains is the Fragrant Mountain, which constantly resounds with the sounds of singing, music, and instrumental performance."

On the mountain there are two caves: the first is named Day (Zhòu), and the second is named Good Day (Shànzhòu). They are composed of the seven treasures of the devas, soft, fragrant, and pure, like celestial garments. The Gandharva King Wondrous Sound (Miaoyin) dwells within them together with five hundred gandharvas.
To the north of the Cave of Good Day (Svadivasa) was a king of *śāla* trees named Supratiṣṭhita, surrounded on all four sides by eight thousand tree-kings.

Beneath the tree-king Supratiṣṭhita dwelt an elephant king, also named Supratiṣṭhita, who rested under this tree. His body was pure white, his seven parts were firmly planted upon the ground, and he possessed the power of flight. His head was crimson, interspersed with multicolored hair; his six tusks were slender and tapered, inlaid with gold.
He was followed and surrounded by eight thousand elephants; beneath each of the eight thousand tree-kings, there was likewise an elephant of similar appearance.

"To the north of the King of Trees, Supratiṣṭhita, there is a great bathing pool named Madhūya, fifty yojanas in length and breadth. It is surrounded by eight thousand smaller bathing pools. Its waters are cool and free from any impurity. The perimeter is lined with embankments made of the seven precious gems. Encircling the pool are seven rows of railings, seven layers of nets, and seven rows of trees, all composed of the seven precious gems: golden railings with silver crossbars, silver railings with golden crossbars, crystal railings with lapis lazuli crossbars, lapis lazuli railings with crystal crossbars, ruby railings with agate crossbars, agate railings with ruby crossbars, and musaragalva railings with crossbars of various jewels."

From the golden silk nets hung silver bells; from the silver silk nets hung golden bells; from the crystal silk nets hung lapis lazuli bells; from the lapis lazuli silk nets hung crystal bells; from the red pearl silk nets hung agate bells; from the agate silk nets hung red pearl bells; and from the musaragalva silk nets hung bells made of various jewels.

As for the golden trees, they have golden roots and branches with silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees have silver roots and branches with golden leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees have crystal roots and branches with lapis lazuli flowers and fruits; the lapis lazuli trees have lapis lazuli roots and branches with crystal flowers and fruits; the red pearl trees have red pearl roots and branches with agate flowers and fruits; the agate trees have agate roots and branches with red pearl flowers and fruits; and the musaragalva trees have musaragalva roots and branches with flowers and fruits made of various jewels.

Furthermore, the bottom of that pond was strewn with golden sand, and encircling it on all sides were stairways made of the seven treasures: gold steps with silver treads, silver steps with gold treads, crystal steps with lapis lazuli treads, lapis lazuli steps with crystal treads, red pearl steps with agate treads, agate steps with red pearl treads, and musaragalva steps with various other precious treads.
On both sides of the steps there are precious balustrades.

Furthermore, within that pond grow four kinds of flowers—blue, yellow, red, and white—with various colors interspersed; the flowers are as large as chariot wheels, and their roots are like chariot hubs. From these flower-roots flows a sap, white in color like milk and sweet in taste like honey.

Surrounding the four sides of the pond are various gardens, pavilions, groves, and bathing pools, where all kinds of flowers bloom; the trees are cool and refreshing, and the fruits and blossoms are abundant. Countless birds sing together in harmony, and it is likewise so throughout.

When the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita, desiring to sport, entered the pond to bathe, he immediately thought of eight thousand elephant kings. At that time, the eight thousand elephant kings also thought to themselves:
"The Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita is now thinking of us; we ought to go to where the Elephant King is."
Thereupon, the herd of elephants immediately moved forward and stood before him.

At that time, the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita proceeded with eight thousand elephants to Lake Mādhura. Among those elephants, some held parasols for the king, some grasped precious fans to fan the elephant king, and others performed music and dance as they preceded and followed him.

At that time, the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita entered the pond to bathe, where musical performances were provided and they enjoyed themselves together. Some elephants washed the king's trunk; others washed his mouth, head, tusks, ears, belly, back, tail, or feet. Among them, some pulled up lotus roots, washed them, and gave them to the king to eat; others took four kinds of flowers and scattered them over the king.
At that time, after the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita had bathed, partaken of food and drink, and enjoyed himself with his companions, he emerged onto the bank and stood beneath the Supratiṣṭhita tree.
Then those eight thousand elephants each entered the pond to bathe, eat, and drink, and enjoyed themselves together.
Having finished, they emerged and went to where the elephant king was.

At that time, the Elephant King was preceded and followed by eight thousand elephants as they proceeded to the site of the Well-Abiding Tree King. Among them were some who held parasols to shade the Elephant King, some who held precious fans to fan the Elephant King, and some who performed songs and music as they led the way.

At that time, the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita, having approached the king of trees, sat, lay down, walked, and roamed about as he pleased; the other eight thousand elephants likewise each stayed beneath their respective trees, sitting, lying down, walking, and roaming about as they pleased.

Within those groves, there were trees with a circumference of eight *vyāma*, others of nine to ten *vyāma*, and even fifteen *vyāma*; only the royal *pārijāta* tree of the well-dwelling elephant king had a circumference of sixteen *vyāma*. When the branches and leaves of the eight thousand *pārijāta* trees fell, a pure breeze would blow them far away to the edge of the forest; furthermore, when the eight thousand elephants voided their excrement and urine, various *yakṣas* and *bhūtas* would clear them away to the edge of the forest.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The elephant king Supratiṣṭhita possesses great supernormal power, and his merit is such that, though he is a beast, he receives such blessings."

**Chapter 2: Uttarakuru** The *Lokadhātu-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the fourth part of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, spoken by the Buddha, Chapter Two: Uttarakuru. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: "In the world of Uttarakuru there are many mountains.

Beside those mountains are various gardens, groves, and bathing pools where diverse flowers bloom. The trees are cool and refreshing, and their fruits and blossoms grow in great abundance. Countless birds sing together in harmony."
Furthermore, within that mountain there are many flowing streams; their waters flow gently and smoothly, without any sudden turbulence. Various flowers cover the surface as they drift slowly along.

On both sides of the banks grow numerous trees with supple branches and lush, abundant flowers and fruits. Soft grasses grow upon the ground, curling to the right like the feathers of a peacock, fragrant like the *vārṣika* flower, and as soft as celestial garments. The ground is so yielding that when one steps upon it, it sinks four inches, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to its original state. The terrain is as level as the palm of a hand, without any elevations or depressions.

“Monks! On the four sides of that continent of Uttarakuru, there are four Anavatapta lakes, each one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Their waters are clear and free from impurity; their edges are lined with embankments made of the seven precious gems. Even down to the countless birds singing together in harmony, they are no different in their splendor from Lake Mādhura.”

From each of those four great lakes issues a great river ten yojanas in width; their waters flow smoothly and gently, without any turbulence, covered above by various flowers as they drift slowly along.

On both sides of the bank were many trees with supple branches and lush, abundant flowers and fruits; the ground grew soft grass that curled to the right, its color like that of a peacock’s plumage and its fragrance like that of the *pāṭala* flower. It was as soft as celestial raiment, and the earth itself was so yielding that when one stepped upon it, it sank four inches, returning to its original state once the foot was lifted. The ground was as level as the palm of a hand, without any unevenness.
Furthermore, that land has no ditches, ravines, pits, or hollows, nor any thorns, stumps, or brushwood;
it is also free from mosquitoes, gadflies, vipers, snakes, bees, scorpions, tigers, leopards, and other malevolent beasts. The ground consists entirely of various jewels, devoid of stones or sand;
the yin and yang are harmonious and gentle, the four seasons are mild and agreeable, and the climate is neither cold nor hot.
Free from all afflictions and calamities, the ground is moist and fertile, with no dust or filth arising; it is as if anointed with oil, free of drifting particles.
A hundred grasses grow perpetually, without distinction between winter and summer. The trees are lush and flourishing, their flowers and fruits abundant.
From the earth grows soft grass that curls to the right, its color like that of a peacock’s throat.
The fragrance is like that of the pāṭali flower, and it is as soft as celestial robes;

the ground is so supple that when one steps upon it, it sinks four inches, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to its original state. The ground is as level as the palm of a hand, without any elevations or depressions.

"In that land, there is always naturally occurring non-glutinous rice; it grows spontaneously without being sown and is free of husks and chaff, like a cluster of white flowers, resembling the food of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, complete with every flavor."

In that land, there are always natural cauldrons and pots. There is a mani-jewel called "Blazing Light" which is placed beneath the cauldron; when the rice is cooked, the light extinguishes. Thus, it requires no firewood and no human labor.

In that land there is a tree called *Kubjaka*, whose leaves overlap one another so closely that rain cannot leak through; the men and women there dwell beneath it. There are also fragrant trees seventy *li* high, with flowers and fruits growing in profusion.

When the fruit ripens, its skin and shell split open of their own accord, and a natural fragrance issues forth. Some of these trees are sixty *li* high, some fifty or forty; the smallest are five *li* high. All are thickly covered with flowers and fruits, and when the fruit ripens, the skin and shell split open naturally, emitting a spontaneous fragrance.

Furthermore, there are clothing trees seventy *li* high, with abundant flowers and fruits; when their fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of garments. These trees may be sixty, fifty, or forty *li* high, and even as small as five *li*, all of them being lush with flowers and fruits and yielding various garments.

Furthermore, there are trees of adornment seventy li in height, their flowers and fruits lush and abundant; when their fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various articles for adorning the body. These trees may be sixty, fifty, or forty li in height, with the smallest being five li tall; all are lush with flowers and fruits, yielding various articles for adorning the body.

Furthermore, there are garland-trees seventy *li* in height, with flowers and fruits growing in profusion. When their fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of garlands. Some trees are sixty, fifty, or forty *li* high; even the smallest are five *li* high, all of them likewise possessing abundant flowers and fruits that produce various kinds of garlands.

Furthermore, there are vessel-trees seventy li in height, with flowers and fruits growing in profusion. When their fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of vessels.
