These trees may be sixty, fifty, or forty li in height; even the smallest are five li tall, all of them bearing flowers and fruits in abundance and yielding various vessels.

Furthermore, there are fruit trees seventy *li* high, their flowers and fruits lush and abundant; when the fruits ripen, their skins split open of their own accord, yielding various kinds of fruit. Some trees are sixty, fifty, or forty *li* high, while the smallest are five *li* high; all are luxuriant with flowers and fruit, producing every variety of fruit.

Furthermore, there are musical instrument trees seventy *li* high, with abundant flowers and fruit. When the fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of musical instruments. These trees may be sixty, fifty, or forty *li* high, and even as small as five *li* high; all are lush with flowers and fruit and produce various musical instruments.

"In that land there is a pond named Sudarśana, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Its waters are clear and transparent, free from any impurity. Its banks are lined with embankments made of the seven treasures. Surrounding the four sides of the pond are seven layers of railings, seven layers of decorative nets, and seven rows of trees; even the countless birds singing in harmony is likewise as described before."

To the north of that Lake Sudarśana there is a tree named Āmra, seven *li* in circumference, rising one hundred *li* in height, with branches and leaves spreading out in all directions for fifty *li*.

To the east of that Lake Sudarśana flows the river Suprabhā, one yojana in width. Its waters flow gently without eddies, and various kinds of flowers cover the surface of the water. On both banks, trees grow in dense profusion; their branches and twigs are supple, and they abound with flowers and fruit. Soft grasses grow upon the ground, curling to the right; their color is like that of a peacock’s throat, their fragrance like that of the vārṣika flower, and their texture as soft as celestial raiment. The ground is so yielding that when one steps upon it, it sinks four inches, returning to its original state once the foot is lifted. The earth is as level as the palm of a hand, without any unevenness.

Furthermore, within that river there are many jeweled boats. When the people of that region wish to enter them to bathe and play, they leave their clothes on the bank and board the boats in midstream. Having finished their play and entertainment, as they cross the water, they encounter whatever clothes they find and put them on; those who emerge first put on what they first find, and those who emerge later put on what they later find, without seeking out their own original garments.
Next they arrive at the fragrance trees; the trees bend their branches down, and the people take various kinds of mixed fragrances with their hands to anoint their bodies.
Next they reach the clothing trees; the trees bend their branches down, and the people take various kinds of mixed garments with their hands to wear as they please.
Next they arrive at the Tree of Adornments; the tree bends down, and the people take various ornaments from it with their own hands to adorn themselves.
Next they arrive at the Garland Tree; the tree bends down, and the people take various mixed garlands from it with their own hands to place upon their heads.
Next they arrive at the Tree of Vessels; the tree bends down for them, and with their own hands they take various precious vessels.

Having taken the vessels, they next arrive at the Tree of Fruits; the tree bends down for them, and with their own hands they take various exquisite fruits—some they eat, some they hold in their mouths, and some they strain for their juice to drink.

Next, they arrive at the trees of musical instruments; the trees bend themselves down, and the people take various instruments from them, tuning the strings and striking them, harmonizing the notes with exquisite sounds as they proceed toward the groves to enjoy themselves as they please for one day, two days, or up to seven days, after which they depart again, having no fixed abode.

"From the south of the Sudarśana Lake flows the River of Exquisite Form; from the west of the Sudarśana Lake flows the River of Exquisite Flavor; and from the north of the Sudarśana Lake flows the River of Radiant Light—it is likewise so."

To the east of Lake Sudarśana is a grove named Sudarśana, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Surrounding the four sides of the grove are seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of decorative nets, and seven rows of trees, interspersed with various colors and composed of the seven precious substances. On the four sides of the grove are four great gates, and the surrounding railings are likewise made of the seven precious substances.
The garden was pure and clean, free of thorns and brambles; its ground was level and even, without ditches, ravines, pits, hollows, hills, or mounds.
It was also devoid of mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, fleas, lice, vipers, snakes, bees, scorpions, tigers, wolves, and other predatory beasts.
The earth consisted entirely of various jewels, with no stones or sand, and the Yin and Yang elements were in harmonious balance.
It is supple; the four seasonal winds are harmonious and gentle, being neither cold nor hot, and free from manifold afflictions and calamities.
Its ground is moist and lustrous, devoid of dust and filth, like the earth smeared with oil where wandering dust does not arise.
A hundred grasses grow perpetually without distinction between winter and summer; the trees are lush and flourishing, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The earth produces moisture.
The grasses coil and wind to the right, their color like that of a peacock’s plumage, their fragrance like that of the *pāṭala* flower, and they are as soft as celestial garments.
The ground is supple and yielding; when one steps upon it, it sinks down four inches, and when the foot is lifted, it returns to its original state.

"In that garden, natural non-glutinous rice grows perpetually; it is free of husks and chaff, appearing like a cluster of white flowers, endowed with every flavor, and resembling the food of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."

In that garden there were always natural cauldrons and pots. There was a maṇi jewel named Flame-Light which was placed beneath the cauldron; when the rice was cooked, the light would extinguish. Thus, it required no firewood and no human labor.

In that garden there is a tree named Curving-Body (*Ku-gong*); its leaves overlap one another so closely that even when it rains from heaven, no water leaks through, allowing the men and women to dwell beneath it.

There are also fragrant trees, seventy *li* in height, with profuse flowers and fruit; when the fruit ripens, the rind splits open of its own accord, emitting various kinds of incense. Other trees are sixty, fifty, or forty *li* high, down to those as tall as five *li*, all of which have profuse flowers and fruit that emit various kinds of incense. Even the musical instrument trees are likewise.

The people of that land go to that garden to play and enjoy themselves for one day, two days, or up to seven days; the Sudarśana Garden is unguarded by anyone, so they play as they please and then depart.
"To the south of Lake Sudarśana is a grove named Mahāsudarśana.
To the west of Lake Sudarśana is a grove named Nandanavana.
To the north of Lake Sudarśana is a grove named Pāruṣyaka; it is likewise so."

In that land, during the middle and latter watches of the night, the Dragon King Anavatapta repeatedly gives rise to pure clouds at the appropriate times, raining sweet dew throughout the world for as long as it takes to milk a cow. With water of eight qualities, it moistens and saturates everything universally; yet the water does not remain stagnant, and the ground is free of mud, just as a garland-maker sprinkles water on flowers to prevent them from withering, keeping them moist, fresh, and radiant.

At that time, after midnight in that land, the sky was free from clouds and mist, clear and serene; a cool breeze rose from the sea, pure and gentle, blowing lightly against the bodies of those there, bringing joy to their entire beings.

That land is abundant and its population is flourishing; whenever food is required, one places natural non-glutinous rice in a cauldron and sets a flaming-jewel beneath it. The rice becomes cooked spontaneously, and the light of the jewel extinguishes of its own accord.
Whoever came was allowed to eat as much as they desired; yet the host did not rise, and the rice was never exhausted.
If the host rose, the rice would then be completely served out.

The rice was fresh and pure, like a cluster of white flowers; its flavor was perfect, like the food of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When they ate this rice, they were free from all ailments, their physical strength was sufficient, their countenances were harmonious and joyful, and they experienced no decline.

Furthermore, the people of that land are similar in physical build and identical in appearance, such that they cannot be distinguished from one another; their countenances are youthful, like those of men about twenty years of age in Jambudvīpa. Their teeth are even, upright, and pure white, closely set without any gaps. Their hair is a deep blue-black, free from dust or grime; it hangs down eight finger-widths, ending level with their eyebrows—neither too long nor too short.

When the people of that land give rise to a desire for lust, they gaze intently at women and then depart; the woman follows after them to the groves. If the woman is the man’s father, mother, or a blood relative such as a paternal or maternal cousin—someone with whom sexual intercourse is improper—the trees do not bend to provide shade, and they each disperse.

If they are not their father, mother, or paternal or maternal relatives, but are those with whom sexual intercourse is permissible, the tree bends its trunk and turns its shade over them; they enjoy themselves as they please for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, after which they disperse.
That woman became pregnant and gave birth after seven or eight days; whether it was a boy or a girl, she placed the infant at a great crossroads where four roads meet and departed, leaving it there.
Whenever practitioners passed by its side, she would extend her finger for them to suck; from her finger, she produced sweet milk that nourished the child’s body.
After seven days had passed, the child grew to the size of those people—the boys among the boys and the girls among the girls.
"When those people pass away, they do not weep or wail; they adorn the corpse and place it at a crossroads, then abandon it and depart.
There is a bird named Ucchvāsaka who takes up that corpse and carries it to another region."
Furthermore, when the people of that land defecate or urinate, the ground opens up for them; once they have finished, the ground closes back up of its own accord.
The inhabitants of that land have no attachments or cravings, nor do they accumulate possessions; their lifespans are always fixed, and upon death, they are all reborn in the heavens.
For what reason is that person’s lifespan fixed?

Because in a previous life that person practiced the ten wholesome actions, when their body perished and their life ended, they were reborn in Uttarakuru with a lifespan of one thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, the lifespans of those individuals are exactly equal.

Furthermore, those who kill fall into the evil realms, while those who do not kill are born in the good realms. Likewise, those who commit theft, sexual misconduct, double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, frivolous speech, covetousness, jealousy, or hold wrong views fall into the evil realms;

whereas those who do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not use double-tongued, harsh, lying, or frivolous speech, and are free from covetousness, jealousy, and wrong views, are born in the good realms.

If there are those who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, and do not practice double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, or frivolous talk; and who do not harbor covetousness, jealousy, or wrong views—when their bodies perish and their lives end, they will be reborn in Uttarakuru, where their lifespan is one thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, the lifespans of those two are exactly equal.
Furthermore, one who is stingy, greedy, and unable to practice charity will fall into the evil realms after death;
whereas one who opens their heart without parsimony and is able to practice charity will be reborn in a good realm.

If there is someone who gives to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, as well as to the poor, beggars, the diseased, and those in distress, providing them with clothing, food, vehicles, flower garlands, scented ointments, couches, and dwellings; and furthermore, constructs stūpas and temples, making offerings of lamps and candles—when such a person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they will be reborn in Uttarakuru, where their lifespan is one thousand years, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Therefore, the lifespans of those people are exactly equal.
For what reason is Uttarakuru called superior?

The inhabitants of that land do not formally undertake the ten wholesome actions; rather, their every movement naturally accords with the ten wholesome actions. When their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn in the heavenly realms, a place of goodness. For this reason, those people are called the "Superior" inhabitants of Uttarakuru.
As for Uttarakuru, what is its meaning?
Among the three continents, its land is the highest and most excellent; therefore it is named Uttarakuru. *Uttara* means "highest" in the language of Qin.
Chapter 3: The Universal Monarch (*Cakravartin*). The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this world there is a universal monarch who possesses the seven treasures and four divine virtues."
How does a Wheel-Turning Sage King achieve the seven treasures?

First is the golden wheel treasure; second is the white elephant treasure; third is the dark-blue horse treasure; fourth is the divine jewel treasure; fifth is the jade woman treasure; sixth is the householder treasure; and seventh is the military commander treasure.
What is the accomplishment of the precious golden wheel of a Wheel-turning Sage King?

When a Wheel-turning Sage King appears in the land of Jambudvīpa, born of the Kṣatriya caste as one consecrated by the pouring of water, on the fifteenth day of the month when the moon is full, he bathes in fragrant water and ascends to the top of a high palace to enjoy himself with a retinue of court ladies. Suddenly, the precious golden wheel of heaven appears before him; it has a thousand spokes, its radiance and color are perfect, it is made of celestial gold, fashioned by celestial artisans, and is not of this world. The diameter of the wheel is fourteen feet.
Having seen this, the Wheel-Turning Sage King thought to himself in silence:
"I have previously heard such words from the elders of old:

'If a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated lineage, on the fifteenth day when the moon is full, bathes in fragrant water and ascends the Dharma Palace surrounded by court ladies, a golden wheel will suddenly appear before him—spontaneously formed, with a thousand spokes, perfect in color and brilliance, crafted by celestial artisans and not of this world, measuring fourteen feet in diameter; he is then called a Wheel-Turning Sage King.'"
"Now that this wheel has appeared, could it not be this very thing?
I should now test this precious wheel-treasure.

Thereupon, the Wheel-turning King summoned his fourfold army and, facing the golden wheel-treasure, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and stroked the golden wheel with his right hand, saying:
"Go toward the east and turn according to the Dharma; do not deviate from the constant rule.
The wheel then turned toward the east.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning King immediately led his fourfold army to follow behind it. Four deities preceded the precious golden wheel as guides, and wherever the wheel came to rest, the king halted his carriage.

At that time, the minor kings of the eastern regions, seeing the Great King arrive, took golden bowls filled with silver grain and silver bowls filled with golden grain, and went to the King’s location. Bowing their heads, they addressed him, saying:
"Excellent!..."
"Great King!

Now this land in the east is prosperous and joyful, abounding in rare treasures; its people are numerous, their natures are gentle and harmonious, and they are compassionate, filial, loyal, and obedient. We pray only that the Holy King may govern here, and we shall serve at your side, receiving your commands."
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King said to the minor kings:
"Stop! Stop!"

"Virtuous ones! You shall have already paid me homage; you must now govern by means of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), ensuring there is no partiality or injustice. Do not allow unrighteous conduct to exist within the realm. Do not kill living beings yourselves, and do not teach others to kill, nor to steal, engage in sexual misconduct, use double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, or frivolous chatter; do not harbor greed, jealousy, or wrong views. This is what I call being governed according to my teachings."

When the minor kings had heard these instructions, they immediately followed the Great King on his tour of the various kingdoms as far as the eastern sea. He then proceeded to the south, the west, and the north; wherever the wheel arrived, the kings of those lands each offered up their territories, just as the minor kings of the east had done.

In this Jambudvīpa, there is a place renowned for its rich soil and fertile fields, where precious treasures abound, and the forests and waters are pure. Upon a level and expansive site, the wheel traveled around; it measured twelve yojanas from east to west and ten yojanas from south to north. During the middle of the night, a celestial deity constructed a city wall within that space. The city had sevenfold enclosures, with seven rows of railings, seven layers of decorative nets, and seven rows of trees, all beautifully adorned and composed of the seven precious gems, even to the point where countless birds sang together in harmony.

Once this city had been built, the precious golden wheel again measured out a territory within the city, four yojanas from east to west and two yojanas from south to north. During the middle of the night, the devas constructed a palace therein; its walls were sevenfold and composed of the seven treasures, and so on, until the countless birds singing in harmony, which was likewise the case here.
Once the palace had been constructed, the precious golden wheel remained suspended in the air above it, complete and motionless.
The Wheel-Turning Sage King leaped for joy and said:
"This precious golden wheel is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
This is the accomplishment of the precious gold wheel.
What is the accomplishment of the precious white elephant?

At dawn, while the Wheel-Turning Sage King is seated upon the main terrace, the precious elephant suddenly appears before him of its own accord. Its fur is pure white; it stands steadily on seven parts of its body; it has the power to fly; its head is variegated in color; it has six tusks that are slender and tapered, inlaid with genuine gold.
At that time, having seen this, the king thought to himself:
"This elephant is noble and excellent; if it were well-trained, it would be fit for riding.
He immediately tested its training and found that all its capabilities were fully prepared.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test his elephant himself, mounted it and departed from the city at dawn; he traveled around the four seas and returned by mealtime.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning King leaped for joy and said:
"This precious white elephant is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage-King.
This is the perfection of the precious elephant.
"What is the accomplishment of the blue horse-treasure (*aśvaratna*) of a Wheel-Turning Sage King?

At that time, while the Wheel-Turning Sage King is seated upon his main hall at dawn, the horse-treasure suddenly appears before him; it is deep blue in color with crimson mane and tail, its head and neck like those of an elephant, and it possesses the power to fly."
At that time, having seen this, the king thought to himself:
"This horse is noble and excellent; if it were well-trained, it would be fit for riding.
He immediately tested its training, and found that all its capabilities were fully prepared.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, wishing to test the horse-treasure for himself, mounted it at dawn and traveled out of the city, circling the four seas before returning by the time of the midday meal.
Then, the Wheel-Turning King leaped for joy and said:
"This dark-blue horse treasure is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
This is the accomplishment of the dark-blue horse treasure.
"What is the accomplishment of the divine jewel treasure?

At that time, when the Wheel-Turning Sage King is seated upon the main terrace at dawn, a divine jewel spontaneously appears before him; its substance and color are pure and transparent, free from any blemish or impurity."
At that time, having seen it, the king said:
"This jewel is exquisite; if it possesses radiance, it may illuminate the interior of the palace.

Then, the Wheel-Turning King, wishing to test this jewel, immediately summoned the fourfold army and placed the precious jewel atop a high banner. In the darkness of night, he carried the banner out of the city.
The radiance of that jewel illuminated one yojana, causing the people within the city to rise and engage in their labors, believing it to be daytime.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King leaped for joy and said:
"Now this divine jewel is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
This is the accomplishment of the divine jewel-treasure. What is the accomplishment of the jade-woman treasure?

At that time, the jade-woman treasure suddenly appeared, her complexion radiant and her countenance upright. She was neither tall nor short, neither coarse nor delicate, neither too pale nor too dark, and neither too rigid nor too supple. In winter her body was warm, and in summer it was cool. From every pore of her body issued the fragrance of *candana* sandalwood, and from her mouth issued the scent of the *utpala* lotus. Her speech was gentle and soft, and her movements were composed and serene; she would rise before others and sit after them, never failing in propriety.
At that time, having seen her, the Wheel-Turning Sage King was without attachment; he did not dwell upon her even for a moment, much less draw near to her.
Then, having seen her, the Wheel-Turning Sage King leaped for joy and said:
"This Jewel of a Woman is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
This is the accomplishment of the Jewel of the Woman. What is the accomplishment of the Jewel of the Householder?

At that time, a householder-man suddenly appears of his own accord; his treasure store is naturally and spontaneously of immeasurable wealth. By virtue of the householder’s past merit, his eyes can see through to hidden treasures beneath the earth; whether they have an owner or no owner, he perceives and knows them all. Those with an owner he is able to protect, while those without an owner he takes for the King’s use.
Then, the Householder Jewel went to the king and said:
"Great King! As for whatever needs to be provided, there is no need for concern; I myself am capable of arranging it."
When the Wheel-Turning Sage King wished to test the householder-treasure, he immediately ordered his ships to be prepared for recreation upon the water and said to the householder:
"I require gold and jewels; give them to me quickly."
The householder replied, "Great King, please wait a moment; we must reach the shore.
The king immediately pressed him, saying:
"I must have it now; I shall obtain it immediately.

Then, at the king’s strict command, the householder-treasure knelt on the ship and placed his right hand into the water. A jeweled vessel emerged from the water following his hand, like a worm climbing a tree; the householder-treasure was just like this, placing his hand in the water until jewels followed his hand out, filling the ship. He then addressed the king, saying:
"As for the jewels you required earlier, how many do you need?"
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King said to the householder:
"Stop! Stop!"
"I have no need for anything; I was merely testing you just now. You have already made an offering to me.
When the householder heard the king's words, he immediately caused the precious objects to sink back into the water.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King leaped for joy and said, "This Jewel of the Householder is truly an auspicious omen for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
This constitutes the accomplishment of the Householder Jewel.
What is the accomplishment of the Military Commander Jewel?

At that time, the Military Commander Jewel suddenly appears; he is possessed of brilliant strategy and fierce prowess, with singular resolve in his heroic schemes. He immediately goes to the king’s presence and says:
"Great King! As for the task of suppressing and punishing [the enemy], there is no need for concern; I myself am capable of accomplishing it.
At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King, wishing to test the Treasure of the Military Commander, immediately assembled the fourfold army and addressed them, saying:

"In your current military operations: those who have not yet assembled, assemble; those already assembled, dismiss. Those who have not yet arrayed, array; those already arrayed, disband. Those who have not yet departed, depart; those already departed, halt."

At that time, having heard the king’s words, the Jewel of the Military Commander immediately ordered the fourfold army: those not yet assembled were to assemble, and those already assembled were to be dismissed; those not yet arrayed were to be arrayed, and those already arrayed were to be disbanded; those who had not set out were to set out, and those who had already set out were to halt.
At that time, having seen this, the Wheel-Turning Sage King leaped for joy and said:
"This Treasure of the Military Commander is truly an auspicious sign for me; I am now truly a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
This constitutes the accomplishment of the seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning Sage King. As for the four divine virtues:

first, he possesses longevity and does not die prematurely, such that none can equal him; second, his body is robust and free from ailment, such that none can equal him; third, his countenance is upright and handsome, such that none can equal him; fourth, his treasuries are overflowing with wealth, such that none can equal him. These are the seven treasures and four virtues accomplished by a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
At that time, after a long interval, the Wheel-Turning Sage King ordered his carriage to go out for an excursion to the rear garden, and he addressed his charioteer:
"You must drive with skill and care. Why is this so?..."
"I wish to observe closely the people of the land to see if they are at peace and free from affliction.
At that time, the people of the country who were watching by the roadside spoke again to their attendants:
"You must walk slowly; we wish to observe closely the majestic countenance of the Holy King."

At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage King nurtured the people and all creatures with compassion, as a father loves his children; the citizens admired the king as children look up to their father. They offered all their rare and precious treasures to the king, praying that he would graciously accept them and bestow them as he saw fit.
At that time, the king replied, "Stop! O people!"

"I have my own treasures; you may use them for yourself. When the Wheel-Turning Sage King governed this Jambudvīpa, the ground was level and even, free of thorns, pits, hollows, or mounds. There were no mosquitoes, gadflies, bees, scorpions, flies, fleas, snakes, vipers, or wicked insects. Stones, sand, tiles, and rubble naturally sank away, while gold, silver, and precious jewels appeared upon the earth. The four seasons were harmonious, being neither cold nor hot. The ground was soft and supple, devoid of dust and filth; it was as smooth as if anointed with oil, pure and lustrous, without any impurity.

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King governs the world, the earth is likewise: springs of water gush forth from the ground, pure and inexhaustible; soft grasses grow there, evergreen through both winter and summer; trees are lush and flourishing, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The ground produces soft grass, the color of a peacock’s throat, fragrant like the *vārṣika* flower, and as supple as celestial raiment. When one treads upon the ground, it sinks four inches; when the foot is lifted, it returns to its original state without any hollow remaining. There is naturally non-glutinous rice, free of husks and chaff, complete with all flavors.
At that time there was a fragrant tree, its flowers and fruits flourishing; when the fruit ripened, it split open spontaneously, emitting a natural fragrance whose scent was rich and pervasive.
Furthermore, there are clothing trees with abundant flowers and fruits; when their fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of garments.
There are also adornment trees with flourishing flowers and fruits; when their fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of ornaments.
Furthermore, there are garland-trees with abundant flowers and fruit; when the fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of garlands.
There are also vessel-trees with abundant flowers and fruit; when the fruit ripens, the rinds split open of their own accord, producing various kinds of vessels.
Furthermore, there are fruit trees with abundant flowers and fruits; when their fruits ripen, the rinds split open of their own accord, yielding various kinds of fruit.
There are also musical instrument trees with abundant flowers and fruits; when their fruits ripen, the rinds split open of their own accord, yielding a multitude of musical instruments.

"When a Wheel-Turning Sage King rules the world, the Dragon King Anavatapta rises after midnight to produce great dense clouds that fill the entire world and send down heavy rain. Like the time it takes to milk a cow, he rains down water of eight flavors; its moisture is pervasive and universal, yet there is no standing water on the ground, nor any mud. Moistening and saturating everything, it causes grasses and trees to grow."

It was just as when a garland-maker sprinkles water upon a flower garland to make the flowers fresh and lustrous, preventing them from withering; the nourishing moisture of the timely rain was likewise so.

Furthermore, at a certain time after midnight, when the sky was clear and bright, free from the obscuration of clouds, a cool breeze rose from the sea—pure, harmonious, and gentle—which, upon touching the body, produced bliss.
When the Sage-King ruled, the five grains of this Jambudvīpa were abundant and cheap; the population was flourishing, and wealth and treasures were so plentiful that there was no lack of anything.

At that time, the Wheel-Turning Sage-King governed the country with righteousness and without oppression, practicing the ten virtuous deeds; likewise, the people at that time also cultivated right view and were endowed with the ten virtuous deeds.
After a long time, that king developed a grave illness and passed away.
At that time, he was like a musician who, having eaten slightly too much, felt a slight discomfort in his body and then died, being reborn in the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, the Jewel of the Woman, the Jewel of the Householder, the Jewel of the Military Commander, and the officials and citizens of the kingdom performed music and dance to bury the body of the Holy King.

The king’s Jewel of the Woman, Jewel of the Householder, Jewel of the Military Commander, and the officials and citizens of the realm bathed the king’s body with fragrant water; they wrapped it in five hundred layers of fine cotton cloth, wrapping it in successive layers as prescribed, and lifting the king’s body, they placed it within a golden coffin and poured scented oil over it before setting it inside an iron outer casket.

Furthermore, he encased the exterior with a wooden coffin and layered heavy garments over it; then, having piled up various fragrant woods and layered them upon the body, he performed the cremation. At the crossroads, he erected a stupa made of the seven treasures, one yojana in length and breadth, adorned with variegated colors and fashioned from the seven precious gems.
Each of the four sides of that stūpa has one gate, surrounded by railings made of the seven precious substances.

The open space on the four sides of the stūpa measures five yojanas in length and breadth. There are sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees. The golden wall has silver gates; the silver wall has golden gates; the lapis lazuli wall has crystal gates; the crystal wall has lapis lazuli gates; the red pearl wall has agate gates; the agate wall has red pearl gates; and the musāragalva wall has gates of various jewels.

As for its railings: there were golden railings with silver crossbars, silver railings with golden crossbars, crystal railings with lapis lazuli crossbars, lapis lazuli railings with crystal crossbars, red pearl railings with agate crossbars, agate railings with red pearl crossbars, and musaragalva railings with crossbars of various jewels.

Beneath the golden lattices hung silver bells; beneath the silver lattices hung golden bells; the lapis lazuli lattices hung crystal bells; the crystal lattices hung lapis lazuli bells; the red pearl lattices hung agate bells; the agate lattices hung red pearl bells; and the musaragalva lattices hung bells made of various jewels.

The gold trees had silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees had gold leaves, flowers, and fruits; the lapis lazuli trees had crystal flowers and leaves; the crystal trees had lapis lazuli flowers and leaves; the red pearl trees had agate flowers and leaves; the agate trees had red pearl flowers and leaves; and the musaragalva trees had flowers and leaves made of various jewels.
The walls of those four gardens further have four gates, surrounded by railings.

Moreover, upon the walls there are pavilions and jeweled terraces; on all four sides of the walls are groves of trees and gardens, with flowing springs and bathing pools where various flowers grow. The trees are lush and flourishing, the fruits and blossoms are abundant, a myriad fragrances waft about, and exotic birds warble plaintively.

Once the stupa was completed, the Jewel of the Woman, the Jewel of the Householder, and the Jewel of the Military Commander, along with all the officials and citizens of the entire nation, came to make offerings to this stupa. They bestowed gifts upon the poor and needy: providing food to those who needed food, clothing to those who needed clothing, and precious elephant and horse carriages to satisfy the needs of the multitude, giving whatever they desired according to their wishes.
Such are the matters concerning the majestic power and meritorious virtues of a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
[End of] Volume XVIII of the *Dīrgha Āgama* Spoken by the Buddha.
[Beginning of] Volume XIX of the *Dīrgha Āgama* Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Section Four: The Chapter on Hells, Part Four of the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*. Chapter Four: The Chapter on Hells.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Surrounding these four continents from the outside are eight thousand continents; surrounding those eight thousand continents is a great ocean of water; and surrounding that great ocean of water is a great mountain of diamond."

Outside of Mount Vajra, there is a second Great Vajra Mountain; between these two mountains, it is profound and dark, such that even the gods of the sun and moon, despite their great power, cannot cause their light to reach that place.
There are eight great hells; each of these great hells has sixteen minor hells.

The first great hell is named Sañjīva (Reviving); the second is Kālasūtra (Black Rope); the third is Saṃghāta (Crushing); the fourth is Raurava (Screaming); the fifth is Mahāraurava (Great Screaming); the sixth is Tapana (Heating); the seventh is Pratāpana (Great Heating); and the eighth is Avīci (Uninterrupted).

In that Saṃjīva Hell there are sixteen minor hells, each minor hell measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. The first minor hell is named Black Sand; the second, Boiling Excrement; the third, Five Hundred Nails; the fourth, Hunger; the fifth, Thirst; the sixth, Single Copper Cauldron; the seventh, Many Copper Cauldrons; the eighth, Stone Mill; the ninth, Pus and Blood; the tenth, Measuring Fire; the eleventh, Ash River; the twelfth, Iron Balls; the thirteenth, Adze and Axe; the fourteenth, Jackals and Wolves; the fifteenth, Sword Trees; and the sixteenth, Cold Ice.
"What is meant by the Hell of Conceptualization (Saṃjīva)?

The sentient beings therein grow iron claws upon their hands; these claws are long and sharp. Filled with mutual rage and harboring thoughts of malice, they tear at one another with their claws; as soon as the flesh falls away with each stroke, they imagine themselves dead.
A cold wind then blows, the skin and flesh regenerate, and they immediately revive and stand up."
They think to themselves,
"I am now alive," while other sentient beings say:
"I think you are alive. Because of this perception, it is called the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.

Furthermore, in the Saṃjīva Hell, the sentient beings therein harbor thoughts of malice and harm one another, provoking each other to conflict. They seize natural swords and blades; these weapons are so sharp that they hack and stab one another, flaying, peeling, and carving the flesh until their bodies are shattered upon the ground. They perceive themselves as being dead; yet—
A cold wind blows, and his skin and flesh are restored; he soon revives and stands up.
He thinks to himself: "I am now alive."
Other sentient beings say,
"I think you are alive.
For this reason, it is called the Saṃjñā Hell (the Hell of Perception).

"Furthermore, in the Saṃjīva Hell, the sentient beings therein harbor thoughts of malice and harm toward one another; they provoke and harass each other, seizing swords and blades with their hands—blades that are extremely sharp—and together they hack and stab, flaying, peeling, and carving each other into pieces, imagining themselves to be dead.
When a cold wind blows upon them, their skin and flesh grow back, and they immediately revive and stand up."
He says of himself,
"I am alive," while other sentient beings say:
"I think you are alive. For this reason, it is called the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.

Furthermore, in the Saṃjīva Hell, the sentient beings harbor thoughts of malice toward one another and harass each other in turn. They grasp oil-soaked blades; these blades are extremely sharp, and they hack, stab, flay, and carve one another, thinking they have died.
A cold wind blew upon him, and his skin and flesh were restored; he soon revived and stood up.
He said to himself, "I am alive!"
Other sentient beings say,
"I think you are alive.
For this reason, it is called the Saṃjñā Hell (the Hell of Perception).

"Furthermore, in the Saṃjīva Hell, the sentient beings therein harbor thoughts of malice and harm toward one another, repeatedly harassing each other. Grasping small knives with blades so sharp they cut and pierce one another, flaying, peeling, and carving each other's flesh; they imagine themselves dead.
Then, a cold wind blows upon them, their skin and flesh grow back, and they immediately revive and stand up."
He says to himself,
"I am alive," while other sentient beings say:
"I think you are still alive.
For this reason, it is called the Hell of Thought (Āpāyika).

After the sentient beings therein have long endured their retributions, they emerge from the Hell of Thought and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection; yet, drawn by their past transgressions, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Black Sand Hell.

At that time, a hot wind suddenly arose, blowing hot black sand that struck his body; his entire frame became as black as a dark cloud. The hot sand scorched his skin, penetrating through the flesh to the very bone. Within the bodies of these offenders, black flames burst forth, swirling around their bodies before re-entering within them, causing them to endure various agonies as they were burned, seared, and consumed by the heat.
Due to the causes and conditions of their offenses, they undergo this bitter retribution; because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they are prevented from dying.

Having suffered for a long time here, they emerge from the Black Sand Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection. Yet, led by their past karma, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Boiling Excrement Hell.

In that hell, boiling excrement and iron balls naturally appear before them; the sinners are driven and coerced to embrace the iron balls, which burn their hands and arms, reaching up to their heads and faces, leaving no part unscathed.

Furthermore, they are made to seize and grasp [the food], which is then placed in their mouths; it burns their lips and tongues, passing from the throat down to the abdomen, penetrating through until there is nothing that is not scorched and rotted.
There are iron-beaked insects that gnaw and devour the skin and flesh, penetrating to the bone and reaching the marrow; the suffering is bitter and acrid, and the distress is immeasurable.
Because their retribution is not yet exhausted, they do not yet die.
"Having long suffered in the Boiling Excrement Hell, they emerge from it and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection, until they reach the Iron Nail Hell."

Having arrived, the hell-wardens throw him down, pinning him supine upon a bed of hot iron; they stretch out his body and drive nails into his hands, his feet, and his heart, until five hundred nails have covered his entire body. In bitter agony and excruciating pain, he wails and groans.
As their remaining retribution was not yet exhausted, they did not die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerged from the Iron Nail Hell and fled in terror, seeking rescue and protection, until they reached the Hungry Ghosts Hell.
The wardens of hell came and asked,
"What do you seek by coming here? They replied:

"I am hungry. Upon this, the wardens immediately seize him and throw him onto a glowing red-hot iron plate, stretching out his body. They hook open his mouth with iron hooks and place a red-hot iron ball inside. It sears his lips and tongue, passing from the throat down to the belly; everything it touches is scorched and consumed without exception. In bitter agony and intense suffering, he wails and weeps piteously.
As their remaining karma was not yet exhausted, they did not die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerged from the Hungry Hell and, fleeing in terror and seeking rescue and protection, arrived at the Thirsty Hell.
The hell-wardens asked,
"What do you seek by coming here? They replied:
"I am thirsty.

The hell-warden immediately seizes him and throws him onto a red-hot iron plate, stretching out his body. He hooks open his mouth with a red-hot iron hook and pours molten copper into it; it burns his lips and tongue, passing from the throat down to the belly, penetrating through until nothing remains unscorched or rotted. In bitter agony and intense suffering, he wails and cries out in lamentation.
As their remaining karma was not yet exhausted, they did not die.

After suffering for a long time, they emerged from the Thirsty Hell (Kṣut-tṛṣṇā-naraka) and fled in terror, seeking rescue and protection; yet, drawn by their past transgressions, they arrived suddenly and unconsciously at the Copper Cauldron Hell (Tāmra-sthālī-naraka).

The hell-wardens, with eyes blazing with rage, seize the feet of the offenders and cast them headlong into the cauldron. As the water surges and boils, they are whirled up and down; from the bottom to the rim, and from the rim to the bottom, or sometimes in the belly of the cauldron, their bodies are boiled until they are completely decomposed.

It is like boiling beans: as they surge and boil with the broth, turning back and forth, rotting from both within and without; so too it is for the sinner in the cauldron, who follows the broth up and down, wailing and crying out in grief as ten thousand poisons assail him all at once.
Because their remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, they do not die.

After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Copper Cauldron Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection; yet, drawn by their past offenses, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Many Copper Cauldrons Hell.

The Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. The hell-demons, with eyes blazing with rage, seize the feet of the offenders and cast them headlong into the cauldrons. As the boiling water surges and seethes, they are tossed up and down, revolving from the bottom to the mouth and from the mouth to the bottom; sometimes they remain within the belly of the cauldron, their entire bodies rotting and disintegrating.

It is like boiling beans; as they surge and boil with the broth, turning upward and downward, they become thoroughly decomposed both inside and out. The sinners in the cauldron are just the same: carried up and down by the broth, from the mouth to the bottom and from the bottom to the mouth; sometimes their hands and feet appear, sometimes their waists and bellies, and sometimes their heads and faces. The hell-wardens hook them with iron hooks and place them into other cauldrons, where they wail and cry out in bitter, agonizing torment.
Because their remaining retribution is not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die.

After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Hell of Many Copper Cauldrons and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection; however, dragged by their past karmic retribution, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Stone Grinding Hell.

The Stone Grinding Hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. The hell-wardens, filled with great rage, seize the offenders and throw them onto hot stones; they stretch out their hands and feet and press heavy, scorching stones upon their bodies, turning and grinding them until their flesh and bones are pulverized, pus and blood flow forth, and they suffer excruciating agony, wailing in bitter lamentation.
Because their remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, they do not die.

After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Stone Grinding Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection; yet, dragged by the retribution of their past deeds, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Pus and Blood Hell.

The Pus-and-Blood Hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Within this hell, pus and blood emerge spontaneously, boiling and surging forth. The sinners run hither and thither within it; the boiling, hot pus and blood scald their bodies, causing their hands, feet, heads, and faces to all become putrid and ruined. Furthermore, they take up the pus and blood to eat themselves;

it scalds their lips and tongues, passing from the throat down to the belly, penetrating through until nothing remains uncorrupted. The bitter poison and acrid pain are such that the various torments are difficult to endure.
Because their remaining offenses were not yet exhausted, they were not permitted to die.

After suffering for a long time, they finally emerged from the Pus and Blood Hell; terrified and frantic, they ran about seeking rescue and protection, but drawn by their past karma, they suddenly and unknowingly arrived at the Measuring Fire Hell.
The Mānava Hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Within this hell, there is a great mass of fire that spontaneously appears before one.

Its flames are fiercely blazing, and the hell-wardens, filled with rage, drive the offenders forward. Holding iron measures in their hands, they compel them to measure the mass of fire. As they measure the fire, it burns their hands and feet and spreads throughout their entire bodies; tormented by such bitter heat and pain, they groan and wail aloud.
Because their remaining retribution for past offenses was not yet exhausted, they were not permitted to die.

After enduring suffering for a long time, they finally emerged from the Hell of Measuring Fire; terrified and fleeing in haste, seeking rescue and protection, they were nonetheless drawn by the牵引 (karmic attraction) of their past karma and, without realizing it, suddenly arrived at the Hell of the Ash River.

The Hell of the Ash River (Kṣāranadī) is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and five hundred yojanas in depth. Ashy hot water surges and boils, emitting foul vapors that billow and swirl; the crashing waves produce a terrifying roar from the bottom to the surface. Iron spikes, eight inches long and sharp-pointed, cover the ground from bottom to top. Along the banks grow swords and blades, and on both sides stand hell-wardens, foxes, and wolves. Furthermore, upon the banks stands a forest of sword-trees, whose branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all swords and blades with edges eight inches long.

The sinners enter the river, rising and falling with the waves, tossing about and sinking; iron spikes pierce their bodies, penetrating them from both inside and out, causing their skin and flesh to rot and decay as pus and blood flow forth. Their suffering is manifold, and they wail with bitter lamentation.
Because their remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, they are not permitted to die.
After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Ash River Hell and reach its bank; there, sharp swords upon the shore slice and pierce their bodies, maiming and destroying their hands and feet.
At that time, the hell-wardens asked the sinners,
"Having come here, what do you seek? The sinners replied:
"We are hungry! the prisoners cry.

The wardens immediately seize them and throw them onto glowing red-hot iron, stretching out their bodies. With iron hooks, they pry open their mouths and pour molten copper into them; it burns their lips and tongues, passing from the throat down to the belly, penetrating through until there is nothing that is not scorched and rotted.
Furthermore, there are jackals and wolves with long, sharp teeth that come to bite the offenders, devouring their flesh raw.

Thus, after the offenders have been boiled in the River of Ashes, pierced by sharp spikes, and had molten copper poured into their mouths, they are devoured by the jackals and wolves; they then immediately scramble up the Sword Trees (*asipattravana*). When climbing the Sword Trees, the blade-edges point downward; when descending the Sword Trees, the blade-edges point upward. As they grasp with their hands, their hands are severed; as they tread with their feet, their feet are severed. The sword-blades pierce their bodies, penetrating through from the outside to the inside; skin and flesh fall away, pus and blood flow out, until finally only white bones remain, held together by tendons and veins.

At that time, there were iron-beaked birds atop the sword-trees that pecked at their skull bones until they broke, devouring their brains; thus, they suffered bitter and acrid agony, wailing and crying out in grief.
Because their remaining offenses were not yet exhausted, they were not allowed to die.

They returned once more to enter the Ash River Hell (*Kṣāranadī-naraka*), where they were tossed up and down by the waves, overturned and submerged. Iron thorns pierced their bodies, penetrating from both inside and out; their skin and flesh rotted away, and pus and blood flowed out until only white bones floated on the surface. When a cold wind blew upon them, their muscles and flesh were restored, and they immediately stood up. In a state of panic, they fled in all directions seeking rescue and protection, but dragged along by the retribution of their past deeds, they unknowingly and suddenly arrived at the Iron Ball Hell (*Ayoguḍa-naraka*).

The Iron Ball Hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Once the offenders have entered, hot iron balls spontaneously appear before them. The hell-wardens drive them forward and seize them; their hands and feet are scorched and ruined, and their entire bodies burst into flames. They wail in bitter agony as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, they are not permitted to die.

After suffering for a long time, they eventually emerge from the Iron Ball Hell and flee in terror, seeking refuge and protection; yet, dragged by their past karmic retributions, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Axe and Hatchet Hell.

The Hell of Axes and Hatchets is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Once the offenders have entered this hell, the wardens, filled with rage, seize these sinners and hurl them onto glowing red-hot iron. With heated iron axes and hatchets, they split their hands, feet, ears, noses, and bodies; the suffering is so bitter and acrid that they wail and shriek in lamentation.
As their remaining karma was not yet exhausted, they did not die.

After suffering for a long time, they emerged from the Hell of Axes and Hatchets, fleeing in terror and seeking rescue and protection; however, drawn by their past transgressions, they were unaware that they had suddenly arrived at the Hell of Jackals and Wolves.

The Śṛgāla-wolf Hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Once the offenders have entered, swarms of śṛgāla wolves come vying with one another to seize and tear them; they gnaw and bite, dragging and pulling them about until the flesh falls away and the bones are wounded, with pus and blood flowing forth. Their suffering is manifold, and their lamentations are bitter and agonizing.
Because their remaining karmic retributions were not yet exhausted, they were not permitted to die.

After suffering for a long time, they finally emerged from the Śṛgāla-vyāghra hell and fled in terror, seeking refuge and protection; yet, drawn by their past karma, they suddenly and unconsciously arrived at the Sword-Tree Hell.

The Sword-Tree Hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. When sinners enter that forest of sword-trees, a great violent wind arises and blows, causing the leaves of the sword-trees to fall upon their bodies; when they strike their hands, the hands are severed, and when they strike their feet, the feet are severed, such that there is no part of their body, head, or face that is not wounded and destroyed.
There is an iron-beaked bird that perches upon their heads and pecks at their two eyes; they endure ten thousand forms of agony, wailing with bitter and piercing cries.
Because their remaining retribution is not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die.

"Having endured suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Sword-Tree Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection; yet, led by their past transgressions, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Cold-Ice Hell."

The Cold Ice Hell is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth; once the offenders have entered it, a great cold wind blows upon their bodies, causing their entire frames to freeze and blister until their skin and flesh fall away. In bitter agony and distress, they wail and cry out, and only then do they die.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The Black Rope Great Hell has sixteen minor hells surrounding it on all sides; each is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, extending from the Black Rope Hell to the Cold Ice Hell.”
For what reason is it called the Black Rope Hell?

Its wardens seize those offenders and throw them onto glowing-hot iron; they stretch out their bodies and mark them straight with hot iron cords. Following the lines of the cords, they hack with hot iron axes, slicing the offenders into hundreds and thousands of pieces. It is just as a craftsman marks wood with a cord and follows the lines with a sharp axe to cut it into hundreds and thousands of segments.
The punishment of those sinful persons is likewise such that their bitter suffering and agony are beyond measure;
yet, because their remaining retribution is not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die.
This is called the Black Rope Hell.

Furthermore, the wardens of the Black Rope Hell seize those offenders and throw them onto hot iron; they stretch out their bodies and mark them with iron cords before sawing them apart. Just as a craftsman marks wood with a cord and then saws it, so too are those offenders treated; their bitter and agonizing pain is beyond measure.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra*).

Furthermore, in the Black Rope Hell, the wardens seize those offenders and throw them onto hot iron, stretching out their bodies. They place hot iron cords upon their bodies, which burn through the skin and penetrate the flesh, scorching the bones and boiling the marrow. The bitter and acrid agony is beyond measure.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is named the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra-naraka*).

Furthermore, the wardens of the Black Rope Hell suspend countless hot iron ropes, intersecting one another, and drive the offenders to walk between them. A violent, evil wind suddenly arises and blows against the iron ropes, which fall upon their bodies, burning through the skin and penetrating the flesh, scorching the bones and boiling the marrow. Their agonizing sufferings are manifold and beyond calculation.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
hence it is named Black Rope (*Kālasūtra*).

Furthermore, the wardens of the Black Rope Hell drive the offenders with garments made of hot iron rope, which burn through the skin and penetrate the flesh, scorching the bones and boiling the marrow. Their agonizing sufferings are manifold and beyond calculation.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is named the Black Rope Hell.

After those offenders have long endured suffering there, they emerge from the Black Rope Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection. Yet, dragged by their past karma, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Black Sand Hell, and so on, until they reach the Cold Ice Hell; thereafter, their lives end in the same manner.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Crushing Great Hell has sixteen minor hells surrounding it on all sides, each measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth."
Why is it called the Crushing Hell?

Within this hell there are great stone mountains that stand facing one another. When the offenders enter between them, the mountains spontaneously close together, crushing their bodies until their flesh and bones are ground to powder. The mountains then return to their original positions, much like throwing a piece of wood against another, which rebounds and separates; the punishment of these offenders is likewise such, involving myriad forms of bitter torment beyond measure.
Because their remaining offenses have not yet been exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Crushing Hell (Samghāta).

Furthermore, in the Crushing Hell there are great iron elephants with bodies ablaze with fire, which come roaring and trample upon the offenders, rolling over them until their bodies are crushed to pieces and pus and blood flow forth. They suffer bitter and acrid agony, wailing and crying out in grief.
Because their remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is named "Crushing" (Tuiya).
Furthermore, as for the hell-wardens within the Crushing Hell:

They seize various criminals and place them within grinding stones; they grind them with the stones until their bones and flesh are pulverized and their pus and blood flow out, enduring bitter and agonizing suffering beyond all measure.
Because their retribution for the sins has not yet been exhausted, they are not allowed to die;
thus it is named "Crushing" (Duiya).

Furthermore, the wardens of the Crushing Hell seize those sinners and lay them upon a great stone, pressing them down with another large stone. Their bones and flesh are ground to pulp, pus and blood flow out, and they endure bitter, acrid agony as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, this place is named "Crushing.

Furthermore, the wardens of the Crushing Hell seize those offenders and lay them within iron mortars, pounding them from the feet to the head with iron pestles until their skin and flesh are ground to pulp and pus and blood flow out. Their suffering is bitter and acrid, as ten thousand poisons assail them all at once.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is named "Crushing.

After those offenders have long endured suffering, they emerge from the Crushing Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection. Yet, led by their past karma, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Black Sand Hell, and so on until the Cold Ice Hell; thereafter, their lives end, and it is likewise for each subsequent realm.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The Great Hell of Screaming is surrounded on all sides by sixteen minor hells, each measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.”
For what reason is it called the Hell of Screaming?

Its wardens seize those sinners and hurl them into large cauldrons where boiling hot water surges and seethes, cooking the sinners as they wail and scream in bitter agony; ten thousand poisons assail them all at once.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is called the Hell of Screaming (*Raurava*).

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Hell of Screaming seize those offenders and cast them into large iron cauldrons where boiling hot water surges and seethes, cooking the offenders as they wail and scream in bitter, piercing agony.
Because their remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, they do not die;
therefore, it is called the Hell of Screaming (*Raurava*).

Furthermore, in the Hell of Screaming, the various hell-wardens seize those offenders and place them within large iron cauldrons where boiling hot water surges and seethes, cooking the offenders as they wail and shriek in bitter agony and distress.
Because their remaining retributions for past sins are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is called the Hell of Screaming (*Raurava*).

Furthermore, in the Hell of Screaming, the various hell-wardens seize those sinners and cast them into small cauldrons where hot water surges and boils, cooking the sinners as they wail and shriek in bitter, acrid agony.
Because their remaining karmic offenses have not yet been exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is called the Hell of Screaming (*Raurava*).

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Hell of Screaming seize those offenders and cast them onto great griddles, where they are repeatedly scorched and broiled, wailing and screaming in bitter agony and distress.
Because their remaining karma has not yet been exhausted, they do not die;
thus, this place is called Raurava (Screaming).

After suffering for a long time, they emerge from the Raurava Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection. Yet, dragged by their past karmic retributions, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Kālasūtra Hell, and so on, until they reach the Arbuda (Icy) Hell, where they remain until the end.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Great Screaming Hell has sixteen minor hells surrounding it on all sides.
For what reason is it named the Great Screaming Hell?"

The various hell-wardens seize those sinners and place them inside great iron cauldrons; as the boiling hot water surges and seethes, it cooks the sinners, who wail and shriek, crying out in great distress, their suffering and bitterness so intense that ten thousand poisons assail them at once.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is named the Hell of Great Wailing (Mahāraurava).

Furthermore, in the Hell of Great Wailing, the various hell-wardens seize those offenders and hurl them into large iron cauldrons where boiling hot water surges and seethes, cooking the offenders. They wail and shriek with great cries, suffering bitter and acrid agony as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is called the Hell of Great Screaming.

Furthermore, the wardens of the Great Screaming Hell seize those sinners and place them inside iron cauldrons where boiling hot water surges and seethes. They cook the sinners therein, who wail and shriek in agony; the bitter poison of suffering is so intense that ten thousand poisons strike at once.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is named the Great Screaming Hell (*Mahāraurava*).

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Great Screaming Hell seize those offenders and throw them into small cauldrons where boiling hot water surges and seethes, cooking the offenders until they wail and scream, crying out in great distress. As bitter pain and anguish assail them like ten thousand poisons at once, it is called the Great Screaming Hell.

"Furthermore, in the Great Screaming Hell, the various hell-wardens seize those offenders and cast them upon a great griddle, roasting them repeatedly from both sides. They wail and shriek, crying out in great lamentation; their suffering is bitter and acrid, as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously."
Because their remaining offenses have not yet been exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
thus it is named the Great Screaming Hell.

After suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Great Screaming Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection. Yet, dragged by their past karmic retributions, they do not realize that they have suddenly arrived at the Black Sand Hell, and so on, until they reach the Cold Ice Hell, whereupon their lives come to an end.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Great Hell of Burning and Roasting (Tapana) is surrounded on all sides by sixteen minor hells. For what reason is it named the Great Hell of Burning and Roasting?"

At that time, the hell-wardens placed the sinners within an iron city; the city blazed with fire, glowing red both inside and out, scorching and roasting the sinners until their skin and flesh were singed and rotted away. Their suffering was bitter and acrid, as ten thousand poisons converged upon them all at once.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Hell of Burning and Roasting.

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Hell of Burning and Roasting lead those offenders into an iron chamber. That chamber is ablaze with fire, glowing red both inside and out, scorching and roasting the offenders until their skin and flesh are charred and rotten. Their suffering is bitter and acrid, as if ten thousand poisons were to strike them all at once.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Hell of Burning and Roasting.

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Hell of Burning and Roasting seize those offenders and place them upon iron towers. These towers are ablaze, glowing red both inside and out, roasting and burning the offenders until their skin and flesh are scorched and putrefied. Their suffering is bitter and acrid, and ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, they do not die;
for this reason, it is called the Hell of Burning and Roasting (*Tapana*).

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Hell of Burning and Roasting seize those offenders and hurl them into large iron cauldrons. These cauldrons are ablaze with fire, glowing red both inside and out, roasting and scorching the offenders until their skin and flesh are charred and putrid. Their suffering is bitter and acrid, as if ten thousand poisons were to strike them all at once.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Hell of Burning and Roasting.

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Hell of Burning and Roasting seize those offenders and hurl them onto great iron griddles. These griddles are ablaze with fire, glowing red both inside and out, burning and roasting the offenders until their skin and flesh are scorched and putrefied. Their suffering is bitter and acrid, as if ten thousand poisons were to strike them all at once.
Because their remaining offenses have not yet been exhausted, they are not allowed to die.

After suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Hell of Burning and Roasting; terrified and frantic, they run about seeking rescue and protection. Yet, drawn by the power of their past karma, they do not realize that they have suddenly arrived at the Hell of Black Sand, and so on through to the Hell of Cold Ice, where their lives finally end—just as it was before.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Great Hell of Scorching Heat has sixteen minor hells surrounding it on all sides, each measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth."
What is called the Great Roasting Hell?

There, the hell-wardens place the sinners within an iron city. That city is ablaze, glowing red both inside and out, roasting and scorching the sinners with intense heat. Their skin and flesh are singed and mangled; they suffer bitter pain as ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Great Roasting Hell (*Mahātapana*).

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Great Roasting Hell take the offenders into iron chambers. These chambers are ablaze with fire, glowing red both inside and out, roasting and burning the offenders. They undergo intense roasting and burning until their skin and flesh are scorched and putrefied; their suffering is bitter and acrid, as if ten thousand poisons were to strike them all at once.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Great Roasting Hell (Mahātapana).

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Great Roasting Hell seize those offenders and place them upon iron towers. These towers are ablaze with fire, glowing red both inside and out, roasting and scorching the offenders. Under this intense roasting and scorching, their skin and flesh are singed and putrefied, and they endure bitter, acrid pain as if ten thousand poisons were attacking them simultaneously.
Because their remaining offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
therefore, it is called the Great Roasting Hell (*Mahātapana*).

Furthermore, the various wardens of the Great Roasting Hell seize those offenders and place them inside a great iron cauldron. The fire within the cauldron blazes so that both its interior and exterior are glowing red, roasting and scorching the offenders. Under this intense roasting and scorching, their suffering is bitter and acrid, and ten thousand poisons assail them simultaneously.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die; for this reason, it is called the Great Roasting Hell (*Mahātapana*).

Furthermore, within the Great Roasting Hell there spontaneously appears a great fire pit with fiercely blazing flames. On both banks of the pit are great mountains of fire. The hell-wardens seize those offenders and impale them upon iron forks, setting them upright in the midst of the fire to roast their bodies. They are roasted intensely and repeatedly until their skin and flesh are scorched and putrefied. Their suffering is bitter and acrid, and ten thousand poisons assail them all at once.
Because their remaining karmic retribution is not yet exhausted, they do not die.

After suffering for a long time, they finally emerge from the Great Roasting Hell and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection. Yet, dragged by their past karma, they unknowingly and suddenly arrive at the Black Sand Hell, and so on until the Cold Ice Hell; only then does their life end, and it is likewise so in each case.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The Avīci Great Hell has sixteen minor hells surrounding it on all sides, each measuring five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.”
What is meant by the Avīci Hell?

There, the hell-wardens seize those offenders and flay their skin from foot to crown; they then wrap that very skin around the offender's body, place them upon a fiery chariot wheel, and swiftly drive the chariot back and forth over the glowing iron ground. Their bodies are crushed and mangled, their skin and flesh fall away, and they endure bitter, agonizing pain as ten thousand poisons assail them all at once.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are prevented from dying; for this reason, it is called the Avīci (Uninterrupted) Hell.

Furthermore, the Great Avīci Hell has a great iron city. On its four sides, great fires break out: flames from the east reach the west, flames from the west reach the east, flames from the south reach the north, flames from the north reach the south, flames from above reach below, and flames from below reach above. The blazing flames swirl and turn without any intervening space. The offenders are within them, running hither and thither, their bodies scorched and roasted until their skin and flesh are charred and putrefied. Their suffering is bitter and acrid, as if ten thousand poisons were to strike at once.
Because their remaining karmic retributions are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, within the Great Avīci Hell there is an iron city where fires blaze forth intensely. The offenders are inside, and the flames lick their bodies until their skin and flesh are scorched and rotted away; the pain and bitterness are extreme, as if ten thousand poisons were to strike them all at once.
Because their remaining karmic offenses are not yet exhausted, they are prevented from dying;
for this reason, it is called the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, when the sinners within the Great Avīci Hell have remained there for a long time, the gates finally open, and those sinners rush toward them.
As he runs, flames issue forth from all his limbs and joints, just like a strong man carrying a great torch of dry grass while running against the wind, its flames blazing fiercely.
When the sinner flees, it is likewise so.

As he runs toward the gate, the gate closes of its own accord; the sinner stumbles and falls upon the ground of glowing red-hot iron, which sears and roasts his body until his skin and flesh are scorched and putrefied. His suffering is bitter and acrid, as if ten thousand poisons were to strike him all at once.
Because their remaining karmic offenses are not yet exhausted, they are not permitted to die;
for this reason, it is called the Avīci Hell (the Uninterrupted Hell).

Furthermore, as for the offenders within the Avīci Hell, whatever they behold with their eyes, they see only foul colors; whatever they hear with their ears, they hear only foul sounds; whatever they smell with their noses, they smell only foul odors; whatever they touch with their bodies, they encounter only painful sensations; and whatever they think of with their minds, they contemplate only unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, for these sinners, there is not even a moment’s respite from suffering during the blink of an eye; therefore, it is called the Avīci Hell (the Uninterrupted Hell).

After the sentient beings therein have long endured their suffering, they emerge from Avīci and flee in terror, seeking rescue and protection. Yet, dragged by their past karmic retributions, they do not realize that they have suddenly arrived at the Black Sand Hell, and so on, until they reach the Cold Ice Hell, whereupon their lives end; it is likewise in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If one performs unwholesome deeds with the body, And likewise with speech and mind,
One shall fall into the Saṃjīva Hell, Trembling with fear, the hair on one's body standing on end."
If one harbors evil intentions toward one’s parents, the Buddha, or the śrāvakas,
one will fall into the Black Rope Hell, where the suffering is beyond description.
Merely committing the three unwholesome deeds and failing to cultivate the three wholesome practices [leads to such a fate].
Falling into the Saṃghāta Hell, their suffering is beyond description.
Those who harbor malice and poison, whose hands are stained with the blood of killing,
and who commit various evil deeds, fall into the Raurava Hell.
Constantly practicing various wrong views, Enveloped by the net of craving,
They commit these base and vile deeds, And fall into the Great Howling Hell.
Constantly performing acts of burning and roasting, They burn and roast all sentient beings.
Falling into the Hell of Burning and Roasting, one suffers burning and roasting through the long night.
Having abandoned the karma of virtuous fruits and the pure path of virtuous fruits,
one performs various base and evil deeds and falls into the Great Hell of Burning and Roasting.
These are the most grievous of sinful deeds, karmic acts that inevitably lead to rebirth in the evil realms;
one falls into the Avīci Hell, where the suffering endured is beyond measure.
There are the Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra hells, as well as the two hells of Saṃghāta and Raurava.
Saṃjīva and Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta and Raurava, Mahāraurava and Tāpana, Pratāpana,
And Avīci as the eighth— these eight great hells are ablaze with the color of fire.
Due to the calamities of past evils, there are sixteen minor hells.
