The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Between those two great Vajra Mountains, a great wind arises called Aṅka. If this wind were to come here to these four continents and the eight thousand continents, it would blow this great earth and all the famous mountains, including Sumeru, the king of mountains, ten *li* or even a hundred *li* off the ground, causing them to fly through the air and be utterly pulverized."
It is like a strong man grasping light chaff in his hand and scattering it into the air;
even if a great wind were to come and blow across this world, it would be just the same.
Because these winds are blocked by two great adamantine mountains, they do not come.
Bhikṣus! You should know that these adamantine mountains provide great benefit, and they are also brought about by the karmic retribution of sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the wind between those two mountains is blazing and fiercely hot; if that wind were to come here to these four continents, all the sentient beings, mountains, rivers, oceans, grasses, trees, and forests therein would surely wither and dry up."
It is just as when fresh, moist grass is cut during the height of summer and placed in the sun; it withers and dries up immediately.
Such is the nature of that wind; if it were to come to this world, its scorching heat would likewise consume and parch everything in this manner.
Because these two vajra mountains obstruct this wind, it is prevented from coming.
Bhikṣus! You should know that these vajra mountains provide great benefit, and they are also the result of the karmic retribution of sentient beings' actions.
"Furthermore, the wind between those two mountains is foul-smelling and impure, pungent, filthy, and acrid; were it to reach this world, it would cause all these sentient beings to lose their sight."
Because these two great adamantine mountains obstruct this wind, it is prevented from coming.
Bhikṣus! You should know that these adamantine mountains bring about much benefit, and they are also the result of the karmic retribution of sentient beings’ actions.
Furthermore, between those two mountains there are ten additional hells:
first, Thick Cloud; second, Cloudless; third, Ha-ha; fourth, How-Alas; fifth, Bleating Sheep; sixth, Sugandhika; seventh, Utpala; eighth, Kumuda; ninth, Puṇḍarīka; and tenth, Padma.
What is the Thick Cloud Hell?
In that hell, the bodies of the offenders are produced spontaneously, resembling thick clouds; therefore, it is named Thick Cloud.
Why is it called Cloudless?
The sentient beings who undergo punishment within that hell are born with bodies that naturally resemble lumps of flesh; therefore, it is named "Cloudless" (Anabhraka).
Why is it named "Ha-ha"?
The sentient beings undergoing punishment within that hell experience such piercing agony that they all cry out "he-he";
therefore, it is named He-he. Why is it named Na-ai?

The sentient beings undergoing punishment within that hell endure such piercing and agonizing suffering that they have no refuge; they all cry out, "What can be done? (nàhē), and for this reason it is named Nàhē.
Why is it named "Ram's Cry"?

The sentient beings undergoing punishment within that hell experience such piercing agony that when they wish to raise their voices to speak, their tongues cannot move; their cries are as straight and simple as the bleating of sheep, and for this reason it is called the "Ram-Howling" Hell.
Why is it called *sugandhika*?
Within that hell, the entire prison is black, like the color of the *sugandhika* flower;
therefore, it is named *sugandhika*. Why is it called *utpala*?
In that hell, the entire region is blue, like the *utpala* flower; therefore, it is named *Utpala*.
Why is it named *Kumuda*?
In that hell, the entire region is red, with the color of the *kumuda* flower; therefore, it is named *Kumuda*.
Why is it called Puṇḍarīka?
Because within that hell, the entire prison is white, like the color of the puṇḍarīka flower;
therefore, it is named Puṇḍarīka. Why is it called Padma?
"In that hell, the entire prison is crimson, like the color of the *padma* flower; therefore, it is named 'Padma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
'Suppose there were a granary with a capacity of sixty-four *hu*, filled to the brim with sesame seeds. Suppose a person were to live for a hundred years..."
Take away a single sesame seed; when they are thus exhausted, one has still not finished receiving their retribution in the Ghanodadha (Thick Cloud) Hell.
Twenty lifespans in the Ghanodadha Hell equal one lifespan in the Atapa (Cloudless) Hell;
twenty lifespans in the Atapa Hell equal one lifespan in the Hahava Hell; and twenty lifespans in the Hahava Hell [equal one lifespan in the next hell].
A lifespan in the Nahe Hell is equal to one [lifespan] in the [preceding] hell; twenty lifespans in the Nahe Hell are equal to one lifespan in the Ram-Howling (Eḍamūka) Hell;
twenty lifespans in the Ram-Howling Hell are equal to one lifespan in the Sūcīndra Hell;
and twenty lifespans in the Sūcīndra Hell are equal to one lifespan in the Utpala Hell.
Regarding the lifespans in the hells: twenty lifespans in the Utpala hell are equal to one lifespan in the Kumuda hell;
twenty lifespans in the Kumuda hell are equal to one lifespan in the Puṇḍarīka hell;
and twenty lifespans in the Puṇḍarīka hell are equal to one lifespan in the Padma hell.
Twenty lifespans in the Padma Hell constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*); twenty such intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).
Within the Padma Hell, the flames are fiercely blazing; even when a sinner is a hundred *yojanas* away from the fire, they are already scorched by its heat.
At sixty yojanas away, both his ears were already deaf, and he could hear nothing;
at fifty yojanas away, both his eyes were already blind, and he could see nothing more.
The bhikṣu Kokālika, having harbored an evil mind and slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, at the dissolution of his body after death, fell into this Padma Hell.
At that time, the Brahma King spoke this verse:
“When a man is born, an axe is in his mouth;
it is by means of evil speech that he cuts himself.”
To praise those who should be censured, and to censure those who should be praised—
this is an evil karma of speech, for which the body shall suffer its retribution.
To acquire wealth through technical skills involves only slight transgression.
To slander the worthy and the noble is a most grievous sin.
For a lifespan of a hundred thousand *anabhraka* heavens and forty-one *bṛhatphala* heavens,
one who slanders the sages shall suffer this calamity, because of the evil committed by mind and speech.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That Brahmā spoke these verses as words of truth, which were approved by the Buddha. Why is this so? Because—"
I, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, also speak this meaning:
"When a person is born, an axe is in his mouth;
it is by means of evil speech that he cuts himself."
To praise those who should be censured, and to censure those who should be praised—this is an evil karma of speech, for which one receives retribution in the body.
To acquire wealth through technical skills carries but slight fault; however, [the fault of such verbal karma is far greater].
To slander the noble and holy is a most grievous sin.
For a lifespan of one hundred thousand *anabhraka* heavens and forty-one *abhasvara* heavens,
one who slanders the sages shall suffer such calamity, due to the evil wrought by mind and speech.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Within the Great Vajra Mountains to the south of Jambudvīpa lies the palace of King Yama, the seat of his governance, measuring six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its city has sevenfold walls, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees; even up to the countless birds singing together in harmony, it is just as described before."
However, three times each day and night, a great copper cauldron spontaneously appears before King Yama.
When the cauldron emerges from within the palace, the king becomes terrified upon seeing it and retreats outside the palace.
If the cauldrons were moved outside the palace, the King would see them and be struck with fear, abandoning them to enter within the palace.

There are great hell-wardens who seize King Yama and lay him upon hot iron; they pry open his mouth with iron hooks and pour molten copper into it, burning his lips and tongue, passing from the throat down to the belly, penetrating through until nothing remains unscorched or rotted.
"Once they have finished undergoing their retribution, they will again enjoy themselves together with various court ladies.
It is the same for those ministers who likewise received blessings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There are three messengers. What are the three?
First is old age; second is illness; third is death.
There are sentient beings who commit evil with their bodies, speak evil with their mouths, and harbor evil thoughts in their minds; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into hell.”
The hell-wardens lead this sinner before King Yama; having arrived, they say:
"This person was summoned by the celestial messengers; we pray that Your Majesty will interrogate him thoroughly."
The king asked the criminal,
"Did you not see the first messenger?
The criminal replied:
“I have not seen such a person.
The King spoke again, saying:

“When you were among men, did you ever see an old man with white hair and fallen teeth, whose vision was dimming, whose skin was wrinkled and flesh sagging, who walked bent over with a staff, groaning as he went, his body trembling and his strength failing?”
"Do you see this person?
The sinner replied, "I see him."
The King spoke again, saying:
"Why do you not reflect for yourself:
'I, too, am like this'?"
That person replied, "At that time,
I was negligent and did not realize it myself.
The king spoke again:
"You were negligent yourself; you failed to cultivate your body, speech, and mind, nor did you reform your evils to follow the good. Now I shall cause you to know the suffering of negligence.
The King further declared:

"The punishment you now receive is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor of Śakra Devendra, nor of your ancestors, nor of your friends, servants, or messengers, nor is it the fault of śramaṇas or brahmins."
"You have committed evil yourself; you shall now receive its retribution for yourself.
At that time, after King Yama had questioned the offender regarding the first divine messenger, he further questioned the offender regarding the second divine messenger, saying:
"How is it that you did not see the second divine messenger?"
He replied, "I have not seen him.
The king asked again:

"When you were formerly a human being, have you ever seen people who were gravely ill and suffering, lying upon beds and mats in a place reeking with excrement and urine? Their bodies lay there, unable to rise or move; they required others for food and drink; their hundred joints ached and pained, and as they wept and groaned, they were unable to speak."
"Do you see this? He replied, "I see it."
The king replied again:
"Why do you not reflect for yourself:
'I, too, shall likewise experience such suffering from illness'?"
The sinner replied, "At that time,
I was negligent and did not realize it myself.
The King spoke again:
"You were yourself negligent and failed to cultivate your body, speech, and mind, nor did you reform your evils to follow the good; now I shall cause you to know the suffering of negligence.
The King further declared:

"The punishment you now receive is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor the fault of Śakra Devendra, nor your ancestors, nor your friends, servants, or messengers, nor the fault of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"You committed evil yourself; you now receive the fruit thereof.
Then, after King Yama had questioned the offender with the second divine messenger, he questioned him again with the third divine messenger, saying:
"Why did you not see the third divine messenger?"
He replied, "I did not see it.
The king asked again:

"When you were formerly a human being, have you ever seen a person die, their body destroyed at the end of life, with all the sense faculties forever extinguished, the body stiff and upright like a withered tree, abandoned in a cemetery to be devoured by birds and beasts, or placed in a shroud or coffin, or burned with fire?"
"Do you see this? The sinner replied,
"I truly see it."
The king replied again:
"Why do you not reflect for yourself:
'I too shall die; I am no different from him'?"
The sinner replied, "At that time,
I was negligent and did not realize it myself.
The king spoke again:
"You were negligent yourself; you failed to cultivate your body, speech, and mind, nor did you reform your evil ways to follow the good. Now I shall cause you to know the suffering of negligence.
The King further declared:

"The punishment you now receive is not the fault of your parents, nor the fault of your brothers, nor that of the Lord of Devas, nor your ancestors, nor your friends, servants, or messengers, nor the fault of śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas."
"You committed evil yourself; you now receive the consequences yourself.
At that time, King Yama, having interrogated him thoroughly regarding the three divine messengers, immediately handed him over to the hell-wardens.
At that time, those hell-wardens immediately led the offenders to the Great Hell; that Great Hell was one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and one hundred yojanas deep below.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In the four directions there are four gates, The streets and alleys all correspond with one another;
The prison walls are made of iron, And above they are covered with iron nets."
With iron for its lower ground, natural flames burst forth;
extending a hundred yojanas in length and breadth, it stands firm and unshakable.
Black flames and smoke billow upward, so fiercely blazing they are difficult to behold.
"There are sixteen minor hells, where the fire blazes due to one's evil deeds.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, King Yama thought to himself:"

"The sentient beings of the world are deluded and ignorant; they commit evil deeds with their bodies, and evil with their speech and minds. When their lives subsequently come to an end, there are few who do not undergo this suffering."

If sentient beings in the world can reform their evils and cultivate good conduct through body, speech, and mind, they will experience happiness after the end of their lives, just like those celestial deities.

If, when my life comes to an end, I am reborn among human beings and should encounter a Tathāgata, I shall shave off my hair and beard within the True Dharma, don the three dharma-robes, leave the household life to practice the Way, and with pure faith cultivate the pure holy life. Having accomplished what was to be done and severed the cycle of birth and death, I shall realize it for myself in this present life and not undergo further existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Though one has seen the divine messenger, If one still remains negligent,
That person will always harbor sorrow And be born in a lowly and base place."
If there is a person of wisdom who beholds the messengers of the devas,
they will draw near to the Dharma of the Noble Ones and not become heedless.
Seeing the fear inherent in rebirth, arising from birth, old age, sickness, and death, they remain vigilant.
Without grasping, there is liberation; birth, old age, sickness, and death are exhausted.
One attains the state of peace and security, realizing the unconditioned in the present;
having crossed over all sorrows and fears, one is certain to enter parinirvāṇa.
Chapter 5: On Dragons and Birds. The Buddha spoke the *Lokadhātu-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, the fourth part of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Chapter Five: On Dragons and Birds. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of dragons."
What are the four? First, birth from eggs; second, birth from a womb; third, birth from moisture; and fourth, birth by transformation. These are the four kinds.
There are four kinds of garuḍas. What are the four? First, those born from eggs;
second, those born from wombs; third, those born from moisture; and fourth, those born by transformation. These are the four kinds.

Beneath the waters of the great ocean lies the palace of the Naga King Sāgara, eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its palace walls are sevenfold, with seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of decorative nets, and seven rows of trees surrounding it in solemn adornment; all are composed of the seven precious substances, and even the countless birds singing in harmony is likewise so.

Between Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, and Mount Khadiraka, there are the palaces of the two dragon kings, Nanda and Upananda. Each palace is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth; their walls are sevenfold, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven precious gems, even down to the countless birds singing together in harmony, which is likewise the case here.
"On the northern shore of the great ocean there is a great tree named Kūṭaśālmali, which is shared by the dragon kings and the garuḍas.
The circumference of its base is seven yojanas, its height is one hundred yojanas, and its branches and leaves spread fifty yojanas in all four directions."

To the east of this great tree are the palaces of the egg-born Nāga kings and the egg-born Garuḍas; each of these palaces is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Their palace walls are sevenfold, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven precious gems, even down to the countless birds singing together in harmony, which is likewise the case here.

To the south of the Kūṭaśālmali tree are the palaces of the womb-born dragon kings and the womb-born garuḍas. Each of these palaces is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Their palace walls are sevenfold, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures. Even up to the countless birds singing together in harmonious lamentation, it is likewise so.

To the west of the Kūṭaśālmali tree are the palaces of the moisture-born nāgas and the moisture-born garuḍas; each palace is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Their walls are sevenfold, with seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of jeweled nets, and seven rows of trees surrounding them, all adorned and fashioned from the seven precious gems. Even up to the countless birds singing in harmony, it is exactly as described before.

To the north of the Kūṭaśālmali tree are the palaces of the spontaneously born Nāga King and the spontaneously born Garuḍa; each of these palaces is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Their palace walls are sevenfold, with seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of jeweled nets, and seven rows of trees surrounding them, all adorned and fashioned from the seven precious substances. Furthermore, it is likewise that countless birds there warble in harmony with one another.

"When a golden-winged garuḍa born from an egg wishes to seize and eat a nāga, it flies down from the eastern branch of the Kūṭaśālmalī tree and strikes the great ocean with its wings; the waters part for two hundred yojanas, and it seizes and eats the egg-born nāgas at will and with ease. However, it cannot seize nāgas that are womb-born, moisture-born, or transformation-born."

"When a garuḍa born from a womb wishes to seize and eat a nāga born from an egg, it flies down from the eastern branch of the tree and strikes the great ocean with its wings; the ocean waters part to the left and right for two hundred yojanas, and it takes the egg-born nāga to eat it at its own will and pleasure."

When a garuḍa born from an egg wishes to eat a dragon born from an egg, it flies down from the southern branch of the tree and strikes the waters of the great ocean with its wings, parting the waters to a distance of four hundred yojanas on both sides; it then seizes and eats the egg-born dragons as it pleases and with complete mastery, yet it cannot seize and eat dragons born from moisture or by transformation.

"When a moisture-born garuḍa wishes to eat an egg-born nāga, it flies down from the eastern branch of the tree and strikes the great ocean with its wings; the ocean waters part for two hundred yojanas on both sides as it seizes and eats the egg-born nāga at its own will."

When a moisture-born garuḍa wishes to eat a womb-born nāga, it flies down from the southern branch of the tree and strikes the waters of the great ocean with its wings; the ocean waters part for four hundred yojanas, and it seizes and eats the womb-born nāga at its own will and pleasure.

When a moisture-born garuḍa wishes to eat a moisture-born nāga, it flies down from the western branch of the tree and strikes the waters of the great ocean with its wings, parting the sea on both sides for eight hundred yojanas; it then seizes and eats the moisture-born nāga at its own will and pleasure, yet it is unable to seize and eat a transformation-born nāga.

"When a *nirmāṇakāya* garuḍa wishes to eat an egg-born dragon, it flies down from the eastern branch of the tree and strikes the waters of the great ocean with its wings; the ocean waters part for two hundred *yojanas*, and it seizes the egg-born dragon to eat it at its own will."

When a magically born garuḍa wishes to eat a womb-born nāga, it flies down from the southern branch of the tree and strikes the waters of the great ocean with its wings; the ocean waters part for four hundred yojanas on both sides, and it seizes the womb-born nāga to eat it at its own will and ease.

When a magically born garuḍa wishes to eat a moisture-born nāga, it flies down from the western branch of the tree and strikes the waters of the great ocean with its wings; the ocean waters part to a distance of eight hundred yojanas, and it seizes the moisture-born nāga to devour it.

When a magically born garuḍa wishes to eat a magically born nāga, it flies down from the northern branch of the tree and strikes the waters of the great ocean with its wings; the ocean waters part to the left and right for sixteen hundred yojanas, and it seizes the magically born nāga to eat it at its own will and ease.
These are the dragons who are eaten by the garuḍas.
Furthermore, there are great dragons whom the garuḍas cannot catch.
Which ones are they?

The Dragon King Sāgara, the Dragon King Nanda, the Dragon King Upananda, the Dragon King Airāvata, the Dragon King Suparṇa, the Dragon King Ālu, the Dragon King Karkoṭaka, the Dragon King Gopāla, the Dragon King Aparājita, the Dragon King Ghaṇṭa, the Dragon King Gopaṇṭa, the Dragon King Anavatapta, the Dragon King Susthira, the Dragon King Uśanasapāda, and the Dragon King Takṣaka—all these great dragon kings are not seized and devoured by garuḍas; furthermore, any dragons who dwell in their vicinity are likewise not seized and devoured by garuḍas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there are sentient beings who uphold the dragon precepts, direct their minds toward the dragons, and fulfill the dharma of the dragons, they will be reborn among the dragons."
If there are sentient beings who uphold the precepts of the garuḍa, direct their minds toward the garuḍa, and fulfill its dharma, they will be reborn among the garuḍas.
Or if there are sentient beings who uphold the precepts of the hare-owl, direct their minds toward the hare-owl, and fulfill its dharma, they will fall among the hare-owls.

If there are sentient beings who observe the dog-vow, or the cow-vow, or the deer-vow, or the mute-vow, or the Maṇibhadra-vow, or the fire-vow, or the moon-vow, or the sun-vow, or the water-vow, or the vow of making fire-offerings, or who observe the defiled practices of asceticism, they form this thought:

"I observe these mute-practices, Maṇibhadra-practices, fire-practices, sun-and-moon-practices, water-practices, fire-offering-practices, and various ascetic practices; by means of these merits, I desire to be reborn in heaven."
“This is a false view,” the Buddha said.
“I declare that such a person with false views will certainly go to one of two places: either they will be born in hell, or they will fall into the four modes of birth.”
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and such a view:
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false;
the self and the world are impermanent; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The self and the world are finite: this is true, all else is false;
the self and the world are infinite: this is true, all else is false;
the self and the world are both finite and infinite: this is true, all else is false."
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
This life-principle is the same as this body; this alone is true, all else is false.
This life-principle is one thing and the body is another; this alone is true, all else is false."
"It is neither that there is a life-principle nor that there is no life-principle;
this alone is true, all else is false. There is neither a life-principle nor a body;
this alone is true, all else is false. Or someone might say:
"There is such a self after death; this alone is true, all else is false. Others say:
"There is no such self after death; this alone is true, all else is false."
Or some say: "It is thus and it is not thus that one dies; this alone is true, and all else is false.
Again, they say:
“‘It is neither existent nor non-existent; such is the state after death; this alone is true, all else is false.

If those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas hold such a doctrine and such a view, asserting that ‘the world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false,’ they do so because they possess within their conditioned formations the view of self, the view of a life-principle, the view of a body, and the view of the world.
Therefore, they speak thus: ‘The self and the world are eternal.’”
Those who speak of impermanence hold views of a self, a life-principle, a body, and a world regarding the conditioned formations; therefore, they say:
"The self and the world are impermanent."
Those who say that it is both eternal and non-eternal are practicing the view of a self, the view of a life-principle, the view of a body, and the view of a world; therefore they say:
"The world is both eternal and non-eternal."

When he says that it is neither eternal nor non-eternal, it is because he holds views of a self, views of a life-principle, views of a body, and views of a world regarding conditioned phenomena; therefore, he says:
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal."

“When he says, ‘The self and the world are finite,’ he holds views regarding the formations (saṃskāra) such as the view of a self, the view of a life-principle (jīva), the view of a body (kāya), and the view of the world. He says:

‘The life-principle is finite, the body is finite, and the world is finite; from the first conception until the cemetery, this body composed of the four great elements (mahābhūta) thus transmigrates for at most seven births. When the formations of body and life are exhausted, I enter the pure assembly.’”
Therefore, he says: "The self is finite.

As for those who say that the self and the world are infinite, they possess views of a self, views of a life-principle, views of a body, and views of a world regarding conditioned formations; thus they speak:
"Lifespan is boundless and the body is boundless.

The world is boundless; from the initial conception in the womb until the final resting place in the cemetery, this body composed of the four great elements thus transmigrates for up to seven births. When the activities of body and life are exhausted, I shall enter the pure assembly."
This person says:
"The self and the world are infinite.
That person speaks thus:
"This world is finite or infinite.
In this regard, he holds views regarding formations: the view of a self, the view of a life-principle, the view of a body, and the view of the world:

"The life-principle is finite or infinite; from the initial conception until the cemetery, this physical body composed of the four great elements thus transmigrates for up to seven births; when the formations of body and life are exhausted, I enter the pure realm."
Therefore, he says: "I am both finite and infinite. He speaks thus:
"I hold that the world is neither finite nor infinite.
Within these formations, one holds the view of self, the view of a life-principle, the view of a body, and the view of the world, thinking:

"The life-principle and the body are neither finite nor infinite; from the initial conception until the cemetery, this physical body composed of the four great elements thus transmigrates for up to seven births. When the formations of body and life are exhausted, I enter the pure assembly."
Therefore, it is said:
"I am neither finite nor infinite.
As for those who say "the life-principle is the same as the body," they hold the view that there is a life-principle in this body and a life-principle in other bodies; therefore, it is said:
"The life-principle is the same as the body.
To say that "the life-principle is different from the body" means that one holds the view that there is a life-principle in this body, but no life-principle in other bodies; therefore, it is said:
"The life-principle is different from the body."

When he says that the body and life are neither existent nor non-existent, it is because he holds the view that there is no life in this body, yet holds the view that there is life in other bodies; therefore, he says:
"neither existent nor non-existent."
When he says there is no life-principle (*jīva*), this refers to the view that this body is without a life-principle and the view that other bodies are without a life-principle; therefore, he says:
"There is no life-principle and no body."
When he says, "There is such a thing as this death," it is because that person sees that while there is life now, there will later be another body and life through which one wanders;
therefore, he says, "There is such a thing as this death."
Regarding the statement "there is no such thing as death in this way": he says that there is life in this world, but no life in the next world;
therefore, he says, "there is no such thing as death in this way."

Regarding the statement, "There is such a self after death, yet there is no such self after death": he says that while the life of this world is cut off and extinguished, the life of the next world continues on;
therefore, he says, "There is such a life after death, yet there is no such life after death."

Regarding the statement, "He dies in such a way that he neither exists nor does not exist": this refers to the claim that both the present body and life are annihilated, and the subsequent body and life are also annihilated;
therefore it is said, "He dies in such a way that he neither exists nor does not exist."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In the distant past, there was a king named Ādarśamukha (Mirror-Face). At that time, he gathered those born blind together in one place and said to them:
'You who were born blind, do you know what an elephant is like?'"
He replied: "Great King! I did not recognize him; I did not know him."
The King spoke again, saying:
"Do you wish to know what his form and appearance were? They replied:
"I wish to know," they said.
At that time, the king immediately commanded his attendants to bring the elephant so that the blind men might feel it with their own hands.

Among them, one who felt the trunk said, "This is the elephant. Another who felt the tusks said so; another who felt the ears; another who felt the head; another who felt the back; another who felt the belly; another who felt the thighs; another who felt the shoulders; another who felt the feet; and another who felt the tail. To each of them, the king spoke:
"This is an elephant. Then, King Ādarśamukha withdrew the elephant and asked the blind son,
"What kind of thing is an elephant?"

Those blind sons who had grasped the elephant’s trunk said the elephant was like a curved yoke; those who had grasped its tusks said it was like a pestle; those who had grasped its ears said it was like a winnowing basket; those who had grasped its head said it was like a cauldron; those who had grasped its back said it was like a mound; those who had grasped its belly said it was like a wall; those who had grasped its thighs said it was like a tree; those who had grasped its shoulders said it was like a pillar; those who had grasped its footprints said it was like a mortar; and those who had grasped its tail said it was like a rope.

Each disputing with the others and mutually asserting right and wrong, saying "this statement is thus" and "that statement is not so," they did not cease their talk and eventually came to blows and strife.
At that time, seeing this, the king laughed with great joy.
Then, King Ādarśamukha spoke these verses:
“A multitude of blind people have gathered here, vying with one another in dispute.”
"The elephant's body was originally a single entity; it is through the arising of diverse characteristics that 'is' and 'is not' are produced.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The various non-Buddhist heterodox teachers are also like this. Not knowing the Truth of Suffering, nor the Truth of Origination, the Truth of Cessation, or the Truth of the Path, they each give rise to divergent views and mutually judge one another as right or wrong. Claiming themselves to be right, they then engage in disputes and litigation."

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are able to know, as it truly is, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering, they will reflect upon themselves, dwell in mutual harmony, share the same experience, follow the same teacher, and blend like water and milk, causing the Buddha-dharma to flourish and abide in peace for a long time.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"If a person does not know suffering, Does not know the origin of suffering,
And likewise does not know the place Where suffering can be brought to total cessation,"
Furthermore, they are unable to know the cessation of suffering, its origin, and the path;
they lose the liberation of mind and lose the liberation by wisdom.
Unable to fathom the root of suffering, they do not understand the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
If one can truly know suffering, Know the origin from which suffering arises,
And also know that place where suffering is utterly extinguished,
Furthermore, if one can skillfully discern The Noble Path that leads to the cessation of the accumulation of suffering—
Thus one attains liberation of mind, and likewise liberation through wisdom.
Such a person can thoroughly exhaust the root of the aggregate of suffering,
ending birth, old age, sickness, and death— the very source of existence.

“Monks! Therefore, you should diligently apply skillful means to contemplate the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.”
The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra, Volume Nineteen. The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra, Volume Twenty.
Translated during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian.
Chapter Six: The Asuras, Part Four of the *Lokasthāna-sūtra*. Chapter Six: The Asuras. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“Beneath the great ocean waters to the north of Mount Sumeru lies the city of the Rāhu-asuras. It is eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. This city has sevenfold enclosures, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around its perimeter and composed of the seven treasures. The city wall is three thousand yojanas high and two thousand yojanas wide.”

The city gates were one thousand yojanas high and one thousand yojanas wide; the golden walls had silver gates, and the silver walls had golden gates, and so on, until even the countless birds singing in harmony was likewise the case.

The small city governed by that Asura King, situated within the great city, is named Cakravāṭa; it is sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. The city has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around its perimeter and composed of the seven precious jewels. The city wall is three thousand yojanas high and two thousand yojanas wide.

The city gates were two thousand yojanas high and one thousand yojanas wide; the golden walls had silver gates, and the silver walls had golden gates, and so on, until even the countless birds singing in harmony was likewise the case.

Within that city, a separate council hall was established named Saptaśrīṣa. Its walls were sevenfold, with seven rows of railings, seven layers of nets, and seven rows of trees surrounding it, all exquisitely adorned and composed of the seven precious gems. The foundation of the council hall was made entirely of musāragalva; its pillars and beams were made entirely of the seven precious gems. The central pillar of the hall had a circumference of one thousand yojanas and a height of ten thousand yojanas. Beneath this pillar stood the Seat of the True Dharma (Saddharmāsana), measuring seven hundred yojanas in length and breadth, carved with intricate patterns and composed of the seven precious gems.

The hall has four doors and is surrounded by railings; there are seven tiers of terraces and pavilions, with seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of decorative nets, and seven rows of trees, all adorned all around and composed of the seven precious substances. Even so, the various birds sing together in harmony, just as described before.

To the north of that assembly hall is the palace of the asuras, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures; even down to the countless birds singing together in harmony, it is likewise so.

To the east of that council hall is a grove named Śāla, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is enclosed by sevenfold walls, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven precious substances; even down to the countless birds singing in harmony and melodiously, it is exactly as described before.
To the south of that council hall is a grove named Supreme Excellence, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, like the Śāla Grove.
To the west of that council hall is a grove named Śyāmā, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, also like the Śāla Grove.
To the north of that council hall is a grove named Nandana, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth, resembling the Śāla grove.

Between the Śāla and the Atimuktaka groves grows a pārijāta tree; its trunk is seven yojanas in circumference and it rises a hundred yojanas high, with branches and foliage spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.

There are seven layers of tree walls, seven layers of railings, seven layers of jeweled nets, and seven rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures; even the countless birds singing in harmony with one another is likewise so.
Furthermore, between the two groves of Śyāmā and Nandana lies the Pāṇḍuka Lake; its waters are cool and refreshing, free from any impurity.

It is surrounded by sevenfold jeweled moats with paved embankments, adorned on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all fashioned from the seven precious gems.

Within that pond, four kinds of flowers grow; each flower and leaf is one yojana in length and breadth, and its fragrance spreads for one yojana as well. Their roots are like the hubs of chariot wheels, and from them flows a sap white in color like milk and sweet in taste like honey, while countless birds sing together in harmony.

Furthermore, along the banks of that pond were pavilions with seven tiers of steps, sevenfold gates and walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned on every side and composed of the seven precious substances; even the countless birds there warbling in harmony was likewise as described above.

"The palaces of that Asura King and his ministers and subordinates measure ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth; some are nine thousand, eight thousand, or as small as one thousand *yojanas*. Their palace walls are sevenfold, with seven layers of railings, seven layers of decorative nets, and seven rows of trees surrounding them, all exquisitely adorned and made of the seven treasures. Even up to the point where countless birds sing together in harmony, it is likewise so."

The palaces of those minor asuras are one thousand, nine hundred, or eight hundred yojanas in length and breadth; even the smallest palace is one hundred yojanas. All of them have sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, adorned all around and composed of the seven treasures. Furthermore, it is likewise that countless birds sing together in harmonious, plaintive melodies.

"To the north of that council hall, there is a staircase made of the seven treasures leading into the palace; furthermore, there is a staircase leading to the Śāla Garden, another leading to the Extremely Wondrous Garden, another leading to the Śyāmā Garden, another leading to the Forest of Joy Garden, another leading to the Jambu Tree, another leading to the Pāṇḍuka Lake, another leading to the palace of the Great Minister, and another leading to the palace of the Lesser Asuras."
When the asura king wishes to go to the Sālavana grove for recreation and sightseeing, he immediately thinks of the asura king Vemacitra; the asura king Vemacitra, in turn, thinks to himself:
"The asura king Rāhu is thinking of me."
He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, surrounded by a vast multitude of attendants, and approached the presence of the Asura King Rāhu, standing to one side.
At that time, the Asura King again thought of the Asura King Prahāsa, and the Asura King Prahāsa thought to himself:
"The King is now thinking of me."
He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, surrounded by a vast multitude of attendants, and approached King Rāhula, standing to one side.
At that time, King Asura again thought of King Śambara Asura, and King Śambara Asura likewise thought to himself:
"Now the King is thinking of me."
He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, surrounded by a vast multitude of attendants, and approached King Rāha, standing to one side.
At that time, the king again thought of the minister Asura. The minister Asura, in turn, thought to himself:
"Now the king thinks of me.
He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, surrounded by a vast multitude of attendants, and went before King Rāgha, standing to one side.
At that time, the king again thought of the minor asura; the minor asura likewise thought to himself, "The king is now thinking of me.
He immediately adorned himself and, together with a great multitude, went before King Rāhu and stood to one side.

At that time, King Rāhula, wearing precious robes and riding in a jeweled chariot, was surrounded before and behind by an immeasurable multitude as he proceeded to the Śāla grove. There arose a natural wind that blew the gates open of their own accord;
there arose a natural wind that blew the ground clean;
and there arose a natural wind that blew flowers onto the ground until they reached the knees.

At that time, after King Rāhu had entered this garden, he enjoyed himself together with [his retinue] for one day, two days, and even up to seven days. Having finished his enjoyment, he returned to his own palace.
Thereafter, his excursions to the most exquisite gardens—the Śyāmā Garden, the Nandana Garden, and others—were likewise of this nature.
At that time, King Rāhu was constantly attended on his left and right by five great asuras:
the first named Dharaka, the second named Vīrabala, the third named Māṇava, the fourth named Mūrdhaga, and the fifth named Vinardana.
These five great asura kings constantly attend and guard him on his left and right.
King Rāhu’s palace is situated beneath the great ocean, with the ocean waters above it, sustained by four winds:
first, the Wind of Abiding; second, the Wind of Sustaining; third, the Wind of Immovability; and fourth, the Wind of Solidity.
He holds the waters of the great ocean suspended in mid-air like floating clouds; ten thousand yojanas away from the palace of the asuras, they never fall.
Such are the karmic rewards, merits, and majestic powers of the King of the Asuras.

**Chapter Seven: The Four Heavenly Kings** The *Lokadhātu-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, the fourth part of the *Dīrgha Āgama* spoken by the Buddha, Chapter Seven: The Four Heavenly Kings. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"To the east of Sumeru, the king of mountains, at a distance of one thousand yojanas, is the city of the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, named Bhadrauttara. It is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. This city has sevenfold walls, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around its perimeter and composed of the seven treasures. Even so, it is likewise filled with countless birds singing together in harmony."

One thousand yojanas to the south of Mount Sumeru is the city of the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, named Sudarśana. It is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. The city has sevenfold walls, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all beautifully adorned and composed of the seven treasures. Furthermore, it is just as described before, with countless birds singing together in harmony.

To the west of Mount Sumeru, at a distance of one thousand *yojanas*, there is the city of the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa, named Cakravāḷa Sudarśana. It is six thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. This city has seven tiers of walls, seven rows of railings, seven layers of nets, and seven rows of trees, all adorned around its perimeter and composed of the seven precious jewels; even the countless birds singing together in harmony is likewise as described before.
One thousand yojanas to the north of Mount Sumeru resides the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa. This king has three cities:
the first is named Bhīṣma, the second Devasaṃmata, and the third Viśvāvasu.

Each is six thousand yojanas in length and breadth; each city has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures, even down to the countless birds singing in harmony, which is likewise the case here.

"To the north of the city of Saṃbhavā there is a grove named Gavyūti-mukha, four thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures; even up to the countless birds singing in harmony with one another is likewise as described."

In the center of the park-city is a pond named Nalini, forty yojanas in length and breadth. Its waters are clear and transparent, free from any impurity. Its banks are lined with embankments made of the seven treasures, adorned on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all fashioned from the seven treasures. Within it grow lotus flowers of blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated colors, whose radiance illuminates half a yojana. Their fragrance wafts for half a yojana; furthermore, the roots of these flowers are as large as chariot hubs, and from them flows a sap white as milk and sweet as honey. Even the countless birds that gather there, singing together in harmony, are likewise so.

"Except for the palaces of the sun and moon, the palaces of all the Four Great Kings are forty yojanas in length and breadth; they have sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, adorned all around and composed of the seven treasures, even down to the countless birds singing in harmony with one another—it is exactly like this."
Those palaces are forty yojanas, twenty yojanas, or at their smallest, five yojanas in length and breadth.

From the city of Saṃjñāya there are jeweled stairways leading to the city of Bhadraśilā; further, stairways lead to the city of Sudarśana, and further stairways lead to the city of Cakravāḍasudarśana; furthermore, stairways lead to the cities of Bhīṣma and Devānām-indra; further, stairways lead to the Gavyūti garden; further, stairways lead to the Nandana lake; and further, stairways lead to the palaces of the ministers of the Four Great Kings.

"When the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa wishes to go to the Caitraratha Garden for recreation, he immediately calls to mind the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra likewise thinks to himself:
'Now King Vaiśravaṇa is calling me to mind.'"

He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, surrounded before and behind by countless gandharva deities, and approached the presence of the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, standing to one side.
At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa again thought of King Virūḍhaka, and King Virūḍhaka likewise thought to himself:
"Now King Vaiśravaṇa is thinking of me."
He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, surrounded before and behind by countless kumbhāṇḍa spirits, and approached the presence of King Vaiśravaṇa, standing to one side.
King Vaiśravaṇa again thought of Virūpākṣa, and Virūpākṣa thought to himself:
"Now King Vaiśravaṇa is thinking of me.
He immediately adorned himself and mounted his precious chariot, surrounded before and behind by countless nāgas and devas, and went before King Vaiśravaṇa, standing to one side.
King Vaiśravaṇa again thought of the ministers of the Four Heavenly Kings, and those ministers of the Four Heavenly Kings likewise thought to themselves:
"Now King Vaiśravaṇa is thinking of us."
He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, with countless devas leading and following him before and behind, as he went before the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa and stood to one side.

At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa adorned himself, donned robes of precious ornaments, mounted a jeweled chariot, and together with countless hundreds of thousands of devas, proceeded to the Gavyūti-mukha Garden.
There is a natural wind that blows the gates open of its own accord;
there is a natural wind that blows upon the ground to make it clean;
there is a natural wind that blows flowers onto the ground until they reach one's knees.
At that time, the king enjoyed himself in the park for one day, two days, and even up to seven days; having finished his excursions and observations, he returned to his own palace.
King Vaiśravaṇa is always attended on his left and right by five great spirit-chiefs:
the first is named Pañcāla, the second Dantura, the third Haimavata, the fourth Takkara, and the fifth Śveta.
"These five spirits constantly follow and attend him as his guardians.
Such are the karmic rewards, merits, and majestic powers of King Vaiśravaṇa.
Chapter 8: The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven From the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the fourth division, the *Lokadhātu-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, Chapter Eight: The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Atop the summit of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, lies the city of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. This city has sevenfold enclosures, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all beautifully adorned and composed of the seven precious jewels. The city is one hundred yojanas high and sixty yojanas wide at the top."

The city gates are sixty yojanas high and thirty yojanas wide; there is one gate every five hundred yojanas. Each individual gate is guarded and protected by five hundred spirits for the sake of the Thirty-three Heavens. The golden walls have silver gates, and the silver walls have golden gates; even up to the countless birds singing together in harmony, it is likewise so.

Within that great city there was another smaller city, sixty thousand yojanas in length and breadth. This city had sevenfold walls, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all beautifully adorned and composed of the seven precious substances. The city wall was one hundred yojanas high and sixty yojanas wide. The city gates were five hundred yojanas apart from one another; each gate was sixty yojanas high and thirty yojanas wide. At each city gate, five hundred spirits stood as sentries by its side, guarding the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

There are cities of gold with gates of silver, cities of silver with gates of gold, cities of crystal with gates of lapis lazuli, cities of lapis lazuli with gates of crystal, cities of red pearls with gates of agate, cities of agate with gates of red pearls, and cities of musaragalva with gates of various jewels.

As for those railings: there were golden railings with silver crossbars, silver railings with golden crossbars, crystal railings with lapis lazuli crossbars, lapis lazuli railings with crystal crossbars, ruby railings with agate crossbars, agate railings with ruby crossbars, and musaragalva railings with crossbars made of various jewels.

Upon those railings were jeweled lattices: beneath the golden lattices hung silver bells; beneath the silver lattices hung golden bells; the lapis lazuli lattices hung crystal bells; the crystal lattices hung lapis lazuli bells; the ruby lattices hung agate bells; the agate lattices hung ruby bells; and the musaragalva lattices hung bells made of various jewels.

As for the gold trees, they have golden roots and branches with silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees have silver roots and branches with golden leaves, flowers, and fruits; the crystal trees have crystal roots and branches with lapis lazuli flowers and leaves; the lapis lazuli trees have lapis lazuli roots and branches with crystal flowers and leaves; the red pearl trees have red pearl roots and branches with agate flowers and leaves; the agate trees have agate roots and branches with red pearl flowers and leaves; and the musaragalva trees have musaragalva roots and branches with flowers and leaves made of various jewels.

These sevenfold walls had four gates, each gate equipped with railings. Above the sevenfold walls were galleries, towers, and pavilions that surrounded them on all sides. There were gardens and bathing pools where various precious flowers grew in a vibrant array of colors. Rows of jewel-trees stood in order, their blossoms and fruits flourishing profusely. Fragrant breezes arose from all directions, delighting the hearts of men. Thousands upon thousands of species of extraordinary birds—wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and other exotic varieties—sang together in harmony.

In the center of that small city lies the palace of the Naga King Elapatra, measuring six thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its palace walls are sevenfold, with seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of jeweled nets, and seven rows of trees surrounding it, all exquisitely adorned and composed of the seven precious gems; even the countless birds singing together in harmonious, plaintive melodies is likewise as described before.

Within that city of Sudarśana is the Hall of the True Dharma (Saddharmasabhā), measuring one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. It is adorned all around with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all fashioned from the seven precious substances.

The foundation of its hall was made entirely of pure gold, covered above with lapis lazuli. The pillars within the hall were ten yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height. Beneath these pillars was spread the imperial throne of the Heavenly Lord, one yojana in length and breadth, interspersed with various colors and fashioned from the seven precious gems. The seat was soft, as supple as celestial raiment, and on both sides of it, to the left and right, were sixteen additional seats.

“The hall has four gates surrounded by railings made of the seven treasures; its stairways and paths are five hundred yojanas in length and breadth. There are sevenfold gate-towers, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all beautifully adorned and made of the seven treasures, even down to the countless birds singing in harmony, which is likewise so.”

To the north of the Hall of Good Vision is the palace of Śakra, extending one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. Its palace walls are sevenfold, with seven rows of railings, seven layers of nets, and seven rows of trees surrounding it in a circular array, all adorned and fashioned from the seven precious gems; even down to the countless birds singing in harmony and lamenting together, it is likewise so.

To the east of the Hall of Good Vision (Sudṛśa) is a grove named Roughness (Karkaśa), measuring one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned on every side with the seven treasures; even down to the countless birds singing in harmony, it is exactly as described before.

In the Coarse and Rough Garden there are two stone mounds adorned with celestial gold; one is named Bhadra and the other Subhadra. Each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and the stones are as soft as celestial garments.

"To the south of the Palace of Good Vision, there is a grove named Citraratha, one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It has sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures; even up to the point where countless birds sing together in harmony, it is likewise so."

Within that garden are two stone mounds composed of the seven precious gems: the first is named Day (Dhava) and the second is named Good Day (Sudhava). Each is fifty yojanas in length and breadth; these mounds are soft, as supple as celestial garments.

To the west of the Hall of Good Vision is a grove named Variegated, measuring one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is enclosed by sevenfold walls, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around its perimeter and composed of the seven treasures; even down to the countless birds singing in harmony, it is just as described before.

Within that garden were two stone mounds: the first named Sudarśana and the second named Anusudarśana. Adorned with celestial gold and composed of the seven precious jewels, each was fifty yojanas in length and breadth. These mounds were soft, as supple as celestial garments.

To the north of the Hall of Good Vision is a grove named Great Joy, measuring one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is enclosed by sevenfold walls, with sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven precious gems; even the countless birds singing in harmony is likewise as described above.

In that garden there were two stone mounds: the first named Nandi and the second named Mahānandi. They were adorned with musāragalva, measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth; these mounds were soft, as supple as celestial garments.

Between the Karkaśa Garden and the Citraratha Garden lies the Nanda Pond, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth. Its waters are clear and transparent, free from any impurity. It is surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of jeweled moats with paved embankments, seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of jeweled nets, and seven rows of trees, all exquisitely adorned and composed of the seven precious gems.
On the four sides of that pond were four stairways, surrounded by railings interspersed with the seven treasures; even so, countless birds sang together in harmony, just as before.

Furthermore, within that pond grow four kinds of flowers—blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated hues such as crimson and pale green—interspersed together. Each flower’s leaves provide shade for one yojana, and its fragrance wafts for one yojana. Its roots are like the hubs of chariot wheels; their sap flows out, white in color like milk and sweet in taste like honey.
On the four sides of that pond there are further groves.

Between the Grove of Various Trees and the Grove of Great Joy, there is a tree named Jambū, seven yojanas in circumference and one hundred yojanas in height, with branches and leaves spreading fifty yojanas in all directions.

Outside the trees was an empty pavilion, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with sevenfold palace walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures; even the countless birds singing in harmony was likewise so.

"The remaining palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are each one thousand yojanas in length and breadth. They have sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around their perimeters and composed of the seven treasures; even up to the countless birds singing in harmony with one another is likewise the same."

Those palaces vary in length and breadth from nine hundred, eight hundred, down to a minimum of one hundred yojanas; they have sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter, even unto the countless birds singing in harmony with one another, which is likewise the case here.

The various celestial palaces of the minor devas are one hundred yojanas in length and breadth; some are ninety or eighty, while the smallest are twelve yojanas. Their palace walls are sevenfold, surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of decorative nets, and seven rows of trees, all composed of the seven precious gems. Even up to the countless flocks of birds singing in harmony with one another, it is likewise so.

"To the north of the Sudarśana Hall, there is a flight of stairs leading to the palace of Śakra; to the east of the Sudarśana Hall, there is a flight of stairs leading to the Pāruṣyaka Grove; furthermore, there is a flight of stairs leading to the Citraratha Grove, another flight of stairs leading to the Miśraka Grove, another flight of stairs leading to the Mahānandana Grove, another flight of stairs leading to the Mahānandana Lake, another flight of stairs leading to the Pārijātaka tree, another flight of stairs leading to the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, another flight of stairs leading to the palaces of the various devas, and another flight of stairs leading to the palace of the Naga King Elāpattra."

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, desires to go for a stroll and sightsee in the Rough and Harsh Garden (Kharasvabhāva-udyāna), he immediately thinks of his ministers of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and those ministers of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately think to themselves:
"Now Śakra is thinking of me."
He immediately adorned himself and mounted a precious chariot, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude before and behind, and approached Śakra; he stood to one side.
Śakra then thought of the other devas, and those devas thought to themselves:
"Now Śakra is thinking of us."
He immediately adorned himself and, accompanied by the hosts of devas, went before Śakra and stood to one side.
Śakra then thought of the nāga king Elapatra, and the nāga king Elapatra likewise thought to himself:
"Now Śakra is thinking of me."

The Dragon King immediately transformed his body to manifest thirty-three heads; each head had six tusks, each tusk had seven bathing pools, each bathing pool had seven great lotus flowers, each lotus flower had one hundred petals, and on each petal were seven jade maidens who played music, sang, and danced upon them with clapping hands.
Then, having performed this transformation, that Nāga King approached Śakra and stood to one side.

At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, adorned with various precious ornaments and garlands upon his body, sat upon the foremost head of the Nāga King Elapatra; on either side of him were sixteen celestial kings, each sitting in succession upon the heads of the Nāgas.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by an incalculable retinue of devas, proceeded to the Kharjūravatī Garden.
A natural wind blew, causing the gates to open of their own accord;
another natural wind blew, sweeping the ground clean.
There was a natural wind that blew the flowers onto the ground; the flowers accumulated until they reached the knees.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, sat at will upon the two stone mounds, Bhadra and Subhadra, while the thirty-three kings each sat in their respective order. Furthermore, there were various devas who were not permitted to attend him as he viewed the gardens and groves, nor were they allowed to enter the park to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
Why is this? It is because their fundamental practices and merits differ.
Furthermore, there are gods who can see the groves but cannot enter them, and thus cannot enjoy the five sensory pleasures together with one another.
Why is this so? It is because their fundamental practices and merits differ.
Furthermore, there are other devas who are able to see and enter [the palace], yet they do not obtain the five sensual pleasures to enjoy together.
Why is this so? It is because their fundamental practices and merits differ.
Furthermore, there are other devas who have attained entry and vision, enjoying themselves with the five desires.
Why is this? It is because their fundamental practices and merits were identical.
"They sported within the gardens, delighting themselves with the five desires for one day, two days, up to seven days; having thus enjoyed themselves, they each returned to their palaces."
It was likewise when Śakra, Lord of the Devas, went to visit the Citraratha Park, the Miśrakāvana Park, and the Nandana Park.
For what reason is it called the Rough and Harsh Garden (Khadiraka-vana)?
When entering this garden, the body becomes coarse and rough.
For what reason is it called the Garden of Painted Pleasure?
Upon entering this garden, various painted colors spontaneously appear upon the body for one's enjoyment.
Why is it called the Grove of Mixture?

Because on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of every month, with the exception of the Apsarases, they release their various court ladies to sport and play in intermingled company with the devaputras; for this reason, it is called the Grove of Mixture.
For what reason is it called the Garden of Great Joy?
Because when one enters this garden, there is entertainment and delight; therefore, it is named Great Joy.
For what reason is it called the Hall of Good Dharma?
Because one contemplates the sublime Dharma within this hall and experiences pure bliss, it is called the Hall of Sublime Dharma (Sudharmā).
Why is it called the Jambu tree?
This tree has a deity named Manda who constantly performs music and dance for his own amusement; therefore, it is called Jambu.
Furthermore, the branches and twigs of that great tree spread out in the four directions, and its flowers and leaves are as luxuriant as a great cloud of jewels; therefore, it is named Pārijāta.
To the left and right of Śakra-devānām-indra, there are always ten great devaputras who follow and attend upon him.
What are these ten? First is named Indrā;

second is named Gopī; third is named Virūḍhaka; fourth is named Virūpākṣa; fifth is named Dhara; sixth is named Brahmā; seventh is named Jīvaka; eighth is named Haimavata; ninth is named Vairūṭya; and tenth is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
Śakra Devānām Indra possesses great supernormal power, and his majestic virtue is such as this.
Among the water flowers esteemed by the people of Jambudvīpa—
namely, the utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, and sugandhika flowers— they are soft, fragrant, and pure.
As for the flowers that grow on land:
the *vimukta* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *pāṭala* flower, the *sumanā* flower, the *vārṣika* flower, and the *kanyā* flower.
The various flowers of the waters and lands in Aparagoyānī, Uttarakuru, Pūrvavideha, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of the garuḍas are likewise so.
In the palaces of the asuras, there are water-born flowers:
the utpala, the padma, the kumuda, and the puṇḍarīka—soft, fragrant, and pure.
Terrestrial flowers:
the *sughosa*, the *utpala*, the *mahotpala*, the *karkarava*, the *mahākarkarava*, the *mandārava*, and the *mahāmandārava*.

The various flowers prized by the Four Heavenly Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, as well as those from both water and land, were likewise so.
“The devas possess ten qualities. What are these ten?
First, they can fly away in infinite numbers.
Second, they can fly back in infinite numbers.”
Third, there is unimpeded departure;
fourth, there is unimpeded arrival;
fifth, the celestial body has no skin, bones, sinews, veins, blood, or flesh.
Sixth, his body is never impure with the discharge of feces or urine.
Seventh, his body never experiences exhaustion.
Eighth, the celestial maidens do not give birth.
Ninth, his celestial eyes do not blink.
Tenth, his body assumes colors according to his will: if he desires blue, it becomes blue; if he desires yellow, it becomes yellow; and red, white, and all other colors appear according to his will.
These are the ten qualities of the devas.
Humans possess seven colors.
What are these seven?
Some are golden in color, some are fire-colored, some are blue, some are yellow, some are red, some are black, and some are the color of Māra.
The seven colors of the devas and asuras are likewise so.
"O bhikṣus! The light of a firefly is not equal to that of a lamp; the light of a lamp is not equal to that of a torch; the light of a torch..."
The brilliance of that [fire] is not equal to the brilliance of accumulated fires;
the brilliance of accumulated fires is not equal to the radiance of the palaces, city walls, necklaces, garments, and bodily colors of the Four Heavenly Kings;
and the radiance of the palaces, city walls, necklaces, garments, and bodily colors of the Four Heavenly Kings is not equal to the radiance of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The radiance of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is not equal to the radiance of the Yāma Heaven;
the radiance of the Yāma Heaven is not equal to the radiance of the Tuṣita Heaven; the radiance of the Tuṣita Heaven is not equal to the radiance of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
the radiance of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is not equal to the radiance of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; [the radiance of] the Paranirmitavaśavartin...
The radiance of Īśvara is not equal to the radiance of the palaces, garments, and bodily colors of the Brahmakāyika devas;
the radiance of the palaces, garments, and bodily colors of the Brahmakāyika devas is not equal to the radiance of the Ābhāsvara devas;
the radiance of the Ābhāsvara devas is not equal to the radiance of the Śubhakṛtsna devas; [the radiance of] the Śubhakṛtsna devas...

The radiance of the Fruitful Heaven (Phalguṇa) does not equal the radiance of the Heaven of Radiant Fruit (Bṛhatphala); the radiance of the Heaven of Radiant Fruit does not equal the radiance of the Heaven of No-Perception (Asaṃjñisattva);
the radiance of the Heaven of No-Perception does not equal that of the Heaven of No-Action (Abhāsvara); the radiance of the Heaven of No-Action does not equal that of the Heaven Without Heat (Atapa);
and the radiance of the Heaven Without Heat does not equal that of the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa). The radiance of the Heaven of Good Vision...
The radiance of the Mahāsudṛśa devas is not equal to that of the Akaniṣṭha devas;
the radiance of the Akaniṣṭha devas is not equal to that of the Kṛtsnāvakrāntika devas; and the radiance of the Kṛtsnāvakrāntika devas is not equal to the radiance of the Buddha.

From the light of fireflies up to the radiance of a Buddha, were all such lights gathered together, they would not equal the radiance of the Truth of Suffering, nor the radiance of the Truths of Origination, Cessation, and the Path.

Therefore, monks! Those who seek light should seek the light of the truth of suffering, the truth of its origin, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path; you should practice in this way.
"The people of Jambudvīpa are three and a half cubits tall; their garments are seven cubits long and three and a half cubits wide.
The people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha are likewise three and a half cubits tall; their garments are seven cubits long and three and a half cubits wide.
The people of Uttarakuru are seven cubits tall; their garments are fourteen cubits long and seven cubits wide, and weigh only one *liang*."
The Asuras are one yojana in height; their robes are two yojanas long and one yojana wide, weighing six *zhū*.
The Four Heavenly Kings are half a yojana in height; their robes are one yojana long and half a yojana wide, weighing half a *liǎng*.
The Trāyastriṃśa gods are one yojana in height; their robes are two yojanas long and one yojana wide, weighing six *zhū*.
The bodies of the gods of the Yāma Heaven are two yojanas in height; their garments are four yojanas long and two yojanas wide, weighing three *zhū*.
The bodies of the gods of the Tuṣita Heaven are four yojanas in height; their garments are eight yojanas long and four yojanas wide, weighing one and a half *zhū*.
The bodies of the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven are eight yojanas in height; their garments are sixteen yojanas long and eight yojanas wide, weighing one *zhū*.

The gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) are sixteen yojanas in height; their robes are thirty-two yojanas in length and sixteen yojanas in width, and weigh half a zhu.
The various heavens above each wear clothing according to their respective bodies.
"The lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa is one hundred years; few exceed this, while most fall short.
The lifespan of the people of Aparagoyānī is two hundred years; few exceed this, while most fall short."
The people of Aparagoyānī have a lifespan of three hundred years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The people of Uttarakuru live for a full thousand years, with no increase or decrease.
The hungry ghosts have a lifespan of seventy thousand years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The lifespan of dragons (*nāga*) and garuḍas is one kalpa, though some may have less.
The lifespan of asuras is one thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings is five hundred celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven have a lifespan of one thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The gods of the Yāma Heaven have a lifespan of two thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The gods of the Tuṣita Heaven have a lifespan of four thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The lifespan of the gods in the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations is eight thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The lifespan of the gods in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations is sixteen thousand celestial years, with few exceeding it and many falling short.
The lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is one kalpa, though there are some for whom it is less.
The lifespan of the Ābhāsvara devas is two kalpas, though there are some for whom it is less.
The lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna devas is three kalpas, though there are some for whom it is less.
The gods of the Fruitful Heaven have a lifespan of four kalpas, though some may have less.
The gods of the Heaven of Non-conception have a lifespan of five hundred kalpas, though some may have less.
The gods of the Heaven of No-Action have a lifespan of one thousand kalpas, though some may have less.
The lifespan in the Atapa Heaven is two thousand kalpas, though some may have less.
The lifespan in the Sudṛśa Heaven is three thousand kalpas, though some may have less.
The lifespan in the Sudarśana Heaven is four thousand kalpas, though some may have less.
The lifespan in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven is five thousand kalpas, though there may be some reduction.
The lifespan in the Ākāśānantyāyatana Heaven is ten thousand kalpas, though there may be some reduction.
The lifespan in the Vijñānānantyāyatana Heaven is twenty-one thousand kalpas, though there may be some reduction.
The lifespan of the gods in the Heaven of No-Perception (Akaniṣṭha) is forty-two thousand kalpas, though some may have less.
The lifespan of the gods in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is eighty-four thousand kalpas, though some may have less.

This defines the extent of sentient beings; this defines the extent of the life-span; this defines the extent of the world; and this defines what is called birth, aging, sickness, and death—the realm of coming and going, the collection of elements and sense-bases.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All sentient beings subsist by means of four kinds of nutriment. What are these four?"
Edible food is the first, contact-food is the second, mental volition-food is the third, and consciousness-food is the fourth.
The food consumed by various sentient beings differs accordingly.
The people of Jambudvīpa take various kinds of cooked rice, parched grain, flour, fish, and meat as solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), and clothing and bathing as smooth-food (ślakṣṇa-āhāra).
The people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha likewise take various kinds of cooked rice, parched grain, flour, fish, and meat as solid food, and clothing and bathing as smooth-food.
The people of Uttarakuru consume only naturally grown non-glutinous rice; they take its celestial flavor as solid food, while clothing and bathing serve as the food of smoothness and refinement.
The nāgas and garuḍas take turtles, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises as their solid food (kavaḍīkārāhāra), and bathing and clothing as their smooth-food (ślakṣṇāhāra).
The asuras take pure solid food as their solid food, and bathing and clothing as their smooth-food.
