The Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven take pure morsel-food as their food of morsels; they take bathing and clothing as their food of fine and smooth sensations.
The various heavens above take the joy and bliss of meditative concentration as their food.
What kind of sentient beings subsist on the food of contact?
Sentient beings born from eggs subsist on the food of contact.
What is the nutriment of mental volition?

There are sentient beings who, by means of the nutriment of mental volition, maintain their existence, develop their faculties, and continue their life-span; this is called the nutriment of mental volition.
What is the nutriment of consciousness?
The sentient beings of the hells and the gods of the formless realm—these are called the nutriment of consciousness.
"The people of Jambudvīpa sustain their lives by means of gold, silver, precious gems, grain, silk, slaves, and servants through cultivation and trade."
The people of Aparagoyānī sustain their livelihood by trading cattle, sheep, and precious gems.
The people of Pūrvavideha sustain themselves by trading grain, silk, and pearls.
The people of Uttarakuru have no marketplaces for trade or commerce by which they sustain themselves.
The people of Jambudvīpa have marriages and social interactions, with men taking wives and women being married.
The people of Aparagoyānī and Pūrvavideha likewise have marriages, with men taking wives and women being married.
The people of Uttarakuru have no marriage; there is no giving or taking of wives among men and women.
However, the nāgas, garuḍas, and asuras do have marriage; there is indeed the giving and taking of wives among their men and women.
The Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and even up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven also have marriage, with men taking wives and women being wedded.
From the heavens above these, there are no longer males or females.
The men and women of Jambudvīpa engage in sexual union, their bodies touching one another to bring about the union of yin and yang.
The people of Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, and Uttarakuru likewise touch body to body to bring about the union of yin and yang.
The nāgas and garuḍas also form yin and yang through the mutual physical contact of their bodies.
The asuras form yin and yang by the proximity of their bodies and through their breath.
It is likewise for the Cāturmahārājika and Trāyastriṃśa devas.
In the Yāma Heaven, they form the union of yin and yang by drawing near to one another;
in the Tuṣita Heaven, they form the union of yin and yang by holding hands;
in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, they form the union of yin and yang by gazing intently at each other.
In the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), there is a temporary manifestation of the union of yin and yang;
from the heavens above this, there is no longer sexual desire.

"If there are sentient beings who commit evil with their bodies, speak evil with their mouths, and harbor evil thoughts in their minds, when their bodies perish and their lives end, their subsequent consciousness ceases and the initial consciousness of the hell realms arises. Due to consciousness, name-and-form arise; due to name-and-form, the six sense bases arise."

There may be sentient beings who commit evil through body, speak evil with their mouths, and harbor evil thoughts in their minds; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall among the animals. Thereafter, the final consciousness ceases and the initial consciousness of an animal arises. Due to consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); due to name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

There may be sentient beings who perform evil deeds with the body, speak evil words with the mouth, and harbor evil thoughts with the mind; when their bodies disintegrate and their lives end, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). Thereafter, the final consciousness ceases and the initial consciousness of a hungry ghost arises. Conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

There may be sentient beings who perform wholesome deeds of body, speak wholesome words of mouth, and maintain wholesome thoughts of mind; when their bodies perish and their lives end, they are reborn among human beings. Thereafter, the consciousness of the previous state ceases and the initial consciousness of the human state arises. Conditioned by this consciousness, there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

“Or there may be sentient beings who practice good through body, speak well with speech, and intend well with mind; when their bodies disintegrate at the end of life, they are reborn among the Four Great Kings. Thereafter, the prior consciousness ceases and the consciousness of the Four Great Kings first arises. With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arise; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.”
When that deva is first born, appearing like a human child of one or two years of age, he manifests spontaneously and sits upon the lap of the deva;
the deva then says: "This is my son."
Due to the ripening of his past actions, natural wisdom arose within him, and he thought to himself:
"By what conduct have I been born here now?
He then further reflected:

"In the past, while in a human body, I practiced good deeds with my body, spoke good words with my mouth, and maintained good thoughts with my mind. Because of these actions, I have now been born in the heavens.
Should I eventually pass away from here and be reborn again as a human, I shall purify my body, speech, and mind, and practice all virtuous deeds with even greater diligence."

Not long after the child was born, he felt hungry of his own accord. Before him appeared a natural precious vessel filled with celestial food of a hundred flavors, naturally pure. If one’s merit was great, the color of the rice was white; if their merit was middling, the color of the rice was blue; if their merit was inferior, the color of the rice was red.
The child reached for the food with his hand and placed it in his mouth; it was naturally digested, like clarified butter cast into fire. When the child had finished eating, he felt thirsty;

there appeared a natural precious vessel filled with ambrosial nectar (*amṛta*). For those with great merit, the color of the nectar was white; for those with middling merit, the color was blue; and for those with lesser merit, the color was red.
The child took that nectar and drank it; the nectar was digested of its own accord, like clarified butter cast into fire.
Once the child had finished eating and drinking, his body grew large, equal to that of the other devas, and he entered the bathing pool to wash and cleanse himself for his own amusement.
Having enjoyed himself, he emerged from the bathing pool and went beneath the fragrant trees; the fragrant trees bowed down, and he took various perfumes with his hands to anoint his body.
He then went to the Karpāsa-cotton tree; the tree bent down for him, and he took various garments and put them on his body.
He then went to the ornamentation tree; the tree bent down for him, and he took various ornaments to adorn himself.
He proceeded again to the Garland Tree; the tree bent down for him, and he took a garland and placed it upon his head.
He proceeded again to the Vessel Tree; the tree bent down for him, and he immediately took a precious vessel.
He proceeded again to the fruit trees, which bent their branches for him; he took the naturally occurring fruits, either eating them, chewing them, or straining out the juice to drink.

He proceeded again to the musical instrument trees, which likewise bent their branches for him; he took celestial musical instruments and sang with a clear and wondrous voice, harmonizing the strings as he moved toward the various groves.

Seeing countless celestial maidens playing drums and lutes, singing and laughing as they face one another, that deva wanders about in pleasure and consequently gives rise to defiled attachment; looking east, he forgets the west, and looking west, he forgets the east. When first born, he reflects to himself:
"By what conduct have I now attained birth here?"
While he was thus dwelling and observing, he completely forgot this thought.
Thereupon, there were female attendants and retinues.

"If there are sentient beings who perform good deeds with their bodies, speak good words with their mouths, and maintain good thoughts with their minds, then at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Following that, the final consciousness ceases and the initial consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, there is name-and-form (nāmarūpa); conditioned by name-and-form, there are the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana)."
When that deva is first born, appearing like a two- or three-year-old child of Jambudvīpa, spontaneously manifested upon the lap of the deva, the deva immediately says:
"This is my son; this is my daughter."
It is also like this.

There may be sentient beings who, having performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, are reborn in the Yāma Heaven after the dissolution of the body at the end of life. When those devas are first born, they are like three or four-year-old children of Jambudvīpa.

There are some sentient beings who, having performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven upon the dissolution of the body after death; when first born in that heaven, they are like children of four or five years of age in this world.

There are some sentient beings who, having performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, at the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in the Heaven of Mastery over Transformations (Nirmāṇarati). When first born in that heaven, they are like children of five or six years of age in this world.

There are some sentient beings who, having performed wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, at the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*). When first born into that heaven, they are just like children of six or seven years of age in this world; it is exactly so for them as well.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three fast days in a half-month. What are the three? They are: the eighth day, the fourteenth day, and the fifteenth day."
The fast on the eighth day of the month, the fast on the fourteenth day, and the fast on the fifteenth day—these are the three fasts.
For what reason is there a fast on the eighth day of the month?
It is because on the eighth day of every month, the Four Great Kings instruct their messengers, saying:

"Go forth and traverse the world; observe and examine the myriad people to see whether there are those who are filial and obedient toward their parents, respectful and compliant toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, who honor their elders, observe the precepts and fasts, practice giving, and provide relief to the poor and destitute."

At that time, having received the king’s instructions, the messenger traveled throughout the world to investigate. He identified those who were filial toward their parents, who honored śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, who were respectful and obedient to their elders, who maintained the precepts and observed the fasts, and who practiced charity for the destitute. Having completed his observations, he saw that there were those in the world who were unfilial toward their parents, who did not respect their teachers and elders, who did not cultivate the fasts and precepts, and who did not relieve the destitute. Returning, he reported to the king:
"O Heavenly King!..."

"In this world, those who are filial toward their parents, respectful and attentive toward their teachers and elders, pure in their observance of the fasts and precepts, and generous in giving to the poor and destitute, are very few! Very few!
When the Four Heavenly Kings heard this, they were filled with sorrow and displeasure, and replied:
"Alas, what is this! The people of the world are mostly wicked;

they are unfilial toward their parents, do not serve their teachers and elders, do not cultivate the precepts of fasting, and do not give alms to the poor and destitute. They diminish the hosts of the devas and increase the hosts of the asuras."

If the messenger sees someone in the world who is filial toward their parents, reverently serves their teachers and elders, diligently practices the fasts and precepts, and bestows alms upon the poor and destitute, he returns and says to the Heavenly King:
"In the world there is a person who is filial toward their parents, reverently serves their teachers and elders, diligently practices the fasts and precepts, and gives to those in dire straits."
Upon hearing this, the Four Heavenly Kings were filled with great joy and proclaimed: "Excellent! We have heard these virtuous words;

there are those in the world who are filial toward their parents, respectful and attentive to their teachers and elders, diligent in practicing the fasts and precepts, and generous in giving to the poor and destitute. Thus, they increase the hosts of the devas and diminish the hosts of the asuras."
"Why observe the fast on the fourteenth day?
On the occasion of the fourteenth-day fast, the Four Heavenly Kings address the crown prince, saying:

'You must travel throughout the world to observe the myriad people, to know whether there are those who are filial and obedient toward their parents, respectful and diligent in serving their teachers and elders, and devoted to practicing the fast and precepts, giving alms to the poor and destitute.'"

Having received the King’s command, the Prince immediately traveled throughout the world to observe the myriad people. He learned that there were those who were filial toward their parents, who honored their teachers and elders, who diligently practiced the fasts and precepts, and who gave alms to the poor. Having completed his observations, he saw those in the world who were unfilial toward their parents, who did not respect their teachers and elders, who did not practice the fasts and precepts, and who did not give to the poor. Returning, he addressed the King, saying:
"O Heavenly King!..."

"In this world, those who are filial toward their parents, respectful and obedient toward their teachers and elders, pure in the cultivation of fasts and precepts, and who provide relief to the poor and destitute, are extremely few!
Extremely few!
Having heard this, the Four Heavenly Kings spoke with sorrow and displeasure:
"Alas! How lamentable it is!

The people of the world are largely wicked; they are unfilial toward their parents, do not serve their teachers and elders, do not cultivate the precepts of fasting and abstinence, and do not succor the poor and destitute. Thus, they diminish the hosts of the devas and increase the hosts of the asuras."

If the Prince sees anyone in the world who is filial toward their parents, respectful and attentive toward their teachers and elders, diligently observes the precepts of fasting, or practices charity toward the poor and destitute, he immediately returns and says to the King:
"O Great King!..."

"In the world there are people who are filial toward their parents, respectful and obedient toward their teachers and elders, diligently practice the fasts and precepts, and give to those who are poor and destitute.
Having heard this, the Four Heavenly Kings were filled with great joy and proclaimed: "Excellent!"

I have heard these virtuous words: that there are those in the world who can practice filial piety toward their parents, honor and respect their teachers and elders, diligently cultivate the precepts of fasting, and practice giving to the poor and needy; thereby increasing the hosts of devas and diminishing the hosts of asuras.
For this reason, there is the fast on the fourteenth day. Why is there a fast on the fifteenth day?

At the time of the fifteenth-day fast, the Four Heavenly Kings personally descend to traverse the world and observe the myriad people: "Is there anyone in the world who is filial toward their parents, respectful in serving their teachers and elders, diligent in practicing the fast and precepts, and generous in giving to the poor?"

Seeing that many people in the world are unfilial toward their parents, do not serve their teachers and elders, are not diligent in observing the fasts and precepts, and do not give alms to the poor and destitute,
the Four Heavenly Kings then went to the Hall of Good Dharma and addressed Śakra,
saying: "Great King!..."

"You should know that the sentient beings of the world for the most part are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, do not cultivate the fasts and precepts, and do not give alms to the poor and destitute.
When Śakra and the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard this, they were filled with sorrow and displeasure, saying:
"Alas, what a tragedy this is!"

The people of the world are for the most part evil: they are unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, do not cultivate the fasts and precepts, and do not give alms to the destitute; thus they diminish the hosts of the devas and increase the hosts of the asuras.

If the Four Heavenly Kings see people in the world who are filial toward their parents, respectful and diligent in serving their teachers and elders, earnestly practicing the fasts and precepts, and giving alms to the poor and destitute, they return to the Hall of Good Dharma and say to Śakra:

"There are people in the world who are filial toward their parents, respectful and diligent in serving their teachers and elders, earnestly practicing the fasts and precepts, and giving alms to the poor and destitute."
When Śakra and the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard these words, they were all greatly delighted and cried out: "Excellent!

There are indeed those in the world who are filial toward their parents, respectful and attentive toward their teachers and elders, diligent in practicing the fasts and precepts, and generous in giving to the poor and needy; this increases the hosts of devas and diminishes the hosts of asuras."
"For this reason, there is the fast of the fifteenth day.
For this reason, there are three fasts.
At that time, Śakra, wishing to cause the devas to experience redoubled joy, spoke these verses:
“Those who always, on the eighth day of the month, and on the fourteenth and fifteenth days,
receive the teachings and practice the fast and precepts, are like me.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This verse spoken by Śakra was not well-received, nor was it well-spoken; it is not acceptable to me. Why is that?"
That Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has not yet exhausted lust, anger, and delusion; he is not yet liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.
I say that such a person has not departed from the root of suffering.

If there is a bhikṣu of mine who is an arhat with outflows exhausted, who has accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, attained his own benefit, destroyed all fetters of existence, and is liberated through equanimity.
Such a bhikṣu should recite this verse:
“On every eighth day of the month, And on the fourteenth and fifteenth days,
Those who receive the teachings and practice the fast and precepts Are my equals.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That bhikṣu who spoke this verse is one who has rightly received [the teaching] and rightly explained it; he is approved by me."

Why is this so? Because when that bhikṣu has exhausted lust, anger, and delusion, he is liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; I say that such a person has departed from the root of suffering.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In all the houses and dwellings where people reside, there are spirits and deities; none are empty.
In all the streets, lanes, and crossroads, as well as among the slaughterhouses, market stalls, and burial mounds, there are spirits and deities; none are empty."

All spirits and deities are named according to that upon which they depend: those who depend on people are named after people; those who depend on villages are named after villages; those who depend on cities are named after cities; those who depend on nations are named after nations; those who depend on lands are named after lands; those who depend on mountains are named after mountains; and those who depend on rivers are named after rivers.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"All trees, even those as small as a chariot axle, have spirits and deities dwelling within them; there is not a single one that is empty."
When all men and women are first born, there are always spirits and deities who follow and protect them;
when they die, those guardian spirits withdraw their vital essence, and the person then dies.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Suppose there were non-Buddhist brahmins who asked,
'Venerable sirs!'"
If all men and women, at the very moment of their initial birth, are followed and protected by spirits and deities;
when they are about to die, those protecting spirits withdraw their vital essence (*ojas*), and the person then dies.
"Why is it that some people among us today are afflicted by ghosts and spirits, while others are not?
If such a question should arise, you should answer them as follows:

"Worldly people engage in unrighteous conduct, holding perverted and inverted views, and commit the ten evil deeds; among such people, whether there be a hundred or a thousand, there may be but one who is protected by a deity."

For example, just as a single person may tend a herd of cattle or a flock of sheep, numbering perhaps hundreds or thousands, so it is with those who practice unrighteousness, hold perverted and inverted views, and commit the ten unwholesome deeds; among such people, even if there be hundreds or thousands, there is but a single deity who protects them.

If there is a person who practices wholesome dharmas, perceives with right faith and conduct, and is endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action, such a person is protected by hundreds of thousands of deities.
It is, for example, like a king or a royal minister who is guarded by hundreds of thousands of people.
It is the same for them: by practicing wholesome dharmas and being endowed with the ten virtuous actions, such a person is protected by hundreds of thousands of deities.
For this reason, among the people of the world, there are those who are afflicted by ghosts and spirits, and there are those who are not afflicted by ghosts and spirits.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The people of Jambudvīpa surpass those of Aparagoyānī in three respects.
What are these three?”
First, being courageous and possessing a powerful memory, one is able to perform karmic deeds.
Second, being courageous and possessing a powerful memory, one diligently cultivates the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Third, being courageous and possessing a powerful memory, a Buddha appears in that land.
In these three matters, [the people of] Aparagoyānī surpass [those of] Jambudvīpa.
There are three matters in which the people of Aparagoyānī surpass those of Jambudvīpa. What are these three?
First, they have many cattle; second, they have many sheep; third, they have many pearls and jade.
By these three matters, they surpass Jambudvīpa.
Jambudvīpa has three matters by which it surpasses Pūrvavideha.
What are these three?
First, being courageous and possessing strong memory, one is able to perform karmic actions.
Second, being courageous and possessing strong memory, one is able to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya).
Third, they are courageous and possess strong memories; thus, a Buddha appears in that land.
By these three matters, it excels Pūrvavideha.
Pūrvavideha has three matters by which it excels Jambudvīpa. What are these three?
First, its land is extremely vast; second, its land is extremely great; third, its land is extremely wondrous.
By these three qualities, it surpasses Jambudvīpa.
“In Jambudvīpa there are three matters that surpass those of Uttarakuru.
What are these three?
First, they are courageous, possess strong memory, and are able to perform karmic actions.”
Second, they are courageous and possess strong memory, enabling them to practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Third, courageous and possessing strong memory, a Buddha appears in their land.
By these three matters, they surpass those of Uttarakuru.
Uttarakuru has three further matters by which it excels Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, there is no sense of being bound or dependent; second, there is no sense of self; third, the lifespan is fixed at one thousand years.
In these three matters, Jambudvīpa excels the hungry ghost realm;
in those same three matters, the people of Jambudvīpa also excel the hungry ghost realm.
However, the hungry ghost realm excels Jambudvīpa in three other matters.
What are these three?
First, long life; second, a large body; and third, receiving for oneself what was done by others.
By these three matters, they surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
The people of Jambudvīpa also surpass the nāgas and garuḍas in the aforementioned three matters;
however, the nāgas and garuḍas, in turn, surpass the people of Jambudvīpa in three other matters.
What are these three?
First, longevity; second, physical stature; and third, palaces.
By these three things, they surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
"The Jambudvīpa surpasses the asuras in three matters;
the asuras, in turn, surpass the Jambudvīpa in three matters.
What are these three?"
First, their palaces are lofty and vast; second, their palaces are magnificently adorned; third, their palaces are pure.
By these three qualities, they surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
The people of Jambudvīpa surpass the Four Heavenly Kings in these three matters.
Furthermore, the Four Heavenly Kings surpass the people of Jambudvīpa in three matters.
What are these three?
First is long life, second is physical excellence, and third is abundant pleasure.
By these three things, they surpass those of Jambudvīpa.

Furthermore, the people of Jambudvīpa also surpass those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven by means of these same three things.
These devas further possess three things that surpass those of Jambudvīpa.
What are these three?
First, longevity; second, physical beauty; and third, abundant pleasure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are twelve kinds of sentient beings in the desire realm. What are these twelve?"

First, hell; second, animals; third, hungry ghosts; fourth, humans; fifth, asuras; sixth, the gods of the Four Great Kings; seventh, the Trāyastriṃśa gods; eighth, the Yāma gods; ninth, the Tuṣita gods; tenth, the Nirmāṇarati gods; eleventh, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods; twelfth, the Māra gods.
There are twenty-two types of sentient beings in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*):
first, the Brahmakāyika devas; second, the Brahmapurohita devas; third, the Brahmakāyika-pariṣadya devas;
fourth, the Mahābrahmā devas; fifth, the Ābhāsvara devas; sixth, the Parīttābhā devas; seventh, the Apramāṇābhā devas.
1. The Heaven of the Gods; 2. The Heaven of the Thirty-three; 3. The Yāma Heaven; 4. The Tuṣita Heaven; 5.
The Nirmāṇarati Heaven; 6. The Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; 7. The Heaven of the Four Great Kings; 8. The Ābhāsvara Heaven; 9. The Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; 10. The Parītta-śubha Heaven;
11. The Apramāṇa-śubha Heaven; 12. The Śubha-kṛtsna Heaven; 13. The Bṛhatphala Heaven; 14. The Parītta-bṛhatphala Heaven; 15. The Apramāṇa-bṛhatphala Heaven; 16. [The Avṛha Heaven].
16. The Heaven of Adorned Fruits; 17. The Heaven of No-Thought;
18. The Heaven of No-Action; 19. The Heaven Without Heat; 20. The Heaven of Good Vision; 21.
The Heaven of Great Good Vision; 22. The Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
There are four kinds of sentient beings in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). What are these four?

First, the devas of the knowledge of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); second, the devas of the knowledge of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); third, the devas of the knowledge of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); and fourth, the devas of the knowledge of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are four great celestial deities. What are the four? They are: the earth deity, the water deity, the fire deity, and the wind deity."
First is the earth deity, second is the water deity, third is the wind deity, and fourth is the fire deity.
In the past, the earth deity gave rise to a wrong view and said:
"Within the earth there is no water, fire, or wind."
At that time, knowing what this earth deity was thinking, I went to her and said:
"You should give rise to the thought:
'Within the earth there is no water, fire, or wind.'"
"Is it so? The earth deity replied,
"Within the earth, there is truly no water, fire, or wind."
I then said to him: "Do not give rise to this thought, thinking that there is no water, fire, or wind within the earth. Why is this so?"
“Within earth there are water, fire, and wind; however, because the earth element is predominant, it receives the name ‘earth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“At that time, I preached the Dharma to that earth deity in successive order to eliminate his wrong views, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him with discourses on generosity, morality, and rebirth in heaven; I taught that sensual desire is impure, that the outflows of the higher realms are a source of affliction, and that the way of escape is supreme.”
I expounded and revealed the pure brahmacarya.

At that time, knowing his mind was pure, supple, joyful, free from hindrances, and easily transformed, I followed the constant dharma of all Buddhas and proclaimed, distributed, and revealed the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Accumulation of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
At that time, the earth deity, while still upon her seat, became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
It was like a clean, white garment that easily takes on color.

He was likewise; with his mind purified through faith, he attained the Dharma-eye, became free from doubt, and gained certainty in the Dharma. No longer falling into the evil realms nor proceeding toward other paths, he achieved fearlessness and addressed me, saying:

"I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha. For as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, deceive, or drink intoxicants. Please accept me as a laywoman (*upāsikā*) within the True Dharma."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the water deity gave rise to a false view and said:
'Within water there is no earth, fire, or wind.'"
At that time, the earth deity, knowing that such a view had arisen in the mind of the water deity, went to the water deity and said:
"You have indeed given rise to this view, saying:
'In water there is no earth, fire, or wind.'"
"Is it so? He replied, "It is indeed so."
The earth deity said:
"Do not give rise to this view, thinking that there is no earth, fire, or wind within water. Why is this so?
“Within water there are earth, fire, and wind, but because the water element is predominant, it receives the name ‘water.

At that time, the Earth Deity preached the Dharma for him, removing his wrong views and instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him with discourses on generosity, morality, and rebirth in heaven; she explained how sensual desire is impure, how the outflows above are a source of affliction, and how the way of escape is supreme;
she further expounded and revealed the pure holy life.

At that time, the Earth Deity, knowing that the Water Deity’s mind was supple, joyful, faithful, and resolved, and that he was pure, free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and easy to transform, followed the constant custom of all Buddhas by preaching the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, expounding and revealing them in detail.
At that time, that water deity immediately distanced himself from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Just as a clean white cloth easily takes on dye, so too was he;

with a pure mind of faith, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, became free from doubt, and was certain to attain the fruit. No longer falling into evil destinies or wandering toward other realms, he achieved fearlessness and addressed the earth deity, saying:

"I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. For as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from lying, and refraining from drinking intoxicants. Please accept me as a laywoman (upāsikā) within the True Dharma."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the fire deity gave rise to a wrong view, saying:
'Within fire, there is no earth, water, or wind.'"
At that time, the earth deities and water deities, knowing that the fire deity had conceived this view, spoke together to the fire deity, saying:
"Do you truly give rise to this view?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The two deities spoke:
"Do not give rise to this view. Why is that?
Within fire there are earth, water, and wind; it is simply because the fire element (tejo-dhātu) is predominant that it receives the name 'fire'."

Then, the two deities immediately preached the Dharma for them, removing their evil views and instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them with discourses on generosity, morality, and rebirth in heaven; they explained that sensual desire is impure, that the outflows of higher realms are a source of affliction, and that the way of escape is supreme;
they thus expounded and revealed the pure holy life.

The two deities perceived that the god of fire had a supple mind, was filled with joy and faith, was pure and free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and was easily capable of being transformed. Then, according to the constant practice of all Buddhas, they proclaimed, expounded, and revealed the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
At that time, the Fire Deity immediately became free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Just as a clean white cloth easily takes on color, so it was with him;

his faith was purified, and he attained the Dharma-eye, free from doubt. Having decisively attained the fruit, he would not fall into the evil realms nor turn toward other paths, but achieved fearlessness. He addressed the two deities, saying:

"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha. For as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and drinking intoxicants. Please accept me as a lay follower (*upāsikā*) within the True Dharma."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the Wind Deity gave rise to a false view and said:
'Within wind there is no earth, water, or fire.'"
The deities of earth, water, and fire, knowing that the deity of wind had conceived this evil view, went to him and said:
"Have you truly given rise to this view? He replied:
"It is indeed so," [he replied]. The three deities said:
"Do not give rise to this view."
"Why is this? Within wind there are earth, water, and fire; however, because the wind element is predominant, it receives the name 'wind.

" At that time, the three deities preached the Dharma for him, removing his wrong views and instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him with discourses on generosity, morality, and rebirth in heaven; they taught that sensual desire is impure, that the outflows are a source of affliction, and that the way of escape is supreme.
He expounded and revealed the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*).

The Wind Deity, perceiving through his threefold divine knowledge that the other Wind Deity’s mind was supple, joyful, faithful, and resolved, free from the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and easy to transform, [the Buddha], according to the constant dharma of all Buddhas, taught the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering, proclaiming and revealing them.
At that time, the Wind Deity immediately distanced himself from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Just as a clean white cloth easily takes on dye, so it was with him:

his mind of faith became pure, and he attained the Dharma-eye. Free from doubt, he was certain of attaining the fruit; he would not fall into the evil realms nor turn toward other paths, but achieved fearlessness. He then addressed the Three White Deities, saying:

"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha. For as long as life lasts, I shall not kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, deceive, or drink intoxicants. I pray that you will accept me as an upāsikā within the True Dharma; with a heart of compassion for all, I shall not harm any living being."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of clouds. What are the four?
First is white, second is black, third is crimson, and fourth is red. That which is white has an excess of the earth element;
that which is black has an excess of the water element; that which is crimson has an excess of the fire element; and that which is red has an excess of the wind element.

These clouds are at various distances from the earth—ten, twenty, thirty, up to forty-four thousand *li*—except for the period immediately following the beginning of a kalpa, when the clouds rise as high as the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
There are four kinds of lightning. What are the four?

The lightning of the eastern direction is named Body Radiance; the lightning of the southern direction is named Invincible; the lightning of the western direction is named Flowing Flame; and the lightning of the northern direction is named Fixed Clarity.
For what reason do these flashes of lightning appear within the clouds of space? At times the bodily radiance comes into contact with the indestructible (*durjaya*);

at times the bodily radiance comes into contact with the flowing flame (*jvālā*); at times the bodily radiance comes into contact with the light of meditative concentration (*samādhi-prabhā*). At times the indestructible comes into contact with the flowing flame; at times the indestructible comes into contact with the light of meditative concentration; and at times the flowing flame comes into contact with the light of meditative concentration.
For this reason, flashes of lightning arise within the clouds in space.
Furthermore, for what reason does the sound of thunder arise within the clouds in space?

Sometimes the earth element in space comes into contact with the water element; sometimes the earth element comes into contact with the fire element; sometimes the earth element comes into contact with the wind element; sometimes the water element comes into contact with the fire element; and sometimes the water element comes into contact with the wind element.
For this reason, the sound of thunder arises within the clouds in the void.
There are five causes and conditions for which a physiognomist may predict rain that cannot be definitively known, causing the diviner to be bewildered.

What are the five? First, when clouds are accompanied by thunder and lightning, diviners predict that it will rain; however, because the element of fire is excessive, it burns the clouds and no rain falls. This is the first cause of delusion for the diviners.

Second, when there are thunder and lightning in the clouds, diviners predict that it will rain; yet, if a great wind arises and blows the clouds apart so they enter among the mountains, for this reason, the prognosticators are deluded.

Third, when clouds are accompanied by thunder and lightning, diviners predict that it will rain; however, at such times, the great Asura seizes the floating clouds and places them within the great ocean. Due to this cause and condition, the prognosticators are led astray.

Fourth, when there are thunder and lightning in the clouds, diviners predict that it will rain; yet because the masters of the clouds and the masters of the rain are negligent, lustful, and disorderly, no rain eventually falls. Due to these causes and conditions, the diviners are deluded.

Fifth, when clouds gather with thunder and lightning, diviners predict that it will rain; yet because the common people of the world act with unrighteous negligence, engage in impure conduct, and are characterized by stinginess, greed, jealousy, and inverted views, they cause the heavens not to send down rain. Due to these causes and conditions, the diviners are led into error.
"These are the five causes and conditions by which a physiognomist cannot definitively predict rain.
Thus spoke the Buddha. *The Long Discourses of the Buddha*, Volume Twenty;
*The Long Discourses of the Buddha*, Volume Twenty-One.
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Chapter Nine: The Three Calamities. The *Ji shiji jing* (Sutra on the Record of the World), Part Four, Chapter Nine: The Three Calamities.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four things that endure for a long time, immeasurable and limitless, which cannot be calculated by means of days, months, or years. What are these four?

First, when the gradual onset of world-catastrophes occurs and this world is destroyed, the intervening period is long-lasting, immeasurable and limitless, and cannot be calculated by means of days, months, or years.”

Second, after this world has been destroyed, there is a period of intermediate voidness in which no world exists for a vast and remote duration that cannot be calculated by means of days, months, or years.
Third, when heaven and earth first arose and were about to be completed, the intermediate duration was so long that it cannot be measured by days, months, or years.
Fourth, once heaven and earth were completed and remained for a long time without destruction, this duration likewise cannot be measured by days, months, or years.
"These four things endure for a long time, being immeasurable and limitless; they cannot be calculated by means of days, months, or years.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are three calamities in the world."
What are these three?
First is the calamity of fire, second is the calamity of water, and third is the calamity of wind.
There are upper limits for these three calamities.
What are the three? First, the Ābhāsvara Heaven; second, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; and third, the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
When the calamity of fire arises, it reaches as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven, with the Ābhāsvara Heaven serving as its limit.
When a calamity of water arises, it reaches as far as the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven; the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven is its limit.
When a calamity of wind arises, it reaches as far as the Bṛhatphala Heaven; the Bṛhatphala Heaven is its limit.
What is the calamity of fire?

When the calamity of fire is about to arise, the people of this world all practice the True Dharma; their right view is unerring, and they cultivate the ten wholesome actions. While they are practicing these dharmas, someone who has attained the second dhyāna leaps upward into the midst of space and, abiding upon the Path of the Sages, the Path of the Gods, and the Path of Brahmā, cries out in a loud voice:
"O Worthy Ones!..."
"You should know that the joy of the second dhyāna, which is without directed thought and sustained examination, is the joy of the second dhyāna.
Then, having heard these words, the people of the world looked up and said to him: "Excellent!"
"Excellent! I only pray that you will explain to me the second dhyāna path, which is without directed thought (vitarka) and without sustained thought (vicāra).
Then, having heard his words, the being in the air immediately explained to him the second dhyāna path, which is without directed thought and without sustained thought.

Having heard his teaching, the people of this world immediately cultivated the path of the second dhyāna, which is without applied thought or sustained thought; at the dissolution of the body after death, they were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

"At that time, the sentient beings in hell, having completed their retribution and ended their lives, were reborn in the human realm; they further cultivated the second dhyāna, which is without vitarka and without vicāra, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

Sentient beings among animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmā heavens, having ended their lives, were reborn in the human realm; they cultivated the second dhyāna, which is without vitarka and without vicāra, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven."
By this cause and condition, the realm of hell is exhausted; the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, and so on up to the Brahma heavens are all exhausted.
At that time, first the hells are exhausted, and then the animals are exhausted;
once the animals are exhausted, the hungry ghosts are exhausted.
When the hungry ghosts have all perished, the asuras perish;
when the asuras have all perished, the Four Heavenly Kings perish;
when the Four Heavenly Kings have all perished, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven perishes.
When the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is exhausted, the Yāma Heaven is exhausted;
when the Yāma Heaven is exhausted, the Tuṣita Heaven is exhausted;
when the Tuṣita Heaven is exhausted, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is exhausted.
When the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven has been exhausted, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is exhausted;
when the Nirmāṇarati Heaven has been exhausted, the Brahmā Heaven is exhausted;
and when the Brahmā Heaven has been exhausted, then humanity is exhausted, leaving nothing behind.

When all people have perished without exception and this world has fallen into ruin, a calamity ensues; thereafter, the heavens do not send down rain, and the hundred grains, grasses, and trees wither and die of their own accord.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All conditioned dharmas are deeply loathsome; one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."

After a long period of time, a great black windstorm arose and blew upon the waters of the great ocean. The ocean waters, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, were blown apart on both sides, and the sun palace was taken up and placed halfway up Mount Sumeru, forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth, within the path of the sun; because of this, two suns appear in the world.
“When two suns have appeared, all the small rivers, streams, canals, and flows in this world will completely dry up and vanish.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All that is conditioned is deeply loathsome; you should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.”

After a long period of time, a great black windstorm arose; it blew the ocean waters, which were eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, apart on both sides, and took the sun palace and placed it halfway up Mount Sumeru, forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth, within the solar path. Because of this, three suns appeared in the world.

When the three suns have appeared, all these great waters—the Ganges River, the Yamunā River, the Varuṇā River, the Aciravatī River, the Mahī River, the Sindhu River, and the Gaṅgā River—all will completely dry up and vanish without remainder.

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon; all that is compounded is utterly loathsome and should inspire weariness, for one must seek the path of liberation that transcends the world."

After a long period of time, a great black windstorm arose; it blew the ocean waters, which were eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, apart on both sides, and took the sun palace, placing it halfway up Mount Sumeru within the solar path. Due to this, four suns appeared in the world.

When four suns have appeared, all the springs, fountains, and deep pools in these worlds—including the Mahā-sudarśana Lake, the Anavatapta Lake, the Catur-dhāraka Dhāyanti Lake, the Utpala Lake, the Kumuda Lake, the Puṇḍarīka Lake, and the Vimala Lake—all fifty yojanas in length and breadth, will completely dry up and vanish.

"Therefore, know that all things are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon; all conditioned phenomena are deeply loathsome, and one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."

After a long time had passed, a great black windstorm arose and blew upon the waters of the great ocean, causing them to part on both sides. It took up the sun palace and placed it halfway up Mount Sumeru within the sun’s orbit; because of this, five suns appeared in the world.
When five suns have appeared, the waters of the great ocean gradually diminish by a hundred *yojanas*, continuing until they are reduced by seven hundred *yojanas*.

By this one may know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon; all that is conditioned is utterly loathsome, and one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
At that time, the great ocean gradually diminished until only seven hundred yojanas, six hundred yojanas, five hundred yojanas, four hundred yojanas, and so on down to one hundred yojanas remained.

By this it should be known that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon; all that is conditioned is deeply loathsome, and one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
At that time, the waters of the great ocean gradually diminished until they were seven yojanas deep, then six yojanas, five yojanas, and so on, down to a single yojana remaining.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All that is compounded is utterly loathsome; you should seek the path to transcendence and liberation."
Thereafter, the seawater gradually receded until it was at the height of seven *tāla* trees, six *tāla* trees, and so on, down to one *tāla* tree.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All that is conditioned is utterly loathsome; you should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.”

Thereafter, the seawater gradually receded, until seven men, six men, five men, four men, three men, two men, and finally one man remained; it reached their waists, then their knees, and finally their calves and ankles.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All that is conditioned is utterly loathsome; you should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."
Thereafter, the seawater became like water after a spring rain, or like water in a cow’s footprint, until it finally dried up completely, not even wetting a person's finger.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All conditioned things are utterly loathsome; one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."

After a long time had passed, a great black windstorm arose, blowing up sand from the ocean floor eighty-four thousand yojanas deep and casting it onto both shores. It seized the sun palace and placed it halfway up Mount Sumeru within the solar path; because of this, six suns appeared in the world.

When the six suns have appeared, the four continents, the eighty thousand worlds, all the mountains, great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, will all emit smoke and burn fiercely; just as when a potter first fires his kiln, so it shall be when the six suns appear.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All that is conditioned is deeply loathsome; you should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."

After a long period of time, a great black windstorm arose, blowing the sands from the bottom of the ocean for eighty-four thousand yojanas and casting them onto both shores. It seized the sun palace and placed it halfway up Mount Sumeru within the solar path; because of this, seven suns appeared in the world.

Once the seven suns have appeared, these four continents, as well as the mountains, great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, throughout the eighty thousand worlds, will all burn intensely; it will be just like the flames rising from a kiln when a potter fires it—the same occurs when the seven suns appear.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All that is compounded is deeply loathsome; one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."
These four continents, as well as the mountains of the eighty thousand worlds and Mount Sumeru, were all ablaze;

at that same time, the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven, and the Brahmā Heaven were likewise all ablaze.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Therefore, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All conditioned dharmas are utterly loathsome; one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."

When these four continents, up to the Brahma Heaven, have been completely consumed by fire, the wind blows the flames as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven; when the newly born devas there see these flames, they all become terrified and say: "Alas!..."
"What is this? The elder devas said to the newly born devas:
"Do not be afraid; that fire has come here before, and it stopped right at this point."
Because they recollect the preceding fire-light, they are called the Ābhāsvara (Light-Recollection) devas.

When this four-continent world, up to the Brahma-heaven, has been completely consumed by flames, Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, gradually collapses, shrinking from one hundred yojanas and two hundred yojanas, up to seven hundred yojanas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon. All that is conditioned is deeply loathsome; you should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world."

When these four continents and everything up to the Brahma Heaven have been consumed by flames until they are ablaze, thereafter the great earth and Mount Sumeru will be entirely reduced to nothing but ashes.

Therefore, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon; all that is conditioned is utterly loathsome, and you should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
When this great earth has been consumed by fire, the water beneath it will be exhausted, and the wind beneath the water will be exhausted.

Therefore, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and decay, and cannot be relied upon; all that is conditioned is utterly loathsome, and one should seek the path to transcendence and liberation from the world.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When the calamity of fire arises, the heavens no longer send rain, and the hundred grains, grasses, and trees wither and die of their own accord.
Who would believe this?"
Only those who have seen it for themselves would naturally know this;
even so, as far as the water beneath the earth is exhausted and the wind beneath the water is exhausted—
who could believe it?
If there are those who witness it alone, will they not know for themselves?
This constitutes the calamity of fire.
How does the kalpa of fire come to an end and restore itself?

After a long time had passed, a great black cloud arose in the void and reached as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven, raining down everywhere with drops as large as chariot wheels. It rained in this manner for countless hundreds of thousands of years until the water gradually rose to a height of countless hundreds of thousands of yojanas, reaching even unto the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
“At that time, four great winds arose and held this water in place.
What are these four? First is the Wind of Abiding; second is the Wind of Sustaining; third is the Immovable Wind; and fourth is the Firm Wind.”

Thereafter, this water receded by hundreds of thousands of yojanas, and even by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of yojanas. From the four sides of the water, a great wind arose called Saṃgha; it blew upon the water, causing it to stir and tossing up the waves until foam was gathered. The wind blew this away from the water, and in mid-air it naturally solidified, transforming into celestial palaces adorned with the seven treasures. By means of these causes and conditions, the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas came into being.

As that water further diminished to countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of *yojanas*, a great wind arose from the four directions called Saṃgha; it blew upon the water, causing it to move, tossing up waves and gathering foam. Driven by the wind, the waves separated from the water and became naturally solidified in mid-air, transforming into celestial palaces adorned with the seven treasures. By this causal condition, the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven came into being.

"As that water further diminished to countless thousands of millions of yojanas, a great wind arose on all four sides called Saṃgha; it blew upon the water, causing it to move, tossing up the waves and gathering the foam. The wind blew the foam away from the water, where it naturally solidified in mid-air, transforming into celestial palaces adorned with the seven treasures. By this causal condition, the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas came to exist."

As that water further diminished to countless hundreds of thousands of yojanas, there arose a *saṃghāta* wind that blew upon the water, causing it to stir and tossing up waves; foam was produced and accumulated, which the wind then blew away from the water. In the midst of space, it naturally solidified, transforming into celestial palaces adorned with the seven treasures. Through these causes and conditions, the Tuṣita Heaven palace came into being.

As the water further receded to countless hundreds of thousands of yojanas, there arose a *saṃghāta* wind that blew upon the water, causing it to stir and tossing up surging waves. Foam was produced and accumulated; the wind then blew this away from the water, and in mid-air it naturally solidified, transforming into celestial palaces. Through these causes and conditions, the palaces of the Suyāma Heaven came to exist.

The water further diminished until it reached countless hundreds of thousands of yojanas; upon the surface of the water was a layer of foam sixty-eight thousand yojanas deep, its edges being limitless. It was just like the springs and flowing streams here in this world, where there is foam upon the surface of the water—the same was true there.
“By what causes and conditions does Mount Sumeru exist?

A turbulent wind arises and blows these water-bubbles to create Mount Sumeru, sixty-eight thousand *yojanas* in height and eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth, composed of four precious substances: gold, silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.”
For what cause and condition do the four palaces of the asuras exist?

Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the waters of the great ocean, blowing the water-foam against the four sides of Mount Sumeru to erect great palaces, each eighty thousand yojanas in length and breadth, which spontaneously transformed into palaces made of the seven treasures.
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions do the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings exist?

Later, turbulent winds blew the foam from the waters of the great ocean, which spontaneously transformed into palaces made of the seven treasures at a height of forty-two thousand *yojanas* halfway up Mount Sumeru; for this reason, they are called the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings.
By what causes and conditions do the palaces of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven come to exist?
Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the great masses of water, and on Mount Sumeru they spontaneously transformed into palaces made of the seven treasures.
"Furthermore, for what reason does Mount Khadiraka exist? Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the great masses of water foam;

not far from Mount Sumeru, it spontaneously transformed into a mountain of jewels. Its base enters the earth for forty-two thousand yojanas, and its length and breadth are forty-two thousand yojanas. Its boundaries are limitless, and it is composed of the seven treasures interspersed with various colors. For these reasons, Mount Khadiraka exists."
Furthermore, by what cause does Mount Īṣādhara exist? Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the great mass of water foam;

not far from Mount Gādhalā, it spontaneously transformed into Mount Īṣādhara. It is twenty-one thousand yojanas high and twenty-one thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its edges are boundless, it is interspersed with various colors, and it is composed of the seven treasures. For these reasons, Mount Īṣādhara exists.

Thereafter, turbulent winds blew upon the foam of the great waters, and not far from Mount Īṣādhāra, it naturally transformed into Mount Yugandhara. It is twelve thousand yojanas high and twelve thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its boundaries are limitless, variegated with intermingled colors, and composed of the seven treasures. By these causes and conditions, Mount Yugandhara exists.

Thereafter, turbulent winds blew upon the foam of the great waters; not far from Mount Cūḍālā, it spontaneously transformed into Mount Apalāla. It is six thousand yojanas high and six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, its boundaries being limitless, variegated with interspersed colors, and composed of the seven treasures. For these reasons, there is Mount Apalāla.

"Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the foam of the great waters; not far from Mount Apanilou, it naturally transformed into Mount Miliṃdara. It is three thousand yojanas high and three thousand yojanas in length and breadth, its boundaries being limitless, variegated with intermingled colors, and composed of the seven treasures. By this causal condition, Mount Niliṃdara came to exist."

Thereafter, turbulent winds blew upon the foam of the great waters, and not far from Mount Nimiṃdhara, it spontaneously transformed into Mount Vinataka. It is twelve hundred yojanas high and twelve hundred yojanas in length and breadth; its boundaries are limitless, it is variegated with intermingled colors, and it is composed of the seven treasures. For these reasons, there is Mount Vinataka.

Thereafter, winds of disorder blew upon the great water's foam; not far from Mount Vinidha, it spontaneously transformed into the Vajravalaya Mountain. It is three hundred yojanas high and three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, its boundaries being limitless, variegated with intermingled colors, and composed of the seven treasures. For these causes and conditions, there exists the Vajravalaya Mountain.
"Why are there palaces for the moon and the seven suns?

Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the great masses of water foam, which naturally transformed into the palace of the moon and the palaces of the seven suns. Variegated and interspersed, they were composed of the seven treasures; blown by black winds, they returned to their original places. By these causes and conditions, the palaces of the sun and moon came to exist."

"Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the great masses of water's foam, which naturally transformed into the four continents and eighty thousand worlds. By these causes and conditions, there came to be the four continents and the eighty thousand worlds."

Thereafter, turbulent winds blew upon the great water's foam, which, across the four continents and the eighty thousand continents, spontaneously transformed into the Great Diamond Ring Mountains (*vajramaṇḍala-parvata*). These mountains were sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas* in height and sixteen thousand eight hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth; their boundaries were limitless, they were as firm as diamond and indestructible. By these causes and conditions, there came to be the Great Diamond Ring Mountains.

After a long time had passed, clouds appeared spontaneously, filling the sky and raining down everywhere with drops as large as chariot wheels. The water overflowed until it submerged the four continents and reached the height of Mount Sumeru. Subsequently, turbulent winds blew upon the earth, creating great chasms into which all the mountain streams flowed; thus the ocean was formed, and by these causes and conditions, the waters of the four great oceans came into being.
There are three causes and conditions for the saltiness and bitterness of the ocean waters. What are these three?

First, there are natural clouds that fill the void of space and reach as far as the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven), raining everywhere to wash the celestial palaces and cleanse the world below. From the palaces of the Brahmakāyika Heaven and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, down to the palaces of the Yāma Heaven, the four continents, the eighty thousand worlds, the various mountains, the great mountains, and Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains—all are washed and cleansed. The foul, salty, bitter, and impure fluids from all these places flow downward into the ocean, merging into a single flavor; therefore, the ocean water is salty.

Second, in the past, a great seer cast a spell upon the ocean waters, causing them to remain perpetually salty and bitter so that humans could not drink them; for this reason, they are salty and bitter.

Third, the waters of that great ocean are inhabited by various sentient beings whose bodies are immense—measuring one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, up to seven hundred yojanas—and as they breathe in and out, and discharge their excrement and urine into it, the seawater becomes salty.
"This is what constitutes a fire calamity.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What constitutes a water calamity?"

When the calamity of water arises, the people of this world all uphold the true Dharma and right view, not holding wrong views; they cultivate the ten wholesome courses of action and, having cultivated these virtuous deeds, [pass away].

At that time, there was one who had attained the third dhyāna, which is without joy; he leaped upward into the air and, abiding upon the path of the noble ones, the path of the devas, and the path of Brahmā, cried out in a loud voice:
"O worthy ones!
"You should know that there is no joy in the bliss of the third dhyāna; there is no joy in the bliss of the third dhyāna.
When the people of the world heard these words, they looked up and said to him: "Excellent!"
"Excellent! I pray that you will explain to me this path of the third dhyāna, which is without joy.

Then, having heard these words, the being in the air immediately expounded the path of the third dhyāna, which is without joy. Having heard his teaching, the people of this world immediately cultivated the path of the third dhyāna; when their bodies dissolved and their lives ended, they were reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.

"At that time, when the sentient beings in the hells have completed their retribution and their lives end, they are reborn in the human realm; there they further cultivate the path of the third dhyāna, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they are reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.

When the lives of animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmā Heaven, and the Ābhāsvara Heaven come to an end, they are reborn in the human realm; there they cultivate the path of the third dhyāna, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, they are reborn in the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven."
By this cause and condition, the realm of hell was exhausted; the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, the Four Heavenly Kings, and so on up to the Ābhāsvara Heaven were all exhausted.
At that time, first the hells will be exhausted, and then the animals;
once the animals are exhausted, the hungry ghosts will be exhausted;
once the hungry ghosts are exhausted, the asuras will be exhausted.
When the asuras have all perished, the four heavenly kings perish;
when the four heavenly kings have all perished, the Trāyastriṃśa gods perish;
when the Trāyastriṃśa gods have all perished, the Yāma gods perish.
When the Yāma Heaven has ended, the Tuṣita Heaven ends;
when the Tuṣita Heaven has ended, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven ends;
when the Nirmāṇarati Heaven has ended, the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven ends.
When the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas have perished, the Brahmā devas perish;
when the Brahmā devas have perished, the Ābhāsvara devas perish;
and when the Ābhāsvara devas have perished, thereafter humanity perishes without remainder.
When all people have perished without exception and this world has been destroyed, it becomes a calamity.

Thereafter, after a long time, a great black cloud suddenly arises, reaching as high as the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, raining down everywhere with torrential showers of pure hot water. This water boils and surges, scorching and parching the celestial palaces of the gods until they are all utterly consumed, leaving nothing behind.
Just as clarified butter placed in a fire is consumed by boiling until nothing remains, so too is the celestial palace of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

From this one should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change, and not to be relied upon; all conditioned things are deeply loathsome, and one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
"Subsequently, this rain further drenched the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, boiling and consuming them until not a trace remained.
Just as clarified butter placed in a fire leaves nothing behind, so too it was with the palaces of the Brahmakāyikas."

Thereafter, this rain further drenched the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, and the Yama Heaven, boiling and consuming them until not a trace remained.
Just as clarified butter placed in a fire is consumed without remainder, so too are those celestial palaces.

Subsequently, this rain further drenches the four continents, the eighty thousand continents, and all the mountains, great mountains, and Sumeru Kings; it sears and evaporates them until nothing remains.
It is just as when ghee is placed in a fire: it is boiled away and consumed until nothing remains. Such is the case here as well.

Therefore, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change, and not to be relied upon; all that is conditioned is utterly loathsome, and one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
Thereafter, this water will scorch and parch the great earth until nothing remains; once the subterranean waters are exhausted, the winds beneath the waters will also be exhausted.

Therefore, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change, and unreliable. All that is conditioned is utterly loathsome; one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna devas will be scorched and utterly consumed.
Who would believe this?”
Only those who possess true insight can know this:
when the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas are scorched away and utterly consumed, even the waters beneath the earth are exhausted, and the winds beneath the waters are exhausted.
Who would believe this?
Only those who have seen it themselves would know.
This is the calamity of water.
"How does the destruction by water come to an end?

After a long period of time, a great black cloud arises and fills the void, reaching as far as the Subhakṛtsna Heaven, raining down everywhere with drops as large as chariot wheels. For countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, the water gradually rises until it reaches the Subhakṛtsna Heaven."
There are four great winds that sustain this water and keep it in place.
What are these four? First is the Wind of Abiding; second is the Wind of Sustenance; third is the Immovable Wind; and fourth is the Solid Wind.

Thereafter, this water receded by countless hundreds of thousands of yojanas. Great winds arose from the four directions called Saṃgha; they blew upon the water, causing it to stir and tossing up the waves until foam accumulated. The wind blew this foam away from the water into the void of space, where it naturally transformed into the celestial palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, adorned with the seven treasures. Through these causes and conditions, the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven came to exist.

The water receded by countless hundreds of thousands of yojanas; then, the Saṃghāta wind blew upon the water, causing it to surge and toss with waves, raising froth that accumulated together. Blown by the wind away from the water, this remained suspended in mid-air, naturally transforming into the celestial palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas, adorned with the seven precious gems;
thus it continued until the seawater became uniformly salty and bitter, just as it is during the time of the fire calamity.
"This is what constitutes the calamity of water.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What is the calamity of wind?"

When the calamity of wind arises, the people of this world all uphold the true Dharma and possess right view, not wrong view; they cultivate the ten wholesome courses of action and practice virtuous conduct. At that time, there is a person who attains the pure protective mindfulness of the fourth dhyāna and dwells in the air upon the noble path, the celestial path, and the Brahma path, proclaiming aloud:
"O worthy ones!
"Protecting mindfulness and pure, the bliss of the fourth dhyāna; protecting mindfulness and pure, the bliss of the fourth dhyāna.
Then, having heard his voice, the people of this world looked up and said to him: "Excellent!"
"Excellent! We pray that you will explain to us the path of the fourth dhyāna of pure mindfulness.

At that time, having heard these words, the being in the air immediately explained the path of the fourth dhyāna. Having heard his explanation, the people of this world immediately practiced the path of the fourth dhyāna; when their bodies dissolved and their lives ended, they were reborn in the Fruitful Heaven (Ābhāsvara-deva).

"At that time, the sentient beings in hell, having completed their retribution and ended their lives, are reborn in the human realm; they further cultivate the fourth dhyāna, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, are reborn in the Fruitful Heaven (Bṛhatphala).

Sentient beings among the animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, and those from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, when their lives end, are reborn in the human realm; they cultivate the fourth dhyāna, and upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, are reborn in the Fruitful Heaven."

By virtue of these causes and conditions, the realm of hell was exhausted; the realms of animals, hungry ghosts, asuras, the Four Heavenly Kings, and so on up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven were all exhausted.
At that time, the hells were first exhausted, and thereafter the animals were exhausted;
once the animals were exhausted, the hungry ghosts were exhausted;
once the hungry ghosts were exhausted, the asuras were exhausted.
When the asuras have all perished, the Four Heavenly Kings perish;
when the Four Heavenly Kings have all perished, it continues in this manner through successive stages until the Śubhakṛtsna devas perish;
once the Śubhakṛtsna devas have all perished, thereafter humanity is entirely exhausted without remainder.
When all people have perished without exception and this world has been destroyed, it becomes a calamity.

After a long period has passed, a great wind arises called Mahāsaṃghāta; reaching as far as the Bṛhatphala Heaven, this wind spreads in all directions, blowing through the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven and the Ābhāsvara Heaven, causing the palaces to strike one another until they are shattered like fine dust.

It is just as if two strong men were to take up two bronze mallets and strike them against one another until they are completely shattered without remainder; the collision of the two palaces was likewise so.

By this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change, and cannot be relied upon. All that is conditioned is utterly loathsome and should be detested; one must seek the path of liberation that transcends the world.

"Subsequently, this wind blew through the palaces of the Brahmakāyika devas and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas; the palaces struck one another until they were shattered like fine dust, with nothing remaining."

It is just as if two strong men were to take up two bronze maces and strike them against one another until they are completely shattered with nothing remaining; the collision of the two palaces was likewise so.
