From this you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change, and not to be relied upon. All that is conditioned is utterly loathsome and distressing; you should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.

Thereafter, this wind blew upon the palaces of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations, the Tuṣita Heaven, and the Yāma Heaven; the palaces struck one another until they were shattered like fine dust, leaving nothing behind.

It was as if a strong man were grasping two bronze maces and striking them together, shattering them completely until nothing remained; in that same way, those palaces were shattered until nothing remained.

By this one should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change and transformation, and not to be relied upon. All that is conditioned is utterly loathsome; one should seek the path of liberation that transcends the world.

"Subsequently, this wind blew the mountains, great mountains, and Sumeru, the king of mountains, throughout the four continents and the eighty thousand worlds, placing them in the void at a height of one hundred thousand yojanas; the mountains struck one another until they were shattered like fine dust."

It is just as if a strong man were to take light chaff in his hand and scatter it into the air; the four continents and Mount Sumeru would be completely shattered and dispersed in exactly the same way.

By this it may be known that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change, and unreliable; all that is conditioned is utterly loathsome and should inspire weariness, and one ought to seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
Thereafter, the wind is exhausted throughout the great earth; the water beneath the earth is exhausted; and the wind beneath the water is exhausted.

Therefore, you should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to change, and not to be relied upon. All that is conditioned is deeply loathsome; one should seek the path to liberation that transcends the world.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven and the Ābhāsvara Heaven would be crushed like fine dust if their palaces were struck against one another.
Who could believe this?"
Only those who have seen it for themselves can know it.
Thus it continues until the waters beneath the earth are exhausted, and the winds beneath the waters are exhausted.
Who could believe this?
Only those who have seen it for themselves are able to believe it.
This is the calamity of wind.
"How does the calamity of wind subside?"

After a long time had passed, a great black cloud spread throughout the void as far as the Bṛhatphala Heaven, and it sent down a heavy rain with drops as large as chariot wheels; this torrential rain fell for countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, and the waters gradually rose until they reached the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
At that time, there were four winds that sustained this water.
What are these four? The first is named the Sustaining Wind, the second the Supporting Wind, the third the Immovable Wind, and the fourth the Solid Wind.

Thereafter, this water gradually diminished by countless hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*. From the four sides of the water, a great wind arose called Saṃgha; it blew upon the water, causing it to stir and tossing up the waves until foam accumulated. Driven by the wind, the foam separated from the water and, suspended in mid-air, naturally transformed into the celestial palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven. Variegated in color and composed of the seven precious gems, it was through these causes and conditions that the palaces of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven came to exist.

The water receded by countless hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*. Then, the *saṃghāta* wind blew upon the water, causing it to surge and toss with waves; foam arose and accumulated, and the wind blew it away from the water so that it remained suspended in mid-air, spontaneously transforming into palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, variegated in color and composed of the seven precious gems;
even the single flavor of the salt-bitter ocean water became like that at the time of the fire calamity.
This is the calamity of wind.
These are the three calamities; these are the three repetitions. Chapter Ten:
On Combat The Buddha spoke the *Mahāsamaya-sūtra*, the fourth part of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Chapter Ten: On Combat. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the devas and the asuras fought together.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, saying:
'Go now and engage them in battle. If you are victorious, seize the asura Vimalacitra, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and bring him to the Sudharma Hall; I wish to behold him.'"
At that time, after the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven had received the instructions of Śakra, they each adorned themselves.
Then, Vemacitrin, the asura, summoned the asuras and addressed them, saying:
"Go now and engage in battle with them. If you are victorious, seize Śakra Devānām Indra, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and bring him to the Saptaparṇa Lecture Hall; I wish to behold him."
Then, having received the instructions of the asura Vemacitrin, the various asuras each adorned themselves for battle.
Thereupon, the hosts of devas and asuras engaged in combat; the devas were victorious, and the asuras retreated.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven seized the Asura King, bound him with the fivefold fetters, and led him to the Sudharma Hall to present him to Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
At that time, the Asura King, seeing the happiness in the heavens, conceived a longing for it and thought to himself:
"This place is exceptionally sublime; I can dwell here. Why should I return to the palace of the Asuras?"
When this thought arises, the five bonds are immediately released and the five pleasures appear before him.
If an asura conceives the thought of returning to his original palace, the five bonds bind him once more and the five pleasures depart of their own accord.
At that time, the bonds by which the asuras were fettered became even more firm. The fetters of Māra are even more severe than these. To reckon in terms of "self" and "person" is to be bound by Māra;

not reckoning in terms of "self" and "person" is to be released from Māra’s bondage. Attachment to "I" is a bond; attachment to "mine" is a bond. "I shall exist" is a bond; "I shall not exist" is a bond. Form is a bond; formlessness is a bond; both form and formlessness are bonds. Having perception is a bond; being without perception is a bond; having neither perception nor non-perception is a bond. "I" is a great affliction, a boil, and a thorn.

Therefore, the noble disciple knows that "I" is a great affliction, a boil, and a thorn; he abandons the notion of self and cultivates the practice of non-self, viewing that "self" as a heavy burden, as negligence, and as existence.

The existence of a self is conditioned; the non-existence of a self is conditioned; form is conditioned; the formless is conditioned; both form and the formless are conditioned; perception is conditioned; non-perception is conditioned; both perception and non-perception are conditioned. Conditioned things are a great affliction, a thorn, and a wound.
Therefore, the noble disciple, knowing that conditioned phenomena are a great affliction, a thorn, and a wound, abandons the conditioned and practices for the unconditioned.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the devaputras and the asuras were at war.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra summoned the Trāyastriṃśa devas and addressed them, saying:"
"Go now and engage in battle with the asuras; if you are victorious, seize the asura Vimalacitra, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and bring him to the Sudharma Hall, for I wish to behold him."
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, having received Śakra’s instruction, each immediately adorned themselves.
Then, Vemacitrin the asura again commanded his asuras, saying to them:
"Go now and engage in battle with them. If you achieve victory, seize Śakra Devānām-indra, bind him with the fivefold bonds, and bring him to the Saptaparṇa Hall; I wish to behold him."
At that time, having received the instructions of the asura Vimalacitra, the various asuras each adorned themselves for battle.
Thereupon, the hosts of devas and asuras engaged in combat; the devas were victorious, and the asuras retreated.
The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven seized the asura and bound him with the fivefold fetters, leading him to the Sudharmā Hall to show him to Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
As they wandered about upon the Sudharmā Hall, the asura king saw Śakra from afar and reviled him with harsh words from within his fivefold fetters.
At that time, the attendant of the Lord of Devas spoke these verses before the Lord of Devas:
"O Lord of Devas, why do you feel such terror? You manifest your own weakness and inferiority;
When Mañjuśrī reviles you face to face, You remain silent and listen to his harsh words."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied to his attendant in verse:
"He possesses no great power, nor do I stand in fear of him.
Why should a man of great wisdom contend with one who lacks wisdom?"
At that time, the attendant again spoke in verse to Śakra, saying:
"If we do not subdue this fool now, I fear it will become increasingly difficult to endure later.
It is fitting to apply the staff and the whip, so that the fool may reform his ways of his own accord."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again spoke in verse to his attendant, saying:
"I have always said that the wise should not contend with the foolish;
when the foolish revile and the wise remain silent, the wise are thereby proven superior."
At that time, the attendant again spoke in verse to Śakra, saying:
"The reason the Heavenly King remains silent is that he fears it might impair the conduct of the wise;
yet that foolish and deluded man thinks the King harbors fear."
"Foolish and lacking self-reflection, he claims he can rival the King;
risking his life, he comes to provoke me, wishing to make the King retreat like an ox.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again spoke in verse to his attendant:
"That fool, ignorant and lacking insight, thinks that I harbor fear;
yet I contemplate the ultimate truth, for patient silence is supreme."
The worst among evils is to give rise to anger toward one who is angry;
to remain unangered in the face of anger is the supreme victory in battle.
For a person has two motivations: acting for oneself and acting for others.
When the multitude quarrels and litigates, he who does not retaliate is the victor.
People have two motives— acting for their own sake and for the sake of others—
and seeing one who does not engage in dispute, they call him a fool.
If a person possesses great strength yet can endure those who are weak, this strength is the foremost; it is the highest among all forms of patience.
When a fool considers himself strong, that strength is not true strength at all.
"One who possesses the power of patience in accordance with the Dharma—this power cannot be thwarted.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, was Śakra, the Lord of Devas, anyone else?"
Do not form such a view.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, was none other than myself.
During that period, I practiced patience and did not act with violence; I also constantly praised those who were able to practice patience.
"If there are wise people who wish to propagate my Way, they should cultivate patience and silence, and harbor no anger or contention.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven fought with the asuras."
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra said to the asura Citta:
"For what purpose do you adorn yourselves with weapons and harbor hearts of anger and malice to engage in battle and strife?"
"Now we shall debate the principles of the Way together with you, so that we may know who is victorious and who is defeated. Then the Asura Citta said to Śakra:
"Even if one were to lay aside all weapons and cease from contention to merely discuss the meaning of the Way, who would know who is victorious and who is defeated?"
Śakra instructed him, saying:
"Simply engage in debate; among your assembly and my celestial host, there are those with wisdom who will know who has won and who has lost."
Then the asura said to Śakra: "You speak the verse first. Śakra replied:
"You are an elder deity; you should speak first.
At that time, Citta the Asura immediately addressed Śakra with this verse:
"If we do not subdue the fool now, I fear it will become even more difficult to endure later."
"It is fitting to apply the rod and the whip, so that the fool may reform his ways.
When the Asura had spoken this verse, the assembly of Asuras immediately rejoiced greatly and cried out "Excellent! in loud voices;
only the host of devas remained silent and spoke no word.
Then, the Asura King said to Śakra:
"It is your turn to speak a verse.
At that time, Śakra immediately spoke a verse for the sake of the Asura:
"I have always said that the wise should not contend with fools;
when the fool reviles and the wise remains silent, the wise thereby triumphs over that fool."
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had spoken this verse, all the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven were filled with great joy and raised their voices in praise;
at that time, the assembly of Asuras remained silent and speechless.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, said to the Asura:
"It is now your turn to speak a verse. Then, the Asura spoke this verse:
“The reason the Heavenly King remains silent is that he fears it might impair the conduct of the wise;
yet those foolish and deluded people claim the King harbors fear.”
"Foolish and lacking self-reflection, he claims he can rival the King;
risking his life, he comes to provoke us, wishing to make the King retreat like an ox.
When the Asura King had spoken this verse, the host of asuras leaped for joy and, raising their voices, acclaimed it as excellent.
At that time, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa devas remained silent and spoke no word. Then, the Asura King said to Śakra:
"It is now your turn to speak a verse."
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, spoke this verse for the sake of the asuras:
“That fool, lacking wisdom and insight, Thinks that I harbor fear;
But I contemplate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*): To endure and remain silent is supreme.”
The worst among evils is to give rise to anger toward one who is angry;
he who does not yield to anger when faced with anger is the most victorious in battle.
Furthermore, there are two conditions for a person: acting for oneself and acting for others.
When the multitude engages in disputes, he who does not retaliate is the victor.
A person has two motivations: acting for oneself and acting for others.
Seeing one who does not engage in dispute, one does not call them foolish.
If a person possesses great strength yet is able to endure those who are weak, this strength is the foremost; it is the highest among all forms of patience.
When a fool considers himself strong, that strength is not true strength at all.
"The power of one who possesses the patience of the Dharma—this power cannot be thwarted.
After Śakra Devānām-Indra had spoken this verse, the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods leaped for joy and raised their voices in praise;
the host of asuras remained silent and speechless.
At that time, the hosts of devas and asuras each withdrew slightly and said to one another:

"The verses spoken by the Asura King contain offenses; they give rise to enmity over swords and blades, produce the roots of strife and litigation, prolong various fetters of resentment, and plant the seeds of the three realms of existence."

The verses spoken by Śakra, Lord of the Devas, are such that they cause no disturbance, do not give rise to swords or blades, do not engender strife or litigation, do not increase the bonds of enmity, and sever the root of the three realms of existence.
"What the Lord of Devas has said is good; what the asuras have said is not good.
The devas are victorious, and the asuras are defeated.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, was Śakra Devānām Indra anyone else?
Do not conceive such a thought. Why is this?"
"I am that very person.
At that time, by means of gentle words, I defeated the host of asuras.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the devas again fought with the asuras.
At that time, the asuras were victorious and the devas were defeated.

Then Śakra-devānām-indra, riding a precious chariot with a thousand spokes, fled in terror. On the way, he saw a nest atop a śimśapā tree containing two young ones; he then addressed the charioteer in verse, saying: [The verse follows]"
“There are two birds upon this tree; you should turn your chariot and avoid them.
Even if the bandits should harm me, do not injure the lives of these two birds.”
At that time, having heard the verse of Śakra, the charioteer immediately stopped the chariot and turned it away from the bird.
At that moment, the front of the chariot was facing the asuras; seeing from afar that the precious chariot had turned toward them, the asura hosts said to one another:
"Now Śakra, Lord of the Devas, riding upon his thousand-spoked precious chariot, is turning toward our host; he surely wishes to fight again, and we cannot withstand him."
The hosts of asuras then retreated and dispersed; the devas were victorious, and the asuras withdrew.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, who else could the Śakra have been?"
Do not form such a view. Why is this?
It is none other than my own body.
At that time, I gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all sentient beings. O bhikṣus!
You who have left the household life to practice the Way within my Dharma should likewise give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and take pity upon the masses.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the devas and the asuras fought together.
At that time, the devas were victorious and the asuras retreated."

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, having returned to his palace after victory in battle, constructed another hall named "Most Victorious" (Jiaye), measuring one hundred yojanas in length from east to west and sixty yojanas in width from south to north.
The hall consists of one hundred bays; in each bay there is a sevenfold open pavilion, and upon each pavilion there are seven jade maidens, and each jade maiden has seven attendants.

Śakra Devānām Indra also does not worry about providing garments, food and drink, or ornaments for his various celestial maidens; rather, they receive their blessings according to what they have created in the past. Because he built this hall with a heart of joy after defeating the asuras in battle, it is named the Hall of Supreme Victory (Vaijayanta).
Furthermore, among all the halls and pavilions within the thousandfold world-system, none can equal this hall; therefore, it is named "Most Victorious.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, the asura conceived this thought:"

"I possess great majesty and my supernatural powers are not slight; yet the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the various sun and moon deities constantly dwell in the void, traveling freely above my head. Now, would it not be fitting for me to take those suns and moons to serve as earrings, so that I may travel about with sovereign ease?"
At that time, the Asura King’s wrath blazed intensely; he immediately thought of striking the Asuras, and as he struck them, he further thought:
"Now the Asura King thinks of us; we should quickly adorn ourselves."

He immediately commanded his attendants to prepare weapons and armor, mounted a precious chariot, and, escorted before and behind by countless hosts of asuras, went before the Asura King and stood to one side.
At that time, the king again thought of the asura Śambara; Śambara the asura then thought to himself:
"Now the king thinks of me; we should quickly prepare ourselves."

He immediately commanded his attendants to prepare weapons and armor, mounted his precious chariot, and, escorted before and behind by countless hosts of asuras, went before the Asura King and stood to one side.
At that time, the king again thought of the asura Vemacitra; the asura Vemacitra, in turn, thought to himself:
"Now the king thinks of me; we should quickly prepare ourselves."
He immediately commanded his attendants to prepare weapons and armor, mounted a precious chariot, and, escorted before and behind by countless asura hosts, went before the king and stood to one side.
At that time, the king again thought of the minister Asura; the minister Asura then thought to himself:
"The king is now thinking of me; we should quickly prepare ourselves."

He immediately commanded his attendants to prepare weapons and armor, mounted a precious chariot, and, escorted before and behind by countless asura hosts, went into the presence of the king and stood to one side.
At that time, the king again thought of the minor asuras, and the minor asuras likewise thought to themselves:
"Now the king thinks of us; we should quickly adorn ourselves."
He immediately adorned himself, fully equipped his weapons, and accompanied by countless multitudes, went before the King and stood to one side.

At that time, Rāhu, the Asura King, likewise adorned himself, donned a jeweled armor, mounted a precious chariot, and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of Asura hosts armed with weaponry, emerged from his realm, intending to go and battle with the devas.

At that time, the dragon kings Nanda and Upananda coiled their bodies seven times around Mount Sumeru, shaking the mountains and valleys. A thin veil of clouds spread across the sky, raining down drop by drop; then, striking the waters of the great ocean with their tails, they caused the waves to surge up until they reached the summit of Mount Sumeru.
At that time, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven immediately thought to themselves:
"Now thin clouds have spread slightly, and drops of rain fall gently; the waves of the ocean surge as he has come here."
"This must be because the asuras intend to come and engage in battle; therefore, these extraordinary omens have appeared.

At that time, the countless billions of dragon troops from within the ocean, all bearing spears, halberds, bows, arrows, swords, and blades, clad in heavy jeweled armor with their weapons fully arrayed, went out to meet the asuras in combat. When the dragon hosts were victorious, they pursued the asuras into their palaces.
If the hosts of nāgas retreat and do not return to their palace, they immediately hasten to the abode of the garuḍa spirits and inform them, saying:
"The host of asuras wishes to wage war against the devas; I went forth to confront them in battle, but they have now gained the victory.
You all must prepare your weapons and join forces together to fight against them."

At that time, having heard the dragon’s words, the various spirits immediately adorned themselves, prepared their weapons, and donned heavy jeweled armor; they joined the host of dragons to battle the asuras, and when they achieved victory, they pursued the asuras into their palaces.
If they do not return to their own palaces in a timely manner, they will immediately retreat and flee to the realm of the *kumbhāṇḍa* spirits who carry flowers, and shall address them, saying:
"The hosts of Asuras wish to fight with the gods; we have fought against them and they have now achieved victory.
You all must prepare your weapons and join forces together to battle them."

"When the various flower-holding spirits heard the dragon's words, they immediately adorned themselves, prepared their weapons, and donned heavy jeweled armor. Joining their strength together, they fought with the Asuras; when they achieved victory, they pursued the Asuras into their palaces."
If they do not return to their own palaces in a timely manner, they immediately retreat and flee to the realm of the *asura* spirits of Constant Joy, where they address them, saying:
"The hosts of *asuras* wish to fight with the devas; we went out to meet them in battle, but they have now gained the victory.
You must prepare your weapons and join forces with us to wage war against them."

At that time, having heard these words, the spirits known as the Constantly Joyful (Nityapramudita) immediately adorned themselves, prepared their various weapons, and donned heavy jeweled armor. United in their strength, they fought against the Asuras; when they achieved victory, they pursued the Asuras into their palaces.
If they do not return to their own palaces at the proper time, they immediately retreat and flee to the Four Heavenly Kings, reporting to them:
"The hosts of Asuras wish to fight with the devas; we opposed them in battle and they have now gained the victory.
You all must prepare your weapons and join forces together to wage war against them."

At that time, having heard these words, the Four Heavenly Kings immediately adorned themselves, prepared their various weapons, and donned heavy jeweled armor. Joining their strength together, they fought against the asuras; when they achieved victory, they pursued the asuras into their palaces.
If they are unsuccessful, the Four Heavenly Kings will immediately go to the Sudharma Hall and address Śakra Devānām Indra and the various gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, saying:
"The Asuras wish to fight with the gods; now the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven should adorn themselves, prepare their weapons, and all join forces to go and battle them."
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, commanded an attendant deva and said to him:
"Go with my words and announce to the devas of Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmitavaśavartin:
'The Asuras, along with countless hosts, intend to come and wage war. Now, all you devas should adorn yourselves, prepare your weapons, and assist me in battle.'"

Then, having received the command of Śakra, that attendant deva immediately went to the Yāma heaven, and so on, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, speaking in the voice of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and said to them:
"The innumerable hosts of Asuras have come to wage war; now you gods should adorn yourselves and prepare all your weapons to assist me in battle."

At that time, having heard these words, the Yama-deva king immediately adorned himself, prepared his various weapons, donned heavy jeweled armor, and mounted a precious chariot. Surrounded before and behind by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial hosts, he stationed himself on the eastern side of Mount Sumeru.

At that time, having heard these words, the devaputra of Tuṣita immediately adorned himself, prepared his various weapons, donned heavy jeweled armor, and mounted a precious chariot. Surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial hosts, he took his station on the southern face of Mount Sumeru.
At that time, having heard these words, the devaputra of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven also arrayed his military forces and stationed himself on the western side of Mount Sumeru.
At that time, having heard these words, the devaputra of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven also arrayed his military forces and stationed himself on the northern side of Mount Sumeru.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately thought of the Trāyastriṃśa gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The Trāyastriṃśa gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three then thought to themselves:
"Now Śakra thinks of us; we should quickly adorn ourselves."

He immediately commanded his attendants to prepare various weapons and mounted a precious chariot; surrounded before and behind by countless billions of devas, he went before Śakra, Lord of Devas, and stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, again thought of the other devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, and those other devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven immediately thought to themselves:
"Now Śakra thinks of us; we should quickly adorn ourselves."

He immediately commanded his attendants to prepare various weapons and mounted a precious chariot; surrounded before and behind by countless billions of devas, he proceeded to the presence of Śakra and stood to one side.
At that time, Śakra again called to mind the artisan spirit Viśvakarman, who immediately thought to himself:
"Now Śakra calls me to mind; I should quickly prepare the adornments."

He immediately commanded his attendants to prepare various weapons and armaments, mounted his precious chariot, and, surrounded by thousands upon thousands of followers before and behind him, proceeded to stand before Śakra.
At that time, Śakra again thought of the Dragon King Susthita; the Dragon King Susthita immediately thought to himself:
"Now that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thinks of me, I should go there now."
He immediately went before Śakra and stood there.

At that time, Śakra adorned himself, prepared his various weapons, donned a precious armor upon his body, and mounted the head of the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita. Surrounded by countless devas and spirits in front and behind, he departed from his celestial palace to go and battle with the asuras.

That which is called formidable weaponry—swords, blades, spears, lances, bows and arrows, axes, hatchets, battle-axes, whirling discs, and nooses—all these weapons and armor are made of the seven precious gems; yet when their sharp edges are brought against the bodies of the asuras, their bodies are not wounded, for the blades merely touch them.

The hosts of asuras took up swords and blades of the seven treasures, spears and lances, bows and arrows, axes and adzes, battle-axes, revolving wheels, and nooses; though they brought their sharp edges to bear upon the bodies of the devas, they merely touched them and were unable to cause any injury or damage.
Thus it is that the gods who dwell in the realm of desire engage in battle with the asuras;
desire is the cause, and desire is the condition. *The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra, Volume Twenty-one* *The Dīrgha Āgama Sūtra, Volume Twenty-two*
Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
Chapter Eleven: The Three Intermediate Kalpas, from the Fourth Division of the *Lokasthāna-sūtra*.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are three intermediate kalpas. What are the three?
First is the kalpa of weapons; second is the kalpa of famine; and third is the kalpa of pestilence.”
What is the kalpa of weapons?

Originally, the people of this world had a lifespan of forty thousand years; subsequently, it gradually decreased to twenty thousand years, then further decreased to ten thousand years, then to one thousand years, then to five hundred years, then to three hundred years and two hundred years, until now, when the human lifespan is approximately one hundred years, with more decreasing than increasing.
Thereafter, the human lifespan will continue to diminish until it reaches ten years; at that time, girls will be married at only five months of age.

At that time, all the fine flavors existing in the world—ghee, honey, rock sugar, and dark rock sugar—all such delicious tastes naturally vanished; the five grains would not grow, and there would be only weeds and tares.
At that time, there will be no more fine garments of brocade, silk, *karpāsa* cotton, or *kṣauma* linen; there will be only coarse-woven grass clothing.

At that time, this earth will produce nothing but thorns, mosquitoes, gadflies, bees, scorpions, vipers, snakes, and venomous insects. Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, the seven treasures, pearls, and jade will naturally sink into the ground, leaving only stones, sand, and foul impurities filling it.
At that time, sentient beings only increased in the ten unwholesome actions; they no longer even heard the name of the ten wholesome actions, let alone having anyone who practiced them.

At that time, those who were unfilial toward their parents, disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, and capable of committing evil deeds would receive offerings and be honored and treated with respect by others; it was just as those today who are filial toward their parents, respectfully serve their teachers and elders, and are capable of performing good deeds receive offerings and are honored and treated with respect by others.
It is just the same for those people who, by committing evil, obtain offerings;
when their lives end, they fall among the animals, just as people today are born into the heavens.
At that time, when people saw one another, they harbored hearts of malice and harm, desiring only to kill each other.
It was just like a hunter who, upon seeing a herd of deer, desires only to slaughter them, without a single thought of goodness.
Such were these people; they desired only to kill one another, without a single virtuous thought.

At that time, there was not a single level spot among the ditches, ravines, valleys, mountain ridges, or mounds of this earth. As people traveled back and forth, they were struck with terror and dread, their hair standing on end.

"At that time, during the seven days, the kalpa of swords and blades arises. At that time, whatever grasses, trees, tiles, or stones people grasp in their hands all transform into swords and blades; these blades are so sharp that whatever they are aimed at is severed, and they strike one another down in succession."

Among them, those who possessed wisdom, seeing the signs of mutual slaughter by weapons, fled in terror to enter mountain forests, ravines, and uninhabited places, where they remained hidden for seven days, saying to themselves in both mind and speech:
"I do not harm others; let no one harm me."
For seven days, that man sustained himself by eating the roots of grasses and trees; after the seven days had passed, he emerged from the mountain forest.
At that time, he encountered another person, and with great joy he said:
"I see a living person! I see a living person!"
"Just as parents who have been separated from an only child for a long time, upon seeing one another again, leap for joy and cannot contain themselves;
so too did he leap for joy and could not contain himself."
At that time, for seven days the people wept facing one another; then, for another seven days, they enjoyed themselves together, rejoicing and celebrating.
At that time, when people’s bodies perish and their lives end, they all fall into the hells. Why is this?
It is because these individuals constantly harbor anger and maintain harmful intentions toward one another, lacking compassion and benevolence; this constitutes the kalpa of weapons.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What is the kalpa of famine?

At that time, the people mostly practice what is not the Dharma; their views are perverted and inverted, and they commit the ten unwholesome actions. Because they practice evil, the heavens do not send down rain; the hundred grasses wither and die, and the five grains do not ripen, leaving only stalks and straw."
What is meant by famine?

At that time, the people gather and sweep up the remains of grain from fields, streets, alleys, roads, and lanes, as well as from heaps of refuse, to sustain their lives; this is what is meant by famine.

Furthermore, when suffering from hunger, a person gathers various skeletal remains from streets, marketplaces, slaughterhouses, and among burial mounds; they boil these bones to make broth which they drink to sustain themselves. This is known as "white-bone starvation."
Furthermore, during the kalpa of famine, the five grains that are sown all transform into grasses and trees. At that time, people gather their flowers, boil them to extract the juice, and drink it.

Moreover, during times of famine, the flowers of the grasses and trees fall and are covered beneath the soil; at that time, people dig into the earth to take these flowers and boil them for food, thereby sustaining themselves. This is known as the "famine of grasses and trees."
At that time, sentient beings, upon the dissolution of the body and the end of life, fall among the hungry ghosts (preta). Why is this?

It is because during the kalpa of famine, these individuals constantly harbored stinginess and greed, lacked a mind for giving and benefiting others, refused to share, and did not consider those in distress; thus it was called the kalpa of famine.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"What is the kalpa of pestilence?
At that time, the people of the world practice the True Dharma, possess right view, and do not hold perverted views; they are endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action."

Suppose spirits from other worlds come here, while the local spirits become negligent and licentious, unable to protect people. These spirits from other worlds then harass the people of this world, beating them with clubs and staffs, seizing their vital essence (*ojas*), causing their minds to become disordered, and driving them away by force.
It is just as when a king commands his generals to provide protection, yet from another direction, bandits come to invade and harass; these negligent people plunder the villages and the kingdom.
It is the same in this case: spirits from other worlds come here, seize people of this realm, beat and strike them with staves, extract their vital essence, and drive them away by force.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Even if the spirits and deities here do not engage in heedless lust, if powerful spirits and deities from other worlds come, these local spirits will become terrified and flee; those great spirits will then harass this person, beating them with clubs and staves, seizing their vital essence, and killing them before departing."
For example, suppose a king or a royal minister dispatches various generals to guard the people; these generals are pure and prudent, remaining free from negligence.
Yet, from another region, there comes a fierce and powerful general with a vast multitude of men and troops to destroy villages and cities, plundering people and property.

It is just the same with him: even if the local ghosts and spirits here do not dare to be negligent, when powerful ghosts and spirits from other worlds arrive, these local ghosts and spirits will flee in terror; those great spirits will then harass this person, beating and striking them with staves, extracting their vital essence, and killing them before departing.
At that time, during the kalpa of pestilence, when the people’s bodies were destroyed and their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
Why was this? It was because the people of that time directed hearts of loving-kindness toward one another and repeatedly asked after each other’s welfare.
"Is your illness abating?
Is your body at ease?
Because of these causes and conditions, one attains birth in the heavens.

Therefore, it is called the *plague kalpa*. These are the three intermediate kalpas. Chapter 12: The Original Causes of the World (*Lokadhātu-pūrvanimitta-varga*) The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “In the fourth part of the *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Lokasthāna Sūtra*, this is the twelfth chapter, ‘The Original Causes of the World. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Mahāsammata. He ruled over the four continents and possessed great power and majesty. At that time, the people lived for eighty thousand years. They were free from illness and sorrow, and they enjoyed all manner of pleasures. Their bodies were naturally radiant, and they did not require clothing or shelter. They sustained themselves by gathering food from the earth, which tasted like honey. As time passed, their lifespan gradually decreased, and their physical stature diminished accordingly. When their lifespan reached sixty thousand years, they began to experience various afflictions. Because of these afflictions, they sought to build houses for protection. This was the beginning of the construction of dwellings. As their lifespan continued to decrease, they eventually reached ten thousand years. At that point, the taste of the food from the earth changed, becoming like the flavor of rice. Because of this change, the people’s greed increased, and they began to hoard and steal. From this arose the concept of property, and they established boundaries to prevent theft. To govern these matters, they appointed a leader who was honored and respected by all; he was called the ‘Kṣatriya King. Thus, the system of governance and social order was established. [The text continues with the evolution of society, the decline of morality, the appearance of the five corruptions, and the eventual onset of the *kalpa* of famine, plague, and warfare. “Thus, it is called the *kalpa* of plague. These constitute the three intermediate kalpas. [End of Chapter 12] The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “In the future, after a long period of time, the lifespan of human beings will increase again until it reaches eighty thousand years. At that time, the world will be filled with peace and prosperity, and all beings will enjoy longevity and happiness. However, as the cycle of decline resumes, the lifespan will again diminish until it reaches ten years. During this period of extreme degeneration, the people will be plagued by famine, disease, and conflict. This is known as the *kalpa* of calamity. After this period of suffering, the lifespan will once more begin to increase, eventually returning to eighty thousand years. Thus, the cycle of the world’s formation, endurance, destruction, and emptiness continues eternally. [The Buddha further explains the causes and conditions of the world’s existence, the nature of sentient beings, and the ultimate goal of liberation. “Bhikṣus, you should understand that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. You must cultivate the path with diligence to transcend the cycle of birth and death and attain the state of Nirvāṇa. [The Buddha concludes the discourse on the origins and destiny of the world. “Bhikṣus, this is the twelfth chapter, ‘The Original Causes of the World,’ from the *Lokasthāna Sūtra* in the fourth division of the *Dīrgha Āgama*. The Buddha having spoken thus, the bhikṣus, having heard his words, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. [End of the *Lokasthāna Sūtra*]

"After the calamity of fire has passed and this world and its heavens are about to be reconstituted, there are certain beings whose merit, karma, and lifespan have been exhausted; they pass away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and are reborn in the empty Brahma-abode. There, they develop a mind of attachment, taking delight in that place and wishing for other beings to be born there with them."

Having formed this thought, other beings whose merit, karma, and lifespan were exhausted passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven at the dissolution of their bodies and lives, and were reborn in the realm of the empty Brahmā.
At that time, the Elder Brahmā thought to himself: "I am the Great Brahmā, King of Brahmā;

there is no one who created me, for I exist naturally and spontaneously without any inheritance. Within a thousand worlds, I possess the greatest sovereignty; I am skilled in all profound meanings, possessed of abundant wealth, and capable of creating all things. I am the father and mother of all sentient beings."
Then the Brahmās who arrived later thought to themselves:

"That previous Brahmā is the Great Brahmā King, the Sovereign of Brahmā. He exists spontaneously; there is no one who created him. He is the most honored and supreme within a thousand worlds, requiring no inheritance, well-versed in all meanings and principles, possessed of abundant wealth, able to create all things, and the father and mother of sentient beings; from him we have come to exist."
That Brahmā King’s countenance and appearance are always like those of a youth; therefore, the Brahmā King is named "The Youth.

At times, when this world is once again formed as a world, many sentient beings are born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. They are born spontaneously by transformation, taking joy as their food, with bodies that illuminate themselves with light, flying through the air by means of supernormal power, dwelling in peace and happiness without obstruction, and possessing long lifespans.
Thereafter, this world transformed into a great expanse of water, overflowing everywhere.
At that time, the world was plunged into great darkness; there were no sun, moon, stars, day, or night, nor were there months, years, or the reckoning of the four seasons.

Thereafter, when this world was about to undergo transformation once more, there were other sentient beings whose merit, karma, and lifespan had been exhausted; they passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn here in this world. They were all born by transformation, taking joy as their food, with bodies that illuminated themselves with light, traveling through the air by supernormal power, dwelling in peace and happiness without hindrance for a long time in this world.

At that time, there were no distinctions of male or female, noble or humble, superior or inferior, nor were there different names; because they were born together as a multitude, they were called "sentient beings" (sattva).

At that time, on this earth, a natural essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) emerged, solidifying upon the ground like clarified butter (ghṛta). When the essence of the earth emerged, it was likewise like fresh ghee, its flavor as sweet as honey.
Thereafter, sentient beings tested it with their hands to discover what flavor it had; upon first tasting it, they found it pleasant and thus developed an attachment to its taste.

As they continued to taste it repeatedly in this manner, greed arose, and they began to scoop it up with their hands. Gradually, this evolved into the practice of hand-gathering food (*piṇḍa-bhojana*). When other sentient beings saw them eating incessantly, they imitated them and ate as well, continuing without ceasing.
At that time, the bodies of these sentient beings became coarse and rough, their radiance gradually faded away, and they no longer possessed supernormal powers, being unable to fly.
At that moment, as there were yet no sun or moon, the light of the sentient beings vanished; consequently, heaven and earth were plunged into great darkness, no different from before.

After a long period of time, a great violent wind blew upon the waters of the great ocean, eighty-four thousand *yojanas* deep, causing them to part on both sides. It seized the sun palace and placed it halfway up Mount Sumeru within the solar path, so that it rises in the east and sets in the west, revolving throughout the world.
"On the second day, when the sun-palace emerges from the east and sets in the west, sentient beings may say:
'This is that very same [sun] from yesterday,' or they may say:"
"It was not yesterday.
On the third day, [the sun] circled Mount Sumeru, rising in the east and setting in the west; at that time, sentient beings said, "This must surely be one day."
"Sun" (rì) is explained as meaning the cause of prior illumination; therefore, it is called "sun.
There are two meanings of "sun":
first, abiding in its constant course; second, its palace.

“Because it provides a wide view in all four directions, the palace is circular; it is temperate and pleasant, composed of celestial gold interspersed with crystal. Two parts are made of celestial gold, pure and unadulterated, transparent inside and out, with light shining far and wide; one part is made of crystal, pure and unadulterated, transparent inside and out, with light shining far and wide.”
"The Sun Palace is fifty-one *yojanas* in length and breadth; its walls and floor are as thin as catalpa or cypress wood.

There are sevenfold walls, sevenfold railings, sevenfold nets, sevenfold jeweled bells, and sevenfold rows of trees, all adorned around the perimeter and composed of the seven treasures: golden walls with silver gates, silver walls with golden gates, lapis lazuli walls with crystal gates, crystal walls with lapis lazuli gates, red pearl walls with agate gates, agate walls with red pearl gates, musaragalva walls with gates of various jewels, and walls of various jewels with musaragalva gates."

Furthermore, its railings consist of gold railings with silver crossbars, silver railings with gold crossbars, lapis lazuli railings with crystal crossbars, crystal railings with lapis lazuli crossbars, red pearl railings with agate crossbars, agate railings with red pearl crossbars, railings of various jewels with musaragalva crossbars, and musaragalva railings with crossbars of various jewels.

Golden nets with silver bells; silver nets with golden bells; crystal nets with lapis lazuli bells; lapis lazuli nets with crystal bells; red pearl nets with agate bells; agate nets with red pearl bells; musaragalva nets with various jewel bells; and various jewel nets with musaragalva bells.

The gold trees had silver leaves, flowers, and fruits; the silver trees had gold leaves, flowers, and fruits; the lapis lazuli trees had crystal flowers and fruits; the crystal trees had lapis lazuli flowers and fruits; the red pearl trees had agate flowers and fruits; the agate trees had red pearl flowers and fruits; the musaragalva trees had various jewels for flowers and fruits; and the various jewel trees had musaragalva flowers and fruits.

The palace walls have four gates, each with seven steps, surrounded by railings. Multi-storied pavilions, terraces, and towers, as well as gardens and bathing pools, stand in orderly succession. They produce various precious flowers, arranged in perfectly aligned rows. There are all kinds of fruit trees with flowers and leaves of diverse colors; their fragrances waft far and wide in the four directions, while flocks of birds of various species sing together in harmony.
"The palace of that sun is sustained by five winds:
first, the sustaining wind; second, the nourishing wind; third, the receiving wind; fourth, the revolving wind; and fifth, the regulating wind."
The main hall where the Sun Deity resides is constructed entirely of pure gold and is sixteen yojanas in height. The hall has four gates, surrounded by railings.
The seat of the Sun Deity measures half a yojana in length and breadth; it is composed of the seven treasures, pure and soft like celestial garments.

The Sun Deity himself emits light that illuminates the golden palace; the light from the golden palace illuminates the solar mansion, and the light from the solar mansion issues forth to illuminate the four continents under heaven.
The lifespan of the Sun Deity is five hundred celestial years; his descendants succeed one another in an unbroken lineage without any variation.
That palace does not decay and endures for an entire kalpa.
When the solar palace moves, the Sun Deva has no intention of moving; he says, "I am walking" or "I am staying," while constantly enjoying himself with the five sensual pleasures.

When the Sun Palace travels, hundreds of thousands of great celestial deities lead and follow it; they proceed with joy and without weariness, delighting in swiftness, and for this reason the Sun Deity is named "Swift."

“The body of the Sun Deity emits a thousand rays of light: five hundred rays shine downward and five hundred rays shine sideways. This arises from the merit of his past karma; thus he possesses these thousand rays, and for this reason the Sun Deity is named ‘Thousand Rays.’”
What are the merits of past karma?

There may be a person who makes offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, relieves those in poverty and distress, and bestows food and drink, clothing, medicinal decoctions, elephants, horses, carriages, dwellings, and lamps. They distribute these gifts at the appropriate times according to what is needed, never opposing the wishes of others, and thus honor the various worthy and holy ones who uphold the precepts.
By means of those various and innumerable causes and conditions of the light of Dharma-joy, the virtuous mind rejoices.
Just as a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated lineage experiences a joyful and virtuous mind upon first ascending the throne, so too is it with this.

By reason of these causes and conditions, when his body perishes and his life ends, he becomes the Sun Deity (Āditya), attaining a solar palace with a thousand rays of light; therefore it is said that through wholesome karma one obtains a thousand rays of light.
"Furthermore, for what reason is it called 'Light of Past Karma'?

There may be someone who does not kill, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, and does not practice double-tongued speech, harsh speech, lying, or frivolous talk; who does not covet, does not harbor ill will, and does not hold wrong views. By these causes and conditions, their wholesome mind is filled with joy."

It is like a great bathing pool at a crossroads, pure and free from impurity; there is a person traveling from afar who, exhausted by fatigue, heat, and thirst, enters this pool to bathe and find coolness, experiencing joy and delight.
Those who practice the ten wholesome deeds likewise experience such joy in their virtuous minds.

When such a person’s body perishes and their life ends, they become a Sun Deity (Āditya), dwelling in a sun palace with a thousand rays of light; for this reason, they are called "Light of Wholesome Karma."
“Furthermore, for what reason is he named ‘Thousand-Rayed Light’?

There may be someone who does not kill, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not deceive, and does not drink intoxicants. By virtue of these causes and conditions, with a virtuous and joyful mind, at the dissolution of the body after death, they become a Sun Deity King, dwelling in the sun palace and possessing a thousand rays of light. For this reason, he is named ‘Thousand-Rayed Light of Wholesome Karma.’”
"Sixty moments of thought constitute one *laya*; thirty *layas* constitute one *muhūrta*; and one hundred *muhūrtas* constitute one *upamā*.
When the sun-palace travels south for six months, it moves thirty *li* per day; it reaches its southernmost limit without exceeding Jambudvīpa, and the same applies when the sun travels north."
“For what reason is the sunlight scorching?
There are ten causes and conditions. What are these ten?”

First, outside Mount Sumeru there is Mount Khadiraka, forty-two thousand yojanas in height and forty-two thousand yojanas in width at its summit; its perimeter is immeasurable, and it is composed of the seven precious gems. When the sun’s light shines upon the mountain, it generates heat upon contact; this is the first reason for the scorching heat of the sun’s rays.

Second, beyond Mount Khadiraka lies Mount Īṣādhara, twenty-one thousand yojanas in height and twenty-one thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with an immeasurable circumference. It is composed of the seven precious jewels; when the sun’s rays strike the mountain, they become hot upon contact. This is the second cause for the scorching heat of the sun’s rays.

Third, beyond Mount Īṣādhara lies Mount Yūthīdhara, rising twelve thousand yojanas in height and spanning twelve thousand yojanas in length and breadth; its circumference is immeasurable and it is composed of the seven treasures. When the sun’s rays strike this mountain, they generate heat upon contact; this is the third cause for the scorching heat of the sun's rays.

Fourth, beyond Mount Yugandhara there is a mountain named Sudarśana, six thousand yojanas high and six thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with an immeasurable circumference, composed of the seven treasures. When the sun’s rays strike this mountain, they become hot upon contact; this is the fourth reason why the sun’s rays are scorching hot.

Fifth, beyond Mount Sudarśana lies Mount Aśvakarṇa, three thousand yojanas high and three thousand yojanas in length and breadth, with an immeasurable circumference. It is composed of the seven precious substances; when the sun’s rays strike the mountain, they become hot upon contact. This is the fifth reason why the sunlight is scorching.

Sixth, beyond the Horse-Sacrifice Mountain (Aśvamedha-parvata) lies Mount Nimindhara. It is twelve hundred yojanas high and twelve hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with an immeasurable circumference. It is composed of the seven treasures; when the sun’s rays strike the mountain, they become hot upon contact. This is the sixth reason why the sunlight is scorching.

Seventh, beyond Mount Nimiṃdhara lies Mount Vinataka, six hundred yojanas high and six hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with an immeasurable circumference. It is composed of the seven precious substances; when the sun’s rays strike the mountain, they produce heat upon contact. This is the seventh reason why the sunlight is scorching hot.

Eighth, beyond Mount Vinataka is Mount Vajravalaya, three hundred yojanas high and three hundred yojanas in length and breadth, with an immeasurable circumference, composed of the seven precious substances. When the sun’s rays strike this mountain, they become hot upon contact; this is the eighth cause for the heat of the sun’s rays.

Furthermore, ten thousand yojanas above, there is a celestial palace named Nakṣatra, composed of lapis lazuli. When the sunlight shines upon it, heat is generated by the contact; this constitutes the ninth cause for the scorching heat of the sun's rays.
"Furthermore, the palace of the sun illuminates the great earth; through contact, heat is generated. These are the ten conditions by which the sunlight becomes scorching.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"By these ten causes and conditions, The sun is named 'Thousand Rays.'"
"The light is blazing and hot; this is what the Buddha-Sun has taught.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"For what reason are the palaces in winter cold and unapproachable, possessing light yet being chilly?"
There are thirteen conditions by which [water] is luminous yet cold. What are these thirteen?
First, between Mount Sumeru and Mount Khadiraka there is water, eighty-four thousand yojanas in breadth and immeasurable in circumference; from this water grow various flowers:
When the utpala, kumuda, padma, puṇḍarīka, and sugandhika flowers are touched by the rays of the sun, they become cool; this is the first condition whereby the sunlight becomes cool.

Second, between Mount Khadiraka and Mount Īṣādhara there is water, forty-two thousand yojanas in width and forty-two thousand yojanas in length, with an immeasurable circumference. Within this water grow various kinds of flowers; when touched by the rays of the sun, they produce coolness. This is the second reason why the sunlight becomes cool.

Third, between Mount Īṣādhara and Mount Yugandhara there is a body of water, twenty-one thousand yojanas wide and immeasurable in circumference, wherein various flowers grow. When struck by the rays of the sun, it becomes cool; this is the third reason why the sunlight is cool.

Fourth, between Mount Sudarśana and Mount Jyotiṣka there is a body of water, twelve thousand yojanas wide and immeasurable in circumference, where various flowers bloom; when touched by the rays of the sun, it becomes cool. These are the four conditions by which the sunlight becomes cool.

Fifth, between Mount Sudarśana and Mount Aśvakarṇa there is a body of water six thousand yojanas wide, in which various flowers grow; when touched by the rays of the sun, it becomes cool. These are the five conditions by which the sunlight becomes cool.

Sixth, between Mount Aśvakarṇa and Mount Nimindhara there is a body of water, twelve hundred yojanas in width and immeasurable in circumference, where various flowers grow. When struck by the rays of the sun, it becomes cold; this is the sixth reason why the sun’s rays become cold.

Between Mount Nimindhara and Mount Vinataka there is water, six hundred yojanas in width and immeasurable in circumference, where various flowers grow. When touched by the rays of the sun, it becomes cool; this is the seventh reason why the sunlight is cool.

Between Mount Vinataka and Mount Cakravāḍa there is water, three hundred yojanas wide and immeasurable in circumference. It produces various kinds of flowers, and when touched by the rays of the sun, it becomes cool; this is the eighth reason why the sunlight is cool.
Furthermore, when the sun's rays shine upon the great oceans and rivers of this Jambudvīpa, they produce coldness upon contact; this is the ninth reason why the sun's rays are cold.

In the land of Jambudvīpa, rivers are few; in the land of Aparagoyānī, water is abundant. When the sun’s rays shine upon it, they produce cold by their contact. These are the ten conditions by which the sun’s rays become cold.
The rivers of Aparagoyānī are few, while the waters of Pūrvavideha are many; when touched by the light of the sun, they become cold. This is the eleventh reason why sunlight becomes cold.

In the region of Aparagoyānī the rivers are few, while in Uttarakuru they are many; when the sun's light shines there, it produces cold upon contact. This is why the sun's light is cold in these twelve cases.
Furthermore, the light of the sun palace illuminates the waters of the great ocean; where the sunlight shines, it produces cold upon contact. This is the thirteenth reason why the sunlight is cold.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"By virtue of these thirteen conditions, The sun is named 'Thousand Rays.
Its radiance is pure and cool; Such is what the Buddha-sun has taught."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The lunar palace sometimes suffers a deterioration of its substance, becoming full or waning, and its radiance diminishes; for this reason, the lunar palace is called 'deteriorated'."
The moon has two meanings: first, it refers to its abiding in a constant course;

second, it refers to its palace. It appears circular because it is seen from afar in all four directions. Its climate is cool and warm, temperate and pleasant. It is composed of celestial silver and lapis lazuli: two parts are celestial silver, pure and unadulterated, transparent inside and out, with light shining far and wide; one part is lapis lazuli, pure and unadulterated, transparent inside and out, with light shining far and wide.

The moon palace is forty-nine yojanas in length and breadth; its walls and floor are as thin as catalpa or cypress wood. There are seven tiers of palace walls, seven tiers of railings, seven tiers of jeweled nets, seven tiers of precious bells, and seven rows of trees surrounding it, all adorned with the seven treasures. Furthermore, countless birds sing together in harmony.
That lunar palace is sustained by five winds: first, the sustaining wind;
second, the nourishing wind; third, the receiving wind; fourth, the revolving wind; and fifth, the regulating wind.
The main hall where the Moon Deity resides is constructed of lapis lazuli and is sixteen yojanas high. The hall has four gates, surrounded by railings.
The throne of the Moon Deity measures half a yojana in length and breadth; it is composed of the seven precious gems, pure and soft, like celestial garments.

The body of the Moon Deity radiates light that illuminates the lapis lazuli palace; the light from the lapis lazuli palace shines upon the moon palace, and the light from the moon palace issues forth to illuminate the four continents.
The life span of the Moon Deva King is five hundred celestial years; his descendants succeed one another without any change in lineage.
His palace does not decay and endures for an entire kalpa.
When the moon palace moves, the Moon Deva King has no intention of traveling; he merely says, "I am moving" or "I am staying," while constantly delighting himself with the five sensual pleasures.

When the Moon Palace travels, countless hundreds of thousands of great celestial deities constantly lead the way; they delight in it without weariness and delight in its swiftness, and for this reason the Moon Deity is named "Swift."

“The body of the Moon Deity emits a thousand rays of light: five hundred rays shine downward and five hundred rays shine sideways. Because of the merit of his past karma, he possesses these rays of light; therefore, the Moon Deity is named ‘Thousand Rays.’”
What are the merits of past karma?

There are people in the world who make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, bestowing upon the poor and destitute food and drink, clothing, medicinal decoctions, elephants and horses, carriages, dwellings, and lamps. They distribute these gifts at the proper times according to what is required, never opposing the wishes of others, and they make offerings to the virtuous and noble ones who uphold the precepts.
It is like these various and innumerable joys of the Dharma, the radiance of a virtuous mind.
Just as a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated lineage, upon first ascending the throne, experiences the joy of a virtuous mind, so too is it with this.

By these causes and conditions, when his body perished and his life ended, he became the Moon Deva-son; because the moon palace possesses a thousand rays of light, it is said that through good karma one obtains a thousand rays of light.
"Furthermore, by what karma does one obtain a thousand rays of light?

There are people in the world who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, and do not practice double-tongued speech, harsh words, lying, or frivolous chatter; they do not harbor covetousness, malice, or wrong views. By these causes and conditions, their virtuous minds are filled with joy."

It is like a great bathing pool at the crossroads that is pure and free from impurity; there is a person traveling from afar who, being utterly exhausted, parched, and thirsty, enters this pool to bathe, becoming cool and refreshed, filled with joy and happiness.
The same is true for one who practices the ten wholesome actions with a joyful and virtuous mind.

When such a person’s body disintegrates and their life ends, they become a Moon Deva King, dwelling in the lunar palace with a thousand rays of light; for these reasons, they are named "Thousand-Rayed of Wholesome Karma."
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions does one obtain a thousand rays of light?

There are people in the world who do not kill, do not steal, do not engage in sexual misconduct, do not deceive, and do not drink intoxicants; by these causes and conditions, their wholesome minds are filled with joy."
When his body perished and his life ended, he became the Moon Deva-son, dwelling in the lunar palace with a thousand rays of light; for this reason, he was named Thousand-Rayed of Virtuous Karma.
Sixty *nāḍikās* constitute one *lava*; thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; and one hundred *muhūrtas* constitute one *upamā*.

When the sun’s palace travels south for six months, the sun moves thirty *li* per day; it reaches its southernmost limit but does not go beyond Jambudvīpa. At that time, the moon’s palace travels south for half a year, yet it likewise does not go beyond Jambudvīpa;
the same applies when the moon travels north.
"For what reason does the lunar palace slightly diminish?
There are three causes and conditions by which the lunar palace slightly diminishes:
first, when the moon emerges from the constellation Viśākhā, this is one cause for the moon's diminution."

Furthermore, within the lunar palace there are various ministers dressed in blue garments who ascend in succession; wherever they dwell, that place becomes blue. For this reason, the moon wanes. These are the two conditions by which the moon diminishes day by day.

Furthermore, the sun palace possesses sixty rays of light; when these rays shine upon the moon palace, they obscure it so that it does not appear. For this reason, in the places where it is obscured, the moon diminishes.
These are the three conditions by which the moonlight diminishes.
Furthermore, by what conditions does the moonlight gradually become full?
There are again three causes and conditions that cause the moonlight to gradually become full.
What are these three?
First, the moon faces the four cardinal directions; therefore, the moonlight is full.

Second, all the ministers of the moon palace wear blue robes, and on the fifteenth day, the Moon Deity sits in their midst to enjoy themselves together; his radiance shines everywhere, eclipsing the light of the other devas, and thus his light is universally complete.
It is just as when a great torch is lit among many lamps and candles, it eclipses the light of all those lamps.
The Moon Deity is likewise; on the fifteenth day, amidst the assembly of devas, he eclipses all other lights, and his radiance alone shines forth. This is the second causal condition.

Third, although the Sun Deity has sixty rays of light that shine upon the Moon Palace, on the fifteenth day the Moon Deity is able to reflect its radiance back, preventing it from being obscured; these are the three causes and conditions by which the Moon Palace remains full and without diminution.
"Furthermore, for what reason does the moon have a dark shadow?
It is because the shadow of the Jambu tree falls upon the moon; therefore, the moon has a shadow.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The mind should be like the moon—cool and free from heat—and when arriving at the house of a donor, one should maintain focused mindfulness without distraction.
Furthermore, for what reason do the various rivers exist?”

Because of the sun and moon there is heat; because of heat there is baking; because of baking there is sweat; because of sweat, rivers and streams are formed; thus, there are rivers and streams in the world.
By what causes and conditions do the five kinds of seeds exist in the world?

There was a great chaotic wind that blew seeds from the world of Non-defeat (Abhavya) to grow in this land; these are the five types of seeds: first, root-seeds; second, stem-seeds; third, joint-seeds; fourth, hollow-seeds; and fifth, seed-seeds. These constitute the five seeds.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, five types of seeds emerge in the world.
When it is midday in this Jambudvīpa, it is sunset in Pūrvavideha, sunrise in Aparagoyānī, and midnight in Uttarakuru;
when it is midday in Aparagoyānī, it is sunset in Jambudvīpa, sunrise in Uttarakuru, and midnight in Pūrvavideha.
When it is midday in Uttarakuru, the sun sets in Aparagoyānī, rises in Pūrvavideha, and it is midnight in Jambudvīpa;
when it is midday in Pūrvavideha, the sun sets in Uttarakuru, rises in Jambudvīpa, and it is midnight in Aparagoyānī.
To the east of Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha is the west; to the west of Jambudvīpa, Aparagoyānī is the east;
to the west of Aparagoyānī, Uttarakuru is the east.
Uttarakuru is in the west, and Pūrvavideha is in the east.
As for why Jambudvīpa is named Jambu, there is a mountain of gold beneath it thirty yojanas high; because it was produced from the Jambu tree, it is therefore called Jambu-gold.
The Jambū tree has fruits like mushrooms, and their flavor is like honey.
The tree has five great branches: four branches on the four sides and one branch at the top. The fruit on the eastern branch is eaten by the Gandharvas;
the fruit on the southern branch is eaten by the people of the seven kingdoms:
The first is called Kuru; the second, Kurava; the third, Videha; the fourth, Bhadravideha; the fifth, Mandā; the sixth, Pāra; and the seventh, Pāri.
To its west, the solitary fruits are consumed by sea creatures;
to its north, the solitary fruits are consumed by birds and beasts.
The solitary fruit atop it is consumed by the celestial beings of the constellations (*nakṣatra*).
To the north of the seven great kingdoms, there are seven great black mountains:

the first is called Bare Earth (*Nagnabhūmi*), the second White Crane (*Śvetabakā*), the third Lizard (*Gṛhagodhikā*), the fourth Immortal Mountain (*Ṛṣiparvata*), the fifth High Mountain (*Uccaparvata*), the sixth Meditation Mountain (*Dhyānaparvata*), and the seventh Earth Mountain (*Mṛtparvata*).

Upon these seven Black Mountains dwell seven Brahmin seers; the abodes of these seven seers are: first, Śobhana; second, Suprabha; third, Śaṅkha; fourth, Ṛṣi; fifth, Rakṣita; sixth, Gaṇana; and seventh, Vardhana.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“At the beginning of the kalpa, after sentient beings had consumed the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa), they remained in the world for a long time. Those who ate much became coarse and haggard in complexion, while those who ate little remained radiant and lustrous. Thereupon, they came to recognize the superiority and inferiority of their complexions and physical forms, and they began to criticize one another, saying:
‘I am superior to you; you are not my equal.’”
Because their minds were preoccupied with "self" and "other," and because they harbored contention and rivalry, the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) vanished.
Furthermore, the skin of the earth emerged, resembling thin cakes in appearance, pure in color, flavor, and fragrance.
At that time, sentient beings gathered in one place, wailing in grief and beating their breasts, saying:
"Alas, what a calamity!
Now the essence of the earth no longer appears."
"Just as a person today who has obtained a sumptuous delicacy praises it as excellent, yet later loses it and suffers distress, so too did he suffer distress, regret, and remorse."

Later, they began eating the earth's crust and gradually grew accustomed to its taste. Those who ate much became coarse and haggard in appearance, while those who ate little remained radiant and well-nourished. Only then did they realize that the complexions and physical forms of sentient beings varied in quality, leading them to judge one another as right or wrong, saying:
"I am superior to you; you are not my equal."
Because their minds were fixed upon self and other and they harbored strife and competition, the surface of the earth withered away.

Thereafter, a layer of earth-skin emerged again, becoming increasingly coarse and thick; its color was like celestial flowers and its texture as soft as celestial garments, and its taste was like honey.

At that time, the sentient beings again took food in common and remained in the world for a long duration. Those who ate much saw their complexions deteriorate, while those who ate very little had radiant complexions. Only then did they come to recognize the superiority or inferiority of one another’s complexions and physical forms, and they began to criticize each other, saying:
"I am superior to you; you are not my equal."
Because their minds were preoccupied with self and other, harboring contention and rivalry, the surface of the earth was consumed and exhausted.
Subsequently, there appeared naturally grown non-glutinous rice, free from husks and chaff; it required no seasoning yet possessed all manner of exquisite flavors.
At that time, the sentient beings gathered together and said:
"Alas, what a calamity!
Now the surface of the earth has suddenly ceased to appear."
"Just as people today, when encountering calamity or misfortune, cry out,
'Alas, what suffering!
so too did those sentient beings at that time lament and wail in such distress."

Thereafter, sentient beings together took up and ate non-glutinous rice; their bodies became coarse and ugly, and they developed male and female forms. As they gazed at one another, thoughts of desire arose, and they engaged in impure acts in secluded places.
Other sentient beings saw this and said:
"Alas, this is wrong!
How can such a thing happen among sentient beings who have come into existence together?"
When that man who had committed the impure act was rebuked by others, he immediately repented his transgression, saying,
"What I have done is wrong," and he threw himself to the ground.
When that woman saw the man prostrate himself on the ground, repenting his transgression and refusing to rise, she immediately brought him food.
Other sentient beings, seeing this, asked the woman,
"To whom do you wish to give this food that you carry?"
He replied, "I shall send food to those sentient beings who repent for their transgressions and have fallen into unwholesome conduct.
Because of these words, the world came to know him by the name "The Unwholesome Husband."
Because she delivered food to her husband, she was consequently named "wife" (*bhāryā*).

Subsequently, sentient beings became lustful and dissolute; as unwholesome dharmas increased, they built houses to shield themselves from view. Due to these causes and conditions, the name "house" (*śālā*) first came into being.
Thereafter, as the lustful indulgence of sentient beings increased further, they eventually became husbands and wives.

Other sentient beings, whose lifespan, karma, and merit were exhausted, passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn here; because they dwelt within a mother’s womb, the world thus acquired the name "conception in the womb."
At that time, he first built the city of Campā, next the city of Vārāṇasī in Kāśī, and after that, the city of Rājagṛha.
He began building at sunrise, and they were completed at sunrise.
For this reason, there arose in the world the names of cities, towns, and districts governed by kings.

At that time, when sentient beings first ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice, it ripened in the evening after being harvested in the morning, and ripened in the morning after being harvested in the evening; once harvested, it grew back again, without stalks or straw.
At that time, there was a sentient being who thought to himself in silence:
"Why do I weary myself by harvesting day after day?
I shall now gather it all at once to provide for several days."
Immediately, they harvested together and accumulated several days' worth of grain.
Later, the other people said to this person:
"Now we should go together to gather non-glutinous rice."
The man replied, "I have already accumulated enough; there is no need for you to take more.
If you wish to take some, go as you please."
Later, another person thought to himself:
"If the former man was able to gather enough provisions for two days, how could I not be able to gather enough for three days?
That man then accumulated provisions for three days.
Furthermore, another person said,
"Come, let us go together to fetch provisions. This man replied:
"I have already taken three days' worth of provisions.
If you wish to take some, do as you please.
This person thought to himself:
"He was able to take provisions for three days; why should I not be able to take provisions for five days?

Having taken provisions for five days, because the sentient beings vied with one another to accumulate surplus grain, the non-glutinous rice (śāli) then produced husks and chaff. Once harvested, it did not grow back, and withered stalks appeared.
"At that time, sentient beings gathered in one place, wailing in grief and beating their breasts, saying:
'Alas, what is this! They lamented and reproached themselves, saying:"

"Originally, we were all born by transformation, taking mindfulness as our food, with bodies that illuminated themselves with light, traveling through the air by supernormal power, dwelling in peace and happiness without hindrance.
Later, the 'taste of the earth' (pṛthivī-rasa) first appeared, endowed with both color and flavor; at that time, we consumed this taste of the earth and remained in the world for a long time."
