Those who ate much became coarse in appearance, while those who ate little remained radiant; thereupon, sentient beings harbored notions of "self" and "other," giving rise to arrogance and saying:
"My complexion is superior; yours is inferior."
Because of the pride arising from quarreling over the color [of the food], the essence of the earth (pṛthivī-rasa) vanished.
Thereupon, a crust of earth (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) appeared, complete with color, fragrance, and flavor.
We then again took it together and ate it, dwelling in the world for a long time.

Those who ate much became coarse and haggard in appearance, while those who ate little remained radiant and lustrous; thereupon, sentient beings harbored notions of "self" and "other," giving rise to arrogance and saying:
"My complexion is superior, yours is inferior."
Because of the pride arising from the color of that [earth], the surface of the earth was consumed.
Then a new crust of earth (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) arose, which was increasingly coarse and thick, and possessed color, fragrance, and flavor.
We then again took it together and ate it, dwelling in the world for a long time.

Those who ate much became coarse and haggard in appearance, while those who ate little remained radiant; thereupon, sentient beings harbored notions of "self" and "other," giving rise to arrogance and saying:
"My complexion is superior; yours is inferior."
Because of the pride arising from quarreling over the color [of the rice], the earth’s skin vanished.
Then, naturally grown *śāli* rice appeared, complete in color, fragrance, and flavor.

We then gathered it together to eat; what was harvested in the morning ripened by evening, and what was harvested in the evening ripened by morning. It grew back as soon as it was gathered, so there was no need for harvesting.
"Because we were then competing with one another to accumulate [grain], husks and chaff began to appear; once harvested, it would no longer grow, and only roots and stalks remained.
We should now jointly demarcate our fields and houses and divide them according to boundaries."
At that time, they immediately divided the fields with distinct boundaries, calculating "this" as belonging to themselves and "that" as belonging to others.
Subsequently, they began to hide their own rice and steal the grain from the fields of others.
Other sentient beings, having seen this, said:
"What you have done is wrong; what you have done is wrong.
Why do you conceal your own property and steal the wealth of others?"
He immediately rebuked him, saying:
"Do not commit theft again from now on.
Even though he was thus admonished, he did not stop and continued to steal. Others then rebuked him again, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; why do you not stop?
He then struck him with a staff, led him before the assembly, and addressed the people, saying:
"This man hid his own non-glutinous rice and stole grain from another's field."
The thief spoke again, saying,
"That man beat me. Upon hearing this,
the crowd was filled with distress and wept, beating their breasts as they said:
"Is it that as the world degenerates, evil dharmas arise?
Thus, he gave rise to the suffering of anxiety, entanglement, and feverish affliction; this is the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death, leading to a fall into the evil realms.
Because there were distinctions between fields, houses, and boundaries, disputes arose, leading to enmity and resentment that no one could resolve. [They thought:

"We should now establish a single impartial lord who will protect the people well, rewarding the good and punishing the evil; we, the multitude, shall each contribute a portion from our own shares to provide for him."
At that time, there was one person among the assembly who was tall and large in stature, handsome in appearance, and possessed of great majesty and virtue. The multitude said to him:
"We now wish to establish you as our leader to protect the people well, rewarding the good and punishing the evil; we shall all contribute by reducing our own portions to provide for you."

Upon hearing this, the man accepted the role of leader; he rewarded those who deserved reward and punished those who deserved punishment, and thus the title of "Ruler by Consent" (minzhu) first came into being.
The first Minzhu had a son named Zhenbao. Zhenbao had a son named Haowei. Haowei had a son named Jingzhai.
Jingzhai had a son named Dingsheng. Dingsheng had a son named Shanxing.
The son of Sukṛta was named Gṛhapati; the son of Gṛhapati was named Rasāgra;
the son of Rasāgra was named Rasādhya; the son of Rasādhya was named Jalapati;
the son of Jalapati was named Śatajñāna; the son of Śatajñāna was named Kāma.
Śikṣita had a son named Śubhakāma; Śubhakāma had a son named Saṃyojanaprahāṇa;
Saṃyojanaprahāṇa had a son named Mahāsaṃyojanaprahāṇa; Mahāsaṃyojanaprahāṇa had a son named Ratnagarbha;
Ratnagarbha had a son named Mahāratnagarbha; Mahāratnagarbha had a son named...
He was called Suppabuddha; Suppabuddha had a son named Mahāsuppabuddha; Mahāsuppabuddha had a son named Asoka; Asoka had a son named Dīpa;
Dīpa had a son named Jotipāla; Jotipāla had a son named Gopaka; Gopaka had a son.
His name was Śakra; Śakra had a son named Balada; Balada had a son named Dṛḍharatha;
Dṛḍharatha had a son named Daśaratha; Daśaratha had a son named Śataratha; Śataratha had a son named Dṛḍhadhanus; Dṛḍhadhanus had a son...
His name was Śata-dhanus; Śata-dhanus had a son named Go-pāla; Go-pāla had a son named Su-cinti.
From Su-cinti onward there were ten lineages, through which the Cakravartin kings continued in succession without interruption.

First is named Gaṇu-ku, second is named Tāla-pa, third is named A-yat-mo, fourth is named Chi-shi, fifth is named Ka-leng-ka, sixth is named Chan-po, seventh is named Ku-la-po, eighth is Pañjara, ninth is Mi-si-lo, and tenth is Śrama.

King Gaṇu had five wheel-turning sage-kings; King Tālaba had five wheel-turning sage-kings; King Ayama had seven wheel-turning sage-kings; King Dhārmika had seven wheel-turning sage-kings; King Kalinga had nine wheel-turning sage-kings; King Campaka had fourteen wheel-turning sage-kings; King Kurava had thirty-one wheel-turning sage-kings; King Vaṃśaja had thirty-two wheel-turning sage-kings; King Miśraka had eighty-four thousand wheel-turning sage-kings; and King Śrama had one hundred and one wheel-turning sage-kings. Finally, there was a king named Mahāsudarśana.

“King Śrīmagha had a son named Uruvilvā; Uruvilvā had a son named Kauravya; Kauravya had a son named Nigroḍha; Nigroḍha had a son named Siṃhahanu; Siṃhahanu had a son named King Śuddhodana; King Śuddhodana had a son named Bodhisattva; and the Bodhisattva had a son named Rāhula.”
From this original cause, the name "Kṣatriya" arose.
At that time, there was a sentient being who thought to himself:

"All family lineages and worldly possessions in this world are like thorns, boils, and sores; I should now renounce them, enter the mountains to practice the Way, and contemplate in a place of stillness."

At that time, he immediately distanced himself from the thorns of household life and entered a quiet place in the mountains. He meditated beneath trees and went out into the village every day to beg for alms.
When the villagers saw him, they increased their respect and made offerings, all praising him together:
"This man is truly able to renounce the burdens of home and enter the mountains to seek the Way, for he is capable of abandoning evil and unwholesome dharmas."
For this reason, they were called "brāhmaṇas.
Among the assembly of brāhmaṇas, there were those who were unable to practice meditation; they would leave the mountain forests and wander among human settlements, saying of themselves:
"I am not able to sit in meditation."

Because of this, he was called the "Brahmin Without Meditation. Passing through a village below, he practiced unwholesome dharmas and administered poisonous methods; as these characteristics arose from him, he was consequently named "Poison."
Due to these causes and conditions, there are brahmin castes in the world.
Among those sentient beings, some practice various occupations to provide for their own livelihood; because of this, there are householder castes in the world.
"Among those sentient beings, there were those who practiced various crafts and skills to sustain their livelihood; because of this, the Śūdra caste came to exist in the world.
After these Śākya clans had first appeared in the world, the śramaṇa caste subsequently arose."
Among those of the kṣatriya caste, there are some who reflect to themselves:
"The worldly attachments of affection are defiled and impure; what is there worth craving or clinging to?
Thereupon, they leave their homes, shave off their hair and beards, don the dharma robes, and seek the Way.
"I am a śramaṇa! I am a śramaṇa!
Among those of the brāhmaṇa caste, the householder caste, and the śūdra caste, there are some who reflect to themselves:
"Worldly affection is defiled and impure; how can it be worth coveting?
Thereupon, he left his home, shaved off his hair and beard, donned the dharma robes, and sought the Way, saying: "I am a śramaṇa!"
"I am a śramaṇa!

"If among the kṣatriya assembly there are those who practice unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind, having practiced such unwholesomeness, when their bodies perish at the end of life, they experience nothing but suffering."

Whether they be Brahmins, householders, or Śūdras, if they practice unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind, then having practiced such unwholesomeness, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will experience nothing but suffering.

If one of the kṣatriya caste practices good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good thoughts of mind, then at the breaking up of the body after death, they will experience exclusively happiness.

The same applies to those of the brāhmaṇa, gṛhapati, and śūdra castes: if they practice good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good thoughts of mind, then at the breaking up of the body after death, they will experience exclusively happiness.

Within the body of one born of the kṣatriya caste there are two kinds of conduct, and in speech and mind there are likewise two kinds of conduct. Having engaged in these two kinds of bodily and mental conduct, at the dissolution of the body after death, they experience the retribution of suffering and pleasure.

Whether they be brahmins, householders, or śūdras, if they engage in two kinds of bodily conduct and two kinds of verbal and mental conduct, then having engaged in those two kinds of bodily and mental conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, they will experience the retribution of suffering and pleasure.

“Among the kṣatriyas, one who shaves off hair and beard, dons the three dharma robes, leaves the household life to seek the Way, and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment—having left the household life for the sake of the Way with firm faith, cultivating the unsurpassed holy life—he realizes it for himself in this very life:
‘Birth and death are ended; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence.’”

Whether they be brahmins, householders, or śūdras, if they shave off their hair and beard, don the three dharma robes, leave the household life to seek the Way, and cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment—having left home for the sake of the Way with firm faith, practicing the unsurpassed holy life and realizing within this very life:
"Birth and death are exhausted; the holy life is established; there will be no further existence."
Among these four types, the one who has emerged through the perfection of clear knowledge and conduct and attained arhatship is the most supreme.
At that time, Brahmā spoke this verse:
“The Kṣatriya born is the most excellent, Able to gather all lineages;”
“Perfectly endowed with clarity and conduct, he is the foremost among gods and humans.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“The verse spoken by that Brahmā was well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it was rightly received, not wrongly received, and it is approved by me.”
Why is this so? I, the present Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, have also spoken this verse:
“The Kṣatriya born is supreme, Able to gather all lineages;”
"Having perfected the realization of knowledge and conduct, he is the foremost among gods and humans.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Complete with the Long Āgama, I take refuge in the All-Knowing One; may all the multitudes be at peace, and may sentient beings abide in the unconditioned—may I also be included therein.

The Buddha-spoken *Dīrgha Āgama*, Volume Twenty-two: Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa; the Śramaṇas, the Udumbara, the Upatiṣya, Maudgalyāyana, Yaśas, Kauṇḍinya, and the King; the gods of the Trayastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens; the Kāla-gaṇḍa, the Kalaviṅka, the Ghaṭa-karṇa, the Pāṭala, the Pūrṇa, and the Aniruddha take refuge. They take refuge in the Dharma and do not take refuge in others. Pāpīyan, Śāṇakavāsin, Vatsagotra, Mārgaliya, Gośālīputra, Sañjayin, Ajita Keśakambalin, Kakuda Kātyāyana, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Maskarin Gośālīputra, Ajita Keśakambalin, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, and the Unborn (Ajita) who has not yet seen the Unborn—these enter the womb with purity.
These are the pure ones: Dhanañjaya, Kātyāyana, and Māṭhara. Niyan-dau and Niyan-dau.
